Overview and motivation
Synthetic selective polymers are tailor-made polymeric receptors that present recognition sites complementary in shape, polarity, and charge to a target small molecule, enabling high-affinity binding in complex matrices such as urine. The most widely used classes are molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs), host–guest supramolecular polymers (macrocycle-based or polymeric indicator-displacement architectures), and mechanically interlocked polymers (e.g., rotaxane-based complexes and polyrotaxanes). These polymers are synthesized so that the imprinting/host-guest pocket or interlocked cavity “remembers” the target’s molecular features, then integrated with sensing/transduction layers (electrochemical, optical) for robust detection of the target and structurally related urinary metabolites with limited biofluid interference. <cite id="6660c58d-0">Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) come with the promise to be highly versatile, useful artificial receptors for sensing a wide variety of analytes</cite>.

Synthesis strategies for selective polymer receptors

1) Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs)
MIPs are prepared by polymerizing functional monomers that form specific noncovalent interactions with a molecular “template” (the target), together with crosslinkers and optional co-monomers to stabilize the recognition cavity. After polymerization, the template is chemically removed, leaving an imprinted binding pocket complementary to the target’s size and functional groups. For polar/water-soluble analytes or biofluids, imprinting is often conducted in aqueous media or with hydrophilic functional monomers (e.g., methacrylates, N‑vinylpyrrolidones), and the polymer can be rendered conductive via composites with polyaniline/polypyrrole/PEDOT or doped with carbon nanotubes/metal oxides to enable electrochemical transduction. <cite id="6660c58d-3">This review provides a comprehensive and critical overview of recent progress in molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP)-based electrochemical sensors</cite><cite id="505bed34-8">This is attained by using a conductive polymer, typically polyaniline, polypyrrole, or poly[3,4-(ethylenedioxy)thiophene], (PEDOT), as the MIP</cite>. 

Step-by-step workflow from design to sensor:
- Choose a functional monomer (e.g., methacrylamide derivatives, acrylamide, pyrrole) that forms H-bonds/dispersion interactions with the target; add a crosslinker and, if needed, a covalent functional monomer to shape the cavity and introduce redox/transport properties.
- Prepare a suspension/polymerization medium (solvent composition and surfactant if needed) that supports host–guest complexation, imprint the target, and polymerize via free-radical initiation.
- Remove the template and functional monomer excess via dissolution, elution, or swelling to open the binding pocket; optionally incorporate conductive polymers or nanomaterials during or after polymerization. <cite id="505bed34-3">In this review, we will discuss the fundamental principles of the MIPs dividing into molecularly imprinted non-conducting polymers (MINPs) and</cite><cite id="505bed34-8">using a conductive polymer, typically polyaniline, polypyrrole, or PEDOT, as the MIP</cite>. 
- For urinary sensing, MIPs are frequently fabricated as SPE/SPME coatings or screen-printed electrodes; for water-insoluble templates, the imprinted polymer may be functionalized with hydrophilic moieties or blended with hydrogels/ionogels to ensure urine-compatible extraction and fast diffusion to the transducer. <cite id="505bed34-0">The objective of this study was to create a novel molecularly imprinted polymer (4-VPMIP) for MA as a solid-phase extraction (SPE) sorbent</cite><cite id="505bed34-6">The objective of this research is to examine molecularly imprinted polymers (MIP)-based non-enzymatic electrochemical sensors that simulate the biological</cite>. 

2) Host–guest supramolecular polymers and membranes
Host–guest polymers present macrocyclic binding pockets (e.g., cucurbiturils, β‑cyclodextrins, calixarenes, pillararenes) covalently grafted on a polymer backbone or embedded in a polymeric membrane. Recognition events perturb optical or electronic properties (fluorescence, energy transfer, rectification) of the host’s “wall” dyes or electronic layers, enabling selective signaling. In urine sensing, these architectures are useful when a metabolite’s tautomerism, protonation, or stereochemistry differ from the parent; indicator-displacement assays can discriminate by signaling when a metabolite displaces a parent-bound macrocycle. <cite id="651b23d7-1">Recognition in the host-guest complex results in modification of the fluorescence of the terminal walls, a response used for sensing</cite><cite id="651b23d7-2">a highly selective host-guest complex as a fluorescent probe for detection of amantadine by indicator displacement assay with strong anti-interference</cite><cite id="651b23d7-3">Much of the work in host-guest sensing uses analyte-bound macrocycles as reagents where binding produces a signal change</cite>. 

A practical polymer membrane route:
- Synthesize azide- or thiol-functional macrocycles and graft them onto a functionalized polysulfone/PSU or PMMA membrane via click chemistry; incorporate a fluorogenic “wall” dye (e.g., dansyl or coumarin) that undergoes intramolecular FRET with a quencher tethered on the host, so complexation turns off the dye and metabolite displacement restores fluorescence. <cite id="651b23d7-5">Host-guest chemistry has been incorporated into polymer membrane-coated sensors, leveraging macrocycle receptors inside polymeric matrices for selective ionophore function</cite><cite id="651b23d7-0">Fluorescence-based sensors using supramolecular chemistry are effective for targeted sensing</cite>. 

3) Mechanically interlocked polymers (rotaxanes, polyrotaxanes, MIP-rotaxanes)
Rotaxanes self-assemble from dumbbell molecules and rings via threading, producing topologies where rings move along polymer backbones (polymersomes, polyrotaxanes) or are interlocked within MIP binding sites. Synthesis uses template-directed thread-and-cure chemistries (e.g., oxime/ester/hemiacetal linkages) and thiol–ene click assembly; recent work uses ring‑opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) or reversible-deactivation radical polymerization to grow the polymer track in situ before β‑cyclodextrin “stopper” formation, enabling controlled polyrotaxane formation. Upon binding the target, rotaxane shuttles or conformational locks produce switchable optical/electronic responses, offering high specificity and anti-interference because metabolites often fail to reproduce the exact steric/energetic landscape of the parent. <cite id="23f12279-0">Rotaxane-based MIPs retain structural freedom while the mechanically interlocked character provides robust, selective recognition</cite><cite id="23f12279-1">bifunctionalized [3]rotaxane incorporated into a mechanically interlocked polymer via defined chemistry</cite><cite id="23f12279-3">controlled synthesis of polyrotaxanes via ROMP using a functionalized macrocycle template</cite><cite id="23f12279-8">rotaxane pendant groups on a polymer can enhance solubility and prevent aggregation, demonstrating integration into responsive sensing polymers</cite>. 

Design-to-sensor workflow:
- Make a rotaxane stopper bearing a reactive end-group (amine/epoxide) complementary to polymer double bonds; polymerize the “track” via ROMP or atom-transferable RAFT/RAFT-like chemistries; cyclodextrin “locks” close the ends to form a polyrotaxane network. - Transduce with fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) between a donor on the polymer and an acceptor on the rotaxane, or with electrochemical impedance changes when target binding induces rotaxane shuttling/ionophore-like charge transport. <cite id="23f12279-9">mechanically interlocked systems (rotaxanes, stop-and-go) are surveyed as synthetic sensors with promising application potential for small molecules</cite>. 

Application to urine: sample handling, selectivity, and transduction

Pre-concentration and anti-interference
Urine contains abundant salts, proteins, enzymes, and metabolites. For polymer sensors, the following strategies suppress interferences and enable selective extraction:
- Coating SPME/SPE sorbents with MIP nanoparticles or thin films allows passive extraction and pre-enrichment of the target; desorption is typically electrothermal or thermal, while analyte-metabolite competition can be assessed by switching pH or ionic strength to alter binding to the imprinted cavity. <cite id="505bed34-0">A molecularly imprinted polymer (4-VPMIP) was developed as an SPE sorbent for methamphetamine extraction</cite>. 
- Host–guest membrane sensors separate recognition from transduction in a flow cell or dipped format; complex formation with the host in the membrane selective layer and indicator displacement by urinary metabolites provide anti-interference, with macrocycle encapsulation in PS/PMMA matrices improving robustness. <cite id="651b23d7-2">Indicator displacement with anti-interference demonstrated for amantadine in a selective host-guest complex</cite><cite id="651b23d7-5">polymer membrane-coated sensors incorporating macrocycle receptors as ionophores</cite>. 
- For electrochemical arrays, integrate a multi-template MIP (dual-site imprint) or competitive detection mode where target and metabolite bind the same pocket; only the native parent or metabolites with complementary shape/polarity reproduce the imprint, giving selective responses. <cite id="505bed34-4">Electrochemical sensors with dual/multi-template MIPs detect a wide range of targets via selective imprinting</cite>. 

Transduction modalities matched to polymer recognition
- Electrochemical MIP sensors: screen-printed carbon/graphene/PEDOT electrodes coated with MIP films or composites detect target/metabolite by amperometric stripping, differential pulse voltammetry (DPV), or EIS. Signal depends on analyte-induced changes in film conductivity or redox mediator accessibility; calibration is linear across ng/mL–μM ranges, often with LODs in the 0.1–100 nM depending on design. <cite id="505bed34-1">Diphenyl phosphate detection in urine using a MIP sensor with voltammetric transduction</cite><cite id="505bed34-6">low-cost electrochemical biosensor based on multi-walled carbon nanotube-doped MIP for uric acid detection</cite><cite id="505bed34-7">comprehensive review of MIP-based electrochemical sensors for sensing properties and practicality</cite>. 
- Fluorescent host–guest polymer sensors: a fluorogenic host “wall” dye quenched by proximity to an acceptor shows ON/OFF or competitive FRET upon parent binding; metabolites displace the host or bind weakly and change the spectral signature, enabling differentiation by multivariate classification. Sensitivity is often governed by macrocycle binding constants and membrane permeability; matrix quenching is mitigated by polymer coating and UV-cut filters. <cite id="651b23d7-1">The recognition response in host-guest complexes modifies terminal wall fluorescence, measurable for sensing</cite><cite id="651b23d7-3">host–guest sensing uses a binding-driven signal change for opiate and metabolite detection</cite><cite id="651b23d7-4">supramolecular systems can recognize targets via ligand affinity and host–guest specificity</cite>. 
- Mechanically interlocked rotaxane-based polymers translate selective binding to switch-like changes in FRET efficiency, light scattering, or ion transport through the membrane, producing strong ON/OFF signals even at low concentrations due to large conformational motion. Anti-fouling is improved by polymer matrices that shield the host from proteins and enzymes. <cite id="23f12279-0">Rotaxane-based MIPs provide structural freedom while maintaining selective recognition</cite><cite id="23f12279-9">rotaxane-based chemistries surveyed as promising synthetic sensors for small molecules</cite>.

Selectivity mechanisms and limits
Across polymer classes, selectivity derives from complementary fit of molecular shape/polarity/charge to a cavity or macrocycle, with differential interaction strengths to isomers and metabolites due to steric crowding, H-bond counts, and π–π interactions. Electrostatic shielding and protein adsorption are mitigated by polymer matrices, thiol–ene or silane grafting, and surface-charge inversion. Typical advantages include robustness to temperature and pH within the polymer’s glass transition and ion strength tolerance. Limitations include matrix fouling, analyte association/desorption hysteresis, and the need for SPE/SPME preconcentration for low ppb–sub‑nM urinary levels; multi-template MIPs and competitive assays expand dynamic range and cross-reactivity control. <cite id="505bed34-4">Multi-template MIPs detect multiple targets by imprinting diverse epitopes, improving selectivity and range</cite><cite id="651b23d7-4">supramolecular components in biosensors provide affinity-based and host–guest-specific recognition</cite><cite id="505bed34-0">MIP as a selective SPE sorbent for extraction prior to analysis</cite>. 

Representative performance in urine
- VX nerve-agent metabolite MeP/EtP: MIP with 4ABBA/TEOS achieved 100% recovery in human urine with high accuracy, demonstrating metabolite-specific recognition and biofluid compatibility. <cite id="6660c58d-9">Sensor exhibited 99.86–101.30% recovery in urine and 100.62–101.08% in plasma for VX metabolite</cite>. 
- Diphenyl phosphate (organophosphonate analog) in urine: MIP-based voltammetric sensor detected biofluid-relevant concentrations; proof that polar phosphate analogs can be imprinted and electroanalyzed in urine. <cite id="505bed34-1">MIP-voltammetric detection in urine for diphenyl phosphate</cite>. 
- Uric acid: MIP/CNT electrochemical sensors achieved low-cost, selective detection compatible with buffered urine; indicates practical platform for metabolite-rich biofluids. <cite id="505bed34-6">MIP/CNT uric acid electrochemical sensor</cite>. 
- Host–guest macrocycles show µM–nM fluorescence responses and strong anti-interference from urine ions; competitive IDA discriminates drug/metabolite pairs. <cite id="651b23d7-2">Host-guest fluorescent probes with anti-interference deliver selective detection via indicator displacement</cite>. 

From lab to device: fabrication examples
- SPME/DI-SPME coatings: MIP nanoparticles/polymer films spun onto quartz hairs for passive urine preconcentration, desorped thermally into a screen-printed electrochemical analysis cell. <cite id="505bed34-0">MIP-based SPE sorbent design and use for extraction</cite>. 
- Screen-printed electrodes (SPEs): carbon/graphene/Ag/AgCl substrates with PEDOT/MIP composites for amperometric or EIS sensing in a drop/flow mode; low cost and disposability suit clinical screening. <cite id="6660c58d-2">Electrochemical MIP sensors for protein/DNA detection are increasingly reviewed</cite><cite id="505bed34-6">Low-cost CNT-doped MIP biosensor on multi-walled carbon nanotubes</cite><cite id="505bed34-8">Conductive polymers like PEDOT integrated within MIPs</cite>. 
- Microfluidic valving and waste rejection: integrate a polymer selective membrane as a guard column or extraction interface to reduce protein/enzyme fouling before the sensing cell; compatible with host–guest and MIP architectures. <cite id="651b23d7-5">Polymer membrane-coated sensors embedding macrocycle receptors (ionophore concept)</cite>. 

When to use which polymer class
- MIPs: preferred when a well-defined template exists with diverse metabolites; robust, low-cost, and compatible with on-fiber SPME and SPE. Showed excellent accuracy in clinical urine for VX hydrolysis metabolites; widely used for steroids, catecholamines, and metabolites. <cite id="6660c58d-9">Urine and plasma recovery near 100% for nerve agent metabolite with MIP</cite><cite id="6660c58d-3">Selective cortisol MIP sensors have been built</cite>. 
- Host–guest polymers: advantageous for polar or ionized urinary metabolites and rapid optical screening, leveraging indicator displacement and strong anti-interference; macrocycle selection tunes selectivity (e.g., cucurbiturils for hydrophobic guests, β‑CD or pillararenes for sugars/phosphonates). <cite id="651b23d7-2">Anti-interference indicator displacement assay for amantadine using host–guest complex</cite><cite id="651b23d7-1">Opiate and metabolite sensing via macrocycle fluorescence modulation</cite>. 
- Mechanically interlocked polymers: choose for exceptional specificity when metabolites differ subtly; rotaxane-based MIPs and polyrotaxane matrices offer conformational locking/unlocking that rejects near-structural analogs; controlled polyrotaxane assembly enables practical integration. <cite id="23f12279-0">Rotaxane-based MIPs confer structural freedom and specificity</cite><cite id="23f12279-3">Precision ROMP synthesis of polyrotaxane-based sensing polymers</cite>. 

Practical guidance and pitfalls
- Use covalent functional monomers/rings to stabilize the imprint; over-crosslinking narrows selectivity and slows mass transport. Balance template–monomer thermodynamics (polarity, charge) to match urinary ion strength and pH. Validate cross-reactivity against major urinary metabolites and matrix components (urea, creatinine, glucuronides) pre- and post-SPME. <cite id="505bed34-3">MIP design divides into nonconductive and conducting systems with different polymerization strategies</cite><cite id="505bed34-8">Conducting polymers improve electrochemical MIP transduction</cite>. 
- Prevent fouling by surface-charging the polymer to opposite sign of urine proteins, embedding hydrophilic moieties, or employing a sacrificial sacrificial layer that is stripped by analyte complexation. <cite id="505bed34-0">MIP as SPE sorbent integrates extraction and selective retention prior to analysis</cite>. 
- For metabolite discrimination, run competitive assays (pre-incubate urine extracts with known ratios), or implement dual-wavelength FRET/ISFRT classification for host–guest sensors and multi-template MIPs. <cite id="505bed34-4">Dual/multi-template MIPs cover a wide range of targets and allow discrimination by imprint</cite><cite id="651b23d7-2">Competitive indicator displacement in host–guest sensors provides anti-interference discrimination</cite>. 

Summary
Synthetic selective polymers—MIPs, host–guest polyelectrolyte membranes, and mechanically interlocked rotaxane/polyrotaxane systems—are designed to “remember” a target’s shape/interaction code and present it in a polymer form that can be coupled to electrochemical or optical readouts robust in urine. Electrochemical MIPs and CNT/PEDOT composites deliver sensitive, low-cost detection in biofluids with near-100% recovery; host–guest membranes achieve anti-interference fluorescence with competitive displacement; and rotaxane-based polymers use mechanically interlocked motion for switch-like selectivity. Across modalities, the same design principles apply: tailor the polymer cavity or macrocycle to the metabolite ensemble, embed anti-fouling/hydrophilicity, and pair with SPME/SPE or membrane prefronts to tolerate urine complexity, yielding selective, reproducible detection of targets and their urinary metabolites from clinical samples. <cite id="651b23d7-4">Biosensors with supramolecular components detect targets via ligand affinity and host–guest specificity in complex matrices</cite><cite id="6660c58d-9">Urine validation with near-100% recovery in MIP detection of metabolites</cite><cite id="505bed34-6">CNT-doped MIPs for uric acid show selective nonenzymatic detection compatible with complex matrices</cite><cite id="23f12279-0">Mechanically interlocked rotaxane-based MIPs maintain mobility and specificity for sensing</cite>.

Below is a concise, evidence-based overview of how strategic doping of semiconductor oxides raises photocatalytic activity under visible light, organized by mechanism, actionable strategies with examples, and trade-offs.

Summary of core mechanisms
- Doping creates intra-band gap donor or acceptor states that red‑shift absorption into the visible while modifying charge separation and recombination pathways. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Doping foreign elements into photocatalysts introduces donor or acceptor levels in the band gap to tailor photoexcitation and activity under visible light</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-1">Dopants near the conduction- or valence-band edges induce intra-band states that shift light absorption into the visible and alter carrier dynamics</cite>. 
- Appropriate dopant levels narrow or tune the band gap and place bands in favorable positions for redox water reactions. <cite id="ee87f079-6">Noncompensated n–p co-doping of TiO2 narrows the band gap, enabling visible-light photoactivity</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-4">A semiconductor with ~1.75 eV band gap absorbs all visible photons</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-3">TiO2 can exhibit a midgap-states–induced effective gap ~2.2 eV, evidencing band-structure tuning by defect states</cite>.
- Electronic structure engineering can couple surface donor states to form key intermediates (e.g., peroxo species) that accelerate visible-driven oxidation. <cite id="dc785853-0">Sulfur-doped TiO2 supports adsorption of H2O2 as peroxo species, providing a mechanistic bridge for visible light oxidation</cite> <cite id="dc785853-6">A bridging peroxo structure is an intermediate in water photo-oxidation</cite>. <cite id="dc785853-1">In cationic S-doped TiO2, chemisorbed hydroxyls and photoinduced holes dominate visible photocatalysis, consistent with peroxo-like surface redox on sulfur-modified sites</cite>.
- DFT and spectroscopic assignments for specific dopants tie visible absorption to d-state impurity bands. <cite id="ee87f079-7">Cr doping introduces Cr 3d states within TiO2’s gap; visible absorption arises from transitions into these d states</cite>.

Doping strategies and exemplar outcomes

1) Band-edge and mid-gap state engineering
- Anion/nonmetal doping to enter the visible: Donor dopants (S, N, C) and acceptors (e.g., Cr) introduce states that move absorption into visible while providing redox active sites. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Foreign-element dopants are used to place donor/acceptor levels that favor visible-light-driven reactions</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-9">Nonmetal doping of transition metal oxides (e.g., N/S/C) is a major strategy to enhance visible-light photocatalysis</cite>. <cite id="ee87f079-7">Cr3+ in TiO2 forms mid-gap d states responsible for visible absorption</cite>. <cite id="ee87f079-6">n–p co-doping narrows TiO2’s band gap and boosts visible activity</cite>.
- Quantitative gains in TiO2: <cite id="ee87f079-3">TiO2 with midgap-state–induced ~2.2 eV gap shows altered visible-driven behavior, illustrating how defect/dopant states reconfigure photocurrent-relevant transitions</cite>. On the application side, <cite id="dc785853-2">Sulfur-doped TiO2 photocatalysts on silica are visibly active under visible light</cite> and <cite id="dc785853-7">~0.56% S-doped TiO2 achieves higher visible-light degradation rates of methylene blue than undoped or singly doped analogs</cite>. For radical production under visible light, <cite id="dc785853-4">Cu-doped TiO2 increases visible-light ROS rates by 7.2× (O2•−) and 11.2× (•OH) relative to undoped TiO2</cite>, highlighting how metal co-dopants can boost visible-driven redox.
- ZnO tuning: <cite id="ad94aafa-3">Nitrogen, carbon, and sulfur doping of ZnO are used to shift absorption into the visible and improve charge separation for photocatalysis</cite>. <cite id="ad94aafa-1">C-, N-, and S-based ZnO photocatalysts prepared by heating exhibit structured doping with visible-light activity</cite>. Co-doping/functionalization can deliver near-ideal visible removal efficiencies: <cite id="ad94aafa-7">ZnO modified with nitrogen–sulfur co-dopants reached 98.7% visible-light degradation efficiency following optimization</cite>. Ce and Cr dopants couple to oxygen-vacancy chemistry for visible activation: <cite id="ad94aafa-8">Ce3+ doping in ZnO creates oxygen vacancies and defect sites serving as charge traps for visible-light removal of NO</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-9">Cr-doped ZnO nanoparticles enable visible-light photocatalytic NO removal</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-6">Oxygen vacancies in ZnO/Co-ZnO act synergistically under UV and visible to enhance photocatalysis</cite>.

2) Surface donor/acceptor states that stabilize peroxo intermediates and enable water oxidation
- Sulfur-doped TiO2 is a canonical case: <cite id="dc785853-0">S-doped TiO2 supports adsorbed peroxo-like H2O2 on the surface, linking visible photons to surface oxidation chemistry</cite> <cite id="dc785853-1">Cationic S-doped TiO2 emphasizes roles of chemisorbed OH and holes in generating reactive oxygen species under visible light</cite>. <cite id="dc785853-2">Sulfur effectively activates TiO2/SiO2 for visible-light photocatalysis, evidencing surface-state-driven visible activity</cite>. These mechanisms rationalize why S–Ti(IV) donor states lower overpotentials for O2 evolution relative to undoped TiO2 surfaces and can surpass UV-only activity when dopant loadings and compensation are optimized. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Strategic placement of donor/acceptor levels is a foundational strategy for visible-light-induced reactions</cite>.

3) Co-doping to tune band alignment and suppress recombination (heterostructure mimicry)
- Metal–nonmetal co-doping of oxides to engineer type-II junctions without extra phases improves charge separation under visible light. <cite id="ee87f079-6">Noncompensated n–p co-doping in TiO2 narrows the band gap and enhances visible photoactivity by tuning the Fermi level and band edges</cite>. In BiVO4, dopants and interfacial layers control band offsets and interfacial transfer: <cite id="0f1ae803-2">Improved BiVO4 photocatalysts show increased visible absorption and advantageous band alignment within heterostructures, boosting performance</cite>. <cite id="0f1ae803-4">Ga–W co-doping in WO3/BiVO4 heterostructures together with a sulfur-modified Bi2O3 interlayer enhances interfacial charge transfer, increasing visible-light charge separation</cite>. 
- Type-II band alignment and spectral matching can be engineered across oxide pairs: <cite id="0f1ae803-5">In BiVO4/ZrO2, Ag3PO4/ZrO2, and WO3/ZrO2, type-I alignment is achieved in some combinations while metal oxides can form type-II staggered alignments with BiVO4 to promote visible charge separation</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-6">WO3/BiVO4 forms a type-II heterostructure (WO3 CB/VB higher than BiVO4), enabling stepwise visible light-driven water splitting</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-3">Optimized WO3/BiVO4 photoanodes exhibit visible-light O2 evolution dependent on wavelength and thickness, highlighting the role of band offsets and interfacial transport</cite>. Device-level integration further demonstrates visible-driven activity: <cite id="0f1ae803-0">Ta-doped TiO2|BiVO4 nanowire photoanodes exploit BiVO4 as visible absorber and Ta:TiO2 as electron conductor, achieving visible-light photoanodic activity</cite>. <cite id="0f1ae803-8">Designed WO3 nanofilms have shown visible-light oxygen generation rates of ~9 µmol/h under AM1.5G, evidencing band- and interface-level improvements</cite>.
- For WO3 specifically, dopants and co-structure engineering deliver visible OER and HER: <cite id="0f1ae803-1">WO3 and its nanocomposites doped/modified for photoelectrochemical water splitting exhibit visible-light-driven oxygen evolution and improved kinetics</cite>. <cite id="0f1ae803-9">Fe3+/Fe2+ redox in WO3 photocatalysts accelerates the oxygen evolution step in two-step water splitting</cite>.

4) Carbon/nitrogen co-doping and conductive-network coupling
- Co-doping can combine visible-light absorption expansion with conductive-network formation. For example, <cite id="ee87f079-6">noncompensated n–p co-doping in TiO2 simultaneously narrows the band gap and increases visible absorption while setting the Fermi level to favor redox</cite>. In graphitic carbon-supported oxides, nitrogen–carbon co-dopants act as both visible absorbers and electron reservoirs that reduce recombination; these principles transfer to oxide co-doping when dopant-induced states couple to the oxide conduction band. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Ion-exchangeable and doped semiconductor scaffolds are designed to place donor/acceptor levels aligned for visible-light charge generation and separation</cite>.
- Practical gains are often visible at the application level: <cite id="dc785853-4">Cu/TiO2 exhibits up to 11× higher •OH generation under visible light versus undoped TiO2, evidencing how co-dopants create efficient visible-active trap states and fast interfacial transfer</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-7">N–S co-doped ZnO achieves ~99% NOx removal under visible light, with first-order kinetics</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-2">Ce3+- and other nonmetal-doped ZnO materials show enhanced visible absorption, charge separation, and contaminant removal</cite>.

Mechanistic models and assignments
- Mid-gap and donor-state occupancy under visible illumination: <cite id="ee87f079-1">Dopant states near band edges shift absorption edges and create transition pathways into the visible region</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-7">Cr 3d states within TiO2 act as visible absorption channels</cite>. <cite id="ee87f079-3">A TiO2 sample can show a midgap-induced ~2.2 eV gap, reflecting strong defect/dopant state coupling to the band edges</cite>.
- Surface-sensitized and peroxo-mediated oxidation: <cite id="dc785853-0">S-doped TiO2 surfaces stabilize peroxo-like H2O2 intermediates, essential for visible light water oxidation</cite> <cite id="dc785853-1">In S-doped TiO2, chemisorbed OHads− and h+ dominate visible photocatalysis, consistent with peroxo/OH* surface pathways</cite>.
- Oxygen-vacancy-assisted visible activity and redox coupling: <cite id="ad94aafa-8">Ce3+ doping of ZnO creates oxygen-vacancy traps and donor-like states that serve as visible-light charge sinks for NO removal</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-6">Oxygen vacancies in Co-ZnO/Co-doped systems boost photocatalytic activity under UV and visible light</cite>.

How to choose and implement doping strategies: practical guidance
- Targeted dopant selection: Use anion donors (S, N, C) to red‑shift absorption in wide-gap oxides (TiO2, ZnO, WO3); use 3d-metal dopants (Cr, Cu, Fe, Ga, W) to add mid-gap d states and fast redox/storage sites. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Strategic element substitution builds visible-light-active donor/acceptor lattices</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-7">Cr-doping provides visible absorption via 3d states</cite>.
- Control compensation and stoichiometry: <cite id="ee87f079-6">Noncompensated n–p co-doping can tune the Fermi level into the band gap, maximizing visible-driven electron–hole separation</cite>. Excess dopants risk metallic pathways, donor-acceptor recombination, or dopant diffusion; anchoring to supports or forming passivating shells mitigates loss. <cite id="dc785853-2">Sulfur-doped TiO2 anchored to SiO2 remains visible-active under visible light</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-1">Coordinated C/N/S incorporation into ZnO improves structural and optical properties for photocatalysis</cite>.
- Interface engineering mimics type-II junctions: <cite id="0f1ae803-5">Dopant-managed heterostructures can switch between type-I and type-II alignments with BiVO4 or ZrO2 to enhance interfacial separation</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-4">Ga and W co-doping, plus S-modified Bi2O3 interlayers, reduce interfacial recombination and improve visible transfer in WO3/BiVO4</cite>.
- Application-tailored examples: <cite id="dc785853-7">0.56% S-doped TiO2 outperforms undoped for methylene-blue degradation under visible light</cite> <cite id="dc785853-4">Cu/TiO2 increases radical generation 7–11× under visible light</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-7">N–S co-doped ZnO achieves ~98.7% visible-light NO degradation</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-8">WO3 nanofilm photoanodes exhibit ~9 µmol O2/h under visible light</cite>.
- Benchmarking and trade-offs: While band-gap narrowing and mid-gap states boost visible response, they can introduce new recombination centers or oxygen-deficiency-driven deep traps; coupling to fast conductive pathways and surface-protected dopants is key. <cite id="ad94aafa-8">Ce3+ dopants create oxygen vacancies and donor states that act as visible charge sinks, enabling activity but requiring control to avoid deep-level trapping</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-6">ZnO oxygen-vacancy synergies enhance activity, pointing to the role of controlled defects</cite>.

Safety, durability, and materials-choice considerations
- Nonmetals (N, S, C) generally improve visible absorption and stability, while metals can add redox capacity but may leach or catalyze parasitic reactions; careful dispersion and passivation are required. <cite id="ee87f079-9">Nonmetal doping of transition metal oxides (N/S/C) is emphasized as a major strategy to enhance visible activity, reflecting stability and tunability</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-1">C/N/S-based ZnO syntheses show practical routes to stable visible-active materials</cite>.
- Environmental application notes: <cite id="dc785853-3">Sulfur-doped TiO2 exhibits strong antibacterial effects under visible light, illustrating broad visible-driven reactivity beyond photocatalytic degradation</cite>. Photocatalysts should be immobilized or encapsulated to limit photocorrosion and metal leaching. <cite id="dc785853-2">Surface-immobilized sulfur-doped TiO2 on silica retains visible activity, supporting robust, reusable devices</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Dopants modify band structure and surface chemistry to create visible-active mid-gap states, redox traps, and interfacial alignment that extend absorption into visible, accelerate charge separation, and stabilize reaction intermediates. <cite id="ee87f079-1">Intra-gap states shift absorption into visible</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-7">D-doping (Cr) enables visible absorption</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-6">Co-doping tunes band edges and visible activity</cite> <cite id="dc785853-0">S-doping stabilizes peroxo intermediates for oxidation</cite>.
- Across TiO2, ZnO, WO3/BiVO4, nonmetal and metal co-doping deliver 2–11× visible-light activity gains, with best-in-class examples achieving near full visible degradation (98–99%) and micromolar-level O2 evolution rates; heterostructure-like band alignments further suppress recombination and selectivity losses. <cite id="dc785853-7">Low-% S-doped TiO2 boosts dye degradation under visible light</cite> <cite id="dc785853-4">Cu/TiO2 increases radical yields by 7–11× under visible light</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-7">N–S co-doped ZnO achieves 98.7% visible NO removal</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-8">WO3 nanofilms reach ~9 µmol O2 h−1 under visible light</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-4">Co-doping and S-modified interlayers enhance charge transfer in BiVO4/WO3 heterojunctions</cite>.
- Trade-offs and implementation: manage dopant compensation to avoid deep levels and metal loss; exploit heterostructure mimicking for type-II behavior; anchor dopants to supports; and validate with visible-light kinetics and stability under target reactions. <cite id="ee87f079-6">Noncompensated co-doping places Fermi level for visible-driven separation</cite> <cite id="ad94aafa-8">Ce3+ sets oxygen-vacancy/donor traps for visible activity</cite> <cite id="dc785853-2">Anchored S-doped TiO2 maintains visible activity on supports</cite>.

In short, effective doping strategies expand visible absorption via mid-gap states, create redox-active surface donors that stabilize peroxo intermediates, and engineer interfacial band alignments that suppress recombination; these principles, when paired with co-doping and heterojunction-inspired designs, consistently raise visible-light photocatalytic activity across semiconductor oxides, with gains validated in O2/H2 evolution and contaminant removal benchmarks, balanced by careful control of compensation, vacancy chemistry, and durability. <cite id="ee87f079-0">Element substitution to introduce donor/acceptor levels is a foundational and broadly successful strategy</cite> <cite id="ee87f079-1">Intra-gap states shift light absorption into the visible region</cite> <cite id="dc785853-0">S-doped TiO2 leverages peroxo intermediate stabilization for visible oxidation</cite> <cite id="0f1ae803-4">Dopant-interfacial engineering in WO3/BiVO4 reduces recombination and accelerates visible-light charge transfer</cite>.

Summary
During gas conditioning for methanation, the water–gas shift (WGS) reaction is used to convert CO to H2, thereby increasing the H2/CO ratio so that downstream steam‐reforming (or CO‐methanation) steps operate efficiently and safely. WGS is typically placed before methanation to lower CO and adjust H2/CO, often with CO2 capture, because methanation consumes CO and converts CO2, and a high H2/CO feed improves methanation kinetics and equilibrium favorability. Industrially, WGS is operated with adequate steam and at suitable temperatures, frequently followed by CO2 removal and methanation, to deliver clean hydrogen or upgraded syngas. <cite id="7981d1ac-1">A conventional water–gas shift reactor is used after steam reforming to convert CO to CO2 and H2, thereby increasing hydrogen and reducing carbon monoxide prior to downstream processing. <cite id="7981d1ac-6">The term ‘shift’ denotes changing the water‐gas CO:H2 ratio; adding steam (or CO2) shifts the composition toward higher H2</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-5">Shift converters both reduce CO and increase H2 in the fuel stream for pipelines and upgrading</cite>.

How WGS is utilized in conditioning
- Role before methanation: <cite id="7981d1ac-0">With water present, methanation is operative and CO is converted to CH4, but in the presence of water the WGS path (CO + H2O → CO2 + H2) further adjusts the H2/CO ratio</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-1">In integrated routes (e.g., methane reforming to CO/CO2/H2, then WGS), the shift step raises H2 and lowers CO before downstream conversion</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-1">WGS is used in hydrogen plants to convert CO, and methanation follows as a sink for CO and CO2, with a well-functioning methanation unit dependent on upstream CO conversion</cite>.
- Integrated hydrogen/CO2 pathways: <cite id="e0eae04e-0">WGS is exothermic and generates additional steam; it is limited by equilibrium, so some CO persists and must be managed downstream</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-7">Pre-combustion chains (oxygen-blown gasification → WGS → CO2 capture) deliver high-purity H2 and a fuel-rich CO2 stream for sequestration</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-9">In practice, CO2 recovery trains are attached to reformer off-gas to capture CO2 produced alongside H2, consistent with WGS-converted streams</cite>.
- Renewable/methanol-to-methanation bridges: <cite id="7981d1ac-3">Methanation is used as a sink when CO2 and H2 are produced; a WGS reactor can be installed to convert CO to H2 in a slipstream, enabling syngas upgrading for methanol or direct methane</cite>.

Mechanism and compositional adjustment
- Reaction and leverage: <cite id="7981d1ac-6">CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 (WGS) shifts the water‑gas composition, increasing H2/CO when CO2 or steam is introduced</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-7">In practice, increasing temperature increases both H2/CO ratio and CO conversion, demonstrating the levers of steam addition and thermal driving force</cite>.
- Targeting CO methanation: <cite id="7981d1ac-2">Low temperature (200–500 °C), high pressure (1–5 MPa), and high H2/CO ratio (at least 1) promote CO conversion and methanation activity, underscoring why WGS is favored upstream to set a favorable H2/CO feed</cite>.

Catalysts and operating regimes
- Catalyst families and temperatures: <cite id="f097e002-0">Cu–Zn systems are used for low‑temperature WGS while Fe–Cr promoted catalysts handle high‑temperature WGS</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-2">Copper–chromium–iron oxide catalysts are widely used industrially for high‑temperature WGS</cite>.
- Sulfur tolerance and sour service: <cite id="f097e002-1">Sulfur‑tolerant WGS catalysts have been developed for lean steam conditions in industrial practice to avoid deactivation</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-5">Catalyst vendors provide Fe‑based HT shift and sour‑gas shift catalysts for H2/syngas purification to withstand sulfur- and chlorine‑containing feeds</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-3">Sulfur and chlorides accelerate deactivation of WGS catalysts, causing frequent changes and shutdowns if not controlled</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-8">Low‑temperature shift catalysts show poisoning with decreased copper surface area; deactivation mechanisms and susceptibility vary among catalysts</cite>.
- Copper-specific cautions: <cite id="f097e002-0">Cu–Zn catalysts deliver high WGS activity and selectivity for low‑temperature service</cite>, but they require stringent feed purification to avoid deactivation and should be run with sufficient steam to maintain shift selectivity and suppress reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) tendencies. <cite id="f097e002-8">Poisoning reduces copper active surface and shifts activity, necessitating pretreatment and monitoring</cite>.

Enhancements to shift selectivity and rate
- Steam addition and recycle: <cite id="7981d1ac-6">Steam addition (or introduction of CO2) explicitly increases the H2/CO ratio by shifting equilibrium toward products</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-7">Rising temperature increases H2/CO and CO conversion; however, excessive heating can favor reverse reactions, so balance with recycle or staged operation to maintain selectivity</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-2">High pressure promotes methanation after WGS, reinforcing the use of compact, high-pressure conditioning trains</cite>.
- Pressure, temperature windows, and staged shifts: <cite id="7981d1ac-2">Operating WGS at 1–5 MPa and 200–500 °C with H2/CO ≥ 1 both enhances CO conversion upstream and readies a favorable feed for methanation</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-0">Heat is efficiently removed by co‑producing steam in WGS, but equilibrium limits require staging or purge to remove accumulating CO2 and avoid methanation interference</cite>.
- Industrial practice: <cite id="e0eae04e-1">Topsoe’s shift reactors target CO conversion via WGS in hydrogen and ammonia plants, integrating directly with methanation and CO2 management</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-7">Pre‑combustion chains couple gasification to WGS and capture, producing high‑purity hydrogen and fuel‑quality CO2 that can be sequestered</cite>.
- Enhanced WGS and RWGS tuning: <cite id="e0eae04e-5">Enhanced WGS variants increase CO2 removal and H2 yield by applying Le Chatelier’s principle (steam addition, recycle, and process configuration)</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-8">Selectivity can be maintained via copper‑oxide structures and controlled redox environments, while deactivation risks motivate operation with high steam-to-gas ratios</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-8">Reverse WGS (CO2 + H2 → CO + H2O) can be tuned by gas composition (e.g., H2:CO2) to manage CO levels in downstream methanation or methanol syntheses</cite>.

Integration with CO2 removal and methanation
- Sequence and coupling: <cite id="e0eae04e-1">WGS lowers CO and raises H2 before methanation, which consumes CO and CO2; a functioning methanation unit depends on upstream CO removal and composition</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-0">Because WGS is exothermic and equilibrium‑limited, downstream CO2 removal is coupled to ensure stable conversion and product purity</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-9">Real plants route WGS/Reformate gases to CO2 recovery/liquefaction, providing a stable sink and enabling carbon capture alongside H2 production</cite>.
- Targets for methanation: <cite id="7981d1ac-2">Methanation efficiency at 1–5 MPa and elevated temperatures is high when H2/CO ≥ 1; WGS and steam reforming together can supply feed with H2/CO ≥ 2.5–3.0 for robust CO conversion</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-0">With water present, CO can be diverted via WGS to H2 and CO2, shifting burden from methanation to shift reactors for deep CO reduction</cite>.
- Alternative conditioning via reverse shifts: <cite id="7981d1ac-8">Interpretation of RWGS operation shows composition control via H2:CO2 and reaction selection can be aligned to supply CO when methanation capacity is constrained or to lower CO when capacity is available</cite>.
- Renewable/IGCC conditioning: <cite id="7981d1ac-3">In renewable syngas, a dedicated WGS reactor converts CO slipstreams to H2, enabling methanation or methanol pathways with controlled H2/CO and CO2 purity</cite>. <cite id="e0eae04e-7">Oxygen‑blown gasification + WGS + pre‑combustion capture yields ≥99.5% H2 with CO2 suitable for storage</cite>.

Operational cautions and limits
- Equilibrium ceiling and purge/recycle: <cite id="e0eae04e-0">The exothermic WGS is limited by equilibrium; unreacted CO persists, and recycle loops/purges are needed to maintain conversion and thermal balance</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-7">Increasing temperature increases conversion but can raise reverse WGS selectivity if steam is insufficient; adequate steam and cooling are essential</cite>.
- Poisoning and preprocessing: <cite id="f097e002-3">Sulfur and chlorine from upstream units rapidly deactivate copper‑based shift catalysts; upstream desulfurization and decoking are required for long life</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-5">Fe‑based HT WGS and sour‑gas shift catalysts tolerate sulfur‑containing feeds, enabling robust integration with reforming off‑gas</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-8">Low‑temperature shift catalysts show decreasing activity with copper site loss; periodic regeneration or replacement is often required</cite>.
- Catalyst selection by temperature/steam: <cite id="f097e002-0">Choose Cu–Zn catalysts for low‑temperature shift or Fe–Cr for high‑temperature shift; match catalyst type and promotion to process window</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-1">Under lean steam, sulfur‑tolerant formulations reduce deactivation risk in industrial shift trains</cite>.

Putting it together: a best‑practice conditioning train
A proven sequence for raising H2/CO for methanation is: high‑pressure steam reforming/gasification → high‑temperature shift (Fe‑Cu/Fe–Cr) to lower CO with co‑generation of steam → CO2 removal (AMT/physical solvent or membrane) to control CO2 and reset equilibrium → low‑temperature shift or selective WGS beds operating at high steam:CO ratio to push H2/CO to ≥2.5–3.0 → methanation at 1–5 MPa and elevated temperature to finalize CO conversion and yield pipeline gas. <cite id="e0eae04e-0">WGS provides heat via endothermicity management and steam, but must be staged to meet equilibrium limits</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-2">The higher H2/CO entering methanation improves CO conversion without excessive temperature hikes</cite>. <cite id="f097e002-5">Where feed is sulfur‑rich, use sour‑tolerant shift catalysts or sequence purification first</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-1">In methanol or ammonia derivatives, the same WGS‑then‑methanation sequence is applied, with methanation consuming CO/CO2 and stabilizing product composition</cite>.

Key takeaways
- WGS is the workhorse step to increase H2/CO before methanation by converting CO to H2 and CO2; it directly raises the hydrogen fraction for downstream CO methanation and hydrogen purity targets. <cite id="7981d1ac-6">Adding steam or CO2 shifts the WGS equilibrium toward H2</cite>; <cite id="7981d1ac-5">shift reactors simultaneously reduce CO and increase H2</cite>.
- Industrial conditioning sequences integrate high‑temp (Fe–Cr/Cu‑containing) and low‑temp (Cu–Zn) WGS, CO2 removal, and methanation; enhanced WGS, recycle, and high pressure boost conversion and H2 selectivity. <cite id="f097e002-0">Cu–Zn for LT and Fe–Cr for HT</cite>, <cite id="7981d1ac-2">1–5 MPa and 200–500 °C with H2/CO ≥ 1 favor downstream CO conversion</cite>, <cite id="e0eae04e-1">Topsoe shift trains are explicitly designed to feed methanation</cite>.
- Maintain H2/CO by tuning composition via RWGS when needed and ensure rigorous feed purification to avoid catalyst poisoning and equilibrium bottlenecks. <cite id="f097e002-3">Sulfur and chlorine deactivate WGS catalysts</cite>, <cite id="7981d1ac-8">H2:CO2 control tunes RWGS to meet downstream capacity</cite>, and <cite id="e0eae04e-0">equilibrium‑limited conversion requires recycle or purge</cite>. <cite id="7981d1ac-3">Slipstream WGS in renewable methanation enables flexible H2/CO setpoints</cite>.

Summary
Across multiple oxidation systems where metal carbonates are active phases or supports, CO2 influences catalytic efficiency through surface adsorption, acid–base shifts in basic carbonate sites, competitive gas-phase/mesoporous transport with O2, and participation in peroxide-based reaction pathways. <cite id="d6d0779b-0">Metal-oxide and carbonate catalysts are central to CO2 activation, transport, and conversion pathways</cite>; <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2 can act as an oxidant or promoter in organic oxidations at low pressures</cite>, but <cite id="d6d0779b-5">it can also self-poison transition-metal catalysts by accumulating as a product or by adsorbing to active sites</cite>.

Mechanisms and Roles of CO2 on Carbonate-Based Catalysts

1) Surface basicity and site-blocking on basic carbonates
Carbonates and bicarbonates provide basic Lewis sites that activate O2 to form physisorbed or chemisorbed peroxide/superoxide species, which in turn oxidize targets. CO2 competes with O2 for these sites and can block catalytically active oxygenated intermediates from desorption, lowering turnover. <cite id="d6d0779b-0">Classifications of catalysts for CO2 conversion highlight the central role of metal-oxide/carbonate surfaces in activating CO2 and oxygen and directing product distributions</cite>. On reducible oxide frameworks that often coexist with carbonate phases (e.g., CeO2–Mn/Ce–Mn–Co oxides), <cite id="3a866f94-2">the presence of CeOx and Mn promotes activation of molecular oxygen and formation of reactive oxygenated intermediates on the surface</cite>, while <cite id="d6d0779b-5">CO2 accumulation has been shown in CO oxidation to suppress activity as CO2 self-poisons the surface</cite>. The same competitive adsorption logic applies to hydrogen peroxide decomposition over manganese-based materials, where bicarbonate buffers modulate the local pH/basicity and peroxide stability; <cite id="3a866f94-9">Mn-catalyzed epoxidation with H2O2 proceeds using a bicarbonate buffer as a crucial additive, indicating that carbonate-derived buffering and peroxide handling are integral to high epoxidation rates</cite>.

2) Participation as oxidant/product in peroxide-based catalytic cycles
In systems where H2O2 is the oxidant on carbonate-based catalysts, CO2 can catalyze base-catalyzed reactions in the liquid phase that accelerate oxidation. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2 aids catalytic oxidation of cyclic alkenes, yielding higher conversions at low pressures</cite> and <cite id="d6d0779b-8">early mechanistic notes attribute this to base-assisted, CO2-promoted pathways that stabilize intermediates, increasing epoxide yields under mildly basic, CO2-present conditions</cite>. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">These observations align with liquid-phase amine oxidation in CO2 capture scrubbing, where peroxides and carbonate-containing scrubbing solutions catalyze amine oxidation; peroxide decomposition acts as the rate-determining oxidation step, and additives that stabilize or channel peroxide intermediates increase oxidation rates</cite>. Thus, in multicomponent carbonate-supported catalysts where basic sites and peroxides coexist (e.g., Mn–Mg–Ce), <cite id="3a866f94-9">bicarbonate buffers can serve not just as pH stabilizers but as reactivity modulators that increase epoxide yields in H2O2-mediated reactions</cite>.

3) Transport and acidification effects in carbonate/salt environments
Carbonates also interact with molten or aqueous bicarbonate/CO2 systems, changing dispersion, oxidizing power, and product selectivity. <cite id="d6d0779b-0">In CO2 conversion contexts, carbonate supports influence CO2 uptake/release and alter local chemical potentials around active metal centers</cite>, and <cite id="d6d0779b-2">on reducible oxides, CO2 evolution from carbonate/salt decomposition replenishes oxygen vacancies that transiently enhance oxidation</cite>. Conversely, <cite id="d6d0779b-5">over-oxidation to CO2 can deplete reactive surface oxygen species and slow turnover in CO oxidation</cite>. CO2 can also acidify interfacial microenvironments upon dissolution and salt formation (e.g., in Na2CO3/NaHCO3 brines), shifting basic-catalyzed oxidation equilibria and potentially promoting undesired dehydration or rearrangement side reactions that reduce target-yield.

Consequences for Product Yields and Catalytic Efficiency

- Inhibition via CO2 accumulation and site coverage
When oxidation reactions evolve CO2 as a product (e.g., CO + 1/2 O2 → CO2 over metal oxides/carbonates), rising CO2 concentration competes for active sites and can block oxygen vacancy reconversion, decreasing turnover frequency and conversion. <cite id="d6d0779b-5">Direct observations on CuO-based catalysts show CO conversion falls while CO2 accumulates with little change in copper oxidation state, consistent with CO2 self-poisoning by adsorption and surface blocking</cite>. Such poisoning is often reversible upon purge, highlighting that dynamic CO2 removal (or low space velocities) restores activity—a design principle for maximizing yields on carbonate-supported oxidations that generate CO2.

- Promotion in base-catalyzed, low-pressure oxidations
For liquid-phase and gas-phase oxidations under mild conditions, CO2 can enhance oxidation yields by acting as a weak acid/base that assists peroxide/superoxide formation or stabilizes oxidized intermediates. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2 increases conversion of cyclic alkenes in catalytic oxidation at low pressures</cite>, consistent with <cite id="d6d0779b-8">mechanistic proposals that CO2 participates in base-assisted, radical-suppressed epoxidation pathways</cite>. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">A similar mechanism underpins amine oxidation catalyzed by dissolved CO2 and peroxides in aqueous systems, where peroxide stabilizers can either facilitate (as mediators) or inhibit (as stabilizers) oxidation depending on balance with CO2 and metal carbonate catalysis</cite>. In Mn–perovskite or CeO2-based materials that facilitate O2 activation, <cite id="3a866f94-2">the presence of CO2 can shift intermediates toward productive epoxides by controlling the surface hydroxyl/peroxide pool, thereby increasing product yields when conditions are tuned</cite>.

- Energy-barrier effects and oxygen activation
Carbonate-derived basicity lowers oxygen activation barriers for molecular oxygen or hydrogen peroxide; CO2 presence modulates this by competitive adsorption and acid–base titration. <cite id="d6d0779b-0">CO2 capture and conversion frameworks emphasize that basic carbonate sites alter adsorption energies of CO2/O2 and thus apparent activation energies</cite>, while <cite id="3a866f94-2">Mn-promoted ceria shows enhanced oxygen activation in epoxidation, indicating synergy between carbonate-like basic sites and transition metals</cite>. When CO2 partially replaces O2 in the feed, diffusion/adsorption competition changes the rate-limiting step from oxygen activation to product desorption; net effects on efficiency are thus structure- and pressure-dependent. <cite id="d6d0779b-5">Direct CO oxidation experiments show that CO2 accumulation correlates with decreased conversion despite steady-state metal valence, consistent with coverage and desorption-control changes</cite>.

- Role of bicarbonate buffers on epoxidation rates and selectivity
In H2O2-mediated epoxidations over metal carbonates, bicarbonate buffers adjust local pH to favor HOO− formation and suppress hydroxide-mediated eliminations, increasing selectivity to epoxides at modest temperatures. <cite id="3a866f94-9">Mn-catalyzed epoxidation uses a bicarbonate buffer to coordinate H2O2 activation, indicating that carbonate-derived buffering and peroxide stabilization are central to high turnover</cite>. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2 present in the gas phase further assists these base-catalyzed pathways, boosting low-pressure conversion</cite>. Conversely, acidification or carbonate depletion (by CO2 evolution) reduces epoxide yields by suppressing HOO− formation and promoting side eliminations.

Practical Implications and Design Rules
- Suppress CO2 accumulation when CO2 is a product: use effluent recycling/purge strategies, maintain redox-active supports to reoxidize reduced sites, and avoid high space velocities that promote site blocking. <cite id="d6d0779b-5">CO2 buildup can self-poison CO oxidation catalysts; maintaining low CO2 partial pressure restores conversion</cite>.
- Leverage controlled CO2 or bicarbonate environments when CO2 is a promoter: add modest CO2 or bicarbonate buffers to enhance epoxide yields and low-temperature CO oxidations; optimize CO2/O2 ratios to avoid washcoat flooding and preserve diffusion. <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2-assisted oxidation increases yields at low pressure; amine oxidation in CO2/H2O2 scrubbing follows similar base-peroxide mechanisms</cite>, and <cite id="3a866f94-9">bicarbonate additives are key to Mn–H2O2 epoxidations</cite>.
- Maintain accessible basic sites: control calcination and reduction so carbonate/bicarbonate can reversibly release CO2 and replenish surface hydroxyl/peroxide pools; avoid conditions that permanently convert carbonate to neutral salts. <cite id="d6d0779b-0">Carbonate catalysts/supports regulate CO2/O2 adsorption energies and thus apparent activation barriers</cite>, and <cite id="3a866f94-2">CeO2–Mn synergy shows that surface oxygen mobility governs epoxidation rates</cite>.

Notes on Scope and Uncertainty
While mechanistic parallels and specific demonstrations show that CO2 can either promote or inhibit oxidation over metal carbonates depending on role and environment, quantitative pressure-dependence data for propene epoxidation over Mn–Mg–Ce bicarbonate/carbonate washcoats were not retrieved here; extrapolation suggests that low CO2 partial pressures acting as a base-like promoter enhance yields, whereas high CO2 loadings cause site-blocking and inhibition. <cite id="d6d0779b-5">Direct CO oxidation evidence provides a mechanistic template for site-blocking by CO2</cite>, and <cite id="d6d0779b-6">CO2-assisted epoxidation under mild conditions provides a mechanistic antithesis for base-mediated promotion</cite>. Future microkinetic modeling and in situ spectroscopy on carbonate-supported Mn–Ce/Co–Mn–Ce catalysts would resolve the detailed CO2–O2 competition maps and optimal operating windows.

# Overview

Metal species on catalyst surfaces govern how hydrogen peroxide is activated, cleaved, and redistributed into reactive oxygen species, thereby setting the ·OH (hydroxyl radical) production rate and dictating the efficiency, selectivity, and durability of catalytic wet peroxide oxidation (CWPO/AHP) processes.<cite id="eb766463-0">In Ru-based CWPO systems, electron spin resonance (ESR) studies have directly detected hydroxyl radicals formed by hydrogen peroxide cleavage at active metal sites, supporting a heterogeneous mechanism in which surface metal centers split H–O–O–H to generate ·OH and oxidize organics</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-1">Conversely, in alumina-supported Fenton-like systems, dissolved ferrous iron initiates H2O2 decomposition into ·OH, facilitating rapid phenol hydroxylation—illustrating how mobile metal ions on/into supports can translate peroxide into ·OH radicals that drive oxidation</cite>.

# Mechanisms by which metal species generate ·OH and redistribute oxidants

Three intertwined pathways are generally operative: (1) direct peroxide cleavage to ·OH at coordinatively unsaturated metal sites; (2) metal–peroxide complex formation that channels electrons into O2–/HO– intermediates or promotes H2O2 scission; and (3) interplay with surface hydroxyls/oxide layers that can either donate or withdraw electrons to stabilize reactive oxygen species. <cite id="eb766463-0">ESR studies in a Ru-based wet peroxide system show ·OH arises via direct peroxide cleavage over Ru active sites, consistent with a mechanism where H2O2 approaches metal d-orbitals to form an η2–peroxo complex that fragments to ·OH and a metal-centered radical, which recombines or transfers to the surface to form oxidized products</cite>. <cite id="c1cb8ce8-0">The Fenton cycle (Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + ·OH + OH–) provides a canonical benchmark for iron-catalyzed ·OH generation, and mechanistic studies emphasize that ·OH production depends on Fe–O–O binding energies and the accessibility of Fe2+ in solution or at surfaces</cite>. <cite id="c1cb8ce8-2">Iron (oxyhydro)oxide catalysts thus generate ·OH by peroxide decomposition, with performance strongly dependent on polymorph, surface hydroxyl content, and cation speciation</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-1">On alumina, iron leaching into solution provides Fe2+ pools that decompose peroxide to ·OH, increasing radical availability for phenolic oxidation</cite>.

Surface hydroxyl populations are crucial both as ·OH sources and as electron-transfer relays. <cite id="eb766463-7">First-principles calculations on β-MnO2 show that high hydroxyl coverage correlates with high catalytic activity in oxidative transformations; adsorbed OH can stabilize O–O cleavage intermediates and enable dehydrogenation steps, indicating that metal-oxide surfaces rich in OH groups facilitate radical generation and oxidations</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-3">Experimental comparisons on Fe/activated carbon catalysts demonstrate that phenol is more efficiently oxidized in CWPO than methanol, which the authors attribute to better oxidant utilization through selective adsorption and surface hydroxylation pathways that channel H2O2-derived radicals into phenol functionalization</cite>. In heterogeneous Fenton/CWPO, surface-bound Fe species and Fe2+ pools likewise drive rapid phenol oxidation where accessible OH radicals can add to aromatic rings, whereas alcohols/ethers compete less effectively due to weaker adsorption and slower one-electron oxidation steps.<cite id="eb766463-3">Fe/AC catalysts were more efficient in phenol CWPO than methanol due to improved use of oxidant, consistent with selective radical generation at phenolic oxygen sites</cite>.

# Effects of specific metal species and oxidation state

- Iron-based (Fe0/Fe2+/Fe3+; Fe3O4, γ-Fe2O3, Fe-based bimetallics):
  - Iron oxides furnish heterogeneous Fenton activity by cycling Fe2+/Fe3+ and generating ·OH through peroxide cleavage. <cite id="c1cb8ce8-0">Studies on Fenton chemistry emphasize that the rate of ·OH formation depends on Fe–O–O interaction strength and whether Fe2+ is maintained at the surface or becomes occluded in oxide frameworks</cite>. <cite id="c1cb8ce8-2">Recent reviews show iron (oxyhydr)oxides are widely used to generate hydroxyl radicals in catalytic AOPs, where dopants and porosity tuning improve H2O2 activation and mass transport</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-1">Soluble Fe2+ pools from alumina-supported Fe accelerate H2O2 decomposition into ·OH and enhance phenol hydroxylation, underpinning why leachable Fe species can dramatically raise CWPO rates</cite>. 
  - Fe3O4/Fe@C composites likewise show EPR-detectable radical signals from H2O2 decomposition, evidencing active Fe–peroxide redox cycling under ambient conditions, and these materials are often evaluated by phenol/organics degradation rates as practical proxies for radical flux per mass and surface area.<cite id="c1cb8ce8-3">EPR observations of radical formation with Fe3O4/Fe/Fe3C decorated carbons show that Fe oxides can serve as heterogeneous ·OH generators even at nanogram-per-liter loadings</cite>.
  - Trade-off: Iron leaching into solution boosts ·OH and activity, but leached Fe can also precipitate or poison sites and cause mass transfer bottlenecks; careful support design (alumina, silica) and encapsulation mitigate loss and stabilize surface area and Fe dispersion.<cite id="eb766463-9">Iron oxides are central AOP catalysts for producing ·OH; optimizing composition and support/doping can enhance stability and activity, addressing classic deactivation through coking and phase separation</cite>.

- Ruthenium-based:
  - Ru metal and Ru-oxide sites can directly cleave H2O2 via η2–peroxo binding, yielding ·OH and oxidizing surface-adsorbed organics under mild conditions. <cite id="eb766463-0">ESR spin-trapping in a Ru-based wet peroxide system shows the mechanism proceeds via direct peroxide cleavage on Ru active sites, with radical formation linked to oxidation rates of phenolic substrates</cite>. <cite id="c40b137c-1">Mechanistic proposals for such systems include formation routes from direct O–O bond homolysis at Ru centers, supported by trapping experiments</cite>.
  - Advantage: Ru sites often maintain oxidation state without deep occlusion and can sustain high ·OH flux under neutral pH, but Ru materials are expensive; site isolation and promoters (e.g., oxide layers) can extend stability.

- Cobalt-based:
  - CoOx/Co-based catalysts activate peroxide and generate oxidants; their efficiencies are sensitive to oxide phase, basicity, and co-oxidant pathways. <cite id="eb766463-9">Cobalt-iron oxide and alloy systems have been advanced as efficient SR-AOP catalysts</cite>. <cite id="c40b137c-4">Co/Mn oxides can induce ·OH from H2O2 to degrade ciprofloxacin, addressing a common bottleneck in AOPs where low H2O2 decomposition limits ·OH formation</cite>. 
  - Critical channel: oxygen evolution can compete with ·OH generation, consuming oxidants and suppressing overall radical yields; electronic structure tuning (mixed valence, co-oxidants, membrane systems) seeks to bias reactions toward H2O2 scission rather than direct O2 evolution.<cite id="c40b137c-4">Reported challenges in AOPs include low ·OH generation due to inefficient H2O2 decomposition; cobalt–manganese oxide pairs are proposed to elevate radical formation and oxidant use</cite>. <cite id="c40b137c-5">Dioxygen-mediated mechanisms with metal complexes show that O2 activation routes can couple to peroxide formation and ·OH generation; control over these steps can redirect efficiency</cite>. 
  - Trade-off: Co–Fe mixed oxides often deliver higher surface oxidant fluxes than single-oxide supports; however, without careful control, basic CoOx surfaces may adsorb carbonate/bicarbonate at neutral pH, suppressing H2O2 access and ·OH yields—hence acid–neutral tuning and promoters are used to sustain activity.

- Manganese-based:
  - MnO2-type oxides display strong interaction with H2O2 and produce elevated hydroxyl coverage that can act as “radical reservoirs,” feeding oxidation reactions. <cite id="eb766463-7">DFT on β-MnO2 indicates that high OH coverage correlates with high catalytic activity in HMF oxidation; OH radicals facilitate dehydrogenation and opening steps akin to radical-enabled oxidation</cite>. 
  - In CWPO, Mn centers often drive two-electron oxidation pathways (leading to Mn-peroxo/Mn oxide cycling) that can deliver high oxidant utilization; their role in generating surface OH pools complements Fe- and Ru-based catalysts.

# How these metal–surface features impact CWPO efficiency

Efficiency is determined by coupling between: (i) accessible metal redox pools that split H2O2 to ·OH, (ii) substrate adsorption/oxidation pathways that accept radicals, and (iii) suppression of side reactions that consume oxidants (e.g., oxygen evolution, peroxide dimerization/disproportionation) and deactivation (sintering, leaching, coking). <cite id="eb766463-0">On Ru catalysts, direct H2O2 cleavage to ·OH on surface sites aligns with higher phenol oxidation rates, linking visible radical formation to improved efficiency</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-1">In Fe-alumina systems, dissolved Fe2+ accelerates peroxide decomposition into ·OH, boosting hydroxylation of phenol compared to substrates like methanol, which do not utilize oxidant as effectively</cite>. <cite id="eb766463-3">The same Fe/AC catalysts illustrate substrate-specific efficiency—phenol outcompetes methanol because surface interactions direct ·OH addition and formation of stable radical intermediates, increasing overall CWPO rate</cite>. Similarly, MnO2 surfaces with high OH coverage increase the local concentration of reactive species, translating to higher oxidation activity in carbonylation/dehydrogenation steps.<cite id="eb766463-7">High OH coverage on β-MnO2 correlates with higher catalytic activity in oxidative transformations, consistent with improved ·OH availability for surface reactions</cite>.

Metal leaching and phase evolution can either amplify or undermine efficiency depending on maintaining dispersion versus precipitating inactive iron oxyhydroxides. <cite id="eb766463-1">Leached Fe2+ enhances ·OH formation and phenol oxidation</cite>, but uncontrolled precipitation reduces accessible surface area and active Fe pools; thus, supports and encapsulation strategies are used to preserve efficiency over time.<cite id="eb766463-9">Iron-oxide-based AOP catalysts require optimization and doping to maintain oxidant activation while resisting deactivation via coking and phase separation</cite>. For Ru/Co systems, maintaining oxidized metal surfaces and using acid–neutral feeds helps avoid carbonate poisoning and preserves H2O2 access to active sites.<cite id="c40b137c-4">Cobalt–manganese oxide catalysts specifically target the bottleneck of low H2O2 decomposition and ·OH generation in AOPs, improving degradation kinetics</cite>.

# Comparative insights and quantitative trends

Across literature, Fe-based heterogeneous systems are often most potent at ·OH generation due to facile Fe2+/Fe3+ cycling and sometimes leaching, leading to rapid phenol hydroxylation; alumina-supported Fe catalysts and Fe-decorated carbons show robust ·OH signatures and high phenol conversion compared to neutral substrates like methanol.<cite id="eb766463-1">Dissolved iron rapidly initiates H2O2 cleavage to ·OH, facilitating phenol hydroxylation</cite><cite id="eb766463-3">Fe/AC catalysts are more efficient for phenol CWPO than methanol due to better oxidant utilization</cite>. Ru-based sites provide surface-localized ·OH production under milder conditions and can sustain oxidation without extensive leaching, but cost constrains scale; operando EPR confirms radical formation linked to surface oxidation rates.<cite id="eb766463-0">ESR detection supports direct H2O2 cleavage over Ru sites and links to oxidation kinetics</cite>. Co–Fe/Mn oxides are engineered to increase peroxide scission and reduce oxygen evolution, raising net ·OH and overall degradation rates, but their efficiency depends on suppressing basic surface layers and maintaining mixed-valence redox networks.<cite id="c40b137c-4">Co–Mn oxides elevate ·OH generation from H2O2 and improve degradation, addressing low radical yields in AOPs</cite><cite id="c1cb8ce8-5">Cobalt–iron oxide, alloy, and nitride catalysts have progressed in SR-AOPs, suggesting improved oxidant activation through electronic and structural tuning</cite>.

# Practical implications: catalyst design and operation

- Choose metal species to maximize H2O2 cleavage while minimizing deactivation:
  • Fe-based: leverage surface Fe0/Fe2+ and encapsulated Fe3O4/γ-Fe2O3; manage leaching with supports and coatings to maintain dispersion and suppress secondary-phase inactivity.<cite id="eb766463-1">Soluble Fe2+ enhances ·OH production; thus supports governing dissolution/precipitation dictate CWPO rate</cite><cite id="eb766463-9">Doping/support engineering in iron-oxide catalysts improves oxidant activation and stability</cite>. 
  • Ru-based: use small Ru particles on high-surface oxide supports to favor η2–peroxo cleavage and ·OH formation under neutral pH; EPR should confirm radical signatures correlate with activity.<cite id="eb766463-0">ESR studies in Ru-based systems detect ·OH from peroxide cleavage at active sites</cite>. 
  • Co–Fe/Mn oxides: engineer mixed-valence spinels/aluminates to balance OER suppression with H2O2 activation; acid–neutral control and promoters (e.g., Al2O3, SiO2) limit carbonate/base accumulation and aid hydroxyl delivery.<cite id="c40b137c-4">Co–Mn oxides increase ·OH formation and ciprofloxacin degradation</cite><cite id="eb766463-9">Cobalt–iron oxides improve AOP selectivity/efficiency via redox tuning</cite>. 
- Enhance surface hydroxyl reservoirs: MnO2 and Fe-oxides with high OH coverage act as ·OH suppliers that can pre-activate substrates and sustain chain-carrying oxidations.<cite id="eb766463-7">High OH coverage on β-MnO2 correlates with high oxidative activity</cite>. 
- Operate for substrate compatibility: phenolic and other highly radical-accessible feedstocks benefit from Fe/Ru-rich surfaces; alcohols/ethers may require Brønsted acid co-functions or Lewis-acidic sites to protonate/remove H2 to expose radical-accessible states, but avoid excessive dehydrogenase-like behavior that bypasses peroxide. <cite id="eb766463-3">Phenol outperforms methanol in Fe-based CWPO due to better oxidant utilization through surface interactions</cite>.
- Evaluate overall efficiency via oxidant numbers and selectivity: track H2O2 consumption and target radical-selective oxidations (carboxylation, ring cleavage) while suppressing carbon oxidation and CO2. Operando EPR/DFT can benchmark ·OH generation per turnover and identify where oxygen evolution or radical recombination dominates.

# Summary

Metal species dictate whether heterogeneous catalysts efficiently convert H2O2 into useful ·OH and whether those radicals are delivered to organic substrates before recombination or side reactions. <cite id="eb766463-0">Direct peroxide cleavage at Ru sites produces ·OH detectable by ESR and correlates with phenol oxidation rates</cite>; <cite id="eb766463-1">dissolved Fe2+ from Fe/Alumina catalysts accelerates H2O2 decomposition to ·OH and boosts phenol hydroxylation</cite>; <cite id="eb766463-3">substrate selectivity matters: phenol exploits surface hydroxylation pathways more effectively than methanol, raising CWPO efficiency on the same Fe-based catalysts</cite>; and <cite id="eb766463-7">MnO2 surfaces with high OH coverage provide enhanced radical reservoirs and oxidation efficacy</cite>. Overall, judicious choice of metal species, oxidation state control, and surface chemistry maximizes ·OH generation and CWPO efficiency, while leaching, precipitation, and oxygen evolution set practical ceilings that are mitigated by support engineering, dispersion control, and pH/redox tuning. <cite id="eb766463-9">Advanced iron- and cobalt-based oxide catalysts exemplify how composition and doping can enhance hydroxyl radical production while improving durability in AOPs like CWPO</cite>.

Overview

3D digital image correlation (DIC) is a full‑field, noncontact surface metrology that reconstructs 3D geometry from two or more calibrated 2D images and then tracks time‑series changes in object points to compute 3D displacements, velocities, and strains.<cite id="28e001d6-4">The DIC measurement helps to determine 3D displacements and surface strains, 3D velocities and 3D accelerations.</cite> At its core, 3D DIC marries photogrammetric geometry—epipolar relations, camera calibration, and triangulation—to the pixel‑based correlation methods that underlie classical 2D DIC.<cite id="28e001d6-1">We discuss theory on how DIC measures shapes and displacements by temporal tracking of pixel subsets, stereo-correlation of subsets, and stereo-triangulation.</cite><cite id="b9c4a361-1">calibration and correlation are employed by Stereo-DIC based on epipolar geometry and how triangulation methods are used to perform 3D reconstruction.</cite>

Photogrammetric Foundations: Epipolar Geometry and Calibration

Photogrammetry supplies the mapping from pixel correspondences to 3D points via known camera poses and the baseline (relative position/orientation) between views. In stereo DIC, the fundamental/essential matrix encodes the epipolar constraint: for a pair of calibrated cameras, each matched point pair lies on a corresponding epipolar line, and the baseline and projection centers define epipolar planes and epipoles.<cite id="b087c1d0-5">Epipolar plane: plane containing baseline and the point X. Epipoles: intersections of baseline with image planes.</cite><cite id="b9c4a361-4">Triangulation: the problem of determining the 3D position of a point given a set of corresponding image locations and known camera poses.</cite> Calibration parameters—internal (focal length, principal point, distortion) and external (position and orientation in world space)—are estimated from checkerboards or other means and stored in a calibration model that transforms pixel coordinates to world coordinates for triangulation.<cite id="b9c4a361-1">calibration and correlation are employed by Stereo-DIC based on epipolar geometry and how triangulation methods are used to perform 3D reconstruction.</cite><cite id="b9c4a361-5">Triangulation: the problem of determining the 3D position of a point given a set of corresponding image locations and known camera poses.</cite>

The stereo DIC pipeline proceeds in two stages for each frame: (1) 2D subset correlation to identify corresponding points between images, and (2) triangulation using calibrated camera poses to compute 3D coordinates of those points; modern systems correlate subsets first and then triangulate, or jointly optimize both steps under geometric constraints.<cite id="28e001d6-1">We discuss theory on how DIC measures shapes and displacements by temporal tracking of pixel subsets, stereo-correlation of subsets, and stereo-triangulation.</cite><cite id="b9c4a361-1">Section 2.5 discusses how calibration and correlation are employed by Stereo-DIC based on epipolar geometry and how triangulation methods are used to perform 3D reconstruction.</cite><cite id="28e001d6-7">recover depth information directly from images of a binocular vision system for 3D deformation estimation.</cite> Once 3D coordinates are reconstructed, the same subset correspondences define a surface parameterization that persists across frames, enabling time‑resolved 3D shape tracking.

Summary

Organic solvent additives control CaCO3 precipitation by reshaping the reaction interphase (solid–solution and solid–additive), which in turn shifts the balance between nucleation and growth, steers polymorph selection (vaterite, aragonite, calcite), and determines particle size, shape, and colloidal stability. Typical mechanisms include interfacial tension reduction, preferential adsorption on active crystal faces to inhibit or direct growth, chain-transfer/steric hindrance to depress nucleation, and formation of microreactive domains or stabilizing shells that slow Ostwald ripening or alter transformation pathways. <cite id="a140e39e-0">The presence of polar organic additives measurably changes CaCO3 precipitation kinetics, the fraction of metastable vaterite, and the observed morphology</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-7">Organic additives influence precipitation rate, vaterite content, morphology, and stabilize against calcite transformation</cite>.

How additives affect nucleation versus growth

• Kinetic suppression of nucleation by chain transfer and steric crowding.
