Hydrophilic polymers such as poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) adsorb onto nascent CaCO3 surfaces and create kinetic barriers that enhance polymorph-specific nucleation selectivity; PVA-coated substrates preferentially yield vaterite nuclei, demonstrating that interfacial crowding can “gate” which polymorph is selected at early stages. <cite id="88f50fd5-2">PVA enhances the selectivity of polymorph nucleation by pre-adsorbing on the fiber and modifying early-stage surface energetics</cite>. Surfactant–polymer templates (e.g., CTAB with PVA/PEG/PVAc) likewise direct PCC crystallogenesis by binding to specific lattice faces and constraining step dynamics, shifting the system from uncontrolled nucleation into template-controlled growth. <cite id="fabcbf39-5">Surfactant–polymer templates (CTAB, PVA, PEG, PVAc) significantly influence PCC morphology by altering growth along specific crystallographic planes</cite>.

• Facilitation of heterogeneous nucleation on additive interfaces. Alcohol–surfactant co-precipitation strategies can act as heterogeneous nuclei or electron-donating microenvironments that accelerate vaterite formation; mechanistic evidence shows synergistic additive–substrate interactions guide phase selection during precipitation. <cite id="88f50fd5-0">An alcohol–surfactant-assisted co-precipitation strategy provides a controlled route to vaterite with altered nucleation/growth pathways</cite>. In some systems, glycol/glycerol or ethanol–water co-solvents depress surface tension and solubility, enabling faster attainment of supersaturation and heterogeneous nucleation at droplet interfaces or along organic templates. <cite id="88f50fd5-3">Common alcohol regulators (ethanol, ethylene glycol, glycerol) are used to control CaCO3 polymorphism by modulating nucleation/growth equilibria</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-0">Polar organic solvents are explicitly used to shape the course of CaCO3 precipitation, including rates and polymorph outcomes</cite>.

• Intermediary amorphous shells that buffer nucleation/growth. Organic additives such as poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) or silane-bearing molecules can form amorphous calcium carbonate–polymer or CaCO3–silicate shells that slow primary nucleation while permitting oriented aggregation, thereby delaying Ostwald ripening and promoting uniform size distributions prior to crystallization. <cite id="fabcbf39-1">Additives can finely adjust vaterite morphology by guiding mesoscale transformation of amorphous calcium carbonate into crystalline polymorphs</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-6">Polymer additives (e.g., PEG) modulate CaCO3 precipitation pathways and microstructure during polymer-induced mineralization</cite>.

Effects on polymorph selection (vaterite, aragonite, calcite)

• Stabilizing metastable phases via interfacial energy tuning and kinetic trapping. Alcohols and glycols stabilize vaterite by lowering surface energy barriers and modulating CO3^2–/HCO3– speciation near the growing face. Isopropanol selectively stabilizes vaterite and can route its transformation into aragonite or calcite under controlled conditions, evidencing additive-programmable phase evolution. <cite id="88f50fd5-1">Isopropanol mediates rapid and selective vaterite synthesis and governs subsequent transformations to aragonite or calcite</cite>. Ethanol–water co-solvent systems similarly maintain a hydrophilic interphase that favors vaterite formation and retards calcite overstep, improving vaterite stability compared to pure water. <cite id="88f50fd5-8">The “alcohol–calcium” method yields more stable vaterite than an ethanol–water binary solvent method due to thermodynamic and kinetic stabilization of the metastable phase</cite>.

• Face-specific adsorption and face-selective growth inhibition. Surfactant tails adsorb to calcite {001} or aragonite {110} to suppress specific growth rates, promoting alternative polymorphs; polymer brushes (PVA/PEG) produce comparable face-selective steric barriers that raise polymorph selectivity. The net outcome depends on additive–face affinity and the energy penalty for maintaining a metastable lattice versus the activation barrier for phase change. <cite id="88f50fd5-2">PVA enhances vaterite nucleation selectivity by pre-adsorbing to fiber surfaces, consistent with face-specific interfacial energy modification</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-5">CTAB–PVA/PEG/PVAc templates reconfigure growth anisotropy in PCC via surfactant–polymer adsorption to active planes</cite>. In general, solution chemistry interacts with additive interfacial energy to permit vaterite formation at early times when nucleation barriers are lowered, with later Ostwald ripening tending to favor calcite or aragonite unless stabilized. <cite id="88f50fd5-4">Relative contributions of polymorphs at the nucleation stage indicate calcite is thermodynamically favored at the crystal surface at early times, illustrating the role of surface energies in polymorph competition</cite>.

• Direct templating of polymorph-dependent morphologies. Additives can impose curvature, alignment, and branching morphologies via micelle/polymer scaffolds or layered adsorption. Reviews document that functionalized organic molecules template nucleation and growth directionality, producing plate-like, rod-like, or spherical morphologies in concert with polymorph shifts. <cite id="a140e39e-1">Organic additives with complex functionalization template CaCO3 nucleation and growth alignment, shaping final morphology</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-5">Calcite tends to rhombs, aragonite to acicular, and vaterite to spheres/agglomerated forms when precipitated unconfined</cite>.

Impact on morphology (size, shape, habit)

• Size and habit control by growth inhibition and Ostwald-ripening asymmetry. Surfactant–polymer templates reduce step mobility on {001} and {110} faces, yielding smaller particles with controlled facets (rhombs for calcite, rods/plates for aragonite), and suppress twinning via zeta-potential-like stabilization (indirectly inferred by consistent face-selective adsorption). <cite id="fabcbf39-5">CTAB, PVA, PEG, and PVAc produce marked morphology modification in freshly precipitated CaCO3, evidencing additive-controlled habit</cite>. Mesoscale intermediates formed with additives (core–shell amorphous/vaterite) can be transformed to yield uniform crystallites with reduced secondary nucleation during growth. <cite id="fabcbf39-1">Additive-assisted intermediates allow finely adjusted vaterite microparticle morphology during transformation</cite>.

• Alcohol-driven microenvironments produce smooth or porous spherical vaterite. Ethanol/glycerol create microhydrophobic pockets and lowered interfacial tension that promote rapid spherical nucleation and compact or porous shells; tuning alcohol/water and surfactant ratios switches between smooth spheres and branched/defected morphologies. <cite id="88f50fd5-0">Alcohol–surfactant co-precipitation provides controlled vaterite with altered shape and surface texture</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-3">Ethanol, ethylene glycol, and glycerol act as alcohol regulators to control nano-CaCO3 polymorphism and habit</cite>.

Colloidal stability, aggregation, and Ostwald ripening

• Stability via face-selective adsorption and charge/dispersion control. Amphiphilic molecules adsorb to crystal faces to reduce surface energy and electrostatic recombination probability; zeta potential is indirectly reflected in face-specific growth suppression and decreased aggregation of PCC particles in surfactant/polymer-modified systems. <cite id="fabcbf39-5">Surfactant–polymer templates significantly influence PCC crystal morphology, consistent with face-selective adsorption that stabilizes colloids against restacking</cite>. Bio-inspired additive strategies exploit phase dependence of bioactivity and tailor Ostwald ripening pathways; Ostwald kinetics differ across calcite/aragonite/vaterite, allowing additive-induced pathway branching that enhances stability of the desired phase. <cite id="fabcbf39-7">Calcium carbonate bioactivity and Ostwald ripening are phase-dependent; tailoring pathways allows stability and bioactivity control of calcareous biomaterials</cite>.

• Polymer shells and silane/POSS linkers raise interparticle barrier and slow ripening. PAA or PEG shells reduce direct contact, while POSS–silyl linkers tether particles to silica surfaces; both slow diffusion-mediated mass transfer needed for ripening and suppress secondary nucleation, preserving narrow size distributions and metastable vaterite over longer induction times. <cite id="fabcbf39-1">Additives guide mesoscale transformations that produce morphology-stable vaterite microparticles</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-6">Polymer addition (e.g., PEG) during CaCO3 precipitation alters particle pathways and stabilizes microstructures</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-8">Additives can prevent transformation from vaterite to calcite by affecting growth rates and stabilization</cite>.

• Liquid–liquid partitioning and solubility tuning alter ripening rates. Alcohol/water co-solvents change the solubility product apparent kinetics by partitioning CO3^2–/Ca2+ and facilitating interdiffusion at curved or additive-modified interfaces, making vaterite smaller spheres slower to transform and less prone to aggregation; careful HCO3–/CO3^2– control can lock in plate-like calcite or acicular aragonite by aligning additive adsorption to those morphologies. <cite id="88f50fd5-3">Alcohols such as ethanol and glycols regulate polymorph selection by controlling nucleation/growth equilibria</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-0">Organic solvents are used to control CaCO3 precipitation rate and final composition</cite>.

Representative additive classes and routes

1) Alcohols and glycols (ethanol, isopropanol, ethylene glycol, glycerol)
- Mechanism: Lower surface tension; hydrophobic microdomains; solvent-mediated chain transfer and CO3^2– sequestration.
- Outcomes: Faster vaterite nucleation; smooth or porous spherical particles; stabilized vaterite against calcite; tunable anisotropy when combined with surfactants. <cite id="88f50fd5-1">Isopropanol selectively stabilizes vaterite with controllable conversion to aragonite/calcite</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-8">An alcohol–Ca2+ route improves vaterite stability versus ethanol–water alone</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-0">Alcohol–surfactant co-precipitation yields controlled vaterite morphology</cite>.

2) Surfactants (ionic/secondary, e.g., CTAB/SDS) and polymer templates (PVA, PEG, PVAc, PAA)
- Mechanism: Face-selective adsorption reduces {001}/{110} step mobility; steric hindrance reduces collision–coagulation.
- Outcomes: Smaller, faceted calcite rhombs; rod-like/aragonite-like prisms; higher polymorph selectivity; reduced aggregation. <cite id="fabcbf39-5">CTAB, PVA, PEG, PVAc significantly modify PCC morphology</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-2">PVA enhances vaterite nucleation selectivity via interfacial adsorption</cite>.

3) Silane/POSS or bio-inspired coupling agents and polymer–silica hybrids
- Mechanism: Covalent tethering to mineral surfaces; creation of rigid shells with functional moieties that discourage layer exchange or Ostwald ripening.
- Outcomes: Prevention of vaterite-to-calcite conversion; more uniform, well-dispersed particles; porosity-preserving crystallization. <cite id="a140e39e-8">Additives prevent vaterite-to-calcite transformation by affecting growth and stabilization</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-1">Additive-guided intermediates allow stable vaterite microparticles</cite>.

Practical guidance and trade-offs

- To favor vaterite or aragonite and obtain spherical/porous particles, introduce alcohols (ethanol/glycerol) or isopropanol, optionally with mild surfactant, to enhance early nucleation and stabilize the metastable phase; maintain mild supersaturation to avoid secondary nucleation and overgrowth. <cite id="88f50fd5-1">Isopropanol selectively stabilizes vaterite with controlled transformation</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-0">Alcohol–surfactant co-precipitation yields controlled morphology</cite>.
- To obtain calcite rhombs or aragonite acicular rods and narrow size distributions, use surfactant–polymer templates to inhibit dominant faces and promote anisotropic growth; choose PVA/CTAB for calcite, surfactant systems adjusted for aragonite {110} growth, and control ionic strength to reduce aggregation. <cite id="fabcbf39-5">CTAB/PVA/PEG/PVAc templates strongly influence PCC habit</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-2">PVA-enhanced nucleation selectivity supports vaterite-to-calcite guidance</cite>.
- For colloidal stability and slow Ostwald ripening, add soluble polymers or introduce POSS/silane linkers to form a steric or covalent shell; tune alcohol fraction to reduce interparticle diffusion and promote dispersion. <cite id="fabcbf39-1">Additives guide transformations into morphology-stable vaterite particles</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-6">PEG-assisted polymer-induced precipitation controls particle formation pathways</cite> <cite id="a140e39e-8">Additives can prevent vaterite-to-calcite conversion and stabilize particles</cite>.

Notes on carbonate chemistry and conditions

Additives operate in concert with solution chemistry; maintaining CO3^2– vs HCO3–, pH, and Ca2+ activity underpins interfacial energy differences seen in polymorph selection. While calcite is often thermodynamically favored at surfaces, kinetic barriers imposed by additive adsorption and Ostwald-ripening asymmetry allow transient stabilization of vaterite or aragonite and can redirect growth once supersaturation fields relax. <cite id="88f50fd5-4">Surface energetics show calcite as most stable at early nucleation, highlighting interfacial energy control</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-7">A grain-boundary kinetics model explains how additives and templates guide precipitation pathways through interfacial processes</cite>.

Key takeaways

Organic solvent additives act at the solid–solution interface to decouple nucleation and growth, bias polymorph-dependent surface barriers, and construct colloidal stabilizers that control size, shape, and stability. Through alcohols/glycols to tune wetting and microenvironments, surfactants/polymers to impose face-selective adsorption and growth anisotropy, and polymer/silane shells to slow ripening, the precipitation outcome is programmable: metastable vaterite spheres in alcohol-rich, low-ionic-strength systems; oriented calcite/aragonite prisms under surfactant–polymer templates; and dispersion-stable colloids via polymer or POSS-mediated shells. <cite id="a140e39e-0">Organic solvents influence precipitation rate, polymorph content, morphology, and stabilization</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-1">Alcohols such as isopropanol selectively stabilize vaterite and control conversions</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-5">Surfactant–polymer templates strongly modify PCC morphology</cite> <cite id="88f50fd5-8">Alcohol–calcium methods stabilize vaterite better than ethanol–water alone</cite> <cite id="fabcbf39-7">Phase-specific Ostwald ripening pathways can be tailored to stabilize desired polymorphs</cite>.

Overview
Low-load carbon nanotube (CNT) reinforcements (commonly sub‑1% to ~2–3 wt% in polymer matrices) can modestly but measurably enhance several mechanical properties when dispersion and interfacial bonding are well controlled, including tensile strength and stiffness, impact resistance and crack energy dissipation, fatigue endurance and creep resistance, interlaminar shear and fracture toughness, and surface hardness/nanohardness.<cite id="c8988221-0">CNT polymer composites have been reported to show enhanced mechanical strength and related property synergies that motivate interest in mechanical reinforcement.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-9">CNTs’ high elastic modulus and tensile strength can transfer to composites via effective load sharing at favorable wt% levels.</cite>

Properties commonly improved by low CNT additions
- Tensile strength and modulus (in-plane):
  • Many polymer systems show increases in tensile strength and Young’s modulus as CNTs form percolating, load-bearing networks at low mass fractions; improvements are attributed to better stress transfer and CNT–polymer interfacial load sharing.<cite id="911e03dc-1">Studies report significant tensile strength gains linked to effective CNT load transfer in polymer matrices.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-2">CNTs’ high Young’s modulus and low density make them attractive nanofillers that can stiffen polymer composites at low loading.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-8">In carbon fiber/epoxy/epoxy hybrids, nanoparticle-type fillers at practical loadings can slightly raise quasi‑static and fatigue strengths, with nanotubes among effective reinforcements.</cite>  
  • Example quantitative changes are matrix- and processing‑specific; for instance, in a TPU matrix, tensile strength and Young’s modulus increased when CNTs were introduced, with reported neat baseline and increased values, illustrating the additive effect on stiffness and strength when dispersion is optimized.<cite id="c8988221-6">For a polyurethane matrix, neat values of tensile strength 52 MPa and modulus 412 MPa were reported, later increased after CNT incorporation, evidencing stiffness/strength improvements at composite state.</cite>
- Impact resistance and energy absorption:
  • Low CNT addition can raise impact strength and reduce damage size (dent depth) by percolating nanonets that absorb energy and blunt cracks; nanoparticle additions have been shown to increase maximum impact force, reduce damage area, and mitigate dent depth.<cite id="f362a6f8-5">Adding nanoparticles into the matrix raised maximum impact force and reduced damage area and dent depth, showing improved impact response.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-5">Post‑impact tensile fatigue behavior improved when nanoparticles such as CNTs were incorporated, indicating better damage tolerance under impact.</cite>
- Fatigue resistance and creep:
  • At low content and good dispersion, CNTs can improve fatigue strength and endurance limit and help suppress matrix cracking and interfacial slip; creep resistance may also improve due to delayed relaxation along the CNT backbone and stress transfer to resist deformation over time.<cite id="f362a6f8-5">CNT additions improved post‑impact tensile fatigue performance and alleviated dent depth, tying impact and fatigue improvements together.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-6">CNT reinforcement has been reported to improve polymer toughness, stiffness, and creep resistance.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-6">CNT networks and interfacial bonding can raise fatigue performance in polymer composites.</cite>
- Interlaminar shear strength (ILSS) and interlaminar fracture toughness:
  • CNTs bridging across interfaces and delamination cracks can raise ILSS and mode I delamination toughness; improvements are often measured via mechanical tests and fracture mechanics, with studies showing that MWCNTs improve CFRP fracture toughness via toughening mechanisms in the polymer/void/interphase system.<cite id="0b1a3767-9">ASTM D6415 measures interlaminar tensile strength via a 90° four‑point loading configuration; such ILSS improvements with CNTs are a primary candidate for quantification.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-6">Mode I interlaminar fracture toughness can be calculated per ASTM D5525 using compliance‑based methods (e.g., DCB/SENB geometries), a common route to quantify CNT‑induced toughening.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-7">The addition of multi‑walled CNTs can enhance interlaminar fracture toughness of CFRP laminates.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-0">ASTM/ISO standards for Mode I, II, and mixed‑mode interlaminar fracture toughness rely on LEFM assumptions; compliance‑extrapolation methods (SENB/DCB) are standard to quantify improvements.</cite>
- Surface hardness and nanohardness:
  • CNT percolation at low loading can raise macroscopic hardness/scratch resistance and nanoscale hardness and elastic modulus, probed by nanoindentation; the strong C–C sp2 network underpins this nanohardness benefit.<cite id="c8988221-9">CNT nanofillers elevate scratch/contact hardness and wear resistance in composites owing to their robust sp2 carbon structure.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-8">CNT/epoxy additions of 0.1–0.5 wt% have been evaluated for nanoscale hardness and stiffness via nanoindentation in related nanocomposites literature.</cite>
- Tribological benefits (wear and coefficient of friction):
  • While not strictly “mechanical strength,” low CNT additions reduce wear rate and COF by forming lubricating graphitic structures and wear maps shift in favorable directions in polymer composites, which is commonly measured with standardized tribometer protocols; these correlate with surface integrity and nanohardness changes.<cite id="c8988221-5">CNTs exhibit wear resistance orders of magnitude better than steel and low COF ~0.06–0.1; composites with CNTs show tribological improvements measurable by standard wear tests.</cite>

How improvements are typically measured
- Tensile and flexural properties:
  • Monotonic properties are quantified by standardized tensile and flexural testing on dogbone or I‑shape specimens and reported as engineering stress–strain. ASTM D3039 governs composite tensile testing on standard specimens; for polymers, ASTM D638 (dogbone) and D6272 (textile-reinforced matrices) are used; flexural properties follow ASTM D790/D6486, with strain‑control and crosshead rates selected in the test method.<cite id="0b1a3767-5">ASTM D3039 defines specimen geometry, loading, and data reduction for tensile properties of polymer matrix composites.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-8">ASTM D638 (D6272 for textiles) specifies tensile testing of plastics/composites, including strain‑controlled rates and stress–strain reporting.</cite>  
  • Load transfer and interfacial quality are often inferred from modulus/strength gains and compared to neat and control‑matrix references at identical wt% and processing to isolate CNT effects.<cite id="911e03dc-1">Observed tensile strength increases are attributed to improved CNT–polymer load sharing, evaluated via mechanical testing at matched compositions and conditions.</cite>
- Impact resistance and energy:
  • Unnotched Izod/Charpy impact strengths are measured per ASTM D256 (impact hammer with notched specimens; energy absorbed plotted vs. loading rate); non‑destructive fall‑weight impact and high‑speed video quantify dent depth and damage area; these setups directly probe whether CNTs raise absorbed energy and reduce damage at a given contact force.<cite id="0b1a3767-3">High‑speed mechanical testing quantifies crack growth resistance and related damage under impact loading, with standard force/displacement protocols.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-5">CNT‑modified composites showed increased maximum impact force and reduced dent depth/damage area, quantified under controlled impact protocols.</cite>
- Fatigue and creep:
  • Fatigue is evaluated by cyclic loading at fixed stress/strain amplitudes, reporting S‑N curves, fatigue strength at a given cycles, and residual strength after impact; ASTM D6419/industry protocols specify fully reversed fatigue testing for polymer composites and related nanocomposites. Post‑impact tensile retention and low‑cycle fatigue recovery are compared to quantify damage tolerance gains.<cite id="f362a6f8-5">Improved post‑impact tensile fatigue performance and reduced dent depth were quantified, demonstrating better fatigue/damage tolerance with nanotube addition.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-6">Creep and fatigue benefits have been reported alongside stiffness/toughness increases when CNTs are uniformly dispersed.</cite>
- Interlaminar shear and fracture toughness:
  • ILSS follows ASTM D6415 (open‑face/internal or 90° four‑point configuration) using coupons with controlled fiber angle and CNT distribution; mode I interlaminar fracture toughness (GIC, KIC) uses DCB or ENF/SENB geometries per ASTM D6641/ISO VDMA and D6411/ASTM D6418 data reduction (load–deflection curves, compliance‑extrapolation, R‑curve analysis).<cite id="0b1a3767-9">ASTM D6415 defines interlaminar tensile strength via 90° four‑point loading; ILSS gains from CNTs are quantifiable using this method.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-6">ASTM D5525 and related procedures compute Mode I interlaminar fracture toughness from SENB/DCB compliance; these methods quantify CNT‑enhanced delamination resistance.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-0">Standardized ASTM/ISO frameworks assume LEFM to extract G or K from load–displacement, enabling consistent comparison of CNT effects across laminates.</cite>  
  • Hybrid or multi‑scale reinforcement studies combine CNTs with fibers and quantify how ILSS and delamination resistance change versus neat and fiber‑only controls at identical low CNT loadings to isolate the nanotube effect.<cite id="911e03dc-4">Multi‑scale CNT/fiber systems show improvements in ILSS/toughness quantified per ASTM methods.</cite>
- Nanoindentation and wear/contact mechanics:
  • To detect hardness and modulus increases at low wt% (e.g., 0.1–0.5%), nanoindentation (e.g., nanoindenter with continuous stiffness measurement, CSM) measures reduced indent depth and higher elastic modulus; wear is quantified with pin‑on‑disk or ball‑on‑plate tribometers, tracking mass loss and COF.<cite id="0b1a3767-8">Nanoindentation protocols quantify modulus/stiffness and hardness increases in nanofilled epoxies at sub‑wt% levels, complementing macroscopic tests.</cite><cite id="c8988221-5">Tribological improvements in CNT‑modified composites are reflected in reduced wear rate and lower COF under standardized sliding protocols.</cite>
- Microstructural and failure analysis:
  • SEM/TEM of fracture surfaces and R‑curve behavior complement energy‑based tests, revealing crack path deflection and CNT bridging—mechanistic underpinnings of toughness gains; processing variables like CNT waviness can reduce modulus if not aligned, underscoring the need for dispersion control and sometimes alignment to realize benefits.<cite id="911e03dc-3">CNT waviness reduces elastic modulus and increases strain but does not preclude strength gains if interfacial bonding is strong and alignment/dispersion are optimized.</cite>

Practical notes on low addition and trade-offs
- Effective low-load improvements require dispersion/functionalization: poorly dispersed CNTs provide negligible or negative effects on strength/modulus and can even reduce fatigue life through stress concentrators; covalent functionalization and surfactant/sonication are often used to achieve percolation at sub‑1 wt% without agglomeration.<cite id="c8988221-9">CNT–polymer interfacial and structural performance is highly sensitive to dispersion and functionalization state.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-4">CNTs hybridized with conventional carbon fibers can raise tensile and bending strength while improving damping, provided the matrix/interphase supports load transfer.</cite>
- Load sharing, alignment and modulus: if CNTs are well distributed but not highly aligned, modulus increases are more reliable than strength gains; some models predict waviness reduces axial modulus but raises ductility/strain; optimizing dispersion and mechanical alignment can lift both stiffness and strength at identical loadings.<cite id="911e03dc-3">CNT waviness lowers composite elastic modulus and raises ultimate strain, emphasizing alignment/dispersion control to realize stiffness/strength gains.</cite>
- Hybrid reinforcement: combining low CNT additions with continuous fibers often yields complementary improvements: fibers carry in‑plane loads with high specific strength, while CNTs bolster ILSS/fracture toughness, energy absorption, and fatigue crack blunting; quantification contrasts hybrid vs. fiber‑only and neat laminates under the same ASTM protocols.<cite id="f362a6f8-1">Hybrid reinforcement with MWCNTs can increase tensile properties versus neat controls.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-6">CNT additions improve toughness, stiffness, and creep resistance in polymer composites used with high‑modulus fibers.</cite>

Summary
- Improved properties with low CNT addition: tensile strength and stiffness (best with good dispersion/alignment), impact strength and energy absorption, fatigue/damage tolerance and creep resistance, interlaminar shear and delamination fracture toughness, and surface hardness/nanohardness; tribological improvements (lower wear, COF) are also common and measurable.<cite id="911e03dc-1">Significant tensile strength improvements arise when load transfer to CNTs is effective at low loadings.</cite><cite id="f362a6f8-5">CNT‑modified composites exhibit higher impact force and improved post‑impact fatigue response.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-9">ASTM D6415 and related standards quantify ILSS and interlaminar toughness gains due to CNT bridging.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-6">Mode I interlaminar fracture toughness gains are quantified via DCB/SENB methods with ASTM procedures.</cite>
- Typical measurement: tensile/flexural per ASTM D3039 (or D638/6272 for polymers), impact per ASTM D256 (Izod/Charpy) with dent depth/energy metrics, fatigue per ASTM D6419 with S‑N behavior and post‑impact recovery, ILSS per ASTM D6415 and fracture toughness per ASTM D6641/D5525 (DCB/SENB), creep under sustained load, and nanoindentation plus tribometry for hardness/wear; SEM of fracture surfaces correlates mechanisms with measured gains.<cite id="0b1a3767-5">ASTM D3039 defines tensile testing for polymer matrix composites.</cite><cite id="911e03dc-8">ASTM D638/6272 specify tensile behavior for polymers and textiles, enabling controlled comparisons at low CNT loadings.</cite><cite id="0b1a3767-6">ASTM D5525 procedures are used to calculate Mode I delamination toughness.</cite>  
- Realization hinges on achieving a percolating, well‑dispersed CNT network via functionalization/processing; alignment can further unlock modulus and strength at identical wt% compared to disorganized networks.<cite id="911e03dc-3">Dispersion/alignment tradeoffs (modulus vs. ductility) and interfacial bonding govern whether low additions translate to net mechanical gains.</cite>

Summary
Industrial production of spherical calcium‑salt crystals relies on controlling nucleation–growth kinetics and pathways to steer polymorph selection and anisotropy toward isotropic, spherulitic, or encapsulated morphologies. Across calcium salts, consistent levers include supersaturation management, temperature programming, seeding and controlled additive/impurity environments, and often anti‑solvent or constrained/guided growth; organic molecules and interfacial engineering reduce anisotropy and promote rounded shapes. Below, we distill the key methodologies and operational parameters that have demonstrated success for spherical/rounded morphology, with emphasis on CaCO3 (the most studied system), plus insights from CaSO4 (gypsum) and calcium phosphates where morphology depends on the same thermodynamic–kinetic controls.

Key Methodologies

1) Thermodynamic pathway and supersaturation management
- Select supersaturation mode and magnitude. Calcium salt crystallization exhibits multiple metastable and stable polymorphs; morphology is set by the supersaturation pathway and rate (SSGR), which dictates the balance of primary nucleation, secondary nucleation, and growth. Temperature programming across the metastability gap (e.g., fast formation of vaterite/calcite intermediates) reduces anisotropic edge growth and promotes spherulitic nuclei coalescing into near‑spherical aggregates in CaCO3 systems. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Temperature and supersaturation determine the phase and particle morphology in CaCO3 precipitation diagrams used for process design</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">Operating parameters including temperature, pH, and supersaturation govern polymorphism, microstructure, and growth kinetics</cite>. 
- For CaSO4·2H2O (gypsum), the supersaturation pathway directly controls the nucleation–growth trade‑off and the formation of acicular or more equant platelets, evidencing that “spherical” morphology is a mobility/impurity‑limited outcome of isotropic growth fronts rather than strictly a thermodynamic phase. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum crystallization is highly sensitive to the supersaturation pathway, with different nucleation–growth balances producing distinct morphologies</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Precipitation design diagrams for CaCO3 show temperature/supersaturation windows mapping to morphologies, a concept that generalizes to pathway‑dependent salts</cite>.

Practical parameters: 
- Maintain low SSGR during early supersaturation bursts (chemical dosing or antisolvent addition) to favor nuclei merging into larger isotropic embryos, then raise SSGR in a second stage to promote isotropic face growth; stage timing and dose rate are critical. <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Supersaturation formation rate can be controlled by additive protocols to select polymorphism</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite grows as monocrystalline cubical particles at 30 °C from metastable vaterite; temperature and supersaturation ratio govern growth mode</cite>.
- Use early supersaturation at subzero or near‑ambient temperatures to form vaterite/calcite spherulitic nuclei, then warm to enable isotropic calcite conversion and growth; a canonical case shows spherulites when 0.2 M Na2CO3 is injected into CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with moderate stirring. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite crystals formed by instantaneous 0.2 M Na2CO3 addition into 0.2 M CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with 300 rpm stirring</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Besides supersaturation, temperature significantly affects the growth mode toward spherulitic vs. anisotropic forms</cite>.

2) Polymorph engineering (vaterite → calcite; calcite orientation)
- Spherical morphology often arises from vaterite or magnesium‑calcite intermediates that have lower anisotropy, followed by conversion to calcite. Process conditions are tuned so that vaterite is kinetically trapped and later transforms to calcite with isotropic spherulitic structures. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite forms under metastable, low‑temperature, high‑supersaturation conditions</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Calcite is thermodynamically stable while vaterite is metastable/less stable, consistent with morphology shifts upon transformation</cite>.
- Mg2+ impurities and Sr2+ can stabilize spherical nanoparticles and alter growth symmetry; such foreign ions and chelation chemistry can be exploited as morphology‑directing agents in solution. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ substitution stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3 systems in molecular dynamics, indicating ion‑induced morphological isotropy</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ addition alters polymorph selection and morphology, shifting supersaturation formation and phase outcomes</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Control Ca2+/CO32−/HCO3− redox and complexation; maintain CO2 partial pressure to suppress aragonite and steer toward vaterite/calcite with slower anisotropic growth faces exposed last. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">CaCO3 precipitation diagrams tie pH/temperature/supersaturation to polymorph outcomes (calcite vs aragonite vs vaterite)</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">pH and temperature windows can be selected to preferentially produce a polymorph that exhibits rounded morphology</cite>.
- Phase transformation engineering: use temperature “sweeps” across the aragonite–calcite gap, or aging, to convert elongated polymorphs into more isotropic structures prior to final growth. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite growth from vaterite and its temperature dependence underpin strategies that combine early metastable nucleation with later growth</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Thermodynamics of polymorph stability (calcite most stable, vaterite least) guide aging and temperature programming</cite>.

3) Anti‑solvent addition and continuous crystallization
- Anti‑solvent programming (e.g., ethanol) is a powerful industrial lever to instantaneously raise supersaturation, trigger nucleation on existing nuclei, and then control growth via residence time and cooling. In CaCO3, lecithin‑containing media under gas diffusion enable spherulitic vaterite; analogous strategies in continuous loop reactors with staged antisolvent injection yield narrow size distributions and increased isotropy by keeping shear and growth face exposure uniform. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media modulate CaCO3 crystallization pathways; differing lecithins shift growth to spherulitic vaterite morphologies</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic CaCO3 formation under rapid supersaturation and low temperature with controlled stirring</cite>.
- Continuous antisolvent crystallizers allow precise dosing and mixing profiles; process variables such as solvent ratio, feed rate, and temperature profile set the SSGR and polymorph selection, yielding near‑spherical particles when anisotropy is suppressed. <cite id="6dfcb41c-7">Continuous antisolvent addition processes and systems control crystallization by dosing organic antisolvent and managing residence and interphase exchange</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-9">Rapid process design methods in agrochemical crystallization emphasize antisolvent and mixing profile design to obtain target morphologies</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Start with a supersaturation “bang,” then dilute and cool to slow anisotropic face growth; shape becomes more spherical as growth rate becomes diffusion‑limited and shear causes uniform rounding. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Design diagrams map temperature/supersaturation to morphology; higher supersaturation at low T favors early nuclei formation and later isotropic growth</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Low‑T rapid addition yields spherulitic nuclei; controlled stirring conditions demonstrate reproducibility</cite>.
- Use a two‑stage antisolvent feed (burst then taper) with downstream temperature rise to promote coagulation/merging of spherulitic embryos before slower isotropic facets predominate. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Temperature and supersaturation ratio affect growth mode; combining temperature steps with supersaturation steps switches between spherulitic and anisotropic growth</cite>.

4) Seeding and distribution control
- Seeded crystallization narrows size distribution and stabilizes a target polymorph; industrial protocols use in‑line recycle to maintain uniform seed concentrations. Seeding can either suppress or promote certain faces, thus reducing spindly growth and favoring rounded spherulites in CaCO3. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design must consider process parameters (e.g., polymorph, kinetics, mixing, residence time) to control morphology and monodispersity</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-3">Seeding within controlled pH and temperature regimes tunes polymorphism and morphology</cite>.
- Recycle‑type crystallizers allow operating windows where secondary nucleation is minimized while growth remains isotropic; CFD and population balance coupling identify safe shear/residence‑time zones. <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Simultaneous bulk/surface analysis in CaCO3 crystallization highlights the roles of flow rate, metal ion nature, and supersaturation in microstructure and polymorphism</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-9">Crystallization kinetics relate to surface structure and morphological control in CaCO3</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Seed in the metastable zone edge to select calcite or aragonite depending on temperature/ionic strength, while avoiding secondary nucleation bursts that fragment spherulites. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Metastable zones for CaCO3 are bounded by temperature and supersaturation; seeding in the metastable window selects phase and shape outcomes</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Control of pathway and polymorph via supersaturation in CaSO4 suggests analogous seeding boundaries for morphology control</cite>.

5) Interfacial engineering: organic additives, surfactants, chelators, and templating
- Amphiphilic additives and phospholipids adsorb on {01-2} or {10-4} faces, reducing growth asymmetry and promoting spherulitic growth; for CaCO3, lecithin media robustly favor vaterite spherulites when CO2 dissolution is managed. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media differentially influence CaCO3 crystallization, enabling reproducible spherulitic vaterite morphologies under gas diffusion</cite>.
- Trace metal ions (Mg2+, Sr2+) act as heterogeneously nucleating species or lattice substituents that stabilize spherical nanocrystals and suppress elongated growth, offering low‑cost morphology control at ppm levels. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3 dynamics, showing substituent‑induced morphological isotropy</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ ions can reorganize polymorphism and morphology through supersaturation kinetics</cite>.
- Biomineralization‑inspired templating (e.g., biomimetic silica or organic matrices) can direct CaCO3 to aragonite/vaterite with rounded morphologies; these concepts translate to industrial seed designs and antisolvent‑assisted precipitation. <cite id="4441a4bd-0">Apatite morphologies on silica surfaces vary with solution conditions and interfacial interactions</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic template design controls hydroxyapatite crystal and aggregate morphology, illustrating interfacial programming</cite>.

Practical parameters:
- Use nonionic surfactants (e.g., SDS/CTAB/zwitterionic) at sub‑CMC to coat prismatic faces and slow {01-2} growth; optimize adsorption kinetics vs. desorption under flow. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Organic media (lecithin) control CaCO3 polymorph selection and morphology; surfactant chemistry modulates interfacial kinetics</cite>.
- Maintain Mg2+/Sr2+ within controlled ranges to “glue” isotropic nanocrystals into spheres or to stabilize the spherulitic precursor; avoid excessive Fe/Ca that create different polymorphs and needle morphologies. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ promotes spherical nanoparticles</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ affects nucleation/growth pathways</cite>.

6) Reactor hydrodynamics, residence time, and CFD‑guided design
- Spherical crystals require isotropic exposure of crystal faces and uniform growth probability; CFD plus population balance models identify zones with shear low enough to avoid edge‑face fragmentation but sufficient to promote uniform diffusion and coalescence. Loop‑reactor antisolvent designs are tuned for short induction times, rapid growth, and recycle that smooths size distribution and shape. <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow rate and supersaturation influence polymorphism and microstructure; surface structure governs morphology</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-9">Process design frameworks tailor mixing, temperature, and antisolvent profiles to achieve morphology targets</cite>.
- In CaCO3 spherulitic growth, moderate stirring promotes spherulite formation, whereas vigorous shear can shatter spherulites into irregular polygons; industrial practice thus targets a Dn/Df window where growth outpaces fragmentation. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulites formed at 5 °C with 300 rpm stirring in CaCl2–Na2CO3 mixing</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding parameter design must account for mixing regimes that minimize irregular secondary nucleation while sustaining growth</cite>.

7) Field‑assisted or “constrained growth” strategies
- Electric fields and ultrasound can alter interfacial energy and growth selectivity to suppress prismatic growth; for CaCO3, constrained environments (e.g., lecithin microcompartments) produce spherical nanocrystals that assemble into larger rounded aggregates. While many proofs are bench‑scale, the mechanisms (isotropic nucleation, constrained growth, and uniform antisolvent exchange) translate to industrial atomization/filming‑and‑growth or field‑assisted crystallizers. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">CaCO3 crystallization in tailored constrained environments (lecithin) yields vaterite spherulites with controlled growth</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic templating controls crystal/aggregate morphology for Ca phosphates, showing that constrained growth and templating can program shape</cite>.

Cross‑Salt Lessons (beyond CaCO3)

- Gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O). Morphology is governed by the same kinetics: supersaturation pathway and mineral chemistry. Industrial seeding in a loop reactor, temperature windows, and gypsum aging promote equant platelet growth; careful control reduces acicular morphologies. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">The supersaturation pathway in gypsum controls nucleation–growth balance, leading to different morphologies; tuning this pathway enables more equant forms</cite>.
- Calcium phosphates (hydroxyapatite, dicalcium phosphate). Morphology varies with Ca/P ratio, solution pH, supersaturation, and seed structure; nanocrystalline, rod‑like, or flake/hexagonal morphologies arise under different conditions. Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis and seeding design are key to obtain uniform or spherical/rounded aggregates. <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis yields hydroxyapatite and nanocrystalline calcium‑deficient apatite; pH and S control morphology</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-0">Apatite morphology depends on solution interfaces and conditions</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Calcium orthophosphate crystallization and dissolution show that phase selection and morphology depend on ionic conditions and ratios</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding design with crystalline structure of seed minerals enables targeted morphology</cite>.

Industrial Parameter Set for Spherical Calcium Salt Crystals

Core control variables (same across salts)
- Supersaturation: generate rapidly then regulate. Use staged antisolvent dosing or CO2 gas‑diffusion to spike S, then dilute/cool to slow anisotropic face growth; target SSGR windows that favor spherulitic nuclei merging and isotropic growth. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Rapid Na2CO3 addition at 5 °C produces spherulitic CaCO3; stirring and temperature set reproducibility</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Antisolvent addition systems and protocols control SSGR for polymorph selection</cite>.
- Temperature program: “cold‑seed‑warm‑grow.” Form nuclei at low T (vaterite/calcite spherulites), then warm to encourage isotropic conversion and growth; avoid high T that yields cubical/anisotropic calcite. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite grows cubically at 30 °C; lower T favors spherulitic formation</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Temperature itself, beyond S ratio, affects growth mode to spherulitic/aggregative forms</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-8">Thermodynamics (calcite stable, vaterite metastable) underpin cold nucleation/warm growth strategies</cite>.
- Polymorph: deliberately select and convert. Use Mg/Sr ions or surface additives to stabilize spherical vaterite or magnesium‑calcite; then convert to calcite via aging/anneal to close porosity and round aggregates. <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles in CaCO3</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Sr2+ and lecithin modulate polymorph selection and morphology</cite>.
- Seeding/reactor design: maintain uniform seed in recycle‑type crystallizers; avoid secondary nucleation hot spots; use population‑balance‑guided residence times. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design considers polymorph, kinetics, mixing, and residence time</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow rate and supersaturation alter microstructure and polymorphism; process parameters are tuned to control</cite>.
- Interfacial chemistry: include nonionic surfactants, phospholipids, or controlled levels of Mg2+/Sr2+ to suppress {01-2} face growth and promote isotropic spherulite growth; control impurities (Fe/CO3 depletion) to prevent elongated morphologies. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media produce spherulitic vaterite CaCO3; interfacial composition controls morphology</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ substitution promotes spherical nanoparticles</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics and residence time: CFD‑coupled PBM to locate antisolvent dosing zones away from shear hot spots; maintain moderate turbulence for diffusion and uniform growth without shattering spherulites. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">300 rpm stirring conditions are compatible with spherulitic CaCO3 growth</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing regimes in seeding must be designed against morphology risks</cite>.
- Pathway engineering: in CaSO4 and Ca phosphates, explicit control of supersaturation pathway (chemical vs. antisolvent), pH, and Ca/P redox avoids acicular forms; maintain pH and Ca/P near target to stabilize the desired equant polymorph. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum morphology depends on supersaturation pathway</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Phase selection is tied to solution stoichiometry and supersaturation</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation and pH control apatite nanocrystal formation</cite>.

Concrete operating windows and examples
- Bench‑to‑industrial scaling example (CaCO3): Inject 0.2–0.5 M carbonate into 0.2–0.5 M Ca salt solution at 5–10 °C in a stirred tank or loop reactor; use antisolvent (ethanol) burst then taper to moderate SSGR; maintain 100–500 rpm to promote merging without fragmentation; age at 25–35 °C to convert vaterite/calcite spherulites into dense spheres; lecithin or SDS at sub‑CMC improves sphericity. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Spherulitic calcite formed by instantaneous 0.2 M Na2CO3 addition into 0.2 M CaCl2·2H2O at 5 °C with 300 rpm</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin‑containing media enable spherulitic vaterite with controlled crystallization</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Temperature shifts from 30 °C to lower T favor spherulitic growth</cite>.
- Calcium phosphate fertilizer (dicalcium phosphate dihydrate, Ca(H2PO4)2·H2O): maintain Ca/P near 1.6–1.7 with controlled CO2/acid titration, low SSGR, and seeding of DCPD to obtain equant granules; higher Ca/P shifts to more acidic, amorphous precipitates that autoaggregate into near‑spherical particles. <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Lower Ca/P increases acidity and solubility; controlling stoichiometry selects crystalline forms</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-1">Supersaturation‑controlled synthesis yields nanocrystalline apatite under defined pH/S conditions</cite>.
- Gypsum fertilizer/chemicals: operate in the metastable “wet” belt with slow antisolvent addition, recycle to maintain seed, and temperature profiles that favor equant platelets; impurity control (e.g., Al/Si) reduces elongated forms. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation pathway engineering in gypsum adjusts nucleation–growth balance to achieve morphology targets</cite>.

Monitoring and feedback
- Maintain target S(r) across the reactor via inline conductivity/pH/optical sensors; adjust antisolvent split to hold SSGR steady; use seed holdup probes and PBM to manage residence time distribution. <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Continuous antisolvent addition processes and systems provide feedback/adjustment to control supersaturation</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding strategy design includes monitoring and control of process parameters</cite>.
- Track polymorph and shape online (Raman/polarization microscopy, DLS/SEM inline vision) and adjust temperature and impurity setpoints accordingly. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Precipitation design diagrams tie polymorph/morphology to temperature/supersaturation and guide corrective actions</cite>.

Limits, trade‑offs, and failure modes
- Overdosing antisolvent or high shear produce irregular polygonal fragments from spherulites; avoid nucleation “spikes.” <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Moderate stirring yields spherulites; conditions must be tuned to avoid irregular forms</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing regimes that induce irregular secondary nucleation can degrade morphology</cite>.
- High temperature skews growth toward cubical/anisotropic calcite even when supersaturation is high; cool‑form‑warm‑grow strategies are needed for spherical targets. <cite id="6dfcb41c-1">Calcite growth at 30 °C tends to cubical morphology; spherulites require lower T</cite>.
- Organic additives can clog interfacial exchange or alter zeta potential in complex industrial mixtures; screen grades and dosing to balance interfacial isotropy with filtration/drying performance. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin media strongly modulate CaCO3 crystallization pathways; formulation is critical</cite>.

Practical Starting Protocol (generic calcium salt)
1) Define target polymorph/shape (e.g., vaterite/calcite spherulites for CaCO3; equant gypsum; equant apatite/DCPD for Ca phosphates). 
2) Set stoichiometry window (Ca/P or Ca/SO4) to favor the target polymorph; add acid/CO2 control pH for supersaturation. 
3) Seed loop reactor with recycle; tune antisolvent addition to create a fast S spike then taper, with temperature profile that drops early (5–15 °C) then rises for isotropic growth. 
4) Add a mild surfactant/phospholipid or controlled Mg2+/Sr2+ to suppress anisotropy; maintain moderate turbulence (100–500 rpm) and uniform residence time. 
5) Age/anneal to complete conversion and densify spheres; monitor S(r), polymorph, and size distribution; adjust antisolvent split and recycle ratio via inline analytics. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation pathway control in gypsum underpins such staged programs</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">Rapid low‑T addition and stirring create spherulitic cores</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-7">Antisolvent continuous addition provides feedback loops to hold supersaturation</cite>.

Summary of Key Parameters to Tune
- Supersaturation profile and rate (SSGR), temperature program across metastability, and polymorph selection. <cite id="8a449bcf-0">Temperature/supersaturation design maps directly onto morphology/polymorph selection</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-3">Temperature significantly affects growth mode toward spherulitic/aggregative</cite>.
- Hydrodynamics: moderate stirring (≈100–500 rpm), short induction zones away from high‑shear, uniform residence time. <cite id="6dfcb41c-0">300 rpm yields spherulitic CaCO3; stirring level matters</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Mixing must be engineered to avoid irregular nucleation</cite>.
- Interfacial modifiers: surfactants/phospholipids and trace Mg/Sr as heteroatoms or templates to suppress anisotropy. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin/lecithin media control polymorph and promote spherulitic morphology</cite> <cite id="6dfcb41c-2">Mg2+ stabilizes spherical nanoparticles</cite>.
- Seeding density and CFD/PBM‑guided recycle design to maintain monodisperse, isotropic growth. <cite id="4441a4bd-6">Seeding design spans polymorph, kinetics, and residence time control</cite> <cite id="8a449bcf-4">Flow and supersaturation alter microstructure; recycle design mitigates</cite>.
- Pathway choice (chemical vs. antisolvent; pH and ionic strength) to avoid elongated polymorphs in CaSO4 and Ca phosphates. <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Gypsum morphology varies with supersaturation pathway; choose pathway for equant shape</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-5">Phase/morphology selection depends on stoichiometry and supersaturation</cite>.

Outlook
Field‑assisted and microfluidic strategies (ultrasound/electrics) are emerging to directly impose isotropy; leveraging what works industrially—lecithin/phospholipid templating and antisolvent‑staged dosing—can yield spherical calcium salts at scale. Translating bench‑scale lecithin‑constrained vaterite growth to spray‑drying or atomizing growth modes, with controlled antisolvent quenching, remains a practical route to spherical CaCO3; similar logic applies to apatite and gypsum via seed design and hydrodynamics. <cite id="8a449bcf-6">Lecithin‑constrained CaCO3 growth demonstrates scalable principles transferable to industrial reactors</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-2">Organic template design demonstrates morphology programming that can be adapted to process environments</cite> <cite id="4441a4bd-8">Supersaturation‑pathway control in gypsum enables industrial‑scale shape engineering</cite>.

# Summary

During pellet roasting (shaft furnace or belt/rotary kiln processes), silica in iron ore and coal/ash interacts with iron oxides to form viscous silicate melts and iron silicate phases that accumulate as deposits on pellet surfaces and within inter-particle voids. These reactions and the resulting slag films control sticking, swelling, caking, and permeability, while their microstructural integration alters pellet strength, reducibility, and resistance to degradation during subsequent direct or indirect reduction. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica is a common gangue and, when present, modifies bonding and reducibility by forming glassy phases with Fe2O3 and CaO during firing</cite><cite id="143d4d64-1">Alumina and silica enhance slag bonding and mechanical resistance in iron ore pellets under high-temperature reduction, with specific roles in sticking, swelling, and breakage</cite><cite id="143d4d64-5">Increasing SiO2 content changes sintering indexes and microstructure, indicating that silica modifies intergranular glass formation and porosity in iron-bearing agglomerates</cite><cite id="143d4d64-7">A glassy slag phase consisting of SiO2, CaO, and Fe2O3 forms during pellet firing, and variations in this phase content influence porosity and mechanical behavior</cite><cite id="143d4d64-3">Coal ash minerals (SiO2, Al2O3) mix into pellet powders and promote silicate formation during simulated deposit formation</cite>.

# Chemical and Phase Pathways: Iron Oxides with Silica

Silicon oxides present as free quartz or in silicate form reduce at lower temperatures (typically below ~800–1000 °C) to Si and FeSi, reacting with hematite to form intermediate iron oxides and, at higher temperatures, iron silicates; concurrently, oxygen partial pressure drops during roasting favor Fe3+↔Fe2+ disproportionation and magnetic/iron-rich spinels. <cite id="b0bdbad1-5">Free silica attracts potassium from furnace gases that further promotes iron reduction; as the reduction proceeds, a glass forms that integrates iron and silica species</cite>. As roasting progresses to indirect-reduction conditions, iron oxides evolve via hematite → maghemite/γ‑Fe2O3 → magnetite/Fe3O4 → iron(II) silicate/olivine/fayalite trends depending on oxygen activity and SiO2 availability. <cite id="942e7aa9-0">Thermodynamic parameterization of the FeO–Fe2O3–SiO2 system shows phase equilibria and reaction trends across temperature and oxygen partial pressure, capturing the competition among ferric iron oxide phases and silica species</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-4">Optimized thermodynamics of Fe–O–Si enable prediction of stable iron silicate phases, their solvus conditions, and tie lines across oxygen activity relevant to roasting/indirect reduction</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-9">Iron-rich phyllosilicate (clay-like) formation depends on pH, silica dissolution rate, and redox conditions; at lower oxygen potential, iron-bearing interlayered silicates (2:1 and 1:1 types) form in reaction with FeO and SiO2</cite>. Silicon-rich intermetallics (FeSi) can evolve upon oxygen ingress during roasting, re‑oxidizing to FeSiO3/iron silicates and potentially depositing on pellet surfaces or bridging particles, thus coupling reduction–oxidation kinetics with deposit adherence. <cite id="b0bdbad1-5">A self‑perpetuating cycle of K deposition, Fe oxidation/reduction, and glass formation integrates silica and iron species into adherent films</cite>.

Alumina in the ore/feedstock buffers melt viscosity and basicity: at high T, Al2O3–SiO2–FeOx pseudoternary melts exhibit low viscosities when silica is present and higher viscosities in CaO–Al2O3–SiO2 systems; alumina also promotes crystallization of mullite/kaolinite groups and phase separation that can limit caking or promote frit bonding. <cite id="143d4d64-1">The presence of alumina enhances slag bonding and mechanical resistance of pellets under thermal stress, improving tolerance to sticking/swelling forces</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-6">In the CaO–(Fe2O3)–SiO2 system near 1240–1270 °C, phase separation and crystallization windows open, enabling buffering of slag viscosity and deposit adherence by Al2O3</cite>.

# Deposit Formation Mechanisms and Kinetics

- Early-stage film formation: At roasting and pre‑reduction zones (∼600–1000 °C), SiO2 and acidic ash constituents (Al2O3, SiO2, K2O) react with Fe2O3 to form thin silicate/leucite/clinopyroxene‑like films and Fe–Si intermetallics. Gas–solid interactions supply alkalis that lower the melting temperature of silica and promote liquid film nucleation on pellet surfaces, enhancing sticking and adhesion of adjacent pellets. <cite id="b0bdbad1-5">Potassium is deposited from furnace gas, interacts with silica, and promotes iron reduction until a glassy layer forms that cements particles together</cite><cite id="143d4d64-3">Silicic/aluminous ash from coal mixes into the pellet bed; reaction products (silicates) accumulate during “deposit formation” experiments on sinter-like structures</cite>.

- Growth and caking: As temperature and oxygen potential shift toward indirect reduction (above ∼1000 °C), viscous FeO–SiO2–Al2O3 slags become more mobile, enabling inter‑particle diffusion bonding and growth of fused zones; the onset of crystallization (mullite formation, olivine/clinopyroxene in Fe–Mg–Si systems) raises viscosity and can arrest caking. <cite id="942e7aa9-1">Iron-silicon phase relations show a sequence of silicide formation; upon oxygen exposure, these intermetals oxidize to iron silicates that can span particle spacings and form adherent clogged layers</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-6">At 1240–1270 °C, phase equilibria in CaO–Fe2O3–SiO2 indicate windowed crystallization that can either reduce fluidity (if solids precipitate) or promote viscous flow (if liquid remains), dictating deposit mobility and caking</cite>.

- Swelling/sticking and permeability loss: Reduced pellets experience swelling due to gas evolution and phase transformations; silica-bearing glasses and iron silicates fill pores and interstices, decreasing porosity and effective gas permeability, exacerbating temperature gradients and mechanical stresses that break pellets or plug furnace voids. <cite id="143d4d64-9">Sticking and breakage of pellets at high temperatures are characteristic hazards in shaft furnaces handling silica- and alumina-bearing feeds</cite><cite id="143d4d64-7">Formation of a continuous SiO2–CaO–Fe2O3 glassy phase during roasting is linked to densification and changes in physical–mechanical indices</cite>.

# Influence on Pellet Characteristics

- Strength and bonding: Silica reduces bonding quality versus pure Fe2O3-only networks; in its absence pellets often show greater secondary porosity and weaker interparticle bonding; conversely, controlled silica/ash-derived silicates can produce fritted bridges that raise apparent strength but may embrittle under cyclic reduction. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica does not readily react with hematite and instead reduces the amount of secondary crystalline bonding, with consequences for reducibility and mechanical integrity</cite><cite id="143d4d64-8">Low‑silica “acid” pellets can exhibit quartz and slag textures; changes in basicity alter modal composition and textural types, affecting strength</cite><cite id="143d4d64-1">Silica and alumina increase slag bonding and resistance to force in pellets undergoing sticking/swelling, indicating strengthened interparticle links when silicate phases are present</cite>.

- Reducibility and surface reactivity: Silica-rich layers and fayalite/iron silicate coatings act as glassy barriers and slow diffusion of H2/H2O and CO/CO2, decreasing near-surface reducibility; lower silica generally improves reducibility by preserving hematite-derived lattice paths and reducing glass build‑up. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica content reduces hematite’s secondary reaction extent, thereby impairing reducibility relative to silica‑lean analogs</cite><cite id="143d4d64-7">Glassy slag phases formed from SiO2–CaO–Fe2O3 densify pellets; such transformations correlate with reduced porosity and altered reducibility profiles</cite>.

- Microstructure and permeability: Increased SiO2 raises liquid-phase sintering during roasting, decreasing macroporosity and increasing interparticle necks; beneficially, this can raise mechanical integrity at ambient but detrimentally lowers gas permeability and RDI performance. Fluxing (MgO/CaO) and silica control crystallization of high‑T phases (perovskite/olivine) that restore permeability by forming rigid frameworks rather than sticky amorphous films. <cite id="143d4d64-5">Sintering indices vary with SiO2: porosity and strength trends shift as silicon participates in glass formation, illustrating permeability–strength trade-offs</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-9">Iron-rich phyllosilicates form depending on pH/silica availability, and these layered silicates can build compacted, less permeable, interparticle bonding layers</cite>.

# Mitigation Strategies Arising from Fe–O–Si Interactions

- Flux design and basicity tuning: Raising basicity (MgO/CaO) shifts the Fe–O–Si phase field away from sticky silica‑rich melts and promotes formation of higher‑T crystalline silicates (e.g., perovskites, phyllosilicates) and ferrite spinels, improving viscosity control and reducing caking. <cite id="143d4d64-1">Adjusting basicity and alumina content enhances slag bonding and resistance to sticking/swelling forces</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-1">Phase boundaries in Fe–Si systems guide selection of alloying and process temperatures to avoid metastable silicides prone to film growth</cite>.

- Alumina buffering and microstructure control: Adding Al2O3 reduces melt viscosity, increases liquidus temperature windows, and encourages mullite crystallization that provides rigid bridges with better mechanical tolerance; it also stabilizes alkalies to reduce gas‑phase attack. <cite id="143d4d64-1">Alumina improves mechanical resistance to sticking and swelling, buffering silica effects</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-6">Aluminous slags show phase separation windows that increase apparent viscosity and suppress continuous liquid bonding at high basicity</cite>.

- Si content management and reactive gas control: Lowering free SiO2 or controlling gas composition (suppressing K/Na deposition) reduces early‑time film nucleation and sticking; in high‑silica feeds, staged roasting or self‑reduction can be tuned to crystallize Fe–Si products at elevated T to avoid amorphous caking. <cite id="143d4d64-2">For high‑silica acidic pellets, regulating the liquid phase composition improves properties, but too much high‑silica feed degrades furnace slag quality</cite><cite id="b0bdbad1-5">Potassium–silica interactions accelerate reduction and glass formation; controlling gas‑phase alkalis reduces silica-driven adhesion</cite>.

- Anti-swelling/coating/porosity retention: Reserving some unreacted hematite and maintaining a porous network via silica control improves RDI by preserving reducible iron surface area and gas pathways; nano‑silica or silica fume can be judiciously used to form micro‑crystalline interlayers that limit viscous melt penetration. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica’s limited reactivity with hematite allows retention of reducible Fe2O3 phases and surfaces</cite><cite id="143d4d64-8">Quartz- and slag-dominated textures under different basicity regimes show how porosity and phase fractions govern swelling and strength</cite>.

# Putting It Together: Interaction Map and Practical Implications

- Chemical interactions: SiO2-rich phases reduce Fe2O3 to Fe-containing liquids/intermetals and FeSi; Fe2O3 evolves to Fe3O4/FeO at higher T; silica and alumina jointly control viscosity and crystallization (liquid phase fraction, nucleation of mullite/olivine, phase separation). <cite id="942e7aa9-0">Thermodynamic modeling of FeO–Fe2O3–SiO2 captures reaction loops across T and oxygen activity</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-6">High‑T phase equilibria reveal crystallization/segregation windows that set viscosity thresholds for deposit mobility</cite><cite id="143d4d64-1">Alumina increases bonding strength while silica fosters glassy adhesion; their balance controls sticking/swelling</cite>.

- Deposit formation: Early silica‑alkali glass films cause surface sticking; viscous high‑T slags penetrate pores and create interparticle necks that clog permeability; at still higher T, selective crystallization of iron silicates/mullite can harden or crack deposits, altering fouling morphology. <cite id="143d4d64-3">Silicate formation mechanisms observed during simulated deposit building in pellet/cinder mixes explain bulk caking</cite><cite id="b0bdbad1-5">Gas‑phase K lowers the effective SiO2 melting point and promotes rapid film growth during reduction</cite>.

- Pellet performance: Silica generally reduces reducibility and strength unless buffered/mitigated via basicity and alumina; too little silica lowers strength and raises reducibility but may worsen furnace slagging upstream. Optimal feeds balance Si/S to avoid sticky deposits while leaving sufficient reducible hematite surfaces, with pellet microstructure engineered to tolerate swelling and maintain permeability. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica reduces secondary reactions and thus reducibility when left uncontrolled</cite><cite id="143d4d64-2">Fluxed high‑silica pellets show improved properties when liquid phase is regulated, but excessive silica worsens furnace slag</cite><cite id="143d4d64-7">SiO2–CaO–Fe2O3 glassy phases formed during roasting control porosity and mechanical indices, linking microstructure to performance</cite>.

# Conclusions and Recommendations

- The Fe2O3–SiO2 interaction during pellet roasting proceeds via silica reduction to Si/FeSi and subsequent formation of Fe–O–Si melts and iron silicate phases; oxygen activity, temperature, and ash chemistry govern whether the system resides in a sticky glassy regime or a crystallized, more robust phase network. <cite id="942e7aa9-0">Trend prediction across FeO–Fe2O3–SiO2 shows how redox and temperature dictate stable phases</cite><cite id="143d4d64-3">Silica-rich, ash-laden deposits and interlayers build readily in pellet beds under typical roasting/reduction</cite>.

- These interactions drive deposit formation through (i) rapid silica–alkali glass film nucleation that adheres pellets, (ii) viscous high‑T slag penetration and neck growth that cake the charge, and (iii) crystallization of iron silicates/kaolinite‑like phases that harden or embrittle deposits; alumina and basicity are the primary levers to tune viscosity, crystallization, and adhesion. <cite id="b0bdbad1-5">K–SiO2 cycles accelerate film formation and Fe reduction</cite><cite id="942e7aa9-6">Viscosity and phase separation windows in CaO–Fe2O3–SiO2 allow rheology control</cite><cite id="143d4d64-1">Alumina strengthens pellet resistance under sticking/swelling loads</cite>.

- Pellet characteristics reflect this chemistry: lower silica improves reducibility but can reduce mechanical integrity at roasting/ambient; regulated liquid phase and balanced basicity improve strength and RDI by promoting favorable crystallization and maintaining gas permeability. Process controls should minimize free quartz near 600–1000 °C, suppress alkali-assisted silica glassing, and encourage high‑T crystallization of rigid silicate frameworks to limit fouling and maintain permeability. <cite id="143d4d64-0">Silica reduces hematite’s secondary bonding, lowering reducibility, so silica control is key</cite><cite id="143d4d64-2">Fluxing and liquid-phase control in high-silica pellets recover properties but must avoid furnace slag degradation</cite><cite id="143d4d64-5">SiO2-driven sintering changes porosity and compressive strength trends, guiding feed optimization</cite>.

Summary
Assessing dispersion and agglomeration of carbon-based fillers (carbon nanotubes, graphene/graphene oxide, carbon black, graphene fibers) in polymer composites relies on a core toolkit spanning microscopic imaging and spectroscopic/chemical probes, complemented by electrical percolation measurements. Below are the commonly employed approaches, what they reveal, and representative evidence.

Microscopy (structure, distribution, and interfaces)
- Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), including high‑voltage imaging and EDS: SEM is used to visualize filler loading, bundling, exfoliation, and fracture-surface interfacial contact; quantitative indices can be estimated from high‑acceleration SEM images by measuring geometric and contact-area features of CNTs in the matrix and agglomerates within the composite <cite id="c42fee1a-2">SEM images at high accelerating voltages can quantify multiple parameters characterizing CNT dispersion (e.g., contact with matrix, bundle size, and bridging/interfacial features) in polymer composites</cite>. Reviews and experimental work show SEM as a primary method for evidence of agglomerates in polymer matrices and for interfacial integrity discussions <cite id="d274ad5a-7">SEM images provide typical dispersion examples of nanotubes in polymers and guide methods to extend to other polymeric systems</cite> <cite id="ac4b12b9-0">XPS and FTIR analyses in CNT–polymer systems are used alongside observations that CNTs often exist as agglomerates; robust interfacial adhesion is emphasized as critical for performance</cite>.
- Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM): TEM discriminates exfoliated individual nanosheets versus bundled/agglomerated structures within polymer domains and shows polymer–carbon interfaces at nanometer resolution; classic studies on CNT–polymer interfaces and graphene-related materials leverage TEM to interpret reinforcement vs. agglomeration mechanisms <cite id="d274ad5a-2">Transmission Electron Microscopy has been used to investigate CNT–polymer adhesion, revealing how interfaces and exfoliation state govern mechanical reinforcement</cite> <cite id="d274ad5a-4">Mechanisms of mechanical reinforcement for graphene-related materials in composites are discussed with structural considerations TEM informs</cite>.
- Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): Tapping-mode phase/amplitude maps distinguish aggregated vs. well-dispersed carbon domains; near-contact resonance AFM and friction/elasticity imaging can resolve interfacial adhesion and relative orientation of nanotubes and graphene nanosheets within the matrix; AFM contrasts with Raman are highlighted as complementary for spatial heterogeneity in carbon composites <cite id="cc414a90-1">Raman imaging visualizes phase separation and locates CNTs with high spatial resolution; AFM, SEM, and TEM provide structure correlates, while Raman adds density/layer information</cite> <cite id="ccb412b9-5">Raman spectroscopic characterization of carbon materials with AFM, SEM, and TEM comparisons notes that Raman approximates lateral size and thickness while microscopies quantify morphology</cite>.
- Optical and polarized light microscopy: Bright-field/dark-field or differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy is routinely used to assess aggregation and morphology of carbon black and opaque nanocarbon fillers in polymer tinted films and composites, tracking primary particle coalescence, network formation, and sedimentation signatures in processing studies <cite id="c42fee1a-6">Dispersion of CNTs and nanofibers is a crucial processing step; microscopy is central to diagnosing dispersion defects and interfacial issues in polymer nanocomposites</cite> <cite id="d274ad5a-9">Homogeneous dispersion of CNTs in rubber is key, and microscopic diagnostics are emphasized at multiple scales</cite>.
- Quantitative image analysis workflows: Algorithms applied to SEM/TEM/AFM images compute dispersion/agglomeration indices (e.g., interfacial contact area per filler, number and size of agglomerates, aspect ratio and curvature), often in tandem with microscopy to link processing to structure <cite id="c42fee1a-9">Quantitative algorithms analyze dispersion of inclusions in polymer composites via image analysis, enabling standardized indices</cite> <cite id="cc414a90-0">Dispersion and agglomeration indices are commonly derived from quantitative image analysis of SEM images of nanocomposites</cite>.

Spectroscopy (chemistry, interfacial bonding, heterogeneity)
- Raman spectroscopy and mapping: Raman identifies carbonaceous phases, quantifies nanotube/chunk density and disorder via I<sub>2D</sub>/I<sub>G</sub>, I<sub>G</sub> full-widths, and spatially resolved mapping shows heterogeneous distributions, percolation networks, and interaction with polymer phases; confocal Raman can be non-destructive in composites <cite id="cc414a90-2">Raman can identify CNTs, assess their dispersion, evaluate nanotube/matrix interactions, and detect polymer phase separation in composites</cite> <cite id="cc414a90-1">Raman imaging provides non-destructive, high-spatial-resolution localization of CNTs and visualization of polymer phase separation</cite> <cite id="cc414a90-5">Raman mapping of chirality-pure nanotubes reveals environmental interactions, and has been extended to excitation mapping of chiral species and their surrounding medium</cite> <cite id="ccb412b9-5">Raman mapping provides spatially resolved imaging of defect density and layer distribution for graphene in composites (albeit approximate geometry vs. AFM/SEM)</cite>. Reviews emphasize Raman as a multi-faceted probe for dispersion state and interfacial quality across carbon fillers in polymers <cite id="cc414a90-8">Raman spectroscopy has been used extensively for multiwalled carbon nanotubes and their composites, enabling assessment beyond morphology to structural changes</cite>.
- Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) and ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy: FTIR identifies functional groups, detects load transfer/chemical interaction (e.g., epoxy C–O shifts upon CNT interaction), and monitors residual CNT–CNT interactions in composites; mapping over sample surfaces correlates IR signatures with dispersion/exfoliation zones and interfacial oxidation/functionalization <cite id="acb412b9-2">FTIR analysis (e.g., hydrogen bonding) probes nanofiller–epoxy interactions, helping infer dispersion and interfacial bonding</cite> <cite id="ac274ad5a-6">Comparative IR/XPS studies show how surface modification improves polymer–CNT adhesion, aligning with better dispersion</cite>. In carbon‑black/polymer systems, near‑IR absorbance and IR spectral band changes are linked to aggregate size, adsorption, and interfacial coupling, supporting spectroscopic classification of dispersion quality <cite id="c42fee1a-6">Dispersion state control is tied to interfacial interactions; spectroscopic diagnostics support interfacial coupling assessment</cite>.
- X‑ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS): Surface‑sensitive XPS quantifies elemental composition, oxidation states, and bonding at polymer–carbon interfaces; shifts/relative intensities of C1s (epoxy/carbonyls vs. graphitic sp<sup>2</sup>) and adventitious O/C ratios indicate degree of interfacial oxidation/hybridization and whether agglomerates present largely unreacted carbon–carbon interfaces <cite id="acb412b9-0">XPS is used with CNT composites where CNTs commonly exist as agglomerates; robust interfacial adhesion correlates with modified surfaces</cite>. Reviews document XPS alongside FTIR to diagnose agglomeration mechanisms and remedies in graphene/CNT composites <cite id="acb412b9-1">Agglomeration in polymer nanocomposites driven by graphene and CNTs is tied to surface energetics; interfacial functionalization/processing are remedies</cite>.

Electrical network and percolation diagnostics (related to agglomeration)
