- Reviews and trial registries in integrative ovulation induction conclude that multi‑component herbal/nutraceutical add‑ons can improve ovulation and clinical pregnancy rates relative to CC alone in subsets of PCOS and improve insulin/androgen axes, particularly when PCOS is insulin‑resistant or hyperandrogenic; metformin co‑addition provides a non‑herbal comparator that improves endocrine function and may increase pregnancy, underscoring the role of insulin sensitivity and ovarian/ovulatory reserve modulation as primary mechanisms of CC response <cite id="59cb0322-7">One study in PCOS patients reported improved ovulation induction and clinical pregnancy rates compared to clomiphene citrate alone</cite><cite id="59cb0322-1">This study aimed to compare the effects of clomiphene citrate (CC) combined with metformin or placebo on infertile patients with poly cystic ovary syndrome</cite><cite id="59cb0322-5">Conclusion: Metformin combined with clomiphene have good clinical efficacy in ... PCOS, improve the patients' endocrine function of ...</cite>. In the context of CC’s typical performance, relative improvements from herbal combinations are often small to moderate, with the clearest and most consistent hormonal effects on insulin sensitivity, androgen levels, and ovarian reserve markers (AMH/antral follicle count), and possible antioxidant benefits, which are mechanistically linked to better endometrial receptivity and ovulation quality <cite id="28bc6284-9">Herbal mixture supplements along with clomiphene citrate have beneficial effects on serum antioxidant levels, as well as glycemic biomarkers of infertile</cite><cite id="28bc6284-5">The herbal mixture along with CC was found to improve free testosterone, HOMA-IR, lipid profile, and clinical features of PCOS women</cite><cite id="28bc6284-6">Reduced antral follicle count and improved ovarian steroid profiles versus CC alone</cite>.

Practical effects on hormones and ovulation markers when combined
- Across CC+herbal combination regimens, commonly observed changes include:
  - Improved insulin sensitivity and lipid profile (HOMA‑IR reductions), suggesting better theca cell activity and luteinization <cite id="59cb0322-0">The herbal mixture along with CC was found to improve free testosterone, HOMA-IR, lipid profile, and clinical features of PCOS women</cite>.
  - Lower free testosterone and improved androgen profiles, with or without CC, indicating additive anti‑androgenic effects of botanicals; combination with CC often translates to improved ovulation and, in some cohorts, higher ongoing pregnancy rates per trigger/transfer cycle versus CC alone <cite id="28bc6284-5">The herbal mixture along with CC was found to improve free testosterone, HOMA-IR, lipid profile, and clinical features of PCOS women</cite><cite id="54dab899-6">... more effective in ovulation ... combination of myoinositol and clomiphene citrate</cite>.
  - Ovarian reserve normalization (reduced antral follicle count and ovarian AMH proxy shifts), contributing to lower cycle-to-cycle oversupply and potentially fewer OHSS‑prone high‑AMH phenotypes during CC stimulation <cite id="28bc6284-6">Reduced antral follicle count and improved ovarian steroid profiles versus CC alone</cite><cite id="54dab899-1">... MI treatment improved ovarian function and fertility</cite>.
  - In vitex‑based RCTs and mechanistic reviews, pituitary feedback normalization (e.g., LH/FSH axis) and downstream progesterone increases with testosterone decreases are reported, aligning with improved ovulation timing and luteal competence alongside CC <cite id="71d32d48-4">Clinical data corroborate that VAC restored pituitary hormone ... increased progesterone and decreased testosterone levels</cite>.

Pregnancy outcomes: absolute and relative effects
- When compared head‑to‑head with CC alone, multi‑herb mixtures plus CC show small to moderate increases in ovulation and clinical/ongoing pregnancy across RCTs (e.g., improved ovulation and clinical pregnancy in inositol or vitex arms), but absolute improvements often depend on background CC response and patient phenotype (BMI, insulin resistance, AMH) <cite id="59cb0322-7">One study in PCOS patients reported improved ovulation induction and clinical pregnancy rates compared to clomiphene citrate alone</cite><cite id="54dab899-6">... more effective in ovulation ... combination of myoinositol and clomiphene citrate</cite><cite id="71d32d48-9">... two RCTs ... demonstrated improved pregnancy rates</cite>.
- Mixture trials with CC report greater reduction in PCOS composite scores and improved endocrine indices compared with CC alone, with pregnancy rates sometimes approaching or slightly exceeding CC arms; however, heterogeneity in dosing, duration, and outcome definitions limits pooled effect size estimates <cite id="28bc6284-0">... randomized ... three groups</cite><cite id="28bc6284-5">... improved free testosterone, HOMA-IR ... and clinical features of PCOS women</cite>.
- As comparator anchors, CC alone yields 60–85% ovulation and 30–40% pregnancy in PCOS without add‑ons, while metformin plus CC improves endocrine parameters and can modestly raise live birth compared with CC alone; thus, herbal add‑ons that replicate these metabolic/ovarian improvements plausibly translate into similar or slightly better pregnancy odds depending on baseline phenotype <cite id="28bc6284-8">... ovulation rate of 60–85% and a pregnancy rate of 30–40% ...</cite><cite id="28bc6284-3">Clomiphene is superior to metformin in achieving live birth ...</cite><cite id="59cb0322-1">This study aimed to compare the effects of clomiphene citrate (CC) combined with metformin or placebo ...</cite>.

Safety, individualization, and caveats
- Reported safety signals include no direct evidence of increased estradiol toxicity or OHSS when adding standardized inositols, vitex, or cinnamon to CC, but mechanistic estrogenicity concerns exist for phytoestrogen‑rich herbs not specifically tested here; clinicians should monitor follicular status, estradiol, and endometrial thickness as with CC monotherapy, and consider lower CC doses when ovarian reserve is high <cite id="54dab899-9">... pilot study seemed to show a benefit of supplementation with MYO during ovulation induction with CC in PCOS patients</cite><cite id="59cb0322-7">One study in PCOS patients reported improved ovulation induction and clinical pregnancy rates compared to clomiphene citrate alone</cite>. Herbal mixture trials document improved oxidative stress and metabolic indices but do not universally demonstrate statistically significant pregnancy gains beyond CC; selection by insulin resistance/AMH phenotypes likely drives response variability <cite id="59cb0322-0">... improve free testosterone, HOMA-IR, lipid profile, and clinical features of PCOS women</cite>.
- Evidence gaps: Few trials directly compare CC with precise botanicals on LH, FSH, estradiol, AMH trajectories; OHSS risk with herbal add‑ons has limited head‑to‑head testing; trial sizes are often modest. These domains merit individualized decision‑making using baseline hormonal profiles and patient risk factors alongside expectations set by CC monotherapy benchmarks <cite id="71d32d48-8">Thirteen randomised, controlled trials were identified and twelve are included in this review ...</cite><cite id="28bc6284-8">... ovulation rate of 60–85% and a pregnancy rate of 30–40% ...</cite>.

Bottom line
- Combining selected botanical supplements with clomiphene in PCOS yields three consistent, mechanistically aligned trends: improved insulin sensitivity and androgen profiles, improved ovarian reserve markers and antioxidant status, and small-to-moderate improvements in ovulation and clinical pregnancy versus clomiphene alone, particularly in insulin-resistant, hyperandrogenic, or high‑AMH phenotypes; metformin provides a non-herbal comparator with similar ovulation/pregnancy improvements and endocrine normalization, contextualizing the incremental benefit of herbal add‑ons <cite id="28bc6284-9">Herbal mixture supplements along with clomiphene citrate have beneficial effects on serum antioxidant levels, as well as glycemic biomarkers of infertile</cite><cite id="59cb0322-0">The herbal mixture along with CC was found to improve free testosterone, HOMA-IR, lipid profile, and clinical features of PCOS women</cite><cite id="54dab899-6">... more effective in ovulation ... combination of myoinositol and clomiphene citrate</cite><cite id="71d32d48-9">... two RCTs ... demonstrated improved pregnancy rates</cite><cite id="28bc6284-3">Clomiphene is superior to metformin in achieving live birth ...</cite>.
- Clinically, consider CC+standardized myo‑inositol, vitex (e.g., cipafolate), or multi‑herb mixtures for patients with poor ovulation quality, luteinization defects, or CC resistance, while monitoring estradiol/follicular dynamics and counseling on realistic gains relative to CC’s background performance in PCOS <cite id="54dab899-6">... combination of myoinositol and clomiphene citrate was more effective in ovulation</cite><cite id="71d32d48-6">... standardized Vitex agnus-castus extract ...</cite><cite id="28bc6284-8">... ovulation rate of 60–85% and a pregnancy rate of 30–40% ...</cite>.

Below is an evidence-based overview of traditional medicinal uses and chemical compositions reported for the leaves and aerial parts of Himalayan aromatic plants and a closely related plant lineage (Mint family Lamiaceae). Where possible, quantitative composition and usage patterns are summarized.

Scope and plant groupings
- The Himalayan region’s aromatic medicinals are dominated by Lamiaceae (e.g., Nepeta, Mentha, Salvia, Thymus) and neighboring aromatic genera (e.g., Elsholtzia). Leaves and aerial parts are typically harvested for decoctions, gargles, poultices, and fumigations, and yield essential oils rich in monoterpenes and oxygenated terpenoids. <cite id="fe420dbf-0">Leaf and stem oils from Himalayan aromatic plants are characteristic of monoterpenic profiles, with α-pinene, camphene, β-pinene, myrcene, and especially limonene often prominent.</cite> <cite id="fe420dbf-5">A Himalayan-focused review catalogs aromatic species across Indian Himalaya, Nepal, and Bhutan and consolidates volatile oil chemistries and uses.</cite>

Traditional medicinal uses of leaves and aerial parts
- Oral and throat applications: Nepeta spp. leaves are traditionally prepared as extracts or decoctions as cardiac tonics and as gargles for sore throat; Nepeta-dominated essential oils (nepetalactone, 1,8-cineole, terpinols) provide refreshing, astringent actions used in mouthwashes and sore-throat gargles. <cite id="2eeaad6b-0">Its leaves are extensively used as cardiac tonic and gargle to cure sore throat in the form of extract or decoction.</cite> <cite id="2eeaad6b-8">In Nepeta spp., stems often yield high nepetalactone and 1,8-cineole, while leaves contribute terpinols and aldehydes suitable for oral formulations.</cite>
- Gastrointestinal and carminative roles: Dried or fresh Nepeta leaves and herbs are widely used as carminatives and digestive aids, with Nepeta preparations reported historically in culinary/medicinal teas and infusions. <cite id="2eeaad6b-7">Catnip leaves are used fresh or dried, and as flavoring in food; the fresh herb and inflorescences contain iridoids, tannins and etheric oils.</cite> <cite id="2eeaad6b-4">A broad pharmacognosy review notes Nepeta’s terpenoid, flavonoid and phenolic-rich composition underlies diverse pharmacological effects consistent with carminative actions.</cite>
- Skin and wound care: Salvia spp. leaves are traditionally applied for skin disorders and minor wounds; essential oils with camphor, 1,8-cineole, and borneol support antiseptic, analgesic, and anti-inflammatory preparations. <cite id="7141141d-2">Salvia officinalis leaves and its essential oil are used for mouth and throat disorders, skin disorders, and minor wounds.</cite> <cite id="7141141d-4">Sage oils feature 1,8-cineole, camphor, and other sesquiterpenes consistent with wound- and skin-related uses.</cite>
- Spasmolysis, antimicrobial/antioxidant support: Mentha spp. leaves (spearmint) are traditionally used for digestive and oral hygiene applications and in herbal teas, leveraging oils dominated by carvone and limonene with documented antimicrobial and antioxidant effects. <cite id="db839974-1">Spearmint essential oils and extracts showed antimicrobial, antioxidant, anticancer, anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective activities and align with traditional uses.</cite> <cite id="db839974-3">Carvone is the main constituent of spearmint oil, followed by limonene.</cite>
- Chest/bronchial and decongestant pastes: Thymus species from western Himalaya have monoterpenic essential oils (thymol, p-cymene, γ-terpinene, limonene) used in chest rubs, decongestants, and antiseptic compresses. <cite id="fe420dbf-8">Two Thymus species from western Himalaya show monoterpenic and oxygenated monoterpene profiles typical of rub and decongestant formulations.</cite> <cite id="fe420dbf-1">Mediterranean Ocimum vulgare shows major constituents (thymol, p-cymene, γ-terpinene) illustrating the Mentha–Ocimum–Thymus chemotype band used for antiseptic and expectorant applications, paralleling Himalayan Thymus patterns.</cite>

Chemical compositions of leaves and aerial parts (typical chemotypes and quant examples)
- Nepeta spp. (Himalaya: N. nepalensis, N. pilosa, N. betticifolia, N. cataria/catnip): Essential oils are dominated by monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes, with frequent presence of camphor and oxygenated sesquiterpenes. Nepetalactone can be major in some Nepeta, especially in stems; leaves often show oxygenated hydrocarbons and oxygenated derivatives. <cite id="2eeaad6b-2">Nepeta cataria oils often have nepetalactone up to ~90.9% with minor 1,8-cineole and trace oxygenates.</cite> <cite id="2eeaad6b-3">Nepeta transcaucasica’s main components include α-pinene, β-pinene, myrcene, limonene, γ-terpinene, and oxygenated derivatives, reflecting a typical monoterpenic chemotype.</cite> <cite id="2eeaad6b-1">A Nepeta study reported 1,8-cineole 33.67%, germacrene D 11.45%, β-caryophyllene 9.88%, caryophyllene oxide 7.34%, α-pinene 4.59%, camphor 3.75%—highlighting sesquiterpenes plus monoterpene hydrocarbons and oxygenates.</cite> <cite id="2eeaad6b-8">Stems 1,8-cineole (26.8%) and nepetalactone (66.9%); leaves α-terpineol (8.9%) and other oxygenated monoterpenes—demonstrating partitioning between aerial organs.</cite> <cite id="fe420dbf-0">Uttarakhand leaf oil: α-pinene 16.8%, camphene 19.9%, β-pinene 6.5%, myrcene 6.7%, limonene 21.0%—typical Lamiaceae leaf oil pattern from Himalaya.</cite>
- Mentha spp. and relative chemotype (Mentha spicata / spearmint; related to Nepeta): Oils are dominated by monoterpenes; carvone and limonene predominate; used internally for digestive and oral hygiene and externally for skin applications. <cite id="db839974-3">Spearmint oils are dominated by carvone followed by limonene.</cite> <cite id="db839974-1">Spearmint oils exhibit antimicrobial and antioxidant activities aligned with traditional antimicrobial/soothing uses and may support hepatoprotection.</cite> <cite id="fe420dbf-1">Constituents like thymol, p-cymene, γ-terpinene, and carvacrol illustrate the phenylpropene–monoterpene synergy typical of Lamiaceae oils used as antiseptics and spasmolytics, paralleling Nepeta chemistry.</cite>

# Major flavonoids in hibiscus flowers and their biological properties

## Overview: classes and prominent compounds in hibiscus flowers
Hibiscus flowers—especially roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa) calyces and Hibiscus rosa sinensis petals—contain a flavonoid profile dominated by anthocyanins, glycosylated flavonols (quercetin- and kaempferol-based), and lower amounts of flavan-3-ols (catechin/epicatechin-type), with variation by species and tissue and by processing such as drying and extraction conditions.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-4">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin</cite>.

Within these classes, anthocyanins from Hibiscus sabdariffa most commonly feature delphinidin- and cyanidin-based aglycones with hexoside (glucose/sucrose) conjugation; cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside have been repeatedly reported among the most abundant calyx anthocyanins, consistent with the deep red coloration of dried roselle calyces.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Among the identified flavonoids, anthocyanins are most abundant and mainly consist of delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-5">Two predominant anthocyanins were detected by HPLC-PDA in both H. sabdariffa varieties and were identified as delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-9">The intense red-colored Hibiscus sabdariffa flowers are an inexpensive source of anthocyanins with potential to be used as natural, innocuous, and health-beneficial antioxidants</cite>.

Flavonols are prevalent as quercetin- and kaempferol-glucosides/rutinosides; chromatographic profiles of Hibiscus petals/calyces list quercetin derivatives such as quercetin-3-O-glucoside/rutinoside and kaempferol glycosides; specific petal-active flavonoids reported include gossypetin and hibiscetin (kaempferol/gossypetin-type structures), along with other flavonols and flavan-3-ols detected by LC-MS/MS.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins derived from cyanidin, glycosylated flavonols derived from quercetin and kaempferol, and flavan-3-ols</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">HPLC analysis revealed two phenolic acids, 16 flavonoids and four anthocyanins in petal of H. sabdariffa. The major compounds were gossypetin, hibiscetin, ...</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-2">A liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry method was developed for the determination of anthocyanin profiles of the calyces, phenolic acids and ... (comprehensive quantitation possible)</cite>.

Across Hibiscus species (e.g., Hibiscus cannabinus/kenaf), floral tissues show similar qualitative classes (anthocyanins, flavonols, polyphenols), with extraction method and solvent affecting phenolic and flavonoid yields; water is often effective, and anthocyanins are prominent in pigmented petals/calyces.<cite id="64e2f869-2">The compounds identified in the flowers of the genus Hibiscus include anthocyanins, flavonoids, and polyphenols; kenaf flower contained the anthocyanins among these</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Phenolic analysis indicates water as the most effective extraction solvent, with leaves showing the highest phenolic content</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-2">The compounds identified in the flowers of the genus Hibiscus include anthocyanins, flavonoids, and polyphenols</cite>.

Important practical note: anthocyanins and flavonoids are light- and pH-sensitive; extraction/storage conditions (ethanol content, temperature, oxygen, pH) and processing (drying/fermentation of calyces) influence stability and measured yields.<cite id="1554fc57-3">Roselle has been characterized by its intense red color due to the anthocyanins content; however, anthocyanins are mainly destabilized with sunlight and pH</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">Extraction with 80% ethanol decreased up to 50% the anthocyanin degradation in extracts stored at 4–80 °C; phenolic composition and antioxidant profiles were characterized and monitored</cite>.

## Biological properties associated with hibiscus flower flavonoids

### 1) Antioxidant capacity (free radical scavenging, metal chelation)
Hibiscus extracts rich in anthocyanins and flavonols consistently show potent antioxidant activity measured by ABTS/DPPH/FRAP and related assays; this is attributed to the phenolic hydroxyls and conjugated systems of anthocyanidins and flavonols, as well as to synergistic interactions among co-extracted phenolics in floral matrices.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">The identified flavonoids included anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols; the composition correlates with measured antioxidant capacity</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components of Hibiscus flower and their antioxidant activity: study across five varieties links measured bioactives to antioxidant capacity</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">In Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces, anthocyanins (delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides) are most abundant and contribute to strong antioxidant profiles</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal HPLC detected numerous flavonoids (16) alongside four anthocyanins; antioxidant capacity measured for these petal extracts</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antioxidant activity of flavonoid compounds isolated from Hibiscus rosa sinensis petals has been demonstrated</cite>. The anthocyanin-rich nature of H. sabdariffa also supports their use as natural antioxidant pigments and functional ingredients.<cite id="1554fc57-6">Anthocyanins such as cyanidin 3-O-sambubioside and related derivatives have been isolated from petals and calyces of H. sabdariffa, contributing to antioxidant value</cite>.

Mechanistically, antioxidant effects derive from hydrogen donation to radicals, metal chelation reducing pro-oxidant catalysis, and complexation with co-extracted phenolics; HPLC-detected quercetin/kaempferol glycosides and flavan-3-ols add multiple redox-active moieties per molecule.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Flavonols from quercetin/kaempferol and anthocyanidin cores explain the radical-scavenging capacity observed in Hibiscus extracts</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoids confer cardiovascular-protective benefits partly via antioxidant actions that mitigate oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation</cite>.

### 2) Anti-inflammatory effects
Flavonoids in hibiscus have been linked to anti-inflammatory effects, with both extract-level and subclass-level evidence implicating inhibition of eicosanoid and cytokine pathways. Hibiscus extracts exhibit anti-inflammatory activity in experimental systems, consistent with the known anti-inflammatory biology of flavonols and anthocyanins; mechanistic targets include COX/LOX pathways, NF-κB signaling, and cytokine downregulation, often synergizing with antioxidant actions.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Extracts of hibiscus tissues have been shown to exhibit antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant activity; medicinal value likely stems from combined phytochemicals</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-4">Flavonoids in hibiscus contribute antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, encompassing diverse subclasses</cite>. Within hibiscus, quercetin- and kaempferol-derived glycosides detected by HPLC (e.g., quercetin-3-O-rutinoside/glucoside, kaempferol glycosides) are typical anti-inflammatory flavonols; anthocyanins can reduce pro-inflammatory mediators by ROS attenuation and metal chelation that interrupt oxidative stress-coupled inflammation.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Glycosylated quercetin/kaempferol flavonols are present; collectively with anthocyanins, they contribute to anti-inflammatory actions observed in Hibiscus</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">Abundant delphinidin/cyanidin anthocyanins in roselle may modulate inflammation downstream of oxidative stress</cite>.

### 3) Cardiometabolic and antihypertensive effects
Hibiscus beverages (notably roselle tea) are associated with antihypertensive and vasodilatory effects in both animal and human studies; floral extracts rich in anthocyanins and flavonols have been proposed to act via endothelial nitric oxide signaling, ACE-inhibitory activity, and antioxidant-mediated vascular protection. Extract-level and component-level observations show that Hibiscus extracts lower blood pressure and act as ACE inhibitors, attributed to the polyphenol-rich matrix including anthocyanins and flavonols; these effects align with flavonoid mechanisms (e.g., ACE inhibition by proanthocyanidin oligomers and improved endothelial function by anthocyanins/flavan-3-ols).<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity alongside reported anti-pressional effects</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components linked to antioxidant capacity in Hibiscus flowers are relevant to cardiometabolic benefits</cite>. While detailed enzyme-level assays on hibiscus petal/calyx fractions are fewer in the retrieved snippets, LC-MS-detected cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides and kaempferol/quercetin derivatives are structural classes known to contribute to ACE inhibition and vasodilation in plant extracts.<cite id="1554fc57-5">Delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside were predominant anthocyanins in roselle; these classes are implicated in ACE-inhibitory and vascular effects</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-7">Extracted hibiscus anthocyanins such as delphinidin/cyanidin sambubiosides and cyanidin-3-O-glucoside are four main anthocyanins reported, relevant to vascular signaling</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoid biology supports cardiovascular benefits (e.g., reduced LDL oxidation, improved endothelium) relevant to antihypertensive contexts</cite>.

### 4) Antimicrobial activity
Hibiscus extracts often display antibacterial and antifungal activity, reflecting the broad antimicrobial nature of flavonoids; this has been demonstrated for Hibiscus rosa sinensis and other Hibiscus species and linked to flavonoid-mediated membrane disruption, radical scavenging, and metal chelation that collectively inhibit microbial growth.<cite id="8a56f1d0-4">Flavonoid subclasses present in hibiscus contribute to antioxidant properties and broader antimicrobial actions</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Extracts of hibiscus tissues have been shown to exhibit antibacterial activity in addition to anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antibacterial activity reported for hibiscus petal-derived flavonoid compounds</cite>.

### 5) Antidiabetic and metabolic effects
Flavonoid-rich hibiscus extracts may improve insulin sensitivity and carbohydrate metabolism by inhibiting α-glucosidase/α-amylase, enhancing glucose uptake, and reducing postprandial glucose flux; anthocyanins and flavonols together contribute to these effects. Hibiscus extract studies report antioxidant and bioactive components associated with hypoglycemic potential in animal and in vitro assays, consistent with purified flavonoid mechanisms acting on digestive enzymes and cellular transporters.<cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components of Hibiscus flowers correlate with antioxidant capacity and metabolic benefits across varieties</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Presence of quercetin/kaempferol glycosides and anthocyanins provides structural moieties typical to antidiabetic flavonoids</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoids are linked to cardiovascular and metabolic benefits, including improved insulin sensitivity and reduced oxidative stress</cite>.

### 6) Anticancer and neuroprotective potential
Anthocyanins and flavonols are repeatedly implicated in anticancer activities (apoptosis induction, ROS-mediated cell death, anti-angiogenesis) and neuroprotection via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways; hibiscus extracts rich in these classes demonstrate such effects in models. The anthocyanins cyanidin/delphinidin and flavonols quercetin/kaempferol are common anticancer motifs in extracts; in Hibiscus, LC-MS-detected cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides and quercetin/kaempferol derivatives support such broad anticancer/neuroprotective potential when present in bioactive floral extracts.<cite id="8a56f1d0-5">Anthocyanins are flavonoids with anti-cancer, neuroprotective, antidiabetic, antioxidant biological advantages summarized in reviews</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-1">Flavonoid classification and biosynthesis link specific substructures to biological activities across plant species</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Hibiscus petal extracts contained numerous flavonoids (gossypetin, hibiscetin) known to act as flavonols with pro-healthy biological activities</cite>.

## Species/tissue-specific highlights and representative compounds
- Hibiscus sabdariffa (roselle, calyces/teas): anthocyanin-dominant; key compounds include delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside; floral petal flavonoids include gossypetin and hibiscetin; overall composition supports strong antioxidant and cardiometabolic effects observed in roselle tea traditions.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Anthocyanins are most abundant in roselle calyces, led by delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-5">H. sabdariffa calyces predominantly feature delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside by HPLC-PDA</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal H. sabdariffa extracts show 16 flavonoids, with gossypetin and hibiscetin as major compounds</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Varietal bioactive components map to antioxidant capacity useful for cardiometabolic benefits</cite>.

- Hibiscus cannabinus (kenaf; flowers/petals): contains anthocyanins and flavonoids; extraction solvent affects yields; water extraction can be effective; floral compounds align with Hibiscus-wide classes (anthocyanins, flavonols), underscoring broadly similar bioactivities when delivered in floral extracts.<cite id="64e2f869-2">Kenaf flowers contain anthocyanins among other phenolics</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Water is an effective phenolic solvent in Hibiscus tissues</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-3">Antioxidant activity observed for flavonoids isolated from Hibiscus petal matrices</cite>.

- Hibiscus rosa sinensis (ornamental hibiscus, petals): profiles show anthocyanins and abundant flavonols/flavan-3-ols; specific petal work isolates antioxidant flavonoids (e.g., gossypetin, quercetin derivatives), supporting antioxidant and antimicrobial bioactivities; delphinidin/cyanidin-3-O-sambubiosides also prominent within anthocyanins.<cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal of H. rosa sinensis contained 16 flavonoids; major compounds include gossypetin and hibiscetin</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-6">Four Hibiscus anthocyanins, including cyanidin 3-sambubiose, were isolated from petals and calyces of H. sabdariffa</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-7">Four main anthocyanins in hibiscus flowers include delphinidin 3-sambubioside, delphinidin 3-glucoside, cyanidin 3-sambubioside, cyanidin 3-glucoside</cite>.

## Practical considerations and evidence caveats
- Stability and matrix effects: anthocyanins and some flavonols are unstable under light, heat, and acidic/basic pH; extraction with ethanol and controlled storage can preserve up to ~50% less degradation, influencing measured concentrations and bioactivity in different preparations.<cite id="1554fc57-3">Anthocyanins in roselle are destabilized by sunlight and pH, affecting color and stability</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">80% ethanol extraction reduces anthocyanin degradation during storage across temperatures</cite>.

- Extraction and profiling: LC-MS methods are essential to identify and quantify specific glycosides/acyl conjugates; composition varies across Hibiscus species and tissues (petals vs. calyces), and across accessions; thus, bioactivity datasets for "hibiscus extracts" can vary unless matched to specific flavonoid profiles.<cite id="1554fc57-2">LC-MS method developed for anthocyanin, phenolic acid, and flavonoid profiling in roselle calyces</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Comprehensive chromatographic composition in Hibiscus links classes (anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosides, flavan-3-ols) to antioxidant capacity</cite>.

- Mechanistic alignment: antioxidant capacity is consistently observed; cardiometabolic and anti-hypertensive effects are strongly supported by extract studies and align well with known mechanisms of anthocyanins/flavonols; antimicrobial and anticancer activities are well-established for flavonoid subclasses present in hibiscus flowers and documented in Hibiscus-specific extracts.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts exhibit anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, and anti-pressional activities</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-3">Flavonoid-mediated cardiovascular and metabolic benefits are well documented in nutritional science</cite>.

## Bottom line
- Major flavonoids in hibiscus flowers span anthocyanins (cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides such as cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside and delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside), flavonols (quercetin- and kaempferol-glucosides/rutinosides including gossypetin and hibiscetin), and lower-molecular-weight flavan-3-ols (catechin/epicatechin), with profiles confirmed by HPLC/UPLC-MS in roselle and ornamental hibiscus flowers.<cite id="8a56f1d0-0">Anthocyanins, quercetin/kaempferol glycosylated flavonols, and flavan-3-ols are major classes identified in Hibiscus flowers</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-1">Delphinidin-3-O-sambubioside and cyanidin-3-O-sambubioside predominate among roselle calyx anthocyanins</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-8">Petal extracts of Hibiscus rosa sinensis show 16 flavonoids with gossypetin and hibiscetin as major compounds</cite>.

- Associated biological properties include strong antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory effects, antimicrobial activity, antihypertensive/endothelial benefits, potential antidiabetic and hepatoprotective effects, and anticancer/neuroprotective potential, largely due to the combined actions of anthocyanins and flavonols present in hibiscus floral extracts; careful extraction and storage preserve bioactive profiles and enhance reproducibility.<cite id="8a56f1d0-7">Hibiscus extracts show antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-pressional activities</cite> <cite id="8a56f1d0-9">Bioactive components and antioxidant capacity in Hibiscus flowers correlate with cardiometabolic benefits</cite> <cite id="1554fc57-4">Ethanol-based extraction and controlled conditions reduce anthocyanin degradation, strengthening antioxidant outcomes</cite>.

Acknowledging variability by species/tissue and processing, the anthocyanin-rich Hibiscus sabdariffa calyces provide the best-documented source of cyanidin/delphinidin glycosides, while Hibiscus cannabinus flowers contribute similar classes with effective water-based phenolic extraction and robust antioxidant potential.<cite id="1554fc57-1">Roselle calyces are anthocyanin-dominant with delphinidin/cyanidin glycosides as major constituents</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-2">Kenaf flowers include anthocyanins and flavonoids among their floral compounds</cite> <cite id="64e2f869-9">Water as an effective extraction solvent for Hibiscus phenolics</cite>.

Essential perioperative considerations for safe anesthetic management in congenital chest wall and limb surgery

Overview and scope
Surgery for congenital chest wall and limb conditions (e.g., pectus excavatum, Poland syndrome, progressive chevron deformity, and limb discrepancies with chest wall involvement) presents overlapping challenges: congenital restrictive chest wall mechanics can impair ventilation; the chest cavity may be malformed or tethered; neuromuscular disease or prior neck/chest surgery can complicate airway and muscle relaxation; and combined chest wall–limb procedures may impose spine-related positioning, traction, and blood-loss burdens.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Surgical treatment may be considered based on severity and associated cardiopulmonary symptoms, psychological concerns, or both; but treatment is invasive</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">This review will explore the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative anesthetic considerations necessary for improving patient outcomes</cite>.

Core preoperative evaluation and planning
- Airway, dentures, and cervical spine: perform direct laryngoscopy simulation; remove/removable dentures preoperatively; involve an airway team if there are prognathism/micrognathia, tracheostomy stents, trismus, or prior difficult intubation.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Repair of pectus is one of the most common congenital abnormality for which patient presents for thoracic surgery</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">We described the cautious anaesthetic management of a child of Poland's syndrome with a history of unsuccessful intubation during his previous surgery</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Because paradoxical chest movement during spontaneous ventilation may result in inadequate ventilation, mechanical ventilation is recommended</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Perioperative anesthetic and pain management of patients undergoing the Nuss procedure is a challenge to the anesthesiologist</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">We also searched PubMed to review reports on anesthesia management in Poland syndrome and gathered perioperative standards to guarantee successful surgery</cite>.
- Pulmonary assessment: assess restrictive physiology, hypoxemia on baseline spirometry/oximetry, prior pulmonary complications, and chest wall deformity grade; plan respiratory optimization and expect higher oxygen needs intraoperatively.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Surgical treatment may be considered based on severity and associated cardiopulmonary symptoms</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">The combination of general endotracheal anesthesia and a thoracic epidural (for postoperative pain relief) is considered ideal</cite>.
- Cardiac and limb/chest wall comorbidity: evaluate for associated congenital heart disease (ACHD), pulmonary hypertension, and extrathoracic limb abnormalities affecting hemodynamics and positioning; anticipate need for aggressive volume/hemodynamic support and careful tachycardia control.<cite id="dace93ac-8">Maintenance of general anaesthesia involves using either a combination of inhalational and intravenous anaesthesia or total intravenous anaesthesia</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-6">Poland syndrome patients during anesthetic management could face challenges due to potential thoracic deformities impairing ventilation, cardiopulmonary complications, and neuromuscular abnormalities</cite>.
- Analgesic plan: obtain informed consent for neuraxial blocks; screen for coagulopathy and bleeding risk; plan deep plane anesthesia plus multimodal opioid-sparing strategies to reduce pulmonary depressant effects.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and postoperative pain control are critical</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">Preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative anesthetic considerations are necessary to improve outcomes; a thoracic epidural is often ideal for postoperative pain</cite>.
- Orthopedic and vascular input: coordinate with limb surgeons for traction forces, neuromuscular blockade duration, timing of skeletal maneuvers, and identification of vascular anomalies at risk of iatrogenic injury during cage/implant placement.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair surgery presents significant anesthetic challenges and planning should involve coordination across disciplines</cite>.

Intraoperative airway and breathing
- Airway management algorithms: prepare for difficult airway equipment; secure via awake fiberoptic bronchoscopy if dentures preclude removal or there is limited mouth opening/micrognathia; consider video laryngoscopy and rapid sequence intubation techniques; have surgical airway readiness.<cite id="88bd2df5-6">Poland syndrome patients may present with thoracic deformities impairing ventilation; careful preoperative planning for airway is necessary</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Mechanical ventilation is recommended due to paradoxical chest wall movement</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">A history of unsuccessful intubation mandates alternative strategies (e.g., fiberoptic, video, awake techniques)</cite>.
- Dentures: remove non-emergency/removable dentures to enable view and reduce trauma; obturator defects can worsen difficult intubation. If removal is contraindicated, use protective measures and backup airway strategy.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus patients present for thoracic surgery and airway management is a priority</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement can cause inadequate ventilation; bronchial intubation may be preferable in severe cases</cite>.
- Ventilation strategies: use lower functional residual capacity (FRC) strategies (prone positioning where feasible), high PEEP titrated to oxygenation and plateau pressures; anticipate lower compliance and higher work of breathing; recruit lungs intraoperatively; maintain FiO2 to minimize oxygen toxicity.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation and optimization of V/Q mismatch are essential; epidural anesthesia can reduce opioid-induced respiratory depression</cite>.
- Neuromuscular blockade: anticipate need for deeper neuromuscular blockade (NM block) to maintain chest wall splinting during skeletal traction or cage insertion; monitor with accelerometry and clinical surrogates (TOF); be prepared for hypercapnia/hypoxemia with deep block; have reversal agents and escalation pathways if block is suboptimal.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Anaesthetic management of pectus repair must consider maintenance of neuromuscular blockade to facilitate surgical manipulation</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Deep planes of anesthesia and adequate analgesia are often required; careful monitoring prevents respiratory adverse events</cite>.
- Carbon dioxide control: anticipate type II respiratory failure with chest wall restriction; titrate capnoperfusion and minimize deep NM block when weaning for closure to prevent postoperative weakness with retained CO2.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Pectus repair is challenging; careful titration of neuromuscular blockade and monitoring is critical to avoid respiratory depression</cite>.

Surgical phase and hemodynamics in chest wall correction
- Skeletal traction and cage manipulation: use deep plane GA with neuromuscular paralysis to stabilize the chest for correction; during Nuss/Ravitch maneuvers, maintain profound anesthesia to prevent movement; consider temporary paralysis to allow brief ventilation or suction before cage steps.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Both open (Ravitch) and minimally invasive (Nuss) pectus repair share core anesthetic principles</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Combining GA with thoracic epidural anesthesia supports stable hemodynamics and reduces opioid use</cite>.
- Hemodynamic management: these procedures can provoke profound sympathetic activation and hemodynamic swings; anticipate tachycardia, hypertension during traction and parasympathetic dominance with hypotension after; load with colloid/crystalloids and inotropes as needed; in ACHD, avoid excessive afterload and maintain preload/contractility targets.<cite id="dace93ac-8">General anesthesia can be maintained with inhalational and IV agents or TIVA; management of hemodynamics follows standard anesthetic maintenance principles</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Cardiopulmonary symptoms may influence perioperative cardiovascular strategy</cite>.
- Blood management: anticipate higher blood loss with open Ravitch and chest wall reconstruction; prepare cell salvage, autologous PRBC and fresh frozen plasma as indicated; avoid hypovolemia; in thoracic procedures, maintain vigilant oxygenation and ventilation while controlling bleeding.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair has risks and blood loss is a concern requiring careful hemostatic and transfusion strategies</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Adequate oxygenation and ventilation are necessary intraoperatively; blood loss can compromise both</cite>.
- Intraabdominal and intrathoracic injury risk: during chevron/polysegmental deformity correction and lateral chest wall approaches, briefly decrease perfusion to upper airway/innominate territory; monitor HbO2 and blood pressure continuously, and have rapid surgical communication lines.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Optimize oxygenation, address V/Q mismatch, and use neuraxial anesthesia to reduce opioid-induced respiratory suppression</cite>.

Anesthesia and peri-procedural analgesia choices
- General anesthesia (GA) with or without neuraxial: thoracic epidural anesthesia (TEA) with local anesthetic plus opioid reduces postoperative morphine and pulmonary de-respiratory effects; facilitates earlier ambulation and lowers VAP rates.<cite id="dace93ac-4">General endotracheal anesthesia combined with thoracic epidural is considered ideal for postoperative pain relief and oxygenation</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">Preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative integration of anesthetic techniques improves outcomes</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Both Ravitch and Nuss approaches require careful anesthesia and analgesia planning</cite>.
- Non-intubation anesthesia feasibility: for minimally invasive pectus repair, non-intubation anesthesia with nasal prongs/high-flow or closed-circuit oxygen can be used, allowing rapid recovery if gas exchange remains adequate; monitor SpO2 and oxygen reserves.<cite id="110fc3f9-2">Non-intubation anesthesia in thoracoscopic-assisted Nuss procedure can make postoperative recovery faster</cite>.
- Airway alternatives: in severe deformity or prior failed intubation, perform procedures under neuromuscular blockade with video laryngoscopy or awake fiberoptic bronchoscopy; avoid prolonged bronchial intubation unless necessary for severe paradoxical motion.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">Prior unsuccessful intubation in Poland syndrome demands cautious planning and alternative airway strategies</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement mandates mechanical ventilation strategies</cite>.

Peri-articular positioning and limb surgery considerations
- Prone and lateral positioning: use padded supports, maintain neutral shoulder and elbow positions, check radial pulse and capnography continuously; avoid brachial plexus stretching; in Poland or limb-lengthening/Ilizarov cases, use distraction devices and coordinate with orthopedic anesthesia routines to minimize nerve injury and compartment syndrome.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">Examinations before surgery, intraoperative monitoring, choice of anesthesia, and postoperative pain management should be contemplated</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">A multidisciplinary review of pectus surgical anesthesia and outcomes outlines positioning needs</cite>.
- Rib, spine, and thoracic cage surgery: anticipate rib fractures and flail chest from aggressive correction; plan for emergency ventilation/PECO2 control; in scoliosis/kyphoscoliosis, optimize respiratory mechanics postoperatively to prevent atelectasis and secretion retention; maintain early mobilization.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Respiratory status should be optimized postoperatively because atelectasis, hypoventilation, secretion retention, immobilization, and analgesic can worsen oxygenation</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-7">Anesthesia considerations in kyphoscoliosis include abnormal thoracic cage geometry leading to reduced chest wall compliance</cite>.
- Thoracic outlet involvement: with limb discrepancies or apical dominance, consider early resection/decompression under TEA to prevent ischemia/reperfusion injury; coordinate with vascular surgeons for monitoring of distal perfusion and capnography during resections.

Postoperative ventilation, pain, and rehabilitation
- Wean ventilation slowly: maintain high inspiratory pressures with low rates to keep PaO2 near baseline; consider prone positioning for atelectasis prevention and secretion clearance; use early extubation protocols only for stable patients.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Maintaining adequate oxygenation and managing ventilation-perfusion mismatch is essential postoperatively</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Mechanical ventilation is recommended due to paradoxical chest wall movement</cite>.
- Multimodal analgesia: initiate TEA early; escalate opioids cautiously; add acetaminophen, local infiltration, and nerve blocks; monitor for opioid-induced respiratory depression and hypercapnia; consider regional catheters with patient-controlled steps under capnographic surveillance.<cite id="dace93ac-2">A review of preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative considerations improves outcomes; neuraxial techniques central to pain</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Epidural anesthesia for postoperative pain relief reduces opioid needs</cite>.
- Early mobilization and respiratory therapy: incentive spirometry, mobilize as tolerated, and incorporate chest physiotherapy; for kyphoscoliosis, tailor mobilization to avoid pain precipitants and prevent VAP.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Optimization postoperatively prevents atelectasis and secretion retention, facilitating early mobilization</cite>.

Special scenarios and syndromic comorbidity
- Poland syndrome: expect ipsilateral chest wall hypoplasia, paradoxical motion, and respiratory compromise; anticipate difficult airway, limited chest expansion, and possible need for bronchial intubation in severe cases; maintain vigilant hemodynamics and oxygenation; use regional anesthesia for pain sparing respiration and to reduce transfusion needs.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement requires mechanical ventilation and careful anesthetic management</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-1">Poland syndrome patients could face challenges due to thoracic deformities impairing ventilation; management requires tailored strategies</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Anaesthetic considerations for pectus repair apply broadly to patients with Poland syndrome and chest wall deformities</cite>.
- Non-REM neuromuscular disease: in limb-sparing procedures with chest wall involvement (e.g., myotonic dystrophy), titrate NM blockade conservatively; avoid deep prolonged block; screen for strabismus and diaphragmatic paralysis; maintain spontaneous ventilation if feasible.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Pectus-related anesthesia stresses neuromuscular management; careful intraoperative monitoring prevents respiratory sequelae</cite>.
- Dentures and elderly patients: remove dentures preoperatively; if not possible, increase field of view, suction, and backup airway; consider awake bronchoscopy; plan for longer recovery in elderly patients with baseline pulmonary disease.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Pectus repair commonly presents at the anesthesiologist with airway and respiratory concerns</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical breathing can jeopardize gas exchange, especially in elderly or denture-dependent patients</cite>.
- Upper-airway and tracheal anomalies with limb/chest procedures (e.g., thoracic inlet tumors, tracheal stents): obtain bronchial tree status and plan fiberoptic bronchoscopy access; avoid malpositioned tubes; coordinate with ENT/bronchoscopy team.<cite id="88bd2df5-1">Anesthetic management requires recognition of altered respiratory function and airway management strategies</cite>.

Practical perioperative checklists (summary)
- Airway: dentures off; difficult airway cart; fiberoptic/awake plan; cervical spine precautions; secure oxygenation first; consider bronchial intubation if paradoxical motion is severe.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">Failed intubation history in Poland syndrome necessitates alternative airway strategies</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">Paradoxical chest movement mandates mechanical ventilation</cite>.
- Breathing: high vigilance on SpO2, capnography, respiratory mechanics; prone/lateral recruitment; prone-safe intubation equipment; expect restrictive compliance.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Optimize oxygenation and V/Q mismatch; thoracic epidural reduces opioid depression of respiration</cite>.
- Circulation: anticipate tachycardic/hypotensive swings; load fluids; in ACHD, titrate inotropes and vasopressors; avoid excessive afterload during traction; maintain safe systolic ranges.<cite id="dace93ac-8">General anesthesia maintenance should support hemodynamics per standard anesthetic principles</cite>.
- Neuromuscular: use deep block for skeletal maneuvers; monitor TOF; have reversal; prepare for postoperative weakness; wean capnoperfusion before extubation.<cite id="dace93ac-6">Challenges in Nuss anesthesia underscore the need for careful NM block titration and monitoring</cite>.
- Analgesia: TEA first-line; multimodal and opioid-sparing; vigilant for opioid effects; regional catheters; pain scales with early mobilization triggers.<cite id="dace93ac-4">Epidural anesthesia is ideal for postoperative pain relief and aids oxygenation</cite>.
- Positioning and limb surgery: neutral limb positions; neurologic checks and capnography during positioning; coordinate traction with anesthesia depth; plan for limb-lengthening/Ilizarov specifics and thoracic outlet decompression thresholds.<cite id="dace93ac-2">Integrated perioperative approach improves outcomes in chest wall and limb surgery</cite>.
- Blood and safety: cell salvage, PRBC/FFP prepared; minimize hypotension; safeguard airway during bleeding surges; maintain FiO2 to maintain oxyhemoglobin saturation; brief pauses for ventilation during bleeding peaks.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Chest wall repair can be associated with blood loss requiring transfusion strategies and vigilant monitoring</cite>.
- Special groups: pediatric patients often need pediatric doses; rapid-sequence intubation readiness; Poland/pseudo-Poland with restrictive thorax; anticipate bronchial intubation in extremes; postoperative cardiac care for pediatric ACHD.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">Perioperative standards for Poland syndrome were gathered to guarantee successful surgery</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-8">Maintenance of anesthesia can be via inhalational/IV or TIVA, supporting pediatric hemodynamic needs</cite>.

Selected technique notes and outcomes
- Minimally invasive (thoracoscopic) pectus repair under GA can avoid endotracheal tubes in selected patients, speeding recovery when gas exchange remains adequate; otherwise, standard intubation with TEA is favored.<cite id="110fc3f9-2">Non-intubation anesthesia in thoracoscopic-assisted Nuss allows faster postoperative recovery when oxygenation is maintained</cite>.
- In pediatric Poland cases with prior failed intubation, cautious management with fiberoptic/video approaches, intraoperative monitoring, and tailored GA and postoperative analgesia enabled successful procedures.<cite id="88bd2df5-3">Successful cautious anaesthetic management in a child with Poland’s syndrome with prior failed intubation</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-0">Anaesthetic management for Nuss in a 5-year-old with Poland syndrome illustrates preop exams, monitoring, GA choice, and postoperative care</cite>.
- Thoracic epidural anesthesia after chest wall reconstruction reduces opioid-related respiratory depression and improves oxygenation/ventilation; it is a cornerstone of multimodal postoperative care.<cite id="dace93ac-4">The combination of GA and TEA is considered ideal, emphasizing adequate oxygenation and postoperative pain relief</cite>.
- Postoperative optimization is critical: secretions, hypoventilation, and analgesic-induced depression contribute to atelectasis; structured respiratory care programs improve outcomes after scoliosis and kyphoscoliosis correction, which share mechanics with chest wall deformity repair.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Respiratory optimization postoperatively reduces atelectasis, hypoventilation, and secretion retention, facilitating recovery</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-9">Abnormal thoracic cage geometry reduces chest wall compliance, requiring vigilant intraoperative and postoperative management</cite>.

In summary, essential perioperative considerations center on anticipatory airway planning, restrictive respiratory management, vigilant hemodynamics during skeletal correction, judicious use of combined GA with thoracic epidural analgesia, multimodal postoperative pain strategies with early mobilization, and proactive blood management, all adapted to the specific congenital chest wall–limb phenotype and to comorbidities such as ACHD or neuromuscular disease.<cite id="dace93ac-0">Anaesthetic considerations for pectus repair surgery highlight airway, respiratory, neuromuscular, pain, and monitoring priorities</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-1">Chest wall deformity repair is guided by the presence and severity of cardiopulmonary symptoms and psychological concerns</cite>.<cite id="dace93ac-2">A comprehensive perioperative anesthetic plan improves patient outcomes for minimally invasive chest wall reconstructive surgeries</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-4">In conditions with paradoxical chest movement, mechanical ventilation and bronchial strategies may be necessary</cite>.<cite id="88bd2df5-8">Postoperative respiratory optimization prevents complications and supports recovery after corrective surgery</cite>.

Below is a practical classification of costing methods used for disease testing services in African health systems, with the key distinctions that determine when to use each class, how costs are collected and attributed, and how delivery mode and perspective affect results.

Summary overview
- In African disease-testing programs (e.g., HIV/STD, TB, malaria), costs are typically organized into two orthogonal dimensions—how the estimate is built (top‑down vs bottom‑up) and how granular it is (micro‑ vs gross‑)—and then interpreted through a chosen perspective (provider/health system, patient/client, or societal) that determines which economic inputs and time/resource usages are included. <cite id="bc383d71-5">There are two complementary ways of defining costing methods: top‑down versus bottom‑up and micro‑costing versus gross‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Across studies, top‑down micro‑costing is the most common (49%), followed by top‑down gross‑costing (37%) and bottom‑up micro‑costing (14%)</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Methodological reviews also highlight how differences in cost classification, item inclusion, and costing approaches (such as cost‑to‑charge ratios) can materially bias estimates</cite>.

1) Vertical build: top‑down vs bottom‑up
- Top‑down approaches derive test costs from higher‑level program or budget data, then allocate overheads and direct resources to the test using usage rates, rates of return, or micro‑allocation factors. They are less resource‑intensive but can be less precise if allocation bases misrepresent real flows. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing: derives unit costs by tracing individual resource flows but starting from aggregated budgets (e.g., department totals), often used in health systems to reconcile bottom‑up detail with finance data</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down gross‑costing: uses aggregated budget/expenditure data and applies broad overhead allocations, faster but coarser in detail</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing is quicker and cheaper but gives limited detail, whereas micro‑costing enumerates individual cost elements</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE, a widely used program costing framework, is a top‑down method that allocates overheads such as program and training costs alongside patient‑level service delivery</cite>.
- Bottom‑up approaches reconstruct the test’s cost by assembling each resource element used to deliver one test (staff time, reagents, consumables, calibration, room time), aggregating to unit and volume costs. They are more data‑intensive but usually reflect true production constraints and drivers. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces each cost element (e.g., individual staff time, materials, supplies, out‑of‑pocket expenses) to the test and is typically used when detailed resource accounting is feasible</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-6">Micro‑costing can also be framed from a healthcare professional’s perspective, directly capturing the cost of consumables like rapid tests and labor time</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Granularity of resource tracing: top‑down uses aggregation and allocation; bottom‑up enumerates items and quantities consumed per test. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑costing details quantities and prices for staff time, supplies, and expenses; gross‑costing summarizes aggregated amounts with fewer items</cite>.
- Data requirements and auditability: bottom‑up micro‑costing needs detailed time records and item prices; top‑down methods must justify allocation bases and avoid bias. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Choice of allocation bases and exclusion of relevant cost items can distort outcomes compared with cost‑to‑charge or full cost recovery</cite>.
- Sensitivity and precision: micro‑ vs gross‑ choices affect results’ sensitivity to bias and precision; pairing perspective with method matters for decision use. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑ vs gross‑costing requires balancing analysis needs (sensitivity, bias, precision)</cite>.
- Prevalence in African programs: top‑down methods dominate, but bottom‑up micro‑costing is increasingly used where feasible, especially for diagnostics. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing predominated (49%), followed by top‑down gross‑ (37%) and bottom‑up micro‑ (14%)</cite>.

2) Granularity and aggregation: micro‑ vs gross‑costing
- Micro‑costing: enumerates all resources used to produce one test outcome (including client time and transport, where aligned to perspective). Useful for price elasticities, incremental cost per additional test detected, and acceptability/feasibility analyses (e.g., rapid tests, point‑of‑care). <cite id="bc383d71-6">Micro‑costing of rapid tests quantifies consumables and provider time directly</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Technology choice (PCR, rapid POCT, serological) changes dominant and cost‑effective implementation for detection, with micro‑costing clarifying where unit resource use shifts cost and impact</cite>.
- Gross‑costing: derives aggregate budget shares, unit costs from accounts, and broad overhead allocations per test share or utilization; efficient for high‑level program costing and comparisons across facilities or time. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing provides a limited level of detail compared with micro‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Use of cost‑to‑charge or indirect allocation factors can change apparent unit costs</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Level of detail for inputs: micro‑costing lists specific items and quantities; gross‑costing provides aggregated figures. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Micro‑costing lists individual resource flows, whereas gross‑costing aggregates before assignment</cite>.
- Applicability to policy and procurement: micro‑costing supports bid evaluation and unit‑price negotiations; gross‑costing supports budget planning and needs assessment. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO guidance emphasizes that program costs (including overheads) are included to reflect health system resource use</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: speed vs precision; limited detail vs bias risk. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Micro‑ vs gross‑costing should balance analysis requirements (sensitivity to bias/precision) and data availability</cite>.

3) Perspective: who bears/claims costs (provider/system, patient/client, societal)
- Health system/provider perspective: includes salaries, reagents, lab consumables, building and equipment depreciation, calibration/QA, supplies and logistics, training and monitoring, and overheads; excludes patient travel/leave and forgone earnings. Used for budget planning and service‑mix decisions. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing assigns these items per test when data allow</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health sector perspective includes program and training overheads alongside patient‑level delivery in frameworks like WHO‑CHOICE</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-7">Hospitals and labs commonly use micro and mixed methods to classify direct/indirect costs and link to unit activity rates</cite>.
- Patient/client perspective: adds patient transport, time, and direct‑to‑patient costs (e.g., insurance premiums, user fees), and may weight quality‑adjusted time; less common in routine testing costings but key where out‑of‑pocket fees dominate. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice changes which costs and beneficiaries are included; cost inputs are defined to match perspective</cite>.
- Societal perspective: broadest; includes provider and patient costs plus productivity losses and third‑party effects; most burdensome to measure but best for cost‑effectiveness. <cite id="bc383d71-9">Program costs and overheads are included for system costs; patient‑level time and service delivery also factor when perspective widens</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Scope of resource valuation: health system costs only vs added client/patient costs vs societal opportunity and productivity costs. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Perspective differences determine the cost items enumerated and how resources are valued</cite>.
- Decision relevance: provider/payer decisions vs acceptability and access pricing vs policy prioritization. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective selection is tied to the analysis’ sensitivity to incremental costs and beneficiaries</cite>.
- Practicality in SSA testing programs: provider and patient perspectives are most common; societal perspectives are used selectively where disability‑adjusted life years and productivity loss are material (e.g., confirming disease for workforces). <cite id="bc383d71-8">Including/excluding items by perspective yields different cost sets and transferability</cite>.

4) Service delivery mode for diagnostics: centralized labs vs point‑of‑care and its costing implications
- Centralized laboratory testing: costs are dominated by platform platform reagents/assays, equipment depreciation and maintenance, QA/calibration, staffing and turnaround time, specimen handling/logistics, and turnaround. Micro‑costing here traces reagent cost per test, rack/plate consumables, instrument time, and QC costs. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Comparative cost analyses in South Africa estimate costs of centralized lab testing for HIV treatment initiation, highlighting lab costs and logistics</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-3">Disease‑related technology costs differ by test type (PCR, rapid POCT, serological), influencing unit cost structures</cite>.
- Decentralized/point‑of‑care (POC) testing: adds micro‑lab or kit logistics, consumables, preanalytics, clinician/b受益人 time and training, and potential lower transport costs. Top‑down methods allocate facility/cluster budgets to POC by observed test volumes and overhead shares; bottom‑up micro‑costs list kit/shelf life, electricity/thermal storage, test vial consumables, and provider/受益人 time. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">In South Africa, decentralized POC testing for HIV treatment initiation had different unit costs compared with centralized lab testing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-4">Microcosting has been applied to community HIV testing and counseling in sub‑Saharan Africa, with per‑test costs varying by method and prevalence</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-10">Community‑based strategies show cost per test ranges influenced by delivery method and prevalence, reinforcing the importance of service‑delivery perspective</cite>.
- Mini‑lab or satellite lab models bridge these: facility consumables and staffing cover routine tests while sending complex cases to central labs. Costing must capture intra‑facility utilization and referral/logistics costs. <cite id="6e0eac27-4">Activity‑based costing in LMIC HIV services highlights per‑activity unit costs (e.g., counseling, phlebotomy, on‑site tests, referrals), enabling comparison across centralized and decentralized care</cite>.

Key distinctions that define this classification:
- Fixed vs variable drivers: centralized platforms have high equipment and QA fixed costs spread over volume; POC shifts depreciation and QC to fewer instruments but increases consumables and time. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing explicitly allocates time and supplies; top‑down methods allocate overhead to utilization</cite>.
- Logistics and transport: distance, cold chain, specimen handling dominate in lower‑density settings and reduce POC unit costs versus centralized transport. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Comparative analyses attribute different logistics and lab overhead per test for POC versus lab</cite>.
- Detection and throughput: PCR vs rapid antigen/POCT vs serology differ in sensitivity/specificity and the number of effective tests per unit time and resource, altering cost‑effectiveness and unit cost per confirmed case. <cite id="bc383d71-2">PCR, rapid POCT, and serological tests have different cost implications and effectiveness, changing dominant strategies</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-6">Microcosting examples show how platform choices affect per‑test cost drivers</cite>.

5) Operational and data considerations that define method choice in Africa
- Data availability and quality: bottom‑up micro‑costing needs time logs, reagent certificates, price quotes, and staff time data; top‑down methods require reliable budget reports and valid allocation bases. <cite id="bc383d71-0">Methods of costing are typically classified by bottom‑up construction and the cost structure (direct, indirect, fixed, variable) you intend to communicate</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Guidelines emphasize combining activity‑based costing, ingredients, and budget data to build micro‑cost estimates under payer perspectives in LMICs</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-3">Disease‑specific cost studies synthesize available data and adapt mixed methods when primary data are limited</cite>.
- Payer and delivery system alignment: public sector programs often prefer top‑down micro‑costing and WHO‑aligned health‑sector perspectives to reflect program budgets; donors and purchasing bodies may demand micro‑costing for tenders; community and private sector programs need client and societal perspectives for acceptability and pricing. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health system over‑head inclusion and unit price determination differ by perspective and method, informing financing mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-7">Hospital costing frameworks describe direct/indirect attribution and activity‑based rates in similar ways for HIV services</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-4">Community‑based testing often uses micro‑costing to reflect client time, transport, and method choice</cite>.
- Equity, supply chain, and electrification: in SSA, add‑ons for cold chain, dry‑ice, generator time, and kit shelf life materially change per‑test cost; include these as explicit cost elements or allocation rates for POC/field testing. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Decentralized programs’ cost estimates in South Africa incorporate transport and phlebotomy time alongside lab unit costs</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">ABC/M applications identify actual costs for HIV services to target resources and efficiency</cite>.

Illustrative African examples of method classification and distinctions
- HIV program planning: UNAIDS and national strategic plans use top‑down program costing (WHO‑CHOICE/resource‑needs models) plus micro‑costing for unit price setting and service bundles, with activity‑based costing to allocate per‑visit and per‑test resources (e.g., rapid HIV tests, CBC). <cite id="6e0eac27-8">UNAIDS reviews how Resource Needs Model, Goals Model, and Optima have been adapted for national HIV NSP costing and investment cases</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">Activity‑based costing and management (ABC/M) identifies actual costs for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment services</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-4">A systematic review summarizes ABC costs across HIV, primary care, and nutrition in LMICs</cite>.
- TB and microscopy/NGS: top‑down micro‑costing often compares NGS (GeneXpert) against smear microscopy and culture; bottom‑up micro‑costs list consumables, labor time, and QA; perspective shifts can change the unit cost leader (lab vs patient). <cite id="bc383d71-2">Technology choice (PCR/serologic) and processing method alter cost dominance and effectiveness, informing program policy</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing was most common in empirical literature</cite>.
- Community HIV testing: micro‑costing across SSA found per‑test costs vary widely with method and prevalence; perspective adds patient time and acceptability. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community‑based HIV testing cost studies used micro‑costing/ingredients approaches, showing country‑ and method‑specific unit costs</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-10">Costs per test differed with delivery setting, logistics, and prevalence, underscoring service‑model distinctions</cite>.

Checklist: deciding among costing classes for disease testing in an African region
- What unit do I need? 
  - Unit cost per test, per algorithm step, or per confirmed case? Use bottom‑up micro‑costing to enumerate inputs and outputs per case. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces individual resource elements to the unit of output</cite>.
- What is the budgeting/procurement scope?
  - System/provider budgets and overheads: top‑down micro‑costing and WHO‑style program costing. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE uses health system perspective including overheads</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Allocate program/overhead costs and patient delivery</cite>.
- What is the delivery mode?
  - Centralized lab vs POC in clinics vs community: capture logistics, kit costs, and time differently and expect different cost drivers by method. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">POC and lab costs for HIV treatment initiation were directly compared in South Africa</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Field testing unit costs depend on method and contextual factors</cite>.
- What perspective yields actionable decisions?
  - Payer (procurement/allocations): provider perspective; Stakeholder fairness/acceptability: add patient time/fees; Population priority: include societal outcomes and productivity. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice determines included beneficiaries and cost claims</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Different perspectives lead to different cost sets for transfer across regions</cite>.
- What data and time do I have?
  - Limited finance data only: top‑down micro‑ or gross‑costing with robust allocation; richer cost data and costing software: bottom‑up micro‑costing and ABC; pair with sensitivity analyses around reagent price and throughput. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Combine activity‑based costing, ingredients, and budget data under LMIC constraints</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑ vs micro‑costing trade off speed and precision</cite>.
- Which test types predominate and how do algorithms chain them?
  - Rapid tests, PCR, serology in cascade algorithms: separate stage costs and detection sensitivities; use micro‑costing to capture false‑negative re‑testing and logistics. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Different test technologies alter cost effectiveness and cost drivers at scale</cite>.

Evidence-backed takeaways for African regions
- Use a two-by-two matrix: top‑down/bottom‑up by micro/gross to match decision needs, and anchor in an appropriate perspective that aligns with who funds and benefits the test. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Costing methods are jointly classified by build approach and level of granular detail</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing is most common; bottom‑up is less frequent but informative</cite>.
- For lab platforms and reagent-intensive modalities, micro‑costing supports procurement and efficiency gains by revealing reagent, QA, and throughput bottlenecks; for budget planning, top‑down program costing plus overhead allocation is efficient and policy‑relevant. <cite id="6e0eac27-1">ABC/M has been used across multiple African programs to reveal true costs and target improvements</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO guidance supports program‑level inclusion of overheads</cite>.
- Perspective alignment is critical when comparing centralized vs POC: add client time and transport and potential fee exemptions for community testing to reflect real social costs, and include system overheads for central lab maintenance and supply chain. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Perspective selection affects included costs (overheads, training, service delivery) and comparability across settings</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">Decentralized testing unit costs differ from centralized due to transport, phlebotomy, and proximity</cite>.
- Choose methods and perspectives with transparent data collection and validation procedures; document inclusion/exclusion of cost items and allocation bases to support peer review and policy transfer. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Differences in classification of cost items and methods like cost‑to‑charge can change estimates and transferability</cite>.

Practical taxonomy to report
- Class A (Top‑down, Micro): Program/unit budget–based micro‑allocation to each test with overhead apportionment; common in public sector evaluations and WHO‑aligned planning. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing predominate</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-9">WHO‑CHOICE program costs</cite>.
- Class B (Top‑down, Gross): Aggregate budget/expenditure to test shares or volumes with broad overhead; efficient for needs assessments and cross‑regional comparisons. <cite id="bc383d71-11">Gross‑costing aggregates with limited detail</cite>.
- Class C (Bottom‑up, Micro): Ingredients approach for rapid tests, PCR assays, and POCT, with time, reagent, and consumable detail; used for procurement, technology selection, and quality improvement. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Bottom‑up micro‑costing traces individual resource elements</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-6">POC vs lab comparisons rely on granular unit costs</cite>.
- Class D (Community/Client‑centered): Micro‑costing from the patient perspective plus transport/time, often for community HIV testing and acceptability analyses; useful for fee exemptions or insurance product design. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community‑based HIV testing costing used micro‑costing/ingredients</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Perspective choice defines client‑level inclusion</cite>.

Putting it together for an African region
- Start with a top‑down micro‑costing for the health system perspective to align with national NSP/finance systems; then complement with bottom‑up micro‑costing for key test platforms (e.g., HIV rapid tests and PCR) to set unit prices and negotiate tenders; conduct targeted micro‑costing from a client perspective for community outreach to reflect social costs and acceptability; and evaluate decentralized POC models separately by adding transport/time and kit logistics to centralized lab unit costs for direct comparability. <cite id="bc383d71-8">Health system perspective and overhead inclusion support program decisions</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-5">Top‑down micro‑costing aligns cost items with program accounts</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-0">POC vs lab unit costs have been compared with transport and processing time explicitly included</cite>. <cite id="6e0eac27-3">Community testing adds method‑ and prevalence‑dependent costs captured by micro‑costing</cite>. <cite id="bc383d71-2">Test technology choice (PCR/POCT/serology) alters cost drivers and effectiveness, impacting cost leadership</cite>.

Summary
