During SARS-CoV-2 infection, host defense cytokines and inflammation induce the catabolic enzyme indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase 1 (IDO1; also known as IPR), which catalyzes the initial, rate‑limiting step of tryptophan degradation into the kynurenine pathway (KP). This shift away from serotonin synthesis and toward KP metabolite production serves both antiviral and immunomodulatory roles while contributing to immune dysfunction in severe COVID‑19. In certain tissues and severities, IDO2 can be induced as well, with distinct endothelial and disease-associated patterns, but IDO1 is generally the key inducible driver of systemic KP activation in COVID‑19.

Mechanism of enzyme induction
- Interferon and inflammatory cytokines: Increased IFN‑γ, IL‑1, and IL‑6 during COVID‑19 are implicated in upregulating IDO expression, with IFN‑γ acting as a principal inducer in antigen‑presenting and other immune cells; this transcriptional program is broadly conserved in innate immune responses to infection. <cite id="228b1a41-0">During COVID‑19, IFN‑γ, IL‑1, IL‑6 likely induce the IDO enzyme, the first and rate‑limiting enzyme of the tryptophan catabolism pathway</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-1">Activation of the KP by COVID‑19 is mediated by IDO induction by proinflammatory cytokines, with potential TDO induction by cortisol</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-2">These cytokines are known to activate the enzyme indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase 1 (IDO‑1), catalysing the first step of tryptophan catabolism</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-3">Interferon lambda upregulates IDO1 expression in respiratory epithelial cells after influenza virus infection</cite> <cite id="4807d070-9">During infection, increased levels of IFN‑γ, IL‑1β, IL‑6, and ROS may induce indoleamine‑2,3‑dioxygenase (IDO), activating tryptophan catabolism</cite>.
- Interferon signaling context: Interferons orchestrate IDO induction across innate immune contexts; interferon‑γ is canonical, and interferon‑inducible programs in epithelial and endothelial compartments are documented, supporting a convergent antiviral program that includes tryptophan catabolism. <cite id="3ce78692-5">Indoleamine 2,3‑dioxygenase is an IFN‑γ‑induced enzyme catalyzing tryptophan degradation</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-8">IDO1 regulation in human lung epithelial cells was investigated by coronaviruses and inflammatory cytokines, indicating interferon/viral context drives IDO1 expression</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">Activation of IDO1 in immune cells during COVID‑19 leads to kynurenine release, AhR activation, and downstream immune modulation</cite>.
- Tissue and severity specificity: Although both IDO isoenzymes are relevant, expression patterns shift with disease course and severity. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominates in early/mild pneumonia and in lung tissues of patients with long COVID, whereas IDO2 predominates in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 expression, with pathology linked to specific kynurenine breakdown products generated</cite> <cite id="4807d070-0">After SARS‑CoV‑2 infection leading to early/mild pneumonia, inflammatory stimuli trigger endothelial IDO1 expression, kynurenine accumulation, and vascular effects</cite>.

Role in tryptophan catabolism
- KP diversion and tryptophan scarcity: Once induced, IDO1 converts L‑tryptophan to N‑formylkynurenine, initiating a cascade that channels tryptophan away from serotonin toward KP metabolites (kynurenine, 3‑hydroxykynurenine, quinolinic acid, etc.). This catabolic shift reduces precursor availability for tryptophan下游 metabolites (serotonin, melatonin) and yields immunomodulatory KP products. <cite id="228b1a41-0">IDO is the first and rate‑limiting enzyme of tryptophan catabolism, and its induction in COVID‑19 redirects tryptophan into catabolism</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">COVID‑19 alters metabolism into the kynurenine pathway, which regulates inflammation and immunity</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection stimulates proinflammatory cytokine secretion, activating IDO1 and promoting immunosuppression through kynurenine pathway products</cite>.
- Systemic and cellular remodeling: Metabolomics studies report selective KP activation during severe disease, consistent with increased IDO1/IDO2 activity and substrate depletion. <cite id="228b1a41-3">Clinical studies suggest selective enhancement of the KP in patients with severe COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-7">IDO1 is induced by proinflammatory cytokines and infection‑induced inflammation triggers tryptophan catabolism in infectious contexts</cite>.
- Re-expression in long COVID: Endothelial and tissue IDO1 expression observed in long COVID lung biopsies ties persistent inflammation to sustained KP flux and potential vascular dysfunction. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 prevails in lung tissues from patients with long COVID</cite>.

Immunologic consequences of KP activation (how the enzyme shapes immunity in COVID‑19)
- T cell suppression and immune evasion: By depleting tryptophan and accumulating kynurenine and downstream metabolites (e.g., 3‑HK, QA, quinolinic acid), IDO1/KP products suppress T cell proliferation, alter T cell receptor signaling, promote T cell exhaustion/activation exhaustion, and can activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) pathways in immune cells. This creates a feedback loop that dampens antiviral adaptive immunity during infection and contributes to persistence and fatigue in long COVID. <cite id="4807d070-8">Activation of IDO1 in immune cells releases kynurenine and activates AhR, integrating tryptophan catabolism into immune signaling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">Selective KP activation in COVID‑19 is linked to immune regulation and inflammation control, consistent with immunomodulatory effects of KP metabolites</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">IDO1‑mediated KP activation promotes an immunosuppressive system during SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="7817455">The KP’s immunosuppressive system during infection includes tryptophan depletion and kynurenine‑mediated T cell suppression, directly linking IDO1 activity to T cell exhaustion</cite>.
- Endothelial immunomodulation and vascular leak: Endothelial IDO1 induction causes kynurenine accumulation within the vessel wall and local immune compartments, promoting an anti‑inflammatory/immunosuppressive milieu and potentially contributing to vascular leak and remodeling that complicate severe COVID‑19. <cite id="4807d070-0">Inflammatory stimuli after SARS‑CoV‑2 infection trigger endothelial IDO1 expression and kynurenine accumulation with vascular effects</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 prevalence in long‑COVID lung tissues aligns with persistent endothelial/parenchymal immunomodulation</cite>.
- Antiviral and protective versus pathogenic tension: Interferon‑driven IDO activation can have antiviral benefits by limiting tryptophan availability to replicating viruses and shaping antigen‑presenting cell function; however, excessive/chronic IDO1/KP activation skews immunity toward suppression and exhaustion in COVID‑19, especially with dysregulated interferon signaling. <cite id="3ce78692-5">IDO is an IFN‑γ‑induced, antiviral enzyme that degrades tryptophan</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">IDO1 activation during COVID‑19 drives immune signaling changes (kynurenine/AhR) that intersect with antiviral and immunosuppressive effects</cite>.

Tissue context and disease phase
- Early/mild disease: Lung epithelium and endothelium express IDO1 in response to interferons and inflammatory cues following infection, diverting tryptophan catabolism locally to limit viral replication and modulate infiltrating leukocytes; this phenotype often precedes systemic dominance of other mediators. <cite id="4807d070-0">Post‑infection, inflammatory stimuli trigger endothelial IDO1, kynurenine accumulation, and vascular remodeling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominance is observed in early/mild pneumonia</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-8">Coronaviruses and inflammatory cytokines regulate IDO1 in human lung epithelial cells</cite>.
- Severe/fatal disease and long COVID: Sustained high‑grade inflammation and/or type II/type I cytokine dysregulation favor broader IDO2 induction in certain cells (notably endothelium) and tissue‑resident macrophages, which can bias KP toward neurotoxic/quadinine‑like metabolites with worse outcomes; in long COVID, persistent endothelial and tissue IDO1 activity sustains KP flux and immune dysfunction. <cite id="228b1a41-1">Potential TDO and IDO induction by cortisol and cytokines further increase KP flux</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 vs IDO2 imbalance associates with early/mild versus severe/fatal courses, with IDO2 predominance in severe/fatal cases</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2–induced IDO2 activity yields disease‑relevant kynurenine breakdown products</cite>.

Clinical patterns and biomarkers
- Metabolomics corroboration: KP activation in blood and tissue during severe disease matches the pattern expected when IDO enzymes are induced; these alterations correlate with inflammation and poor outcomes, and have motivated IFN‑γ itself as a biomarker link to persistent symptoms. <cite id="228b1a41-6">Targeted/untargeted metabolomics identified KP alterations in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="4807d070-4">SARS‑CoV‑2 triggers IFN‑γ production, associated with fatigue, muscle ache, and depression</cite>.

Putting it together
- Which enzyme is induced: The primary, inducible enzyme is IDO1 (IPR), with notable induction by interferons and proinflammatory cytokines typical of COVID‑19; in certain cells and disease phases, IDO2 and sometimes tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) suppression further tilt metabolism toward KP activation. <cite id="228b1a41-0">IDO is induced by IFN‑γ, IL‑1, IL‑6 in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-2">Cytokines activate IDO1 to catalyze tryptophan catabolism</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-1">Activation of the KP by COVID‑19 is mediated by IDO induction by cytokines and potential TDO induction by cortisol</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2 infection induces IDO2 activity with disease‑relevant metabolites</cite>.
- What it does in tryptophan catabolism: By catalyzing the first committed step, IDO1 gates irreversible conversion of tryptophan into KP metabolites, depleting tryptophan and creating immunomodulatory gradients that locally suppress T cell function and promote AhR‑linked signaling, thereby integrating antiviral defense with immunopathogenic consequences in severe and long‑COVID settings. <cite id="228b1a41-0">As the rate‑limiting enzyme, IDO activation redirects tryptophan catabolism during COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="4807d070-8">IDO1 activation in immune cells releases kynurenine and activates AhR, coupling tryptophan catabolism to immune signaling</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-6">KP shifts regulate inflammation and immunity during SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite>.

Nuances and unresolved issues
- Isotype and tissue specificity remain under study, with converging data for IDO1 predominance early/mildly and IDO2/endothelial dominance in severe/fatal disease; TPH1 suppression by cortisol may complicate serotonergic metabolism in hospitalized patients. <cite id="228b1a41-1">Potential TDO induction by cortisol and cytokine‑driven IDO induction together increase KP flux</cite> <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 vs IDO2 endothelial imbalance stratifies disease severity and long COVID lung tissues</cite>.
- While clinical metabolomics substantiates KP activation, causal attribution to specific isoenzymes in vivo benefits from cell‑type‑resolved measurements; nonetheless, interferon/cytokine induction mechanisms and metabolite‑linked immune dysfunction align with the IDO/KP paradigm across preclinical and translational data. <cite id="228b1a41-6">KP activation is observed and linked to immune regulation</cite> <cite id="4807d070-2">Cytokine‑driven IDO1 activation promotes immunosuppression via kynurenine</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-3">Respiratory viral interferons can upregulate IDO1 in airway epithelium, supporting cross‑virus relevance</cite>.

Practical implication
- Blocking or modulating the KP (e.g., IDO1/IDO2 inhibitors) in severe or long‑COVID has been proposed to restore tryptophan availability, improve T cell function, and limit pathologic metabolite accumulation; this strategy is being examined with the caveat that some KP products have antiviral or reparative roles at low levels, so dosing/timing are critical. <cite id="228b1a41-4">IDO1 predominance in lung tissues of long COVID suggests local KP targeting as a strategy to break immune‑metabolic dysfunction</cite> <cite id="3ce78692-2">SARS‑CoV‑2–induced IDO2 activity with disease‑relevant kynurenine breakdown products supports isoenzyme‑targeted modulation</cite>.

# Summary

Proteins can modulate the effects of proinflammatory cytokines through direct neutralization, receptor interception, intracellular signaling reprogramming, and epigenetic or cellular reprogramming of cytokine-producing cells. These mechanisms translate into therapeutic benefits in multiple inflammatory diseases, as shown by recombinant and fusion protein biologics (e.g., TNF inhibitors), cytokine agonists/analogs (e.g., IL-10), engineered receptor-derived peptides/binders, and endogenous anti-inflammatory proteins (e.g., annexin A1). Below are representative mechanisms, evidence, and therapeutic examples.

# Mechanisms by which proteins modulate proinflammatory cytokines

- Inhibition of cytokine production and signaling by TNF family blockers
  - TNF is a central driver of inflammation; soluble TNF receptor fusion proteins (e.g., etanercept; infliximab) bind TNF with high affinity and act as "decoy receptors," preventing TNF from engaging membrane TNF receptors and upstream NF-κB–dependent signaling, thereby attenuating TNF-driven cytokine cascades (e.g., IL-1, IL-6) and inflammatory gene expression programs. <cite id="1de81f7b-0">The similarity of clinical results observed for infliximab and etanercept suggests the mechanistic equivalence of blocking TNF access to membrane receptors versus neutralization in vivo</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-2">Etanercept is a soluble TNF receptor competitor for TNF binding sites and is indicated for rheumatoid arthritis</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-6">Etanercept's therapeutic effects arise by acting as a decoy receptor for TNF-α, neutralizing this key proinflammatory cytokine</cite>.
  - Beyond TNF binding, TNF antagonists also affect cytokine networks indirectly—e.g., by reducing joint destruction and altering Th17/Treg balance—and clinical trials show rapid and sustained efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease, supporting their broad anti-cytokine mechanism. <cite id="1de81f7b-4">Treatments with TNF antagonists (infliximab or etanercept) are highly clinically efficacious and delay joint destruction</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-3">TNF inhibitors were the first rationally designed biologic drugs for rheumatoid arthritis</cite>.

- Anti-inflammatory cytokines reprogramming myeloid and adaptive cells
  - IL-10 is a potent inhibitor of proinflammatory cytokine responses. It suppresses TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 production by macrophages and inhibits TLR4/TLR9–induced signaling, acting via STAT3-dependent pathways to reprogram gene expression in innate cells, thereby dampening cytokine cascades. <cite id="a578b52b-0">Interleukin-10 is arguably the most potent anti-inflammatory cytokine, produced by many immune cells</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-4">IL-10 exerts anti-inflammatory effects through inhibiting production of proinflammatory cytokines, preventing antigen presentation, and affecting multiple immune functions</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-3">IL-10 reduces TLR-induced inflammatory responses; anti-inflammatory mechanism was revealed in a mouse model</cite>.
  - Therapeutic modulation of IL-10 pathway includes direct administration and gene therapy. Local IL-10 expression from DNA/plasmid or variant cytokine constructs downregulates proinflammatory cytokines at sites of inflammation (e.g., joints, liver injury), supporting translational potential. <cite id="a578b52b-7">IL-10 gene therapy via plasmid DNA downregulates pro-inflammatory cytokines through IL-10 expression</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-2">IL-10 inhibits the most typical markers of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF, IL-1)</cite>.

- Smaller protein/peptide binders that sequester cytokines
  - Engineered peptides derived from cytokine receptors can bind and neutralize proinflammatory cytokines, offering a modular route to anti-cytokine therapy. Such receptor-derived binders can be designed to target TNF or IL-6 and have shown anti-inflammatory efficacy in preclinical models. <cite id="291d2d66-5">A peptide derived from cytokine receptors binds proinflammatory cytokines as a therapeutic strategy for anti-inflammation</cite>.

- Growth factors/cytokines shaping T-cell cytokinesis and cytok production
  - TGF-β can restrain inflammatory T-cell responses by suppressing proliferation and cytokine production by naïve and effector T cells (including Th1 and Th2 clones), thereby limiting proinflammatory cytokine secretion. Its actions are context-dependent—beneficial to suppress autoimmunity in some settings but potentially pathologic when excessive—necessitating careful modulation. <cite id="3c3e25ba-9">TGF-β inhibits proliferation and cytokine production by naïve T cells and both Th1 and Th2 T cell clones, contributing to anti-inflammatory control</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-0">TGF-β control of innate immune cells can have severe pathological consequences; interest exists in modulating TGF-β for therapeutic benefit</cite>.
  - Clinical programs modulate TGF-β signaling for immune-mediated diseases, consistent with preclinical evidence of efficacy in autoimmune and chronic inflammatory models. <cite id="3c3e25ba-2">TGF-β has been experimentally manipulated to control autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases, revealing promising therapeutic potential</cite>.

- Endogenous "innate cytokine-buffering" proteins
  - Some endogenous proteins blunt cytokine-driven destructive inflammation. For example, the exoribonuclease POP2 inhibits a key inflammatory pathway, dampening cytokine-mediated responses before they cause tissue damage. <cite id="291d2d66-7">A protein called POP2 inhibits a key inflammatory pathway, calming the body's inflammatory response before it becomes destructive</cite>.

# Therapeutic evidence and examples

- TNF receptor fusion proteins (etanercept, infliximab)
  - Structural mechanism and clinical benefit: Fusion proteins (e.g., etanercept: two TNFR2 extracellular domains fused to Ig-Fc; infliximab: chimeric monoclonal anti-TNF) neutralize or intercept TNF, reversing cytokine storm signaling. Clinical trials established their efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis, with rapid symptom and biomarker improvement and durable remission when dosed appropriately. <cite id="2de81f7b">Etanercept is a recombinant p75 soluble TNFR fused to Fc; it received FDA approval for rheumatoid arthritis and juvenile RA</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-4">TNF antagonists (infliximab, etanercept) show highly efficacious clinical responses and reduce structural joint damage</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-5">Anti-TNF agents bind soluble and membrane TNF and have been effective in rheumatoid arthritis and other TNF-driven diseases</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-3">TNF targeting was the first rationally grounded biologic therapy in rheumatoid arthritis</cite>.
  - Distinct modulation from different agents: Etanercept (decoy) and infliximab (neutralizing antibody) show broadly concordant efficacy in immune-mediated diseases, supporting the validity of TNF-centric cytokine modulation strategies, though disease-specific pharmacodynamics can diverge. <cite id="1de81f7b-1">Etanercept and infliximab are effective in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis via distinct modes of TNF modulation</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-0">Clinical similarity between infliximab and etanercept supports the TNF-interception/neutralization mechanism despite mechanistic differences</cite>.

- IL-10-based therapies
  - In vivo IL-10 delivery lowers cytokines at the disease site. Gene delivery of IL-10 variants in murine models reduces TNF, IL-1, and tissue damage in colitis and liver injury; clinical trials of IL-10 or IL-10–based biologics have targeted inflammatory bowel disease and oncologic inflammation, with mixed outcomes reflecting delivery/immune-context constraints. <cite id="a578b52b-7">Local plasmid IL-10 expression can downregulate proinflammatory cytokines in vivo</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-2">IL-10 is the prototype anti-inflammatory cytokine; its inhibitory action suppresses canonical proinflammatory cytokines</cite>.
  - Disease-modifying effects in chronic inflammation hinge on adequate IL-10 bioavailability and timing; strategies that enhance IL-10 signaling (agonists or delivery systems) target the same cytokine network implicated in Crohn's colitis and infectious inflammation. <cite id="a578b52b-8">Monocyte-derived IL-10 acts to inhibit potentially protective cell-mediated responses, illustrating context-dependent cytokine modulation</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-3">Mouse models revealed IL-10's anti-inflammatory mechanism by reducing TLR-induced responses</cite>.

- TGF-β modulation
  - Preclinical and translational rationale: Because TGF-β restrains Th1/Th2 cytokine production and antigen presentation, manipulating its signaling can ameliorate autoimmunity and chronic inflammation. Clinical pipelines include TGF-β pathway agonists and delivery systems for immune diseases (e.g., inflammatory bowel disease, scleroderma), acknowledging risks of over-suppression due to context dependence. <cite id="3c3e25ba-2">Experimental manipulation of TGF-β controlled autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases with promising therapy</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-9">TGF-β inhibits cytokine production by inflammatory T cell clones, supporting anti-inflammatory utility when dysregulated</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-7">TGF-β clinical modulation programs (e.g., for fibrosis/cancer) highlight breadth of therapeutic exploration</cite>.
  - Safety/efficacy trade-offs: Over-inhibition or over-activation of TGF-β can worsen pathology; this duality underscores why therapeutic agents must target context-specific inflammatory circuits rather than broadly suppress cytokines. <cite id="3c3e25ba-0">TGF-β control of innate immune cells can have severe pathological consequences, necessitating careful modulation</cite>.

- Engineered cytokine binders and receptor analogs
  - Receptor-derived peptides bind cytokines such as TNF/IL-6 to neutralize bioactivity locally, reducing inflammation with lower systemic exposure risk. Preclinical efficacy supports their progression as protein-based anti-inflammatory therapeutics. <cite id="291d2d66-5">A cytokine receptor-derived peptide can bind proinflammatory cytokines, serving as an anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategy</cite>.

# How to pick a protein modulator for therapy

- Target TNF when inflammation is TNF-dominant (RA, spondyloarthritis, Crohn's, severe sepsis). Fusion proteins and antibodies that block TNF engagement/signaling rapidly reduce cytokine storm biomarkers across diseases. <cite id="1de81f7b-0">TNF blockade through receptor interception/neutralization yields clinically concordant benefits across agents</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-3">TNF inhibitors are foundational biologics for rheumatoid arthritis</cite>.
- Augment IL-10 pathways in chronic persistent inflammation (IBD, certain infections, transplant rejection), where innate immune reprogramming is needed to suppress ongoing cytokine secretion. Local IL-10 delivery or IL-10-mimetic proteins can rebalance cytokine networks. <cite id="a578b52b-7">Local IL-10 expression downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines in vivo</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-4">IL-10 suppresses proinflammatory cytokines and antigen presentation</cite>.
- Modulate TGF-β in autoimmunity and fibroinflammatory disease when Th1/Th17 circuits dominate, while monitoring for systemic immunosuppression risks; delivery systems and targeted agonists help mitigate off-target effects. <cite id="3c3e25ba-9">TGF-β restrains cytokine production in inflammatory T cells</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-0">Context dependence creates therapeutic opportunities and pitfalls for TGF-β modulation</cite>.
- Consider engineered peptide binders for rapid, localized cytokine neutralization (e.g., in acute exacerbations), leveraging receptor-derived affinity to reduce dosing and side effects. <cite id="291d2d66-5">Peptide cytokine binders function as anti-inflammatory therapeutics in preclinical models</cite>.

# Representative evidence supporting therapeutic potential

- Head-to-head and long-term clinical success of anti-TNF agents in rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease demonstrates that protein-based cytokine neutralization can safely and durably turn off destructive inflammatory cascades. <cite id="1de81f7b-4">TNF antagonists are highly efficacious clinically and delay joint damage</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-5">Both infliximab and etanercept bind soluble and membrane TNF and are effective in RA</cite> <cite id="2de81f7b">Etanercept's recombinant TNFR:Fc fusion and approvals for RA/JRA document translational maturation</cite> <cite id="1de81f7b-3">They represent the first rational biologic therapies</cite>.
- IL-10 delivery strategies provide proof-of-concept that protein-based cytokine pathway reinforcement can down-modulate cytokine production at sites of inflammation, supporting development of IL-10 agonists and delivery technologies. <cite id="a578b52b-7">Gene-delivered IL-10 downregulates pro-inflammatory cytokines</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-2">IL-10 inhibits canonical proinflammatory cytokines</cite>.
- TGF-β manipulation has rescued autoimmune and chronic inflammatory phenotypes in experimental models and motivates clinical modulation in immune-mediated diseases, with careful attention to dose/timing and tissue specificity. <cite id="3c3e25ba-2">TGF-β experimental modulation controls autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-9">TGF-β suppresses cytokine production by T-cell effectors</cite>.
- Engineered cytokine binders demonstrate feasibility of protein-based "sponges" that neutralize toxic cytokine levels, offering oral or localized therapy options to complement injectables. <cite id="291d2d66-5">Receptor-derived peptides bind and neutralize proinflammatory cytokines</cite>.

# Practical caveats

- Cytokine networks are redundant and context-specific; blocking one axis can shift pathology to another (e.g., TNF suppression can increase IL-6 or IL-1 signaling). Treatments that reprogram cell-intrinsic anti-inflammatory programs (IL-10, TGF-β) may be more durable because they alter cellular homeostasis rather than transiently neutralizing a single cytokine. <cite id="a578b52b-3">IL-10 reduces innate inflammatory signaling by inhibiting TLR pathways</cite> <cite id="3c3e25ba-0">TGF-β's dual roles mean indiscriminate modulation can be pathogenic</cite>.
- Delivery and bioavailability remain key determinants; systemic TNF antibodies face cytokine rebound; local IL-10 gene therapy shows stronger cytokine suppression at the target. <cite id="1de81f7b-5">Anti-TNF agents bind both soluble and membrane TNF, but responses can vary across contexts</cite> <cite id="a578b52b-7">Local IL-10 expression drives cytokine downregulation at the site</cite>.

# Takeaway

Proteins modulate proinflammatory cytokines by directly binding and neutralizing cytokines, intercepting receptors, reprogramming intracellular signaling, or reinforcing endogenous anti-inflammatory cytokine networks. These mechanisms underpin successful therapies across inflammatory diseases—most prominently TNF receptor fusion proteins and IL-10 pathway reinforcement—with growing evidence for TGF-β–based and engineered peptide approaches. The strongest therapeutic support comes from TNF blockers in immune-mediated arthritis and skin/joint inflammation, IL-10 delivery/localization strategies in chronic gut and tissue injury, and context-aware TGF-β modulation in autoimmunity and fibroinflammatory states. <cite id="291d2d66-0">Therapeutic strategies targeting cytokine-driven inflammation are an established approach in disorders with cytokine-mediated pathology</cite> <cite id="291d2d66-4">Inhibiting proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1 is a recognized therapeutic avenue</cite> <cite id="291d2d66-5">Engineered receptors/peptides that bind proinflammatory cytokines offer additional anti-inflammatory therapeutics</cite> <cite id="291d2d66-7">Endogenous proteins like POP2 can blunt destructive inflammatory pathways</cite>.

# Short answer

- Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) such as plasmids, phages, integrative conjugative elements (ICEs), and integrons generate bacterial genetic diversity primarily by moving genes—resistance, virulence, metabolism—and by catalyzing recombination and chromosomal integration; they also accelerate adaptation through rapid access to accessory traits and pangenome acquisition <cite id="9c98c83c-0">Mobile genetic elements are key to the evolution of bacteria and traits that affect host and ecosystem health.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-3">Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are crucial for horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in bacteria and facilitate their rapid evolution and adaptation.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-5">Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are key promoters of microbial evolution. These elements can be located extrachromosomally or integrated into the chromosome.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-4">Mobile elements are known to potentiate gene gain and loss, a major force that can profoundly change bacterial fitness.</cite> 
- They shape host specificity by both relaxing it (enabling access to new niches through new virulence or colonization determinants) and tightening it (via host-range determinants encoded on the element or counter-adaptations like restriction-modification, CRISPR-Cas, and phage anti-CRISPRs) <cite id="9c98c83c-1">Mobile elements can carry genes that make bacteria resistant to antibiotics, harmful to humans, or able to use new food sources.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-7">The host range of MGEs varies widely—some have a broad host range, while others are restricted to a single strain or species.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-8">Indeed, the ability to confer beneficial traits on their hosts is the most conspicuous feature of many MGEs.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-8">Integrative and conjugative elements are “hot” vectors for the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-8">Bacteria utilize CRISPR-Cas adaptive immune systems for protection from bacteriophages; some phages produce anti-CRISPR proteins.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-3">Restriction-modification systems are important barriers to plasmid transfer and have left their mark on plasmids over long evolutionary times.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-5">Temperate phages integrate as prophages and can contribute genes to bacterial pathogenicity.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-0">Lysogeny by temperate phages can take precedence over CRISPR-Cas immunity in some cases.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-9">Temperate phages consistently exhibit higher microdiversity than virulent counterparts in multiple comparisons.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">ICEs/IMEs act as gene shuttles and promote increased large-scale chromosomal transfer events, shaping the host genome structure.</cite>

# Mechanisms by which MGEs create genetic diversity

- Gene flow without phylogenetic constraint: Plasmids and ICEs mobilize phenotypic-carrying modules (resistance, virulence, metabolic pathways) across phylogenetically distant lineages, fueling within- and across-species diversity <cite id="da39d9e4-2">ICEs/IMEs not only act as gene shuttles ferrying various phenotypic genes, but also promote increased large-scale chromosomal transfer events, shaping the host.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-3">Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) are prominent drivers of horizontal gene transfer.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-5">Horizontal gene transfer, mediated by conjugative plasmids, is a major driver of the global rise of antibiotic resistance.</cite> 
- Pangenome expansion via chromosomal integration: Integrative elements excise, transfer, and reintegrate, reshaping chromosomal neighborhoods and enabling mosaic genomes; they also trigger recombinational exchange with donor DNA <cite id="da39d9e4-1">ICEs can excise, replicate, and transfer from cell to cell and then integrate back into the host chromosome.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">ICEs/IMEs promote increased large-scale chromosomal transfer events, shaping the host genome structure.</cite> 
- Recombination hotspots and cassette turnover: Integron systems package gene cassettes at att sites, enabling rapid gain/loss of accessory genes that modify metabolism, virulence regulation, and environmental responses <cite id="da39d9e4-7">Integron cassettes commonly integrate into bacterial genomes via widespread non-classical attG sites.</cite> 
- Mutation amplification upon entry: Some broad-host-range plasmids encode mutagenic functions (umuDC homologues) that elevate mutation rates transiently during invasion, creating allele microdiversity as they spread <cite id="da39d9e4-7">These plasmids frequently encode UmuDC homologues that boost the mutation rate of the bacterial host upon entry.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-7">CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial across phages, highlighting variable selection pressures on host–phage coevolution.</cite> 
- Phage-mediated innovation: Temperate phages deliver accessory cargo (virulence regulators, toxins, colonization factors) and can rewire host fitness; prophage induction can also lyse cells and release genes, shaping ecological dynamics and opportunity for resistant lineages <cite id="6586493d-5">Temperate phages integrate into host chromosomes as prophages, with prior studies detailing roles in bacterial pathogenicity.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-0">Lysogeny by temperate phages can override CRISPR-Cas immunity, influencing diversification trajectories.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-4">Imperfect CRISPR targeting of prophages is assumed to yield large ecological footprints as prophages reactivate and lyse host cells.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-1">Mobile elements can carry genes that allow use of new food sources and antibiotic resistance.</cite> 

# How plasmids and ICEs shape diversity and niche breadth

- Antibiotic resistance and clinically relevant lineages: Conjugative plasmids are a principal engine of ESBL and carbapenemase spread globally, reorganizing clonal complexes via plasmid–chromosome integration and recombination, which increases between-strain diversity and the fitness of resistant subpopulations <cite id="552f38ac-5">Horizontal gene transfer, mediated by conjugative plasmids, is a major driver of the global rise of antibiotic resistance.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">ICEs/IMEs act as gene shuttles and can drive chromosomal transfer events, shaping host genomes.</cite> 
- Broad host range vs. strain specificity: Plasmid host range spans family-level transfers for some narrow-partitioning elements to within-genus constraints for others; the distribution of host compatibility and strain-specific factors explains patchy dissemination of resistance determinants within clinical and environmental communities <cite id="552f38ac-1">Some NHR plasmids can transfer across family-level groups of bacterial hosts, whereas others are apparently restricted within a single bacterial genus.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-2">The DNA phosphorothioation restriction-modification system influences antimicrobial resistance and plasmid stability across species.</cite> 
- “Hot” vectors and fitness effects: ICEs are repeatedly identified as efficient vectors of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, with evidence they catalyze large-scale chromosomal transfer, accelerating adaptive evolution and pangenome turnover within strains and across ecologically connected populations <cite id="da39d9e4-8">Integrative and conjugative elements are “hot” vectors for dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">They promote large-scale chromosomal transfer events, shaping host genome structure.</cite> 
- Microdiversity via temperate phages: Prophage-associated microdiversity exceeds that of virulent phages, consistent with lysogenic maintenance of diverse accessory gene repertoires that seed adaptive divergence when excision or transfer occurs <cite id="6586493d-9">Temperate phages exhibit significantly higher microdiversity than virulent counterparts in multiple comparisons.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-2">Temperate phages replicate either lysogenically as prophages or produce virions, linking host population dynamics to adaptation.</cite> 

# Host specificity: barriers, coevolution, and narrowing/broadening

- Built-in barriers (RM and CRISPR) refine host specificity: Restriction–modification systems impose stringent sequence/CpG specificity, reducing plasmid uptake across species; their signatures are imprinted on plasmid replication origins and partitioning modules, reinforcing strain-specific plasmid maintenance <cite id="552f38ac-3">Restriction-modification systems are important barriers to plasmid transfer and have left evolutionary marks on plasmids.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-2">Phosphorothioation-based systems influence resistance and plasmid stability across hosts.</cite> 
- Immune evasion and shifting boundaries: CRISPR-Cas reduces prophage success, but temperate phages frequently circumvent immunity or trigger prophage reactivation, producing dynamic coevolution that maintains diverse temperate phage populations and can promote niche shifts in host bacteria <cite id="6586493d-0">Temperate phage lysogeny can overtake CRISPR-Cas immunity in some cases.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-8">Bacteriophages encode anti-CRISPR proteins that suppress Cas systems, underscoring arms races and variable fitness landscapes.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-4">CRISPR targeting of prophages depends on imperfect matches, enabling prophage reactivation and lysis that shape bacterial ecology.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-1">Temperate phages enhance microbial adaptation via interactions orchestrating population-level dynamics.</cite> 
- Pathogenicity islands and ecological niche: Pathogenicity islands, often mobilizable by MGEs, encode colonization/virulence determinants and regulatory modules; their movement across strains and species broadens host use of pathogens (e.g., EHEC from environmental to human niches), while chromosomal integration hotspots (att sites) promote repeated turnover and strain-differentiation <cite id="552f38ac-0">Genomic islands are involved in dissemination of variable genes across bacteria.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-8">Pathogenicity islands are large groups of mobile elements associated with pathogenicity.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-7">Integron cassettes integrate via widespread attG sites, enabling rapid cassette turnover.</cite> 
- Species- and strain-level compatibility: Compatibility of plasmids and genomic islands with species- or strain-specific conjugal machinery (trales, relaxases) and chromosomal integration sites dictates whether transfer is successful, producing clonally structured diversity when compatibility is rare and panmictic gene flow when compatibility is common <cite id="552f38ac-1">Plasmid host range varies from family-wide transfer to genus-level restriction, reflecting compatibility with host partitioning systems.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-6">Plasmid host range reflects whether it can transfer, replicate, and persist in the bacterial host.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-1">ICEs integrate after excision and transfer, coupling compatibility with recombination outcomes.</cite> 

# Integration into ecological and evolutionary outcomes

- Pangenome dynamics: MGE-mediated gene turnover expands and reshapes the pangenome; accessory genes are gained/lost rapidly, enabling fluctuating fitness in changing environments and maintaining adaptive potential within bacterial strain complexes <cite id="9c98c83c-3">MGEs crucially drive HGT and rapid bacterial evolution and adaptation.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-3">ICEs are prominent drivers of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">They promote chromosomal transfer events and shape host genome structure.</cite> 
- Within-strain vs. between-strain diversity: Conjugation and ICE activity generate within-strain mosaic genomes and microdiversity via recombination and prophage-mediated gene exchange; plasmid-mediated resistance spreads between strains and clonally structured lineages, elevating between-strain diversity as successful clones expand with particular accessory gene combinations <cite id="552f38ac-5">Conjugative plasmids drive global rise of antibiotic resistance, a clear example of HGT-driven between-strain diversity.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-2">ICEs/IMEs act as gene shuttles and increase large-scale chromosomal transfer, shaping within-host genome architecture.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-9">Temperate phages carry higher microdiversity than virulent phages, consistent with within-population strain differentiation.</cite> 
- Host specificity spectra: Some elements have broad host ranges (e.g., certain plasmids, temperate phages) and seed multi-strain adaptation or new ecological niches, while others are strain- or species-specific, often due to stringent immunity or compatibility constraints, maintaining clonality and narrow host use <cite id="9c98c83c-7">MGE host range varies widely, from single strain to species-level breadth.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-1">NHR plasmids span family-level transfer to genus-level restriction.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-3">RM barriers significantly limit plasmid transfer across species, preserving host specificity.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-8">Prophage-encoded anti-CRISPRs illustrate mechanisms of narrowing effective host ranges through immune suppression.</cite> 

# Examples that tie mechanisms to patterns

- ESBL and carbapenemase outbreaks: Plasmid-mediated resistance cassettes and ICE-borne modules integrate into chromosomes and mobilize via conjugation, fueling rapid, multi-locus resistance diversity and emergent, highly virulent lineages across hospitals and environments <cite id="da39d9e4-8">ICEs are hot vectors for antibiotic resistance dissemination.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-5">Conjugative plasmids are major drivers of global antibiotic resistance rise.</cite> 
- Prophage-borne virulence and adaptation: Temperate phages often encode or regulate virulence traits and can switch between lysogeny and lysis, influencing colonization success and triggering CRISPR-mediated selection waves; in some cases, prophage takeover surpasses CRISPR defenses, accelerating diversification into new niches <cite id="6586493d-5">Temperate phages contribute to bacterial pathogenicity via prophage integration.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-0">Lysogeny can outcompete CRISPR-Cas immunity, guiding adaptive diversification.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-4">Imperfect CRISPR targeting of prophages permits reactivation and ecological impact.</cite> 
- RM- and plasmid-shaped community diversity: Bacterial RM systems and plasmid modification adaptations sculpt which conjugative plasmids persist in each community, producing structured diversity by species and strain; this yields patchy distribution of resistance and niche partitioning even among closely related taxa <cite id="552f38ac-3">RM systems are pervasive barriers to plasmid transfer and leave evolutionary imprints on plasmids.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-2">Phosphorothioation-based systems in RM impact plasmid stability and resistance prevalence across species.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-1">Narrow- vs. broad-host plasmids reflect compatibility across species boundaries.</cite> 

# Synthesis: net effect on diversity and specificity

- Net effect is context-dependent. In nutrient-rich or clinically stressed environments with frequent encounters, MGEs predominantly broaden gene pools, increase microdiversity, and drive rapid adaptive evolution through HGT and prophage-mediated turnover, often expanding host use when new colonization/virulence genes are acquired <cite id="9c98c83c-3">MGEs are crucial for HGT and rapid evolution and adaptation.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-1">MGEs carry genes for antibiotic resistance, pathogenicity, and niche exploitation.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-1">Temperate phages enhance microbial adaptation via population-level interactions.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-8">ICEs act as efficient hot vectors dispersing resistance and virulence genes across lineages.</cite> 
- In systems with strong species- or strain-specific immunity (RM, CRISPR, Acr-mediated), MGEs often drive finer-scale diversification and clonality, maintaining narrow host specificity unless counter-adaptations (plasmid modifications, prophage interference, mutagenesis) emerge to breach barriers, at which point host breadth can rapidly widen again <cite id="552f38ac-3">RM systems are key barriers to plasmid transfer, preserving host specificity.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-8">Phages encode anti-CRISPR proteins that suppress Cas, enabling escape from narrow immunity.</cite> <cite id="6586493d-0">Lysogeny can override CRISPR, allowing adaptation in constrained hosts.</cite> <cite id="da39d9e4-7">MGE cargo and chromosomal integration sites enable rapid gain/loss of determinants, maintaining microdiversity under constraints.</cite> 
- Across ecosystems, MGEs therefore operate as engines and pacemakers of bacterial evolution: they increase genetic diversity via modular gene exchange and mutagenic mobilization, while host specificity is a dynamic outcome of compatibility, immunity, and coevolutionary feedbacks among plasmids, prophages, chromosomal islands, and defense systems <cite id="9c98c83c-0">MGEs are key to bacterial evolution and trait evolution affecting hosts and ecosystems.</cite> <cite id="9c98c83c-7">MGE host ranges vary widely, shaping whether diversity accrues within or across species.</cite> <cite id="552f38ac-6">Plasmid host range depends on whether they can transfer, replicate, and persist in a given host, emphasizing compatibility-mediated specificity.</cite>

Summary
Horizontal transfer of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) relies on mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that package, move, and integrate resistance determinants across bacterial cells and species. Conjugative plasmids, integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs), integron systems, and bacteriophages are the principal MGE mediators, each coupling transfer machinery with gene-cassette architectures that boost acquisition, stability, and reshuffling of resistance traits. <cite id="982a2495-0">Antibiotic resistance genes can spread via HGT through MGEs among bacteria</cite> <cite id="982a2495-8">The characteristics of the major MGEs involved in acquisition and spread of antibiotic resistance are outlined in dedicated reviews</cite> <cite id="41477165-1">Conjugation is a major mechanism driving the spread of antibiotic resistance</cite>.

Mechanisms by MGE class

Conjugative plasmids: transfer machines and mobilome shuffling
- Plasmids encode the core transfer apparatus: a relaxase that cleaves a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) at oriT and an assembly of mating pore proteins (mating pair formation, MPF) that couple donor and recipient membranes for DNA transfer. The relaxase–oriT nucleoprotein complex is exported via the MPF of the conjugative element, mediating unidirectional DNA strand transfer to a partner cell. <cite id="41477165-0">Relaxase interacts with plasmid oriT; the resulting nucleoprotein complex is transported by the MPF of a conjugative element</cite> <cite id="41477165-7">Relaxases are essential for conjugative transfer, cleaving DNA strands and forming covalent phosphotyrosine linkages</cite> <cite id="41477165-4">Conjugation involves pairing through structures in cell membranes and transfer of DNA from one cell to another</cite>.
- Conjugation is a dominant route for AMR dissemination, moving multidrug-resistance modules rapidly across lineages and ecological niches. <cite id="41477165-1">Conjugation drives the spread of antibiotic resistance, rhizobial traits, and complex virulence factors</cite> <cite id="41477165-8">Plasmids are key players in the rapid spread of AMR by transferring resistance genes via HGT</cite>.
- Non-conjugative plasmids can “hitchhike” on mobilizable cargo: oriT-bearing plasmids mobilize other AMR plasmids that lack their own transfer genes, broadening the reach of resistance. <cite id="41477165-2">Conjugative plasmids can facilitate horizontal transfer of diverse antimicrobial-resistance plasmids that lack Mob genes</cite> <cite id="41477165-5">Multiple origin-of-transfer regions might aid the spread of AMR from environmental reservoirs to pathogens</cite>.
- Environmental and population signals further increase transfer rates, enabling “hitchhiking” under antibiotic pressure. <cite id="41477165-4">A small signal triggers bacterial conjugation via a hitchhiking mechanism</cite>.

Integrons and ICEs: chromosomal integration and gene-cassette exchange
- Integrative and conjugative elements (ICEs) integrate into the host chromosome as modular MGEs, remain resident while encoding functions to excise and transfer, and frequently relocate to spread advantageous cargo like AMR genes. ICEs encode self-conjugation modules and can transfer between cells, often under physiological stress, to disseminate beneficial traits. <cite id="95ba196a-0">ICEs are modular MGEs integrated into host genomes, passively copied once mobilized, and encode functions for excision and transfer</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-3">ICEs are frequently located in bacterial chromosomes and encode self-conjugation modules, enabling transfer between cells</cite>.
- Integron systems capture and express AMR gene cassettes: a site-specific integrase recombines at att sites (attI/receiver in the integron, attC/cassettes) to integrate new cassettes, creating arrays that can be transcribed via promiscuous regulatory elements. This enables rapid assembly of multi-gene resistance operons and exchange among donor–recipient lineages. <cite id="95ba196a-1">Integrons possess a recombination system for integration, expression, and exchange of gene cassettes</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-2">Integrons contain a site-specific recombination system able to integrate, express and exchange DNA elements called gene cassettes</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-8">Integration of circular gene cassettes occurs by site-specific recombination between attI and attC, assisted by the integron integrase</cite>.
- Together, ICEs and integrons expand genetic repertoire and fitness landscapes: pairing ICE transfer with diverse cargo allows communities to adapt quickly to antibiotics and other stresses. <cite id="95ba196a-5">By pairing ICE machinery with diverse cargo, bacterial communities expand their genetic repertoire</cite>.

Bacteriophages: specialized and generalized transduction
- Temperate phages mediate HGT via two routes. Generalized transduction packages random bacterial DNA fragments into capsids; upon infection, recipient cells receive chromosomal fragments that can integrate, enabling uptake of ARGs when packaging coincides with resistance genes. Specialized transduction packages specific host genes (often near IS elements) and transfers them with high precision, facilitating rapid transfer of resistance operons or marker genes. <cite id="cbcc13fa-0">Generalized transduction transfers any portion of the donor genome to the recipient by lytic or lysogenic routes</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-1">Phage-mediated HGT occurs via generalized or specialized transduction; generalized transducing particles arise by aberrant packaging</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-3">Specialized transduction transfers a restricted set of bacterial genes to another bacterium</cite>.
- Phage-mediated transfer can be bidirectionally beneficial under antibiotics: phages and bacteria cooperate through DNA integration and other mechanisms, reinforcing survival during antibiotic exposure and creating new opportunities to mobilize adjacent resistance genes. <cite id="cbcc13fa-5">Bacteria and generalized transducing phages cooperate to survive adverse conditions such as antibiotics by phage integration</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-2">Phage lysogenic conversion and transduction contribute to HGT of genetic material</cite>.
- Collectively, phage vectors bridge niches and taxonomic distances, delivering ARGs into novel hosts where integron/ICE machinery can integrate or conjugate them. <cite id="cbcc13fa-0">Generalized transduction implicates transfer of any portion of the donor genome by lytic or lysogenic routes</cite> <cite id="982a2495-3">MGEs are primary facilitators in the global spread of antibiotic resistance</cite>.

Complementary mobilizers and gene-cassette architectures that increase transfer efficiency
- oriT-carrying mobilizing plasmids and broad host-range transfer modules increase the probability of successful mobilization, sometimes enabling transfer of non-mobilizable plasmids and enhancing AMR gene spread across unrelated species. <cite id="41477165-2">OriT-bearing plasmids can mobilize AMR plasmids lacking Mob genes</cite> <cite id="41477165-5">Multiple plasmid origin-of-transfer regions might aid the spread of AMR</cite>.
- Integron backbones provide stable expression platforms; gene cassettes are modular, easily gained/lost, and exchangeable, accelerating the assembly of multi-drug resistance (e.g., aminoglycoside resistance followed by beta-lactamase cassettes) and promoting lateral reshuffling during outbreaks. <cite id="95ba196a-1">Integron systems integrate, express, and exchange gene cassettes</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-2">Integrons use site-specific recombination to integrate and express gene cassettes</cite>.
- ICEs integrate and excise using site-specific recombinases and conjugation modules, pairing with AMR cargo to increase fitness under antibiotic selection; once integrated into chromosomes, ICEs become reservoirs and vectors for subsequent dissemination. <cite id="95ba196a-0">ICEs integrate into host genomes, encode transfer functions, and are passively mobilized once excised</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-3">ICEs encode self-conjugation modules and are frequently located in chromosomes</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-8">attI–attC recombination by integrase integrates circular cassettes</cite>.

Ecological and evolutionary drivers of successful dissemination

Fitness landscapes and gene mosaicism
- ARGs hitchhike on beneficial MGEs and increase fitness by combining modules through integron cassettes; once established, ICEs enable chromosomal integration and further spread. This combinatorial “mosaic evolution” explains rapid emergence of multidrug resistance. <cite id="982a2495-1">Resistant genes spread and are acquired through MGEs, which are essential for facilitating HGT</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-5">Pairing ICE machinery with diverse cargo significantly expands genetic repertoire, enabling adaptation</cite>.
- Stress and antibiotic pressure upregulate transfer: conjugation and specialized transduction increase under sublethal antibiotics; phage-bacterial cooperation is strengthened during drug exposure, increasing transfer efficiency of resistance determinants. <cite id="982a2495-4">This mini-review explores conjugative plasmids’ behavior in environments, including signals controlling transfer</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-5">Bacteria and generalized transducing phages cooperate to survive antibiotics via phage integration</cite>.

Population genetics and reservoirs
- Environmental reservoirs (soil, water, gut microbiomes) serve as mixing vessels where plasmids, phages, and integrons exchange cargo; oriT and att site diversity, along with transient conjugation bridges, route AMR from reservoirs into pathogens. <cite id="41477165-5">Hypothetical networks of origin-of-transfer regions facilitate transfer of AMR from environmental reservoirs to human pathogens</cite> <cite id="982a2495-4">Conjugative plasmids exhibit behaviors and transfer dynamics across environments</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-8">Integron gene cassettes integrate by attI–attC recombination</cite>.

Strategies of the mobilome to disseminate resistance

Packaging, protection, and integration
- MGEs encode packaging signals, relaxases, and integration cassettes that ensure resistance DNA is transported intact and incorporated into new genomes; plasmid ssDNA transfer intermediates and phage-packaged fragments are protected during transit, while site-specific recombinases at integrons drive circular-cassette integration. <cite id="95ba196a-1">Integrons possess recombination systems for integration and exchange of gene cassettes</cite> <cite id="41477165-7">Relaxases cleave DNA and form covalent linkages for conjugation</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-0">Generalized transduction transfers donor DNA fragments to recipient cells by phage</cite>.
- Non-selective routes like generalized transduction increase the chance that ARGs reach recipients, while specialized transduction and conjugation focus on precise, efficient transfer of larger units (plasmids, ICEs), balancing fidelity with reach. <cite id="cbcc13fa-1">Generalized transducing particles arise by aberrant packaging, enabling transfer of random DNA segments</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-0">ICEs integrate into the chromosome and encode transfer functions for dissemination</cite>.

Numbers matter: copy number and mobilization cues
- High-copy-number plasmids and partitioning systems amplify transfer opportunities; mobilizable plasmids and oriT hotspots accelerate conjugation, and environmental signals (quorum sensing, metal stress, antibiotics) trigger transfer programs, collectively increasing ARG dissemination rates. <cite id="41477165-4">Antibiotic pressure elicits conjugation via hitchhiking mechanisms, indicating environmental cues can trigger transfer</cite> <cite id="41477165-5">Multiple origins of transfer aid spread of AMR from reservoirs to pathogens</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-3">ICEs encode self-conjugation to transfer between cells, frequently located in chromosomes</cite>.

Impact and implications

Rising transmission and intervention targets
- MGE-facilitated HGT is a primary engine of ARG dissemination globally, with plasmids, phages, and integrons collectively accelerating the spread of multidrug resistance and enabling rapid evolution of resistance in clinical pathogens. <cite id="982a2495-3">MGEs are primary facilitators in the global spread of antibiotic resistance</cite> <cite id="982a2495-8">The major MGE types involved in acquisition and spread of antibiotic resistance are characterized</cite>.
- Targeting MGE functions—relaxase–oriT transfer, MPF pilus assembly, phage packaging and integration, and integron/intICE recombination—directly impedes ARG transfer. Disrupting conjugation machinery or phage integration reduces resistance propagation under antibiotics. <cite id="41477165-7">Relaxases are essential for conjugation; inhibiting them propagates to conjugation</cite> <cite id="41477165-4">Interrupting conjugation pathways breaks antibiotic-driven hitchhiking</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-5">Inhibiting cooperation between bacteria and generalized transducing phages reduces survival under antibiotics</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-0">ICEs are modular MGEs that can be targeted to prevent excision/transfer</cite>.

Take-home points
- MGEs facilitate HGT of AMR genes by providing transfer machinery, gene-cassette architectures, and mobilization strategies across bacteria and into clinical pathogens. Plasmid conjugation, ICE chromosomal integration, integron cassette exchange, and phage-mediated transduction collectively package, transmit, and integrate ARGs. Stress and antibiotic pressure increase transfer rates, while modularity enables rapid multi-gene resistance assembly. <cite id="982a2495-1">MGEs are essential facilitators of HGT of resistant genes</cite> <cite id="41477165-0">Relaxase–oriT complexes and MPF underpin conjugation-based transfer</cite> <cite id="95ba196a-8">Integron integrase mediates attI–attC integration of gene cassettes</cite> <cite id="cbcc13fa-1">Phages mediate generalized and specialized transduction of bacterial DNA</cite> <cite id="982a2495-3">MGEs are central facilitators of the global ARG spread</cite>.

# Executive summary

Immunocompetent critically ill patients with viral pneumonia typically present with rapidly progressing respiratory failure and radiographic patterns of consolidation, ground-glass opacity, and nodular opacities, often sparing the upper lobes and sparing the lung apices—features that overlap with “atypical pneumonia.” <cite id="1d715476-2">Viral pneumonia commonly shows bronchopneumonia, multifocal airspace consolidation, and ground-glass/nodule patterns on imaging</cite><cite id="1d715476-6">Viral pneumonia is classically an atypical pattern including ground-glass opacity and nodular consolidations</cite><cite id="1d715476-8">High-resolution CT reviews delineate viral pneumonia radiologic phenotypes across pathogens</cite>. In contrast, immunocompromised ICU patients often have bilateral, peripheral, and often extensive GGO/consolidation reflecting primary opportunistic viral pneumonitis (e.g., varicella-zoster virus [VZV], cytomegalovirus [CMV]) or superimposed invasive fungal pneumonia—imaging is essential but insufficient to name the pathogen and must be paired with molecular diagnostics and clinical immune context. <cite id="1d715476-1">Imaging is pivotal for diagnosing pneumonia and guiding ICU care</cite><cite id="1d715476-5">Imaging features and newer modalities are central to recognizing pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts</cite><cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV pneumonia on CT shows bilateral GGOs/halos with multiple nodular shadows</cite><cite id="22d487d6-3">CMV pneumonia in non-AIDS immunocompromised adults shows bilateral mixed GGO and consolidation on HRCT</cite>. Immunologically, immunocompetent critical illness is dominated by a cytokine-driven “storm” with lymphopenia and coagulopathy, whereas immunosuppressed critical illness shows suppressed innate responses with persistent infection and high mortality largely dictated by severity and overall status. <cite id="426162e9-2">Infected critical illness commonly shows lymphopenia and a cytokine storm with IL-6, TNFα, IL-1β elevation</cite><cite id="1d715476-4">Guidelines emphasize testing strategies for severe respiratory infections in immunocompromised ICU patients</cite><cite id="1d715476-7">In immunocompromised ARF with virus detection, mortality is high and driven by severity and poor general status</cite><cite id="426162e9-8">Vaccination and infection trigger strong immune activity, with elevated D-dimer and coagulopathy</cite>.

# Clinical course and immune-pathophysiology

In immunocompetent hosts, severe viral pneumonia (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) is characterized by early viral replication, innate immune sensing, and a prominent neutrophilic and cytokine-driven acute respiratory distress phenotype with hypoxemia and rapid radiographic progression. <cite id="1d715476-2">Immunocompetent viral pneumonia often has multifocal and bronchopneumonia patterns on imaging</cite><cite id="426162e9-1">ARDS from SARS-CoV showed higher plasma IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α</cite>. Therapies that dampen hyperinflammation (e.g., IL-6 blockade) are used in cytokine storm phenotypes. <cite id="426162e9-6">Steroids and IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab) are recommended for cytokine storm/hyperinflammation in inflammatory pneumonia</cite>.

In immunocompromised hosts, key immune axes are blunted (e.g., impaired T-cell function, lymphopenia), allowing primary viral pneumonias (VZV, CMV, adenovirus) or reactivations to dominate, with less bronchiolar/acinari neutrophilic consolidation and more diffuse, bilateral GGO/“granular” shadowing. Systemically, these patients often lack or fail to mount effective inflammatory cytokine cascades, leading to persistent infection with progressive hypoxemia, higher risk of superimposed invasive aspergillosis (Aspergillus) and fungal “pathergy,” and multiorgan involvement without the typical self-limited cytokine storm. <cite id="1d715476-5">PFM review highlights updated imaging features and emphasizes immune context in immunocompromised disease</cite><cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV CT findings include bilateral GGO/halos and nodular shadows</cite><cite id="6f63743c-2">Steroid exposure prolongs mechanical ventilation and ICU stay in severe VZV pneumonia</cite>.

# Presentation and imaging patterns

- Immunocompetent:
  - Clinical course: abrupt viral prodrome, tachypnea/desaturation, sometimes high-yield sputum or throat PCR, and risk of ARDS with secondary bacterial invasion; imaging shows patchy GGO, consolidation, and nodules that confluent rapidly. <cite id="1d715476-2">Viral pneumonia phenotypes include bronchopneumonia (~30%) and multifocal airspace pattern (~25%) with ground-glass/nodules on CT</cite><cite id="1d715476-6">Viral pneumonias present with ground-glass and nodular consolidations (atypical)</cite>.
  - Imaging: chest radiograph/CT often demonstrates peripheral and lower-lobe predominance, GGO, consolidation, and nodular opacities; ultrasound can identify consolidation/hydrostatic edema. <cite id="1d715476-1">Chest radiography, lung ultrasound, and CT all have roles; CT improves resolution for pneumonia</cite><cite id="6f63743c-8">Radiologic CT reviews outline viral pneumonia patterns across pathogens</cite>.

- Immunocompromised:
  - Clinical course: higher baseline comorbidity and steroid use; subtle or atypical respiratory symptoms with rapid deterioration, often bilateral and severe radiographic infiltrates despite low early fever; risk of refractory hypoxemia and sepsis from superimposed bacteria or fungi. <cite id="1d715476-1">Imaging is pivotal but must be integrated with clinical context</cite>.
  - Imaging patterns: bilateral, peripheral, and often extensive GGO with small nodules and scattered consolidation; HRCT classically shows bilateral mixed GGO and poorly defined centrilobular nodules in CMV, and multi-nodular/fusion shadows with bilateral halos in VZV; CT improves diagnostic yield beyond radiography but cannot definitively assign etiology. <cite id="22d487d6-1">In immunocompromised patients, bilateral GGO, minimal consolidation, and small nodules are common CT findings</cite><cite id="22d487d6-2">Radiology reference: CMV infection shows GGOs and thin-section CT patterns in immunocompromised patients</cite><cite id="22d487d6-3">CMV HRCT: bilateral mixed GGO and poorly defined centrilobular small nodules</cite><cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV CT shows multiple fusion nodular shadows with bilateral halos or GGOs</cite>.

# Diagnostic recognition and microbiology

Immunocompetent patients often clear infection with supportive care, antivirals (when available), and antibiotics for secondary infection; imaging correlates, PCR on respiratory samples, and clinical response guide management. <cite id="1d715476-1">Imaging, ultrasound, and CT guide diagnosis and therapy but must be coupled with laboratory testing</cite><cite id="1d715476-2">Viral phenotypes on imaging and PCR help confirm diagnosis</cite>.

Immunocompromised ICU patients require a high index of suspicion for opportunistic viral pathogens (VZV in reactivation/steroid context, CMV in transplant/bone marrow, adenovirus in solid organ and transplant), and for superimposed invasive aspergillosis in neutropenic/severe courses; workup typically includes bronchoscopy with BAL for PCR/NAAT and fungal stains/culture; imaging-based “halos,” branching centrilobular nodules, and air crescents raise alert for necrotizing/fungal superinfection. <cite id="1d715476-4">Contemporary guidelines for severe respiratory infections in immunocompromised hosts advise layered testing strategies</cite><cite id="6f63743c-2">Steroids worsen severity and prolong organ support in VZV pneumonia, suggesting careful steroid review and antiviral therapy</cite><cite id="6f63743c-1">CT improves resolution but etiologic diagnosis in immunocompromised hosts still requires microbiologic testing</cite>. Molecular diagnosis is essential because imaging alone cannot unambiguously identify the pathogen. <cite id="1d715476-3">Recent advances in microbiologic diagnostics (PCR/dNA technologies) target pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts</cite><cite id="6f63743c-9">Approach to pulmonary infection emphasizes CT and PCR for VZV (and influenza) in ICU candidates</cite>.

Immunophenotypic markers that help distinguish mechanisms include profound lymphopenia with elevated inflammatory markers in immunocompetent hyperinflammatory ARDS vs persistent lymphopenia with poor inflammatory response and undetectable cytokines in selected immunosuppressed cases—though these are nonspecific and must be read with clinical immune context. <cite id="426162e9-2">Lymphopenia with IL-6/TNF/IL-1 elevation is common in viral ARDS</cite><cite id="426162e9-8">Strong immune activation associates with lymphopenia and coagulopathy (raised D-dimer)</cite>. The presence of fungal imaging and neutropenia/steroids should trigger Aspergillus-directed evaluation and therapy. <cite id="1d715476-5">Imaging features in immunocompromised hosts and updated diagnostics are linked; fungal complications require targeted evaluation</cite>.

# Complications and extrapulmonary “OPSI-like” disease

Immunocompetent ARDS with viral etiology has frequent secondary bacterial superinfections and fluid overload physiology; management emphasizes proning, ventilator strategies, corticosteroids for bacterial pneumonia, and sometimes anti-IL-6 for hyperinflammation. <cite id="426162e9-9">Steroids improve outcomes in severe community-acquired pneumonia; IL-6 blockade used for hyperinflammation in ARDS</cite>.

Immunocompromised critical illness is marked by frequent “pneumopathy”/organizing pneumonia–like courses and pathergy-like systemic disease: upper-airway/cutaneous/visceral lesions with systemic vasculopathy, shock, and respiratory failure from viral reactivations (notably VZV), sometimes with disseminated fungal involvement in neutropenic/severely debilitated patients. CT “granular,” consolidative patterns with halos and nodules, plus systemic rash and neurologic/cardiac involvement, argue for VZV or mixed infection/fungal superinfection; prompt immune reconstitution and antiviral/fungal therapy are crucial. <cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV severe pneumonia on CT shows bilateral GGO/halo opacities and nodular shadows</cite><cite id="6f63743c-3">Varicella pneumonia can be defined by chickenpox rash with CT infiltrates, highlighting systemic-to-pulmonary synchrony</cite><cite id="6f63743c-7">Corticosteroid tapering after COVID-19 can precipitate severe VZV pneumonia</cite>.

# ICU management: decision rules and pitfalls

- Recognize imaging red flags: bilateral, rapidly progressive GGO/consolidation with centrilobular nodules, halos, or nodular fusion shadows favor opportunistic VZV/CMV or aspergillosis; in immunosuppressed patients without rapid cytokine storm, consider reactivation versus primary infection. <cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV bilateral halos/GGO and nodular fusion shadows on CT</cite><cite id="22d487d6-3">CMV HRCT patterns include bilateral GGO/consolidation and centrilobular nodules</cite>.
- Don’t rely on imaging alone: combine with BAL/bronchoscopy PCR for VZV/CMV/adenovirus and fungal cultures/histology; consider fungal PCR/Aspergillus culture especially in neutropenic courses. <cite id="1d715476-1">Imaging plus directed tests are needed to manage ICU pneumonia</cite><cite id="6f63743c-1">Bronchoscopy with BAL helps identify pathogen in immunocompromised pneumonia</cite><cite id="1d715476-5">PFM reviews emphasize updated clinical and imaging updates, and the need for etiologic testing</cite>.
- Watch for immune phenotype: lymphopenia with cytokine storm supports immunocompetent hyperinflammatory ARDS; profound lymphopenia without robust cytokine rise and steroid exposure should raise suspicion for opportunistic/steroid-triggered reactivation, VZV/CMV, and fungal superinfection. Manage with immune-modulating therapies judiciously (e.g., IL-6 blockade for storm), antivirals, and fungal coverage when indicated. <cite id="426162e9-2">Viral ARDS commonly shows lymphopenia and elevated proinflammatory cytokines</cite><cite id="1d715476-7">Mortality in virus-detected ARF in immunocompromised patients is high, driven by severity and status</cite>.
- Expect extrapulmonary involvement in immunosuppressed critical illness—upper-airway/bulbar involvement, rash, neurologic changes, and multisystem organ failure—guiding broader ICU support and immune modulation. VZV-associated severe pneumonia correlates with prolonged ventilation and ICU stay, particularly under steroids. <cite id="6f63743c-2">Steroid-treated VZV pneumonia shows longer ventilation and ICU length of stay, underscoring de-escalation need</cite><cite id="6f63743c-3">Chickenpox-type rash with CT infiltrates helps anchor varicella etiology</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Immunocompetent ICU viral pneumonia: sharp cytokine storm with lymphopenia and coagulopathy; imaging shows rapid progression of GGO/consolidation/nodules; treat with antivirals, antibiotics for superinfection, ventilation, and cytokine-modulating therapies. <cite id="1d715476-2">Classic imaging phenotypes of viral pneumonia guide recognition</cite><cite id="426162e9-2">Viral ARDS features lymphopenia and cytokine storm</cite><cite id="426162e9-6">IL-6 blockade is recommended for hyperinflammation</cite>.
- Immunocompromised ICU viral pneumonia: bilateral, diffuse GGO/consolidation often from VZV/CMV with atypical presentation; imaging is essential but insufficient without molecular diagnostics and immune context; high mortality for severe ARF regardless of organism and frequent superimposed invasive aspergillosis; manage with immune reconstitution, antivirals, and targeted antifungals. <cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV CT patterns (bilateral GGO/halos, nodular shadows) are classic</cite><cite id="22d487d6-3">CMV HRCT shows bilateral mixed GGO/consolidation</cite><cite id="1d715476-5">Immunocompromised imaging features and diagnostic updates highlight atypical presentations</cite><cite id="1d715476-7">Virus-detected ARF in immunocompromised patients has high mortality driven by severity</cite>.

Key differentiators that aid recognition:
- Imaging distribution and morphology (bilateral, peripheral GGO/granular nodules and halos in immunocompromised vs multifocal/lobe-dominant consolidation in immunocompetent), <cite id="1d715476-2">viral phenotypes include multifocal bronchopneumonia</cite><cite id="6f63743c-0">VZV bilateral halos/GGO</cite><cite id="22d487d6-3">CMV bilateral GGO/consolidation</cite>.
- Immune markers (lymphopenia with cytokine storm and elevated D-dimer/coagulopathy in immunocompetent ARDS vs profound lymphopenia with blunted cytokine response and steroid exposure in immunosuppressed), <cite id="426162e9-2">lymphopenia and cytokine storm with IL-6/TNF/IL-1</cite><cite id="426162e9-8">lymphopenia and raised D-dimer/coagulopathy</cite>.
- Microbiology (non-opportunistic viruses by PCR in immunocompetent vs opportunistic/reactivated viruses and possible fungal superinfection in immunocompromised), <cite id="1d715476-4">testing strategies for severe respiratory infections in immunocompromised hosts</cite><cite id="1d715476-5">PFM review details clinical and imaging updates for immunocompromised pneumonia</cite><cite id="6f63743c-9">Approach to pulmonary infection stresses VZV/flu PCR and bronchoscopy</cite>.
- Outcomes (mortality in immunocompromised ARF correlates tightly with severity and overall status; immunocompetent mortality also rises with severity but can improve with modern therapies). <cite id="1d715476-7">In immunocompromised virus-detected ARF, mortality is high and driven by clinical severity and poor status</cite>.

Summary and definitions
- Fixed partial dentures (bridges) and single crowns are both tooth-supported restorations for replacing missing teeth, but they place different biomechanical demands on abutment teeth and prosthetic structure. Over decades of clinical follow-up, survival and complication-free survival differ across materials and designs; fracture risk compares on timelines due to span, ceramic type, and tooth condition. Below, “risk of fractures” includes crown-root/vertical root fractures (VRF) and other forms of tooth fracture as well as loss of retention or fracture of the prosthetic structure leading to extraction.

Baseline survival patterns (frame of reference)
- A systematic review and meta-analysis reported that the 10‑year probability of survival for tooth‑supported FPDs is about 89.1% and the 10‑year probability of success is about 71.1%, providing a useful baseline against which single crowns can be contextualized, especially where complications include fracture or endodontic-related failure of abutments from loading effects.<cite id="e46eafaa-4">The 10-year probability of survival for fixed partial dentures was 89.1% (95% confidence interval: 81-93.8%) while the probability of success was 71.1%</cite>
- Meta-analytic data also show that survival of tooth-supported FPDs has a hazard over time for abutment loss (often from caries/periodontal issues or fracture), and that survival probabilities are sensitive to span and material (e.g., metal-free zirconia FDPs). For example, posterior zirconia fixed dental prostheses showed an overall survival of 84% after a mean 5 years in a systematic review, illustrating that ceramic, span, and location drive risk.<cite id="e46eafaa-3">The overall survival rate for posterior zirconia based FDPs was 84% after a mean follow period of 5 year (95% CI); this result is comparable to the estimated ... (supporting comparison contexts)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-9">This study used meta-analysis to formulate annual probability estimates for three categories of fixed partial denture or abutment survival and indicated ... (supports time-resolved survival frameworks for FPD)</cite>
- In contrast, single crowns frequently achieve high 5‑ to 10‑year survival across ceramic systems, which shapes comparative fracture risk dynamics. Prospective data on monolithic zirconia crowns reported 98% survival at 5 years and only 6% complication rate, underscoring that modern all-ceramic crowns can minimize prosthetic fracture and loss of retention in the medium term.<cite id="ae74ffc0-5">For the 50 monolithic zirconia crowns analyzed, the survival rate was 98% after 5 years. Only 6% of the crowns presented some type of complication (two porcelain chippings, two screw channel failures, one abutment fracture)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-1">This paper reviews the literature regarding possible complications, complication-free survival, and overall survival of fixed dental prostheses that use ... (provides framework for complication breakdowns across FDPs and SCs)</cite>

Short-term comparisons (≤2–3 years)
