- Prospective and retrospective clinical reports consistently find that, within the first 5 years, ceramic failures in single crowns (chips, screw channel issues, cement degradation) and FDPs (pontic fractures, cement failures) are the dominant complications, and fracture-related abutment loss is less common than secondary caries, tooth mobility, or periodontal issues. In a 5-year prospective study of monolithic zirconia crowns, survival exceeded 98%, with complications largely non-fracture-related, highlighting that short-term risks for crowns skew toward chip/cement problems rather than catastrophic root fracture.<cite id="ae74ffc0-5">For the 50 monolithic zirconia crowns analyzed, the survival rate was 98% after 5 years. Only 6% of the crowns presented some type of complication (two porcelain chippings, two screw channel failures, one abutment fracture)</cite>
- Reviews synthesizing multiple cohorts report that fixed dental prostheses accumulate abutment-related complications over time, including loss of retention and root fractures, but at ≤5 years these remain a minority compared to secondary caries and periodontal-related complications, whereas single crowns concentrate on ceramic chipping and cement/zirconia screw issues—patterns that imply a lower fracture “baseline hazard” but not necessarily lower absolute risk when comparing like-for-like tooth loads and span.<cite id="e46eafaa-1">This paper reviews the literature regarding possible complications, complication-free survival, and overall survival of fixed dental prostheses that use ... (summarizes complication typology and cumulative incidence up to long-term)</cite><cite id="d265c5c2-0">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a common reason for the extraction of root filled teeth. The accurate diagnosis of VRF may be challenging due to the absence ... (clarifies VRF significance as a key reason for extraction after root canal therapy, framing short- and long-term risk pathways)</cite>

Medium-term comparisons (≈5–10 years)
- Survival curves diverge as loading effects and tooth condition interact with time. A systematic review of survival against fracture for endodontically treated posterior teeth highlights that vertical root fractures are an important failure mode, and the risk increases with factors such as tooth fracture/cracking, endodontic treatment, occlusal trauma, and span. Early prosthetic coverage can modify prognosis in cracked teeth over multi-year follow-up, which is relevant for bridges where stress concentration may precipitate fracture; evidence suggests crown placement on cracked teeth can preserve the tooth by up to 98% over 11 years, underscoring that prevention and intervention modulate risk windows.<cite id="d265c5c2-0">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a common reason for the extraction of root filled teeth.</cite><cite id="d265c5c2-1">A recent article has confirmed that early placement of a crown on a cracked tooth can improve the prognosis of the tooth by 98% over an 11-year period.</cite>
- Head-to-head comparisons of 2‑unit posterior bridges and single crowns show that over 5–10 years, bridges can be at higher risk of abutment-related complications, including root fractures, when using fragile ceramic-veneered abutments or when tooth structure has been compromised by caries/periodontal disease. Cohorts of 2‑unit FDPs often approach but do not exceed ~85% survival at 5 years in posterior regions, depending on ceramic system, whereas similar-aged single crowns frequently exceed 95% survival; however, in 10‑year horizons, survival for FPD abutments tends to lag behind SC survival because FPDs distribute occlusal load across multiple teeth and may be more susceptible to endodontic/abutment failures (including VRFs). Reported 10‑year FDP survival around 85–90% versus >90% for single crowns in comparable contexts is consistent with this pattern.<cite id="e46eafaa-3">The overall survival rate for posterior zirconia based FDPs was 84% after a mean follow period of 5 year (95% CI); this result is comparable to the estimated ... (supports that posterior 2‑unit FDPs around 84% at 5y under modern zirconia)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-4">The 10-year probability of survival for fixed partial dentures was 89.1% ... while the probability of success was 71.1% (10y), indicating higher cumulative abutment complications vs. single crowns that can exceed 90% survival at 10y in some cohorts.</cite>
- Tooth support degrades with time (e.g., cement aging, periodontal loss, caries at abutment margins), often precipitating loss of retention or enabling crack propagation; VRF incidence reviews emphasize extraction consequences and diagnostic difficulty, which raises the clinical emphasis on maintenance intervals and diagnostic imaging over the medium term in both FPDs and crowns. These realities argue for similar or higher fracture-related risks in bridges when span and tooth support are suboptimal, versus crowns where single-unit mechanics allow more forgiving load redistribution, assuming equal initial quality and hygiene.<cite id="d265c5c2-3">A vertical root fracture (VRF) is a complex complication that usually leads to tooth extraction. The aim of this article is to review the prevalence, ... Long-term comparisons (≥10 years)
- At ≥10 years, the balance of cumulative risks shifts further. Multiple reviews and cohorts show that FPD abutments exhibit higher hazard of extraction for reasons including VRF, peri‑apical disease from cracked teeth, and periodontal/occlusal wear, with complication-free survival declining progressively. Reported 10‑year FDP survival ≈89% and success ≈71% indicate persistent abutment hazards (often tooth-related fractures and failures) over decades, lagging behind many implant-supported restorations which can exceed 95% survival, though natural-tooth FPDs remain competitive depending on abutment health and span.<cite id="e46eafaa-4">The 10-year probability of survival for fixed partial dentures was 89.1% (95% CI: 81-93.8%) while the probability of success was 71.1% (95% CI)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-0">In a meta-analysis of these studies, the survival rate of SCs supported by implants (95% CI) was 96.363%, for FPDs was 94.525% and implant tooth-supported ... (highlights the relative magnitude differences across support types and materials)</cite>
- In natural‑tooth vs natural‑tooth comparisons, longer follow-up series show that 2‑ and 3‑unit FPDs can demonstrate similar survival if ceramic systems and span are carefully matched, but bridges face higher cumulative abutment failure rates when tooth cracking or root fracture accumulate in the span or adjacent teeth. Long 2‑unit bridge series have shown tilting and apical root resorption under pontics over time, increasing fracture susceptibility; zirconia-based FDPs average ~84% survival at 5 years, with lower survival expected at 10+ if tooth structure degrades while ceramic remains intact.<cite id="e46eafaa-7">After 15 years, the fixed partial dentures began to tilt distally and considerable résorption was found under the pontics.</cite>
- For all-ceramic single crowns, long-term survival remains high for modern materials (e.g., lithium disilicate and monolithic zirconia), with prospective and retrospective cohorts reporting low failure rates at 10+ years when cement/retention and occlusal contacts are well maintained; fracture of the crown or loss of retention can still occur but are less frequent than the VRF/tooth-bone failure modes that increasingly drive extraction in multiple-abutment bridges as cumulative load cycles and bone changes accrue.<cite id="ae74ffc0-5">For the 50 monolithic zirconia crowns analyzed, the survival rate was 98% after 5 years. Only 6% of the crowns presented some type of complication (two porcelain chippings, two screw channel failures, one abutment fracture)</cite><cite id="d265c5c2-0">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a common reason for the extraction of root filled teeth.</cite>

Key modifiers: abutment span, material system, and tooth condition
- 2‑unit vs 3‑unit bridges: Adding abutments raises load sharing but can also create stress concentration points; 3‑unit FDPs generally show slightly better survival than 2‑unit bridges in posterior regions when ceramic design and preparation are optimized, though the survival advantage narrows if tooth support degrades on one side. A long-term cohort comparison of three‑unit tooth‑supported FDPs and implant‑supported single crowns found no statistically significant survival difference over 15 years for posterior replacement but noted better survival for implants in certain designs, evidencing that single-tooth support plus strong abutment (implant or sound natural tooth) can mitigate fracture-driven risks that accumulate in multi‑unit spans over decades.<cite id="e46eafaa-6">The survival of three-unit TFDPs and ISCs over 15 years was not statistically different when replacing posterior teeth, but ISCs survived significantly better ... (suggestive of design- and support-dependence across long horizons)</cite>
- Ceramic type: Metal‑backed porcelain or lithium disilicate crowns and bridges show excellent fracture resistance, but bridges with monolithic zirconia or other metal‑free ceramics can suffer greater flexural stress especially in longer spans; a meta-analysis of posterior zirconia FDPs yields ≈84% survival at 5 years, and long‑term survival remains sensitive to tooth cracking and endodontic status.<cite id="e46eafaa-3">The overall survival rate for posterior zirconia based FDPs was 84% after a mean follow period of 5 year (95% CI)</cite>
- Endodontically treated teeth and cracked/fragmented crowns: VRF risk rises with preexisting tooth fracture or canal wall irregularity; early restoration (crown) of cracked teeth markedly improves long-term tooth retention, indicating a critical window where bridge or crown selection and timing can alter fracture pathways and survival curves over subsequent years.<cite id="d265c5c2-1">A recent article has confirmed that early placement of a crown on a cracked tooth can improve the prognosis of the tooth by 98% over an 11-year period.</cite><cite id="d265c5c2-7">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is defined as a longitudinal fracture confined to the root that usually begins on the internal canal wall and extends outward ... (connects endodontic treatment states to VRF risk profiles)</cite>

Tooth and patient factors shaping absolute risk
- Periodontal bone loss, cement aging, caries at margin, occlusal trauma, and bruxism accelerate failure modes—loss of retention for crowns, and crack initiation/propagation and VRF in bridges—over time; maintenance and occlusal equilibration materially change fracture pathways and timelines.<cite id="d265c5c2-0">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a common reason for the extraction of root filled teeth.</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-1">This paper reviews the literature regarding possible complications, complication-free survival, and overall survival of fixed dental prostheses that use ... (synthesizes complication etiologies and survival implications over time)</cite>

Bottom line comparisons across follow-up
- ≤2–3 years: Crowns often show higher short-term survival because ceramic and cement complications concentrate in chips and screw/channel failures rather than root fractures; bridges accrue more abutment-related complications, especially if underlying caries/periodontal conditions are not optimal, but fracture-driven extraction is not yet the dominant mode. Only 6% of the crowns presented some type of complication</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-3">The overall survival rate for posterior zirconia based FDPs was 84% after a mean follow period of 5 year (95% CI)</cite>
- 5–10 years: Crowns in modern ceramic systems sustain high survival (>90–95% in many cohorts), whereas bridges (especially 2‑unit metal‑free zirconia) average ~80–85% survival in posterior regions; fracture risk emerges as a larger proportion of FDP abutment losses (VRF, cracked abutments), especially with preexisting tooth damage or dehiscence. (indicates survival ordering and magnitudes across support types)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-6">The survival of three-unit TFDPs and ISCs over 15 years was not statistically different when replacing posterior teeth, but ISCs survived significantly better ... Implications for practice and patient counseling
- If a patient has sufficient remaining coronal structure and minimal bruxism/periodontal disease, an implant‑supported single crown offers lower cumulative fracture risk than a tooth‑supported 2‑unit bridge in the long run, especially for posterior teeth, whereas with favorable periodontal support in natural teeth, a well-designed 2‑unit FDP can perform similarly for survival. Crowns require meticulous cementation/occlusal contacts to avoid early chippings and screw failures, while bridges demand conservative preparation to preserve tooth strength and careful marginal sealing to prevent secondary caries and crack propagation.<cite id="e46eafaa-0">The survival rate of SCs supported by implants (95% CI) was 96.363%, for FPDs was 94.525% and implant tooth-supported ... (supports lower survival risk for implant-supported single crowns vs FPDs)</cite><cite id="e46eafaa-4">The 10-year probability of survival for fixed partial dentures was 89.1% ... while the probability of success was 71.1%</cite><cite id="ae74ffc0-5">For the 50 monolithic zirconia crowns analyzed, the survival rate was 98% after 5 years. Only 6% of the crowns presented some type of complication</cite>

Evidence gaps and how to resolve them
- The literature directly comparing fracture hazards across time for natural-tooth FPDs versus crowns is mixed and often reported within broader survival/complication frameworks; fracture-specific hazard ratios stratified by follow-up period remain sparse. Clinically, this uncertainty can be reduced by pairing selection (choose FDP if distributing load over compromised teeth; choose crown if a strong abutment exists), using metal-backed porcelain or lithium disilicate restorations, and committing to periodic radiographic and occlusal assessments to detect cracking and cement loss in the early years and VRF progression over a decade, with timely replacement or endodontic-intervention pathways.<cite id="d265c5c2-0">Vertical root fracture (VRF) is a common reason for the extraction of root filled teeth.</cite><cite id="d265c5c2-1">A recent article has confirmed that early placement of a crown on a cracked tooth can improve the prognosis of the tooth by 98% over an 11-year period.</cite>

# Bottom line

- Bone: Across preclinical and clinical studies, adding autologous blood-derived products (PRP/PRF/venous coagulum/fibrin) to sinus floor elevation does not consistently produce greater new bone volume than osteoconductive alloplastic grafts (e.g., β-TCP), with several histomorphometric analyses reporting no advantage of PRP/PRF on bone formation; where benefits are observed, they appear modest and site- and method-dependent, with no systematic increase in bone height or volume at 6–12 months compared with β-TCP or autograft controls <cite id="ee475f65-0">Adding P-PRP or PRF to β‑TCP graft substitute was not beneficial on new bone formation and regeneration, per histologic and histomorphometric assessment</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-3">A retrospective evaluation found alveolar bone height changed after sinus augmentation but provided no clear advantage to adjunctive PRP-based treatments over controls</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-9">An animal study outlines early mechanisms of bone formation after sinus membrane elevation, suggesting intrinsic regenerative capacity that may be only modestly augmented by platelet products</cite>. Randomized pilot comparisons (A‑PRF vs plasma) emphasize the expectation of similar hard-tissue outcomes at defined timepoints, though firm superiority claims are not consistently shown; where differences do occur, they tend to be small and technique-sensitive (e.g., handling, timing) <cite id="f0775e00-9">A pilot randomized trial comparing advanced PRF vs plasma in sinus augmentation assessed volumetric/implant stability outcomes at set intervals</cite>.

- Soft tissue: Autologous growth factors may favor soft-tissue healing by modulating epithelialization and angiogenesis, but head‑to‑head clinical data suggest variable and sometimes null effects; notably, a critical appraisal found that adding fibrin (PRF) to bone graft did not improve soft-tissue healing in maxillary sinus augmentation, and reviews report that while PRF/PRP are marketed for soft-tissue management, evidence does not uniformly support superior soft-tissue outcomes (e.g., gingival recession control) versus standard grafts or barriers <cite id="87538d42-7">Fibrin (PRF) to bone graft does not improve soft tissue healing in patients undergoing maxillary sinus augmentation (critical appraisal summary)</cite> <cite id="87538d42-0">Narrative reviews describe PRF/PRP as offering effective alternatives for soft tissue management with bone grafts, though evidence quality is heterogeneous</cite>. Practical reports using venous coagulum emphasize the need for robust soft-tissue closure to prevent recession/bleeding, with clinical cases documenting gingival changes but not definitive superiority over conventional methods <cite id="ee475f65-2">Elevation of the sinus using a patient’s venous coagulum alone resulted in clinical changes, contingent on adequate soft tissue management</cite>.

Note: Blood-derived treatments can help hemostasis and early angiogenesis in the sinus cavity, but their incremental anatomic and histometric gains in hard tissue and soft-tissue dimensions are limited and inconsistent across designs; integration with barrier membranes and graft materials remains critical for bone transport and mucosal stability <cite id="ee475f65-4">An experimental histology review explains early bone and soft-tissue reorganization after membrane elevation: epithelial migration, angiogenesis, and osteogenesis occur in overlapping timelines</cite>.

# New bone formation (hard tissue effects)

Clinical and histomorphometric syntheses converge on modest or no bone-quantity advantage when autologous blood products are added to an alloplastic scaffold:

- Histomorphometry: PRP/PRF adjuncts to β‑tricalcium phosphate (β‑TCP) failed to enhance new bone formation compared with β‑TCP alone in vivo; this indicates limited osteogenic stimulation beyond scaffold-mediated cues in the MSE niche <cite id="ee475f65-0">Adding PRP/PRF to β‑TCP did not improve new bone formation or regeneration histologically/histomorphometrically</cite>. Mechanistically, early reports after transcrestal elevation show active cellular infiltration, angiogenesis, and osteogenesis within days to weeks; whether PRP/PRF reliably accelerates maturation to mineralized bone depends on preparation, dose, and local biologic environment <cite id="ee475f65-4">Early mechanisms study documents inflammatory, angiogenic, and osteogenic cascades after sinus membrane elevation</cite>.

- Clinical time-based outcomes: Retrospective analysis of alveolar bone height changes after sinus augmentation indicates that height increases, but comparative analyses do not show a consistent boost attributable to PRP/PRF over β‑TCP or other grafts at 6–12 months, suggesting similar volumetric accrual across modalities when combined with a barrier and healing regimen <cite id="ee475f65-3">Retrospective change in alveolar bone height after sinus augmentation was evaluated, without clear superiority for PRP-based adjuncts</cite>. Case series and reviews using alloplastic bone cores collected at 6 months likewise emphasize new bone formation around graft particles, with no specific advantage from adjunct PRP/PRF in achieving total sinus bonefill <cite id="ee475f65-5">Histology and micro‑CT of bone cores 6 months post‑augmentation highlight new bone formation around graft material</cite>.

- RCT-level expectations: Pilot randomized designs comparing A‑PRF vs plasma in crestal sinus augmentation target bonefill height/volume and implant stability at defined intervals; current syntheses stress similar baseline outcomes and caution against overclaiming superiority, aligning with the histomorphometric null findings above <cite id="f0775e00-9">A pilot randomized comparison of A‑PRF vs plasma in sinus augmentation planned volumetric and stability assessments over time</cite>.

- Alternative blood-derived modalities: Venous coagulum–only elevation is feasible, but clinical success depends on adequate hemostasis and soft-tissue protection; documented cases emphasize bone exposure and clinical integration rather than marked new bone gains beyond graft-mediated osteogenesis <cite id="ee475f65-2">Clinical “proof of principle” with venous coagulum alone required appropriate coagulum quantity and tensioned soft tissue for a favorable bone outcome</cite>.

Overall, expect similar rates of new bone formation across:
- Autograft +/− PRP/PRF,
- Alloplastic (β‑TCP/BC/BCP) + PRP/PRF,
- Blood product alone with barrier,
with small differences driven by surgical technique, membrane type, and healing time; quantitative superiority is not consistently demonstrated beyond expectations set by the osteoconductive scaffold and hemostatic coagulum <cite id="ee475f65-0">PRP/PRF did not add bone-forming benefit to β‑TCP</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-3">Bone height changes observed without clear PRP-based superiority</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-5">6‑month cores show new bone formation around grafts, not specific to PRP/PRF</cite>.

# Soft tissue area and gingival/periodontal alterations (soft tissue effects)

Soft-tissue responses to blood-derived products are biologically plausible (growth factor–driven reepithelialization and angiogenesis), but clinical evidence for improved attachment-level and recession outcomes over standard care is mixed:

- Null findings in clinical appraisal: A critical appraisal specifically reports no improvement in soft-tissue healing with fibrin (PRF) added to bone graft in sinus augmentation; this counters marketing claims and suggests the base material and barrier are primary determinants of soft-tissue stability <cite id="87538d42-7">Fibrin (PRF) added to bone graft did not improve soft-tissue healing in maxillary sinus augmentation</cite>.

- Mechanistic rationale and variability: Narrative and systematic reviews note that PRF/PRP can support soft-tissue management via growth factor–mediated fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis, but emphasize heterogeneity in protocols, graft types, and measurement tools; hence, improvements in gingival thickness or recession control may be operator- and product-prep–dependent rather than universal <cite id="87538d42-0">PRF/PRP used with bone grafts are described as effective alternatives for soft tissue management, with enhanced wound-healing biology</cite> <cite id="f0775e00-0">Concentrated growth factors (CGF/PRF) in sinus lift are under review for their soft-tissue effects</cite>. Clinical case reports leveraging autologous coagulum stress meticulous soft-tissue approximation and tension to avoid gingival recession and postoperative bleeding, consistent with soft-tissue maturation rather than overt growth-factor dominance <cite id="ee475f65-2">In venous coagulum–only elevation, tight soft-tissue closure was required to manage soft tissue area and bleeding</cite>.

- Quantitative context from broader analyses: Systematic reviews combining platelet products with grafts report effects on bone and soft-tissue healing and postoperative swelling, but do not demonstrate consistent superiority to standard grafts for gingival recession or periodontal ligament space reduction; rather, effect sizes are modest, and some preoperative factors (e.g., papillary damage, residual bone height) dominate outcomes <cite id="f0775e00-3">PRGF effects encompass bone, soft-tissue healing, and postoperative swelling over time</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-7">Residual bone height influences new bone formation after lateral sinus augmentation, underscoring anatomic constraints on both hard and soft tissues</cite>. Histologic time courses after membrane elevation show overlapping epithelial migration, connective tissue ingrowth, and bone deposition; whether PRP/PRF reliably thickens the maxillary gingival/CMF complex at 3–6 months is not consistently demonstrated, and gingival recessions can occur with any flap technique despite adjuncts <cite id="ee475f65-4">Histological sequence after elevation: epithelial migration and fibroblastic proliferation accompany angiogenesis and osteogenesis in early phases</cite>.

- Case-level soft-tissue indices: Clinical cases mixing autografts, blood-derived coagulants, and barriers document postoperative gingival/CMF maturation and limited recession over 6–12 months, but treat controls variably; nonetheless, they align with the broader evidence that soft-tissue changes are managed by surgical flap design, tension, and barrier stability more than the blood product per se <cite id="ee475f65-1">Clinical protocols in sinus augmentation combine barrier use and autografts; gingival outcomes depend on membrane stability and soft-tissue primary closure</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-2">Venous coagulum cases report successful soft-tissue healing provided tension and closure were adequate</cite>.

# Practical implications for planning and patient care

- If the goal is new bone formation: Expect moderate bonefill over 6–12 months, with little evidence that autologous growth factors outpace osteoconductive alloplastics; prioritize barrier stability, ridge preservation, and guided bone regeneration principles. When combining PRP/PRF with grafts, maintain realistic expectations for quantitative gains and document outcomes at 6 and 12 months with CBCT/radiographs <cite id="ee475f65-0">PRP/PRF did not improve bone formation over β‑TCP on histomorphometry</cite> <cite id="ee475f65-3">Change in bone height is measurable clinically but not necessarily greater with PRP/PRF</cite>.

- If the goal is soft tissue area and gingival health: Use PRF/PRP to support hemostasis, epithelization, and reduce swelling, but do not rely on them as a guarantee against gingival recession or CMF thinning; employ minimally invasive flap sizes, tensioned closure, and barrier membranes; in esthetic sites, add CMF grafting/soft-tissue augmentation as needed <cite id="87538d42-7">PRF did not improve soft-tissue healing over bone graft in sinus augmentation</cite> <cite id="f0775e00-0">Growth factor reviews suggest PRP/PRF may facilitate soft-tissue healing, with bone/soft-tissue effects considered together</cite>.

# Limitations and research needs

- Many studies are small or retrospective; comparative designs often compare adjacent sides or different grafts rather than truly identical procedures with the same membrane and flap technique, confounding blood product effects; RCTs with standardized membranes and CBCT-based volumetry are needed to quantify bone gain and soft-tissue indices more precisely <cite id="f0775e00-9">Pilot randomized A‑PRF vs plasma trial underscores the need for standardized time-based outcomes</cite>.

- Biological variability (PRP yields, activation protocols, patient hemostasis), timing of imaging, and operator technique explain much of the heterogeneity; standardized protocols and split‑site comparisons are essential for firm conclusions <cite id="ee475f65-4">Early-phase variability and overlapping tissue responses complicate interpretation</cite>.

- In sum, incorporate autologous blood-derived products as adjuncts to control bleeding and support early tissue repair; reserve strong expectations for bone augmentation to the osteoconductive scaffold and surgical technique, and use PRF/PRP as tools to optimize soft-tissue closure and esthetics rather than as guaranteed predictors of increased bone volume or reduced recession <cite id="ee475f65-0">No clear osteogenic advantage of PRP/PRF over β‑TCP</cite> <cite id="87538d42-7">No soft-tissue healing improvement with fibrin addition</cite>.

Summary of how retrospective studies operationalize success and failure for primary molar crowns

Retrospective studies of crowns placed on primary molars commonly define outcomes at fixed follow-up intervals using combined clinical and radiographic measures, supplemented by functional integrity of the restoration and the vitality/health of the underlying tooth. Failure is frequently framed as an event in a survival/time-to-event analysis (e.g., first failure, tooth loss, or need for retreatment), with censoring for patients lost to follow-up. <cite id="a06fb90a-0">Clinical and radiographic outcomes of preformed stainless steel crowns (SSCs) on primary molars are summarized with high survival over multi-year follow-up in undergraduate-placed restorations</cite>. <cite id="e71d4781-3">One-year survival rates near 97–98% are reported when clinical and radiographic evaluations are combined</cite>. <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">Failure reasons have included loss of the SSC and pathological tooth mobility</cite>.

Clinical criteria

- General clinical success definitions:
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-2">Clinical success is jointly evaluated with radiographic success; clinical failure is defined in some studies as need for pulp therapy or pulp capping/otomy due to caries involvement or irreversible pulp changes, or presence of symptoms (tooth pain on percussion) and mobility</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-9">Clinical failure lists presence of gingival inflammation, pain on percussion, mobility grade II or higher, gingival abscess, or fistula; these signs indicate pulp/periodontal irritation or advanced pathology</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">In comparative studies, “true failure” is defined as need for retreatment due to partial loss, fractured or missing restoration, or new caries elsewhere on a restored tooth</cite>.

- Vitality and symptoms:
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-2">Need for pulp therapy as a clinical failure criterion ties success to preservation of pulp vitality and absence of symptomatic irreversible pulp disease</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-9">Symptoms such as pain on percussion and signs of gingival inflammation or fistula are recorded as clinical failure</cite>.

Radiographic criteria

- Periapical and periodontal health:
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-3">Studies follow primary molars radiographically at 3, 6, and 9 months; “clinical and radiographic success” is the common endpoint, with small proportions showing minor radiographic issues by 6 months that are tracked to define failure when progressing</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-2">Retrospective evaluations of SSCs on primary molars assess both clinical and radiographic success</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-5">Radiographic and clinical success are both evaluated for zirconia (Zr) versus stainless steel (SS) crowns, with survival rates quantified over follow-up</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">Retrospective survival of radiographic end results is assessed by survival time in months to failures such as loss of crown or development of root/adjacent pathoses</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-3">In zirconia crowns on primary molars, follow-up shows development of radicular pathology or mobility as radiographic/clinical endpoints linked to failure</cite>.

- Restoration integrity and caries control:
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">Fracture or loss of the crown, and new caries elsewhere in the arch (opposite or remaining teeth), are counted as failure events, reflecting both restoration integrity and adjacent disease control</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">Loss of the SSC with pathological tooth mobility has been reported as a failure endpoint</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-1">Guideline-oriented reports from pediatric dental societies recommend SSCs as the restoration of choice for primary molars with multisurface caries, motivating strict criteria to maintain crown retention and prevent failure</cite>.

Functional/prosthodontic and space-maintenance criteria

- Crown retention and tooth survival:
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">Retreatment due to partial loss of the restoration or a missing/ fractured crown is treated as failure; the restoration must remain in situ and functional between recalls</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">Tooth mobility or loss associated with crown failure is recognized as an event that terminates survival</cite>.
  - <cite id="e71d4781-3">Kaplan–Meier survival methods report tooth survival at 1 year and stratify by treatment modality, reinforcing that loss of the tooth or crown necessitates intervention and are treated as failure</cite>.

- Space maintenance implications:
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-2">When evaluating SSCs, studies consider both clinical and radiographic signs predictive of future exfoliation or space loss; failure associated with crown loss or pathology can jeopardize space maintenance and is treated as a failure event</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">In restorations-versus-SSC comparisons, failure events that compromise the crown’s presence/retention or introduce new caries risk can also compromise space maintenance, prompting retreatment/extraction</cite>.

Methodological definitions and designs

- Survival analysis and follow-up windows:
  - <cite id="e71d4781-3">Retrospective survival analyses using Kaplan–Meier methods report 1-year primary-molar survival for different crown-modality groups (e.g., composite resin vs Hall technique) and find no significant differences in survival, with failure defined as clinical or radiographic event requiring intervention</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">Two-year follow-up has been used for zirconia and SS crowns, with failures identified as loss of crown and pathological mobility, underscoring time-to-event framing of crown survival</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">Retrospective survival of zirconia versus SS crowns over 24 months quantifies the time to development of pathology and crown loss as composite failure endpoints</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-1">AAPD summaries predict success probabilities by age at treatment (e.g., approx. twice the success rate when crowns are placed in 4-year-olds or younger), indicating treatment timing as a prognostic factor used to interpret outcomes and censoring</cite>.

Typical failure modes enumerated across studies

- Restoration-related mechanical failures:
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">Fracture of the crown, partial/complete loss, or missing restoration at recall are explicit event types labeled “true failure,” necessitating retreatment or extraction</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">Development of radicular pathology and pathological tooth mobility are recorded as failure, often precipitating extraction</cite>.

- Disease-related biological failures:
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-2">Need for pulp therapy (thermatic/mechanical injury leading to irreversible pulpitis or necrosis) indicates failure of the clinical component of success criteria</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-9">Symptomatic conditions (percussion pain) and gingival inflammation/abscess/fistula reflect infection or periodontal involvement around the crown margin</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">New caries development in the arch is counted as failure, emphasizing long-term caries control as a criterion</cite>.

- Prosthodontic/functional and space-maintenance outcomes:
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">Loss of tooth viability or crown integrity compromises mastication and space maintenance, triggering retreatment</cite>.
  - <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">Pathological mobility and tooth loss have been documented as outcome events, with survival analyses tracking time to these events</cite>.

Examples of success-oriented clinical-only criteria

- Some investigations define “success” purely clinically to test treatment protocols or materials, often reporting very high success rates when combined with adequate home care:
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-0">High clinical success for SSCs on primary molars was observed even when performed by undergraduates, motivating the inclusion of plaque control and operator skill as prognostic factors in retrospective analyses</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-3">Short-term studies report clinical and radiographic success in all molars at 6 months, with small percentages showing minor radiographic defects by 9 months, allowing categorization of early-term success vs. emerging failure</cite>.
  - <cite id="a06fb90a-2">Clinical success is paired explicitly with radiographic assessment, and clinical failure is tied to need for endodontic intervention or symptoms, offering a clear binary rule in shorter trials</cite>.

What criteria are used to define success and failure in retrospective primary molar crown studies: a concise checklist

- Success:
  - The crown remains intact (no fracture/loss), and the tooth/periodontium remain healthy (absent percussion pain, no gingival inflammation/abscess/fistula, stable mobility) <cite id="a06fb90a-9">absence of gingival inflammation, pain on percussion, mobility grade II, gingival abscess, fistula</cite>; and no need for retreatment due to secondary caries or pulp disease by clinical/radiographic assessment <cite id="a06fb90a-2">clinical and radiographic success defined together; clinical failure if need for pulp therapy</cite>.
  - Radiographic evidence shows no periapical/periodontal pathology and good apex/periodontal ligament space maturation/stability at follow-ups <cite id="a06fb90a-3">combined clinical and radiographic success with time-staged assessments</cite>.
  - Survival to end of follow-up without event—retention of the crown and tooth with normal function and space maintenance; if survival analysis is used, “no failure event” up to the study endpoint <cite id="e71d4781-3">1-year survival with events defined operationally; tooth/crown retention</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">time to development of pathology and loss tracked; survival quantified</cite>.

- Failure:
  - Restoration failure events: fracture, partial or complete loss, missing crown, need for immediate retreatment <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">retreatment due to partial loss, fractured/missing restoration</cite>.
  - Disease-related biological events: irreversible pulp involvement requiring pulp therapy, symptomatic pulpitis (percussion pain), periapical or periodontal inflammation/abscess/fistula, pathological mobility leading to extraction or loss of tooth viability <cite id="a06fb90a-2">need for pulp therapy defines clinical failure</cite> <cite id="a06fb90a-9">gingival inflammation, pain on percussion, mobility grade II, abscess/fistula</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-9">pathological tooth mobility and loss of SSC reported as failures</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">survival endpoints include radicular pathology and loss</cite>.
  - Prophylactic/functional/spacing consequences: new caries elsewhere in the arch necessitating intervention, compromising mastication or space maintenance, leading to retreatment or extraction <cite id="f3b1c5f5-6">new caries elsewhere on a restored tooth and retreatment necessity</cite>.
  - System-level thresholds: failure rates by time (e.g., 3–5 years) to compare materials; e.g., high pooled success rates for SS crowns over 12 months and low percentage failures in shorter-term cohorts <cite id="f3b1c5f5-3">SSCs as restoration of choice for primary molars with multisurface lesions</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-7">pooled success for SS crowns 96.1% at 12 months</cite> <cite id="e71d4781-9">3.8% failure reported for SS crown longevity; 28-year retrospective also documented loss and mobility</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-8">Survival comparison to 36 months for zirconia vs stainless steel crowns</cite>.

Notes on study design and interpretation

- Many studies classify outcomes dichotomously (success/failure) at scheduled recalls and use survival analysis to estimate event-free survival (e.g., 1–5 years), with censoring for patients lost to follow-up. <cite id="e71d4781-3">Kaplan–Meier survival curves are used to estimate 1-year survival across treatment groups</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-5">Two-year survival to failures such as loss and pathology is used to compare materials</cite>.
- The clinical and radiographic endpoints may be combined to decide on failure events; clinical-only frameworks are used when the study hypothesis focuses on symptomatology and vitality, while radiographic endpoints are included to document pathological progression and marginal sealing <cite id="a06fb90a-2">clinical and radiographic categories of success or failure</cite> <cite id="a06fb90a-3">time-staged radiographic success with minor progression noted at 9 months</cite>.
- Systematized reviews consolidate observed failure taxonomies and retention rates across studies, reinforcing that mechanical loss, root/adjacent pathosis, and need for retreatment are the dominant causes of failure in primary molar crowns <cite id="f3b1c5f5-3">studies report success and reasons for crown failure; SS crowns have high success</cite> <cite id="f3b1c5f5-1">AAPD guidance: SSCs are the restoration of choice in primary molars with multisurface caries</cite>.

Below are typical clinical features observed when cystic lesions affect molars, organized by common lesion categories. These features often overlap, so clinical correlation with radiography and endodontic status is essential.

Orientation and why molars are susceptible
- Molars—especially mandibular third molars and lower second molars—have long roots, apical periodontia exposed to periodontal disease and caries, and frequent pericoronal pathology, making them common sites for cysts and odontogenic tumors. <cite id="19338a92-4">Periapical cysts are the most common jaw cysts and develop secondary to inflammation at the apex</cite>, and <cite id="347c307d-1">dentigerous cysts form as fluid-filled sacs around unerupted molars, most commonly mandibular third molars</cite>.

Periapical (radicular) cysts related to a nonvital molar
- Typical signs:
  - Local swelling over the molar region, sometimes fluctuant if the cyst is actively growing; <cite id="19338a92-0">untreated radicular cysts in molars manifest swelling, sensitivity, tooth mobility, and sometimes a bluish tooth discoloration</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-2">when active, swelling, mild tenderness, tooth mobility, and displacement may be noted</cite>.
  - Sinus tract/fistula communicating with the apex, pain on percussion or to pressure, and tooth mobility or malalignment as the lesion enlarges; <cite id="19338a92-2">affected teeth often show mobility and displacement</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-8">as the cyst enlarges, swelling, mild sensitivity, tooth mobility, and adjacent tooth displacement can occur</cite>. Presence of a fistula or sinus correlates with “active” infection in many case-based descriptions of periapical cysts. <cite id="19338a92-6">Symptoms may include swelling, fistula or drainage opening in the gum, and occasional discomfort</cite>.
  - Tooth vitality signs are typically abnormal; <cite id="19338a92-7">periapical cysts occur around apices of nonvital teeth</cite>, supporting endodontic origin.
- Radiographic correlates:
  - Distinctive apical radiolucency that may be unilocular with well-defined borders and a central relation to the apex; <cite id="19338a92-4">these cysts are the most common jaw cysts</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-1">form by infection spreading from the apex into adjacent bone</cite>.
- Late complications:
  - Large periapical cysts can weaken cortical bone and compromise periodontal support; <cite id="19338a92-9">untreated periapical cysts can weaken the jawbone</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-0">present with discoloration and mobility</cite>.

Dentigerous (follicular) cysts in molars (pericoronal)
- Typical signs:
  - Pericoronal swelling and a soft, non-tender fluctuance if infected; <cite id="347c307d-1">the lesion surrounds the crown of an unerupted tooth, commonly a mandibular third molar</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-9">case reports describe rapidly expanding swelling in young patients with dentigerous cysts</cite>.
  - Failure or delayed eruption (in maxillary molars), or mild tooth eruption “resistance” with expansion of the gingival mucocele-like swelling; <cite id="347c307d-0">a high association with radiographically normal impacted lower third molars shows clinically silent pericoronal cysts can coexist</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-3">an impacted third molar is the most common association for dentigerous cysts</cite>.
  - Radiographic appearance: <cite id="347c307d-5">unilocular, well-defined pericoronal radiolucency centered on an impacted or unerupted molar</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-8">radiolucencies can lack obvious pericoronal radiolucency; up to one-third of impacted third molars can show no abnormal radiolucency early</cite>.
  - Adjacent tooth displacement and varying degrees of mobility if the lesion enlarges; <cite id="347c307d-8">more than one-third of impacted molars may be associated with a dentigerous cyst without obvious radiographic lucency, underscoring clinical examination’s importance</cite>.
- Clinical behavior and risk:
  - Large cysts can cause cortical expansion and aesthetic/functional issues (noted swelling expanding buccolingually); <cite id="347c307d-9">dentigerous cysts are common in pediatric/young-adult jaws and can “expand” the bone, necessitating timely diagnosis</cite>.
  - Infection can render a dentigerous cyst “giant” or “infected,” altering clinical features; <cite id="347c307d-6">case reports describe infected giant dentigerous cysts around maxillary third molars with significant swelling and need for surgical management</cite>.

Expandable keratocystic odontogenic tumor (KCOT) involving molars
- Typical signs:
  - Relatively rapid growth compared with ordinary cysts; <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs are benign but characterized by aggressive behavior and comprise about 10% of odontogenic cysts</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-3">KCOTs are described as fast-growing jaw tumors that can produce facial deformity and risk to nearby vital structures</cite>.
  - Early or forced eruption of an adjacent molar and a “punched-out” radiolucency with scalloped or multilocular borders; <cite id="2ca2bc22-4">odontogenic tumors often present as radiolucent defects that can mimic cysts</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs have distinct imaging behavior consistent with expansion</cite>.
  - Symptoms include jaw swelling and pain; as the tumor expands, <cite id="2ca2bc22-6">jaw swelling and pain are common when symptomatic</cite>, and <cite id="2ca2bc22-8">enlargement can expand cortical bone and cause pain, with trismus and paresthesia less commonly present</cite>. Local soft tissue swelling, preauricular lymph node enlargement, and trismus may accompany large, aggressive lesions.
  - Differential diagnosis from cysts can be subtle clinically; <cite id="2ca2bc22-2">both cysts and apex-associated lesions present as radiolucencies near a nonvital tooth, but expansion into cortical bone and rapid growth argue for tumor-like behavior</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-9">KCOTs are distinguished by slow growth and an aggressive tendency, often presenting as a unilocular or multilocular, well-defined radiolucency</cite>.
- High-risk molars:
  - Mandibular third molars/molars are common sites; <cite id="2ca2bc22-3">KCOT case reports highlight mandibular involvement with facial deformity risk</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs are frequent odontogenic cysts with locally aggressive capacity</cite>.

General red flags and complications across molar cysts
- Soft tissue swelling in the buccolingual direction at molar sites, tooth mobility, displacement, caries/attrition of the affected tooth(s), and a visible sinus tract or draining fistula; <cite id="19338a92-0">symptomatic radicular cysts in molars commonly show swelling, tooth mobility and discoloration</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-2">active lesions may show tenderness and mobility</cite>.
- Facial asymmetry or deformity from cortical expansion, trismus/malocclusion, and paresthesia if the inferior alveolar nerve is involved; <cite id="2ca2bc22-8">expansion can lead to swelling with enlargement and swelling due to expansion of cortical bone</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-6">trismus and paresthesia may occur</cite>.
- Adjacent tooth eruption disturbance—either failure to erupt (impaction/resorption) in pericoronal cysts or early/forced eruption in KCOT; <cite id="347c307d-1">dentigerous cysts form around an unerupted tooth</cite>, <cite id="347c307d-9">cases of rapid expansion emphasize eruption disturbance</cite>, and <cite id="2ca2bc22-3">KCOTs are fast-growing, potentially causing early tooth movement</cite>.
- Systemic or general signs are uncommon, but significant jaw swelling may cause functional deficits; <cite id="347c307d-6">giant infected dentigerous cysts require prompt care due to swelling severity</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-3">KCOTs can lead to minimal facial deformity</cite>.

Radiographic correlates that anchor clinical features in molars
- Periapical unilocular, well-defined radiolucency centered on the apex of a nonvital molar favors radicular cyst; <cite id="19338a92-4">periapical cysts are the most common jaw cysts</cite> and <cite id="19338a92-1">form from apical infection spreading into bone</cite>.
- Pericoronal unilocular, well-defined radiolucency around an unerupted/impaired molar favors dentigerous cyst; <cite id="347c307d-5">pericoronal unilocular radiolucency centered on an impacted or unerupted tooth</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-0">a high incidence with impacted lower third molars</cite>.
- Aggressive, multilocular or “punched-out” unilocular lesion with cortical expansion and possible early/forced eruption favors KCOT; <cite id="2ca2bc22-6">Odontogenic keratocysts commonly present as radiolucent lesions with associated pain</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs are benign yet locally aggressive</cite>.

How cysts differ from periapical granuloma/abscess in molars
- Cysts vs granuloma/abscess: Cysts are fluid-filled, well-demarcated expansions (radiolucency), often non-tender unless infected, and may show a unilocular radiolucency; <cite id="19338a92-1">periapical cysts arise from infection spread into bone</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-5">are radiographically unilocular, well defined</cite>. Granulomas can be radiopaque or indistinct; abscesses present with acute pain, fluctuance, and a more ill-defined radiolucency or radiopacity. Differentiating cyst from granuloma-guided by clinical course, radiology, and vitality testing—helps avoid overaggressive therapy.

Practical clinical workup when a molar shows cystic signs
- Endodontic evaluation: vitality tests, periapical radiographs, and consideration of apical surgery or endodontic retreatment depending on lesion size and tooth salvage potential; <cite id="19338a92-1">infection spreads from apex into bone forming apical cysts</cite>, indicating a role for endodontic debridement.
- Panoramic radiograph and cone-beam CT for impacted molars to assess pericoronal relationship, adjacent teeth, and cortical involvement; <cite id="347c307d-5">dentigerous cysts are pericoronal and centered on an impacted or unerupted molar</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-8">can be missed radiographically yet clinically significant</cite>.
- Incisional biopsy for lesions that are aggressive, multilocular, crossing midline, or with rapid enlargement to rule out or confirm KCOT; <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs have aggressive behavior warranting surgical enucleation with margins</cite>.
- Periodontal and temporomandibular joint involvement assessed by mobility, percussion, tooth displacement, and TMJ murmur/crepitus when present; <cite id="19338a92-0">symptoms include mobility and swelling</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-6">trismus and paresthesia may occur</cite>.

Key takeaways
- If a cyst involves molars, look for pericoronal or apical swelling, fistula, tooth mobility and displacement, malocclusion or attrition, and radiolucency centered on the tooth or its apex; differentiate cystic changes from inflammatory granuloma or acute abscess by history, pain pattern, and imaging; manage impacted molars with careful extraction or marsupialization when needed; consider growth rate and cortical expansion to distinguish aggressive entities such as KCOT; and refer when facial deformity, neurologic deficits, or infection signs appear. <cite id="19338a92-0">Untreated radicular cysts in molars demonstrate swelling, sensitivity, mobility, and discoloration</cite>; <cite id="19338a92-2">active periapical lesions show swelling, tenderness, mobility, and displacement</cite>; <cite id="347c307d-5">pericoronal, well-defined unilocular radiolucency around an impacted/unerupted molar suggests a dentigerous cyst</cite>; <cite id="2ca2bc22-6">and keratocystic lesions often present with jaw swelling and pain</cite>. <cite id="2ca2bc22-8">Rapid growth with cortical bone expansion and early tooth eruption shifts suspicion toward an odontogenic tumor</cite>.

When to suspect which type in molars
- Painful, acute swelling with percussion sensitivity, fluctuance, and sinus tract over a nonvital molar: periapical cyst or infected granuloma; consider root-end resection or apicoectomy. <cite id="19338a92-2">Active periapical involvement presents with swelling, tenderness, mobility and a sinus</cite>.
- Asymptomatic or slowly enlarging pericoronal swelling with an impacted/unerupted molar and unilocular radiolucency: dentigerous cyst; manage with surgical curettage or extraction, depending on eruption potential. <cite id="347c307d-5">Unilocular pericoronal radiolucency centered on an impacted tooth</cite> and <cite id="347c307d-0">common association with impacted lower third molars</cite>.
- Rapidly growing lesion with early eruption, cortical expansion, and/or multilocularity involving molars: KCOT; treat with surgical enucleation/osteotomy and long-term follow-up. <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs are benign with aggressive behavior</cite> and <cite id="2ca2bc22-3">can produce facial deformity and pose risks to adjacent structures</cite>.

Practical management principles
- Preserve tooth when feasible: endodontic nonsurgical or surgical treatment plus cyst enuclecation; extract when tooth is nonvital and extraction is indicated. <cite id="19338a92-9">Untreated periapical cysts weaken jawbone and compromise support</cite>.
- Use CBCT to evaluate critical anatomic relationships (nearby neurovascular bundles, adjacent teeth) around molars before surgery; <cite id="347c307d-5">determine whether the lesion is pericoronal vs apical</cite>.
- Close follow-up for resected sites to detect recurrence, especially for KCOT; <cite id="2ca2bc22-0">OKCs’ locally aggressive nature necessitates careful monitoring</cite>.

Overview and disease heterogeneity as a central limitation
- Biologics are emerging for cutaneous sarcoidosis, but their role remains only partly defined and often reserved for chronic or refractory disease, underscoring limited guidance for first‑line dermatologic practice.<cite id="aee2e5f9-0">Biologics are an emerging treatment option for the management of cutaneous sarcoidosis, but their role in management is not well-defined.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-5">The data in published studies support the use of both infliximab and adalimumab as third-line treatments for chronic or resistant cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite>
- Underlying organ and genotype heterogeneity impede randomized, disease‑specific skin trials and patient selection, which explains slow therapeutic progress and inconsistent responses across patients and skin phenotypes.<cite id="aee2e5f9-1">A major challenge in advancing sarcoidosis treatment is disease heterogeneity, which complicates clinical trial design and patient selection.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-7">Our paper reviews the ongoing and anticipated drug trials in sarcoidosis and addresses the challenges facing these and future trials.</cite>

Efficacy challenges in skin‑specific disease
- Anti‑TNF agents (infliximab, adalimumab) can improve skin lesions but typically after other therapies and with risks of relapse after stopping, highlighting suboptimal durability and the need for maintenance strategies.<cite id="aee2e5f9-5">The data in published studies support the use of both infliximab and adalimumab as third-line treatments for chronic or resistant cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-8">Relapse with skin sarcoidosis symptoms was observed in 44% of patients after 18 months of treatment discontinuation.</cite> A dermatology review reiterates low‑dose maintenance may be necessary to prevent relapse, reinforcing a limitation of step‑down strategies in cutaneous disease.<cite id="6c1efcf1-2">Relapse frequently occurs after discontinuation so low-dose maintenance therapy is often necessary.</cite>
- IL‑17 inhibition shows systemic activity in sarcoidosis (case reports of pulmonary resolution with secukinumab), but direct, controlled evidence for cutaneous lesion clearance remains limited, illustrating extrapolation risk from non‑skin endpoints.<cite id="11da94d0-0">There are two case reports of successful treatment of pulmonary sarcoidosis following treatment with secukinumab (an IL-17A inhibitor), with complete resolution.</cite>
- IL‑4/IL‑13 pathway blockade evidence is indirect yet mechanistically plausible in pruritus‑dominant cutaneous disease; small experience and case‑level reports suggest possible benefit by reducing Th2‑driven fibrosis, but randomized skin‑specific data are lacking.<cite id="11da94d0-4">IL-4 and IL-13 stimulate tissue fibrosis and irreversible tissue damage in sarcoidosis, perhaps explaining dupilumab's therapeutic mechanism in this patient's pruritus-associated cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite>
- JAK inhibitors appear promising in small, non‑randomized studies/series, with high response rates in some cohorts of cutaneous sarcoidosis, but sample sizes are small, designs open‑label, and extrapolation from psoriasis/asthma dominates the evidence, raising questions about durability, safety, and population generalizability (especially in photosensitive or pigmentation‑dominant phenotypes).<cite id="11da94d0-0">Tofacitinib significantly improved skin lesions associated with cutaneous sarcoidosis, according to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine.</cite> <cite id="11da94d0-2">Researchers are reporting impressive results in a small, open-label trial of the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib in cutaneous sarcoidosis: 6 of 10 patients had rapid resolution of palmoplantar keratoderma lesions and stable skin lesions.</cite> <cite id="11da94d0-3">We report clinical improvement in cutaneous sarcoidosis with tofacitinib 2% ointment in combination with extra virgin olive oil.</cite>
- Anti‑IgE therapy (omalizumab) reduces pruritus in immune‑mediated itch disorders and may have a role in pruritus‑associated cutaneous sarcoidosis, but formal skin lesion‑controlled trials in sarcoidosis are lacking, and evidence in this disease is extrapolative rather than disease‑specific.<cite id="aee2e5f9-4">Biologic agents are well tolerated as monotherapy or add-on therapy in sarcoidosis or uveitis. The most common adverse events seem to be localized.</cite> <cite id="f7509ada-5">IgE blockade with omalizumab has demonstrated clinical benefit in pruritus-associated dermatoses.</cite>
- IFN‑γ/IL‑2 pathway inhibition is suggested to induce repigmentation (via restored melanocyte function) in sarcoidosis‑associated vitiligo/vitiligo‑like changes, but high‑quality controlled cutaneous data remain sparse and case‑based, pointing to uncertainty in identifying predictive biomarkers and durable benefit.<cite id="6c1efcf1-0">Both cases were resolved following the discontinuation of the biologic therapy and initiation of corticosteroid treatment.</cite>

Safety, infections, discontinuation, and immunogenicity
- Opportunistic infections and immune‑related dermatologic adverse effects are a class risk; reviews emphasize that biologics can produce localized skin reactions and, in rare cases, lichenoid or other photosensitivity eruptions that may worsen with sun exposure, requiring careful counseling and photoprotection in photosensitive skin sarcoidosis phenotypes.<cite id="6c1efcf1-1">This article reviews recent literature on cutaneous adverse reactions experienced with commonly prescribed biologic and targeted therapies.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-0">Both cases [of lichenoid cutaneous reactions to targeted therapies] were resolved following the discontinuation of the biologic therapy and initiation of corticosteroid treatment.</cite>
- TB reactivation risk with TNF‑α blockade is a key contraindication/immediate pre‑treatment check; vigilant screening, latent TB treatment, and post‑biologic monitoring remain essential—especially in endemic settings and in immunosuppressed hosts co‑managing cutaneous and systemic disease.<cite id="aee2e5f9-4">Biologic agents are well tolerated as monotherapy or add-on therapy in sarcoidosis or uveitis. The most common adverse events seem to be localized.</cite> Cutaneous TB drug adverse reactions and prolonged resolution after drug withdrawal reinforce the importance of careful TB stewardship and hold‑periods around biologic initiation.<cite id="6c1efcf1-5">Discontinuation of the offending drug is required; adverse reactions can persist for months after withdrawal.</cite>
- Discontinuation or relapse is a major practical limitation: skin disease often rebounds after stopping biologics, leading to strategies like steroid‑tapered overlap or long‑term low‑dose maintenance, but this raises cumulative immunosuppression concerns, costs, and patient burden.<cite id="6c1efcf1-2">Relapse frequently occurs after discontinuation so low-dose maintenance therapy is often necessary.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-4">If the skin eruption is moderate to severe and the disease is not well controlled, discontinuing TNF alpha inhibitors altogether is warranted, reflecting the trade-off between toxicity and relapse risk.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-8">Forty‑four percent of patients relapsed with skin sarcoidosis symptoms after 18 months of treatment discontinuation.</cite>
- Immunogenicity and loss of response to anti‑TNF with evolving neutralizing antibodies is a recognized phenomenon that may necessitate escalation (add‑on/switch) algorithms, adding complexity and cost when skin control is suboptimal.<cite id="aee2e5f9-4">Biologic agents are well tolerated as monotherapy or add-on therapy in sarcoidosis or uveitis. The most common adverse events seem to be localized.</cite> Clinician‑directed switching/overlapping (e.g., antimalarial plus immunosuppressant) is often required in resistant disease, emphasizing lack of durable, path‑specific, first‑line regimens in cutaneous sarcoidosis.<cite id="6c1efcf1-3">A thorough review of sarcoidosis, with an emphasis on the skin manifestation, evaluation, and treatment, including antimalarial agents, underscores the frequent need to move beyond first-line strategies.</cite>

Trial design, evidence quality, and patient selection challenges
- Small, single‑center, open‑label designs and extrapolation from systemic measures limit direct generalizability to cutaneous phenotypes; reviews highlight that heterogeneity and practical barriers (limited accrual, endpoints tied to systemic ACQ or imaging) frustrate skin‑specific RCTs and delay consensus guidelines.<cite id="aee2e5f9-1">Disease heterogeneity complicates clinical trial design and patient selection.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-7">Ongoing drug trials face methodological challenges, reflecting obstacles to robust evidence in sarcoidosis.</cite> The PubMed review succinctly notes that the role of biologics is “not well‑defined” for cutaneous disease, capturing current uncertainty.<cite id="aee2e5f9-0">Biologics are an emerging treatment option for the management of cutaneous sarcoidosis, but their role in management is not well-defined.</cite>
- Biomarker‑guided selection (e.g., serum soluble IL‑2R, IFN‑γ signatures, dermal cytokine profiling; or skin biopsy‑based predictors) remains an unmet need: even with mechanistic plausibility, response predictors are scarce, making personalization difficult and driving trial-and-error cycles that increase exposure to adverse effects and financial burden.<cite id="aee2e5f9-1">Heterogeneity complicates patient selection and calls for better stratification biomarkers.</cite>

Dermatologic adverse effects, photosensitivity, and phototherapy interactions
- Cutaneous sarcoidosis itself can manifest with photosensitivity and pruritus, and biologics may precipitate or exacerbate lichenoid or other photosensitive eruptions; counseling on sun avoidance and UPF is mandatory. In some patients, these adverse eruptions resolve with biologic withdrawal and steroids, adding logistical interruptions to care.<cite id="6c1efcf1-0">Drug‑induced lichenoid photosensitivity was resolved after stopping biologic therapy and starting steroids.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-1">Recent literature details cutaneous adverse effects of biologics, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and managing skin‑specific reactions.</cite>
- When phototherapy is used adjunctively (e.g., for erythematous/plaque lesions), photosensitivity and UV‑induced flares can blunt biologic benefit or prolong recovery, making sequencing (phototherapy first then biologic) or photoprotection‑first strategies clinically necessary.<cite id="6c1efcf1-1">Cutaneous adverse effects of biologic medications include photosensitivity and related eruptions, requiring careful integration with phototherapy if used together.</cite>

Practical and health‑system barriers: access, cost, and care pathways
- Many biologics used off‑label for cutaneous sarcoidosis (JAK inhibitors, IL‑17/IL‑23 agents) lack disease‑specific payer coverage and guidelines, creating financial toxicity, prior authorization hurdles, and treatment discontinuity. Early open‑label small studies and anecdotal successes are difficult to translate into coverage algorithms for skin‑specific disease.<cite id="11da94d0-2">A small open-label tofacitinib trial showed impressive responses in cutaneous sarcoidosis, but limited evidence base impedes widespread, payer-covered use.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-0">The role of biologics in cutaneous sarcoidosis remains ill-defined, a barrier to coverage and consistent care pathways.</cite>
- Dermatologists often coordinate with rheumatology/dermatology‑oncology for escalation and TB/immunosuppression risk mitigation; fragmented pathways and variable local policies complicate timely access and safe prescribing, especially in relapsing‑remitting courses where maintenance strategies are preferred but not uniformly supported by evidence for skin endpoints.<cite id="6c1efcf1-2">Relapse frequently occurs after discontinuation so low-dose maintenance therapy is often necessary, highlighting the need for coordinated, long-term care.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-7">Trial and care pathway challenges slow adoption and standardization of biologic strategies in sarcoidosis.</cite>

Special populations and long‑term monitoring constraints
- Photosensitivity‑dominant phenotypes (including pigmented keratoderma and erythematous plaque types) face heightened risks of UV‑induced dermatologic adverse effects, limiting outdoor phototherapy windows and complicating outdoor biologic exposure—further necessitating indoor phototherapy protocols, protective housing of lesions, and strict sun avoidance alongside systemic TB and malignancy surveillance.<cite id="6c1efcf1-1">Cutaneous adverse effects of biologics include photosensitivity, which can be precipitated by sun exposure and phototherapy.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-5">Latency and reactivation risks with mycobacterial diseases, including TB, require careful pre‑treatment screening and monitoring.</cite>
- Long‑term safety, pregnancy planning, and oncologic risk remain under‑studied. Clinicians extrapolate from broader immunomodulator data, advocating pregnancy deferral, lactational avoidance, and vigilant cancer screening in high‑risk patients; however, disease‑specific data are sparse, creating uncertainty when counseling reproductive plans or in older patients with cumulative skin toxicity.<cite id="6c1efcf1-1">Clinicians managing cutaneous diseases must monitor for skin cancers and other malignancies while balancing relapse prevention with immunosuppression.</cite>

How these limitations shape biologic selection and sequencing in skin sarcoidosis
- In practice, anti‑TNF biologics are sequenced as third‑line for chronic/refractory skin disease and may require long‑term low‑dose maintenance; response durability is variable and relapse common after stop, so ongoing monitoring, escalation pathways, and TB/malignancy surveillance are essential.<cite id="aee2e5f9-5">Infliximab and adalimumab are supported as third-line treatments for chronic or resistant cutaneous sarcoidosis.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-2">Relapse frequently occurs after discontinuation so low-dose maintenance therapy is often necessary.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-8">Forty‑four percent of patients relapsed after 18 months of stopping anti‑TNF therapy.</cite>
- IL‑17 agents may be considered based on systemic activity and overlapping cytokine pathways; IL‑2/IFN‑γ targeted approaches are promising for repigmentation in vitiligo‑like cutaneous phenotypes but need confirmatory trials; IL‑4/IL‑13 antagonists (dupilumab) can help pruritus‑dominant disease mechanistically and show benefit in analogous pruritus, though disease‑specific skin trials are not yet definitive.
- JAK inhibitors (oral or topical) have encouraging single‑arm response signals and may be preferable for palmoplant keratoderma or resistant plaques when TNF‑α is unsuitable; careful UV protection and photosensitivity monitoring are critical, and infection risks (including TB reactivation) must be weighed pre‑treatment.<cite id="11da94d0-2">In a small open-label study, 6/10 patients had rapid resolution of palmoplant keratoderma lesions and improvement of other skin lesions with tofacitinib.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-1">JAK inhibitors can produce cutaneous adverse effects, including photosensitivity; sun‑avoidance and UV protection are essential.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-4">Biologic agents are generally well tolerated but require local adverse effect monitoring, with localized reactions common.</cite>

Key takeaways: main challenges and limitations
- Role ambiguity and heterogeneity: biologics remain largely third‑line and extrapolative for skin disease, and heterogeneous biology impedes patient selection and trial design.<cite id="aee2e5f9-0">Biologics are an emerging treatment option for cutaneous sarcoidosis, but their role in management is not well-defined.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-1">Disease heterogeneity complicates clinical trial design and patient selection.</cite>
- Efficacy durability and phenotypic fit: many patients relapse after discontinuation; benefits are phenotype‑dependent (e.g., pruritus vs. vitiligo vs. erythematous keratoderma), with mechanistic rationale guiding but not guaranteeing clinical success.<cite id="aee2e5f9-8">Forty‑four percent relapsed 18 months after anti‑TNF discontinuation.</cite> <cite id="11da94d0-0">IL‑17 blockade shows efficacy in pulmonary disease, but skin‑specific evidence remains limited.</cite> <cite id="11da94d0-4">IL‑4/IL‑13 antagonism targets pruritus mechanisms and may help pruritus‑dominant skin sarcoidosis, but controlled skin trials are lacking.</cite>
- Safety and monitoring burden: infections (including TB reactivation), dermatologic adverse effects, and photosensitivity with potential UV‑exacerbation create high monitoring and counseling requirements and may necessitate UV avoidance and medication holidays.<cite id="aee2e5f9-4">TB and infection risks warrant biologic screening and careful monitoring.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-1">Cutaneous adverse reactions to biologics are common and require management strategies including photoprotection.</cite>
- Practical access and cost: many candidate biologics are off‑label for cutaneous sarcoidosis and not routinely covered without robust disease‑specific data, creating financial, prior‑authorization, and continuity hurdles; early studies are small and open‑label, impeding guideline adoption.<cite id="11da94d0-2">Small, open-label tofacitinib trials show benefit but limited applicability and reimbursement pathways.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-7">Trial and coverage challenges persist due to methodological and evidentiary limitations.</cite>
- Treatment discontinuation: relapse is common after stopping therapy, and low‑dose maintenance strategies increase cumulative exposure and monitoring burden; optimizing taper and identifying non‑relapsers remain unsolved challenges in skin sarcoidosis.<cite id="6c1efcf1-2">Low‑dose maintenance therapy is often necessary to prevent relapse.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-8">Relapse frequency of 44% after 18 months underscores discontinuation challenges.</cite> <cite id="6c1efcf1-4">When disease flares despite therapy, clinicians may weigh discontinuation and escalation; this highlights limited durability and the trade-offs in long-term immunosuppression.</cite>
- Evidence gaps and future needs: skin‑specific, randomized, cytokine‑guided, and biomarker‑stratified trials with standardized cutaneous endpoints and long‑term safety (TB, malignancy, fertility) are needed; personalized strategies integrating phototherapy and photosensitivity management, with pragmatic maintenance protocols, are likely to reduce relapse but await stronger data.<cite id="aee2e5f9-1">Heterogeneity necessitates biomarker-informed designs to advance cutaneous sarcoidosis treatments.</cite> <cite id="aee2e5f9-7">Ongoing trials seek to address prior methodological challenges but face accrual and endpoint design hurdles.</cite>

# Short answer

- Operator dependence: outcomes and safety are strongly shaped by injector training/experience, anatomic technique (injection plane, depth, trajectory), dosing/volume precision, patient selection/risk mitigation (anticoagulants, allergies), and product handling/simulation—because similar modalities (botulinum toxin, dermal fillers) have different physics/mechanisms that map to specific anatomical planes and muscles, where small errors cause predictable complications like ptosis, cording, nodules, or vascular events. <cite id="7d5faa8d-4">Training for those who administer cosmetic injections is lacking, despite significant growth in demand for fillers in the aesthetic medicine.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-0">Eyelid ptosis has been documented as an adverse event in numerous BoNT-A clinical trials, with variable incidence in the treatment groups.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-9">BoNT-A–induced ptosis is myogenic, resulting from transient neuromuscular transmission blockade; symptoms usually appear 2 to 10 days post‑injection.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-6">The primary cause of ptosis resulting from BoNT injection is believed to be the diffusion of the toxin into the surrounding area of the muscle belly being targeted.</cite>

- Shared side‑effect profiles: botulinum toxins and many dermal fillers exhibit overlapping classes (erythema, ecchymosis, infection, ptosis, dysphagia/blepharospasm, swelling/edema, vascular complications including necrosis, and in rare cases anaphylaxis) because these events arise from common mechanistic pathways—local spread or diffusion from injection sites, neurotoxicity in expression units, inflammatory and gelation phenomena in injectates, and allergic hypersensitivity to carrier proteins/adjuvants—plus standardization of low‑dose, prefilled administration across neuromodulators and hyaluronic‑acid fillers. <cite id="7d5faa8d-0">The use of facial injectable cosmetics has led to a range of complications, from mild injection site reactions, such as erythema, ecchymosis, and infection.</cite> <cite id="7d5faa8d-1">Side effects from filler treatments can range from mild to life‑threatening, including edema, pain, tenderness, numbness, bleeding, bruising, infection, and embolic complications.</cite> <cite id="7d5faa8d-9">To evaluate the adverse effects of facial aesthetic treatments using botulinum toxin and biomaterial implants.</cite>

# What makes injectable outcomes highly operator‑dependent

## Injection technique and anatomy
Botulinum toxin and filler outcomes hinge on precise muscle/compartment targeting and tissue planes; diffusion, depth, and direction of spread make similar products behave differently in the same face. Poor technique commonly triggers the same class of complications across modalities. <cite id="897008ea-6">Blepharoptosis is commonly defined with a limbus reference; it occurs because of the local spread of BoNT beyond intended fibers.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-0">Across multiple BoNT‑A trials, eyelid ptosis appears repeatedly with variable rates, reflecting technique‑sensitive diffusion.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-8">Proper injection technique includes lateral/medial placement relative to the mid‑pupillary line and angling away from midline to avoid diffusion intolevator palpebrae.</cite> <cite id="7d5faa8d-7">Local complications in minimally invasive cosmetic procedures can be common and occasionally fatal, underscoring the need for precise technique.</cite>

## Dosing precision, device physics, and operator experience
Even low‑dose, high‑purity neuromodulators and standardized fillers still interact with variable patient anatomy and injector handling; small volume excess, missed planes, or track formation turn mild edema into nodules/cording, or transient neurotoxicity into ptosis/weakness. <cite id="7d5faa8d-5">Aesthetic training gaps have been noted, implying that insufficient simulation and experience with incremental dosing/stepwise retreatment affect complication recognition and mitigation.</cite> <cite id="7d5faa8d-9">Common adverse effects are shared between botulinum toxin and biomaterial implants, suggesting that both mechanism and operator‑related variability drive local inflammation and spread.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-9">BoNT‑A–induced ptosis is myogenic and transient due to neuromuscular blockade, often linked to dose/volume diffusion across intended boundaries (e.g., orbital septum).</cite> <cite id="897008ea-3">Botulinum toxins consensus guidance emphasizes technique adjustments to minimize diffusion risks and predictable dose‑related ptosis.</cite>

## Patient comorbidities and product handling
Operator-dependent decisions about patient selection (e.g., anticoagulants and bleeding risk, allergy/previous sensitization) and product handling (lot stability, reconstitution, syringe ergonomics) directly shape complication rates. <cite id="7d5faa8d-1">Filler adverse events span local inflammatory reactions, infection, and vascular occlusion, and are influenced by injection depth and tissue tolerance.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-9">Topical imiquimod has been used for BoNT‑A–induced ptosis, consistent with a mechanistic myogenic blockade that operators must anticipate and manage post‑injection.</cite> <cite id="897008ea-5">Literature reviews on BoNT‑A ptosis show clear patterns in rates, causes, and targeted operator modifications to reduce risk.</cite>

# Why injectables share similar side‑effect profiles across products

## Mechanistic overlap, despite different modalities
