- Mechanism-informed selection: TGR5-predominant therapies are attractive for simultaneous hepatic and vascular risk targeting (apoB/A1 lowering, VLDL reduction), whereas FXR-predominant agents (OCA) more reliably improve steatosis/fibrosis but show variable lipids; combining receptor-selective agents with established cardiometabolic therapies (GLP-1 agonists for glycemia; statins for LDL) may optimize CV risk control in NAFLD. <cite id="021d6d8c-0">FXR integrates lipid and glucose metabolism</cite> <cite id="a2e2f9b6-0">TGR5 activation enhances hepatic energy metabolism and reduces inflammatory steatosis</cite>.

Limitations and questions where randomized evidence remains thin
- Parenteral or oral sodium-based bile salt–glucose interventions lack clear, recent RCTs in NAFLD directly reporting HbA1c, insulin, and lipid changes; existing narrative and mechanistic reviews support bile salts’ role in glycemic and lipid regulation, but head-to-head NAFLD RCTs are limited, and data are heterogeneous. <cite id="98972a42-3">Signaling through bile salts in cardiovascular–metabolic disease is being explored, with bile salt-based therapies under study</cite>.
- Within OCA/related bile-acid therapy, trial heterogeneity in dosing, disease stage, and co-medications contributes to variability in lipid effects; multi-arm RCTs comparing bile-acid receptor–selective agents with standard-of-care GLP-1/statin backgrounds are needed to precisely estimate CV benefit–harm trade-offs and glycemic synergies.
- Lipid endpoints that best reflect CV risk (LDL-P, non-HDL-C, apoB, apoA-I, ratios, inflammation) are underreported in small NAFLD trials; larger FLINT/SELECT successors and next-gen FXR/TGR5 studies with standardized lipid/marker panels and pre-specified CV endpoints are the highest priority to resolve uncertainties.

Bottom line
- In randomized trials across UDCA and OCA/bile-acid receptor agonist programs, bile acid therapies reliably improve liver histology and reduce insulin resistance, with modest improvements in glycemic control and mixed but clinically meaningful effects on lipid profiles in NAFLD/NASH; these changes translate to improved or at least stabilized cardiovascular risk markers when managed carefully, especially by co-optimizing glucose and lipids with standard therapies. <cite id="a612979a-1">UDCA reduces fasting glucose, HbA1c, and insulin</cite> <cite id="2f60bb25-0">OCA improves NASH histology</cite> <cite id="2f60bb25-9">OCA’s LDL/TC increases highlight trade-offs requiring monitoring and co-therapy</cite>. Clinicians should expect insulin-sensitivity improvements with glycemic gains (particularly with UDCA) and histology improvements with OCA, and monitor LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, and apolipoproteins closely; adding standard lipid-lowering therapy when needed can counteract LDL elevations and further lower CV risk in NAFLD/NASH populations. <cite id="2f60bb25-0">Hepatic and metabolic improvements with OCA sustained to 72 weeks</cite> <cite id="2f60bb25-9">OCA increased total and LDL cholesterol versus placebo</cite> <cite id="a2e2f9b6-8">Direct effects on LDL and HDL necessitate monitoring and adjunctive therapy</cite>.

Summary
Multiple strands of evidence converge that how healthcare providers communicate with adolescents with type 1 diabetes (T1D) measurably shapes their willingness and ability to follow self‑management routines (insulin dosing, blood glucose monitoring, medication, follow‑up), often mediated by autonomy, self‑efficacy, and trust. <cite id="1170b329-0">Effective communication between pediatric diabetes patients and their providers has the potential to enhance patient satisfaction and health outcomes</cite>. <cite id="1170b329-8">Provider communication is a key lever for facilitating adherence behaviors in adolescents with T1D</cite>. These effects are demonstrated in trials of motivational interviewing (MI)–based counseling, nurse‑led education, tailored outreach, and communication‑rich team and peer models, with improvements in self‑management behaviors and glycemic control (HbA1c) compared to usual or structured non‑MI care. <cite id="4b2bd661-1">Motivational interviewing approaches in adolescents with T1D have been associated with decreased HbA1c and improved self‑management</cite>. <cite id="ac071bf6-2">Nurse‑led multidisciplinary team management improves HbA1c and quality of life in diabetes populations</cite>. <cite id="1170b329-7">Provider‑facilitated text‑message engagement improves adherence among adolescents with T1D</cite>.

Mechanisms: how provider communication drives adherence
1) Autonomy‑supportive, collaborative exchange. <cite id="c34a7b68-2">Autonomy‑supportive communication by health care providers and parents improves treatment adherence in adolescents with T1D</cite>. <cite id="4b2bd661-3">In adolescents with T1D, nurse‑led MI sessions over six months substantially enhanced general and disease‑specific self‑management skills, consistent with MI’s collaborative, goal‑oriented, change‑focused language</cite>. These findings align with self‑determination theory: when providers affirm choice, rationale, and future goals and invite adolescent reason‑giving, adherence behaviors (testing, dosing) increase via higher self‑efficacy and intrinsic motivation. <cite id="4b2bd661-0">A randomized controlled trial in teens with T1D found MI‑in‑education outperformed structured education on adherence behaviors</cite>.

2) Empathic, tailored information delivery. <cite id="c34a7b68-1">Adolescents face psychological and social obstacles to T1D adherence, including shifting family dynamics</cite>. Empathy and culturally/developmentally appropriate explanations reduce decisional fog and improve medication scheduling adherence; MI‑trained providers explicitly attune to adolescent distress, beliefs, and health literacy to co‑construct plans. <cite id="4b2bd661-9">MI is a collaborative, goal‑oriented communication style designed to strengthen motivation within patients by eliciting change talk and reducing resistance</cite>. <cite id="ac071bf6-0">Nurse‑led DSME improves self‑care practices through tailored, consistent coaching</cite>.

3) Shared decision‑making and realistic goal setting. <cite id="1170b329-1">A T1D adherence review highlights that clinician guidance and communication can mitigate common adolescent barriers (symptom management complexity, access, and psychosocial stress), thereby supporting adherence</cite>. Providers who incorporate adolescent preferences (device use, mealtime insulin ratios) and family input into step‑wise decisions increase perceived fairness and follow‑through, and MI pilots operationalize this by structuring provider questions to elicit pros/cons and values and committing to small, incremental rule changes (e.g., carb counts vs. estimated insulin).

4) Continuity, safety planning, and transition readiness. <cite id="c34a7b68-3">Communication training for parents and providers to make interactions more autonomy‑supportive can improve adolescent adherence</cite>. <cite id="c34a7b68-5">Qualitative analyses show adolescents and parents often disagree on readiness to manage T1D independently, with communication patterns in visits and clinics not consistently promoting self‑management confidence</cite>. <cite id="c34a7b68-6">Qualitative adolescent accounts indicate prevailing health care communication patterns may not promote readiness for independent disease management</cite>. When providers anticipate transition (care coordination across pediatric and adult teams, appointment control, and emergency plan co‑creation), adolescents integrate monitoring and dose adjustments into daily life more reliably.

5) Family involvement and confidentiality. <cite id="1170b329-8">Provider communication within the family context is central to adolescent T1D adherence</cite>. Providers who respectfully scaffold family roles (education sessions with adolescent autonomy safeguards, parent–adolescent communication coaching) often improve nighttime or school‑day adherence; conversely, overbearing directives or secrecy that undermine adolescent privacy can erode cooperation. <cite id="ac071bf6-3">Team‑based approaches built on the Chronic Care Model emphasize relationships, communication, and community linkages to sustain high‑quality chronic care</cite>.

Intervention evidence linking communication style to adherence and glycemic outcomes
- Motivational interviewing–based counseling. <cite id="4b2bd661-0">An RCT in adolescents with T1D comparing MI‑in‑education to structured education found MI improved adherence behaviors</cite>; <cite id="4b2bd661-2">a six‑month nurse‑led MI program in adolescents enhanced self‑management skills and disease‑specific behaviors</cite>. <cite id="4b2bd661-1">A randomized controlled pilot trial reported MI was associated with decreased HbA1c and improved self‑management</cite>. <cite id="4b2bd661-4">MI‑guided analyses of adolescent–provider visits show provider language maps onto autonomy support and predicts engagement in self‑care tasks</cite>. <cite id="4b2bd661-7">A MI framework trial (NCT03906786) targets provider communication to improve type 1 diabetes self‑care</cite>.

- Nurse‑led, team‑supported education and follow‑up. <cite id="ac071bf6-0">Nurse‑led diabetes self‑management education improves self‑care practice and adherence outcomes</cite>. <cite id="ac071bf6-2">Community nurse‑led multidisciplinary management improves HbA1c and quality of life, consistent with improved self‑management and supportive communication across clinicians</cite>. Although much diabetes team research is in type 2 populations, these models generalize to pediatric T1D teams: <cite id="ac071bf6-1">multidisciplinary teams facilitate patients’ self‑management through coordinated, clear communication</cite>. <cite id="ac071bf6-3">The Chronic Care Model highlights communication infrastructure as a core system component for optimal chronic disease management</cite>.

- Technology‑mediated, provider‑facilitated prompts. <cite id="1170b329-7">Engagement with a text‑messaging intervention for adolescents with T1D improved adherence; provider involvement in content and response boosted behavioral activation</cite>. <cite id="1170b329-6">Adolescents report numerous barriers to insulin adherence; provider‑linked mobile strategies explicitly address these barriers through tailored messaging and rapid coaching</cite>.

- Peer‑supported care as a communicative environment. <cite id="ac071bf6-9">Virtual peer groups for adolescents and young adults with T1D lowered HbA1c; peer leaders emulate provider communication by offering normative support, practical troubleshooting, and motivational framing</cite>.

Adolescent preferences, barriers, and dyadic dynamics that communication can address
- Psychological and social barriers. <cite id="c34a7b68-1">Adolescent adherence barriers include anxiety, stigma, and flux in family dynamics, which providers can mitigate by eliciting coping plans, normalizing help‑seeking, and involving supportive families</cite>. <cite id="c34a7b68-2">Autonomy‑supportive provider communication, combined with parental autonomy support, improves adherence</cite>.

- Readiness mismatch and transition. <cite id="c34a7b68-5">Parents and adolescents frequently disagree about readiness to manage T1D, with qualitative analyses indicating clinic communication seldom builds adolescent confidence</cite>. <cite id="c34a7b68-6">Communication patterns often hinder readiness for independent management</cite>. Providers can close this gap by co‑creating transferable routines (e.g., school‑bag checklists with shared decisioning), clarifying roles at home and school, and scheduling pre‑adult visits.

- Confidentiality and trust. <cite id="c34a7b68-0">Effective provider–adolescent communication improves satisfaction and outcomes</cite>. Adolescents report improved adherence when providers respect privacy, coordinate with schools discreetly, and build trust that conversations will not precipitate parental conflict.

Communication competencies clinicians can apply
- Use MI techniques: express interest in the adolescent’s story; roll with resistance; summarize change talk; set concrete, co‑agreed steps. <cite id="4b2bd661-9">MI strengthens motivation by focusing on collaborative change talk, reducing directive pressure</cite>. <cite id="4b2bd661-2">Nurse‑led MI sessions improved self‑management skills, demonstrating feasibility in adolescents over six months</cite>.

- Family‑centered communication: educate parents and adolescents together with clear role negotiation; coach parents in autonomy‑supportive language to improve the home environment. <cite id="c34a7b68-3">Training parents and providers in autonomy‑supportive communication is recommended to enhance adolescent adherence</cite>.

- Health literacy and tailoring: use teach‑back, plain language, visuals; match information to developmental stage and tech literacy. <cite id="ac071bf6-0">Nurse‑led DSME improves self‑care behavior by tailoring education and reinforcement</cite>.

- Previsit planning and transitions: ask about school routines, device use, recent hypoglycemia; co‑create a three‑month “transition toolkit” for home/school with a handoff to adult providers. <cite id="c34a7b68-5">Communication patterns are a key obstacle to readiness; proactive, structured communication improves transition</cite>.

- Safety scripting and SBIRT: brief screening for psychosocial problems that impede adherence (e.g., anxiety), with referral coaching. <cite id="c34a7b68-1">Psychological factors and social stressors are common barriers that require targeted communication and support</cite>.

- Culture‑congruent delivery: incorporate family values, languages, and stigma reduction, with sensitivity to immigration status. <cite id="1170b329-8">Providers’ communication plays a crucial role in facilitating adherence among adolescents and their families</cite>.

Evaluating impact and closing gaps
Clinicians and teams can operationalize these behaviors in visits and messaging and monitor adherence via validated tools and HbA1c. <cite id="4b2bd661-0">Compared with structured education, MI‑oriented counseling improved adherence behaviors in a randomized adolescent T1D trial</cite>, suggesting behavior change as a mechanism. <cite id="ac071bf6-2">Team‑led care improved HbA1c and QOL</cite>, implying system‑level communication infrastructure as a mediator. Qualitative work underscores high‑leverage targets: reducing stigma, aligning with adolescent readiness, and improving family–provider alignment. <cite id="c34a7b68-3">Autonomy‑supportive communication training is a feasible intervention to enhance adherence</cite>.

Open questions. Mechanistic mediation studies that isolate conversational dimensions (e.g., autonomy support score) and link them to self‑efficacy and behavior are still limited in T1D adolescents. Heterogeneity by developmental stage, cultural context, and digital literacy suggests a need for MI plus tailored remote coaching and transition‑specific communication protocols. <cite id="ac071bf6-3">Communication capacity across teams remains a system constraint that warrants measurement and improvement</cite>.

Practical takeaway. Provider communication does not merely “inform” about insulin; it builds a trusting, collaborative partnership, co‑owns a practical self‑management plan, removes contextual barriers at home/school, and transitions responsibilities smoothly to adulthood. <cite id="1170b329-0">When communicated effectively, adolescents report higher satisfaction and better health outcomes</cite>. <cite id="c34a7b68-2">Autonomy‑supportive care yields higher adherence</cite>, and <cite id="4b2bd661-1">can improve glycemic control</cite>, making communication both a behavioral mechanism and a clinical outcome in adolescent T1D.

Summary
Adjusting for smoking, alcohol use, and BMI substantially alters the apparent relationship between diabetes and oral cancer risk. Large population-based studies generally find that a history of diabetes is associated with higher overall head and neck cancer risk, and this includes higher risks for oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers; however, after rigorous adjustment and matching for lifestyle factors and adiposity, most of this excess risk dissipates, leaving at most modest or site-specific residual associations. <cite id="60620c2d-2">The risks of developing oral cavity cancer, oropharyngeal cancer, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma were significantly higher in patients with diabetes mellitus</cite>, yet <cite id="0e763111-9">odds ratios for head and neck cancer increase with greater cigarette and alcohol use and lower body mass index</cite>, and <cite id="ecc1c1b9-1">cases are more likely to be smokers, alcohol drinkers, and have lower BMI than controls</cite>, patterns that point to important confounding.

Background: Established risk factors for oral/oropharyngeal cancer
Smoking and alcohol use are the leading modifiable risk factors for oral and oropharyngeal cancers, with combined exposure producing multiplicative excess risk. <cite id="ecc1c1b9-0">Odds ratios for head and neck cancer increase with greater cigarette and alcohol use and lower body mass index</cite>, and <cite id="60620c2d-5">smoking and drinking alcohol together strongly increase oral cancer risk</cite>. <cite id="60620c2d-6">Smoking and alcohol individually increase oral cancer likelihood, and together can drive up to a 30-fold increase in a patient’s risk</cite>. This strong background confounding is directly relevant to interpreting diabetes–cancer associations.

Diabetes (especially type 2) and oral/oropharyngeal cancer before adjustment
Several observational studies report elevated risks of oral–oropharyngeal cancers among people with diabetes, especially type 2. <cite id="60620c2d-2">Patients with diabetes mellitus have significantly higher risks of oral cavity, oropharyngeal, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma</cite>, and <cite id="7ff80885-3">type 2 diabetes confers elevated risk of oral cancer and precancerous lesions</cite>. Large consortia also note consistent links between metabolic traits and head and neck cancer risk. <cite id="0e763111-2">Obesity and related metabolic disorders, including type 2 diabetes, have been associated with head and neck cancer risk across observational studies</cite>.

Impact of adjusting for smoking, alcohol, and BMI
Adjustment for smoking, alcohol, and BMI exerts three principal effects:

1) Strong attenuation (often near-null) of diabetes-associated risk: Case–control and cohort evidence that carefully matches or adjusts for smoking and alcohol yields little to no excess risk of oral/oropharyngeal cancer among diabetics. <cite id="ecc1c1b9-5">When analyses adjust for BMI and major lifestyle factors, the positive associations observed in unadjusted or crudely adjusted models weaken substantially</cite>. <cite id="0e763111-5">ORs for oral cavity/pharyngeal cancer rose with smoking and alcohol, whereas risk related to lower BMI varied by subsite, indicating that body size and lifestyle confounders materially influence estimates</cite>. These patterns are consistent with pooled data showing that smokers and drinkers have much higher head and neck cancer risks than non–smokers or non–drinkers, implying that failure to adjust explains much of the spurious diabetes signal in non–adjusted analyses. <cite id="0e763111-5">Odds ratios for BMI, smoking, and drinking increased in a dose–response manner for oral cavity and pharyngeal cancers</cite>.

2) Type-specific heterogeneity: The degree of attenuation differs by diabetes type. Type 2 diabetes often reflects shared metabolic and lifestyle risk pathways; after adjustment, many excess risks are reduced or confined to subgroups with additional exposures. <cite id="60620c2d-2">Risks were higher for oral and oropharyngeal cancers among patients with diabetes mellitus</cite>, yet <cite id="60620c2d-9">smoking and alcohol are the two main risk factors linked to head and neck cancers (especially oral cancer), and in case–control settings that pair and match these exposures, the diabetes association tends to vanish</cite>. Conversely, type 1 diabetes—less intertwined with obesity, smoking, and alcohol—shows more robust residual associations when these confounders are fixed. <cite id="7ff80885-1">A pooled analysis across multiple sites reports elevated cancer risks in diabetics and discusses confounding by lifestyle factors; in sub-analyses distinguishing type 1 and type 2, residual associations can remain for type 1 after adjustment, whereas type 2 results can be largely attenuated</cite>. Quantitatively, some site-specific cohorts show that heavier alcohol use raises risk more strongly in diabetics, indicating effect modification. <cite id="0e763111-4">Excess risks varied by anatomical subsite, with notable synergism for hypopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers by BMI, smoking, and drinking</cite>.

3) Independent role of BMI/obesity: After accounting for smoking and alcohol, associations between higher adiposity and oral/oropharyngeal cancer risk may remain, particularly for certain subsites. <cite id="7ff80885-0">A nationwide cohort in Denmark (Wideroff et al.) reported increased mouth/pharynx cancer risks among persons with type 2 diabetes</cite>, but <cite id="7ff80885-9">the association between diabetes and some cancers is stronger among individuals with higher BMI or heavier alcohol consumption, pointing to additive lifestyle–metabolic pathways</cite>. <cite id="0e763111-9">Prospective evidence indicates an inverse association with leanness and direct associations with abdominal obesity and height for head and neck cancers overall</cite>, and <cite id="7ff80885-5">76% of oral cancer risk was attributed to smoking versus 55% to alcohol in one review, underscoring the magnitude of confounding</cite>.

Illustrative adjusted patterns
- Smoking: <cite id="ecc1c1b9-1">Diabetes case series show smokers and drinkers among cases are over-represented</cite>, suggesting that stratifying by smoking status collapses diabetes-related risk in oral cancer once smoking is fixed. Models that include smoking as covariate produce much lower apparent diabetes effects.
- Alcohol: <cite id="60620c2d-6">Combining smoking and alcohol can drive up to a 30-fold increase in oral cancer risk</cite>, so alcohol adjustment reduces the “diabetes effect” by removing a major confounder; some analyses find stronger effect modification in oropharyngeal cancer among diabetics with heavy drinking. <cite id="60620c2d-5">Significant interactions are seen for oropharyngeal cancer odds by sex and exposure levels after adjusting for multiple factors</cite>.
- BMI: <cite id="0e763111-9">Abdominal obesity is positively associated with head and neck cancers, and leanness inversely</cite>, and <cite id="ecc1c1b9-5">lower BMI often enhances oral/pharyngeal risk estimates</cite>. After BMI adjustment, diabetes–oral cancer associations for type 2 cases become weaker (or nonsignificant), whereas for type 1 diabetes, residual risk can persist, highlighting distinct etiologies. <cite id="7ff80885-7">In pooled analyses of metabolic traits, adjustment for type 2 diabetes often attenuates but may not eliminate risk</cite>.

What remains after adjustment and proposed mechanisms
Even after controlling for lifestyle factors and adiposity, several studies report small but statistically significant excesses of oral and oropharyngeal cancer among diabetics, particularly type 1, and among obese individuals with additional alcohol or smoking exposures. <cite id="0e763111-3">Pooled nationwide cohorts have shown mouth/pharynx cancer risks elevated among diabetics</cite>, and <cite id="7ff80885-7">diabetes’ association with some cancers remains stronger among higher BMI and heavier drinkers, pointing to insulin/IGF-1 and inflammatory pathways</cite>. Mechanistic hypotheses emphasize adiposity-driven hyperinsulinemia and chronic low-grade inflammation, plus potential genetic interactions; large consortia suggest that even after multivariable adjustment, metabolic traits remain associated with risk, consistent with these pathways. <cite id="0e763111-2">Obesity and diabetes have been repeatedly linked to head and neck cancer risk in observational studies</cite>.

Practical implications for interpretation and clinical practice
- Do not overstate a direct causal link from diabetes to oral cancer. <cite id="0e763111-5">Because smoking and drinking are strong drivers of oral/oropharyngeal risk, unadjusted estimates of diabetes’ effect are inflated</cite>, while <cite id="0e763111-9">adiposity independently adds risk in a dose–response manner</cite>. Rigorous multivariable adjustment that includes BMI and alcohol yields attenuated associations, and stratification by smoking status often eliminates them.
- Type-specific counseling: For patients with type 2 diabetes, weight management and addressing alcohol use may reduce residual risk even beyond glycemic control; for patients with type 1 diabetes, risk reduction should prioritize lifestyle carcinogen avoidance and careful screening due to limited attenuation by BMI and alcohol.
- Screening intensity: Diabetic patients with heavy smoking/alcohol exposure should undergo heightened oral/oropharyngeal surveillance, with particular attention to oropharyngeal subsite involvement where alcohol and metabolic factors show synergistic signals. <cite id="0e763111-4">Subsite-specific synergism is strongest in hypopharynx/larynx</cite>.

In short, adjusting for smoking, alcohol use, and BMI/obesity typically removes most—but not all—of the observed association between diabetes and oral cancer. The largest changes occur due to the dominant confounding by smoking and alcohol, with BMI contributing additional attenuation for type 2 diabetes but retaining an independent role in overall risk and potentially in residual excess after lifestyle adjustment. <cite id="60620c2d-2">Diabetes is linked to higher oral/oropharyngeal cancer risk before adjustment</cite>, but <cite id="ecc1c1b9-1">matching/adjusting for smoking, alcohol, and BMI materially reduces these excess risks</cite>, leaving a smaller residual signal especially for type 1 diabetes and in specific high-exposure subgroups. <cite id="7ff80885-7">Mechanistically, metabolic pathways and shared lifestyle risk explain these patterns, though additional biological mechanisms may contribute beyond lifestyle confounding</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of clinical evidence indicating that the perceived risk of lactic acidosis with current medications may be lower than initially feared in patients with kidney or liver disease, alongside important caveats.

Key framing and mechanisms
- Lactic acidosis risk depends on impaired lactate production or clearance; renal impairment reduces metformin clearance and can raise arterial lactate, while hepatic impairment impairs lactate production and clearance, both predisposing to lactic or mixed acidosis. <cite id="e14e6ec7-0">Metformin is likely to have lactic acidosis-related adverse effects in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients, such as increased arterial lactate</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-3">Metformin is contraindicated in chronic hepatic disease because of the increased risk of metformin-associated lactic acidosis</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-0">A case of metformin-associated lactic acidosis in a patient with alcoholic liver disease and decompensated cirrhosis illustrates mechanism and clinical severity</cite>.

Metformin in kidney disease
- Modern cohort data refine risk by estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), showing no overall association at preserved kidney function and elevated relative risk only at severe renal impairment. This challenges a blanket notion that metformin “inevitably” raises lactic acidosis risk in all CKD patients. <cite id="680a88d5-0">Metformin use was not significantly associated with incident acidosis at eGFR greater than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-1">There was an increased risk at eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (adjusted HR 2.07; 95% CI 1.33–3.22), whereas no such association was found when eGFR was 45–60 or 60–90 mL/min/1.73 m2</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-5">Meaning: metformin therapy may be safe in patients with eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2</cite>.
- Clinical guidance reflects these stratified risks, emphasizing that renal impairment increases risk but does not render metformin contraindicated in all patients; careful use with dose adjustment and monitoring is advised. <cite id="e14e6ec7-2">Renal impairment is a risk factor for lactic acidosis in patients taking metformin; metformin can still be used with precautions</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-6">Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 per label; use is cautioned at 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2</cite>.
- Population-level summaries and narratives note that absolute rates may be low in carefully selected, stable patients and that some earlier concerns were exaggerated. <cite id="680a88d5-3">Use at 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 was not associated with increased acidosis risk in cohort follow-up, though caution remained appropriate</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-2">Guidance from VA/ESP warns risk rises with renal dysfunction and age, supporting significant precautions rather than generalized avoidance</cite>. <cite id="e14e6ec7-5">Narrative synthesis: metformin use was not associated with increased risk for lactic acidosis overall across kidney function strata</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-9">A large cohort concluded no evidence of increased risk for lactic acidosis when metformin was prescribed under study conditions</cite>.
- Mechanistically, metformin can raise lactate, yet lactic acidosis remains rare overall. When it occurs (including with acute kidney injury), it is clinically severe. These data help frame expectations below early, worst-case warnings. <cite id="e14e6ec7-0">Metformin can increase arterial lactate in CKD</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-7">Case series emphasize metformin-associated lactic acidosis as rare but life‑threatening, sometimes accompanied by acute kidney injury</cite>.

Metformin in liver disease
- Liver disease increases concern due to impaired lactate clearance, but contemporary evidence shows caution rather than universal avoidance, with risk context-dependent. <cite id="5f54c09d-1">Reviews list renal and hepatic insufficiency as absolute contraindications or strong cautions for metformin, reflecting risk for lactic acidosis</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-3">Metformin is contraindicated in chronic hepatic disease because of increased risk of lactic acidosis</cite>.
- Real-world evidence in cirrhosis underscores clinical caution: metformin use was associated with higher mortality and decompensation, supporting restriction in decompensated disease and careful evaluation in compensated disease. <cite id="5f54c09d-4">Metformin use was associated with higher risks of mortality and cirrhotic decompensation in patients with compensated liver cirrhosis</cite>.
- Case reports in alcoholic liver disease highlight that when hepatic failure decompensates, metformin-associated lactic acidosis with multiorgan failure can occur. <cite id="5f54c09d-0">A patient with alcoholic liver disease on metformin developed metformin-associated lactic acidosis with acute decompensated liver failure</cite>.
- Taken together, metformin should be avoided in severe/hepatic failure but can be considered with restrictions in carefully selected patients with preserved hepatic function and no precipitants of lactic acidosis. <cite id="5f54c09d-1">Metformin is contraindicated or not recommended in hepatic insufficiency; alternatives are preferred</cite>.

Zidovudine (AZT) in renal/hepatic impairment (HIV era)
- Early experience with older nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) produced catastrophic, sometimes fatal lactic acidosis—especially in the setting of HIV-associated immunosuppression and renal impairment—driving broad warnings and contraindications. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-2">Reported cases of zidovudine-induced fatal lactic acidosis and hepatic failure in HIV patients</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-3">Guidelines warned of increased lactic acidosis risk with certain NRTI combinations in pregnancy</cite>.
- As clinical experience and antiretroviral strategies evolved, evidence and expert commentary frame lactic acidosis as rare, often asymptomatic, and amenable to risk-factor–guided prevention and drug switching, indicating the risk is not as uniformly high as early warnings implied. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-9">Lactic acidosis is a rare side effect of some HIV medications, especially the older NRTIs; recognition and management are emphasized</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-4">HIV clinical management acknowledges that lactic acidosis may be clinically asymptomatic but can present with acute multiorgan failure</cite>.
- Risk-factor–guided care and switching away from stavudine to zidovudine in higher-risk patients have been proposed to reduce hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis risk, consistent with practice tightening risk rather than broadening it. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-0">A risk-factor guided approach recommends using zidovudine instead of stavudine in higher-risk patients to reduce likelihood of lactic acidosis/hyperlactatemia</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-6">Patients with lactic acidosis risk factors had less LAHL when on zidovudine-containing regimens than stavudine, supporting switching strategies</cite>.
- Contemporary guidance still cautions about monitoring and stopping for symptoms, reflecting residual but manageable risk. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-1">Labeling advises patients to stop zidovudine if they develop symptoms suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity</cite>.

What suggests risk may be lower than previously thought
- Kidney disease: Large, adjusted cohorts show no excess risk at eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m2 and only modestly elevated risk (<2.1 HR) at eGFR <30, with overall findings consistent with “increased risk with renal impairment is the dominant driver, not a uniform doubling across all kidney disease,” and expert summaries endorse use at 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 with precautions. <cite id="680a88d5-0">No association with incident acidosis at eGFR >30</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-1">HR 2.07 at eGFR <30, no association at eGFR 45–60 or 60–90</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-5">Interpretation: metformin therapy may be safe at eGFR 30–60</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-3">Use at 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2 not associated with increased acidosis risk in follow-up, with continued caution</cite>.
- Liver disease: Although hepatic impairment remains a caution, evidence emphasizes context and careful selection rather than blanket avoidance. The absolute incidence remains low overall and rises in settings of decompensation or co-occurring kidney injury; modern cohorts in cirrhosis support restricting metformin and avoid prescribing in severe hepatic failure. <cite id="5f54c09d-1">Hepatic insufficiency is a strong caution/contraindication due to risk of lactic acidosis</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-4">Metformin use associated with higher mortality and decompensation in compensated cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-0">Case report shows fulminant metformin-associated lactic acidosis during decompensation in alcoholic liver disease</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-9">Contemporary narrative: lactic acidosis is rare with older NRTIs in HIV, with emphasis on early detection and management</cite>.
- Cross-class signals: Observational cohorts and clinical reviews of metformin show no overall increased risk of lactic acidosis “under study conditions,” and narrative summaries note no increased overall risk across kidney function strata in carefully monitored patients. <cite id="5f54c09d-9">No evidence of increased risk for lactic acidosis when prescribed under study conditions</cite> <cite id="e14e6ec7-5">Metformin use not associated with increased lactic acidosis risk overall across kidney function</cite>.

Limitations and clinical caveats
- Even when overall absolute risk appears low in carefully selected patients, residual risk persists, especially at severe CKD and in decompensated liver disease; asymptomatic hyperlactatemia can progress to symptomatic acidosis. <cite id="680a88d5-1">Relative risk doubles at eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-4">Metformin-related acidosis curves can be flat/intractable without addressing precipitants</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-0">Decompensated liver disease precipitated severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis</cite>.
- Medication-related lactate toxicity has nontrivial mortality; clinicians should maintain vigilance for clinical features (fatigue/weakness/myalgias → multiorgan failure) and avoid use with radiographic contrast/other nephrotoxic exposures in CKD. <cite id="5f54c09d-7">Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare but life‑threatening; cases may co-occur with acute kidney injury</cite> <cite id="e14e6ec7-8">Contraindications to metformin include impaired kidney function or acid-base disorders; contrast exposure raises risk</cite>.
- For HIV NRTIs, the worst-case lactic acidosis syndromes were largely linked to older regimens and immunosuppression; modern, risk-factor–aware prescribing and switching away from stavudine, with close monitoring, have materially reduced observed incident lactic acidosis. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-0">Zidovudine substitution for stavudine in higher-risk patients reduced likelihood of lactic acidosis/hyperlactatemia</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-6">Patients with risk factors had less LAHL on zidovudine-containing regimens</cite>.

Practical implications
- In CKD patients with eGFR 30–60 mL/min/1.73 m2, consider metformin with reduced dosing, absence of other risk factors, and frequent reassessment; counsel on symptoms and avoid precipitants. <cite id="680a88d5-5">Metformin therapy may be safe at eGFR 30–60</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-6">Label-based restrictions support contraindication at eGFR <30 and caution in 30–60</cite>.
- In decompensated liver disease, avoid metformin; in compensated cirrhosis, avoid if possible; carefully weigh risks and benefits, given associations with mortality and decompensation. <cite id="5f54c09d-4">Metformin use linked to higher mortality/decompensation in compensated cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-1">Hepatic insufficiency remains a strong category of caution/contraindication</cite>.
- For HIV NRTIs, prefer modern regimens and maintain risk-factor–guided strategies; if AZT is used, aggressively monitor for early lactate toxicity and switch promptly if risk rises. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-0">Use zidovudine instead of stavudine in higher-risk patients to reduce lactic acidosis/hyperlactatemia</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-9">Lactic acidosis is rare but requires recognition and management; emphasize patient education and early stoppage for symptoms</cite>.
- Across organ failure, integrate multidisciplinary care to manage predispositions (CKD AKI, liver decompensation) that unmask latent metformin effects or drug–disease interactions. <cite id="e14e6ec7-8">Metformin requires avoidance with conditions that impair acid-base balance (e.g., renal dysfunction, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) and during radiological contrast exposure</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-0">Overlap with liver failure and AKI can precipitate life‑threatening lactic acidosis</cite>.

Summary
- For metformin, large modern cohorts and updated guidance suggest that lactic acidosis risk is not uniformly increased in kidney disease—it is concentrated in severe CKD—so risk may be lower than feared if therapy is restricted and monitored in preserved kidney function. <cite id="680a88d5-0">No association at eGFR >30</cite> <cite id="680a88d5-1">Relative risk 2.07 at <30</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-9">No overall increased risk under study conditions</cite>.
- For both kidney and liver disease, absolute risk remains nonzero and clinical vigilance is required; in liver failure, metformin remains contraindicated or avoided, with alternative therapies preferred. <cite id="5f54c09d-1">Hepatic insufficiency contraindicates or cautions strongly</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-4">Use associated with higher mortality/decompensation in cirrhosis</cite>.
- For zidovudine, early catastrophic lactic acidosis risk has been mitigated by improved antiretroviral choices and risk-factor–aware management; lactic acidosis is now considered rare and often asymptomatic, with guidance emphasizing interruption at symptom onset. <cite id="f5f8d6e7-9">Lactic acidosis is rare with older NRTIs; educate and intervene early</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-0">Switching away from stavudine reduced hyperlactatemia/lactic acidosis risk</cite>.
- Net conclusion: clinical evidence and practice updates indicate that in carefully selected patients with organ impairment, lactic acidosis risk with these medications is often less frequent or clinically underappreciated than early warnings implied, but individualized risk assessment, careful selection, and close monitoring remain mandatory to detect rare, severe cases early. <cite id="680a88d5-5">Metformin may be safe at eGFR 30–60 if used cautiously</cite> <cite id="f5f8d6e7-9">HIV NRTI lactic acidosis is rare when recognized and managed</cite> <cite id="5f54c09d-9">Metformin showed no overall increased risk in large observational cohorts</cite>.

Summary
Growing evidence shows that cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein biomarkers—particularly neurofilament light chain (NFL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)—are elevated after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)/concussion and associate with both injury severity and longer symptom duration, including in sports-related populations. These proteins reflect axonal and glial damage, and higher CSF concentrations measured acutely and subacutely predict greater odds of poor functional outcomes and persistent post-concussive symptoms over months to years, supporting their use as severity and prognosis markers after concussion. <cite id="fdd1ca53-0">NfL concentration is associated with number of concussions and symptom severity scores</cite> and <cite id="aecf4f1a-8">initial high concentrations of NFL and GFAP in CSF relate to poorer outcomes 1 year and 10–15 years after spinal cord injury—demonstrating long-term prognostic value of glial and axonal proteins</cite>. Although not limited to mTBI, these CSF proteins consistently index neuronal injury processes relevant to concussion.

Evidence that CSF biomarkers index concussion severity
- Association with injury burden and symptom severity: Across cohorts that measured CSF and serum, NFL showed robust associations with concussion exposure and symptom severity; CSF and serum NFL correlated with number of concussions (r = 0.44, p < 0.001) and symptom severity measures, indicating that higher axonal damage markers co-occur with more severe clinical presentations in TBI populations that include mild cases <cite id="fdd1ca53-0">NfL is associated with number of concussions and symptom severity scores; both CSF and serum NfL showed associations with number of concussions (r = 0.44, p ...)</cite>. Clinician-facing reviews similarly emphasize GFAP’s diagnostic utility for distinguishing concussed individuals from controls, supporting its sensitivity to injury presence and severity, including in sport settings <cite id="aecf4f1a-7">GFAP has shown high sensitivity and specificity in distinguishing concussed individuals from controls and is now used in some clinical settings</cite>.
- Proteomic profiles in athletes: In sports-related concussions, CSF neuroinflammatory and axonal biomarkers are elevated relative to non-injured controls, and their magnitude correlates with persistent symptoms, linking biochemical injury signatures to clinically severe, prolonged presentations <cite id="aecf4f1a-0">Cerebrospinal fluid levels of neuroinflammatory biomarkers are increased in athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms following sports-related ...</cite>. This indicates that CSF biomarker elevations reflect severity-related neuropathophysiology in athletic mTBI beyond acute symptomatology.
- Mechanistically aligned markers predict worse neurobehavioral function: Cross-sectional and longitudinal TBI cohorts that include mild cases show serum and CSF GFAP, NFL, and tau associate with worse neurobehavioral outcomes over time, suggesting that the same CSF proteins capture severity-related damage after concussion <cite id="aecf4f1a-2">Elevated GFAP within 12 months of TBI predicted poor cognitive outcome (perceptual reasoning)</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-9">Serum GFAP, NfL, and tau concentrations are associated with worse neurobehavioral functioning following mild, moderate, and severe TBI: a cross-sectional ...</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-1">Association of plasma biomarker levels with their CSF concentration and the number and severity of concussions in professional athletes</cite>. A broader review synthesizes that CSF NFL and GFAP show prognostic value across TBI severities, reinforcing their relevance for mTBI prognosis <cite id="aecf4f1a-2">Similarly in this population, elevated GFAP within 12 months of TBI predicted poor cognitive outcome</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-4">This review aims to explore current fluid biomarkers ... biofluid-based predictors of post-concussion symptoms</cite>.

Evidence that CSF biomarkers predict symptom duration and recovery
- Persistent post-concussive symptoms correlate with higher CSF biomarkers: In sports cohorts, athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms exhibit higher CSF neuroinflammatory biomarkers than those who recover, indicating that biochemical injury signatures at injury timeframe forecast extended symptom duration <cite id="aecf4f1a-0">Cerebrospinal fluid levels of neuroinflammatory biomarkers are increased in athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms following sports-related ...</cite>.
- Longitudinal prognostic associations in CSF: In adult traumatic brain injury cohorts with initial CSF NFL/GFAP quantification, higher acute CSF NFL and GFAP concentrations predicted worse 1-year global outcome (GOS-E) and remained predictive 10–15 years later, demonstrating durable linkage between early CSF protein elevations and sustained disability or impaired recovery; this mechanism is directly relevant to concussion severity and prolonged symptoms <cite id="aecf4f1a-8">High concentrations of NfL and GFAP in CSF relate to a poorer outcome 1 year and 10–15 years after an sTBI</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-5">Initial high concentrations of NfL and GFAP in CSF are associated with higher odds for GOS 1–3 outcome 1 year and 10–15 years after</cite>.
- Time course and predictive windows: CSF NFL tends to rise within days to weeks after injury and is “mainly explored to predict TBI outcome,” with levels reflecting axonal damage intensity that can anticipate symptom persistence; such dynamics argue for early CSF measurement as a guide to expected duration of post-concussive symptoms <cite id="5916b423-9">NfL levels tend to rise during the first 2 weeks post-injury and have been so far mainly explored to predict TBI outcome</cite>. Complementary CSF glial markers (GFAP) show biphasic release patterns across subacute and chronic TBI, again linking injury intensity and recovery trajectory to CSF protein trajectories <cite id="5916b423-7">GFap showed a biphasic release in serum, with levels decreasing during the first six months of injury, whereafter increased over the subsequent ...</cite>.
- Athlete-specific prognostication: Professional athletes with higher serum (and paired CSF) NFL/GFAP exhibit more concussions and greater severity; these cohorts underscore that NFL and GFAP capture injury severity and predict longer recovery profiles in high-exposure head-bang sports settings <cite id="aecf4f1a-1">Association of plasma biomarker levels with their CSF concentration and the number and severity of concussions in professional athletes</cite>.

Methodological strength and applicability to concussion
- Diagnostic and stratification utility: Clinician-oriented reviews note GFAP’s high sensitivity and specificity for concussion detection, supporting its use to confirm injury and stratify severity when combined with clinical exams <cite id="aecf4f1a-7">GFAP has shown high sensitivity and specificity in distinguishing concussed individuals from controls and is now used in some clinical settings</cite>. This converges with multi-center evidence that CSF NFL/GFAP show prognostic value across severities, supporting their role in risk stratification for mTBI.
- Domain evidence in sports medicine: Sports-focused CSF studies demonstrate that elevated neuroinflammatory markers specifically track persistent post-concussive symptoms in athletes, providing concussion-relevant evidence that CSF protein biomarkers flag higher risk for prolonged symptomatic recovery and may guide athlete return-to-play pathways <cite id="aecf4f1a-0">Cerebrospinal fluid levels of neuroinflammatory biomarkers are increased in athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms following sports-related ...</cite>.
- Caveats and complementarity: While CSF measurements provide direct CNS fluid evidence, access and invasiveness limit routine use; however, translational studies show strong correlations of serum biomarkers (with paired CSF) to concussion counts and severity in professional athletes, supporting blood surrogates when CSF is not feasible and reinforcing the mechanistic basis of NFL/GFAP for tracking injury severity and duration <cite id="aecf4f1a-1">Association of plasma biomarker levels with their CSF concentration and the number and severity of concussions in professional athletes</cite>.

Overall interpretation
Collectively, CSF-based studies show that NFL and GFAP rise after concussion and correlate with and predict clinical severity and longer symptom duration. In sports cohorts, elevated CSF neuroinflammatory biomarkers specifically mark athletes who fail to recover, while longitudinal sTBI cohorts demonstrate durable predictive value of early CSF NFL/GFAP for worse outcomes over years. These convergent findings support using CSF protein biomarkers—especially GFAP and NFL—as adjuncts to clinical assessment for gauging concussion severity and anticipating symptom duration, thereby informing prognostic counseling and return-to-activity decisions <cite id="aecf4f1a-0">Cerebrospinal fluid levels of neuroinflammatory biomarkers are increased in athletes with persistent post-concussive symptoms following sports-related ...</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-7">GFAP has shown high sensitivity and specificity in distinguishing concussed individuals from controls and is now used in some clinical settings</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-8">High concentrations of NfL and GFAP in CSF relate to a poorer outcome 1 year and 10–15 years after an sTBI</cite> <cite id="aecf4f1a-2">Elevated GFAP within 12 months of TBI predicted poor cognitive outcome (perceptual reasoning)</cite> <cite id="fdd1ca53-0">NfL is associated with number of concussions and symptom severity scores</cite> <cite id="5916b423-9">NfL levels tend to rise during the first 2 weeks post-injury and have been so far mainly explored to predict TBI outcome</cite>.

Below is an evidence-based synthesis of clinical studies, guidelines, and systematic reviews addressing the effectiveness and limitations of parathyroid hormone (PTH)–based treatments (including surgical parathyroidectomy and pharmacologic PTH analogs such as teriparatide) across genetic disorders of calcium–phosphate homeostasis and parathyroid neoplasia.

Overview of target disorders and PTH pathways
- Autosomal dominant multiple endocrine neoplasias (MEN1 and MEN2A) are characterized by germline mutations that predispose to parathyroid adenomas/hyperplasia, frequent multifocal disease, and high recurrence after surgery. <cite id="c3d36c4a-5">MEN-1 patients must be followed for life for involvement of the parathyroid glands, endocrine pancreas, pituitary, adrenal glands, thymus, and other endocrine tissues, reflecting a multiorgan, inherited endocrine neoplasia syndrome</cite>.
- Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) and hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome (HRPT2/CDM) are monogenic disorders with hyperparathyroidism or parathyroid abnormalities that may have atypical PTH/hypercalcemia relationships and distinct genetic counseling and management needs. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia should be considered in patients with long-standing hypercalcemia with low fractional urinary calcium, which helps distinguish it phenotypically from primary hyperparathyroidism</cite> <cite id="6076b493-6">Hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor (HPT-JT) syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by parathyroid tumors in association with fibro-osseous jaw lesions</cite> <cite id="6076b493-9">In HPT-JT syndrome, bilateral neck exploration and en bloc resection of suspicious lesions with lifelong follow-up are recommended</cite>.

Evidence in MEN1/MEN2A and HRPT2 (parathyroid surgery and re-operation)
- Effectiveness: Parathyroidectomy is curative in MEN-associated primary hyperparathyroidism (pHPT), but approach and extent are tailored to genetic risk. <cite id="c3d36c4a-1">In patients with MEN1-associated pHPT, subtotal parathyroidectomy is recommended as the management approach</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-6">If MEN1 or MEN2 are present, bilateral neck exploration is needed, and selective parathyroidectomy is contraindicated because multiple glands are typically involved</cite>. <cite id="c3d36c4a-7">Compared to limited parathyroidectomy, total and subtotal parathyroidectomy were associated with longer recurrence-free survival in overall PHPT cohorts, supporting higher-surety approaches</cite>.
- Limitations and adverse outcomes: Multiglandular involvement and tumor biology in MEN syndromes limit the role of unilateral or limited procedures and elevate reoperation risk. <cite id="c3d36c4a-3">Less-than-subtotal parathyroidectomy should not be abandoned for selected MEN1 patients, but data emphasize its role is limited given a high chance of persistence/recurrence; selected patients can be managed this way</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-9">MEN-associated recurrent primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common clinical manifestation in MEN1, highlighting durable disease control challenges</cite>. <cite id="c3d36c4a-0">Unilateral gland clearance can achieve similar results as total/subtotal in carefully selected patients with PHPT without causing permanent hypoparathyroidism, but such strategies risk missing multifocal disease</cite>. For HRPT2/HPT-JT, surgical aggressiveness is justified by malignant potential and frequent multigland involvement but carries lifelong surveillance burdens. <cite id="6076b493-8">In HPT-JT syndrome, long-term follow-up revealed 20% recurrence of PHPT; given the high risk of malignancy and multiglandular involvement, bilateral neck exploration and en-bloc resection with lifelong postoperative follow-up are recommended</cite>.
- Functional outcomes: When successful, surgery normalizes PTH and calcium and improves bone, kidney, and skeletal outcomes, though these benefits require complete lesion control. <cite id="30c68d3c-4">Parathyroidectomy normalizes PTH and calcium, decreases nephrolithiasis, slows renal function deterioration, and improves bone mineral in appropriately selected hyperparathyroid patients</cite>. However, persistent or recurrent disease attenuates benefit and necessitates reoperation and extended endocrine surveillance. <cite id="6076b493-5">Long-term studies report significantly higher recurrence rates after parathyroidectomy at longer follow-up intervals (e.g., more than 6 months to several years), especially in genetic or multifocal syndromes</cite> <cite id="6076b493-2">Recurrent or persistent PHPT after initial surgery often requires reoperative parathyroid surgery and is associated with greater anatomic complexity due to familial disease patterns</cite>.
- Cross-cutting surgical risks/limitations: Total parathyroidectomy risks transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism; subtotal can leave residual disease in aggressive syndromes. <cite id="c3d36c4a-0">Unilateral clearance can replicate STP outcomes without permanent hypoparathyroidism in selected PHPT cases, though this is conditional on disease unifocality</cite>. In MEN1, bilateral or extended exploration addresses multifocal disease but increases operative morbidity and lifelong endocrine follow-up. <cite id="c3d36c4a-6">Selective parathyroidectomy is contraindicated if MEN1/MEN2 is diagnosed because multiple glands are typically involved and bilateral neck exploration is needed</cite>.

Evidence for teriparatide (recombinant human PTH [1–34]) and related PTH-based therapies
- Efficacy in osteoporosis: Teriparatide is an anabolic PTH analog that reduces new vertebral fractures and increases bone density across populations, including patients with established hyperparathyroidism when used for osteoporosis management. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Randomized teriparatide therapy reduced the cumulative incidence of new vertebral fractures to 3.1% versus higher rates in controls, demonstrating robust antifracture efficacy</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide labeling notes efficacy for glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with significant reductions in vertebral fractures and increased bone mineral density in randomized trials</cite>. More broadly, guideline summaries reiterate improvements in BMD across multiple skeletal sites within months. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-1">After six months of teriparatide therapy, significant improvements in DXA scores are observed, indicating clinically relevant BMD gains</cite>.
- Limitations and safety concerns in hypercalcemic/genetic endocrine disease: Teriparatide can raise calcium in patients with hyperparathyroidism or other hypercalcemic states and is categorically contraindicated in such settings. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Avoid teriparatide in patients with underlying hypercalcemic disorders, such as primary hyperparathyroidism; therapy may precipitate hypercalcemia</cite>. While teriparatide has been studied in osteogenesis imperfecta cohorts and is used off-label in certain rare syndromes, its primary evidence base excludes hyperparathyroidism, and careful calcium surveillance is mandatory. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-3">Teriparatide is a recombinant human PTH (1–34) analog that can be administered to patients with severe osteoporosis and even in the setting of established hyperparathyroidism when the goal is osteoporosis management, underscoring a clear therapeutic distinction</cite>.
- Special situations: In families with suspected inherited hyperparathyroidism, teriparatide should be reserved for treatment of osteoporosis (and other indications as per drug label) when parathyroidectomy is unsuitable or failed; its role in “primary” hyperparathyroid genetic disease is adjunctive rather than curative. <cite id="30c68d3c-6">Because PTH-secreting parathyroid disease drives hypercalcemia, rPTH use is primarily considered for bone complications rather than as a causal therapy for hyperparathyroidism, requiring careful case selection and calcium monitoring</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-9">Teriparatide is typically given for severe osteoporosis (including men) or in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis contexts, not as a replacement for definitive management of hyperparathyroid lesions</cite>.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) and misclassification of “primary” hyperparathyroidism
- Diagnostic effectiveness vs. limitations: FHH can mimic “primary” hyperparathyroidism biochemically but is distinguished by low urinary calcium excretion and family history; misclassification leads to inappropriate parathyroidectomy and persistent hypercalcemia. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">FHH should be considered in patients with long-standing hypercalcemia and urinary calcium less than 100 mg/day (or low fractional excretion), suggesting preserved renal calcium handling rather than classic PHPT</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-1">In younger patients with apparent PHPT, a urinary calcium/creatinine clearance ratio less than 0.01 may indicate FHH, requiring careful phenotyping</cite>. <cite id="30c68d3c-8">Historical calcium values and family history are key to exclude progressive hypercalcemia as in PHPT and to steer away from overtreatment; FHH is characterized by a positive family history and stable biochemistry</cite>.
- Therapeutic implications: When FHH is correctly identified and biochemical complications (e.g., osteoporosis or nephrolithiasis) arise, parathyroidectomy can normalize PTH and calcium when a functioning adenoma is present, but in genetic disease without adenoma, this is ineffective. <cite id="30c68d3c-4">Parathyroidectomy normalizes PTH and calcium in appropriate hyperparathyroid patients and improves downstream bone and kidney measures</cite>. Conversely, performing parathyroidectomy in a true FHH without a functional lesion risks iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism and fails to correct hypercalcemia/steatoencephaly, underscoring the diagnostic gatekeeping role of urinary indices and family history. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">Applying FHH indices such as urinary calcium thresholds prevents misclassification of apparent PHPT as PHPT, which would otherwise drive harmful or ineffective parathyroidectomy</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-6">Workup that integrates urinary indices and family history is crucial to separate FHH from progressive PHPT and guides therapeutic choice</cite>. Teriparatide’s role is niche: treat osteoporosis when indicated despite PTH elevation, with strict calcium monitoring due to risk of calcium rises in hyperparathyroid states. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Use of teriparatide is contraindicated in patients with hypercalcemia and may cause hypercalcemia; in FHH mimicking PHPT, any use must ensure that parathyroid function is not driving hypercalcemia</cite>.

Hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor (HRPT2/CDM) syndrome
- Effectiveness of aggressive surgery: Because of malignant potential and frequent bilateral/intrafocal disease, early bilateral exploration and en bloc resection are recommended; outcomes are improved when multigland involvement or suspicious malignancy is addressed upfront. <cite id="6076b493-8">Long-term series from HPT-JT report 20% recurrence, supporting initial bilateral neck exploration and en-bloc resection for suspicious lesions</cite> <cite id="6076b493-9">Recommendations emphasize lifelong postoperative follow-up due to recurrence potential and possible multifocal disease</cite>.
- Limitations: Despite upfront aggressiveness, recurrence remains significant; management depends heavily on complete disease resection and vigilant long-term imaging/bone-density monitoring. <cite id="6076b493-5">Long-term recurrence after parathyroidectomy is common in genetically driven disease and can occur several years later, requiring continued surveillance</cite>. The need for life-long surveillance in MEN and HPT-JT reflects the principal limitation of surgical cures in autosomal dominant endocrine neoplasias. <cite id="c3d36c4a-5">MEN1 mandates lifetime surveillance across endocrine organs, including parathyroid glands, reflecting the persistent risk of new tumors</cite>.

Phosphate/FGF23-driven genetic disorders and tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO)
- Mechanistic context: X-linked hypophosphatemia, hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia (PHP), and TIO disrupt phosphate/FGF23 signaling and lead to low calcium/PTH set points with rickets/osteomalacia despite elevated PTH or resistance to PTH action; these conditions illustrate why PTH elevation alone does not equal bone turnover risk and why calcium/FGF23 control must precede anabolic PTH therapy. <cite id="30c68d3c-1">Endocrine overviews emphasize distinguishing hereditary causes of hypercalcemia/osteomalacia; urinary indices and family history inform syndrome specificity and downstream treatment</cite>.
- PTH/teriparatide role and limits: In rickets/osteomalacia driven by phosphate dysregulation or tumor burden (e.g., TIO), management priorities include removing the causative lesion, correcting vitamin D/FGF23 pathways, and treating hypophosphatemia; PTH stimulation with teriparatide may be beneficial for bone mass when calcium and phosphate are normalized and tumor burden reduced, but data in genetic/tumor-driven osteomalacia are limited and case–series driven. Pediatric case series and expert reviews support anabolic therapy after stabilization, with close biochemical monitoring, acknowledging small sample sizes. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide’s indication is severe osteoporosis with careful exclusion of hypercalcemia and frequent calcium monitoring; in genetic disorders causing osteomalacia, therapy is reserved for bone-specific indications after correction of underlying abnormalities</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-9">Teriparatide is considered for severe osteoporosis and established hyperparathyroidism when used for osteoporosis; in monogenic phosphate disorders, these indications inform cautious usage after tumor or metabolic stabilization</cite>.
- Clinical outcomes: Key benefits include increased bone mass and reduced fracture risk in eligible patients; risks include hypercalcemia if phosphate/FGF23 abnormalities are incompletely corrected, and tumor regrowth (in TIO) may negate skeletal gains. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Randomized data show strong increases in spinal bone mass and reductions in new vertebral fractures during teriparatide, which can be extrapolated to genetic bone disease when metabolic prerequisites are met</cite>. Thus, in FGF23/PHP and TIO, teriparatide-like PTH analogs are best positioned as adjuncts to definitive tumor/metabolic control, not primary curative agents for the genetic disease itself.

Osteogenesis imperfecta and other skeletal/parathyroid disorders
- In ICD-10-aligned conditions and monogenic osteomalacia/osteogenesis disorders, teriparatide is used off-label to stimulate bone formation when fractures are frequent and linear growth is not a concern; clinical series in endocrine-immunology populations report improved bone turnover and pain, with the caveat of hypercalcemia risk in underlying parathyroid dysfunction and need for strict monitoring. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Use in patients with hypercalcemic disorders is contraindicated; teriparatide can cause hypercalcemia and increases calcium load</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-1">Dose-response clinical experience shows significant BMD gains over 6 months</cite>. Guidance emphasizes individualized benefit–risk given variable skeletal fragility and potential endocrine comorbidity. <cite id="30c68d3c-5">An endocrine guideline approach recommends a layered diagnostic plan and surgery when appropriate; teriparatide-like strategies fit in the osteoporosis component across monogenic and nonsyndromic settings</cite>.

Cross-cutting effectiveness and limitations of PTH-based strategies
- When disease-targeted therapy (surgery for MEN1/HPT-JT, tumor resection for TIO, metabolic correction in FHH/FGF23 disorders) is successful, adjunctive or primary PTH-targeted interventions are effective for:
  - Cure or biochemical control of persistent/recurrent hyperparathyroidism and associated kidney and bone complications. <cite id="c3d36c4a-7">Total/subtotal parathyroidectomy provides longer recurrence-free survival than limited procedures in PHPT</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Teriparatide reduces new vertebral fractures, supporting its use for osteoporosis coexisting with treated hyperparathyroidism</cite>.
- Principal limitations include:
  - Genetic-driven multifocality and recurrence requiring repeat surgery, radiation, or medical therapy for refractory cases. <cite id="c3d36c4a-9">Recurrent PHPT is common in MEN1</cite> <cite id="6076b493-5">Long-term follow-up shows recurrence rates increase over several years</cite>.
  - High risk of hypercalcemia with teriparatide in patients whose hypercalcemia is driven or amplified by PTH-producing tumors or monogenic hypercalcemia; absolute contraindication in this context. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide may cause hypercalcemia and is contraindicated in patients with hypercalcemic disorders, such as primary hyperparathyroidism</cite>.
  - Diagnostic uncertainty in FHH can lead to delays or inappropriate surgery; urinary indices, family history, and careful repeat testing are essential. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">Low fractional urinary calcium should prompt consideration of FHH to avoid overtreatment</cite>.
  - In disorders of phosphate/FGF23 signaling, PTH elevation or resistance may not reflect skeletal turnover risk if phosphate or tumor burden is untreated; PTH analogs should be reserved for stabilized patients. <cite id="30c68d3c-1">Apparent PHPT with low urinary calcium suggests FHH and may explain lack of expected sensitivity to parathyroidectomy or teriparatide</cite>.
  - Surgical risks, including transient or permanent hypoparathyroidism and vocal cord/neurologic complications, and the lifelong surveillance burden in autosomal dominant syndromes. <cite id="c3d36c4a-0">Unilateral procedures are acceptable in selected cases but risk missing multifocal disease</cite> <cite id="6076b493-9">Lifelong postoperative follow-up is recommended after aggressive resections in HPT-JT</cite>.

Practical treatment algorithms derived from the evidence
- MEN1/MEN2A (suspected or diagnosed):
  - First-line: Bilateral neck exploration with subtotal or total parathyroidectomy, depending on burden and genetics, with lifelong calcium/PTH surveillance to detect new lesions early. <cite id="c3d36c4a-1">Subtotal parathyroidectomy is recommended in MEN1-associated pHPT</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-6">Bilateral exploration is needed if MEN1 or MEN2 is present to address multifocal disease</cite>.
  - Options and limitations: Limited surgery reserved for selected, unilateral, low-risk cases; recurrence is common and requires reoperation. <cite id="c3d36c4a-3">Less-than-subtotal resection can be considered in selected MEN1 cases, though selection is narrow</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-7">Total/subtotal approaches improve recurrence-free survival</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-5">Lifelong surveillance is mandated</cite>.
- FHH and “apparent PHPT”:
  - Workup: Urinary calcium fractional excretion and family history to exclude FHH; avoid routine bilateral parathyroidectomy in isolated FHH without a functioning adenoma. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">Urinary calcium thresholds and consideration of FHH alter management from routine parathyroidectomy</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-1">Low urinary calcium/creatinine clearance favors FHH</cite>.
  - If biochemical complications (osteoporosis or nephrolithiasis), consider targeted parathyroidectomy for functioning adenoma; otherwise manage osteoporosis with non-PTH approaches, reserving teriparatide when PTH does not drive hypercalcemia and with strict calcium monitoring. <cite id="30c68d3c-4">Parathyroidectomy normalizes PTH and calcium in appropriate cases and improves bone/lithiasis outcomes</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide increases calcium risk and is contraindicated in hypercalcemia</cite>.
- HRPT2/HPT-JT:
  - Aggressive upfront bilateral exploration, en-bloc resection of suspicious lesions, and lifelong imaging/PTH monitoring; teriparatide considered for coexisting osteoporosis with vigilant calcium tracking. <cite id="6076b493-8">Bilateral en-bloc procedures with lifelong follow-up due to recurrence and malignancy risk</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Teriparatide reduces vertebral fractures, supporting its adjunctive role for osteoporosis</cite>.
- FGF23/phosphate disorders and TIO:
  - Prioritize lesion resection (TIO), vitamin D/FGF23-directed therapy (PHP/FHH), and calcium/alkali/vitamin D correction; initiate teriparatide cautiously if calcium remains within target and prior to skeletal complications; monitor PTH and calcium monthly given tumor regrowth risk and paradoxical hypercalcemic responses. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Teriparatide’s strong antifracture and BMD effects are context-dependent and require metabolic control</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-1">Urinary indices and phenotype distinguish actionable from non-actionable PTH signaling</cite>.
- Osteogenesis imperfecta and monogenic osteomalacia:
  - Teriparatide acceptable off-label for frequent fractures with skeletal maturity preserved to reduce deformity and pain; contraindicated if there is active hyperparathyroidism or prior calcium rises, and used with monthly calcium/PTH checks and bone densitometry. <cite id="f5dbe7c3-1">6-month BMD improvements with teriparatide are clinically meaningful</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide is contraindicated in hypercalcemia</cite>.

Evidence gaps and research directions
- Randomized head-to-head data in genetic endocrine neoplasias comparing surgical and medical strategies are scarce; current high-quality evidence supports surgery as first-line for curative control, with PTH analogs positioned for coexisting osteoporosis and specific genetic bone diseases. <cite id="c3d36c4a-7">Long-term recurrence-free survival advantages of total/subtotal parathyroidectomy vs limited resection suggest surgical strategy superiority in general PHPT</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Prospective randomized trials in osteoporosis validate teriparatide’s anabolic efficacy and provide class external validity when used for bone indications</cite>.
- In FHH and HRPT2 syndromes, prospective studies are needed on standardized urinary biomarkers plus PTH and PTHrP-guided imaging protocols to reduce delayed diagnosis and unnecessary surgery, and on optimized calcium monitoring algorithms for teriparatide use when PTH is elevated but not driving hypercalcemia. <cite id="30c68d3c-0">Low fractional urinary calcium and careful FHH phenotype recognition reduce misdiagnosis-driven surgery</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Calcium surveillance intensity should match hypercalcemic risk</cite>.

Summary
- Clinical effectiveness: Targeted parathyroidectomy is curative and normalizes PTH/calcium with downstream bone and kidney benefits in MEN/HPT-JT and “true” PHPT; teriparatide provides reproducible antifracture and BMD benefits for osteoporosis and is considered as part of care in established hyperparathyroidism when used for osteoporosis; PTH analog therapy may also benefit selected patients with rare monogenic bone disorders after stabilization of the underlying genetic/metabolic problem. <cite id="c3d36c4a-1">Subtotal parathyroidectomy is recommended for MEN1 pHPT</cite> <cite id="c3d36c4a-7">Total/subtotal parathyroidectomy improves recurrence-free survival</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Teriparatide reduces new vertebral fractures to 3.1%</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-1">BMD improvements are seen within 6 months</cite>.
- Key limitations: Genetic syndromes drive multifocality and recurrence despite aggressive surgery; misdiagnosis or overtreatment (e.g., FHH) can cause iatrogenic hypoparathyroidism; teriparatide is contraindicated and risky in hypercalcemic genetic endocrine diseases; and in phosphate/FGF23 disorders, PTH stimulation must follow tumor/metabolic control. <cite id="6076b493-5">Recurrence rates rise over long-term follow-up in genetic disease</cite> <cite id="30c68d3c-0">FHH misclassification can derail therapy because parathyroidectomy in nonfunctioning glands is ineffective and can worsen hypercalcemia</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-6">Teriparatide can precipitate hypercalcemia and is contraindicated in hypercalcemia</cite>. Overall, management hinges on syndrome-appropriate tumor/metabolic control with PTH-based therapy acting primarily as an adjunct for skeletal complications when biochemical triggers are addressed. <cite id="30c68d3c-4">Parathyroidectomy’s downstream benefits are contingent on correct diagnosis and curative lesion control</cite> <cite id="f5dbe7c3-0">Teriparatide’s effects are durable and quantifiable but conditional on exclusion of hypercalcemic drivers</cite>.

# Summary

<cite id="91224bf8-5">Exercise acutely increases skeletal muscle glucose uptake while chronically enhancing insulin sensitivity by increasing mitochondrial capacity and GLUT4 expression in muscle</cite>, with central signaling through the AMPK/mTOR axis. <cite id="b184be3c-0">During exercise, the combined fall in insulin and rise in glucagon normally stimulate glucose output from the liver and muscle glycogenolysis, creating a transient hyperglycemic counter-regulatory drive that is offset by exercise-stimulated muscle glucose uptake</cite>. <cite id="0270cf3e-0">Gastric and intestinal hormones such as GLP‑1 reduce hepatic glucose production (HGP) and enhance muscle glucose uptake via incretin-mediated effects</cite>; chronic physical training improves hepatic insulin sensitivity, contributing to improved whole-body glucose metabolism. <cite id="87a86e77-0">Exercise reverses lipid-induced skeletal muscle insulin resistance, in part by normalizing aberrant mTORC1 activation</cite> and dampening proinflammatory signaling, which restores insulin signaling and glucose disposal. <cite id="b184be3c-6">In patients with type 2 diabetes, impaired glucagon regulation contributes to hyperglycemia, and exercise training supports restoration of hormonal homeostasis that facilitates glycemic control</cite>. Over months, these adaptations translate into modest reductions in HbA1c, especially when combining aerobic and resistance exercise. 

# Physiological mechanisms

1) Acute lowering during and after exercise via muscle glucose uptake
- <cite id="91224bf8-5">An acute bout of exercise increases skeletal muscle glucose uptake in humans</cite>, which can temporarily exceed hepatic glucose output, contributing to rapid post-exercise reductions in plasma glucose. <cite id="b184be3c-0">During moderate exercise, insulin falls and glucagon rises, increasing hepatic and muscle glycogenolysis to supply fuel, but the exercise stimulus simultaneously drives glucose uptake into active muscles</cite>. <cite id="91224bf8-4">PGC‑1α upregulation by exercise increases GLUT4 and mitochondrial proteins, providing greater capacity for oxidative uptake and utilization, which is immediately engaged during exercise</cite>. <cite id="91224bf8-9">These reviews emphasize that exercise-induced GLUT4 redistribution to the plasma membrane and enhanced mitochondrial density are central to increased glucose uptake and oxidation in muscle during physical activity</cite>.

2) Chronic insulin sensitization of muscle and liver
- <cite id="91224bf8-2">Exercise training increases skeletal muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and GLUT4 protein expression and is associated with improved insulin sensitivity</cite>. <cite id="91224bf8-6">Mitochondrial remodeling to exercise enhances metabolic flexibility, facilitating glucose uptake and oxidation</cite>, reducing hepatic reliance to maintain euglycemia. <cite id="0270cf3e-6">Training exerts an insulin-sensitizing effect on the liver, improving whole-body glucose metabolism in patients with type 2 diabetes</cite>.
