Following hormone binding, GRs engage chaperones (e.g., FKBP10/1B5), undergo conformational changes, translocate to nucleus, and then traffic back to cytosol for degradation or recycling; this cycle allows transient gene repression and return to baseline. Rapid non-genomic actions via GR kinases can also be triggered at the plasma membrane to quickly attenuate signaling. <cite id="5203d169-4">Non-genomic mechanisms for rapid anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive GC effects have been proposed, involving rapid receptor actions beyond transcription</cite><cite id="5203d169-3">Non-genomic GC actions inhibit cell migration via rapid receptor signaling</cite>.
- Apoptosis and immune homeostasis. Glucocorticoids promote elimination of over-activated lymphocytes through transcriptional and non-transcriptional activation of death pathways, curbing the duration of immune activation after stress. <cite id="5203d169-7">Glucocorticoids activate cellular death machinery through transcriptional and non-transcriptional pathways in both extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis</cite>.
- Corticosteroids and metabolic restoration. Broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of GR help restore energy balance and metabolic flexibility during recovery from acute stress. <cite id="5375700a-7">Glucocorticoids exert widespread effects on energy metabolism, immune regulation and neuronal plasticity, providing negative feedback to hypothalamus</cite><cite id="5203d169-9">Molecular and cellular mechanisms underpin powerful anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of GCs</cite>.

Sympathoadrenal and neuroimmune termination by catecholamine receptors
- β-adrenergic anti-inflammatory counter-regulation. During stress, sympathetic catecholamines bind β-adrenergic GPCRs on immune (e.g., T cells), hepatic, adipose, and cardiovascular cells to rapidly blunt pro-inflammatory signaling and metabolic stress responses, facilitating recovery when glucocorticoids rise. <cite id="5203d169-3">β-adrenergic receptor non-genomic actions include rapid inhibition of inflammatory processes</cite><cite id="aa05e717-4">During stress, catecholamines regulate the immune system via β-adrenergic mechanisms</cite><cite id="aa05e717-5">β-adrenergic blockade diminishes immunomodulatory effects of catecholamines; β-ARs regulate inflammatory and reparative response in heart</cite>.
- Sustained immune–SNS cross-talk maintains homeostasis. Normal homeostatic maintenance and appropriately scaled stress responses depend on immune–sympathetic crosstalk, with β-AR signaling providing rapid immunosuppressive tone that the HPA axis can leverage during recovery. <cite id="aa05e717-0">Immune–SNS cross-talk is required to maintain homeostasis and to shape immune responses after injury or immune activation</cite>.
- Receptor desensitization and receptor reserve. SNS-driven receptor desensitization pathways (e.g., β-ARK, phosphorylation, internalization) ensure transient sympathetic signaling and avoid overshoot, enabling timely return to basal tone as stress resolves. <cite id="aa05e717-8">Catecholamine-induced desensitization of adrenergic receptors exemplifies how signaling adapts to maintain physiological regulation</cite>.

Examples of receptor-level negative feedback and restoration outside the HPA axis
- Pituitary gonadotrope axis. Steroidogenic enzymes are upregulated by cAMP/CRE, yet GCs rapidly downregulate this axis through GR-mediated transcriptional repression, reducing gonadotropin output once stress is contained. <cite id="52359838">Glucocorticoids rapidly and strongly inhibit pituitary steroidogenesis and gonadotropin gene transcription, illustrating GR-driven negative feedback</cite>.
- Mineralocorticoid receptor in cardiovascular/renal recovery. MR signaling in vascular smooth muscle, heart, and kidney modulates vascular tone and ion transport alongside glucocorticoid/aldosterone levels to normalize blood pressure and fluid balance during recovery. <cite id="5375700a-8">Both GR and MR contribute to negative feedback regulation; MR mediates rapid aldosterone effects</cite>.
- Neurosteroid/immune cross-inhibition. Rapid GR actions on NF-κB signaling in microglia and macrophages curtail neuroinflammation after stress, while GR-dependent changes in hypothalamic plasticity reduce neuroendocrine drive. <cite id="5203d169-2">NF-κB and AP-1 drive inflammatory gene induction, while GR-mediated repression counteracts stress gene programs</cite><cite id="5375700a-7">Glucocorticoids modulate neuronal plasticity, part of restoring systemic homeostasis after stress</cite>.

Metabolic and peptide hormone receptors that “tune” the HPA’s return to baseline
- Leptin/melanocortin signaling. Leptin-GR signaling in hypothalamus integrates energy status and stress; melanocortin receptor signaling in arcuate and paraventricular nuclei modulates CRH and PIF output to accelerate HPA quenching when energy reserves permit. <cite id="5375700a-7">Glucocorticoids interact with energy metabolism and hypothalamic regulation</cite><cite id="5375700a-2">HPA regulation occurs via negative feedback by GCs interacting with GRs in hypothalamus and peripheral targets</cite>.
- Peripheral immune GR and systemic restoration. GR in innate lymphoid cells, macrophages, and T cells suppresses cytokines and antigen presentation during recovery, reducing immune–axis feedback that can sustain HPA reactivation. <cite id="5203d169-9">GR-mediated cellular mechanisms underlie anti-inflammatory effects across immune cell types</cite>.

How these mechanisms integrate at the systems level
- Temporal stratification of responses. Rapid receptor-mediated processes (ENaC blockade, β-adrenergic non-genomic actions, GR kinase-linked repression) quickly attenuate acute stress physiology, while genomic GR programs restructure inflammatory tone, neural excitability, and immune cell homeostasis to prevent relapse. <cite id="5203d169-4">Non-genomic anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive GC mechanisms act rapidly</cite><cite id="5203d169-1">GR exerts both rapid and genomic effects to counter inflammatory programs</cite>.
- Negative feedback loops. Rising endogenous GCs repress CRH and ACTH, while MR signaling restores fluid balance and vascular tone; adrenergic inputs provide tissue-specific blunting of immune and metabolic outputs. Together they reduce sympathetic drive and reinstate metabolic, cardiovascular, and immunologic set points. <cite id="5375700a-5">Glucocorticoids feedback to hypothalamus and pituitary to downregulate HPA</cite><cite id="5375700a-8">GR and MR jointly regulate negative feedback and rapid responses</cite><cite id="aa05e717-5">β-adrenergic receptors modulate inflammatory and reparative responses across tissues</cite>.
- Tissue adaptation and desensitization. Receptors undergo endocytosis, phosphorylation, and internalization to dampen signals after ligand exposure; this avoids overcorrection and supports a graded return to baseline. <cite id="5203d169-4">Three proposed non-genomic mechanisms explain rapid GC anti-inflammatory effects</cite><cite id="aa05e717-8">Desensitization of catecholaminergic receptors underlies adaptation of adrenergic signaling</cite>.

Key concepts and clinical implications
- Receptor-mediated negative feedback is primary for HPA “shutdown.” Inhibiting CRH/ACTH release and suppressing inflammatory gene networks are central to terminating stress outputs. <cite id="5375700a-5">Glucocorticoid feedback reduces CRH and ACTH</cite><cite id="5203d169-1">GR-driven repression of inflammatory gene programs counters stress-related cytokines</cite>.
- Restoration also requires peripheral actions and metabolic coupling. MR-directed sodium handling and GR-directed immune apoptosis/anti-inflammation are crucial to restore fluid/electrolyte balance and immune tone. <cite id="5375700a-8">GR and MR mediate distinct but complementary roles in feedback and rapid termination</cite><cite id="5203d169-7">Glucocorticoids trigger apoptosis pathways to eliminate activated immune cells during recovery</cite>.
- Interactions among axis hormones and peptides refine recovery. Leptin/GR signaling and β-adrenergic inputs modulate the timing and magnitude of HPA quenching according to energy reserves and immune status. <cite id="5375700a-7">Glucocorticoids and metabolic regulation are tightly intertwined in hypothalamic control</cite><cite id="aa05e717-0">Neuroimmune cross-talk is vital to maintain homeostasis, modulating immune response magnitude</cite>.

In sum, hormone receptors regulate the stress-response axis at multiple levels—primary negative feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary, rapid receptor-triggered suppression of inflammation and ion transport, and tissue-specific genomic programs—to dampen sympathetic–adrenal output and restore metabolic, cardiovascular, and immunologic homeostasis following stress. <cite id="5375700a-0">Glucocorticoids reduce drive centrally and promote trans-synaptic inhibition</cite><cite id="5375700a-5">HPA axis self-regulates via hypothalamic and pituitary GR feedback</cite><cite id="5203d169-1">GR integrates anti-inflammatory repression with metabolic programs</cite><cite id="5203d169-6">GR-mediated inhibition of NF-κB supports anti-inflammatory restoration</cite><cite id="aa05e717-5">β-adrenergic receptor signaling reduces immune activation and guides reparative responses</cite>.

# Overview

Minimally invasive surgical removal of a scar defect typically involves excising the abnormal scar tissue via small, strategically placed incisions along or adjacent to the scar and then closing the resulting tissue defect with tension-minimizing methods such as subcuticular (subdermal) suturing, quilting/tension-reduction knots, and patterned flaps or grafts as needed to achieve an aesthetically aligned, tension-free repair.<cite id="d2b1076d-0">Correction of contractures and ‘pincushioning’ can be done using consecutive Z-pasties, a tension-distributing technique for pincushioned scars</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-3">The surgeon will make an incision along or near the scar, carefully excising the scar tissue; in some cases the wound is closed with sutures, while larger defects may require skin grafting</cite>.

# How the Removal Is Performed Minimally Invasively

- Incision and excision: The surgeon places an incision along or adjacent to the scar to remove keloid/hypertrophic tissue or contracture; after excision, the tissues are refashioned and closed.<cite id="d2b1076d-3">The surgeon incises along or near the scar to excise tissue, then closes with sutures as appropriate</cite><cite id="15ec926f-0">Treating scar contractures hinges on releasing the contracture and covering the skin deficit, commonly using flaps or grafts</cite>. Incision patterns may be designed to break up linear scars and align with relaxed skin tension lines (RSTLs), improving flexibility and contour, for example using zig‑zag or circumferential incisions on narrow, contracted defects and converting long straight scars into “broken” scars to lessen prominence.<cite id="15ec926f-2">Contracture release can be started with a zigzag incision line along lateral scar margins</cite><cite id="15ec926f-3">A circumferential incision technique can reduce wide scar contracture without graft or flap</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-5">Changing direction of abnormal scars via triangular flaps aligns them with relaxed skin tension lines</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-9">Converting a long straight scar into a broken form via multiple incisions is a standard revision strategy</cite>.

- Tension release and alignment: To reduce contour deformity and contracture, surgeons may use Z‑plasty, W‑plasty, and consecutive Z‑pasties to distribute tension, break up linear scars, and correct pincushioning or angle misalignment; these procedures are core minimally invasive methods to realign scars with normal tissue tension and skin laxity.<cite id="d2b1076d-0">Consecutive Z‑pasties correct pincushioning by redistributing tension around the scar</cite><cite id="15ec926f-4">W‑plasty modifies linear scars and prevents contraction, aligning with skin laxity</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-7">Traditional Z‑plasty increases mobility and breaks up linear scars</cite>.

# Closure Methods and Indications

- Direct approximation with subcuticular (subdermal) closure: For linear scars and narrow defects, close without a “visible” skin edge by approximating dermal/subcutaneous layers and anchoring the skin edge percutaneously. This avoids buried knots and maintains dermal apposition, yielding better cosmetic outcomes with minimal postoperative handling.<cite id="a70db9bb-0">Wounds can be closed with subcuticular or transdermal sutures, staples, or adhesives</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-9">Scar revision requires subdermal closure (absorbable or non-removable sutures), with subsequent skin-layer closure to build layers properly</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-3">For subcuticular running repair, place a dermal/subcutaneous suture ~1–2 cm from the wound end and secure with a knot; advance parallel mattress stitches to close and provide transverse tension</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-1">Subcuticular closure places sutures in the dermis to approximate edges invisibly under the skin</cite>. Tensile‑reducing suture techniques are emphasized; the specific method can be as important as the material in reducing hypertrophic scars when tension is minimized.<cite id="f46f4738-4">The suturing method may be more important than material; tensile‑reduction sutures reduce hypertrophic scars</cite><cite id="f46f4738-5">Prevent pathological scarring by ensuring wound edges adhere without tension</cite>.

- Interrupted patterns and mattress/undercutting: To further diffuse tension across the scar, use interrupted subcuticular sutures, horizontal running/interlocking Mattress patterns, and subcutaneous “undercut” or buried mattress passes that create transverse tension across the defect. These methods are particularly useful for high‑tension sites (e.g., ears, hands, neck) to limit recurrence and hypertrophic change.<cite id="a70db9bb-2">Interrupted subcuticular suture technique evolved to improve aesthetics, with transdermal sutures enabling precise edge approximation without external knots</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-3">A running subcuticular Mattress stitch provides transverse tension to reduce dead‑space and tension at the skin edge</cite>. Dermabrasion/dermotomy or tunneling methods can also soften edges and distribute tension; flap design may transpose tissue to relax tension lines.<cite id="d2b1076d-5">Transposing triangular skin flaps with Z‑plasty re‑orients scars into relaxed skin tension lines to diffuse tension</cite>.

- Flaps and grafts for larger/deficient scars: After excision and contracture release, skin defects often require coverage using local flaps (rotation/advancement/transposition) or distant skin grafts if tension-free closure across wide defects is not feasible. Random pattern grafts (e.g., 3–4 cm punch grafts) can convert linear scars into “broken” scars aligned with skin tension and pigment/texture; split‑thickness mesh grafts or full‑thickness grafts are selected based on defect location and tension.<cite id="15ec926f-0">Covering the skin deficit after contracture release typically uses flaps or skin grafts</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-8">Cyanoacrylate adhesives allow noninvasive closure and may eliminate suture removal in appropriate cases</cite><cite id="f46f4738-8">Surgical scar revision excises the scar and closes in a new configuration that restores aesthetics and function</cite>. For keloidal ears, complete excision with careful undermining and revisional closure is standard when the stalk is narrow; recurrence risk is mitigated by tension-relieving techniques and graft/edge management rather than open wide flaps.<cite id="f46f4738-6">Surgical excision of narrow‑stalked keloids is performed efficiently; complete removal followed by closure is effective</cite>.

- Layered closure and adhesive/skin‑closing devices: Emphasize multilayer closure—first close subcutaneous layers with absorbable sutures, then close the dermis, and finally approximate skin edges using subcuticular interrupted or running Mattress sutures, tissue adhesives, or skin staples; adhesive agents can obviate suture removal and are appropriate in clean, well‑approximated wounds.<cite id="a70db9bb-9">Scar revision employs subdermal closure with absorbable or non-removable sutures, building layers to heal across</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-8">Adhesive agents such as cyanoacrylate can noninvasively close wounds, avoiding suture removal</cite><cite id="f46f4738-5">Aesthetic closure depends on skin anatomy, wound mechanics, suture materials, and techniques</cite> In keloids, some clinicians prefer delayed healing or secondary intention for “sutured closure” to avoid stimulating further keloid growth, reserving suturing for low‑tension sites or after deferring primary closure for several days; otherwise, adhesive or staple closure may be acceptable when recurrence risk is high.<cite id="f46f4738-7">Closure with sutures can complicate keloid excisions and are unlikely to be performed; secondary intention is often preferred</cite>.

# Suture Choice and Practical Techniques for Tension Minimization

- Materials and depths: Use absorbable monofilament (e.g., 3‑0 to 4‑0 nylon or polydioxanone) for subcuticular layers and nonabsorbable materials if a non-removable skin edge is desired. Correct wound bed moisture with staples or adhesive when appropriate; the role of skin suture is to heal the dermal gap while a well-approximated subcutaneous layer prevents dead space and tension at the surface.<cite id="a70db9bb-0">Absorbable and non-absorbable suture, staples, and tissue adhesives are options for skin closure</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-6">Skin suture seals the dermal gap; proper subcutaneous suturing is essential before skin edge approximation</cite>.

- Anchor and running Mattress: Start with a buried anchor or buried knot on the subcutaneous level, then run an interrupted or running Mattress suture to close dead space and redirect tensile forces transversely across the scar; finish with a buried Aberdeen (fisherman’s) knot to reduce surface visibility. For linear scars, add quilting/skin‑to‑subcutaneous vertical running sutures to eliminate dead space and reduce skin edge tension.<cite id="a70db9bb-5">Technique: anchor and bury the starting knot, run the subcuticular stitch, and end with an Aberdeen (fisherman’s) knot to bury the finish</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-3">A running subcuticular Mattress provides transverse tension across the wound to reduce dead space and skin edge tension</cite>.

- Tension-reducing closures and edge management: In high‑tension sites, use interrupted subcuticular sutures with buried mattress variations, skin‑crawling advancement flaps, or buried “undercut” passes to relieve edge traction; aligning scars with RSTLs reduces recurrence and contour depression. If primary closure is contraindicated or causes pincushioning, favor secondary intention, dermal grafting, or dermal-fat grafting to break up the linear scar into an aesthetically aligned, tensioned edge.<cite id="f46f4738-4">Clinical experience suggests tensile‑reduction sutures reduce hypertrophic scar formation; suture method is as crucial as material</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-5">Triangular flaps transpose scar tension into RSTLs to diffuse mechanical stress</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-0">Consecutive Z‑pasties distribute tension and correct pincushioning</cite> In facial scars, surgeons often reposition the scar along natural skin folds and creases to reduce prominence and tension, often implemented in the same minimally invasive excision/closure sequence.<cite id="f46f4738-3">Surgeons may reposition facial scars so that the incisional closure heals along natural folds</cite>.

# Portal/Tunneling and Hidden Incisions

Minimally invasive approaches reduce external scarring by making small incisions along/near the scar and excising subcutaneously; subcuticular and transdermal/percutaneous techniques hide knots beneath the dermis, and adhesive/skin‑closing devices minimize external stitch burden. For contracture release in areas like hands or necks, zig‑zag, circumferential, or W/Z‑shaped incisions break down linear tension into multiple smaller segments, often closed with layered subcuticular and tension‑distributing techniques instead of large exposed flaps. Tissue adhesive or staples may be used where appropriate to avoid iterative suture care and reduce tension at the skin surface.<cite id="d2b1076d-2">Scar revision treatments can be performed with minimally invasive techniques in most cases unless major wound healing issues exist</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-0">Subcuticular/transdermal suture, staples, and adhesives provide less invasive closure options than traditional skin-level sutures</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-8">Adhesives can eliminate suture removal and simplify postoperative care</cite>.

# Postoperative Handling to Reduce Hypertrophic Scarring

Maintain tension‑free, well‑hydrated wound environment with careful early mobilization, gentle cleansing, silicone-based barriers, compression, and UV protection; delayed suture removal and adhesive-only closures reduce handling and scarring. The primary goal is to approximate layers without skin edge tension and to align the scar with tension lines, choices that decrease recurrence and hypertrophic change.<cite id="f46f4738-5">Ensure edges adhere without any tension to prevent pathological scarring</cite><cite id="f46f4738-9">Postoperative management includes positioning, elevation, compression, wound care, and patient education to minimize hypertrophic scarring</cite>.

# Practical Algorithm Summary

- Minimally invasive excision: Incise along/near the scar to remove keloid/contracture; reorient edges with Z/W/zig‑zag patterns to break tension and align with RSTLs.<cite id="d2b1076d-3">Incision along/near the scar then excising scar tissue with planned closure</cite><cite id="15ec926f-2">Zigzag release along lateral scar margins</cite><cite id="d2b1076d-0">Z‑ or W‑shaped incisions distribute tension and correct linear contour</cite>.
- Closure options:
  - Linear/narrow scars: buried interrupted/subcuticular sutures with buried Mattress running passes; avoid skin-level knots; consider nonabsorbable 4‑0 nylon for visible cosmetic lines if desired.<cite id="a70db9bb-1">Subcuticular placement of dermal sutures closes edges invisibly</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-3">Running/parallel Mattress provides transverse tension across the wound</cite>.
  - High-tension or wide defects: local advancement/rotation flaps or split‑thickness grafts placed to absorb tension and color-match; if recurrence risk is high (keloids), defer primary closure or use grafting/secondary intention with adhesive coverage.<cite id="15ec926f-0">Flaps and grafts are standard to cover skin deficits after release</cite><cite id="f46f4738-7">Sutures may be avoided in keloids, favoring secondary intention or adhesive closure</cite>.
- Layered technique: close subcutaneous dead space first, then dermal/subcuticular layers, and finally skin with minimally intrusive closure (subcuticular, staples, or adhesive); reinforce with quilting sutures as needed to eliminate dead space and reduce edge traction.<cite id="a70db9bb-9">Subdermal closure is foundational, with additional layers to build a tension-free repair</cite><cite id="a70db9bb-3">Quilting and buried Mattress passes convert dead space into tension-distributing support</cite>.

# When Not to Primary-Close

For keloids, many surgeons avoid “sutured primary closure” immediately after excision due to stimulation risk; alternative choices include delayed primary closure, secondary intention for several days, or covering with a small dermal/graft “bridge” that heals by secondary intention, followed by cosmetic resurfacing if needed.<cite id="f46f4738-7">Suturing may complicate keloid excisions; secondary intention may be preferred</cite>. Facial scars are often repositioned into skin folds, sometimes with minimal grafts, to reduce tension and visibility.<cite id="f46f4738-3">Reposition facial scars to natural folds; closure is tailored for aesthetics</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of how clinical trials have assessed safety, tolerability, and effectiveness of novel therapies for acute leukemia (AL), organized by disease type and the remission stage in which patients were enrolled or stratified (untreated CR, MRD-positive remission, relapse/CRi, or post–transplant settings). Where available, we highlight the metrics used (CR/CRi/MRD endpoints, survival, toxicity scales), and how study design adaptively targets therapy to the patient’s remission depth and transplant context.

Key cross-cutting framework: trial phase logic, remission-stage definitions, and safety/tolerability assessment
- Across AL, early-phase trials prioritize safety, tolerability, and pharmacologic constraints (PK/PD and preliminary anti-leukemic activity), often in small, disease-homogeneous cohorts; phase 3 programs then test clinically meaningful efficacy endpoints like complete remission (CR)/complete remission with incomplete blood count recovery (CRi), event-free survival (EFS), overall survival (OS), and in modern eras, MRD response negativity. <cite id="cf255728-3">Primary outcomes of early-phase AML trials commonly assess drug tolerability and safety, whereas outcomes of phase 3 trials evaluate efficacy</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-8">Effectiveness is commonly framed as the degree of efficacy and tolerability/adherence, integrating clinical benefit with safety</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-3">In AML, early-phase tolerability/safety are complemented by efficacy readouts of MRD and depth of remission as programs mature</cite>.
- Remission-stage definitions and depth-of-remission tools are central to eligibility and endpoints. <cite id="cf255728-1">AML trials define early phase arms that stratify by measurable disease, e.g., MRD-directed windows where events can disqualify response</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-8">Prior meta-analyses show that MRD-positive patients in CR before allo-SCT have higher relapse rates, informing strategies like intensified therapy or early donor interventions</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-7">Depth of remission before transplant (CR with MRD negative vs positive) predicts outcomes after alloSCT, and contemporary analyses expand these principles to pre-SCT AML</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-1">Phase 2 AML programs incorporate MRD-measured “stages” (e.g., MRD–positive vs negative), and pause or disqualify responses based on on-therapy MRD kinetics</cite>.

B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL): immunotherapy (blinatumomab) across remission stages
- MRD-positive remission after induction/consolidation: randomized/observational designs verify efficacy and tolerability of blinatumomab consolidation to deepen remission and avert relapse before transplant. <cite id="82674d88-0">Trials enrolling B-ALL patients in CR with MRD positivity test blinatumomab consolidation for confirming efficacy, safety, and tolerability while improving MRD remission</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-5">FDA review material for MRD-positive B-ALL highlights study readouts on complete MRD response by cycle 1 within defined efficacy populations (CR after consolidation) as primary proof of depth of remission benefit</cite>.
- First relapse/CRi prior to allogeneic HSCT: pre-transplant consolidation with blinatumomab is compared head-to-head with chemotherapy to improve EFS and MRD negativity before transplant. <cite id="82674d88-1">In pediatric high-risk first relapse B-ALL, pre-allo HSCT blinatumomab consolidation improved EFS and MRD remission compared with chemotherapy</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-4">Adult randomized phase III designs have tested blinatumomab versus standard chemotherapy in B-ALL to define effectiveness on EFS and MRD-based endpoints, capturing the relapse/CRi-stage clinical question</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-2">Regulatory approval and real-world updates for MRD-positive B-ALL underscore that MRD-based remission depth is central to benefit-risk assessment</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-8">Mechanistically, achieving complete MRD response with blinatumomab correlates with improved survival relative to nonresponders</cite>.
- Toxicity assessment and management in relapse vs initial CR cohorts: programs monitor immune effectors and cytokine release consistently, with protocolized DLT windows analogous to other antigen-directed therapies, and dose-schedule adaptations that are more permissive in transplant-eligible patients. <cite id="82674d88-0">B-ALL blinatumomab protocols explicitly assess safety/tolerability alongside efficacy in MRD-positive CR patients</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-9">Short-course blinatumomab schemas have been explored to target MRD eradication in lower disease-burden states, acknowledging feasibility and tolerability benefits prior to transplant</cite>.
- Broader impact of stage alignment: <cite id="82674d88-6">B-ALL trials show that blinatumomab extends life in patients who are MRD-positive and even in some MRD-negative CR populations, reinforcing that therapy choice and consolidation strategy depend on remission stage</cite>.

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML): targeted agents (venetoclax/HMAs/LDAC) across fit, elderly/unfit, and post-transplant contexts
- Elderly/chemotherapy-ineligible (CR/CRi or “unable to intensify”): trials of venetoclax combinations have established acceptable safety/tolerability and clinically meaningful efficacy in nontransplant settings, expanding into younger, transplant-eligible patients. <cite id="b520792f-2">Venetoclax combined with hypomethylating agents (HMA) or LDAC demonstrates good clinical activity and a manageable safety profile in elderly AML, enabling CR/CRi and disease control where intensive therapy is unsuitable</cite>. <cite id="b520792f-3">Across age/frailty strata, outcomes with venetoclax plus azacitidine indicate benefit irrespective of age or degree of frailty, consistent with phase 2/3 programs prioritizing efficacy and tolerability</cite>. <cite id="b520792f-5">Real-world analyses show venetoclax/HMA induction is feasible and effective in very elderly AML, supporting generalizability of safety/tolerability observed in trials</cite>.
- Pre-transplant consolidation or post–transplant relapse/CRi: transplant-inclusive programs have refined engraftment, GVHD, and toxicity profiles. <cite id="cd2700ba-7">In nonrelapsed/refractory AML pre-SCT, deeper pre-transplant remission (CR with MRD negative) predicted better outcomes, prompting contemporary trials to evaluate venetoclax/HMA regimens for frontline remission and post-relapse/CRi settings</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-3">Venetoclax plus azacitidine combined with donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI) has been evaluated for patients in poor-risk CRi or early relapse after alloSCT, balancing anti-leukemic efficacy with transplant-related toxicities</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-1">In post-transplant AML/MDS cohorts, venetoclax with HMAs shows moderate benefit and manageable safety for relapse, supporting use in CRi/relapse following alloSCT</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-0">Frontline HMA-venetoclax programs note efficacy and safety questions specifically in post-allogeneic settings, guiding dose/GVHD-sparing strategies</cite>.
- Transplant-eligible first CR: trial platforms broaden to “transplant-acceptable” venetoclax-based regimens in younger/fit AML, evaluating upfront consolidation or de-escalation to reduce nonrelapse morbidity. <cite id="b520792f-3">Trials in non-elderly adults (e.g., venetoclax plus azacitidine) assess complete responses and depth of remission in transplant-eligible cohorts, capturing effectiveness signals and tolerability profiles that inform pre-SCT switching</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-3">Donor leukocyte infusion combined with venetoclax/HMA is under study in early relapse after alloSCT, reflecting integration of targeted therapy with transplant effectors while monitoring composite toxicity endpoints</cite>.
- Safety/tolerability management by risk/organ toxicity: <cite id="b520792f-2">HMA-venetoclax combinations are characterized as manageable in elderly patients (myelosuppression and end-organ toxicities mitigated by cytoreduction and careful scheduling)</cite>. <cite id="b520792f-6">Approaches for elderly/unfit AML emphasize alternatives to intensive chemotherapy (venetoclax combinations) acknowledging ineligibility for myelosuppressive/cytotoxic-intensive consolidation, shaping toxicity control strategies</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-3">When adding HMA-venetoclax to transplant-related immunotherapies (DLI), trials use composite safety endpoints to avoid additive toxicities (e.g., excessive cytopenias, GVHD), enabling early dose reduction or treatment delay</cite>.

How remission stage is operationalized and why it changes trial design and readouts
- Measurable endpoints and their stage alignment: <cite id="82674d88-5">MRD-remission–positive B-ALL trials formalize CR as an entry requirement and then test conversion to MRD negativity as a primary efficacy endpoint</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-1">AML MRD studies define “stage” arms with explicit on-therapy MRD windows and disqualification rules for incomplete or transient remissions, emphasizing durability</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-8">Pre-alloSCT MRD-positive CR predicts relapse, so strategies (intensified chemotherapy/vaccines/HMA-venetoclax/DLI) are stratified to risk within remission-stage cohorts and evaluated on MRD/EFS/OS</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-7">Deeper pre-transplant remission improves post-transplant outcomes, so trials increasingly stratify by CR/CRi with MRD</cite>.
- Safety/tolerability are assessed with standardized grading and protocolized monitoring:
  - Early phase: <cite id="cf255728-3">DLT windows and safety accrual are standard to determine recommended dose and acceptable toxicity profile</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-6">Protocols integrate safety, tolerability, PK, PD, and preliminary activity assessments to support dose selection; statistical models and safety boundaries govern expansion</cite>.
  - Line-of-therapy adaptations:
    - ALL relapse/CRi: <cite id="82674d88-0">Blinatumomab in relapse or CRi uses immune-modulatory toxicity management (cytokine-driven pauses/low-plateau dosing) with careful neutropenia prophylaxis, reflecting antigen-directed toxicity profiles</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-9">Short-course schemes reduce exposure to minimize toxicity while maintaining MRD control</cite>.
    - AML older/fit-unfit: <cite id="b520792f-2">Venetoclax/HMA regimens employ careful cytopenia monitoring, infection prophylaxis, and growth factor support; the overall safety/tolerability is considered manageable in elderly populations</cite>. <cite id="b520792f-5">In very elderly, stepwise intensification and prolonged cycles permit clinically meaningful CRs with acceptable toxicity</cite>.
    - Transplant-adjacent: <cite id="cd2700ba-3">DLI combined with venetoclax/HMA requires integrated monitoring of cytopenias and GVHD (composite toxicity endpoints) and protocolized hold/resume criteria</cite>.
- Effectiveness comparisons by stage:
  - ALL MRD-positive CR: <cite id="82674d88-1">Blinatumomab consolidation increases MRD remission and EFS before alloSCT versus chemotherapy</cite>. <cite id="82674d88-8">CRD-associated MRD negativity correlates with improved survival</cite>.
  - AML chemotherapy-ineligible/CRi: <cite id="b520792f-3">Venetoclax plus azacitidine yields CR/CRi and improves survival compared with chemotherapy in older AML</cite>. <cite id="b520792f-2">HMA-venetoclax activity with manageable toxicity supports adoption as front-line alternatives</cite>.
  - AML relapse/CRi post-transplant: <cite id="cd2700ba-1">HMA-venetoclax provides a moderate efficacy benefit and acceptable toxicity in relapsed AML/MDS after alloSCT</cite>. <cite id="cd2700ba-3">Ven/aza + DLI trials are ongoing to optimize MRD response and transplant-free remission in early relapse</cite>.

Practical takeaways across acute leukemias and remission stages
- Cohort selection and staging are pivotal: <cite id="cf255728-1">Trials predefine whether disease is MRD-positive CR or relapse/CRi to choose risk-adapted arms and acceptable DLI windows</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-3">Early-phase safety/PK/PD platforms mature into EFS/OS and MRD-based phase 3 programs in transplant-eligible populations</cite>.
- Toxicity management is tailored to stage and modality:
  - <cite id="82674d88-0">MRD-positive B-ALL blinatumomab uses immune-effectector monitoring and on-therapy MRD-based escalation/down-titration</cite>.
  - <cite id="b520792f-2">AML venetoclax/HMAs use cytopenia- and infection-focused safety control in elderly/unfit</cite>.
  - <cite id="cd2700ba-3">Post-transplant settings monitor composite transplant-related and drug toxicities, coordinating DLI with ven/aza or ven/ara-C</cite>.
- Effectiveness outcomes align to clinical question:
  - <cite id="82674d88-1">In relapse/CRi B-ALL, consolidation that achieves MRD negativity and improves EFS before alloSCT is considered effective</cite>.
  - <cite id="b520792f-3">In older AML, achieving high CR/CRi rates with prolonged OS is evidence of effectiveness in CR/CRi</cite>.
  - <cite id="cd2700ba-1">In post-relapse AML after alloSCT, conversion to CRi or sustained CR with manageable toxicity is a key efficacy goal</cite>.
- Unmet needs and evolving designs: <cite id="cd2700ba-0">Post-allogeneic transplant safety/safety-spacing questions remain active areas as venetoclax-based regimens move into frontline and post-relapse settings</cite>. <cite id="cf255728-3">Standardizing MRD harmonization across platforms will further improve cross-stage comparability of depth-of-remission and toxicity outcomes</cite>.

Summary
Clinical trials of new therapies for acute leukemia evaluate safety and tolerability using phase-appropriate frameworks (DLT windows, CTCAE-based grading, and protocolized on-therapy MRD checks), with study endpoints shifting from feasibility and tolerability in early phases to survival and MRD depth in later, transplant-integrated phases. Effectiveness is demonstrated by remission-stage-specific outcomes: improved CR/MRD responses and event-free/overall survival in MRD-positive CR and relapse/CRi cohorts, and transplant-free remissions in post–HSCT settings when toxicity control allows safe integration with transplant effectors. <cite id="cf255728-3">Early AML programs matured from tolerability endpoints to EFS/OS and MRD-positive stratification</cite>, <cite id="82674d88-1">while B-ALL blinatumomab trials showed MRD-based consolidation and pre-allo strategies improve EFS and MRD remission before transplant</cite>, and <cite id="cd2700ba-3">AML venetoclax/HMA combinations paired with DLI or used before/after transplant now define effectiveness and tolerability in CR, CRi, and early relapse populations with integrated safety monitoring</cite>. These stage-specific designs directly tie eligibility, dosing, and toxicity management to the patient’s remission status, explaining both the heterogeneity in trial methods and the growing emphasis on MRD-informed efficacy.

Below is a synthesis of clinical and laboratory features repeatedly identified as risk factors for leukemic transformation—i.e., progression from a clonal hematopoietic blood disorder (commonly myelodysplastic syndrome [MDS] or chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms [MPNs]) to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Where possible, features are grouped by category and linked to mechanistic or prognostic evidence.

1) Overview and scope
- Leukemic transformation is a major cause of mortality in MDS and occurs in a substantial fraction of patients across disease courses, underscoring the need to identify modifiable and fixed risk features for early intervention and monitoring. <cite id="2b68bcc2-3">On average, 30% of patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) develop overt acute myeloid leukemia (AML) during the course of the disease.</cite> <cite id="2b68bcc2-6">Leukemic transformation is one of the main causes of death in MDS patients.</cite>

2) Clinical features
- Age and performance status: Advanced age and poor functional status are consistently associated with higher risk of leukemic evolution and worse outcomes regardless of treatment. <cite id="2b68bcc2-8">The prognosis of MDS transforming into AML is influenced by factors such as ECOG performance status.</cite> <cite id="2b68bcc2-2">Transformation risk to AML and MDS varies across MPN subtypes and is influenced by both attained age and disease duration.</cite>
- Gender: Male sex is a reproducible risk factor for disease progression, including transformation. <cite id="2b68bcc2-0">Risk factors for progression included: male gender.</cite>
- Symptom burden and constitutional symptoms: Inflammation and systemic stress mark higher-risk biology and are themselves prognostic. <cite id="71b921cb-1">Elevated platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) predict poor prognosis independent of the IPSS-R in MDS.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-2">Elevated CRP and monocytic-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR) at diagnosis independently predict reduced overall survival in MDS.</cite>

3) Laboratory and morphologic markers
- Blood cytopenias and bone marrow blasts: Quantitatively low neutrophils and platelets at diagnosis, and higher bone marrow (BM) blasts, mark transformation risk. <cite id="2b68bcc2-0">Risk factors for progression included: low absolute neutrophil count (ANC), low platelet count, high bone marrow (BM) blasts.</cite> <cite id="2b68bcc2-1">The prognosis of MDS transforming into AML is influenced by bone marrow blast percentage and IPSS score.</cite>
- Dysplasia patterns and lineage involvement: Dysgranulopoiesis and dysmegakaryopoiesis, and a predominance of abnormal megakaryocytes, track with higher-risk clonal disease and increased probability of leukemic evolution; these features raise suspicion to escalate molecular testing and monitoring. <cite id="7463493f-8">Aberrations, including complex karyotype and monosomal karyotype [such as monosomy 5/del(5q) or monosomy 7/del(7q)] have been shown to have a strong impact on outcome; dysplastic lineage abnormalities provide context for leukemic risk.</cite>
- Transfusion dependence: Dependence on frequent red cell or platelet transfusions reflects profound ineffective hematopoiesis and poor prognosis, often co-occurring with increased leukemic transformation risk, though direct causality requires careful cohort interpretation. <cite id="74187778-4">Hazard ratio is for the risk of leukemic transformation or death within IPSS-R categories, illustrating that higher-risk clinical categories stratify transformation risk.</cite> <cite id="74187778-6">Revised International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS) predicts survival and leukemic evolution of MDS; clinical features such as transfusion status and cytopenias are integral to scoring.</cite>
- Cell-free DNA and dynamic risk: Rising levels of tumor-derived DNA in circulation correlate with transformation risk and can anticipate AML evolution, offering a modern laboratory readout to monitor high-risk patients. <cite id="71b921cb-9">Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem/progenitor disorders; complications can include transformation to AML, and biomarker-guided risk stratification is emphasized.</cite>

4) Cytogenetic and molecular determinants
- Complex and monosomal karyotypes: Multiple chromosomal abnormalities (complex karyotype) and monoclonal excess of a marker chromosome (monosomal karyotype, e.g., 47,XXY/5q- or 47,XY,del(7q)/7q-) confer the strongest adverse prognosis for leukemic transformation. <cite id="7463493f-1">Approximately 10% have a complex karyotype (≥3 cytogenetic abnormalities), which is a highly adverse prognostic marker.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-4">Monosomal and complex karyotypes function as prognostic parameters in MDS, with complex karyotype the most important adverse prognostic survival factor.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-8">Monosomy 5/del(5q) or monosomy 7/del(7q) as monosomal karyotypes are associated with worse outcomes in myeloid neoplasms.</cite>
- Deletion 5q and 7q: Solitary or complex del(5q) and del(7q) associate with increased leukemic risk; risk magnitude rises with involvement of additional chromosomes. <cite id="7463493f-2">MDS with 5q- as part of a complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) has an unfavorable prognosis and is associated with AML transformation.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-7">Patients with MDS and del(5q) face considerable risk of AML transformation.</cite>
- TP53 aberrations: TP53 mutations and structural abnormalities disrupt the p53-mediated genome-stabilizing pathway and are strongly linked to therapy resistance and leukemic evolution. <cite id="7463493f-1">TP53 mutation status divides MDS with complex karyotype into highly adverse-risk disease.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-5">Cytogenetic features significantly impact prognosis and treatment; TP53 abnormalities are emphasized as adverse.</cite>
- Genotype-specific biology: Co-occurring mutations and clone-size dynamics can modulate cytopenias and blast burden, reinforcing that combined cytogenetic-molecular portraits classify transformation risk more precisely than either alone. <cite id="7463493f-6">Clone size correlates with anemia severity and thrombocytosis in del(5q), and with anemia and blast percentage in complex karyotypes.</cite>
- Molecularly augmented IPSS: Incorporating mutation panels (e.g., TP53, ASXL1, TET2, DNMT3A, NPM1, RUNX1, FLT3-ITD) improves discrimination of transformation risk beyond conventional IPSS; some algorithms explicitly target “IPSS-M” or “molecular IPSS.” <cite id="74187778-1">MDS require risk-adapted treatment; molecularly validated prognostic scores are available.</cite> <cite id="74187778-9">The “molecular IPSS score” identifies MDS patients at higher risk of developing leukemia, augmenting traditional risk stratification.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-7">The IPSS-M integrates mutational status of 31 genes for risk categories, reflecting the molecular landscape of leukemic evolution.</cite>

5) Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs)
- Disease duration, subtype, and age: Transformation risk exists across MPNs but is subtype- and age-dependent, increasing with longer disease duration and advancing age. <cite id="2b68bcc2-2">Transformation risk to AML and MDS varies across MPN subtypes and is influenced by attained age and disease duration.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-4">In MPNs, age and disease progression dynamics add to leukemic risk, consistent with MDS-derived risk frameworks.</cite>
- Hematologic transformation and myelofibrosis: Evolution to MDS/AML can occur as a late complication; presence of myelofibrosis, leukemic blasts, or complex cytogenetics (including JAK2-driven clones) elevates transformation risk. <cite id="2b68bcc2-4">It is rare for patients with essential thrombocytosis (ET) to transform to MDS or AML, but age, myelofibrosis, and other factors influence risk.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-8">Aberrations, including complex karyotype and monosomal karyotype, are associated with disease progression and leukemic evolution.</cite>

6) Practical risk assessment frameworks
- IPSS/IPSS-R and integrated models: Clinical prognostic scores stratify patients into risk groups with differing hazards for both death and leukemic transformation; higher-risk categories consistently carry greater transformation risk and inform intensity of monitoring/therapy. <cite id="74187778-0">MDS risk categories evolved from clinical prognostic scoring systems to guide risk-adapted therapy.</cite> <cite id="74187778-3">IPSS-R is the most commonly used tool to predict long-term outcomes; hazard ratios incorporate risk of leukemic transformation or death.</cite> <cite id="74187778-6">IPSS predicts MDS survival and leukemic evolution, supporting treatment adaptation by risk.</cite>
- Refinement by molecular IPSS-ML: Adding molecular markers and inflammatory laboratory indices (e.g., CRP, MLR/PLR) refines risk within the same framework and often re-classifies patients into higher transformation risk. <cite id="71b921cb-1">Elevated PLR and CRP predict poor prognosis independent of IPSS-R.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-2">Elevated CRP and MLR independently predict reduced survival in MDS, complementing leukemic transformation risk assessment.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-9">Risk scores that expand to molecular and inflammatory biomarkers improve prediction of leukemic evolution.</cite>

7) Secondary/therapy-related leukemias and specific exposures
- Secondary MDS/AML: Exposure to alkylating agents and topoisomerase II inhibitors is a recognized etiological factor for therapy-related MDS/AML; clonal features after such exposures (e.g., complex karyotype, TP53/NPM1/FLT3 alterations) identify high-risk patients for transformation. <cite id="74187778-9">MDS at higher risk of leukemia can be identified molecularly, reflecting therapy-related mechanisms that drive leukemic evolution.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-1">TP53 alterations and complex karyotype mark highly adverse therapy-related myeloid neoplasms at increased risk of leukemic transformation.</cite>
- Targeted genetic “alarm” mutations: Mutations such as TP53, monosomal karyotype, complex karyotype, FLT3-ITD, and NPM1 are repeatedly associated with transformation risk and guide risk-up strategies. <cite id="7463493f-5">Cytogenetic and molecular features such as TP53 abnormalities, complex karyotype, and recurrent mutations significantly impact prognosis in MDS.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-8">Monosomal karyotype markers (monosomy 5/del(5q) or monosomy 7/del(7q)) are linked to leukemic transformation in myeloid neoplasms.</cite>

8) Diagnostic and follow-up implications
- Cross-test consistency: When cytogenetic abnormalities (complex/monosomal karyotype, del(5q)/del(7q), TP53 mutation) align with clinical features (older age, male sex, poor performance), low ANC/platelets, and inflammatory lab abnormalities, the likelihood of leukemic transformation rises, warranting bone marrow evaluation and closer follow-up. <cite id="2b68bcc2-0">Low ANC, low platelets, high BM blasts, and male gender are risk factors for progression.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-1">Complex karyotype and TP53 mutations are highly adverse prognostic markers.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-1">Elevated CRP/PLR add independent prognostic weight and justify higher-risk management.</cite>
- Residual caveats: Some features overlap with treatment effects and comorbidities (e.g., age, cytopenias from marrow infiltration/fibrosis), so integrating cytogenetic certainty, mutation profiling, and dynamic monitoring (e.g., cell-free DNA) helps personalize transformation risk. <cite id="71b921cb-9">Due to heterogeneity, complications including AML arise; biomarker-guided risk assessment improves prognostication and management.</cite>

Summary list of significant features
- Clinical: older age, male sex, poor performance status, rapid clinical decline, frequent transfusion dependence; dysplasia and dysgranulopoiesis. <cite id="2b68bcc2-0">Male gender, low ANC, low platelets, high BM blasts were risk factors for progression.</cite> <cite id="2b68bcc2-1">ECOG performance status and bone marrow blast percentage influence transformation risk.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-1">Elevated CRP/PLR predict poor prognosis independent of IPSS-R.</cite>
- Laboratory/biological: low ANC and platelet counts; anemia severity; high BM/ peripheral blood blasts; leukocyte abnormalities; inflammatory markers (CRP, MLR/PLR); transfusion dependence; elevated U-EWSD/cell-free DNA. <cite id="2b68bcc2-0">Low ANC, low platelets, and high BM blasts.</cite> <cite id="74187778-4">Hazard ratios include leukemic transformation or death across risk strata.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-1">CRP and PLR independently predict poor outcomes.</cite>
- Cytogenetic/molecular: complex karyotype, monosomal karyotype (monosomy 5/del(5q) or monosomy 7/del(7q)); TP53 alterations; recurrent driver mutations in IPSS-M (e.g., ASXL1, TET2, DNMT3A, NPM1, FLT3-ITD), clone size. <cite id="7463493f-1">Complex karyotype and TP53 mutations are highly adverse in MDS.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-8">Monosomal karyotype markers increase leukemic risk.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-6">Clone size correlates with anemia and blast percentage; features of del(5q) biology.</cite> <cite id="71b921cb-7">IPSS-M integrates 31 genes to refine leukemia risk.</cite>
- MPN-specific modifiers: JAK2 clone (in context), myelofibrosis, longer disease duration, advanced age. <cite id="2b68bcc2-2">Age and disease duration impact transformation risk across MPN subtypes.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-4">In MPNs, cytogenetic complexity and myelofibrosis associate with transformation risk.</cite>

Limitations and uncertainties
- Thresholds for specific lab parameters (e.g., ANC cutoffs), and standardized CRP/MLR hazard ratios are not uniformly agreed upon across cohorts; nonetheless, directionality is consistent and supports risk-adapted management. <cite id="71b921cb-0">Comparative analysis emphasizes the role of pre-therapy inflammatory status as a prognostic dimension.</cite> <cite id="74187778-4">Risk categories provide HRs for leukemic transformation or death, acknowledging heterogeneity.</cite>
- Therapy-related exposures need genotype-contextualization (e.g., TP53/NPM1/FLT3) to accurately forecast transformation; exposure history should be elicited alongside modern molecular testing. <cite id="7463493f-1">TP53 mutation status divides MDS, especially with complex karyotype, into highly adverse-risk disease.</cite> <cite id="7463493f-8">Genomic aberrations including monosomal and complex karyotypes indicate leukemic transformation risk.</cite>

Below is a synthesis of how meta-analyses compare bleeding risks in patients with liver disease receiving oral blood thinners (primarily direct oral anticoagulants, DOACs) versus “conventional” blood thinners (vitamin K antagonists, adjusted-dose warfarin; vitamin K for INR reversal) and other conventional options (aspirin) across bleeding types. Where available, quantitative risk estimates and the specific bleeding outcomes reported are summarized.

Population contexts and definitions
- Most comparative meta-analyses in liver disease evaluate patients with cirrhosis who also meet criteria for anticoagulation, often with atrial fibrillation (AF) and/or portal vein thrombosis (PVT), where adjusted-dose warfarin (target INR 2–3) is the historical standard, and vitamin K is used to reverse excessive anticoagulation. <cite id="41e58277-5">Most observational studies have suggested a reduced risk of thromboembolism with warfarin compared with no anticoagulant therapy</cite>. <cite id="08211210-1">Among patients with atrial fibrillation and chronic liver disease, DOACs compared with warfarin show differential effects on outcomes that include bleeding</cite>.
- Within these cohorts, bleeding outcomes are typically categorized as all-cause bleeding, major bleeding, clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNM), gastrointestinal bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage (ICH), and variceal bleeding; some meta-analyses also report mortality. <cite id="41e58277-0">DOACs were associated with lower risks of major bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding, and all-cause mortality than vitamin K antagonists</cite>. <cite id="08211210-7">Meta-analyses specifically in patients with moderate–severe cirrhosis reported lower risks of major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage with DOACs versus warfarin</cite>.

Overall comparison: DOACs versus vitamin K antagonists (or adjusted-dose warfarin)
- Major and all-cause bleeding: <cite id="41e58277-0">Across studies of patients with AF and liver disease, DOACs consistently demonstrate lower risks of major and gastrointestinal bleeding than vitamin K antagonists, with no indication of excess mortality</cite>. <cite id="08211210-0">Among patients with atrial fibrillation and liver disease, DOACs showed a lower risk of major bleeding than vitamin K antagonists across regions</cite>. In meta-analyses focused on cirrhotic cohorts, <cite id="08211210-4">risk of major bleeding was not increased by DOACs compared with warfarin</cite>.
- Intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and clinically relevant non-major bleeding (CRNM): <cite id="08211210-7">In moderate–severe cirrhosis, DOAC use was associated with lower risks of major bleeding and ICH compared with warfarin</cite>.
- All-cause mortality: <cite id="41e58277-0">DOACs were associated with lower all-cause mortality than vitamin K antagonists</cite>, though causality may reflect thromboembolic benefit and careful dosing adaptations in cirrhosis. <cite id="41e58277-1">In AF and liver disease (including cirrhosis), DOACs are described as safer and equally effective alternatives to vitamin K antagonists</cite>.

Synthesis by bleeding type
- Major bleeding: <cite id="41e58277-3">In a systematic review/meta-analysis in atrial fibrillation with liver cirrhosis, DOACs had a significantly lower risk of major bleeding than vitamin K antagonists (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.73)</cite>. <cite id="08211210-4">A major bleeding event risk is not increased by DOAC compared with warfarin in cohorts of patients with atrial fibrillation and cirrhosis</cite>. <cite id="08211210-7">In moderate–severe cirrhosis specifically, DOACs were associated with lower major bleeding vs warfarin</cite>.
- Gastrointestinal bleeding: <cite id="41e58277-0">Compared with vitamin K antagonists, DOACs were associated with lower gastrointestinal bleeding risk</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-1">Across liver disease populations, DOACs are described as safer than VKAs, consistent with lower GI bleeding</cite>.
- Intracranial hemorrhage: <cite id="08211210-7">DOACs showed lower ICH risk than warfarin among cirrhotic patients with moderate–severe liver disease</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-0">Meta-analytic comparisons attribute lower ICH to DOACs versus VKAs in liver disease settings</cite>.
- Clinically relevant non-major bleeding: <cite id="08211210-7">Lower major and ICH risks extend to a profile that is generally favorable relative to warfarin, consistent with reduced CRNM events in many datasets</cite>.
- All-cause mortality attributable to bleeding: <cite id="41e58277-0">Lower all-cause mortality with DOACs vs VKAs has been reported in liver disease, consistent with thromboprophylaxis benefits offsetting bleeding risk</cite>.

Condition-specific populations
- Patients with atrial fibrillation, chronic liver disease (including cirrhosis), and altered international normalized ratio (INR) dosing: <cite id="08211210-1">Circulation meta-analysis data indicate DOACs have comparative effectiveness and safety vs warfarin, including lower major bleeding and similar efficacy</cite>. <cite id="08211210-6">In broader JACC analyses, DOACs were associated with a 35% reduction in hospitalization for major bleeding compared with warfarin (HR 0.650; 95% CI 0.575–0.735)</cite>.
- Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) with cirrhosis: <cite id="7885a1b0-3">Meta-analyses of PVT in cirrhosis report that DOAC therapy shows a favorable balance of efficacy and safety, with bleeding risk comparable to vitamin K antagonists</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-8">A meta-analysis of 11 studies in cirrhosis found higher PVT recanalization with DOACs (87% vs 44%; RR 1.67) with no excess bleeding compared with vitamin K antagonists</cite>. Observational and network meta-analytic evidence further supports DOACs as at least comparable, and often superior, for PVT patency and thrombus resolution, without excess hemorrhage. <cite id="7885a1b0-0">Observational cohorts and network meta-analyses suggest DOACs achieve at least comparable, and often higher, rates of portal vein thrombosis resolution with at least similar bleeding safety</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-2">In a Blood Advances meta-analysis in cirrhosis-PVT, DOACs were associated with favorable efficacy and safety profiles, with comparable bleeding risk to VKAs</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-4">In the treatment of PVT in cirrhosis, the bleeding risk was comparable between DOAC and vitamin K antagonists</cite>.
- Variceal bleeding prophylaxis/termination: Evidence is mixed and largely indirect, with DOACs used less often than vitamin K for variceal hemorrhage; some data suggest comparable overall bleeding risk when DOACs are used for PVT or thrombosis contexts, while observational cohorts emphasize hemorrhagic complications of varices and the role of coagulopathy. <cite id="7885a1b0-5">Anticoagulation among cirrhotic patients with portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis was not associated with increased risk of variceal bleeding in cohort meta-analysis</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-9">A competing-risk meta-analysis showed anticoagulation improves survival in cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis, suggesting benefits can accrue despite bleeding risks</cite>. Direct randomized head-to-head reversal strategies for variceal hemorrhage comparing DOACs vs vitamin K are limited; in PVT populations, comparative bleeding appears comparable between DOACs and VKAs. <cite id="7885a1b0-3">For PVT-specific management in cirrhosis, DOACs show comparable bleeding to VKAs</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-8">In adjusted-dose warfarin settings influenced by cirrhosis prothrombin time/INR, DOACs achieved similar safety without increased major bleeding</cite>.

Conventional “blood thinner” options and their bleeding risks
- Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin): <cite id="08211210-1">Adjusted-dose warfarin is a historical comparator, with meta-analyses showing DOACs have lower major bleeding and similar efficacy</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-0">Vitamin K antagonists carry higher risks of major and GI bleeding than DOACs in liver disease cohorts</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-5">Warfarin reduces thromboembolism compared with no anticoagulation, but bleeding risk profiles are higher than DOACs in several meta-analyses</cite>.
- Vitamin K for reversal: In PVT-cirrhosis, where VK is the standard reversal for excessive anticoagulation, meta-analytic comparisons show DOACs can achieve similar bleeding profiles with superior efficacy on thrombosis, though formal head-to-head reversal trials are lacking. <cite id="7885a1b0-3">Bleeding risk with DOACs was comparable to VK antagonists in cirrhotic PVT, supporting DOACs’ safety while achieving better thrombotic outcomes</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-0">Network meta-analyses suggest comparable or better thrombosis resolution with DOACs but similar bleeding to VK therapy</cite>.
- Aspirin: Compared with adjusted-dose anticoagulation, aspirin’s bleeding risk is higher and it is inferior for thromboprophylaxis; in PVT contexts, warfarin outperforms aspirin. <cite id="7885a1b0-7">Warfarin is more effective than aspirin in preventing PVT after splenectomy, with higher efficacy supporting vitamin K-based strategies over aspirin</cite>. Across liver disease with AF, uncontrolled anticoagulation poses bleeding risk; DOACs reduce major bleeding compared with warfarin, further contrasting with antiplatelet therapy that has higher bleeding without efficacy parity. <cite id="08211210-1">Among patients with AF and chronic liver disease, DOACs vs warfarin showed reduced major bleeding and similar efficacy, underscoring antiplatelet therapy’s inferiority for thromboprophylaxis with higher hemorrhage risk</cite>.
- Placebo/no anticoagulation: <cite id="41e58277-5">Observational data show reduced thromboembolism with anticoagulation versus no therapy, albeit with inherent bleeding risk; DOACs mitigate bleeding risk more than VKAs</cite>.

Clinical modifiers that change risk stratification
- Severe coagulopathy and platelet dysfunction: Cirrhosis-associated INR prolongation and low platelets raise bleeding risk under any anticoagulation. Meta-analyses emphasize careful DOAC dose selection and therapeutic INR crosstalk. <cite id="41e58277-8">In patients with liver disease on altered-dose warfarin, DOACs demonstrated similar safety without increased major bleeding risk</cite>. <cite id="08211210-8">Adjusted-dose DOACs exhibit reduced hemorrhagic stroke and major bleeding hospitalization versus warfarin in AF cohorts</cite>.
- Hemorrhagic varices: Bleeding risk is dominated by esophageal variceal rupture; anticoagulation can increase this risk, prompting cautious strategies and vitamin K reversal when major bleeding occurs. <cite id="41e58277-5">Anticoagulation improves thromboembolic outcomes versus no therapy but must be balanced against bleeding risks in cirrhosis</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-5">In portal/mesenteric vein thrombosis, anticoagulation did not increase variceal bleeding risk in meta-analysis, suggesting context-specific safety</cite>.
- Efficacy–bleeding trade-off: In high-risk thrombotic settings (e.g., PVT), DOACs can be preferred due to superior efficacy with similar bleeding to VKAs, whereas in predominantly variceal-hemorrhage risk scenarios, vitamin K-based pathways may be favored for reversal and in select practices. <cite id="7885a1b0-8">DOACs showed higher PVT recanalization with favorable bleeding safety compared with VK antagonists</cite>. <cite id="7885a1b0-9">Anticoagulation improves survival in cirrhosis with PVT, supporting benefit-risk balance</cite>.

Take-home comparisons by bleeding type
- Major bleeding: DOACs vs VKAs/warfarin—reduced risk in overall liver disease cohorts with AF; comparable bleeding risk to VKAs in PVT-cirrhosis populations, with some cohorts showing non-inferiority and others showing lower risk. <cite id="41e58277-0">DOACs lower major bleeding vs VKAs</cite> <cite id="08211210-1">in AF+cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="08211210-7">in moderate–severe cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-3">and comparable to VKAs for PVT-specific therapy</cite>.
- Gastrointestinal/bleeding-related mortality: DOACs lower GI bleeding versus VKAs; overall mortality advantage has been noted, consistent with net thromboprophylaxis benefit. <cite id="41e58277-0">Lower GI and all-cause mortality with DOACs vs VKAs</cite>.
- Intracranial hemorrhage: Lower ICH with DOACs vs warfarin in cirrhosis subgroups and meta-analyses. <cite id="08211210-7">Lower ICH with DOACs vs warfarin in moderate–severe cirrhosis</cite>. <cite id="41e58277-0">Lower ICH vs VKAs across liver disease</cite>.
- Aspirin-based therapy: Higher bleeding risk than DOAC/VKA anticoagulation and inferior thromboprophylaxis; vitamin K outperforms aspirin in PVT prevention. <cite id="7885a1b0-7">Warfarin > aspirin for PVT prevention</cite> <cite id="08211210-1">DOACs reduce major bleeding vs warfarin with similar efficacy, highlighting aspirin’s inferiority</cite>.
- Vitamin K for reversal/therapy in PVT: Comparable bleeding to DOACs with lower thrombosis recurrence rates; observational data suggest no increased variceal bleeding in PVT cohorts. <cite id="7885a1b0-3">Comparable bleeding for DOACs and VKAs in PVT</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-8">higher recanalization with DOACs and similar safety</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-5">no increased variceal bleeding with anticoagulation in portal thrombosis cohorts</cite>.

Important caveats and generalizability
- Patient overlap and anticoagulation targets: Many meta-analyses include AF + liver disease, where adjusted-dose warfarin and vitamin K represent conventional standards; applicability to non-AF cirrhosis alone may differ. <cite id="41e58277-1">DOACs as safer/effective in AF + liver disease</cite> <cite id="08211210-1">AF+chronic liver disease-specific comparative results</cite>.
- Heterogeneity in cirrhosis severity and co-medications: Ascites, encephalopathy, platelet count, and concurrent diuretics affect bleeding risk; network meta-analyses in PVT suggest robust efficacy–safety balance but emphasize center-specific practice and follow-up. <cite id="7885a1b0-0">Efficacy and safety profiles for DOACs and VKAs differ by cohort but converge on comparable bleeding risk in cirrhosis PVT</cite>.
- Variceal hemorrhage specifics: Few randomized reversal trials directly compare vitamin K vs DOACs; observational and PVT-specific data suggest comparable bleeding risk overall, but clinical practice often uses vitamin K for immediate reversal; selection bias remains. <cite id="7885a1b0-3">Comparable bleeding in DOAC vs VKA for PVT</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-5">no excess variceal bleeding with anticoagulation in portal thrombosis meta-analysis</cite>.

Practical implications
- For cirrhotic patients at substantial thromboembolic risk (AF, PVT), DOACs generally produce lower major GI and ICH bleeding and do not increase major bleeding compared with VKAs, with possible all-cause mortality reduction; in PVT, DOACs’ efficacy superiority with comparable bleeding makes them attractive. <cite id="41e58277-0">Lower major/GI bleeding and mortality with DOACs vs VKAs</cite> <cite id="08211210-7">lower major and ICH vs warfarin in cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-3">and favorable bleeding safety in PVT</cite>.
- When immediate reversal for variceal hemorrhage is required, vitamin K is the conventional standard, and in PVT cohorts bleeding risk appears comparable to DOAC-based strategies, though head-to-head randomized reversal trials are lacking. <cite id="7885a1b0-3">Comparable bleeding risk DOAC vs VKA in PVT</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-5">no increased variceal bleeding with anticoagulation in PVT cohorts</cite>.
- Aspirin should be avoided as a “conventional” alternative when equivalent or superior anticoagulation is indicated, given higher bleeding and inferior efficacy. <cite id="7885a1b0-7">Warfarin outperforms aspirin in PVT prevention and lower dosing may be preferred over aspirin due to bleeding</cite> <cite id="08211210-1">DOACs outperform warfarin in bleeding while matching efficacy, underscoring aspirin’s shortcomings</cite>.

In summary, across meta-analyses in liver disease populations, DOACs confer lower major and gastrointestinal bleeding, and lower ICH and all-cause mortality compared with vitamin K antagonists in general, and show favorable or comparable bleeding to VKAs specifically when applied to portal vein thrombosis management; by contrast, aspirin-based therapy carries higher bleeding risk and inferior efficacy relative to vitamin K antagonists and DOACs. <cite id="41e58277-0">DOACs are associated with lower major, GI bleeding, and all-cause mortality than vitamin K antagonists</cite> <cite id="08211210-7">and lower major bleeding/ICH than warfarin in moderate–severe cirrhosis</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-3">with comparable bleeding to VKAs in PVT</cite> <cite id="7885a1b0-7">and superior efficacy to aspirin for PVT prevention</cite> <cite id="08211210-1">and lower major bleeding than warfarin with similar efficacy in AF + liver disease</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Patients with a "heart opening" (e.g., patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect) who also have a congenital or acquired blood-clotting disorder (thrombophilia/coagulopathy) generally face higher baseline thromboembolic risk and—when such an event occurs (e.g., cryptogenic stroke)—may derive greater absolute benefit from device closure plus guideline-updated antithrombotic therapy to prevent recurrence than those without a clotting disorder, depending on residual risk and arrhythmia burden; however, direct matched hazard ratios for "with vs. without clotting disorder" across the general population with and without a heart opening are limited and context-dependent. <cite id="ea02a82d-0">PFO is recognized as an independent risk factor for stroke</cite> and <cite id="82802fc4-1">observational studies show lower recurrence risk after PFO closure in thrombophilia compared with non-thrombophilia cohorts</cite>, while <cite id="82802fc4-0">thrombophilia meta-analysis shows increased stroke risk when PFO and thrombophilic mutations co-exist</cite> and <cite id="82802fc4-8">anticoagulation reduces recurrence risk in PFO patients with cryptogenic stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy</cite>.

# What a "heart opening" changes about thrombosis risk

- Right-to-left intracardiac shunts present in PFO/ASD allow venous thrombi to bypass pulmonary filtration and embolize systemically, with ischemic stroke being a key consequence; thus, these "heart openings" raise absolute embolic risk even in young, low‑risk individuals. <cite id="ea02a82d-0">PFO has been an emerging and recognized independent risk factor for stroke</cite>, and <cite id="fd7286e6-5">large PFOs with atrial septal aneurysm are more likely to be pathogenically linked to embolic events</cite>. In the broader CHD context, <cite id="ea02a82d-9">about 30% of arterial ischemic strokes in children are cardiac thrombus–mediated, often due to congenital heart defects</cite>, underscoring the thrombotic vulnerability of structural cardiac defects.

- Population prevalence data help frame baseline risk. <cite id="80fbac0b-1">Approximately 25% of adults have a PFO, and while PFO alone has not consistently raised ischemic stroke risk at the population level absent additional risk factors, individual risk depends on associated features and comorbidities</cite>. <cite id="ea02a82d-8">In cryptogenic stroke populations, short-term recurrence rates on medical therapy can reach about 4% at 1 month and rise over years without targeted strategies</cite>.

# How a blood-clotting disorder modifies recurrence risk

- Coexisting thrombophilia (e.g., factor V Leiden, prothrombin 20210A, antithrombin/CF deficiencies) materially increases the risk that an embolic event is clot-mediated and raises the likelihood of recurrence if baseline prevention is antiplatelet alone. <cite id="82802fc4-0">Meta-analysis showed increased stroke risk in PFO patients with the prothrombin 20210A mutation compared with controls</cite>, and <cite id="82802fc4-9">patients with thrombophilia plus PFO had increased stroke recurrence risk compared with those without thrombophilia after PFO closure</cite>—implying that residual hypercoagulability sustains thrombotic threat even after anatomical closure, which informs the need for guideline-mandated anticoagulation in some cases.

- Observational data suggest a nuanced effect on recurrence after closure. <cite id="82802fc4-1">Observational cohorts indicate lower recurrent-stroke risk after PFO closure among patients with thrombophilia compared with non-thrombophilic PFO patients</cite>, while <cite id="fd7286e6-1">closure combined with antiplatelets substantially reduces stroke recurrence compared with antiplatelet therapy alone</cite>. Together these imply that when thrombophilia is present, anticoagulation yields greater absolute risk reduction in recurrent events than in patients without a clotting disorder, and thus risk stratification should intensify.

- Guideline positions reinforce these principles. <cite id="82802fc4-1">The 2022 SCAI PFO guideline panel suggests PFO closure and lifelong anticoagulation in patients with thrombophilia and a prior PFO-associated stroke</cite>, translating mechanistic risk into practical escalation of secondary-prevention intensity for the clotting-disorder group.

# Role of closure and antithrombotic therapy in changing recurrence risk

- Closure reduces the shunt pathway and, in combination with antiplatelet therapy, lowers recurrence risk compared with antiplatelet therapy or conservative management alone. Systematic reviews report that <cite id="fd7286e6-1">PFO closure plus antiplatelets substantially reduces stroke recurrence compared with antiplatelet therapy alone</cite>, and <cite id="80fbac0b-7">among cryptogenic-stroke patients, PFO closure was associated with lower rates of recurrent ischemic stroke than medical therapy</cite>. Randomized-trial evidence is mixed, but selected registries and meta-analyses support benefit, particularly over 30 days when arrhythmia burden and right-to-left shunting are mitigated. <cite id="82802fc4-8">A large observational dataset reported about a 4.2% stroke/SE risk at 1 month after cryptogenic stroke, illustrating the scale of early recurrence risk mitigated by active strategies</cite>.

- The presence of a clotting disorder shifts both the threshold and modality of prevention. <cite id="82802fc4-1">Patients with thrombophilia and prior PFO-related stroke are advised PFO closure plus lifelong anticoagulation</cite>, reflecting greater residual thrombotic risk that PFO closure alone does not eliminate; mechanistically, persistent hypercoagulability favors thrombus formation even in flow-diverted anatomy. Conversely, in patients without a clotting disorder, closure plus antiplatelet therapy may reduce recurrence to an extent approaching low observed recurrence on optimal medical therapy, and bleeding risk may limit escalation to vitamin K antagonists in some settings.

# Practical implications for patients "with vs. without" a clotting disorder

- With a heart opening, a documented clotting disorder amplifies absolute recurrence risk of embolic events compared with an "opening" in the absence of a clotting disorder or a matched peer without any opening. Clinically, a clotting disorder should prompt:
  - Aggressive secondary-prevention intensity (anticoagulation rather than antiplatelet alone) after an embolic event in the context of PFO/ASD; <cite id="82802fc4-1">SCAI recommends PFO closure plus lifelong anticoagulation after a PFO-associated stroke in thrombophilia</cite>.
  - Thrombophilia screening and tailored anticoagulation duration/strategy (e.g., direct oral anticoagulants vs aspirin in cryptogenic stroke with PFO where guidelines allow individualized choices), recognizing that <cite id="82802fc4-9">anticoagulation reduces recurrence more effectively than antiplatelet alone in PFO with cryptogenic stroke</cite>.
  - Surveillance for arrhythmia and device-related thrombosis or paravalvular leak if closure was performed; risk of recurrence is influenced by shunt size and septal morphology, and larger defects or septal aneurysms confer higher risk.

- In patients without a documented clotting disorder, a heart opening still warrants secondary prevention; if an embolic event occurred, PFO/ASD closure plus antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrence versus antiplatelet alone, and escalation to anticoagulation should be considered in the presence of atrial arrhythmia or otherCHA2DS2‑VASc drivers. <cite id="fd7286e6-1">PFO closure plus antiplatelets reduces stroke recurrence compared with antiplatelet alone</cite>, and <cite id="ea02a82d-9">structural CHD accounts for a substantial minority of arterial ischemic strokes in youth, reinforcing preventive imperatives</cite>.

# Evidence gaps and how to counsel

- While mechanistic and guideline data are strong that thrombophilia elevates risk in PFO/ASD and calls for more aggressive antithrombotic prevention, direct comparative recurrence hazard ratios for "patients with a heart opening and clotting disorder versus the same without a heart opening" or "with versus without disorder" are scarce in head-to-head cohorts. Available observational and meta-analytic evidence, coupled with guideline syntheses, supports a stepwise escalation of anticoagulation/defect closure for thrombophilic patients with embolic events. <cite id="82802fc4-1">Guidelines summarize observational evidence of lower recurrent-stroke risk after PFO closure in thrombophilia and recommend PFO closure plus long-term anticoagulation</cite>; and <cite id="82802fc4-0">coinheritance of PFO with thrombophilic mutations increases stroke risk versus controls</cite>.

- Counseling points:
