- Start with a multimodal pathway that pairs rapid local control for symptomatic disease (surgery/radiosurgery/radiation) with an appropriate systemic backbone dictated by histology/genotype; aim for SRS-first regimens to preserve neurocognition when feasible (1–4 lesions), WBRT when multifocal or multiple lesions, and integrate PCI in resected melanoma BM to reduce intracranial failure after durable systemic control. <cite id="cae124ad-5">SRS alone preferred for 1–4 lesions to protect cognition.</cite> <cite id="04e53b13-1">Systemic immunotherapy extends survival in metastatic melanoma and brain metastases.</cite> <cite id="04e53b13-8">Dual ICI combinations are recommended for melanoma BMs.</cite>
- In metastatic melanoma with limited lesions and good systemic control, consider concurrent PD-1 (or dual ICI) and SRS for optimal local-intracranial synergy; in NSCLC with targetable drivers, combine EGFR/ALK TKIs with WBRT/SBRT and consider integrating PD-1-based ICI where BBB penetration and biomarkers justify it. <cite id="3c903388-1">Combining dual ICBI with SRS plus targeted therapy can improve survival and control in NSCLC BM.</cite> <cite id="04e53b13-2">PD‑1 therapy and SRS are complementary in melanoma/NSCLC BMs, with strong local control data.</cite>
- Use delayed SRS when systemic immunotherapy controls intracranial disease to minimize neurocognitive toxicity; switch to local therapy if disease progresses or lesions are symptomatic. <cite id="3c903388-2">Deferred SRS was associated with higher 12‑month PFS with nivolumab versus sequential ipilimumab, with similar OS, supporting strategy flexibility based on toxicity and control.</cite>
- Expect robust local control with radiosurgery and immunotherapy combinations but balance with IRIS risk and neurocognitive monitoring; involve neuro-oncology, radiation oncology, neurosurgery, and medical oncology early to individualize sequencing. <cite id="3c903388-4">Concurrent SRS and dual ICI achieved durable intracranial control with low grade ≥3 toxicity in real-world practice.</cite> <cite id="cae124ad-1">Multimodal, patient-centered coordination is essential across surgical, radiation, and systemic modalities.</cite>

Summary
Assessing abnormal radiotracer uptake for infectious disease studies uses a standardized, multimodal workflow: careful patient selection and tracer choice; high‑quality acquisition with CT/SPECT fusion; dual-reader interpretation using both qualitative localization and quantitative metrics; validation against clinical outcomes; and final reporting framed by clinical context with attention to physiologic mimics and measurement pitfalls. <cite id="c09e1031-3">Procedures standards emphasize calibrated FDG PET acquisition and interpretation, quantitative definitions, and clinical correlation</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-2">Comprehensive reviews map patient selection to integrated strategies for infection imaging</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-9">Guidelines for cardiovascular infections specify where PET/CT and SPECT/CT add value and how to interpret uptake in infection versus noninfectious inflammation</cite>.

1) Pre-imaging selection, tracer, and acquisition standards
- Tracer selection depends on disease, body region, and background physiology. FDG PET/CT is widely used because infection/inflammation elevate glucose metabolism; leukocyte-labeled white blood cell (WBC) tracers (99mTc or 111In) and gallium‑67 are preferred for specific infections (e.g., cardiac, bone, soft-tissue), especially when infection is suspected but occult. <cite id="c09e1031-5">FDG PET/CT is an established tool across infectious applications</cite> <cite id="539c62f5-0">Leukocytes can be radiolabeled with 99mTc or 111In, with protocol-dependent imaging windows and target organs</cite> <cite id="539c62f5-1">67Ga or 111In-labeled leukocyte scintigraphy with SPECT/CT improves localization over planar imaging</cite>.
- Acquisition standards include dual-modality fusion (CT or SPECT/CT), proper attenuation correction, consistent timing relative to tracer pharmacokinetics, and standardized SUV calibration and shimming. <cite id="c09e1031-8">IAEA SOPs detail adult FDG PET/CT scanning and quantitation, stressing calibration, injected dose, and timing</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-4">SUV measurement relies on device calibration and standardized acquisition; these factors affect quantitation accuracy</cite>.
- Protocols for leukocyte tracers specify timing and blood counts. <cite id="539c62f5-9">For example, indium-111 WBC imaging may include an early chest scan at 6 hours with radiopharmacy requirements on WBC count to ensure labeling yield</cite> <cite id="539c62f5-6">The study demonstrates labeled WBC distribution at serial times to detect focal sequestration sites of infection/inflammation</cite>.

2) Qualitative and quantitative interpretation frameworks
- Qualitative evaluation: localizes abnormal uptake on fused CT, distinguishes focal from diffuse patterns, and correlates intensity with clinical signs. <cite id="c09e1031-2">Reviews advocate integrated strategy—fused hybrid imaging to match tracer uptake to anatomic lesions and clinical context</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-7">Society guidance frames cardiovascular infection imaging in a multimodality algorithm that uses PET/CT and leukocyte SPECT/CT for sites with high specificity of uptake</cite>.
- Quantitative evaluation: uses SUV and volumetric metrics to report absolute uptake and lesion burden; thresholds and ratios can flag abnormality. <cite id="b8d007fe-3">FDG uptake is conventionally quantified with semi‑quantitative SUV, most often SUVmax, despite recognized limitations</cite>. <cite id="c09e1031-3">Guideline standards define SUV methodology and the need for accurate calibration to support reproducible quantitation</cite>. <cite id="b8d007fe-6">Volume‑based metrics—metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and lesion/total lymph node metabolic length (LTL) add lesion‑level quantitation that complements SUVmax</cite>. <cite id="b8d007fe-5">Texture analysis and radiomics can further characterize uptake heterogeneity to enhance differential diagnosis</cite>. <cite id="b8d007fe-2">These quantitative descriptors can be combined with clinical features to improve diagnostic classification</cite>.
- Key determinants of quantitative accuracy must be controlled or reported: injected dose, body weight, blood glucose, device calibration, reconstruction, partial volume effects, and shimming. <cite id="b8d007fe-7">A systematic review details factors that affect SUV accuracy and provides recommendations to minimize errors across serial studies</cite>. <cite id="c09e1031-3">Procedural standards require attention to device calibration and standardized acquisition to ensure reliable SUV interpretation</cite>.

3) Reader-based evaluation, validation, and decision analytics
- Dual-reader interpretation with structured templates reduces variability and improves detection of abnormal uptake. <cite id="c09e1031-3">EANM/SNMMI FDG standards emphasize standardized reporting and recommendation workflows for hybrid studies</cite>. <cite id="c09e1031-7">ASNC/IDCA guidance operationalizes reading and reporting for cardiovascular infections across tracers</cite>.
- Reader studies often estimate test accuracy (sensitivity, specificity) and decision metrics (PPV/NPV, LR) using ROC or RROC analyses in infectious indications. <cite id="c09e1031-2">Infection imaging reviews recommend ROC‑based comparison of tracers/techniques and emphasize that clinical integration is essential for positive/negative predictive interpretation</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-4">Clinical reviews of leukocyte imaging show that when echo or clinical findings are inconclusive, leukocyte SPECT/CT changes diagnostic yield, illustrating PPV/NPV‑driven utility</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-7">99mTc HMPAO leukocyte SPECT/CT has been evaluated as adjunctive to nuclear cardiac stress to improve detection of endocarditis, quantifying incremental yield in ROC‑like settings</cite>.
- Coverage and appropriateness criteria translate accuracy into patient‑level benefit. <cite id="c09e1031-1">A CMS LCD for PET in inflammation and infection sets criteria for medical necessity based on clinical scenarios where PET improves diagnostic certainty over conventional testing</cite>.

4) Tracer‑ and modality‑specific evaluation practices
A) FDG PET/CT for infection
- Clinical questions: differentiate active infection from granuloma/tumor, assess osteomyelitis or prosthetic joint infection, guide surgery/treatment. <cite id="c09e1031-5">Overviews catalog FDG PET/CT applications across infectious diseases</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-6">ASNC/IDCA provides disease‑focused guidance for cardiovascular infection</cite>.
- Readout: focal increased FDG uptake in infected/inflamed tissue versus physiological uptake (mediastinal, hepatic, renal, gastrointestinal) or fibrosis. Quantitative thresholds are relative, so patterns and SUV trends across time (pre/post) matter alongside clinical course. <cite id="b8d007fe-3">SUVmax is common but limited by partial volume and physiological background; combining SUV with spatial context and MTV improves specificity</cite>. <cite id="c09e1031-3">Guidelines recommend calibrated SUV and lesion‑based metrics in clinical context to mitigate physiological mimicry</cite>.
- Image quality: CT fusion localizes uptake; attenuation correction reduces misclassification; shimming harmonizes images across the body. <cite id="c09e1031-8">Standardized FDG PET/CT SOPs emphasize adult‑specific scanning, attenuation correction, and calibration for reliable quantitation in infection/inflammation</cite>.
- Decision utility: in indeterminate febrile illness or hidden sources (PJI, osteomyelitis), abnormal focal uptake raises infection likelihood and can alter management; persistence or increase on follow‑up indicates active or progressing infection. <cite id="c09e1031-7">Guidance documents show PET/CT and leukocyte tracers add value in specific high‑yield scenarios (e.g., endocarditis, musculoskeletal infection)</cite>.

B) Leukocyte radiotracer imaging (99mTc WBC, 111In WBC, 67Ga) and SPECT/CT
- Technique: autologous WBC labeling and serial imaging detect sequestrated leukocytes at infection/inflammation foci; gallium accumulates in areas of active inflammation/infection with skeletal tropism. <cite id="539c62f5-0">99mTc and 111In are the principal isotopes for leukocyte labeling with differing imaging windows and counts of interest</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-6">Indium‑111 WBC scintigraphy visualizes distribution and trapping of labeled leukocytes to localize infection</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-1">SPECT/CT improves spatial localization for 67Ga or 111In‑labeled leukocyte studies over planar imaging</cite>.
- Evaluation: search for focal “cold‑hot” trapping on early/late views; compare with clinical and anatomic correlation (e.g., chest pain with a normal ECG may be adjudicated with leukocyte imaging). <cite id="539c62f5-7">99mTc HMPAO leukocyte imaging with SPECT/CT is beneficial when echocardiographic findings are inconclusive for endocarditis</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-4">Clinical decision rules use leukocyte imaging to raise or lower disease probability when initial tests are equivocal</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-5">Gallium exams may be used when bone scans are inconclusive or show cold defects, with increased activity in inflammatory conditions</cite>.
- Practical constraints: WBC thresholds for labeling, early chest imaging windows, and counts must be met; low WBC or antibiotic use may reduce yield. <cite id="539c62f5-9">Protocols specify minimum WBC counts (e.g., 5,000/mL) and early imaging for chest infections, affecting study interpretation</cite>.

C) Comparative evaluation across tracers
- Choice of tracer affects sensitivity/specificity and anatomic coverage. FDG is broad‑body but confounded by physiological uptake; leukocyte tracers and gallium home in on leukocyte‑mediated inflammation with higher anatomic specificity yet may be less sensitive in non‑inflamed infections. <cite id="c09e1031-2">Reviews discuss FDG’s broad utility versus leukocyte/gallium for localization, with integrated interpretation depending on patient presentation</cite>. <cite id="539c62f5-1">SPECT/CT for leukocyte tracers improves lesion localization and reduces nondiagnostic studies</cite>.
- Reader studies and ROC analyses across centers show incremental diagnostic yield of FDG PET/CT (and leukocyte modalities) over conventional imaging in indeterminate infection and can alter management or reduce need for invasive procedures. <cite id="c09e1031-1">Coverage decisions are based on demonstrable diagnostic value in inflammation/infection; studies supporting LR and PPV/NPV underpin such policies</cite>.

5) Managing physiologic mimics and false positives
- Physiologic uptake (mediastinal, hepatobiliary, renal, gastrointestinal) can mimic infection; careful CT fusion, attenuation correction, and shimming reduce misattribution. SUV thresholds alone are insufficient; pattern, physiologic knowledge, and longitudinal changes are critical. <cite id="b8d007fe-3">SUVmax is susceptible to partial volume and background uptake; clinicians often combine SUV with qualitative localization and clinical context to avoid false calls</cite> <cite id="b8d007fe-7">Known factors influencing SUV accuracy—device calibration, injected dose, body weight, blood glucose—must be controlled to reduce false positives</cite>.
- In leukocyte imaging, physiologic trafficking is expected; focal trapping with clinical correlation defines true infection. <cite id="539c62f5-6">The leukocyte study reflects distribution and sequestration; distribution pattern and site-specific findings guide interpretation</cite>.

6) Reporting and clinical integration
- Structured reports include: clinical question; method (tracer, protocol); imaging findings with localization, intensity, and quantitative metrics (SUVmax/MTV/LTL) where applicable; comparison to prior studies; and likelihood ratios/management implications. <cite id="c09e1031-3">FDG hybrid procedure standards promote recommendation‑based reporting that ties PET findings to clinical action</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-7">Cardiovascular infection guidance emphasizes multimodality reporting to inform antibiotic therapy and surgery</cite>.
- Decision integration: positive results increase posttest probability of infection and may trigger biopsy or targeted therapy; negative results reduce probability if disease is indolent or early; follow‑up with serial PET/CT can monitor response by tracking SUV or MTV dynamics. <cite id="b8d007fe-6">Volumetric and metabolic metrics can track change over time to confirm infection activity or response to therapy</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-3">Guidelines recommend serial FDG PET/CT for monitoring when infection activity is suspected based on initial findings</cite>.

Practical workflow to detect abnormal uptake
1) Select tracer and protocol by indication (FDG for broad infection/inflammation; leukocyte/gallium for localized, leukocyte‑mediated disease).
2) Acquire calibrated, attenuation-corrected hybrid images; ensure consistent timing and counts.
3) Localize lesions on CT; record qualitative pattern and intensity; compute SUVmax with ROI placement and report MTV/LTL when meaningful; add texture/radiomics as needed.
4) Validate against clinical findings using ROC/reader studies where available; compute PPV/NPV within the patient cohort; document LR for pretest–posttest updating.
5) Integrate with labs and other imaging; differentiate physiologic uptake; schedule follow‑up when disease trajectory is uncertain.
6) Report with structured recommendations to your clinician, highlighting sites of abnormal uptake, quantitative benchmarks, and management implications.

Where to look and how to avoid pitfalls
- Use CT fusion to tie uptake to anatomy; correct for attenuation and image harmonization; record blood glucose, WBC, and device calibration to contextualize SUV. <cite id="c09e1031-8">SOPs emphasize attenuation correction and calibration</cite> <cite id="b8d007fe-7">Systematic factors affecting SUV should be reported when interpreting SUV thresholds</cite>.
- In FDG studies, mark physiological backgrounds (mediastinal/renal) to avoid misclassification; in leukocyte studies, note early/late trapping and compare to clinical suspicion. <cite id="b8d007fe-3">SUVmax has well‑known limitations; qualitative context is essential</cite> <cite id="539c62f5-6">Leukocyte uptake patterns distinguish infection/inflammation by sequestration</cite>.
- Choose tracers on clinical scenario, remember coverage criteria, and align study design to measurable decision impact in your population. <cite id="c09e1031-1">LCDS emphasize appropriate clinical use with documented utility</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-2">Integrated strategies improve localization and diagnostic precision across modalities</cite>.

Bottom line
Abnormal radiotracer uptake in infectious-disease imaging is evaluated through standardized acquisition and quantitation (calibrated SUV, MTV/LTL), paired with qualitative anatomical localization, reader‑driven ROC‑style validation against clinical outcomes, and tracer‑ and modality‑specific interpretation that distinguishes infection from physiologic mimics. These frameworks are operationalized by society procedures and reviews and translated into diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations through careful clinical integration. <cite id="c09e1031-3">Procedural standards and EANM/SNMMI guidance underpin FDG PET/CT interpretation and reporting</cite> <cite id="c09e1031-2">A comprehensive roadmap details patient selection to integrated interpretation strategies</cite> <cite id="539c62f5-1">SPECT/CT improves localization for leukocyte/gallium studies</cite> <cite id="b8d007fe-7">Control for factors influencing SUV accuracy to maintain reliable thresholds</cite>.

Overview

High-accuracy delineation of tumor extent is critical in head and neck cancer (HNC) because target volumes (GTV, CTV/PTV) define dose coverage to the entire neoplasm and risk regions, while normal-tissue sparing governs toxicity and quality of life. - PET-CT/PET-MRI for metabolic GTV/CTV: PET-guided target delineation improves concordance with active metabolic tumor burden. Head-to-head studies show PET/CT–derived GTVs correlate better with histologic tumor burden than CT alone and capture non-enhancing microscopic spread along lymphovascular pathways; hybrid PET/MRI further unifies soft-tissue and metabolic delineation for more biologically accurate GTVs. - Risk-adapted PTV margins guided by PET: Higher-resolution PET-informed GTVs and metabolic maps allow tailoring CTV/PTV margins to actual tumor risk rather than uniform shells, which can substantially lower doses to swallowing muscles, salivary glands, and airway surfaces while retaining tumor control. Summary
Steroid synthesis inhibitors used for Cushingoid conditions (e.g., ketoconazole, metyrapone, etomidate, dexamethasone, and 11β‑methylprednisolone/deflazacort) directly modify adrenal steroidogenesis and/or pharmacologically antagonize the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, while many “steroid‑like” drugs share enough molecular similarity with cortisol to spuriously elevate immunoassay readings. Using interference‑free (e.g., LC–MS/MS; targeted immunoassays with specificity panels) cortisol measurements is therefore essential to avoid misclassification, inappropriate therapy changes, and dosing errors in clinically treated patients. <cite id="041082f5-0">Compounds that are structurally similar to cortisol can produce cross‑reactivity in steroid hormone immunoassays, which underlies assay overestimation when endogenous or exogenous corticosteroids are present</cite> <cite id="041082f5-2">This cross‑reactivity and antibody affinity limitations can yield overestimation of total serum and salivary cortisol in clinical assays</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-0">Cross‑reactivity with endogenous steroids can lead to grossly inaccurate immunoassay results in saliva and urine</cite>.

Why interference matters when using steroid synthesis inhibitors
- Shared structure triggers immunoassay cross‑reactivity. Immunoassay antibodies frequently cross‑react with closely related corticosteroids (cortisone, dexamethasone, prednisone/prednisolone, 6‑methylprednisolone, 11‑deoxycortisol), producing falsely elevated “cortisol” levels; specificity varies by assay and reagent lot. <cite id="041082f5-0">Immunoassay cross‑reactivity is driven by structural similarity to cortisol</cite> <cite id="041082f5-9">Some cortisol assays have negligible cross‑reactivity with dexamethasone and low cross‑reactivity with a few glucocorticoids, underscoring assay‑dependent behavior</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-6">Cortisone is abundant in saliva and can cross‑react with salivary cortisol immunoassays</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-2">Specific cross‑reactivity studies document how various glucocorticoids perturb cortisol immunoassays</cite>.
- Drug‑induced changes in the adrenal steroidome distort endogenous profiles. Inhibitors of steroidogenesis (e.g., ketoconazole, metyrapone, etomidate) shift precursor/product ratios and can markedly reduce urinary cortisol excretion while elevating metabolites of precursors; these shifts interfere with immunoassays for urinary free cortisol. <cite id="35d6c442-1">Ketoconazole and metyrapone reduce urinary steroid metabolites and alter urinary free cortisol immunoassay reliability in Cushing syndrome</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-6">During ketoconazole treatment, cross‑reactivity among transformed steroids degrades urinary free cortisol immunoassay reliability</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">In patients taking metyrapone, LC–MS/MS versus immunoassay differences in serum cortisol correlate with metyrapone dose and with serum 11‑deoxycortisol, reflecting conversion to 11‑oxo‑17‑keto compounds</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-0">24‑h urinary free cortisol remains the workhorse follow‑up test in Cushing syndrome precisely because it reflects net suppression of total cortisol output and downstream metabolites</cite>.
- Exogenous/“agonist” effects can mask suppression. Full‑dose dexamethasone suppresses ACTH and lowers cortisol and cortisone; however, it also potentiates test suppression and can interact with immunoassay cross‑reactivity patterns for salivary/serum cortisol. <cite id="a22a6bc5-5">Salivary cortisol decreases more profoundly than plasma cortisol or ACTH with escalating dexamethasone doses</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-3">Dexamethasone is a potent ACTH suppressor; paradoxically, in some assays it does not cross‑react with cortisol, yet it still alters endocrine milieu and reference interpretability</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-1">Dexamethasone suppression testing relies on reliable decreases in cortisol; assay matrix and cross‑reactivity can undermine salivary test reliability</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-9">Higher‑dose dexamethasone tests with urinary free cortisol offer superior suppression detection than low‑dose regimens</cite>.
- Clinical consequences if ignored. Over‑ or under‑estimation of cortisol by immunoassays during inhibitor therapy can lead to misdiagnosis of disease activity, premature therapy withdrawal, unnecessary dose increases, or persistence of overtreatment without physiologic confirmation. <cite id="a22a6bc5-0">Immunoassay cross‑reactivity can cause grossly inaccurate salivary and urinary cortisol results, compromising diagnostic decisions</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-1">Reduced urinary metabolite patterns with ketoconazole/metyrapone can be misinterpreted by immunoassay, risking wrong follow‑up actions</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">Dose‑dependent LC–MS/MS–immunoassay differences during metyrapone therapy confirm that single‑assay readings may not reflect true physiology</cite> <cite id="041082f5-2">Overestimation of serum and salivary cortisol via cross‑reactive endogenous steroids can drive inappropriate clinical management</cite>.

Drug‑specific mechanisms and measurement implications
- Metyrapone (11β‑hydroxylase inhibitor). By blocking cortisol → cortisone conversion, metyrapone increases 11‑deoxycortisol/cortisol intermediates and lowers total cortisol; immunoassays sensitive to 17‑oxo‑ steroid cross‑reactivity will overestimate “cortisol” and fail to recognize true suppression. Dose of metyrapone correlates with LC–MS/MS–immunoassay differences, reflecting the biochemical shift. <cite id="35d6c442-2">Metyrapone reduces serum cortisol by inhibiting adrenal 11β‑hydroxylation, forming the basis for its medical management of Cushing’s syndrome</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">Among patients on metyrapone, LC–MS/MS versus immunoassay differences in serum cortisol increase with metyrapone dose and with serum 11‑deoxycortisol</cite>.
- Ketoconazole (multiple CYP enzyme inhibition). Blocks several enzymes of adrenal steroidogenesis, decreasing circulating cortisol and shifting urinary metabolite patterns; these shifts impair standard UFC immunoassay reliability due to cross‑reactive metabolites, especially in treated patients enrolled in follow‑up. <cite id="bf06da4a-0">Ketoconazole inhibits several adrenal steroidogenic enzymes, lowering cortisol and potentially testosterone</cite> <cite id="bf06da4a-3">Levoketoconazole (the 2S,4R enantiomer of ketoconazole) potently inhibits cortisol production in adrenocortical cells</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-1">Ketoconazole‑induced reductions in urinary metabolites alter urinary free cortisol immunoassay reliability</cite>.
- Etomidate (17α‑hydroxylase/17,20‑lyase inhibitor; peri‑anesthetic). Temporarily lowers cortisol by blocking late steroidogenesis steps; clinicians often discontinue therapy when clinical Cushingoid features resolve, but assay choice affects whether biochemical “normalization” is detected. <cite id="bf06da4a-6">Etomidate decreases corticosteroid synthesis by reversibly inhibiting 17α‑hydroxylase/17,20‑lyase in the adrenal cortex</cite> <cite id="bf06da4a-8">Adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors including etomidate have variable efficacy and risks and remain used for transient suppression of cortisol production</cite>.
- Dexamethasone (glucocorticoid receptor antagonist/agonist; suppression testing and therapy). Strongly suppresses ACTH and lowers cortisol/cortisone; salivary cortisol suppression is profound and dose‑dependent. Clinically, these physiologic alterations must be distinguished from endogenous HPA suppression, and cross‑reactivity in salivary/serum assays must be considered. <cite id="a22a6bc5-5">Salivary cortisol is markedly and dose‑dependently suppressed by dexamethasone compared with plasma ACTH/cortisol</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-3">As a potent ACTH suppressor, dexamethasone’s lack of cross‑reactivity with cortisol contrasts with the need to interpret its biochemical suppression correctly</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-6">Salivary assays are susceptible to matrix and cortisone cross‑reactivity when evaluating patients on exogenous corticosteroids</cite>.
- 11β‑methylprednisolone/deflazacort (synthetic glucocorticoids used therapeutically). These cortisol analogs can activate glucocorticoid action and perturb RAAS; their molecular similarity can trigger immunoassay cross‑reactivity and confound “low‑dose” suppression testing, underscoring the need for specificity or drug adjustment. <cite id="041082f5-1">Glucocorticoid cross‑reactivity is a general mechanism that can elevate cortisol immunoassays regardless of source</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-7">False positives in low‑dose dexamethasone suppression testing can arise when glucocorticoid receptor antagonism is blunted by co‑therapies or when assays are not sensitive to suppression patterns</cite>.

Clinical pitfalls and consequences
- Overestimation during therapy can falsely suggest “active Cushingoid disease,” leading to continued or escalated inhibitor therapy despite physiologic suppression from the drug itself; salivary/serum cortisol patterns during dexamethasone can be misinterpreted without recognizing dose‑related suppression. <cite id="a22a6bc5-1">Salivary cortisol reference intervals and test principles may not account for exogenous glucocorticoid effects, yielding unreliable results and misdiagnosis</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-5">Dexamethasone causes salivary cortisol to fall more than plasma cortisol/ACTH, a pattern clinicians must recognize to avoid over‑diagnosis</cite>.
- Underestimation or masking can miss true pathologic hypercortisolism if assays lack specificity for particular metabolites or fail to capture precursor shifts, particularly during ketoconazole/metyrapone when endogenous conversion patterns change. <cite id="35d6c442-1">Drug‑induced metabolite reductions can mislead urinary free cortisol immunoassays, risking under‑detection of disease activity</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">Correlation of LC–MS/MS vs immunoassay differences with metyrapone dose and 11‑deoxycortisol highlights the need to avoid single‑assay misinterpretation</cite>.
- Assay‑specific differences affect clinical decisions in follow‑up: 24‑h urinary free cortisol remains a sensitive functional test, but its accuracy depends on the assay’s cross‑reactivity panel. <cite id="35d6c442-0">24‑h urinary free cortisol is the most used test for follow‑up in Cushing syndrome because it integrates endocrine suppression</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-6">Adverse cross‑reactivity in treated patients compromises immunoassay reliability for UFC</cite>.
- Confronting interference directly improves outcomes: replacing immunoassays with LC–MS/MS or using immunoassays designed to exclude glucocorticoid cross‑reactivity reduces false positives/negatives and guides appropriate therapy adjustment. <cite id="041082f5-6">Reviews outline common immunoassay interferences with hormones and practical solutions to detect/eliminate them in clinical practice</cite> <cite id="041082f5-9">Selection of assays with low cross‑reactivity to dexamethasone/prednisolone improves cortisol measurement accuracy during glucocorticoid therapy</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-5">Comparative studies show LC–MS/MS provides cortisol measurements less confounded than immunoassays in patients with Cushing’s syndrome</cite> <cite id="bf06da4a-2">Endocrine‑lab reviews emphasize the superiority of mass spectrometry over immunoassay for cortisol measurement in Cushing syndromes</cite>.

What to measure instead: strategies to mitigate interference
- Prefer targeted, interference‑aware methods. Use LC–MS/MS assays with specificity for cortisol or panels that quantify cortisol, cortisone, and dexamethasone/11‑deoxycortisol to detect physiologic shifts during inhibitor therapy and concurrent glucocorticoid exposure. <cite id="35d6c442-4">Simultaneous measurement of cortisol and dexamethasone improves diagnostic performance of the overnight dexamethasone test; metyrapone‑related differences track with 11‑deoxycortisol and dose</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-8">Cross‑reactivity with 11‑deoxycortisol can be managed by using LC–MS/MS methods designed to resolve interfering metabolites</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-0">Mass spectrometry–based cortisol assays are less affected by cross‑reactivity than immunoassays</cite>.
- Adjust testing to drug effects and suppression patterns. In patients on dexamethasone or other GR antagonists/agonists, prefer salivary cortisol timing to plasma/urine, monitor suppression dose‑response, and consider drug “washout” windows; in patients on steroidogenesis inhibitors, combine UFC with dynamic testing and imaging/other biochemical axes. <cite id="a22a6bc5-5">Salivary cortisol demonstrates a dose‑related, greater suppression than plasma after dexamethasone, guiding test selection and dose interpretation</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-7">Minimize false positives in low‑dose suppression testing by recognizing that expected cortisol decreases may be blunted and by setting appropriate thresholds</cite> <cite id="bf06da4a-0">Because ketoconazole suppresses multiple steroid enzymes, clinicians must coordinate biochemical testing with drug effects on adrenal output</cite>.
- Use multi‑axis, longitudinal strategies. Combine serum ACTH with cortisol; monitor UFC trend lines; add late/early morning free cortisol or salivary profiles; and integrate clinical signs and imaging. Recognize that metyrapone and ketoconazole suppress cortisol but elevate 11‑oxo/17‑keto intermediates—measurements that can normalize with tapering, independent of disease activity. <cite id="35d6c442-2">Metyrapone lowers serum cortisol by blocking 11β‑hydroxylation, which informs management of Cushing’s syndrome</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">Dose‑correlated increases in 11‑deoxycortisol and LC–MS/MS–immunoassay differences highlight the need to interpret intermediate metabolites and longitudinal trends</cite> <cite id="bf06da4a-9">In patients with mild or subclinical Cushing’s treated with ketoconazole or metyrapone, careful longitudinal analysis is required to distinguish genuine remission from drug‑induced suppression</cite>.
- Practical lab policy. Maintain assay logs (lot‑to‑lot cross‑reactivity changes), avoid mixing specimens from different therapies, and institute algorithms to escalate to LC–MS/MS when UFC or salivary measures are near thresholds, or when drugs known to interfere are present. <cite id="041082f5-6">Daily practice faces detectable and variable analytical interferences; detection and elimination strategies include assay selection and validation for interference in routine care</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-3">Matrix and method issues can render salivary testing unreliable if cross‑reactivity is unaccounted for, warranting confirmatory methods or adjustments</cite>.

Key takeaways
- Interference‑free assays are needed because steroid synthesis inhibitors themselves shift steroid profiles and because many exogenous/physiologic corticosteroids cross‑react with immunoassays, producing overestimation or masked suppression that misguides clinical decisions. <cite id="bf06da4a-0">Ketoconazole blocks multiple adrenal enzymes, lowering cortisol and altering steroid metabolite patterns</cite> <cite id="041082f5-1">Structurally similar exogenous corticosteroids cause cross‑reactivity, elevating immunoassay cortisol readings</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-1">These drug‑induced shifts compromise urinary free cortisol immunoassay reliability in treated patients</cite> <cite id="a22a6bc5-5">Dexamethasone exerts profound, dose‑related suppression of salivary cortisol, which must be interpreted with assay specificity</cite>.
- LC–MS/MS and targeted, cross‑reactivity‑aware immunoassays, combined with clinical correlation, prevent misclassification and allow appropriate dose adjustments and timely discontinuation of inhibitors without risking disease flare. <cite id="35d6c442-5">Comparative studies favor mass spectrometry over immunoassay for accurate cortisol measurement in Cushing syndromes</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">Metyrapone therapy shows LC–MS/MS–immunoassay differences that correlate with true biochemical shifts</cite> <cite id="041082f5-6">Reviews provide actionable approaches to detect and eliminate interferences in routine endocrine testing</cite>.

Residual uncertainties and best practices
Physiologic and assay variability can confound interpretation even with “interference‑free” immunoassays. To minimize risk, align testing modality with drug exposure (dexamethasone dosing windows for salivary profiles; UFC plus metabolite panels in metyrapone/ketoconazole), document medications that cross‑react or suppress ACTH, and escalate ambiguous results to LC–MS/MS with simultaneous quantification of cortisol, cortisone, and major glucocorticoid metabolites. <cite id="a22a6bc5-3">Dexamethasone’s potent ACTH suppression and assay‑specific non‑cross‑reactivity illustrate the need to couple biochemical interpretation with clinical pharmacology</cite> <cite id="35d6c442-4">In metyrapone‑treated patients, following LC–MS/MS–immunoassay gaps by dose and 11‑deoxycortisol aids patient‑level decisions</cite> <cite id="041082f5-2">Overestimation by immunoassays in serum and salivary samples underscores the importance of method selection and confirmation in patient care</cite>.

Summary and scope
Across multiple studies in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), adherence to healthier dietary patterns—particularly Mediterranean-style diets and calorie-restricted plans—is associated with reductions in body weight, BMI, and waist circumference, together with improvements in hepatic fat and metabolic features of the metabolic syndrome. <cite id="5b896621-0">High adherence to a Mediterranean diet is linked with amelioration of intrahepatic fat and better metabolic syndrome indices in NAFLD</cite>. <cite id="e072d54a-1">Systematic reviews conclude that Mediterranean diet and calorie restriction can improve NAFLD, with limited data suggesting the Mediterranean pattern is effective</cite>.

Randomized trials and controlled interventions: weight, BMI, and waist
- Calorie-restricted and low-fat dietary interventions produce significant anthropometric improvements. <cite id="5b896621-4">In a randomized controlled trial of a low-fat diet (LFD) in NAFLD, participants showed meaningful reductions in weight, waist circumference, and BMI</cite>. <cite id="e072d54a-8">In personalized, calorie-restricted Mediterranean and low-fat diet programs, after three months participants had significant weight loss (>9%) with improvements in waist circumference, body fat percentage, visceral adiposity index (VAI), and other lipid measures</cite>.
- Mediterranean diet programs designed for weight loss show appreciable short-term change, though sometimes less than matched low-fat or hypocaloric diets. <cite id="e072d54a-4">A randomized trial comparing calorie-restricted Mediterranean versus low-fat diets showed both reduced liver fat and improved inflammatory/metabolic risk factors; although body weight reductions were often modest (e.g., −1.0 kg MedDiet vs. −2.4 kg LFD over 12 weeks), liver fat reduction was greater, consistent with diet-driven hepatic and metabolic effects complementing weight loss</cite>. <cite id="b179c42a-5">Trial summaries note that the Mediterranean diet can reduce hepatic fat and improve hepatic insulin sensitivity even without weight loss, indicating that diet composition can alter body composition beyond scale weight</cite>.
- Practical implementation: NAFLD diet programs explicitly target weight loss and build adherence support. <cite id="da19ae72-7">Participants assigned to Mediterranean or low-fat arms engaged in group sessions aimed at weight loss and increasing adherence to the Mediterranean pattern</cite>. <cite id="e072d54a-4">After three months across calorie-restricted diets, substantial reductions in weight, waist, and body fat were observed alongside improvements in cardiometabolic risk markers</cite>.

Dose–response with adherence: “healthy diet” intensity and central adiposity
- Higher adherence aligns with better metabolic/visceral outcomes even when total weight loss is modest. <cite id="5b896621-2">In NAFLD comparing ad libitum Mediterranean versus low-fat diet, the Mediterranean group improved serum adiponectin without significant weight change, demonstrating that diet-induced anti-inflammatory and adiposity redistribution effects can occur independently of large scale weight loss</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-8">Randomized trials of Mediterranean versus low-fat diets show meaningful reductions in weight, waist, and BMI under interventions that are “not sufficiently powered for these secondary endpoints,” underscoring that anthropometric improvements are realistic but moderate in small to medium-sized RCTs</cite>.
- Population-level adherence and central obesity: cross-sectional analyses in NAFLD cohorts link better adherence to healthier profiles. <cite id="5b896621-0">High Mediterranean diet adherence in NAFLD is associated with improved intrahepatic fat and better metabolic syndrome features (including central adiposity and insulin sensitivity)</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-6">Observational work in primary care NAFLD underscores that lower Mediterranean diet scores are linked with higher NAFLD prevalence and metabolic risk, consistent with protective effects concentrated at higher adherence levels</cite>.
- Region-specific evidence confirms the pattern. <cite id="da19ae72-2">Greater Mediterranean diet adherence among women with fatty liver and type 2 diabetes in Asia is associated with greater improvement in hepatic fat and lipid profiles, reinforcing that adherence intensity corresponds to organ and metabolic benefits even as weight and BMI change</cite>.

Mechanisms: diet-driven adiposity redistribution and NAFLD biology
- Diet quality can reduce visceral and waist adiposity and liver fat even with stable or small total weight change. <cite id="9b896621-2">Mediterranean diet interventions improved adiponectin levels and reduced visceral fat in NAFLD without weight loss in one study</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-4">Concurrently, low-fat diet arms achieved meaningful reductions in waist, BMI, and weight, highlighting that dietary fat composition and overall energy balance both matter</cite>.
- Meta-analytic perspectives support a mechanistic shift beyond weight alone. <cite id="e072d54a-1">Systematic review and meta-analysis in Clinical Nutrition conclude Mediterranean and calorie restriction can improve NAFLD; limited data suggest MD may be effective in reducing hepatic fat and improving metabolic risk, consistent with reductions in central adiposity and hepatic steatosis</cite>. <cite id="da19ae72-3">Another systematic review similarly supports the effect of Mediterranean interventions on NAFLD-related outcomes</cite>.

Broader clinical context and comparative guidance
- RCT syntheses and expert summaries converge on Mediterranean diet programs—often calorie-restricted—being effective first-line dietary treatments for NAFLD. <cite id="e072d54a-3">A systematic review and meta-analysis supports current guidelines that dietary interventions, especially Mediterranean-style, are effective for managing NAFLD</cite>. <cite id="da19ae72-7">Group-based programs explicitly target weight loss and adherence to Mediterranean patterns, with demonstrated improvements in visceral adiposity and metabolic risk markers over months</cite>.
- Trials also emphasize that inflammation, lipids, and insulin sensitivity improve with diet, which may parallel and help explain reductions in waist and hepatic fat. <cite id="b179c42a-2">In a randomized MedDiet vs. LFD comparison, both reduced inflammatory markers and liver fat despite modest, sometimes nonsignificant, weight changes, suggesting diet-driven anti-inflammatory and liver-sparing effects</cite>.

Observational and cohort insights in real-world NAFLD
- In clinical cohorts, higher Mediterranean adherence correlates with less NAFLD and better metabolic risk, including lower central obesity. <cite id="5b896621-0">High Mediterranean adherence is associated with improved intrahepatic fat and better metabolic syndrome indices in NAFLD</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-9">Lower adherence is associated with higher prevalence of steatosis, and diet composition beyond weight may drive NAFLD improvement</cite>.
- Ultra-processed/low-adherence patterns relate to cardiometabolic risk and NAFLD burden, complementing the anthropometric improvements from healthier patterns. <cite id="da19ae72-7">Lower Mediterranean adherence predicts higher NAFLD prevalence; diet quality changes influence metabolic syndrome features such as central adiposity</cite>.

Practical implications, magnitudes, and timelines
- What to expect: With structured adherence to Mediterranean or calorie-restricted diets, NAFLD patients commonly experience reductions in weight, BMI, and waist of clinically meaningful magnitudes over months, alongside liver-fat improvement and improved insulin sensitivity and lipids. <cite id="5b896621-4">Three-month LFD yielded meaningful decreases in weight, waist, BMI, and other cardiometabolic risk factors in NAFLD, albeit in a study underpowered for secondary endpoints</cite>. <cite id="9b896621-2">Three months on calorie-restricted Mediterranean programs produced >9% weight loss and improved waist, body fat, and visceral adiposity indices</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-2">Even without large scale changes, adiponectin and visceral fat can improve on Mediterranean diet, demonstrating early metabolic and central adiposity benefits</cite>.
- Importance of adherence: Programs that include group support, education, and monitoring of adherence tend to produce the best anthropometric and liver outcomes. <cite id="da19ae72-7">Mediterranean diet and low-fat arms in trials are delivered with sessions aimed at weight loss and adherence, and participants demonstrate improvements in body composition and metabolic risk markers over months</cite>.
- Nuance around weight vs. risk factors: Diet-led improvements can optimize intrahepatic fat and metabolic syndrome indices—sometimes before or alongside substantial BMI change—underscoring the value of focusing on a Mediterranean pattern even if weight loss plateaus modestly. <cite id="5b896621-2">Mediterranean diet improved liver fat and adiponectin without notable weight loss in NAFLD participants</cite>. <cite id="5b896621-0">Higher Mediterranean adherence improves metabolic syndrome features beyond hepatic fat</cite>.

Caveats and gaps
- Trial sizes often limit precise pooled deltas for BMI and waist across all included studies; many RCTs emphasize hepatic or metabolic endpoints with secondary anthropometrics. <cite id="5b896621-4">A trial noted meaningful reductions in weight, waist, and BMI but lacked power for secondary endpoints, illustrating typical constraints</cite>.
- Real-world, long-term adherence and durable anthropometric change remain variable; diet quality’s protective associations are stronger when paired with behaviors that promote sustained adherence and energy balance. <cite id="5b896621-6">Lower adherence correlates with greater NAFLD prevalence, pointing to the importance of maintaining dietary quality over time</cite>.

Bottom line
- Across randomized trials, meta-analyses, and clinical cohorts, adhering to a Mediterranean or calorie-restricted healthy diet improves NAFLD by reducing body weight, BMI, and waist, and by improving visceral adiposity and metabolic risk—sometimes even when total weight change is modest. <cite id="5b896621-4">Three-month low-fat diet regimens produce meaningful reductions in weight, waist, and BMI in NAFLD</cite>, <cite id="e072d54a-8">calorie-restricted Mediterranean programs achieve >9% weight loss with improved waist and body-fat measures over similar time frames</cite>, and <cite id="5b896621-2">Mediterranean patterns can improve liver fat and adiponectin without weight loss, highlighting diet-driven metabolic and visceral benefits</cite>. <cite id="e072d54a-1">Syntheses conclude that Mediterranean diet and calorie restriction are effective NAFLD interventions with improvements in weight, waist, and liver fat, with emerging evidence that Mediterranean patterns can be effective even without very large weight changes</cite>. The magnitude and durability of anthropometric change are closely tied to dietary adherence and concurrent energy management; maximizing adherence to Mediterranean principles—rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, healthy fats, and modest in energy density—yields the most consistent improvements in BMI, weight, waist circumference, and NAFLD severity. <cite id="5b896621-0">Higher Mediterranean adherence improves intrahepatic fat and metabolic syndrome indices, which include central adiposity and insulin sensitivity</cite>, <cite id="da19ae72-2">greater adherence associates with greater hepatic fat improvement</cite>, and <cite id="da19ae72-7">NAFLD diet programs explicitly targeting weight loss and adherence demonstrably reduce visceral and total adiposity over months</cite>.

# Overview

<cite id="b2265b4b-0">Homocysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid whose blood level is tightly regulated by one‑carbon metabolism; deficiency of B12 or folate disrupts remethylation and betaine pathways, elevating homocysteine and promoting endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular disease</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-1">Because vegetarians and especially vegans obtain fewer B12 and variable folate from plant foods, they are at higher risk of subclinical B12/folate deficiency, which raises homocysteine and is associated with atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease</cite>.

# Mechanisms: How vitamin status manipulates homocysteine metabolism

- Core biochemical cycle. <cite id="502d03ec-0">Homocysteine can be remethylated to methionine using a methyl group from 5‑methyltetrahydrofolate (a folate derivative) or from betaine; methionine is then remethylated to methionine synthase (B12‑dependent) to produce methionine, which reloads folate cycles</cite>. <cite id="502d03ec-4">Impairment of remethylation occurs with dietary folate or vitamin B12 deficiency or functional defects in methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), methionine synthase (MTR), or related enzymes</cite>.

- Alternative routes and cofactors. <cite id="502d03ec-0">Betaine serves as an alternative methyl donor when folate is limiting, but capacity is finite and betaine levels determine overflow to homocysteine</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-4">In folate deficiency, betaine concentrations elevate because remethylation becomes rate‑limiting</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-5">Raising B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) supports transsulfuration via cystathionine beta‑synthase, complementing remethylation; combining folic acid, B6, B12, vitamin E and betaine reduces thrombosis and cardiovascular dysfunction risk in hyperhomocysteinemia</cite>.

- Antioxidant/vascular angle. <cite id="b2265b4b-5">Vitamin E and B2/B6/B12/folate work with betaine to lower homocysteine and reduce vascular oxidative stress, improving endothelial function</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-9">Hyperhomocysteinemia independently increases risk of cardiovascular and central nervous system disorders through effects on folate/choline metabolism and vascular function</cite>.

# Vegetarian diets: why certain vitamins fall short

- B12 scarcity in plant foods. <cite id="13c15bec-7">Vegetarian or vegan diets can cause vitamin B12 deficiency because they contain little or no animal‑source foods, the primary B12 carriers</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Subclinical B12 deficiency in vegans elevates homocysteine, raises stroke and atherosclerosis risk, and increases all‑cause mortality</cite>.

- Folate vs preformed folate. <cite id="13c15bec-2">Serum homocysteine inversely correlates with serum folate, especially among vegetarians and vegans</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-5">Vegans have significantly higher mean plasma homocysteine than omnivores in a well‑matched cohort, reinforcing that folate sufficiency is necessary to keep homocysteine low</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-4">Folate deficiency elevates betaine, pushing homocysteine overflow</cite>.

- B6 and B2 status. <cite id="b2265b4b-1">Deficiency of folate or vitamin B6 can also elevate homocysteine</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-9">Randomized evidence shows that B6 is not universally effective at lowering homocysteine across doses (e.g., mean 16.5 mg showed no significant effect), and folic acid/B12 do reduce levels 5–7%</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-0">Vitamin B12 supplementation produced an additional ~7% homocysteine reduction in randomized trials; high‑dose folic acid and B12 were often effective whereas B6 commonly was not</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-5">B6 acts more downstream via transsulfuration; combining B6/B12/folate with betaine and vitamin E improves vascular outcomes</cite>.

- Population comparisons. <cite id="13c15bec-0">Vegetarians show higher mean homocysteine (≈13.18 µmol/L) and higher hyperhomocysteinemia prevalence (≈29%) versus omnivores (≈10.19 µmol/L; 5%)</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-2">Inverse correlations with folate and B12 persisted when stratified by diet</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-8">Meta‑evidence across countries similarly finds lower B12 and higher homocysteine among vegetarians and vegans</cite>.

# Health risks tied to elevated homocysteine in deficiency contexts

- Endothelial injury and atherosclerosis. <cite id="b2265b4b-0">Elevated homocysteine induces endothelial dysfunction and promotes cardiovascular disease</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Subclinical B12 deficiency associates with greater risk of atherosclerosis, especially stroke, and higher mortality</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-9">Hyperhomocysteinemia is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular and central nervous disorders (e.g., cognitive decline), with mechanistic links to folate/choline metabolism</cite>.

- Mitigation by vitamins. <cite id="b2265b4b-8">Treating hyperhomocysteinemia with folic acid, vitamin B12 and B6 is “extremely successful” in most patients</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-4">A 3‑year trial using folic acid 0.8 mg plus vitamin B12 0.4 mg (and B6 40 mg) lowered homocysteine versus placebo and evaluated stroke/coronary outcomes</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-5">The HOPE‑2 trial specifically tested homocysteine‑lowering vitamins (folic acid and B12) for cardiovascular prevention</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-9">In practice, folic acid/B12 reliably reduce homocysteine whereas B6 effects are inconsistent and often modest outside deficiencies in CBS activity</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-8">Even high‑dose homocysteine‑lowering strategies have shown up to 30% reductions in extreme elevations and highlight antioxidant contributions to vascular protection</cite>.

# How vegetarian mechanisms contribute to elevated homocysteine

- Reduced B12 intake and absorption. <cite id="13c15bec-7">B12 is largely absent from plant foods, requiring active absorption from animal products; vegans therefore face higher B12 deficiency risk</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Mild B12 deficiency in vegans elevates homocysteine into the “moderately increased” range (>10 µmol/L), which raises CVD risk and is best kept below 10 µmol/L with supplementation</cite>.

- Folate status and genetics. <cite id="502d03ec-4">Dietary folate deficiency slows remethylation and drives homocysteine accumulation</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-2">Lower serum folate in vegetarians correlates inversely with higher homocysteine</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Genetic variants affecting methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase or methionine synthase further increase vulnerability to homocysteine elevation on low‑B12/low‑folate diets</cite>.

- Overreliance on betaine pathway. <cite id="502d03ec-0">When folate/B12 are limiting, the betaine‑mediated remethylation pathway must compensate; if capacity is exceeded, homocysteine rises</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-4">In folate deficiency, betaine levels elevate as homocysteine backs up</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-7">Supplementing with betaine plus B6/B12/folate effectively lowers elevated homocysteine in several studies</cite>.

- B6/B2/E contributions. <cite id="b2265b4b-1">B6 deficiency can elevate homocysteine</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-5">Adequate B6 supports cystathionine beta‑synthase and, when combined with antioxidant nutrients (B2, E) and methyl donors (folate, B12, betaine), reduces thrombotic and cardiovascular risk</cite>.

# Quantitative examples in vegetarian cohorts

- Group‑level differences. <cite id="13c15bec-0">Vegetarians had higher mean homocysteine (~13.2 µmol/L) than omnivores (~10.2 µmol/L), with much higher hyperhomocysteinemia rates (29% vs 5%)</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-5">Even in well‑planned vegans, mean plasma homocysteine can exceed omnivores if B12/folate are not supplemented</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-8">Across multiple studies, vegetarians and vegans consistently show lower B12 with higher homocysteine than omnivores</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-1">Vegans often meet recommended B12 with fortified foods (e.g., 5.6 µg/day) but must monitor levels, as homocysteine should be kept <10 µmol/L to minimize CVD risk</cite>.

# Health consequences and pathways

- Cardiovascular. <cite id="b2265b4b-0">Homocysteine promotes endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle injury, and thrombosis, linking deficiency‑driven elevations to atherosclerosis and events</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Mild B12 deficiency associates with increased stroke/atherosclerosis risk in vegans</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-9">Independent risk status supports aggressive correction of B12/folate/B6 and antioxidant strategies</cite>.

- Neurological and thrombotic. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Subclinical B12 deficiency in vegans elevates risk of cognitive decline</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-5">Combined B6/B12/folate, vitamin E, and betaine reduce thrombosis risk and cardiovascular dysfunction in hyperhomocysteinemia</cite>.

# Prevention and treatment: tailoring to vegetarian diets

- Dietary strategies. <cite id="13c15bec-2">Ensuring adequate folate through fortified foods/leafy greens and, in vegans, B12‑fortified products helps lower homocysteine; inverse relationships between folate and homocysteine are strongest in vegetarians</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Vegans should follow B12 recommendations and keep levels sufficient to maintain homocysteine below ~10 µmol/L; maintaining levels below 10 µmol/L minimizes CVD risk</cite>.

- Supplementation. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-0">Randomized data show folic acid and B12 reliably lower homocysteine by 5–7% per unit dose, with B6 sometimes ineffective</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-9">Pragmatically, a B‑complex with folic acid and B12 is effective; vitamin E and betaine can be added for vascular benefit when homocysteine is elevated</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-4">Trials pairing folic acid 0.8 mg with B12 0.4 mg and B6 40 mg demonstrate homocysteine lowering and informed cardiovascular risk reduction</cite>. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-8">Very high homocysteine can drop ~30% with aggressive dosing/folate plus antioxidant strategies, underscoring synergistic methyl donor–antioxidant effects</cite>.

- Monitoring and genetics. <cite id="502d03ec-4">Defects in MTR, MTRR, or MTHFR increase susceptibility to homocysteine elevation with folate/B12 insufficiency and may warrant higher or earlier supplementation</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">MTR/MTRR polymorphisms interact with B12 methylation and should be considered if homocysteine remains elevated on standard doses</cite>.

# Practical guidance and uncertainties

- What to measure. <cite id="b2265b4b-2">Homocysteine elevation is common in vegans if B12 is marginal; keeping B12 ≥200–300 pmol/L (normal range varies) and homocysteine <10 µmol/L is a practical target</cite>. <cite id="13c15bec-2">Higher folate (≥40–60 nmol/L) correlates with lower homocysteine in vegetarians</cite>.

- Where evidence is thin. <cite id="5e4aa4aa-9">While folic acid/B12 reliably lower homocysteine, B6’s efficacy is inconsistent across trials and populations; gene‑diet interactions (MTHFR/CBS/MTR/MTRR) may explain variability but require individualized dosing</cite>. <cite id="b2265b4b-1">Population risk is clear, but translating this into a precise cardiovascular risk reduction per µmol/L lowering depends on baseline risk and comorbidities</cite>.

In summary, vegetarian diets can drive elevated homocysteine through limited B12 intake and variable folate availability, crowding the betaine remethylation pathway and increasing oxidative stress, which together promote endothelial dysfunction and vascular risk; targeted vitamin fortification and supplementation of folate, B12, and B6—with betaine and antioxidants when indicated—effectively lowers homocysteine and mitigates associated risks in vegans and vegetarians <cite id="b2265b4b-0">Homocysteine depends on B12/folate</cite><cite id="502d03ec-0">Remethylation uses folate/B12 or betaine</cite><cite id="13c15bec-0">Vegetarians have higher homocysteine</cite><cite id="b2265b4b-2">Vegan B12 deficiency raises homocysteine and CVD risk</cite><cite id="5e4aa4aa-0">Folic acid/B12 lower homocysteine</cite><cite id="5e4aa4aa-9">Practical B‑complex/folate regimens are effective</cite>.

Overview and scope
Across randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, herbal weight-loss extracts typically produce small absolute weight losses (on average a few kilograms over 8–16 weeks), with clinical significance being mixed and often limited to modest improvements versus placebo, especially when taken with energy-restricted diets or behavioral counseling. Effects and tolerability vary by the specific phytochemical and dose form. <cite id="58dc1be2-0">Psyllium was repeatedly identified as one of the more effective herbal interventions for weight loss in comparative analyses, illustrating that not all botanicals are equivalent</cite>. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">An aggregate analysis of 54 randomized, placebo-controlled trials across 4331 overweight or obese adults reported that, overall, herbal medicines showed limited effectiveness for weight loss compared with placebo</cite>.

Dose–response and clinical significance by extract

• Garcinia cambogia (hydroxycitric acid, HCA)
- Weight-loss effects by dose:
  - Low-to-moderate standardized doses (e.g., 500 mg three times daily, 1500 mg/day of HCA) have repeatedly shown statistically modest effects that are not clearly clinically significant; some small trials in men found no effect on appetite or weight loss at 500 mg three times daily with diet advice <cite id="71548350-6">A smaller two-week study in men found no effect on appetite or weight loss when participants took 500 mg of HCA three times daily with diet advice</cite>. <cite id="71548350-0">Meta-analyses indicate a statistically significant difference in body weight between HCA and placebo groups overall, but average effects can be small</cite>.
  - Higher daily exposure with split dosing before meals (e.g., around 2400 mg/day) in conjunction with a low-calorie diet has shown greater weight loss versus placebo over weeks to months <cite id="71548350-7">A study using 2400 mg of Garcinia cambogia daily divided and taken before meals noted that active treatment lost more weight from a low-calorie diet than placebo</cite>.
- Clinical significance and safety:
  - Signals of short-term efficacy exist, but data are inconsistent and often limited by small samples and short durations; risk of hepatotoxicity and cognitive or gastrointestinal effects have been reported and warrant careful risk–benefit assessment <cite id="71548350-1">Garcinia-based supplements could show short-term weight loss, but the evidence is not conclusive</cite>. <cite id="71548350-4">Some studies suggest benefits in animals; current human research likely shows probable lack of weight-loss benefit overall</cite>. <cite id="71548350-8">Medscape notes suggested weight-loss and lipid-lowering activities with trials supporting use being limited</cite>.
- Practical implication:
  - When active preparations are used with a calorie-restricted diet, total daily HCA exposure around 1800–2400 mg/day has shown superior weight loss vs placebo in at least one RCT; lower daily doses (≤500–1000 mg) often fail to demonstrate meaningful differences beyond diet or lifestyle alone, and effects are small in absolute terms <cite id="71548350-7">Active treatment lost more weight from a low-calorie diet than placebo at ~2400 mg/day split before meals</cite> <cite id="71548350-6">No effect at 500 mg three times daily on weight loss in men over two weeks with diet advice</cite>.

• Green coffee bean extract (GCBE; chlorogenic acid, CGA)
- Weight-loss effects by dose or CGA content:
  - Meta-analyses identify effective ranges of lower doses when standardized for CGA content: 180–200 mg/day of extract containing 40–45% CGA taken for 4–12 weeks showing reductions in body weight or adiposity indices <cite id="c3a42833-2">Green coffee extract (GCE) at 180–200 mg/day containing 40–45% CGA for 4–12 weeks reduced body weight</cite>.
  - Higher daily CGA exposure around 500 mg/day also shows weight loss versus placebo in pooled analyses, though effects are modest <cite id="c3a42833-0">GBCE with CGA 500 mg/day lowers body weight in meta-analysis</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-4">Meta-analysis similarly found GBCE with CGA 500 mg/day lowers body weight</cite>.
- Clinical significance and context:
  - While multiple small RCTs and meta-analyses show statistically detectable, small-to-moderate weight reductions, effect sizes often translate to marginal clinical significance compared with diet-only changes, and benefits are maximized when extracts are combined with caloric restriction and behavior change <cite id="c3a42833-1">Meta-analysis supports GCE supplementation for improving obesity indices</cite>. <cite id="c3a42833-9">A 2023 systematic review in Systematic Reviews summarized a decreasing trend in body weight with GCBE across RCTs</cite>.
- Practical implication:
  - To achieve meaningful weight loss, use standardized GCBE with known CGA content (e.g., 180–200 mg/day of a 40–45% CGA product yields ~72–90 mg pure CGA; higher-dose regimens around 500 mg/day CGA have shown benefits), alongside diet and lifestyle; however, typical absolute losses remain small and not transformative without energy restriction <cite id="c3a42833-2">180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA for 4–12 weeks reduced body weight</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-0">~500 mg/day CGA lowered body weight in pooled trials</cite>.

• Citrus aurantium (“bitter orange”) and related markers
- Weight-loss effects and dose:
  - Trials commonly use synephrine- or N-methyltyramine-containing standardized bitter orange extracts. Evidence from RCTs indicates modest weight loss or BMI reduction versus placebo in some studies when extracts are used alongside diet/exercise, with effects generally small and inconsistent across preparations. <cite id="58dc1be2-5">A broader 2020 meta-analysis across herbal medicines found insufficient evidence for weight loss overall, consistent with many bitter orange trials showing limited effects</cite>.
  - Clinical significance: Benefits, if any, are typically on the order of a few kilograms over months with added behavioral change; adverse events (notably cardiovascular stimulant-type effects) can limit tolerability at higher doses. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Across 54 RCTs, herbal medicines showed limited effectiveness for weight loss compared with placebo</cite>.
- Practical implication:
  - Dose ranges in trials span 200–600 mg of standardized bitter orange extracts taken premeal; weight loss benefits appear modest relative to calorie restriction alone, and safety screening (e.g., heart rate, BP, contraindications with stimulants) is crucial. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Across RCTs, overall herbal weight-loss efficacy is limited</cite>.

• Irvingia gabonensis (“African mango”) and related phytochemicals
- Weight-loss effects and clinical significance:
  - In systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs, Irvingia gabonensis showed statistically and clinically significant weight loss versus placebo in some included trials, particularly for BMI and waist circumference, when doses were adequate and treatment duration was several weeks to months. <cite id="58dc1be2-2">Statistically and clinically significant weight loss compared to placebo was reported for Irvingia gabonensis in meta-analysis</cite>. <cite id="58dc1be2-8">Across 54 RCTs of herbal weight-loss medicines, clinical benefits were limited overall, but Irvingia was among extracts with positive pooled signals</cite>.
- Practical implication:
  - Typical used doses in trials range from 150 to 400 mg of an extract standardized to irgafrin or other markers, with many positive small-to-moderate effects on weight/BMI; benefits should be interpreted in context of concurrent diet and expectation of modest magnitude. <cite id="58dc1be2-2">Irvingia gabonensis demonstrated significant weight loss versus placebo in pooled RCT analyses</cite>.

Across-herb synthesis: What dosing features matter
- Total daily phytochemical exposure and labeling confounding:
  - Trials that report active ingredient concentration are clearer. For HCA, higher daily exposures (~1800–2400 mg/day) paired with diet restriction yielded superior weight loss versus placebo, whereas labels often advertise 500 mg “HCA” capsules but the actual HCA fraction may be low; such lower-exposure regimens have shown little to no effect. <cite id="71548350-7">~2400 mg/day of Garcinia (split premeals) produced greater loss than placebo with a low-calorie diet</cite> <cite id="71548350-6">500 mg TID for two weeks showed no effect on weight loss with diet advice</cite>.
  - For green coffee, standardizing by CGA content (180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA or ~500 mg/day CGA) correlates with measurable reductions; products that rely on “green coffee” without CGA% on label can be hard to compare. <cite id="c3a42833-2">180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA reduced body weight</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-0">~500 mg/day CGA lowers body weight in pooled trials</cite>.
- Behavioral context:
  - Herbal extracts work best when combined with dietary advice, caloric restriction, and exercise; many trials enroll participants on “advice to reduce diet,” and meta-analyses report that isolated herbal supplementation without behavior change yields small effects that may not be clinically meaningful. <cite id="71548350-7">In a low-calorie diet context, higher-dose HCA produced superior weight loss vs placebo</cite> <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Across many RCTs, herbal agents show limited weight-loss effectiveness compared with placebo overall</cite>.
- Duration and trial quality:
  - Short trials (2–4 weeks) are underpowered for weight change; effects become detectable but still modest at 8–12 weeks. Larger and longer RCTs are needed; inconsistency across small, industry-funded, or heterogeneous-dose trials drives uncertainty. <cite id="58dc1be2-5">A meta-analysis (n≈54 RCTs, 4331 participants) reported insufficient evidence for many herbal medicines overall</cite>.
- Adverse events and clinical risk:
  - Liver injury with Garcinia has been reported, and stimulant-type side effects are possible with bitter orange; clinical significance hinges on risk profiling and exclusion criteria. <cite id="71548350-1">Despite possible short-term efficacy with Garcinia, evidence is inconclusive and safety concerns exist</cite>. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Trials show limited efficacy but acknowledge adverse event profiles across botanical agents</cite>.

How to interpret “clinical significance”
- Magnitude of difference vs placebo:
  - Typical weight-loss deltas with herbal extracts range from ~0.5–2.5 kg over 8–16 weeks when taken with basic diet advice; combinations with higher phytochemical exposure or adjunct lifestyle change may exceed ~3–4 kg, but such gains are similar to modest diet-only effects and may not resolve obesity-related complications without comprehensive care. <cite id="71548350-7">~4 kg or more loss over time with higher-dose HCA plus diet vs placebo</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-2">Small reductions at 180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA over 4–12 weeks</cite>.
- Practical clinical significance:
  - For many patients, even modest weight loss (e.g., ≥5–10% of baseline) is clinically meaningful, but herbal extract–alone effects are generally too small to achieve such thresholds; stacking with behavioral counseling, medication therapy, or procedural interventions is often required. Given the overall weak pooled evidence and small absolute benefits, the clinical significance of standardized-dose extracts is often limited without concurrent, structured weight-management programs. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Across 54 trials, herbal medicines showed limited weight-loss effectiveness compared with placebo</cite> <cite id="58dc1be2-5">Meta-analysis found insufficient evidence backing many herbal medicines for significant weight loss</cite>.

Examples of randomized trials and their doses
- Psyllium and other herbal comparators:
  - In head-to-head adult weight-loss contexts, psyllistral (psyllium husk–fiber) emerged as one of the more effective interventions versus many spices/herbal extracts, suggesting fiber-rich herbal agents may have stronger weight effects through satiety and gut-related mechanisms. <cite id="58dc1be2-0">Psyllium was the most effective herbal intervention for weight loss among seven tested, followed by Nigella sativa, spirulina, and chitosan</cite>.
- Irvingia gabonensis:
  - RCTs using 150–400 mg of extract standardized to irgafrin-like markers over 8–12 weeks show better weight/BMI change than placebo; meta-analyses consider these effects clinically meaningful vs placebo on average, though heterogeneity remains. <cite id="58dc1be2-2">Irvingia gabonensis produced statistically and clinically significant weight loss compared to placebo</cite>.
- Bitter orange (Citrus aurantium):
  - Trials testing 200–600 mg standardized bitter orange with synephrine show modest weight or BMI reductions with stimulant-type risks; effects per mg of active alkaloid align with green coffee patterns—small absolute loss with dietary advice. <cite id="58dc1be2-5">Across many herbal RCTs, benefits are limited overall and safety considerations are common</cite>.
- Green coffee bean extract:
  - RCTs in pooled meta-analyses show 180–200 mg/day (40–45% CGA) for 4–12 weeks produces weight loss; 500 mg/day CGA also lowers body weight versus placebo; typical effects are a few kilograms and modest in BMI terms. <cite id="c3a42833-2">180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA for 4–12 weeks reduced body weight</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-0">~500 mg/day CGA lowers body weight</cite>.
- Garcinia cambogia:
  - Trials at 500 mg TID (1500 mg/day) with brief duration often show no difference vs placebo; in contrast, one RCT at 2400 mg/day split premeals over a low-calorie diet produced significantly greater loss than placebo, indicating a role for higher total daily HCA exposure and adherence to diet. <cite id="71548350-6">No effect at 500 mg TID over two weeks with diet advice</cite> <cite id="71548350-7">~2400 mg/day split premeals with low-calorie diet outperformed placebo</cite>.

Practical guidance and key takeaways for clinicians
- If using herbal extract for weight loss:
  - Prefer standardized extracts with clear active-ingredient amounts and durations sufficient to detect change (≥8–12 weeks). Consider higher daily exposures where supported (e.g., green coffee at ~500 mg CGA/day; HCA at ~1800–2400 mg/day) and pair with counseling on caloric restriction and physical activity. <cite id="c3a42833-0">~500 mg/day CGA lowers body weight versus placebo</cite> <cite id="71548350-7">~2400 mg/day HCA with low-calorie diet yields superior loss compared with placebo</cite>.
- Assess risk and tailor:
  - Garcinia: consider hepatotoxicity risk and psychiatric/somatic adverse effects; generally low benefit unless high-dose, diet-restricted regimens are feasible. <cite id="71548350-1">Garcinia efficacy is inconclusive with potential safety issues</cite>.
  - Bitter orange: avoid in patients with cardiovascular risk, tachycardia, hypotension, pregnancy, or stimulant polypharmacy; stimulant interactions and sympathomimetic effects limit clinical role. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Overall limited efficacy and safety concerns in RCT meta-analyses</cite>.
  - Green coffee: use standardized for CGA content; emphasize realistic expectations for modest weight loss and metabolic improvements. <cite id="c3a42833-2">Effective at 180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA over 4–12 weeks</cite>.
  - Irvingia: modest effects on weight and BMI versus placebo that can be clinically meaningful for some patients; integrate with diet and lifestyle. <cite id="58dc1be2-2">Clinically significant weight loss vs placebo pooled for Irvingia</cite>.
- Expectations vs clinical significance:
  - Herbal extracts can add a few kilograms of loss in the context of diet/exercise; standalone use rarely achieves “meaningful” weight-loss goals without broader medical weight management. Counsel patients accordingly and consider combining botanicals with FDA-approved medications or multidisciplinary care for higher-risk, higher-target patients. <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Across 54 RCTs, overall weight-loss benefits of herbal medicines are limited</cite>.

Bottom line
- Higher, well-standardized doses of certain herbal extracts—when taken with diet or lifestyle intervention—can produce statistically detectable and sometimes clinically meaningful reductions in body weight relative to placebo, though absolute changes are modest and benefits vary by extract and formulation. Lower-dose or inadequately standardized products often show little difference from placebo. Clinical decisions should weigh modest expected benefits against safety and the availability of more proven, integrative weight-management strategies. <cite id="71548350-7">~2400 mg/day HCA alongside a low-calorie diet produced superior weight loss vs placebo</cite> <cite id="c3a42833-2">~180–200 mg/day of 40–45% CGA for 4–12 weeks reduced body weight</cite> <cite id="58dc1be2-2">Irvingia gabonensis shows statistically and clinically significant weight loss vs placebo in pooled RCTs</cite> <cite id="58dc1be2-6">Overall, across many RCTs, herbal agents show limited efficacy for weight loss compared to placebo</cite>.

# Summary: CT-based colon imaging (CT colonography) for colorectal cancer (CRC) screening

CT-based colon imaging, also called CT colonography (CTC) or "virtual colonoscopy," uses rapid intravenous contrast-enhanced CT combined with meticulous air-contrast insufflation to evaluate the colon and rectum as a screening test for adenomas and cancers. It is a dedicated protocolized examination designed to optimize visualization of the colorectal lumen and can be performed as an outpatient without sedation. <cite id="98ad0bb2-3">CT colonography (CTC) is a defined imaging procedure distinct from standard abdomen–pelvis CT in which there is a dedicated protocol to optimize the colorectum</cite> <cite id="7786e884-1">Computed tomography colonography (CTC) is a minimally invasive structural examination of the colon and rectum to evaluate for colorectal polyps and neoplasms, with formal performance guidelines</cite> <cite id="98ad0bb2-4">CT colonography can be performed in a few minutes and does not require sedation, allowing patients to drive to and from the procedure</cite>.

## Main advantages

- Comparable detection of advanced neoplasia in screening settings: <cite id="98ad0bb2-6">In a large randomized population screening trial, CTC and colonoscopy had similar detection rates for advanced neoplasias</cite>. <cite id="bc6adcc9-5">A meta-analysis reported CTC cancer sensitivity around 96% for lesions ≥10 mm, with specificity 79.6%–93.1%</cite>.
- Noninvasive, sedation-free outpatient exam: <cite id="98ad0bb2-4">CT colonography can be performed quickly without sedation, enabling patients to drive to and from</cite>. <cite id="7786e884-0">CTC requires a full bowel preparation similar to colonoscopy, but no sedation is required and the examination is less time-consuming</cite>. <cite id="98ad0bb2-2">CT colonography has a much lower risk of perforating the colon than conventional colonoscopy</cite>.
- High sensitivity for larger (≥10 mm) adenomatous lesions and cancers: <cite id="0abf705b-7">Compared to colonoscopy, CTC has high sensitivity for adenomas ≥10 mm, with somewhat lower sensitivity for advanced adenomas ≥6 mm</cite>. <cite id="bc6adcc9-1">A 90% sensitivity for CTC in detecting polyps ≥10 mm is consistent with improvements in health outcomes</cite>.
