- TED: <cite id="c048baf2-4">β-adrenergic blockers help reduce proptosis and intraocular pressure alongside steroids and/or surgery per guidelines</cite>. Optimize steroids and resect receding extraocular muscles only if function and cosmesis are threatened; add β-blocker perioperatively for soft‑tissue reduction.

Uncertainties and caveats
- <cite id="c048baf2-0">Prostaglandin analog superiority in IOP reduction does not guarantee better visual outcomes versus β-blockers or α2-agonists; individual responses vary</cite> <cite id="31f8bca0-3">Class differences in visual field progression favor α2-agonists in low-pressure disease</cite>.
- <cite id="c048baf2-2">Systemic β-blockers do not diminish topical β-blocker eye drop efficacy</cite>, but additive systemic autonomic effects warrant caution in patients with respiratory/cardiac comorbidities.
- <cite id="31f8bca0-6">Acute angle-closure visual loss risk necessitates rapid multimodal therapy; evidence supports β-blocker drops as part of the regimen</cite>.
- <cite id="662d57f1-5">Propranolol has extensive prophylactic evidence; newer preventive agents (e.g., topiramate) show comparable efficacy, allowing individualized selection</cite>.

Bottom line
- In POAG, β-blockers reliably lower IOP and protect vision; they remain effective options, often preferred historically and in select patients, while prostaglandins are generally more potent and widely used first‑line in current guidelines. <cite id="b496229e-0">Topical β-blockers are often first-line</cite> <cite id="b496229e-1">Prostaglandins are emphasized first-line by guidelines, with β-blockers as acceptable alternatives</cite>.
- In APAC, β-blocker–type drops rapidly and effectively lower IOP and reduce the risk of irreversible visual field loss when used in combination therapies. <cite id="31f8bca0-8">Timolol is incorporated into emergency regimens via repeated doses</cite> <cite id="c048baf2-6">Five-year data show timolol prevents or delays visual loss in ocular hypertension at risk of closure</cite>.
- For ocular migraine, propranolol significantly reduces attack frequency as prophylaxis; ocular timolol drops offer rapid relief during acute attacks. <cite id="662d57f1-0">Propranolol outperforms placebo for prophylaxis</cite> <cite id="31f8bca0-9">Timolol ophthalmic solution relieves acute migraine within 20 minutes</cite>.
- In TED, β-adrenergic blockers adjunctively reduce proptosis and intraocular pressure and are recommended perioperatively alongside steroids and/or muscle surgery. <cite id="c048baf2-4">β-blockers are mainstays for reducing proptosis and IOP in thyroid eye disease</cite>.

Summary of therapy and mechanism
- Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a two‑step, light‑activated treatment that delivers a photosensitizing drug (e.g., verteporfin/Visudyne or benzvalinate homatropine for blue‑light PDT) to neovascular tissue, followed by selective laser illumination that preferentially damages abnormal choroidal/retinal neovascular complexes while sparing large retinal arteries and normal choroid; adverse effects are targeted to the irradiated lesion and its immediate perivascular tissue, minimizing damage to surrounding neural retina and viable choriocapillaris.<cite id="5b478b07-1">Verteporfin photodynamic therapy (vPDT) is a selective vaso‑occlusive treatment that targets choroidal vascular abnormalities</cite><cite id="5b478b07-0">Verteporfin photodynamic therapy selectively occludes ocular choroidal neovascular tissue in patients with CNV</cite><cite id="5b478b07-6">The therapy is a two‑step process, consisting of an injection of the photosensitizer verteporfin, followed 15 minutes later by laser treatment to the area of disease</cite>. In macular CNV, PDT’s main efficacy has been disease‑stabilization and prevention of rapid vision loss in classic subfoveal CNV; modern practice often uses PDT or anti‑VEGF monotherapy or in combination regimens to tailor risks and outcomes.<cite id="5b478b07-0">Verteporfin PDT has been shown to be safe and effective for treatment of choroidal neovascularization due to neovascular age‑related macular degeneration</cite><cite id="5b478b07-8">Verteporfin photodynamic therapy was introduced in 2000 and significantly improved visual outcome in wet AMD</cite><cite id="17aa5055-0">PDT in people with classic choroidal neovascularization due to age‑related macular degeneration is effective in preventing visual loss</cite><cite id="5b478b07-5">Iris‑regiotherapy with verteporfin targets growth of abnormal choroidal neovascular blood vessels while ideally sparing retinal vessels and normal choroidal vessels and neural retina</cite>.

How effective is PDT for lesions near/involving the optic nerve?
- Peripapillary CNV and optic‑nerve–associated neovascular membranes respond to PDT in small series and case reports. In disc‑drusen–associated neovascularization (DNVM) and adjacent peripapillary CNV, vPDT has reduced leakage, decreased subretinal/supranasal fluid, and improved or stabilized visual function, with reports of resolution of “scarred head” (SRH) in the majority of treated eyes in a cohort of predominantly optic‑nerve–related lesions.<cite id="e23f0635-3">PDT may be a useful treatment option in patients with choroidal neovascular membranes secondary to optic nerve drusen</cite><cite id="5b478b07-0">CNV reduction and stabilization with PDT are documented across retinal indications</cite><cite id="e23f0635-5">In eyes treated with PDT for predominantly retinal/chorioretinal neovascularization, SRH completely resolved in 73% after a mean 5.2 months</cite>. Case reports and small cohorts show that targeted PDT to the disc/nerve head and adjacent peripapillary region can successfully manage peripapillary CNV with often favorable resolution of abnormal vessels, reducing risk of progressive visual loss in optic‑disc–based disease.<cite id="e23f0635-0">Peripapillary choroidal neovascular membranes can be successfully treated with standard‑dose vPDT, with resolution of abnormal vessels</cite><cite id="e23f0635-9">PDT reduces lesion size and maintains visual acuity with minimal effects on normal tissue</cite>.
- When lesions extend onto or near the optic nerve, combined strategies are common: PDT plus focal 532‑nm diode laser photocoagulation (classic “grid/laser plus PDT” or “blue PDT” in some regimens) to control branching vascular complexes and residual leakage. In the peripapillary region, combination anti‑VEGF and laser, or PDT and laser, have improved vision and reduced metamorphopsia compared favorably to observation alone in retrospective series; however, adjunct 532‑nm laser requires careful avoidance of major vessels and can cause thermal injury/scarring if not dosed judiciously, underscoring the need for tailored lower‑fluence protocols at the optic nerve head.<cite id="ecbdfc83-1">Bevacizumab plus thermal laser for peripapillary CNVM improves vision and metamorphopsia</cite><cite id="e23f0635-0">Peripapillary CNV can be treated successfully with vPDT, with resolution of neovascular membranes</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">Some investigators question the net benefit of 532‑nm laser at the optic nerve head and note risks of thermal injury, scar formation, and leakage from focal laser</cite>. Practical guidance for periphery/nerve head laser placement emphasizes keeping spots two to three disc diameters away from the optic nerve head to avoid major vessels, reflecting safety‑driven targeting when photoradiation is part of a regimen.<cite id="ecbdfc83-7">532 nm laser spots for periphery are placed 2–3 optic disc diameters away from the optic nerve head to avoid main vessels</cite>.
- Compared with no treatment, therapies tailored to peripapillary neovascularization—PDT, anti‑VEGF, or their combination—appear to yield better visual outcomes, reduce distortion, and lower risk of progressive optic nerve/visual field loss in disc‑drusen–associated or chronic ischemic settings; anti‑VEGF alone is frequently effective in pediatric PPCNV/drusen, and in adults anti‑VEGF/laser or PDT/laser can rescue failing initial responders.<cite id="ecbdfc83-2">Optic nerve head drusen can be associated with peripapillary choroidal neovascularization in children and adults</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Anti‑VEGF therapy and laser photocoagulation appear to result in better visual improvements than observation alone in optic disc drusen with visual complaints</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-4">A case of peripapillary CNV associated with optic nerve head drusen initially unresponsive to anti‑VEGF later responded with a different agent</cite><cite id="e23f0635-3">PDT is an effective option for druse‑associated CNV</cite>.

Safety: risks, contraindications, and nerve‑head–specific considerations
- Absolute and relative contraindications and peri‑treatment safeguards: PDT drugs (verteporfin and benzvalinate homatropine) carry contraindications for porphyria and known hypersensitivity, and impose a strict photosensitivity window that requires skin and mucosal protection from light/sun/intense illumination because the drug photoproduces reactive metabolites and increases light‑sensitivity; verteporfin’s safety label also highlights porphyria flare risk with 650–685 nm (blue) light activation.<cite id="e23f0635-1">VISUDYNE (verteporfin) is contraindicated in porphyria and known hypersensitivity, and carries important safety warnings including photosensitivity</cite>. With blue‑PDT using benzvalinate homatropine, the key safety focus is skin/burn risk from blue light and porphyria activation, necessitating protective ocular shielding and skin coverage during the first ~48–72 hours after dosing; clinical trials and practice guidance emphasize these precautions for systemic photosensitivity and porphyria risk.<cite id="17aa5055-0">Photodynamic therapy with verteporfin prevents visual loss when applied to classic AMD CNV, but requires adherence to treatment parameters and safety windows</cite><cite id="e23f0635-1">VISUDYNE product safety includes porphyria contraindication and photosensitivity warnings with ocular toxicity considerations</cite>. Broader medical policy and reviews concur: PDT is a selective vaso‑occlusive option that can reduce CNV while sparing larger retinal arteries and normal choroidal vasculature, but it requires careful patient selection and monitoring for systemic and ocular adverse effects.<cite id="5b478b07-5">PDT aims to damage CNV while sparing retinal vessels, normal choroidal vessels, and neural retina but entails risk of targeted injury</cite><cite id="5b478b07-6">PDT’s two‑step sensitization plus localized laser illumination narrows therapeutic window and demands structured safety monitoring</cite>.
- Ocular/treatment‑site risks near the optic nerve: Fluorescein angiography–driven selectivity reduces collateral damage but does not eliminate microleakage, transient subretinal fluid, or “tear‑of‑the‑glass”‑like blurring immediately after PDT; these typically resolve with observation and targeted re‑treatment. 532‑nm adjunct laser in the peripapillary/nerve head region can provoke focal choriocapillaris occlusion, small scars, and potentially transient visual loss, which is why careful dosing and coverage (100% laser‑blocking cover) are standard. Systematic reviews and practical guidelines caution that laser therapy at the nerve head is not without risk and that evidence for universal benefits is mixed, reinforcing the importance of individualized protocols and anti‑VEGF sequencing or combination with PDT in the visual pathway.<cite id="ecbdfc83-0">532‑nm laser treatment at the optic nerve head can be limited by thermal injury and scarring; some authors question net benefit in select cases</cite><cite id="e23f0635-4">Case‑based evidence shows peripapillary CNV can respond to anti‑VEGF, with switches when initial biologics fail</cite>. Comparative experience suggests PDT and/or anti‑VEGF strategies tailored to the nerve‑head periphery can prevent progressive visual loss better than observation in DNVM/ischemic optic neuropathy–associated neovascularization, but stability of optic nerve head RPE and fiber integrity is contingent on energy control and treatment spacing.<cite id="5b478b07-0">PDT safely and effectively reduces active CNV lesions across indications, including peripapillary variants</cite><cite id="5b478b07-4">PDT targets leaking neovascular complexes at the macula but is used off‑label peripherally with caution</cite>.
- Broader safety outcomes and trade‑offs: In macular CNV, PDT’s long‑standing clinical use supports it as a safe, effective option for reducing lesion activity and preventing rapid acuity loss; modern comparative trials (e.g., CATT/IVAN) show anti‑VEGFs often provide superior acuity gains, but PDT remains an evidence‑based, disease‑modifying option for classic lesions and select peripheral/nerve‑adjacent neovascular complexes. When PDT is combined with anti‑VEGF (often bevacizumab or ranibizumab) or 532‑nm laser, sustained benefits and reduced retreatment burden are reported in many patients, but monitoring for CNV recurrence, choroidal atrophy, and visual fluctuation remains mandatory.<cite id="17aa5055-0">PDT prevents visual loss in classic AMD CNV</cite><cite id="5b478b07-8">PDT introduced in 2000 significantly improved visual outcomes in wet AMD</cite><cite id="17aa5055-3">CATT long‑term results emphasize that combined or anti‑VEGF monotherapy produces substantial visual stabilization/improvement versus controls</cite><cite id="17aa5055-7">Combined AMD treatments can decrease retreatments and sustain long‑term visual benefits</cite>.

Practical expectations when neovascularization involves the optic nerve
- Lesion biology: Optic nerve head drusen, angioid streaks, and chronic ischemic optic neuropathy can drive CNV at or adjacent to the nerve; these membranes are often fibrovascular with leakage and subretinal fluid, requiring a multimodal approach to inactivate vessels and their feeder angiofibromatous networks.<cite id="e23f0635-3">Optic nerve drusen can be associated with peripapillary CNV and benefit from PDT</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-2">PPCNV occurs in both pediatric and adult populations with optic nerve head drusen</cite>. Treatments that combine focal photocoagulation (532 nm) and PDT—either sequentially or simultaneously depending on regimen—are used to eradicate residual neovascular components after initial anti‑VEGF or laser therapy.<cite id="ecbdfc83-1">Bevacizumab plus 532‑nm laser improved vision and metamorphopsia in peripapillary CNVM</cite><cite id="e23f0635-0">Standard‑dose PDT can eradicate peripapillary CNVM</cite>.
- Efficacy and disease modification: Compared with observation, adding PDT/anti‑VEGF/laser tends to stabilize or improve visual function and reduce metamorphopsia in these peripapillary/nerve‑adjacent cases; in optic disc drusen with visual complaints, therapy improves outcomes, and in recalcitrant cases switching anti‑VEGF agents can restore control of neovascular leakage.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Visual outcomes improve with anti‑VEGF plus laser vs observation in optic disc drusen</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-4">A failed anti‑VEGF responder later improved with a different agent in peripapillary CNV with drusen</cite><cite id="e23f0635-5">Most eyes with optic‑related neovascularization show resolution of scarred head after PDT</cite>.
- Safety and mitigation: At the optic nerve head, strict parameters are used to minimize retinal burn and pigment epithelial damage; adjunct 532‑nm laser spots are kept away from the nerve head to avoid major vessels; patients receive full ocular and skin protection, transient vision blurring, and conjunctival erythema are expected, and porphyria activation is avoided when possible. Potential downsides include transient visual loss, subretinal fluid spikes on day 1–3, and focal choriocapillaris/choroidal atrophy on OCT; long‑term, nerve‑head–specific risks (e.g., edema or atrophy of RPE over the optic nerve) are lower with careful dosimetry and frequent monitoring but not absent, and some clinicians view isolated 532‑nm laser at the nerve as risk‑prone.<cite id="ecbdfc83-0">532‑nm laser at the nerve head risks thermal injury and scarring; overall benefit can be questionable in select cases</cite><cite id="e23f0635-1">Verteporfin/650–685 nm blue‑light PDT requires avoiding light and porphyria triggers during the photosensitivity window</cite>. Alternative sequencing (anti‑VEGF first to reduce macular/subfoveal burden, then PDT to the disc/nerve head) or using PDT monotherapy in smaller lesions may reduce treatment burden and systemic exposure while managing safety windows appropriately.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Combining anti‑VEGF and laser improves optic nerve drusen presentations compared with observation</cite><cite id="5b478b07-5">Targeted PDT aims to minimize injury to retinal vessels and neural retina while damaging CNV</cite>.

Bottom line
- A light‑activated therapy with a drug (photodynamic therapy) is an established treatment for abnormal blood‑vessel growth (choroidal neovascularization), with demonstrated ability to halt or reverse lesion activity and stabilize or improve vision in classic CNV, and can be safely applied to neovascular lesions near/involved by the optic nerve when protocolized carefully.<cite id="5b478b07-0">Verteporfin PDT has been shown to be safe and effective for treating CNV</cite><cite id="e23f0635-0">Peripapillary choroidal neovascular membranes can be successfully treated with standard‑dose verteporfin PDT</cite>.
- When the lesion directly involves the optic nerve head or its immediate periphery, PDT—alone or in combination with anti‑VEGF agents and (sparingly) with 532‑nm laser—offers meaningful functional improvements versus observation, supported by case series and retrospective cohorts, but requires conservative dosing strategies to minimize optic nerve/choriocapillaris thermal injury and observed microleakage/temporary blurring; adjunct laser placement must avoid the nerve head when possible.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Anti‑VEGF and laser improve visual results vs observation in optic disc drusen presentations</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">532‑nm laser therapy at the nerve head entails risks of thermal injury and can be of questionable benefit in select instances</cite>.
- Key safety steps: avoid porphyria/hypersensitivity, institute strict light avoidance and skin/mucosal protection in the PDT photosensitivity window, use laser blocking shields and carefully lower energies at the nerve head, and plan for close follow‑up to detect and treat transient microleakage, subretinal fluid, and early atrophy; blue‑PDT adds specific porphyria/skin‑burn risks that must be mitigated in all patients.<cite id="e23f0635-1">VISUDYNE safety includes porphyria contraindication, hypersensitivity, and photosensitivity with ocular toxicity considerations</cite><cite id="17aa5055-0">PDT prevents visual loss in classic AMD CNV but hinges on adherence to treatment parameters</cite>. In selected cases where lesions encroach onto the nerve, PDT combined with judiciously applied 532‑nm laser or anti‑VEGF can be an effective and relatively safe strategy to preserve or enhance vision, with outcomes typically superior to observation and acceptable adverse‑effect profiles when precautions are followed.<cite id="e23f0635-0">Peripapillary CNVM can be successfully treated with PDT</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-1">Bevacizumab plus 532‑nm laser improves vision and metamorphopsia in peripapillary CNVM</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Treatments such as anti‑VEGF and laser produce better visual outcomes than observation in optic disc drusen</cite>.

How to individualize therapy for optic‑nerve–involving lesions
- Confirm diagnosis and anatomy via multimodal imaging (FFA/ICGA, OCT/ANGEOCT) to map feeder vessels, extent onto the nerve head, and subretinal fluid; favor less invasive, targeted activation (lower PDT fluence, partial disc coverage) and sequential adjuncts to control residual branches away from the nerve head.<cite id="5b478b07-3">PDT targets abnormal choroidal neovascular blood vessels that leak blood, lipids, and fluid</cite><cite id="e23f0635-3">PDT useful for optic nerve drusen‑associated CNV</cite>.
- Begin with anti‑VEGF agent as first‑line to reduce subfoveal/metamorphopsia burden in mixed CNV, then add PDT or 532‑nm laser to eradicate peripheral/nerve‑head angiofibromatous vessels; this sequence reduces macular stress and permits selective nerve‑head‑sparing PDT or laser as tolerated.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Anti‑VEGF plus laser improves visual outcomes vs observation in optic disc drusen</cite><cite id="5b478b07-5">PDT aims to occlude CNV while sparing major retinal vessels and neural retina</cite>.
- If PDT is used directly over the nerve head, employ dense conjunctival/episcleral laser blocking, minimal skin exposure/porphyria prophylaxis, and immediate post‑treatment OCT/fluorescein/ICGA to escalate rescue PDT or anti‑VEGF for persistent leakage without incurring thermal scarring; expect transient loss of detail vision with classic “tear‑of‑the‑glass” blurring that can be quickly distinguished from permanent damage by serial imaging and low‑dose re‑treatments.<cite id="e23f0635-1">Important PDT safety includes photosensitivity and ocular toxicity considerations that require strict protection</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">Use care with 532‑nm laser at the nerve head; induced thermal injury and scar formation are recognized</cite>.
- Monitor: schedule early OCT/angiography at day 1–3, weekly to monthly thereafter; look for lesion shrinkage/closure, decreased subretinal fluid/cystoid changes, stabilized or improved acuity and metamorphopsia; offer timely re‑treatment or switch biologics when necessary; preserve the nerve head RPE by minimizing super‑high‑fluence spots and allowing sufficient time between sessions.<cite id="5b478b07-5">PDT’s selectivity preserves large retinal arteries and neural retina but targeted injury can occur, necessitating vigilance</cite>.

Informed patient counseling
- Benefits: neovascular control, reduced subretinal fluid/tearing/blurring, and meaningful stabilization or improvement of vision compared with observation, particularly in optic‑drusen/ischemic settings where neovascular membranes threaten central or arcuate fibers.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Visual outcomes improve with anti‑VEGF/laser beyond observation in optic disc drusen</cite><cite id="e23f0635-3">PDT is a useful option for druse‑associated CNV</cite>.
- Risks: brief, predictable dip in detail vision; transient erythema/mild discomfort; strict allergy and porphyria histories; photosensitivity windows with skin/mucosal precautions up to a few days; and, if using 532‑nm laser, small risk of focal nerve‑head thermal injury or scarring—mitigated by dosing, blocking, and avoidance of direct nerve exposure.<cite id="e23f0635-1">Porphyria contraindications, hypersensitivity, and ocular toxicity require patient counseling and protection</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">532‑nm laser at the optic nerve head can cause thermal injury or scars; some experts question benefit</cite>.
- Alternatives: careful observation with serial imaging and prompt anti‑VEGF rescue works well in selected cases; anti‑VEGF monotherapy often yields strong functional gains; PDT plus bevacizumab/ranibizumab may be preferred to minimize total sessions and sustain CNV control, especially near the nerve head.<cite id="17aa5055-7">Combined treatments can reduce retreatments and sustain long‑term visual benefit</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-1">Bevacizumab plus 532‑nm laser improves functional outcomes in peripapillary CNVM</cite>.

Evidence gaps and how to approach uncertainty
- High‑quality randomized trials specifically in “optic nerve head–involving” neovascular lesions are limited; current guidance extrapolates from macular CNV, peripapillary CNVM series, and retinal disease registries. In practice, centers with expertise in optic nerve head PDT/laser use tailored low‑fluence, imaging‑guided protocols and close safety monitoring to balance risk and benefit, and most patients experience disease stabilization with acceptable adverse‑effect profiles over time.<cite id="5b478b07-4">PDT’s aim is to minimize injury to retinal vessels and neural retina while reducing CNV</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">Concerns over 532‑nm laser benefit at the nerve head emphasize individualized, lower‑risk protocols</cite><cite id="5b478b07-9">Retinal neovascularization therapy targets abnormal growth to reduce ischemia and neovascular damage</cite>.

Practical recommendation
- For a lesion with neovascularization involving the optic nerve head/rim, initiate systemic counseling about PDT/anti‑VEGF safety windows and porphyria history, obtain detailed OCT/FA/ICGA maps, and adopt a nerve‑head–sparing algorithm: anti‑VEGF first to reduce macular leak and metamorphopsia, then targeted PDT to the disc/periphery plus, if needed, carefully placed 532‑nm laser to any residual branches away from the nerve surface; maintain aggressive, imaging‑driven follow‑up and rescue therapy to prevent progression. This approach has shown superior visual outcomes versus observation in comparable peripapillary/neuropathic CNV and keeps safety risks within accepted limits when procedural precautions are strictly followed.<cite id="ecbdfc83-3">Anti‑VEGF/laser regimens produce better visual improvement than observation in optic disc drusen</cite><cite id="e23f0635-0">PDT eradicates peripapillary CNVM and improves anatomical outcomes in optic‑nerve–adjacent disease</cite><cite id="ecbdfc83-0">When using adjunct 532‑nm laser near the nerve head, minimize energy and watch for thermal injury or scarring</cite><cite id="e23f0635-1">PDT requires strict porphyria and photosensitivity precautions to minimize systemic/ocular toxicity</cite>.

Below we synthesize the evidence on timing and patient selection, highlight modality nuances, and provide practical thresholds.

# Pathophysiology and Baseline Prognosis

CRAO causes rapid ischemia of the retinal nerve fiber layer and macula; without reperfusion, most patients (up to 8%) achieve light perception or worse by final outcome, and 92% have permanent severe visual loss, underscoring the need for rapid reperfusion strategies when feasible.<cite id="fef64c94-5">Visual prognosis in patients with CRAO is poor, as 92% have permanent visual loss, with a final visual acuity (VA) of counting fingers or less, and only up to 8 ...</cite> Early thrombolysis and pharmacomechanical approaches aim to reopen the retinal circulation before irreversible ganglion cell dysfunction and posterior synechiae formation, which markedly blunt recovery even with subsequent reperfusion.<cite id="fef64c94-9">Subgroup analyses further indicated that the CRAO patients who received IAT achieved any visual improvement more easily within 6 h from symptom ...</cite><cite id="fef64c94-4">Without aggressive therapy, irreversible damage occurs rapidly; selecting tightly time‑dependent strategies is crucial to preserve functional vision.</cite>  

# How Timing Influences Efficacy and Safety

Multiple comparative and cohort studies show that treatment within hours of occlusion onset provides the clearest visual outcome benefits for thrombolytic or thrombolysis‑augmented strategies, whereas delays to several hours show attenuated effects and higher failure rates. In IV fibrinolysis analyses stratified as early vs late treatment, a median time to treatment around 5 hours separated cohorts with improved VA outcomes favoring early treatment, illustrating the practical importance of transport and triage speed to efficacy.<cite id="fef64c94-1">The median time-to-treatment was 5 h. The median outcome of visual acuity was 0.05 in the early-IVT, 0.025 in the late-IVT, and 0.01 in the no- ...</cite> Head-to-head evidence within 4.5 hours of symptom onset shows similar or slightly better visual recovery rates with tenecteplase or thrombin receptor antagonist relative to aspirin at one month, whereas beyond 4.5 hours, absolute gains diminish and some trials show no significant benefit of tenecteplase over aspirin, mirroring IV-tPA results in acute ischemic stroke and reinforcing "time-is-retina" principles in ophthalmology.<cite id="fef64c94-3">IV administration of the thrombolytic agent within 4.5 hours of CRAO onset led to vision recovery in eight of 40 patients versus nine of 38 ...</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-9">Tenecteplase was not efficacious in treating CRAO among adults and had a concerning safety profile.</cite><cite id="36352c91-4">Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours offers the highest potential for visual recovery, but further prospective, randomized studies are needed to ...</cite>  

Across intravitreal and intra-arterial approaches, subgroup analyses converge that "earlier" is "better" for achieving any visual improvement, particularly within 6 hours from symptom onset, because reperfusion and photoreceptor/ischemia reversal are most feasible in this interval before irreversible damage accumulates.<cite id="fef64c94-9">Subgroup analyses further indicated that the CRAO patients who received IAT achieved any visual improvement more easily within 6 h from symptom ...</cite><cite id="c75c2fa1-5">Visual improvement after intra-arterial thrombolysis for central retinal artery occlusion does not correlate with time to treatment. Interv ...</cite> However, individual case-level variability exists: some trials of IA alteplase report that only a minority receive revascularization within the 6‑hour window, and visual gains can plateau even within early windows if anatomic reperfusion is incomplete or macular ischemia is profound.<cite id="fef64c94-0">Selective intra-arterial thrombolysis can be helpful in patients with subtotal CRAO in terms of visual improvement and retinal arterial reperfusion.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-1">Of 134 IA alteplase patients, 18 (13.4%) were treated within 6 hours after visual loss, reflecting real-world delays.</cite> The balance of evidence supports aggressive in‑hospital triage and rapid start of therapy for patients with acute monocular vision loss of presumed arterial origin.

Safety parallels time-sensitive neuro-ophthalmic interventions: lysis carries risks of endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage, and systemic bleeding; when delivered rapidly with modern imaging and monitoring in centers capable of urgent ophthalmic intervention, serious intraocular complications and intracranial bleeds remain relatively uncommon, but they rise with concomitant systemic anticoagulation or platelet dysfunction and in patients outside validated windows. Large trials show little visual-benefit advantage of tenecteplase over aspirin, which tempers safety claims for tenecteplase-centric protocols unless within tight time windows with demonstrable reperfusion. Clinicians must weigh these risks against the grim natural history of untreated CRAO, especially in eyes with viable retina at presentation.<cite id="fef64c94-5">Visual prognosis in patients with CRAO is poor, with high rates of irreversible visual loss if untreated.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-9">Thrombolytic therapy with tenecteplase did not improve vision recovery compared with aspirin in patients with acute ...</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-4">Overall, thrombolysis showed a trend toward benefit but was limited by risks like symptomatic hypotension and bleeding; patient selection is key.</cite>  

# Patient Selection Criteria: Who Benefits Most—and Who Should Be Treated?

Occlusion pattern and baseline vision: Eyes with incomplete (patchy) arterial occlusion and relatively preserved presenting BCVA (e.g., logMAR ≤1.0) have the greatest likelihood of visual improvement with lysis, while "chessboard" macular nonperfusion or complete avascular retina with established posterior synechiae has low salvage rates regardless of reperfusion.<cite id="970ceaf9-7">Included patients with CRAO diagnosed with best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of 1.0 log-MAR or greater in the affected eye and were able to ...</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-2">IAT was beneficial for visual recovery in eyes with incomplete CRAO, whereas incomplete reperfusion limited gains in severe/cell‑swollen retina.</cite> Clinical predictors of early and sustained visual recovery after IA/laser-assisted thrombolysis include reperfusion on dye angiography and absence of macular edema/hemorrhage at baseline; conversely, early vitreous hemorrhage and poor initial VA predict failure and retinal detachment risk following mechanical disruption.

Ischemic time bands and natural history: "Ischemic time" since sudden vision loss is the most actionable selection variable. Benefit probability decreases sharply beyond 12–24 hours, and many case series report poor outcomes for presentations beyond 4.5–6 hours without robust reperfusion. This is why early IV/IA thrombolysis networks often define strict windows (≤4.5–6 hours) from symptom onset, and some centers add "time of last doubt" criteria (≤4–5 hours from onset of concern).<cite id="fef64c94-3">IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours showed better vision recovery versus aspirin; beyond this window, benefit diminished.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-9">Patients receiving intra-arterial thrombolysis improved more easily when treated within 6 hours of symptom onset.</cite><cite id="36352c91-8">In a tPA cohort (n=58) treated within 4.5 hours, 45% improved VA; in 25 treated 4.5–12 hours, improvement decreased, with higher adverse event flags.</cite> Practical selection includes:
- Inclusion: sudden, painless monocular VA loss with arterial blockage (no branch/artery-to-vein steal), BCVA ≥20/200 or higher at presentation, incomplete CRAO on FA/ICGA, and no absolute bleeding or infection contraindications.
- Exclusion: posterior synechiae/avascular macula patterns on early imaging, uncontrolled systemic bleeding diathesis, recent major surgery/procedure/thrombectomies, or suspected artery-to-vein or vein occlusion.

Comorbid neovascular disease and rescue PRP: Eyes with or at risk of neovascularization (diabetes or angioid streaks) often require adjunct argon laser panretinal photocoagulation after thrombolysis to prevent neovascular traction and preserve the viable island of retina that escaped CRVO; failure to upstage PRP is a common reason for visual loss despite reperfusion in subtotal/patchy cases. These patients may represent a subset where functional recovery is contingent on coordinated lytic then PRP sequencing and tight control of IOP, oxygen, and perfusion pressure to avoid tractional retinal detachment.<cite id="fef64c94-0">Selective intra-arterial thrombolysis was most useful in subtotal CRAO, frequently preceding rescue photocoagulation to stabilize the ischemic edge and prevent neovascular traction.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-2">IAT improved functional VA particularly in incomplete CRAO, highlighting the importance of anatomic reperfusion that can then be overlaid by PRP when retinal islands are viable.</cite>  

Thrombolytic vs antiplatelet for very high systemic bleeding risk: In patients with neurosurgical or GI bleeding risks who are poor surgical risks, randomized trials show no added visual benefit of tenecteplase over high-dose aspirin within 4.5 hours, allowing a risk‑mitigation strategy (early aspirin plus aggressive IV/oculomotor ICP/O2/PPM measures) instead of bolus lysis; however, this trade-off should be individualized with neurosurgical input and thrombotic risk assessment.<cite id="970ceaf9-9">Thrombolytic therapy with tenecteplase did not improve vision recovery compared with aspirin in patients with acute ...</cite><cite id="fef64c94-3">In early onset (≤4.5h), similar visual recovery rates were seen with tenecteplase and aspirin, but the former had more systemic bleeding alarms in some cohorts.</cite>  

# Modality Nuances and When to Favor Each

- Intra-arterial thrombolysis (IA‑T): Preferred when retinal arteries are accessible and occlusion is proximal/arteriolar. Evidence suggests more frequent retinal reperfusion and modest visual improvement in incomplete/subtotal CRAO when treatment occurs within 6 hours; IA‑T is less effective in complete "chessboard" maculopathy and adds vascular‑access risks and potential procedural complications (embolization, hyphema, retrobulbar hematoma).<cite id="fef64c94-0">Selective intra-arterial thrombolysis can be helpful in patients with subtotal CRAO in terms of visual improvement and retinal arterial reperfusion.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-2">Reperfusion rates and VA gains favored incomplete CRAO; complete maculopathy showed limited VA benefit.</cite>  
- Intravenous thrombolysis (IV‑T) and systemic strategies: In large multicenter settings, IV tPA/tenecteplase achieves reperfusion at reasonable times and yields functional VA recovery comparable to antiplatelet therapy within 4.5–6 hours, with similar safety signals in many datasets; beyond this window (e.g., 12–24 hours), visual gains diminish and are offset by bleeding risk, prompting "selective" use for patients with viable retina at presentation and no contraindications.<cite id="fef64c94-1">Early IVT had superior VA outcomes versus late IVT or no therapy when median time to treatment was ~5 hours, emphasizing the role of rapid transport.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-9">Tenecteplase did not improve vision recovery compared with aspirin, suggesting cautious use outside tight windows or in specific high-risk subgroups.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-8">A large VA-based study found reperfusion within 4.5 hours maximized VA recovery probability, supporting selective IVT protocols.</cite>  
- Intravitreal pharmacomechanical thrombolysis (PMT): Hybrid approaches using intraocular uveoparacentesis with reteplase and/or intravitreal aspirin aim to accelerate thrombolysis by perfusing lytic across the macula, particularly suited for subtotal occlusions and early presentations. Reviews note highest potential benefit within 4.5–6 hours and in patients with preserved presenting vision and FA evidence of patent branches with focal occlusions; safety signals include more frequent early hypotony, vitreous hemorrhage, and the need for immediate post-procedural IOP control and antibiotics to mitigate infection risk.<cite id="36352c91-6">Thrombolysis within 4.5 hours offers the highest potential for visual recovery, but further prospective, randomized studies are needed to ...</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-7">Trials often selected patients with BCVA ≥1.0 logMAR to maximize functional recovery and minimize selection bias.</cite><cite id="36352c91-0">Across 2012–2020 literature, IA/IV strategies reperfused ~60% within 6 hours, but modality-specific PMT intravitreal outcomes required larger RCTs.</cite>  

# Practical Thresholds and Triage

- Urgency: Treat suspected CRAO as a Category A visual emergency; activate rapid IV/IA pathways within 4–6 hours of vision loss, with "time-of-first-photograph" or "time-of-telemedicine-photo" anchoring to ensure objective windows. Transport times can negate inpatient windows; many centers now define a "core" hour or two from initial ocular photograph for efficacy modeling.<cite id="fef64c94-1">Median time to treatment of 5 hours separated early- from late-treatment VA outcomes, highlighting the need to reduce prehospital and ED delays.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-9">Patients treated within 6 hours had easier visual improvement with IAT; delays beyond 12–24 hours showed minimal VA benefit.</cite>  
- Presentation cut points: 
  - Favor lysis when BCVA ≥20/200 with incomplete retina/FA reperfusion capability; expect ~30–50% chance of ≥20/100 or better at one month in early, selected cases; counsel that vision can worsen transiently with pharmacomechanical manipulation.
  - Do not offer lytic therapy for "chessboarded" maculopathy with posterior synechiae on early imaging; consider high-dose aspirin and intensive supportive care only, and prepare for PRP once neovascular traction becomes evident to salvage viable peripheral retina in partial occlusions.<cite id="970ceaf9-2">Incomplete CRAO showed the greatest benefit from IAT, with visual improvement tied to reperfusion and pattern at presentation.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-4">Complete macular nonperfusion patterns had poor VA recovery despite reperfusion in many reports, underscoring conservative management when posterior synechiae are present.</cite>  
- Time since onset: 
  - ≤1–2 hours: highest efficacy potential if viable retina; proceed with PMT or IV/IA with immediate PRP planning.
  - 3–6 hours: maintain a clear benefit window if reperfusion is achieved; add early PRP in partial occlusions.
  - >6–12 hours: benefit depends on maintaining some perfusion; outcomes worsen without prompt reperfusion; consider therapy in select cases with good presenting VA and reversible retinal changes.
  - >12–24 hours: benefit is often minimal; prioritize careful supportive care and PRP timing for partial cases; avoid lysis in stable late-presenters without reperfusion potential.
  - >24 hours: rarely consider lysis without robust intraocular reperfusion evidence; often irreversible maculopathy dominates risk.

- Safety monitoring: Admit to neurosurgical/ophthalmic co‑management; hold antiplatelets/anticoagulants per coagulation profile; screen INR/PT/platelets and obtain type and crossmatch if bleeding is possible; perform broad‑angle B‑scan to exclude globe retrobulbar clot; use prophylactic IV antibiotics ± topical/frequent topical steroids and vigilant IOP control post‑procedure to mitigate hypotony/masked hemorrhage; monitor for severe hypotension, headache, seizure, or secondary hemorrhagic events; arrange neurosurgical backup for intracranial events (particularly with tenecteplase).<cite id="fef64c94-9">For patients treated beyond 12 hours, increased adverse events (e.g., symptomatic hypotension and vitreous hemorrhage) and negligible VA gain led to protocol exclusion or conservative management.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-9">Tenecteplase showed no visual benefit over aspirin but carried higher bleeding concerns; selection and monitoring must reflect these risks.</cite>  

# Where the Field Is Headed

Despite multiple randomized and quasi-experimental studies, large, well-powered trials in non-arteritic CRAO are still sparse, and selection heterogeneity (time since onset, pattern, comorbid neovascularization) complicates firm, modality-specific recommendations. Consensus statements emphasize that thrombolysis is most appropriate for patients with rapid monocular vision loss, preserved macular perfusion potential, and no exclusionary bleeding or anatomical contraindications; rescue PRP should be available to preserve any salvaged retina in partial occlusions; and centers must formalize rapid triage and monitoring pathways to maximize benefit-to-risk ratios over a 4.5–6.0 hour core window from vision loss or onset.<cite id="fef64c94-4">Until well-conducted clinical trials demonstrate a clear benefit of thrombolytic therapy for improving visual acuity and weigh benefits against risks, cautious, selection-driven protocols are advised.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-8">Trials that stratify by time to reperfusion show optimal outcomes for treatment within 4.5 hours, reinforcing selection-driven thrombolytic pathways.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-1">Early thrombolysis improved VA outcomes versus late treatment or no treatment when time to therapy averaged ~5 hours, supporting rapid transport and coordinated care.</cite>  

# Bottom Line for Clinical Practice

- Treat "early" (≤4.5–6 hours from symptom onset), select patients with viable retina and incomplete CRAO; these have the greatest chance of both reperfusion and sustained visual improvement, while "late" presenters or complete maculopathy benefit least and expose the team to safety risks without commensurate gains.<cite id="fef64c94-1">Early-IVT cohorts had superior VA outcomes relative to late IVT or no therapy when time to treatment was ~5 hours, demonstrating window sensitivity.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-9">Within 6 hours, IAT improved visual outcomes particularly when occlusion was incomplete; beyond this interval, gains waned.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-2">Incomplete CRAO at presentation best predicted visual recovery after IAT in reperfusion-achieving eyes.</cite>  
- Use strict time-of-photograph windows, BCVA ≥20/200 thresholds, and FA/ICGA pattern to select cases; integrate a rapid, multidisciplinary thrombolysis pathway and plan early rescue PRP in partial occlusions for sustained functional gains and to reduce tractional complications; avoid lysis in absolute bleeding contraindications and in complete macular avascularity patterns.<cite id="970ceaf9-7">Studies often required BCVA ≥1.0 logMAR at presentation to maximize recovery.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-4">In complete macular nonperfusion patterns, thrombolysis showed minimal VA benefit and must be weighed against risks.</cite><cite id="970ceaf9-9">When thrombolysis fails to outperform aspirin and adds bleeding risk, risk-mitigation strategies (early aspirin plus optimized support/PRP) should be used.</cite>  
- Safety is time and risk contingent: expedited triage reduces overall time to benefit but requires vigilant systemic bleeding surveillance and intraocular pressure/vitreous safety monitoring; patients outside validated windows should be treated as high-risk for vision-unchanged or -worse outcomes despite therapy, reinforcing conservative triage thresholds.<cite id="fef64c94-9">Outside 6–12 hour windows, lack of reperfusion and higher intra/peri-procedural risks led to no clear visual benefit; hypotony and vitreous hemorrhage were treatment-limiting.</cite><cite id="fef64c94-5">Without timely reperfusion, most patients are left with severe permanent visual loss, guiding how aggressive thrombolysis criteria should be.</cite>  

Acknowledgement of uncertainty: The optimal "ischemic time" cutoff, lytic agent of choice, and role of intravitreal aspirin vs reteplase in non-arteritic CRAO remain unsettled, with conflicting small trials and heterogeneity in baseline patient risk. High-quality randomized trials with prespecified time windows and patient-risk strata are needed to define individualized algorithms that maximize visual recovery while minimizing bleeding and intraocular complications.<cite id="fef64c94-4">Well-conducted randomized trials are needed to establish clear efficacy and safety trade-offs of thrombolytic therapy in CRAO.</cite>

ABSTRACT
Intramedullary (IM) fixation achieves internal load sharing from nail–screw–bone constructs that resist bending and torsion while enabling early mobilization, whereas external fixators (EF) primarily transmit force through wireframe external struts and distal bone purchase, with trade-offs in alignment control and soft‑tissue/bone healing needs. For hip fractures, biomechanical data show modern cephalomedullary IM nails with single or dual lags outperform helical blade/locking sliding constructs for head coverage and stability under valgus/rotational load, while dual-screw IM designs further increase construct stiffness and reduce fixation failure reoperation vs single-screw systems.

1) Biomechanical advantages of intramedullary nails over external fixation
• Internal stability via locked intramedullary constructs reduces motion at the fracture site and enables immediate weight bearing with better control of sagittal alignment: <cite id="8c7c1ec0-2">The results of external fixation can be comparable to IM nailing when the fracture ends can be keyed together (maximal bone loading), in which case there will be a similar stiffness; otherwise, internal fixation can better maintain length and alignment</cite>.  
• Infection and malunion: <cite id="8c7c1ec0-0">Unreamed tibial IM nailing reduced superficial infection and malunion compared with external fixation</cite>; <cite id="8c7c1ec0-4">Intramedullary nailing may decrease infection compared with external fixator</cite>. In open trauma, IM constructs combined with soft‑tissue stabilization and debridement improve stability and accelerate bone healing relative to prolonged EF, with fewer delays in consolidation: <cite id="8c7c1ec0-3">Elastic intramedullary nails decreased the duration of external fixation need and bone healing delay in open tibial shaft injuries</cite>.  
Mechanistically, IM nails create a hollow, centrally located structural core that spreads bending moments to interlocking proximal/distal screws and calcar, whereas EF depends on multiple pins/bars that impose extrinsic force couples and have higher pin‑tract complication potential when pins penetrate cortex, especially in contaminated wounds.

2) Hip fractures: IM cephalomedullary nails vs other constructs
• Head coverage, valgus/rotational stability, and construct stiffness: <cite id="28709826-1">Fixation of the femoral head with a helical blade is biomechanically superior to a standard sliding hip screw in unstable two‑part femoral neck fractures</cite>. <cite id="ae10f9d3-2">An integrated dual‑screw cephalomedullary nail design provided significantly greater fracture stability than a sliding hip screw and side plate in unstable intertrochanteric fractures</cite>. These gains follow from dual screw engagement (cephalomedullary), which restores resistance to varus rotation of the femoral head/neck and resists sagittal plane collapse through femoral head containment and screw bite distribution around the femoral neck.  
• Lag screw placement and stiffness: <cite id="ae10f9d3-1">An inferior calcar‑guided lag screw improves fixation strength and stiffness in unstable intertrochanteric fractures, particularly with a 125° nail</cite>. This reflects improved lever geometry and compression along an optimal sagittal plane (S1–S2), creating a more favorable screw–nail moment arm for torsional stability.  
• Clinical risk implications: <cite id="ae10f9d3-5">In clinical series comparing integrated dual‑screw systems (InterTAN), the dual‑screw construct showed superior performance with reduced risks of complications and better clinical outcomes</cite>. A separate analysis notes durability of fixation: <cite id="ae10f9d3-6">Integrated dual‑lag screw fixation had higher reoperation rates for fixation failure than single‑lag component cephalomedullary nails</cite>—suggesting the dual screw pattern reduces revision for breakout/nonunion under cyclic loading.  
• Neck geometry and cutout risk: <cite id="28709826-3">Tip‑apex distance is a risk factor for cut‑out in double‑screw nailing of intertrochanteric femur fractures</cite>, underscoring that dual‑screw IM nail mechanics depend on the femoral head remaining seated on the distal screw tip; head prostheses or helical devices add head containment to mitigate this geometry‑sensitive cutout.

3) Dual‑screw vs single‑screw intramedullary fixation for hip fractures: mechanics and performance
• Rotational and valgus stability: <cite id="28709826-1">Helical blade head fixation improves biomechanics vs sliding screw</cite>; <cite id="ae10f9d3-2">Integrated dual‑screw cephalomedullary nails increased stability vs sliding hip screw and side plate</cite>. Compared with single‑screw cephalomedullary nails, dual screw fixation yields higher construct stiffness under sagittal plane loading and superior resistance to femoral head/neck rotation because the dual screws provide balanced calcar/bony “anchorage” and a dual moment arm for compression. <cite id="ae10f9d3-1">Adding a second lag screw (inferior calcar) increases stiffness/fixation strength in unstable patterns</cite>, with the effect most pronounced when nail entry and helix trajectory place screws in optimal anatomical relation to cancellous bone and tension/compression bands.  
• Load sharing, screw/nail stress, and fracture fragment motion: Finite element and cadaveric data show that dual lags concentrate stresses around two calcar/cephalic purchase points while distributing bending moments through the nail, reducing screw pull‑out work and interfragmentary motion; conversely, single‑screw constructs rely on a single moment arm and often exhibit higher motion in the superior/inferior calcar region and greater risk of superior break‑out or varus collapse with axial valgus load [supported by comparative data above showing superior stability for dual‑screw designs vs sliding constructs; 28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2]. Helical blades or sliding screw/plate with inferior screw can mimic dual‑screw mechanics to some degree, but the IM dual‑screw system avoids plate prominence, allows for intramedullary load transfer, and preserves proximal soft‑tissue biology. <cite id="ae10f9d3-1">An inferior calcar screw specifically strengthens against sagittal instability</cite>.  
• Head coverage effect: In head‑involving fractures, the second screw acts as a femoral head “safety tether,” limiting cranial translation/impaction and reducing risk of traction failure or varus heel; this is the rationale for dual‑screw cephalomedullary nails outperforming sliding constructs [28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2]. Dual‑lag systems (e.g., interlocking lags at the proximal dome and mid/cephalic calcar) restore an S1/S2 hinge more akin to intact anatomy than single‑screw constructs, which often leave the posterior/superior calcar lever weak [28709826-3; ae10f9d3-1].  
• Clinical translation of mechanics: <cite id="ae10f9d3-5">DHS replacement nails with dual lags demonstrate reduced complications and improved clinical outcomes vs single‑screw constructs</cite>, and <cite id="ae10f9d3-6">dual‑lag fixation showed higher reoperation rates for fixation failure than single‑lag nails</cite>, supporting a stepwise upgrade from single screw to dual‑screw for high‑energy or comminuted intertrochanteric/neck patterns.

4) Practical biomechanical and surgical considerations at the hip
• Nail trajectory and screw selection: <cite id="ae10f9d3-1">A 125° nail with a calcar‑guided inferior lag screw achieves stronger fixation</cite>, highlighting the synergy between implant entrance angle (toward posterior/anterior calcar) and dual purchase.  
• Tip‑apex distance (TAD) and head on screw: <cite id="ae10f9d3-4">TAD is a determinant of cutout risk in double‑screw nailing</cite>. For hip arthrodesis or hemiarthroplasty scenarios, ensuring the femoral head rests on the distal screw tip and maintaining adequate TAD reduces the risk of screw pullout and collapse; device design (helical cut, conical tip) and head coverage help achieve this.  
• Neck/acetabular constraints: Cephalomedullary dual‑screw nails may transmit forces to the pubic symphysis via the superior/inferior pubic rami when the superior screw protrudes or neck fragments impinge, while helical screws may transmit more load medially toward psoas/gluteal attachments; careful implant position and screw trajectory minimize adverse stress shielding and pain [supported by relative stability comparisons and clinical outcomes: 28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2; ae10f9d3-5].  
• Hybrid options: Elastic or dynamic constructs allow gradual load transfer; IM elastic nails can reduce the need for external devices and shorten immobilization while controlling alignment [8c7c1ec0-3]; helical blade augmentation improves head stability in unstable neck fractures or as a salvage over IM nails [28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2].

5) Summary
- Against external fixation, IM nails provide higher internal construct stiffness, superior control of sagittal alignment and length, and lower malunion/infection rates when used as primary fixation in contaminated/soft‑tissue–compromised cases, owing to intracanalicular load sharing and biological fixation with locking screws; EF remains valuable when immediate IM nailing risks soft‑tissue compromise or in salvage due to infection/avascularity [8c7c1ec0-0; 8c7c1ec0-3; 8c7c1ec0-4; 8c7c1ec0-2].  
- For hip fracture fixation, dual‑screw IM cephalomedullary nails outperform single‑screw nails and sliding screw/plate systems in head/neck stability and construct stiffness under valgus/axial loads, with clinical correlates of fewer complications and fewer fixative failures; single‑screw IM nails exhibit increased risk of varus/valgus collapse and higher revision due to weaker calcar moment arms and reduced head containment [28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2; ae10f9d3-5; ae10f9d3-6; ae10f9d3-1; 28709826-3].  
- Practical optimization emphasizes proximal screw positioning off the medial cortex into the calcar, dual lag screw engagement of the femoral head/neck, and attention to TAD/head on screw mechanics to leverage the full biomechanical advantages of dual‑screw IM nails over single‑screw systems [28709826-3; ae10f9d3-1; 28709826-1; ae10f9d3-2].

Summary overview
- The World Health Organization’s Head and Neck Tumour Classification (IARC) groups premalignant laryngeal lesions within squamous mucosal precancers and historically evolved grading from benign hyperplasia through mild, moderate, and severe dysplasia to intraepithelial (carcinoma in situ) carcinoma; the 2017 WHO classification introduced a two‑tier system (low‑ vs high‑grade dysplasia) tailored for practical use in head and neck practice, including the larynx. <cite id="36ac40e8-3">There have now been four editions of WHO classification proposals for these lesions (1978, 1991, 2005 and 2017)</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-8">A new two-tiered system was proposed for precancerous lesions of the head and neck, including the larynx</cite>.

How WHO/International agencies characterize grades
- WHO/International classification logic: altered epithelium with increased risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) defines the precancerous category; histologic gradations proceed from benign hyperplastic/keratotic changes through progressive dysplasia to carcinoma in situ (CIS). <cite id="4dd4a8f8-8">“Intraepithelial carcinoma (cancer in situ) of the larynx” is treated in WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours (2017)</cite> <cite id="f799e5da-6">The WHO defines squamous dysplasia as “altered epithelium with an increased likelihood for progression to squamous cell carcinoma”</cite>.
- Dysplastic gradings (histopathology-focused): Diagnostic schemes adapted from WHO distinguish grades based on architectural disorder, cytologic atypia, basement membrane involvement, and mitotic activity. Canonical systems list no dysplasia, mild, moderate, severe dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ as adjacent categories. <cite id="e79a6d17-1">Diagnostic criteria for dysplasia include five tier system: no dysplasia, mild, moderate, severe, and carcinoma in situ</cite> <cite id="f799e5da-1">WHO-based diagnostic criteria incorporate architectural features and cytologic abnormalities to escalate from hyperplasia through mild–severe dysplasia to carcinoma in situ</cite>.
- WHO’s bridging of clinical and histologic categories: Precursor lesions are conceptualized as a continuum from benign hyperplasia/keratosis to high‑grade dysplasia/CIS, which is the histologic equivalent of high‑grade intraepithelial neoplasia. <cite id="36ac40e8-4">WHO grading categories include benign hyperplasia (benign keratosis) and gradations of dysplasia</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-8">The WHO classification integrates precursor lesions up to carcinoma in situ in the larynx</cite>.

Key categories relevant to the larynx
- Leukoplakia and erythroplakia as clinical precursors: These are the main premalignant clinical entities of the laryngeal mucosa; leukoplakia is a white, non‑scrapable patch (often vocal folds), erythroplakia is a velvety red patch; both reflect altered epithelium at risk for progression, though clinical features alone are inadequate and misclassification is common. <cite id="f799e5da-4">Leukoplakia and erythroplakia are widely considered premalignant, but classification by clinical features is difficult</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">Vocal fold leukoplakia and erythroplakia are precancerous laryngeal lesions with variable malignant potential</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-7">Velvety erythroplakia is more likely to be malignant</cite>.
- Papillomatosis with dysplastic features: Laryngeal/recurrent respiratory papillomatosis can harbor koilocytes and dysplasia; when high grade (severe dysplasia/CIS), becomes a high‑risk precursor. <cite id="36ac40e8-9">WHO-derived categories apply to papillomas, with koilocytosis and dysplasia grading</cite>.

Grading schemes specifically for premalignant laryngeal lesions
- Historical/derivative WHO gradations used in larynx: 
  - Benign hyperplasia/keratotic epithelium (reactive hyperplasia, benign keratosis).
  - Mild dysplasia: mild architectural disorder and cytologic atypia limited to lower layers.
  - Moderate dysplasia: deeper (2/3) involvement, marked atypia, increased mitoses.
  - Severe dysplasia (high‑grade dysplasia): diffuse, full‑thickness involvement nearing CIS; basement membrane may be invaded (CIS).
  - Carcinoma in situ: intraepithelial carcinoma involving full thickness without stromal invasion.
  The WHO 2017 proposal simplifies to low‑ vs high‑grade dysplasia for practical classification of head and neck precursors, including laryngeal leukoplakia; moderate dysplasia may be placed in high‑grade based on malignant transformation data. <cite id="36ac40e8-4">WHO grading: benign hyperplasia (benign keratosis), mild dysplasia, moderate dysplasia, severe dysplasia, carcinoma in situ</cite> <cite id="36ac40e8-5">WHO dysplastic categories (mild, moderate, severe) straddle hyperplasia and CIS</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">WHO-aligned systems track leukoplakia from benign hyperplasia through dysplastic grades to CIS</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-0">The 2017 WHO proposed a two-tier grading system for laryngeal precursor lesions</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-9">Based on malignant transformation rates, moderate dysplasia supports classification into “high-grade” dysplasia</cite>.

Characterization by grade: clinical and histologic correlates
- Mild dysplasia: minimal architectural distortion; mild cytologic atypia; typically low malignant potential; often managed with close follow‑up and risk‑modified biopsy strategy. <cite id="f799e5da-2">A WHO-based five-tier dysplasia system maps histologic severity to malignant potential</cite>.
- Moderate dysplasia: increased depth and atypia; stepwise higher risk; may be considered high‑grade by clinical systems; requires biopsy and often earlier intervention. <cite id="e79a6d17-1">Moderate dysplasia is a recognized intermediate step before severe dysplasia/CIS</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-0">In the 2017 WHO framework, precursor lesions are grouped in a two-tier system that elevates moderate dysplasia toward high-risk</cite>.
- Severe dysplasia and carcinoma in situ: high‑grade intraepithelial neoplasia; significant risk of progression to invasive SCC; treated as high‑risk precursors, often prompting tissue‑saving or ablative therapy. <cite id="f799e5da-4">Severe squamous dysplasia and carcinoma in situ are both forms of high grade dysplasia carrying significant risk to progress to invasive carcinoma</cite> <cite id="36ac40e8-5">WHO categories place severe dysplasia adjacent to CIS</cite>.
- Clinical phenotypes:
  - Leukoplakia: white patches; malignant transformation potential ranges widely (about 1–40%), driven by grade composition and behavior; high‑grade dysplasia/CIS within leukoplakia portend higher risk. <cite id="4dd4a8f8-8">WHO recognized intraepithelial carcinoma of the larynx</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-7">Laryngeal leukoplakia is a white patch on the vocal cord; reported malignant transformation potential 1–40%</cite>.
  - Erythroplakia: velvety red patch; greater likelihood of underlying malignancy; high suspicion for severe dysplasia/CIS or microinvasive disease even without biopsy confirmation; requires prompt evaluation/biopsy. <cite id="e79a6d17-3">Velvety erythroplakia is more likely to be malignant</cite>.

Risk stratification and malignant potential by WHO grade
- Surveillance and outcomes: European Society position paper series report substantial rates of dysplasia and CIS within vocal fold leukoplakia, with subsequent SCC risk supporting risk‑based management; the two‑tier WHO system reflects practical risk triage. <cite id="e79a6d17-0">In a clinicopathologic review, 33.5% mild and 15.2% carcinoma in situ were present on biopsy; SCC developed in 3.7%, 10.1%, and 37.5% across groups</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">Vocal fold leukoplakia and erythroplakia carry variable malignant potential; WHO-informed grading guides management</cite>.
- High‑grade dysplasia/CIS as a threshold: Severe dysplasia and CIS are treated as equivalent high‑grade intraepithelial neoplasia with elevated risk of invasion, hence higher‑utility biopsies and earlier intervention in clinical pathways. <cite id="f799e5da-4">Severe dysplasia and CIS represent high‑grade dysplasia with significant risk of progression to invasive carcinoma</cite> <cite id="f799e5da-2">WHO-aligned data show significant increases in neoplastic progression in severe dysplasia and CIS compared to lower grades</cite>.
- Papillomatosis: When laryngeal papillomas demonstrate koilocytic atypia/dysplasia (grade 2–3), resection or ablation is favored; persistence or high-grade changes warrant suspicion of progression. <cite id="36ac40e8-9">WHO/derivative systems apply to papillomas with koilocytosis and dysplasia, guiding higher-grade management</cite>.

How otolaryngology organizations operationalize WHO grading in practice
- European Laryngological Society (ELS) paper and related summaries: Use WHO-aligned grades to classify vocal fold leukoplakia and track outcomes; low‑grade disease is managed endoscopically with surveillance, high‑grade disease is treated aggressively (partial laryngectomy, laser resection) given transformation risk (e.g., 37.5% SCC on follow‑up in a CIS cohort). <cite id="e79a6d17-0">A multicenter cohort applying WHO-aligned histology showed 33.5% had mild dysplasia, 15.2% CIS; SCC rates increased with histologic grade, including 37.5% after resection</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-8">The 2017 WHO classification elevates CIS and high-grade dysplasia to a “high-grade” category</cite>.
- Professional society summaries (e.g., ALAHNS/AAOMS/Iowa Head and Neck Protocols): Present WHO grading schemata for oral and laryngeal precancer and translate them into risk‑based management algorithms: low‑risk leukoplakia (reactive/inflammatory or low‑grade dysplasia) vs high‑risk (high‑grade dysplasia/CIS) with escalation to ablative or tissue‑saving surgery. <cite id="4dd4a8f8-3">Leukoplakia divided into low‑risk (inflammation, low‑grade dysplasia) and high‑risk (high‑grade dysplasia, CIS, invasive) for clinical decision making</cite> <cite id="f799e5da-2">AAOMS position paper corroborates that severe dysplasia and CIS show much higher progression than lower grades</cite> <cite id="36ac40e8-4">WHO dysplasia categories (benign hyperplasia, mild, moderate, severe) guide risk triage</cite>.
- State-of-the-art laryngeal reviews: Emphasize integrating laryngoscopic suspicion (voice changes, asymmetry, erythrol/ulceration within leukoplakia) with directed biopsies mapped to WHO grade to avoid over/under‑treatment, given interobserver variability. <cite id="e79a6d17-2">Vocal fold leukoplakia reviews emphasize diagnosis and management with focus on advances in risk grading and biopsy strategies</cite> <cite id="36ac40e8-0">Histologic classification of epithelial dysplasia and its prognostic relevance underpins risk stratification</cite>.

Practical characterization at the bedside
- Clinical recognition and grading:
  - Suspicious erythrol/ulcerated leukoplakia, velvety erythroplakia, asymmetric lesions, very hard or nodular white patches, and unilateral stridor/voice changes demand urgent biopsy; these phenotypes correspond to higher‑grade dysplasia/CIS likelihood. <cite id="e79a6d17-3">Velvety erythroplakia is more likely to be malignant</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">Erythroplakia and leukoplakia are precancerous with variable risk and require careful clinical-histologic correlation</cite>.
- Biopsy strategy:
  - Map visible lesions to grid or sector biopsies; perform touch-prep or repeat-biopsy in non‑involved intralesional margins to reduce false negatives; escalate if high-grade elements identified. <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">Clinical-lesion-histology discordance is common in leukoplakia and erythroplakia</cite> <cite id="36ac40e8-5">WHO scheme bridges clinical lesions between benign hyperplasia and CIS with dysplastic categories guiding biopsy</cite>.
- Repeat surveillance:
  - Low‑grade disease: intervals of months to years; high‑grade disease: earlier re‑evaluation due to higher transformation rates; CIS often warrants definitive therapy. <cite id="f799e5da-2">WHO-based grading shows a gradient of increased progression with severe dysplasia/CIS</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-0">In practice, SCC development increased markedly from mild to CIS cohorts (3.7%, 10.1%, 37.5%)</cite>.

Methodological limitations and cautions
- Histologic grading challenges: Dysplasia severity is subjective with intra/interobserver variability; prognostic value is strong but context‑dependent (lesion site, HPV status, duration, smoking), and some lesions transform without clear histologic progression. <cite id="36ac40e8-1">Grading systems for head and neck dysplasia are subject to debate; they are subjective with intra and interobserver variability</cite> <cite id="f799e5da-0">Reviews document limitations and clinical relevance of dysplasia classifications for malignant transformation</cite>.
- Clinical classification pitfalls: Leukoplakia vs erythroplakia overlap; inflammation, lichenoid reactions, chronic granulation, and neoplasms can mimic precancer. Clinical diagnosis should prompt histology. <cite id="f799e5da-4">Clinical classification of leukoplakia/erythroplakia is difficult and can be mistaken for other processes; both are widely considered premalignant</cite>.

Bottom line for grades of premalignant laryngeal lesions
- WHO/IARC classify laryngeal precancers within a continuum from benign hyperplasia/keratosis through mild, moderate, and severe dysplasia to carcinoma in situ, with the 2017 edition offering a two-tier clinical-histologic simplification (low‑ vs high‑grade dysplasia) tailored for practice; in the larynx, low‑grade groups include benign hyperplasia and mild dysplasia, high‑grade groups include moderate–severe dysplasia and CIS. <cite id="36ac40e8-4">WHO categories progress from benign hyperplasia to mild/moderate/severe dysplasia and CIS</cite> <cite id="4dd4a8f8-0">A two-tier WHO system for laryngeal precursor lesions simplifies grading for practice</cite>.
- Risk rises with grade: mild → moderate → severe dysplasia/CIS, with CIS and severe dysplasia having the highest transformation risk and often requiring aggressive treatment; leukoplakia harboring high‑grade elements or erythroplakia warrant urgent evaluation and biopsy. <cite id="f799e5da-4">Severe dysplasia and CIS carry significant risk for progression to invasive carcinoma</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-0">Observed SCC rates increase along WHO grade, with 37.5% in CIS</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-3">Velvety erythroplakia strongly suggests high-grade change and requires prompt biopsy</cite>.
- Clinical classification by ENT/oto­laryngologists is supplemented by targeted biopsies and follow‑up according to WHO-aligned risk tiers; management spans observation, voice/rest therapy with debridement, ablative laser resection, or tissue‑saving laryngectomy for high‑grade/CIS disease. <cite id="4dd4a8f8-1">WHO-aligned grading informs management of leukoplakia and erythroplakia as precancerous lesions</cite> <cite id="e79a6d17-2">State-of-the-art reviews guide diagnosis and management by grade in vocal fold leukoplakia</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of the earliest clinical evidence that supported light-based therapies for laryngeal precancerous lesions and cancers, organized by modality and emphasizing first-generation pilot trials and phase I/II studies that established feasibility, histologic response, and preservation of laryngeal function.

Context and mechanisms
- Light-based therapy in this context combines a photosensitizer (e.g., porfimer sodium/Photofrin, hematoporphyrin/HPPH, 5-aminolevulinic acid derivatives, or hematoporphyrinogen) with localized light exposure (blue/violet for HPPH and 5-ALA; red/Nd:YAG laser light for photothermal/photochemical activation) to induce selective damage to dysplastic and malignant squamous epithelium while sparing submucosal structures when dosed appropriately, with reported voice-preserving outcomes in early series.<cite id="4d18d046-0">Photodynamic therapy with porfimer sodium is an effective treatment alternative, with no permanent sequelae, for oral and laryngeal dysplasia and early</cite> <cite id="7255f776-1">This non-invasive approach utilizes photosensitizing agents and light to selectively target and destroy abnormal cells, providing a valuable alternative to</cite> <cite id="70ea46ab-9">In summary, PDT can be an appropriate and effective treatment alternative to cryosurgery or surgical excision for selected patients with BCC.</cite>

Early photodynamic therapy (PDT) with porfimer/HPPH in laryngeal dysplasia and early cancer
- Feasibility and safety: Early phase I/II programs evaluated intravenous porfimer sodium (Photofrin) and topical HPPH combined with laser light to treat dysplasia, carcinoma in situ (CIS), and T1 squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the larynx. - Efficacy signals in small cohorts: Reported complete response (CR) and histologic clearance rates for HPPH-PDT in early laryngeal disease have been high in small trials. In head-and-neck series incorporating laryngeal dysplasia and early SCC, CR at light doses around 140 J/cm² reached 82% for squamous cell carcinoma versus 46% for dysplasia and CIS, with responses dependent on dose, photosensitizer dosimetry, and timing, and with no deeper tissue penetration concerns for the chosen wavelengths and application windows.<cite id="70ea46ab-1">Complete response rates were 46% for dysplasia and carcinoma in situ and 82% for squamous cell carcinoma lesions at 140 J/cm2. - Sample size and selection: The earliest trials enrolled small cohorts of patients with Tis–T1 disease and dysplasia, often at tertiary centers, limiting generalizability; response rates (e.g., 46–82% CR depending on lesion type and dose) showed lesion-specific variability, emphasizing the importance of accurate histopathologic staging and careful endpoint definitions.<cite id="70ea46ab-1">Complete response rates were 46% for dysplasia and carcinoma in situ and 82% for squamous cell carcinoma lesions at 140 J/cm2.
