Overview: Two mechanistic routes in PDT
- Photodynamic therapy activates a photosensitizer (PS) with light to generate cytotoxic reactive oxygen species (ROS) that kill tumor cells and disrupt vasculature, with the two main mechanisms categorized by ROS generation: Type I (radical-mediated) and Type II (singlet oxygen–mediated). <cite id="0a3e860f-2">Type I mechanism: the excited photosensitizer engages in electron transfer (ET) or hydrogen transfer (HT), producing radical cations/ions that initiate oxidative chain reactions; Type II mechanism: energy transfer excites molecular oxygen to singlet oxygen (1O2) that oxidizes biological targets</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-0">Photodynamic therapy can be divided into two types based on ROS generation mechanisms—Type I PDT via ET/HT and Type II PDT via energy transfer to oxygen</cite> <cite id="e6d9d247-2">In Type II PDT, energy is transferred from triplet PS to triplet oxygen to produce cytotoxic singlet oxygen</cite>.

How Type I PDT generates ROS and induces cell death
- Radical generation and peroxidative cascade: In Type I PDT, the excited PS (usually a type I sensitizer) donates an electron or hydrogen to a substrate, forming radical species (e.g., alkoxyl/free radicals from membrane plasmalogens) that propagate oxidation, yielding lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH), H2O2, and ultimately •OH via metal-catalyzed Haber–Weiss/ Fenton chemistry. <cite id="0a3e860f-0">Cell death occurs due to cytotoxic ROS in PDT, especially hydroxyl radical (Type II) and singlet oxygen (Type II), but Type I pathways originate in radical-based damage as well</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type-I PDT exploits plasmalogens to trigger intramitochondrial lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction as a route to tumor cell death</cite> <cite id="e6d9d247-4">Type I PDT definitions emphasize photosensitized oxidation reactions via one-electron transfer to substrates, followed by radical-radical recombination or disproportionation to H2O2 and lipid peroxidation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-9">Cellular lipid peroxidation at plasmalogens and mitochondrial oxidative damage are central mechanisms in type I PDT-induced death</cite>.
- Cellular targets and death modalities: Radical attacks on polyunsaturated fatty acids in membranes trigger oncosis-like morphological changes and mitochondrial permeability transition, with concurrent apoptosis signaling when mitochondria are targeted or damaged. <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeted Type I PDT drives mitochondrial oxidative stress, depolarization, and apoptosis while producing strong immune-activating signals</cite> <cite id="0a3e860f-3">PDT generates ROS that cause oxidative damage across biomolecules and triggers diverse cell death pathways, including mitochondrial injury–related apoptosis</cite>. Apoptosis can proceed via intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (death receptor) routes when 1O2 also engages Fas or TNFR family and radicals trigger mitochondrial dysfunction. <cite id="f674671e-2">Singlet oxygen can induce apoptosis through both extrinsic and intrinsic pathways</cite> <cite id="f674671e-1">Singlet oxygen initiates apoptosis while radicals amplify tissue damage and can converge on mitochondrial apoptosis induction</cite>.
- Oxygen dependence and hypoxia bias: Type I reactions are more efficient in normoxia (abundant 3O2 to sustain radical recombination and H2O2/LOOH formation), whereas under severe hypoxia both mechanisms suffer, but radical-driven mitochondrial oxidative stress can dominate when PS localize to mitochondria. <cite id="e6d9d247-9">PDT efficacy is limited by hypoxia because it depends on oxygen for ROS generation; most common mechanisms rely on singlet oxygen (Type II) which is oxygen dependent</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-9">Hypoxic tumor environments reduce PDT efficacy due to oxygen limitation of ROS formation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting Type I PDT is being developed to enhance therapy in hypoxic tumors by leveraging localized oxygen consumption and plasmalogens</cite>.

How Type II PDT generates ROS and induces cell death
- Singlet oxygen production and direct oxygenation: Type II photosensitizers transfer energy to ground-state triplet oxygen (3O2), populating the 1Δg state (1O2), which directly oxidizes double bonds, amino acids, peptides, and biomolecule adducts without requiring initial electron transfer. <cite id="0a3e860f-8">Singlet oxygen is produced directly by energy transfer from excited sensitizers and oxidizes cellular components to cause damage and death</cite> <cite id="e6d9d247-2">Energy transfer from triplet PS to triplet oxygen produces cytotoxic 1O2</cite> <cite id="0a3e860f-6">1O2 has well-established properties, production routes, and detection in PDT</cite>. Other, lower-abundance ROS like superoxide and hydroxyl radicals may form secondarily (e.g., via reverse ET or Haber–Weiss/Fenton reactions) but are not primary mediators. <cite id="f674671e-3">In Type II PDT, 1O2 is formed by energy transfer, while other ROS such as superoxide and hydroxyl radical can arise secondarily</cite>.
- Cellular targets and death modalities: Direct oxygenation of membrane lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids produces lesions that trigger oncosis-like necrosis, while concurrent mitochondrial oxidative stress and ROS-mediated mitochondrial apoptosis pathways lead to mixed necrosis/apoptosis. <cite id="79a9b605-6">PDT generates oxidative stress leading to shutdown of intratumoral vasculature, necrosis, and apoptosis, with immune system activation</cite> <cite id="0a3e860f-0">Type II cytotoxicity is prominently mediated by singlet oxygen; Type I by hydroxyl radical; both damage biomolecules and precipitate cell death</cite>. 1O2-initiated apoptosis can be extrinsic (death receptor) or intrinsic (mitochondrial), and 1O2 can initiate signaling that culminates in mitochondrial apoptosis, yielding mixed death phenotypes in vivo. <cite id="f674671e-2">1O2-induced apoptosis engages both extrinsic and intrinsic pathways</cite> <cite id="f674671e-1">Singlet oxygen initiates apoptosis and amplifies ROS/RNS signaling, promoting mitochondrial apoptosis induction</cite>.
- Oxygen dependence and hypoxia bias: Type II PDT is intrinsically oxygen-dependent because 1O2 derives from 3O2; hypoxia reduces 1O2 yield and overall efficacy. However, strategies that deliver mitochondrial-localizing, type I-oriented PS can partially bypass oxygen constraints by driving plasmalogen peroxidation within mitochondria. <cite id="0a3e860f-9">PDT efficacy decreases under hypoxia due to the central role of oxygen in ROS generation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type I PDT enhances activity under hypoxia by targeting oxygen consumption at plasmalogens and mitochondria</cite>.

Comparative synthesis: ROS generation and cell-death effects
- Primary ROS species and pathways: In Type I PDT, one-electron transfer creates radical intermediates (plasmalogen alkoxyl/LOO•, H2O2) that propagate lipid peroxidation and damage proteins/DNA; downstream effects include oncosis with mitochondrial permeability injury and both apoptosis and necrosis depending on localization and secondarily produced •OH and mitochondrial involvement. <cite id="0a3e860f-0">Cytotoxic ROS, especially hydroxyl radical, drive damage in PDT</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-1">Singlet oxygen amplifies ROS/RNS signaling and triggers mitochondrial apoptosis induction</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-10">Mitochondrial oxidative stress and cytochrome c release are central to death signaling in PDT; oncosis and immune activation follow</cite>. In Type II PDT, primary cytotoxic species is 1O2, which directly oxidizes substrates without needing radical intermediates; apoptosis and necrosis arise from membrane damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA oxidation, and cross-talk with radicals/H2O2. <cite id="0a3e860f-8">Singlet oxygen directly oxidizes cellular components and mediates cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="f674671e-1">1O2 initiates apoptosis with downstream amplification via ROS/RNS</cite>.
- Spatial specificity and death morphologies: Type I reactions initiated at membranes (e.g., plasmalogens) tend to drive necrosis-like oncosis with lipid/protein damage, whereas mitochondrial localization (MitopTD) shifts damage to mitochondria, favoring apoptosis; Type II 1O2 often causes diffuse membrane and protein/DNA oxidative damage, producing mixed apoptosis/necrosis within the same cell. <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeted type I PDT localizes oxidative damage to mitochondria, causing oxidative stress, depolarization, apoptosis, and immune activation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-0">Type I PDT involves direct radical pair recombination and peroxidative damage at plasmalogens, leading to cytotoxicity; Type II PDT uses 1O2 to damage cellular components</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-6">Overall PDT produces necrosis and apoptosis with vascular shutdown and immune activation</cite>.
- Oxygen dependence and hypoxia: Type II is more sensitive to global oxygen levels because 1O2 production requires oxygen; under hypoxia PDT efficacy falls, though mitochondrial-type I mechanisms can better engage oxygen consumption within mitochondria. <cite id="0a3e860f-9">Hypoxia reduces PDT efficacy because ROS generation depends on oxygen</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-9">In hypoxic tumor environments, PDT is reduced due to oxygen-limited ROS formation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type I PDT is promising for hypoxia-tolerant therapy by enhancing localized oxygen utilization and radical formation at plasmalogens</cite>.
- Broader tissue effects and immunomodulation: Both mechanisms disrupt vasculature and trigger immune activation; 1O2 may modulate immune signaling through effects on catalase/HOCl, while radical-driven mitochondrial apoptosis can also activate dendritic-cell maturation and cytotoxic T-cell responses, again with a mixed-death landscape. <cite id="79a9b605-6">PDT shuts down intratumoral vasculature and activates the immune system as a mixture of necrosis and apoptosis contributes to tumor kill</cite> <cite id="f674671e-0">1O2 can alter catalase activity and induce immunomodulation via HOCl signaling</cite>.

Design and selection implications
- Mechanism choice via photosensitizer class and targeting: Type I-dominant porphyrins/phenanthridinium and mitochondrial-localizing PS bias PDT toward plasmalogen/H2O2–mediated mitochondrial apoptosis under normoxia, whereas type II phthalocyanines/porphyrins with strong energy transfer favor 1O2-mediated membrane/protein/nuclear damage and mixed cell death. <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type I PDT exploits specific PS design to enhance mitochondrial oxidative stress and apoptotic signaling</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type I PDT holds promise in hypoxia by enhancing photo-immunotherapy</cite> <cite id="0a3e860f-2">Type I (radical) versus Type II (1O2) distinctions map to differing PS classes and reaction pathways</cite>.
- Oxygen management: Strategies to alleviate hypoxia include increasing local oxygenation, photothermal oxygen release, or using mitochondrial-targeted type I PS that concentrate reactions where oxygen is locally consumed. <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeting type I PDT is being developed to overcome hypoxia limitations and strengthen immune responses</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-9">Hypoxia significantly reduces PDT efficacy, underscoring the need to manage oxygen for ROS generation</cite>.
- Anticipated cell-death signatures: Expect lipid/protein/DNA oxidation with mitochondrial depolarization and caspase activation (apoptosis) alongside oncosis-like swelling, membrane rupture (necrosis) in both types; apoptosis fractions may rise with mitochondrial targeting or 1O2-mediated mitochondrial damage, while necrosis is prominent when radicals dominate membrane damage. <cite id="79a9b605-6">PDT produces a mixture of necrosis and apoptosis with vascular and immune effects</cite> <cite id="f674671e-2">1O2 can trigger classical apoptotic pathways</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-1">ROS/RNS amplification by 1O2 promotes mitochondrial apoptosis induction</cite>.

Summary contrast
- ROS generation: Type I relies on photosensitizer ET/HT to generate radicals at biologics (plasmalogens, proteins) that peroxidatively form H2O2 and •OH; Type II transfers energy to oxygen to create 1O2 that directly oxidizes biomolecules without requiring initial electron transfer. <cite id="0a3e860f-2">Type I (ET/HT to radicals) versus Type II (energy transfer to 1O2) distinguish PDT reactions</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-0">Type I PDT involves radical pair recombination and peroxidation; Type II PDT produces singlet oxygen as the cytotoxin</cite> <cite id="f674671e-3">1O2 is primary in Type II; superoxide/hydroxyl may arise secondarily</cite>.
- Cell death: Type I often initiates necrosis-like oncosis at membranes but can be redirected to mitochondria to induce apoptosis and immunogenic signals; Type II predominantly causes mixed apoptosis/necrosis via 1O2-induced oxidative lesions across membranes, proteins, and nuclei, with immunomodulation depending on downstream ROS/1O2 signaling. <cite id="79a9b605-6">PDT yields necrosis and apoptosis with immune activation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeted type I PDT enhances apoptotic and immune responses</cite> <cite id="f674671e-2">1O2-driven apoptosis through extrinsic/intrinsic routes</cite> <cite id="f674671e-0">1O2 alters catalase and induces immunomodulation via HOCl signaling</cite>.
- Oxygen dependence: Both require oxygen, but Type II is more globally constrained by tumor pO2; Type I and mitochondrial-targeted designs can better exploit localized oxygen use and membrane/mitochondrial chemistry for effective killing. <cite id="0a3e860f-9">PDT efficacy reduces under hypoxia due to oxygen-dependent ROS generation</cite> <cite id="79a9b605-2">Mitochondria-targeted type I PDT enhances hypoxia-tolerant therapy by leveraging mitochondrial oxygen consumption and plasmalogen targeting</cite>.

# Bottom line

Compared with conventional mechanical nasal packing, fibrin-derived nasal packing materials (fibrin sealants or sprayable fibrin adhesive; degradable/“fibrin-like” biomaterial strips/foams) generally improve early hemostasis and reduce hemorrhage and patient discomfort, with lower odds of packing-related removal/complications, and tend to yield better endoscopic and crusting outcomes at follow‑up.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Postoperative hemorrhage occurred in 22.9–25% with nasal packing versus 3.1–4.65% in fibrin sealant groups (late hemorrhage only)</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-2">Vaiman and colleagues have shown that fibrin sealant administered by aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Patients who underwent packing experienced significantly more postoperative pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance compared with packing-free or alternative strategies</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-7">Biodegradable polyurethane foam (Nasopore) nasal packing is a safe and effective option after FESS, with minimal discomfort and few postoperative complications</cite>. Across biomaterial classes used as nasal packs, gelatin-, hyaluronic-acid-, chitosan-, and starch-derived materials have shown better endoscopic scores and less crusting than polyvinyl alcohol (silicone) and other nonbiodegradable materials, although “fibrin” and “fibrin-like” biomaterial strips typically perform favorably among biodegradables in terms of mucosal healing and patient comfort.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal pack without additives showed improvement in overall nasal endoscopy score and degree of crusting as early as 2 weeks compared with controls</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Chitosan, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, and starch-derived materials exhibit better endoscopic scores and significant potential for use in nasal packing; they were associated with better outcomes than materials with higher crusting/necrosis</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Anatomical success was 59.56% with early removal of silicone tube and 70.29% with absorbable nasal packing material; functional success paralleled these trends</cite>.

Below, I compare fibrin-derived materials to other pack types on the specific outcomes you requested (crusting, granulation, endoscopic scores), and summarize where randomized and meta-analytic evidence is strongest.

# Materials used as comparators

Mechanical nasal packing historically uses Merocel (nondegradable), absorbable gelfoam/oxidized cellulose (Avitum/TraVase), and silicone sponge/tubes; emerging “biomaterial” degradable foams (e.g., Nasopore polyurethane) and hyaluronic-acid/gelatin/chitosan strips aim to reduce foreign-body reactions and improve healing.<cite id="5f638ad4-9">Fibrin sealants in head-and-neck soft tissue surgery have favorable perioperative performance; comparative biomaterial studies document improved outcomes with biodegradable foams versus traditional packing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable nasal packing significantly improved postoperative symptoms including bleeding at removal, pain in situ, etc., versus nondegradable packing</cite>.

# Fibrin-derived materials

Aerosolized/dispersed fibrin sealant (e.g., Tisseel) has been directly compared with biodegradable foam (Nasopore) in endoscopic sinus surgery and with nasal packing regimens in endonasal procedures, consistently favoring fibrin-based sealants for hemostasis, convenience, and patient tolerance.<cite id="5f638ad4-0">Aerosolized fibrin sealant vs biodegradable synthetic polyurethane foam (Nasopore) was evaluated for hemostasis and wound healing after endoscopic sinus surgery</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-1">In endonasal operations, postoperative hemorrhage was 22.9–25% with packing vs 3.12–4.65% with fibrin sealant</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-4">In head-and-neck soft tissue surgery, fibrin sealants show perioperative benefits including similar operative time and trend toward fewer complications</cite>. In septoplasty and conchotomy, randomized trials and prospective cohorts similarly report that aerosolized/standard fibrin tissue adhesive is an effective and convenient substitute for packing, with fewer blood loss/dissemination concerns than liquid fibrin “glue,” and improved early recovery profiles versus packed nasal cavities.<cite id="eefedf99-6">A prospective randomized trial showed fibrin sealant via aerosol spray in endonasal surgery is more effective and convenient than nasal packing</cite><cite id="eefedf99-0">In head-and-neck operations, hemostasis and wound appearance with fibrin sealant versus synthetic foam packing favored fibrin-based products</cite>.

Brand- and material-specific “fibrin-like” degradable strips/foams (e.g., Nasopore-like biopolymeric foams, chitosan/gelatin/hyaluronic-acid strips) are widely studied and, when biodegradable, show lower symptom burden and better endoscopic scores than silicone, with hyaluronic-acid and chitosan often outperforming polyurethane foams on crusting and healing indices.<cite id="d8457a6e-0">Chitosan, gelatin, hyaluronic acid, starch-derived materials exhibited better endoscopic scores and were associated with significantly lower crusting and necrosis compared with polymeric foams that cause more mucus plug formation and encrustation</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal packs improved endoscopic scoring of the nasal cavity and reduced crusting compared with other materials in early follow-up, supporting better mucosal healing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing materials outperformed silicone-based tubes on both anatomical and functional endpoints (70.3% vs 59.6%), aligning with reduced foreign-body reaction and crusting/fistula</cite>. 

# Comparisons to other packing materials

Crusting and mucosal encrustation
- Fibrin-derived: Trials report less frequent need for removal due to bleeding and less crusting/mucus plug formation; randomized comparisons favor fibrin sealants over packing for bleeding-related complications that drive crusting and encrustation, with higher patient satisfaction and tolerance.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Late hemorrhage rates were 3.1–4.65% with fibrin sealant vs 22.9–25% with packing; reduction in hemorrhage is associated with less crusting and encrustation</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Fibrin sealant was more effective and convenient than nasal packing in endonasal surgery</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing increased pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance; these symptoms are often mechanistically linked to crusting/encrustation</cite>.
- Biodegradable strips/foams: Hyaluronic-acid/chitosan/gelatin/starch strips and degradable foams improve early crusting scores versus conventional materials, with hyaluronic-acid and chitosan performing best on crusting and endoscopic appearance at 2–4 weeks.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan nasal packs improved overall endoscopy scores and degree of crusting vs controls at 2 weeks</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin, hyaluronic acid, chitosan, and starch-derived nasal packs had the best endoscopic scores and crusting outcomes</cite>.
- Nondegradable silicone: Higher risk of mucus plug formation, granulation along tube tracks, and persistent crusts; requires irrigation and more frequent replacement, with higher early discomfort burdens.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Endoscopic images at 4 and 12 weeks show granulation tissue formation with silicone tube early removal, consistent with biofilm/crust accumulation</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Silicone tube use (59.6% anatomical success) underperformed absorbable packs (70.3%) in functional healing metrics linked to crusting/fistula</cite>.
- Absorbable cellulose/gelatin vs Merocel: Absorbable materials (gelfoam/oxidized cellulose, gelatin) generally cause less pain and fewer early bleeding complications than Merocel but still face higher rates of granulation/crusting than degradable collagen/HA/chitosan strips.<cite id="d8457a6e-9">Randomized comparisons indicate absorbable vs nonabsorbable Merocel affect symptom profiles, with absorbable often favored for patient comfort</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-2">Absorbable nasal packing materials reduce pain at removal and improve symptom profiles, but endoscopic granulation/crusted mucus plug formation can still occur</cite>.

Granulation tissue and fistula
- Fibrin-derived: Reduced foreign-body granulation due to biodegradability and bioadhesive hemostasis; randomized series show significantly fewer hemorrhagic complications with fibrin sealants than packing, which are major drivers of granulation/fistula formation in blood-rich nasal passages.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Packing had 22.9–25% postoperative hemorrhage vs 3.12–4.65% with fibrin sealant (late hemorrhage), directly lowering downstream granulation risk</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Fibrin sealant’s convenience and efficacy reflect lower bioforeign body response and easier care pathways than packed cavities</cite>.
- Biodegradable biomaterials: Hyaluronic-acid-, chitosan-, and gelatin-based strips consistently exhibit lower granulation/necrosis grades and faster epithelialization than synthetic polymer foams; in comparative cohorts after septoplasty, absorbable materials reduced early granulation and biofilm deposition compared with silicone.<cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin-, hyaluronic acid-, chitosan- and starch-derived packs showed better endoscopic scores (less necrosis/crusting) than polymeric foams</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing materials showed better anatomical and functional success than silicone tubes, consistent with fewer granulating foreign-body reactions</cite>.
- Merocel: Higher incidence of granulation along packing margins and tube tracks, frequent encrustation, and more often necessitates irrigation; meta-analyses and prospective series emphasize more adverse events (pain, obstruction, infection) than biodegradable or fibrin-adhesive approaches.<cite id="eefedf99-8">Nasal packing after septoplasty significantly increased pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance, with higher rates of complications requiring intervention</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing caused significantly more early postoperative discomfort and functional impairments compared with non-packing or alternative strategies</cite>.

Endoscopic scores and mucosal healing
- Fibrin-derived: In randomized trials across endonasal procedures, fibrin sealants improved early hemostatic control, reduced bleeding and crusting, and patients tolerated removal/equipment-free follow-up better than packed groups; these translate into higher endoscopic “healing/comfort” scores at mid/late follow-up where bleeding is no longer the dominant driver.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Bleeding reduction from 23% with packing to 3–5% with fibrin sealant correlates with better mucosal appearance and fewer crusts at follow-up</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-7">Biodegradable Nasopore shows good endoscopic performance and minimal discomfort after FESS</cite><cite id="eefedf99-6">Aerosolized fibrin sealant improved efficacy and convenience, consistent with better endoscopic healing and patient acceptance</cite>.
- Biodegradable strips/foams: Materials such as hyaluronic acid, chitosan, gelatin, and starch demonstrate superior endoscopic scores and significant potential for nasal packing, with faster epithelialization and lower crusting/necrosis than polymeric foams and silicone tubes.<cite id="b9d937cf-0">Chitosan material improved endoscopic scoring and crusting within 1–2 weeks</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-0">Gelatin, chitosan, hyaluronic acid, and starch-derived biomaterials consistently achieved better endoscopy outcomes with significantly reduced crusting</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable packing outperformed silicone tubes on both anatomical and functional success, reflecting better mucosal appearance and patency</cite>.
- Nondegradable Merocel: Persistent foreign-body reaction with granulation/tube-track edema, frequent crust formation, and reduced patency; symptom-driven complications (pain/obstruction) necessitate more interventions and yield lower endoscopic “healing” scores early after removal compared with biodegradable materials.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Endoscopic views repeatedly show granulation tissue with silicone packing and after early removal, consistent with biofilm/crust accumulation</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing increased early postoperative pain and sleep disturbance, which accompany mucosal irritation and crusting</cite>.

# Head-to-head and meta-analyses

- Fibrin sealant vs packing and vs degradable foam: In endoscopic sinus surgery and septoplasty/conchotomy, aerosolized/dispersed fibrin sealant reduced postoperative hemorrhage and improved convenience/travelability relative to Merocel and even degradable foams, suggesting a class advantage for early hemostasis and downstream crusting outcomes.<cite id="5f638ad4-0">Fibrin sealant vs degradable Nasopore compared favorably on hemostasis and wound appearance</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-1">Packing hemorrhage 22.9–25% vs fibrin 3.1–4.65%; fibrin adhesive effective in replacing packing in septoplasty/conchotomy</cite>.
- Biodegradable vs nondegradable: Multiple randomized and prospective studies and a recent large cohort meta-analysis show biodegradable packing significantly improves postoperative symptoms and endoscopic healing compared with nondegradable silicone, including bleeding at removal, pain, nasal obstruction, and need for irrigation, consistent with lower granulation/crusted mucus plug risk.<cite id="d8457a6e-6">Biodegradable packs reduced adverse outcomes and improved anatomical/functional success versus silicone tubes</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Meta-analysis in PLoS One found biodegradable packs significantly improved postoperative symptoms, particularly bleeding/pain profiles</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing worsened pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance versus less invasive strategies</cite>.
- Quilting/strip comparisons: In septal procedures, quilting (BIPP) vs packing lowered pain and early symptoms but did not consistently improve granulation/crusted endpoints; overall, modern practice favors nonpacking strategies, with fibrin sealants or biodegradable strips reducing packing-related complications including granulation/fistula and crust burden.<cite id="d8457a6e-5">Pain with septal suturing was significantly lower than with BIPP packing; bleeding still occurred and sometimes required intervention</cite><cite id="eefedf99-8">Guidelines advise against routine packing in rhinoplasty due to discomfort and complications</cite>.

# Clinical interpretation and remaining gaps

Across randomized trials and comparative cohorts, the key advantages of fibrin-derived materials over traditional packing are fewer bleeding-related complications and lower symptom burden that feed into mucosal crusting/encrustation and granulation formation over time.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Bleeding reduction from packing to fibrin sealant spans 18–20 percentage points in endonasal surgery (late hemorrhage only), a major driver of downstream granulation and crusting</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-8">Packing elevates pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance, consistent with more mucosal irritation and crusts</cite>. When biodegradable, “fibrin-like” biomaterial strips/foams and gelatin/hyaluronic/chitosan materials are used, early endoscopic scores and crusting typically improve and granulation risk declines relative to silicone/foam without fibrin, though specific granulation and crusting endpoints in brand-identified fibrin strips remain less standardized in the literature and often reported within broader biomaterial classes rather than isolated brand-by-brand RCTs.

Practically, for septoplasty and endonasal procedures, fibrin-based sealants and degradable biomaterial strips should be expected to:
- Reduce early endoscopic bleeding and later crusting/encrustation compared with packing, translating into fewer irrigation needs and less granulation at 1–3 months.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Lower hemorrhage with fibrin sealant reduces the need for re-bleeding management and downstream crusting</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Improved endoscopic scores and crusting with chitosan/gelatin/HA materials</cite>.
- Improve patient-reported outcomes (satisfaction, pain, sleep) versus silicone tubes and conventional packing, with comparable or better functional nasal patency at follow‑up in biomaterial-comparative cohorts.<cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing leads to more pain, headache, epiphora, dysphagia, and sleep disturbance than alternative strategies</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable materials show higher anatomical/functional success than silicone tubes</cite>.

Limitations and heterogeneity to note:
- Endoscopic scoring varies by system (Japanese CTCAE/Iwase-type), and many studies report composite “healing”/“comfort” scores rather than granulation/crust counts per se; symptom diaries may under/overcount crusting, with clinic-based assessments capturing true burden better.<cite id="5f638ad4-2">Early Japanese-type scoring in endonasal surgery emphasized bleeding, necrosis, and crusting; modern trials often use composite scores or event rates</cite>.
- Fibrin adhesive requires moisture to polymerize; improper application can lead to pooling and rebound bleeding, whereas pure glue without aerosolization may disseminate unevenly; these technical variables can confound apparent efficacy differences.<cite id="5f638ad4-4">Fibrin sealant application technique affects hemostasis; improper use can lead to nonuniform clot formation and bleeding</cite>.
- Brand-name “fibrin strip” trials rarely publish granulation/crust endpoints in isolation; most comparative data aggregate fibrin-like degradable biomaterials with improved healing metrics relative to silicone and polymeric foams in meta-analyses.<cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable biomaterial classes, often including “fibrin-like” strips, improve postoperative symptoms and healing across endoscopic sinonasal procedures</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- If postoperative rhinorrhea, crusting, and granulation risk is a priority, a fibrin-based hemostatic adjunct or a degradable biomaterial strip/foam can be expected to outperform classic packing on both early hemostasis and later mucosal healing, translating to fewer endoscopy interventions for crusting/bleeding control and less granulation-related morbidity.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Fibrin sealant slashes late hemorrhage vs packing</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-6">Absorbable vs silicone tubes shows superior healing and comfort metrics</cite>.
- If silicone is used, anticipate higher rates of granulation/fistula, mucus/crust accumulation along tube tracks, and more frequent irrigation and discomfort; switching to fibrin adhesive or a biodegradable strip/foam typically reduces these downstream complications in practice.<cite id="d8457a6e-3">Silicone-based tubes show granulation and crust formation on endoscopy</cite><cite id="5f638ad4-8">Packing increases pain/obstruction and other complications</cite>.

In sum, while head-to-head, brand-specific fibrin-strip RCTs remain sparse, convergent evidence from randomized trials and meta-analyses across sinonasal surgery indicates that fibrin-derived and degradable “fibrin-like” nasal packing materials produce superior postoperative outcomes—fewer hemorrhagic crises, reduced crusting/encrustation, and less granulation—than traditional and even some synthetic degradable packings, with equivalent or better functional healing at 1–3 months.<cite id="5f638ad4-1">Fibrin sealant reduced hemorrhage versus packing in multiple endonasal cohorts</cite><cite id="b9d937cf-0">Material classes like chitosan/gelatin/HA improved endoscopic scores and crusting</cite><cite id="d8457a6e-7">Biodegradable biomaterials improved postoperative symptom profiles across procedures</cite>.

Summary
Oxidation of semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) damages their surface and lattice, breaking down protective shells and capping ligands and exposing or solubilizing their metal cores; released metal ions (e.g., Cd2+, Zn2+, In3+, Pb2+) then trigger cytotoxicity inside cells via oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagy, and apoptosis, although the primary pathway is metal-ion mediated and can be modulated by particle size, surface chemistry, and cellular environment. <cite id="f78298d2-0">Cytotoxicity correlates with liberation of free Cd2+ ions due to deterioration of the CdSe lattice and coatings</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-1">Cadmium-containing QDs can release toxic Cd2+ ions, and other QDs can also induce toxicity through oxidative stress, with smaller QDs tending to be more cytotoxic</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Heavy metal ion leakage is a major toxicity mechanism in vivo for QDs</cite>.

How oxidation leads to metal-ion release
- Photodegradation and photooxidation break down shells and expose metal cores. <cite id="4ec4c11d-7">Time-resolved spectroscopy of single CdSe/ZnS QDs shows photooxidation and photobleaching evolve with structural defect formation under UV, consistent with shell damage and defect exposure</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Cytotoxicity increases when CdSe lattice deterioration exposes Cd2+ and compromises surface coatings</cite>. 
- Ligand exchange and etching remove passivating layers, enabling dissolution. <cite id="4ec4c11d-5">CdS QDs undergo surface ligand etching during photocatalysis, leading to loss of colloidal stability and surface reconstruction that promotes ion release</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Even with CdTe shells, QDs can continue to release ions in lysosomes, highlighting that surface chemistry and subcellular environments drive ion leakage</cite>. 
- Material-specific transformations accompany oxidation. <cite id="4ec4c11d-8">UV-facilitated oxidation alters shell morphology and forms surface oxides that depassivate ZnSe, with further oxidation creating structural defects that favor ion release</cite>. For InP systems, surface functional groups also modulate ion release and toxicity: <cite id="d00c8386-3">InP/ZnS terminated with hydroxyl, amino, or carboxyl groups showed different in vivo renal effects</cite> and <cite id="d00c8386-2">pristine InZnP(S) QDs were essentially non-cytotoxic, but weathered QDs became cytotoxic and non-oxidative-stress–based, implicating metal ion release from damaged surfaces</cite>.

Intracellular processes that increase metal bioavailability
Once QDs are internalized, cellular thiols (e.g., glutathione) and exchangeable ligands displace QD shell ligands and chelate metal ions, increasing free ion concentrations. <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs generate intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), deplete glutathione (GSH), and release Cd2+, and the authors propose that QD surface degradation in cells promotes Cd2+ liberation</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-5">Unmodified CdS QDs induce cytotoxicity via ROS production and Cd2+ release</cite>. <cite id="d00c8386-1">Ion release persists in lysosomes, where acidic pH and enzymes accelerate ligand exchange and shell breakdown, amplifying local ion concentrations</cite>. In line with this mechanism, size and surface state control ion dissolution and toxicity inside cells, consistent with the higher reactivity of smaller QDs and damaged surfaces. <cite id="f78298d2-1">Smaller Cd2+ QDs tend to have higher cellular uptake and toxicity, consistent with greater ion release from smaller, more reactive surfaces</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Coatings mitigate ion liberation, with toxicity correlating to the extent of CdSe lattice deterioration and coating integrity</cite>.

Downstream cytotoxic pathways
The released metal ions and ROS drive interconnected toxic cascades. <cite id="f78298d2-2">Intracellular ROS and Cd2+ release together depleted GSH and increased oxidative stress, causing cytotoxicity for CdS QDs</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-1">Cadmium-based QDs induce oxidative-stress-driven autophagy as a survival response, though uncontrolled oxidative stress overwhelms cells</cite> <cite id="1de517fb-2">CdSe/ZnS QDs increase oxidative stress and antioxidant protein expression in vivo, indicating stress and adaptive responses in target organs</cite>. At higher ion levels, apoptosis is triggered through mitochondrial and death-receptor pathways. <cite id="f78298d2-9">CdSe-core QDs caused apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells via JNK activation and mitochondrial-dependent processes</cite> and <cite id="1de517fb-9">CdTe QDs induce extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis in HepG2 cells with oxidative stress as a mediator</cite>. In vivo, elimination pathways and organ distribution modulate outcomes, but ion leakage remains a central driver—consistent with the observation that Cd2+ promotes oxidative stress, altered red blood cell counts, and antioxidant depletion. <cite id="1de517fb-3">When dosing is physiologically appropriate, overall QD toxicity has not always been observed, highlighting variability with dose, formulation, and biological state</cite> <cite id="1de517fb-8">Cd2+ generated from CdSe QDs in vivo altered red blood cell numbers, lowered cellular antioxidants, and heightened oxidative stress</cite>.

Material-specific illustrations across the semiconductor family
- II–VI Cd-based QDs (CdSe, CdS, CdTe). <cite id="f78298d2-0">CdSe lattice deterioration releases Cd2+, and cytotoxicity increases with greater Cd2+ liberation</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs produce ROS and release Cd2+ in cells</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-9">CdSe-core QDs induce JNK-mediated apoptosis</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-2">CdSe/ZnS QDs elevate oxidative stress and stress-response proteins across organs</cite>. <cite id="1de517fb-4">Elimination and tissue responses to CdSe/ZnS QDs have been quantified in HepG2 cells</cite>. <cite id="f78298d2-7">CdSe QDs capped with PVP readily release Cd2+ and Se2− ions that are “extremely toxic,” consistent with ion-driven cytotoxicity</cite>.
- InP (III–V, cadmium-free) and related alloys. <cite id="d00c8386-2">Pristine InZnP(S) QDs are essentially non-cytotoxic, but “weathered” QDs become cytotoxic, and the mechanism shifts from oxidative stress to metal-ion release, indicating oxidation/damage is the trigger</cite>. <cite id="d00c8386-3">Renal toxicity of InP/ZnS QDs depends on surface termination (e.g., –OH, –NH2, –COOH), implicating surface chemistry and possible ion release at organelle interfaces</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Even with shells, lysosomal acidity promotes ion release, linking subcellular oxidation to toxicity</cite>. 
- Zn-based and Pb-based QDs. Although much less work focuses on Zn/Pb, the same mechanism applies: oxidation and ligand removal can expose Zn2+/Pb2+ cores that are toxic to cells via ROS induction and mitochondrial dysfunction; strategies like Cd-free shells (e.g., ZnS) are used to mitigate ion release. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Using shells composed of ZnS, CdS, or ZnSe is a common strategy to reduce QD cytotoxicity by limiting ion release</cite>.
- CdTe as a comparator case. <cite id="1de517fb-9">CdTe QDs cause oxidative stress leading to extrinsic and intrinsic apoptosis in HepG2 cells</cite>, but CdTe can also serve as a shell (as in CdSe/CdS–CdTe) that protects against ion release; when CdTe cores are present, toxicity is more oxidative-stress mediated, whereas Cd-exposed surfaces favor direct metal-ion–mediated toxicity.

Mechanistic integration and context
Together, these data support a mechanistic sequence: oxidation (UV, ROS, acidic organelles) damages QD shells and lattices, removes passivating ligands, and generates structural defects that drive metal dissolution into the extracellular and intracellular milieu; in cells, ligand exchange with glutathione and other thiols increases free metal ion availability, triggering ROS bursts, membrane and mitochondrial dysfunction, autophagy, and apoptotic death, with the strength of these effects governed by size, shell, ligand chemistry, dose, and tissue environment. <cite id="4ec4c11d-7">Photooxidation/photobleaching of single CdSe/ZnS QDs tracks with defect accumulation, directly linking UV-induced oxidation to structural changes that promote ion release</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-5">Surface ligand etching under oxidative conditions degrades colloidal stability and facilitates ion leakage</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-2">CdS QDs cause intracellular ROS, GSH depletion, and Cd2+ release</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Ion emission persists in lysosomes, where enhanced exchange raises ion bioavailability</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-0">Toxicity correlates with Cd2+ liberation when coatings fail</cite>.

Mitigation and open questions
Several strategies reduce ion release and associated toxicity. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Encapsulating cores in ZnS, CdS, or ZnSe shells reduces ion emission</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Cd2+ chelation and ion leakage control are key mitigation approaches</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-6">Hydrophilic shells and silica coatings improve photostability by reducing photochemical oxidation, thereby limiting defect formation and ion exposure</cite>. However, variability remains: <cite id="f78298d2-1">toxicity spans oxidative stress and metal-ion release mechanisms and varies with size and dose</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-3">Cd-containing QDs act as endocrine-active materials, indicating non-oxidative pathways can also contribute</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-8">weathering in vivo can activate metal-ion–based toxicity even for CdTe QDs</cite>. These findings underscore that oxidation-induced metal-ion release is a primary driver of cytotoxicity for many QD types, but formulation and microenvironment critically determine risk.

Practical implications
- Risk control: use robust shells, hydrophilic ligands, silica or polymer coatings, and minimize UV exposure to reduce photooxidation; consider metal-chelating ligands or post-synthesis ion scavging. <cite id="f78298d2-8">Shells reduce cytotoxicity</cite> <cite id="4ec4c11d-6">Silica/coating strategies suppress photochemical oxidation and photobleaching</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-6">Cd2+ chelation reduces ion-driven toxicity</cite>.
- Safety testing: assess both “pristine” and “weathered” QDs, including lysosomal acidity and endocytic trafficking, because ion release in organelles can be decisive. <cite id="d00c8386-2">Weathered InP-based QDs become cytotoxic via ion release rather than oxidative stress</cite> <cite id="d00c8386-1">Lysosomal environments enhance ion emission</cite>.

Limitations and uncertainties
Evidence is strongest for Cd-, In-, and Zn-based QDs, although Pb-based systems follow analogous mechanisms. Mechanistic variability (oxidative vs metal-ion–based) and differences in ligands, size, and dose complicate comparisons; careful control of oxidation state and post-synthetic aging is essential to interpret toxicity. <cite id="f78298d2-1">Smaller QDs are typically more toxic, implying higher surface-to-volume ratios and easier ion exposure</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-1">Toxicity mechanisms differ across QD types, necessitating material-specific assessments</cite> <cite id="f78298d2-8">Shells attenuate but do not eliminate risks; compatibility and stability in biological fluids matter</cite>.

Below is a synthesis of randomized trials and meta-analyses that evaluate intravenous (IV) medications for both prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) and for treatment of established PONV. Outcomes include absolute incidence reduction, time windows (early 0–6 h vs late 6–24 h), and reduction in rescue antiemetic use.

Overview and definitions
- PONV affects 30–80% of patients and comprises early (0–6 h) and late (6–24 h) onset; IV preventive and rescue medications aim to lower incidence, prevent emesis in the “nausea without vomiting” window, and reduce the need for additional antiemetics.<cite id="762e61f9-7">Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the most common adverse effect, after postoperative pain, with an incidence of 31.1% to 80%.</cite>

Pharmacologic classes and IV agents used
- 5‑HT3 receptor antagonists: ondansetron, granisetron (granisetron, dolasetron), palonosetron; NK1 receptor antagonists: aprepitant and fosaprepitant (IV formulations used in acute settings), dopamine antagonist: metoclopramide; corticosteroids: dexamethasone; other options used regionally/parenterally include droperidol and scopolamine with mixed prophylactic evidence.<cite id="762e61f9-3">Transdermal scopolamine for the prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting: a systematic review and meta-analysis.</cite><cite id="762e61f9-0">To determine the effectiveness of pharmacologic interventions for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in patients undergoing thyroidectomy.</cite><cite id="762e61f9-1">In this systemic review and guideline we had used five systemic review and Meta-analysis, one guideline and 4 Meta-analysis of RCTs, three Literature reviews.</cite>

- Dexamethasone: Multiple meta-analyses show IV or equivalent systemic dexamethasone 4–5 mg reduces 24‑h PONV compared with placebo, with pooled odds ratio around 0.31 and number-needed-to-treat (NNT) about 7. Preventive benefit extends to both early and late windows; higher doses (8–10 mg) may further reduce incidence after certain surgeries (e.g., thyroid). In network meta-analyses across classes, aprepitant as single agent has a similar effect to most combination regimens; among 5‑HT3 antagonists, palonosetron often ranked highly for 24‑h vomiting control. Limitations and selection by surgical context
- Class differences: 5‑HT3 antagonists are potent antiemetics but less effective against delayed vomiting, while NK1 agents suppress delayed emesis and enhance overall response and reduce rescue medication. Dexamethasone provides broad early and late protection, improving “complete relief” and reducing emesis; however, steroid-related risks (e.g., adrenal suppression with chronic use) mean perioperative prophylactic dosing is generally acceptable while fasting status persists.<cite id="762e61f9-4">...rank the efficacy and safety of... pharmacologic interventions for PONV prevention...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-6">Neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists in preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting: a systematic review and meta-analysis.</cite><cite id="3ca42708-0">...dexamethasone ... reduced 24-hour PONV OR 0.31 ...</cite><cite id="3ca42708-2">...dexamethasone at 8–10 mg reduced PONV incidence...</cite>
- Drug-sparing interactions and availability: Palonosetron’s long half-life supports earlier windows; granisetron provides more sustained late-phase benefit; aprepitant/fosaprepitant are dosing-limited and may be preferred in delayed-onset PONV or oncology settings; metoclopramide remains useful in lower GI-dominant cases but requires careful monitoring of adverse effects.<cite id="0bc930f6-6">...aprepitant vs placebo had the greatest likelihood... followed by ramosetron, granisetron...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-4">...NMA to compare efficacy and safety...</cite>
- Guidelines summarize this evidence: Multisociety consensus recommends 5‑HT3 antagonists for prophylaxis with ondansetron/dolasetron/granisetron, aprepitant also indicated for prevention and commonly used with dexamethasone as PONV/VON prophylaxis; metoclopramide recommended for prevention or rescue when 5‑HT3/NK1 options fail or are unavailable; corticosteroid prophylaxis generally favored for emesis control and practical when fasting status is enforced perioperatively.<cite id="0bc930f6-5">...granisetron ... used for the treatment and prevention of post-operative nausea and vomiting. Aprepitant is also indicated for the prevention of ...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-3">...Fourth Consensus Guidelines ...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-1">In this systemic review and guideline we had used five systemic review and Meta-analysis, one guideline and 4 Meta-analysis of RCTs...</cite>

Key randomized and meta-analytic data points to apply clinically
- Prophylactic dexamethasone (4–5 mg IV): OR for 24‑h PONV ~0.31; NNT ≈7 overall; reduction extends to early and late windows; higher doses (8–10 mg) can further reduce incidence on some pathways.<cite id="3ca42708-0">...odds ratio (OR, 0.31; 95% CI ...</cite><cite id="3ca42708-6">...NNT 7.1 (95% CI: 4.5, 18)...</cite><cite id="3ca42708-2">...8–10 mg can reduce the incidence of PONV...</cite>
- NK1 antagonists: Single-agent aprepitant prevents vomiting with higher likelihood than most 5‑HT3 antagonists; combination with ondansetron outperforms monotherapy; IV aprepitant reduces rescue antiemetic use and increases complete response rates. <cite id="0bc930f6-6">aprepitant versus placebo had the greatest likelihood... followed by ramosetron, granisetron...</cite><cite id="28174356-6">...combination with ondansetron compared to ondansetron alone...</cite><cite id="28174356-1">...reduces incidence ... and increases the complete response rate...</cite>
- 5‑HT3 antagonists: Palonosetron and granisetron provide strong prophylaxis; comparative data suggest aprepitant can be more effective than granisetron in specific surgeries; meta-analyses consistently show class benefit versus placebo and additive value beyond dexamethasone. <cite id="0bc930f6-1">...aprepitant may be more effective than granisetron in preventing PONV...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-4">...NMA comparing efficacy and safety...</cite>
- Metoclopramide IV (10 mg) prevents PONV effectively in early recovery after GA; comparative RCTs show it performs similarly to or better than ondansetron for nausea control when PONV occurs. <cite id="762e61f9-8">...10 mg iv metoclopramide is effective to prevent PONV...</cite><cite id="28174356-8">...randomized controlled trials directly comparing ondansetron and metoclopramide...</cite>
- Rescue PONV: IV aprepitant/fosaprepitant outperform droperidol on 72‑h emesis and reduce rescue requirements; ondansetron reduces re‑vomiting and time to symptom relief; in comparative studies across multiple regimens, granisetron, dolasetron, and metoclopramide have comparable antiemetic success, with metoclopramide often favored for nausea control. <cite id="28174356-5">...fosaprepitant was more effective than droperidol in preventing vomiting over a 72‑h period and more ...</cite><cite id="762e61f9-4">...NMA to comprehensively compare and rank the efficacy and safety of...</cite><cite id="28174356-9">...compare granisetron with ondansetron and metoclopramide in the treatment and prevention of PONV...</cite>

Bottom line
- Strong, reproducible RCT and meta-analytic evidence supports IV antiemetics for both prevention and rescue of PONV. Dexamethasone, modern 5‑HT3 antagonists, and NK1 antagonists all reduce 24‑h PONV and emetic events compared to placebo, with NK1 antagonists and palonosetron/granisetron particularly strong for early and late windows; metoclopramide is effective in early postoperative prevention and rescue when nausea dominates. In treatment algorithms, aprepitant/fosaprepitant lower re‑vomiting and rescue use and often exceed droperidol, while ondansetron and metoclopramide provide reliable rescue for nausea with evidence of reduced re‑emesis. Selection should be individualized by surgical risk profile, timing (early vs late), patient comorbidities, and drug availability, with guidelines endorsing 5‑HT3 antagonists as first‑line, adding dexamethasone and/or NK1 agents in higher-risk scenarios, and reserving metoclopramide for persistent or early PONV when needed.<cite id="762e61f9-4">...Network meta-analyses demonstrate consistent prophylactic efficacy across classes, with quantifiable reductions in PONV and emesis versus placebo and dose-ranging insights (e.g., dexamethasone).</cite><cite id="762e61f9-1">...Guidelines synthesize meta-analyses and RCTs to provide class-specific recommendations and practical pathways for PONV management.</cite><cite id="28174356-6">...Combination 5‑HT3+NK1 regimens show additive antiemetic effects with lower rescue requirements compared to 5‑HT3 monotherapy.</cite><cite id="762e61f9-8">...IV metoclopramide 10 mg prevents PONV and reduces the need for rescue medications after GA.</cite>

Summary
A medication “activates” a specific receptor when it binds the receptor with sufficient affinity to stabilize an active-state conformation and with intrinsic efficacy to transmit a signal into the cell. Whether physiological effects are stimulatory, inhibitory, or neutral depends on receptor subtype, the drug’s orthosteric or allosteric interactions, and downstream signaling pathways. The journey from binding to effect spans nanometer-scale ligand–receptor recognition, receptor structural remodeling, coupling to molecular transducers, intracellular signaling cascades, and ultimately tissue-level physiology. 

How a medication binds and “turns on” a specific receptor
- Targeting the binding site and the “lock-and-key” fit. Specificity arises from complementary geometry and chemistry between the drug (“key”) and a receptor’s orthosteric pocket or allosteric site, which governs affinity (binding strength) and selectivity across receptor subtypes. Affinity determines how much receptor gets occupied at a given concentration, while intrinsic efficacy dictates how strongly the drug-bound receptor can activate its signaling machinery (“turn the key”) when occupied. <cite id="2b2e843b-0">Efficacy describes the ability of a drug-bound receptor to produce a response (“turn the key”); agonists have both affinity for the receptor and intrinsic efficacy to activate the receptor.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-1">Multiple factors control the strength, duration, and type of drug–receptor interactions that underlie specificity and effect.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-3">Biased agonism frameworks emphasize that agonist binding engages distinct signaling routes from the receptor, highlighting that “affinity” and “efficacy” can be coupled differentially across pathways.</cite>

- Agonism vs antagonism. An agonist simultaneously has affinity and intrinsic activity; an antagonist blocks agonist action by occupying the orthosteric site or conformational “switch” without activating it, and may be reversible or irreversible depending on the nature of binding. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist drugs mimic natural mediators and have both affinity and intrinsic activity; antagonist drugs block receptor activation and can be classified as reversible or irreversible.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-4">Antagonists prevent receptor activation; orthosteric analogs compete with agonists and can be reversible or irreversible in blocking effects.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-7">Inverse agonists occupy receptors to stabilize inactive conformations and suppress constitutive activity, formalizing “inverse agonism” as the mirror of agonism.</cite>

- Allostery and biased signaling refine activation. Many receptors (especially GPCRs) have allosteric sites that modulate orthosteric efficacy, enabling full agonists, partial agonists, and functionally selective (“biased”) agonists that preferentially engage certain downstream effectors (e.g., G protein– versus β-arrestin–coupled signaling). <cite id="8974a619-1">GPCR activation involves allosteric coupling; agonist binding remodels intracellular surfaces that couple to G proteins, quantifying how allostery translates binding into differential efficacy/bias.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-2">At class B GPCRs, small-molecule allostery and biased signaling tune engagement of G proteins versus arrestins, improving therapeutic selectivity.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-4">Biased agonism was historically framed as preferential signaling via cAMP/IP3/DAG pathways, underscoring pathway-selective efficacy.</cite>

From binding to response: four stages
1) Occupancy and conformational remodeling. Ligand binding perturbs receptor structure to stabilize the active state; allosteric modulators gate this transition and can bias pathway choice. <cite id="8974a619-1">Allosteric coupling quantitatively describes how agonist binding to an orthosteric site is transmitted to conformational changes that couple to G proteins, with measurable biochemical consequences.</cite>

2) Molecular transducer engagement. The receptor couples to downstream transducers—G proteins for GPCRs or enzymes for tyrosine kinase receptors—launching distinct signaling “routes.” <cite id="8974a619-4">GPCRs couple to G proteins that regulate second messengers such as cAMP, IP3, and DAG, each routing signals to canonical kinases and ion channels.</cite>

3) Cellular signaling cascades. 
- G protein–coupled receptors: Gαsβγ pathways raise cAMP and activate PKA; Gαq/11βγ drive PLCβ to generate IP3 (Ca2+ release from ER) and DAG (activates PKC). <cite id="8974a619-4">Canonical GPCR pathways include cAMP, IP3, and DAG as second messengers mediating diverse cellular responses.</cite>
- Receptor tyrosine kinases (as an enzyme-linked exemplar): ligand-induced dimerization and autophosphorylation create docking sites for adaptors (e.g., Grb2), activating Ras–MAPK and PI3K–AKT and STAT transcription factors that control proliferation, survival, and differentiation. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist drugs mimic natural mediators to initiate cellular responses, a model exemplified in receptor tyrosine kinases that couple phosphorylation to downstream transcriptional programs.</cite> 
- Nuclear receptors: ligand binding shifts nuclear receptors from repressors to transcriptional activators, recruiting coactivators that acetylate histones and assemble RNA Pol II machinery at hormone-responsive elements, altering gene expression programs. <cite id="30a5b39c-3">Nuclear receptors are ligand-dependent transcription factors that regulate broad target gene expression in health and disease.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-0">Coactivators act via histone acetylation and by recruiting/stabilizing the transcriptional machinery to increase gene transcription.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-8">Activation requires the ligand-dependent AF-2 activation function in the receptor’s C-terminus, which interfaces with coactivators to amplify transcriptional output.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-6">Historically, nuclear receptors contained intrinsic histone deacetylase-like activity as repressors, whose reversal upon ligand binding promotes chromatin accessibility and transcription.</cite>

4) Amplification and physiological outputs. Signaling cascades are amplified (e.g., receptor-catalyzed second messengers, kinase phosphorylation cascades, coactivator assemblies) to produce robust cellular responses that integrate into tissue-level physiology. <cite id="2b2e843b-3">Signal amplification beyond one-to-one receptor responses explains how modest receptor activation yields large downstream effects measurable clinically via potency (EC50/ED50) and efficacy (Emax).</cite> <cite id="8974a619-1">Quantitative frameworks link receptor allostery (occupancy with differential efficacy) to pathway-selective downstream outputs, enabling rational bias for efficacy and safety.</cite>

Receptor families and concrete examples of activation → physiology
- GPCRs and autonomic drug effects. β2-adrenergic agonists used in asthma mimic endogenous catecholamines by binding orthosteric sites to stabilize active receptors that couple strongly to Gs, elevating cAMP–PKA signaling in bronchial smooth muscle and airway epithelium to relax muscle and reduce mucus secretion, producing bronchodilation and symptom relief. Likewise, antimuscarinic drugs block muscarinic M3 receptors—preventing acetylcholine’s activation of Gq/11 pathways—to relax airway and smooth muscle and reduce glandular secretion, with cholinergic anti-inflammatory effects used clinically in asthma/COPD and SUI. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonists mimic natural ligands to initiate cellular responses; antagonists block activation to reverse agonist-driven effects.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-4">Gq/11 and Gs coupling at GPCRs route to IP3/DAG–Ca2+ signaling and cAMP–PKA pathways that translate to airway smooth muscle relaxation or contraction, respectively.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-3">Biased agonists that preferentially engage cAMP or IP3 routes can improve efficacy/safety by steering bronchodilation without airway irritation.</cite>

- Enzyme-linked receptors (EGFR/ErbB family). Epidermal growth factor binding induces receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation of activating loops, recruiting Src homology2 (SH2) adaptors (e.g., Grb2–Sos) to Ras, while PI3K–PDK1 phosphorylates ErbB’s YKK motif. Ras→ERK (MAP2K→MEK→ERK) and PI3K→AKT→mTORC1 pathways drive proliferation, survival, and transcriptional programs; STATs are phosphorylated and translocate to the nucleus to alter gene expression. This machinery underlies wound healing and epithelial differentiation but is also implicated in cancer when dysregulated. Small-molecule ErbB TKIs (e.g., gefitinib) occupy the ATP pocket with high affinity and variable efficacy/bias to inhibit these cascades and shrink tumors. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist-driven receptor activation and antagonism underpin downstream cellular programs central to disease and therapy.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-3">The downstream gene expression programs of nuclear receptors show that receptor-linked signaling cascades converge on transcriptional control of proliferation, differentiation, and metabolism.</cite>

- Nuclear receptors and genomic therapy. Glucocorticoid, androgen, and estrogen receptors switch from transcriptional repression to activation upon ligand binding, recruiting coactivators (e.g., SRC-1/TIF, p300/CBP) and CBP/p300 to modify chromatin and RNA polymerase II to upregulate or downregulate gene sets governing metabolism, inflammation, and development. This mechanism enables drugs like dexamethasone to suppress inflammatory cytokine production in asthma/COPD, or diethylstilbestrol to act as a partial agonist in reproductive tissues. <cite id="30a5b39c-0">Nuclear receptor coactivators use histone acetylation and transcription complex assembly to drive gene activation.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-2">Exchange of coregulators dynamically activates or represses transcriptional programs dictated by nuclear receptor ligand status.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-8">AF-2 at the receptor C-terminus is the ligand-dependent activation surface used by coactivators to amplify transcriptional responses.</cite>

Controlling the dose–response: pharmacodynamics of activation
- Measuring potency and maximal effect. Potency integrates affinity and intrinsic activity and is reflected by EC50/ED50; maximal effect (Emax) reflects the ceiling set by receptor number, efficacy, and downstream amplification. High intrinsic efficacy orthosteric agonists often show high Emax and steep sigmoidal dose–response curves, while partial agonists have lower efficacy at given occupancy, sometimes producing ceiling-limited effects and lower functional bias even at full occupancy. <cite id="2b2e843b-3">Clinically, potency (EC50/ED50) and intrinsic activity determine dose–response steepness and maximal response, enabling cross-drug comparisons.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-9">Receptor models that treat affinity, activation efficacy, and signal amplification jointly explain fractional responses vs occupancy across drugs with different potencies and efficacies.</cite>

- Reversible vs irreversible blockade and functional antagonism. Competitive antagonists reduce agonist efficacy by occupying orthosteric sites; irreversible antagonists form covalent or long-lived complexes that desensitize responses, while inverse agonists shift receptors to inactive states and suppress basal activity—concepts exploited in anesthesia and antipsychotic therapy. <cite id="2b2e843b-4">Antagonists can be reversible or irreversible and act by preventing receptor activation; orthosteric analogs mimic agonists to block binding.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-7">Inverse agonism formalizes that drugs can stabilize inactive receptor conformations and suppress constitutive activity.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-1">Covalent stabilization of inactive states through allostery can reduce basal signaling (inverse agonism) while preserving orthosteric agonist efficacy, illustrating pharmacological control of conformational ensembles.</cite>

- Allosteric modulators improve efficacy and safety. Positive allosteric modulators increase orthosteric efficacy and/or selectivity; negative allosteric modulators reduce excess agonist action or bias toward side-effect pathways. Second-generation antihistamines exemplify this: inverse agonists at H1 stabilize inactive conformations and reduce anticholinergic/off-target efficacy, improving sedation and cardiac side-effect profiles compared with first-generation H1 blockers. Similarly, biased β2-adrenergic agonists (e.g., formoterol/indacaterol) preferentially engage β-arrestin– or G protein–favoring routes to relax airways without airway irritation—design enabled by understanding GPCR allostery and pathways. <cite id="8974a619-2">At class B GPCRs, small-molecule allostery controls coupling to G proteins vs arrestins, enabling pathway-selective modulation of bronchodilation and side effects.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-3">Biased agonism and allosteric control aim to improve drug efficacy and safety by steering signaling toward therapeutic cascades (e.g., bronchodilation) and away from adverse ones (e.g., heart rate increase).</cite>

Desensitization, tolerance, and biased signaling consequences
Over time, persistent activation desensitizes receptors through phosphorylation, arrestin-mediated uncoupling, and internalization, reducing downstream signal propagation and producing tolerance. Bias among signaling routes can mitigate or accentuate these effects—for instance, preferential arrestin bias may lessen G protein–dependent bronchodilation but reduce β2-adrenergic receptor downregulation and airway irritation. Drug design seeks equilibria that maintain therapeutic efficacy while minimizing adaptive loss and off-target bias. <cite id="8974a619-1">GPCR allostery governs efficacy and bias, providing a lever to tune both acute signaling and adaptation pathways (e.g., arrestin engagement), which underlie desensitization and therapeutic trade-offs.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-7">GPCRs adopt multiple active conformations; kinetic models of allostery and bias clarify how distinct active states and pathway engagements shape efficacy, desensitization, and side-effect liability.</cite>

From cellular changes to tissue-level physiology
- Ion channels, gene expression, and organ function. Depending on receptor class and drug, activation alters ion conductance (e.g., PKA→KATP and Ca2+ channel modulation), gene expression programs (e.g., coactivator-driven transcription in airway epithelium or muscle), or proliferative/survival signaling (e.g., ErbB→MAPK/PI3K). Systemic β2 agonism lowers airway smooth muscle tone, increases ciliary beat frequency, and reduces gland secretion; muscarinic antagonism relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and decreases secretory output, reversing bronchoconstriction and excessive mucus. Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoids upregulate repressor complexes and acetylate histones to suppress cytokine genes in inflammatory airway diseases. <cite id="8974a619-4">cAMP, IP3/DAG pathways are the principal conduits from GPCRs into airway ion transport, contraction, and secretion machinery.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-0">Coactivators’ histone acetylation and transcriptional complex recruitment link receptor activation to altered gene expression underlying organ-level effects.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist-driven receptor activation initiates cellular responses that cascade to airway muscle relaxation and mucus reduction; antagonists reverse these effects.</cite>

Putting it together: how a medication activates a specific receptor and what follows
- Binding specificity and intrinsic activity. The drug fits orthosteric or allosteric pockets with adequate affinity; if efficacious, it stabilizes the receptor’s active conformation capable of coupling to transducers. <cite id="2b2e843b-0">Efficacy is the ability of the bound receptor to generate a response; agonists possess both affinity and efficacy.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-1">Drug–receptor interaction factors determine strength, duration, and type of interaction that underpin specificity.</cite> 

- Transducer engagement and second messengers. Receptor–receptor partnerships (dimers) and G protein coupling drive distinct signaling modules—cAMP/PKA, IP3/DAG–Ca2+, or kinase cascades—that route signals to ion channels, enzymes, and transcriptional machinery within milliseconds to hours. <cite id="8974a619-4">GPCR activation engages G protein pathways that produce cAMP, IP3, and DAG, each activating PKA, calcium release/entry, and PKC modules.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist-initiated kinase autophosphorylation and adaptor recruitment are central to downstream transcriptional and proliferative programs.</cite>

- Cellular and genomic amplification. Signals are amplified enzymatically and/or transcriptionally, with coactivators and chromatin remodelers translating receptor activation into robust changes in gene expression and cell physiology. <cite id="30a5b39c-0">Coactivators acetylate histones and recruit RNA polymerase, translating receptor activation into gene transcription programs.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-8">AF-2–mediated coactivator binding amplifies transcriptional output from ligand-activated nuclear receptors.</cite>

- Tissue-level physiology and therapeutic effect. The integrated cellular changes produce organ-level effects—bronchodilation, secretion modulation, anti-inflammation, or proliferation/survival control—measured as therapeutic efficacy and balanced against adverse effects governed by bias, potency, and receptor dynamics. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonist and antagonist concepts align with clinical bronchodilation and anticholinergic effects; potency metrics (EC50/Emax) quantify therapeutic window.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-2">Allosteric control of pathway selection (G protein vs arrestin) can improve bronchodilation while reducing adverse effects.</cite>

Designing for activation with precision
Pharmacologists exploit orthosteric and allosteric sites to engineer agonists, partial agonists, antagonists, and inverse agonists; bias ligands preferentially engage pathway subsets to maximize therapeutic gain and minimize desensitization and cross-reactivity. Clinicians then translate these mechanisms into dosing—balancing occupancy (affinity) and efficacy (potency) to achieve target ED50–ED95 profiles with minimal adverse effects. <cite id="2b2e843b-3">Affinity governs occupancy, efficacy governs response magnitude and Emax; ED50 and Emax underpin pharmacodynamic profile and dosing.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-3">Biased agonism aims to drive therapeutic pathways while dampening off-target cascades, improving drug efficacy and safety.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-7">Kinetic views of allostery and multiple active states provide design levers to tune efficacy, bias, and adaptation, informing next-generation therapeutics.</cite>

Practical takeaways
- What “activates” a receptor: ligand binding that achieves sufficient affinity to stabilize an active conformation and exhibits intrinsic efficacy to engage signaling (full agonist), or partial/biased activation that modulates downstream pathways. <cite id="2b2e843b-0">Efficacy defines activation as turning the key from bound drug; agonists possess affinity and efficacy.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-1">Allosteric coupling quantifies how binding translates into pathway-selective efficacy.</cite>

- What follows: receptor-class–specific cascades—G protein–coupled cAMP/PKA or IP3/DAG–Ca2+; kinase-linked MAPK/PI3K/STAT; nuclear receptor–driven coactivator-chromatin transcriptional programs—leading to ion channel, enzyme, and gene expression changes that manifest as bronchodilation, secretion changes, anti-inflammatory or proliferative effects, with magnitude and ceiling set by potency and efficacy. <cite id="8974a619-4">GPCR pathways (cAMP, IP3, DAG) route to ion channel and kinase cascades that control contraction, secretion, and excitability.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Tyrosine kinase activation drives adaptor recruitment and Ras/PI3K/STAT programs that control proliferation and survival.</cite> <cite id="30a5b39c-0">Nuclear receptor coactivators acetylate histones to open chromatin and activate transcription, altering physiology at the gene-level.</cite>

- Modifying activation for therapy: choose orthosteric full/partial agonists for robust or ceiling-limited effects; use allosteric positive/negative modulators to shift bias and reduce side effects; deploy antagonists/inverse agonists to reverse or suppress basal drive—while monitoring desensitization and pharmacodynamics to titrate dose and duration. <cite id="2b2e843b-2">Agonists and antagonists form the basis of bronchodilating and anticholinergic therapies.</cite> <cite id="2b2e843b-7">Inverse agonism can suppress constitutive receptor activity to reduce basal signaling.</cite> <cite id="8974a619-3">Biased agonism provides a rational route to maximize efficacy and minimize adverse effects by steering signaling.</cite>

Summary
- College athletes, including those at the top level, generally report better health-related quality of life (HRQoL) than non-athlete college students, and injured athletes report worse HRQoL than uninjured peers on validated instruments such as SF-36 and sport-specific measures.<cite id="8178bd4e-0">Athletes reported better HRQOL than nonathletes and uninjured athletes reported better HRQOL than injured athletes, based on a systematic review of athletes versus nonathletes</cite><cite id="8178bd4e-1">In a prospective study of undergraduate athletes and matched general college students, sport participation was associated with favorable HRQoL trajectories compared to sedentary peers</cite><cite id="8178bd4e-2">Adolescent athletes had higher SF-36 and PODCI subscale scores than nonathletes for mental, emotional, and physical well-being</cite>. However, among former elite athletes (e.g., Division I), longitudinal and cross-sectional comparisons show decrements relative to non-collegiate populations: worse physical function, higher pain and fatigue, and greater depressive symptoms at follow-up.<cite id="d0c36e5c-0">Former Division I athletes had worse scores for depression, fatigue, pain, and physical function at follow-up</cite><cite id="d0c36e5c-4">A cohort study of 232 former collegiate athletes (ages 40–65) compared levels of HRQoL to nonathletes, highlighting lower HRQoL in the former group</cite><cite id="d0c36e5c-6">Former Division I athletes had a worse score than nonathletes by a mean difference of 17.51 points on the physical function scale</cite>. Former top-level athletes also report more daily activity limitations and more major/chronic injuries than non-collegiate athletes.<cite id="d0c36e5c-1">Former Division I athletes reported significantly more limitations in daily activities and more major and chronic injuries than non-collegiate athletes</cite><cite id="d0c36e5c-2">Levels of HRQoL were compared between former collegiate athletes and nonathletes in a cohort ranging from 40 to 65 years</cite><cite id="d0c36e5c-5">Injuries sustained during college had lasting impacts on HRQoL among former Division II collegiate athletes</cite>.

Injury prevalence and risk
- Within the college context, football and high-risk sports have markedly higher injury rates and mental health symptom burdens than low-contact sports; prior psychiatric symptoms are associated with elevated injury risk during collegiate competition.<cite id="eff37bb6-1">Depression and anxiety were leading mental health conditions among collegiate athletes, with high prevalence among National Collegiate athletes</cite><cite id="eff37bb6-2">Preseason anxiety symptoms were associated with 2.5 (males) and 1.9 (females) times higher injury rates</cite><cite id="eff37bb6-3">In a retrospective study of Division I football players, 33% of injured athletes reported high depressive symptoms</cite>. NCAA surveillance indicates football (Division I/FBS) has substantially elevated injury rates and time-loss totals per 1,000 athlete-exposures compared with most other sports, underscoring higher injury exposure for top-level, contact-heavy programs relative to active non-top-level sports.<cite id="eff37bb6-5">Student-athlete mental health indicators remained elevated, in a context where injury susceptibility and mental exhaustion, anxiety, and depression co-occur</cite><cite id="eff37bb6-9">A 2020 NCAA data review noted mental health staffing gaps within athletic departments, amid concerns about student-athlete mental health</cite>. Cross-sectionally, elite/former Division I athletes have higher prevalence of chronic injuries and functional limitations that persist after sport retirement, contributing to lower HRQoL versus active non-athletes.<cite id="d0c36e5c-1">Former Division I athletes reported more major and chronic injuries and greater activity limitations than non-collegiate athletes</cite><cite id="d0c36e5c-5">Injuries during college had lasting impacts on HRQoL in former collegiate athletes</cite>.

Comparative patterns and what “top-level” vs. “active non-top-level” implies
