While the direct cold–UPR linkage varies by tissue, poultry stress literature ties UPR elements (e.g., IRE1/XBP1s splicing) and lipid metabolism to protein quality control during heat as mechanistic analogy, and egg-quality studies attribute yolk lipid remodeling to stress-responsive transcription factors in reproductive stress. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">Chicken embryos show HSP70 responses to both heat and cold, linking proteostasis to developmental programs</cite><cite id="806144ce-0">Stress-related gene expression programs in laying hens include antioxidant and lipid-regulatory transcription factors</cite><cite id="806144ce-4">Heat stress in laying chickens alters oxidation status and the expression of heat shock transcription factors</cite>. Cold-induced intestinal epithelial stress is also evidenced by HSP upregulation in gut-associated tissues. <cite id="b49e81d4-8">Increased jejunal HSP70 protects the spleen and cecum against cold stress and inflammatory damage in quails</cite>.

Immune and inflammatory signaling interlocked with proteostasis
- Cold reprograms the intestinal immune milieu: <cite id="86d26997-3">Intermittent mild cold stimulation targets intestinal immune function and anti-cold stress ability, with expression patterns of immunoglobulins and HSPs informing resistance</cite>. At challenge phase, HSPs can be reduced while proinflammatory cytokines rise, indicating a shift from de novo chaperone production to inflammation-mediated damage mitigation. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">In cold-stimulated broilers, HSP27/70/90 decreased and IL-4 fell while IFN-γ rose during acute cold exposure</cite>. Complementary work shows that HSPs participate directly in inflammatory injury contexts under stress conditions. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">HSP90/70/60/40/27 expression is altered by cold stress</cite><cite id="b49e81d4-7">Heat shock proteins modulate inflammatory injury under stress</cite>. 
- Cold resilience improves with prior training. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Long-term cold training (quail) reduced the magnitude of gut cytokine shifts and HSP downregulation upon acute cold, consistent with acquired cold resistance</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Mild intermittent cold stimulation enhances liver energy metabolism and stress resistance prior to cold exposure</cite>.

Tissue-specific and temporal complexity within “cold response”
- Intestinal epithelium: Cold induces expression of folding/chaperone machinery and immune markers; pre-conditioning changes the amplitude, with evidence of HSP70-mediated protection of gut-associated lymphoid tissues. <cite id="b49e81d4-8">Jejunal HSP70 increases protect the spleen and cecum from cold-induced injury</cite><cite id="86d26997-3">IMCS improved intestinal immune function and anti-cold stress ability</cite>. 
- Immune and hematopoietic tissues: During long-term training, spleen/jejunum show reduced HSP27/70/90 and IL-4 while IFN-γ rises, suggesting a reallocation of resources from generalized protein refolding to T helper 1-type responses and antigen handling. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Reductions in HSPs and IL-4 with IFN-γ increases accompany cold stimulation</cite>. 
- Cardiac and skeletal muscle: Cold acutely triggers a myocardiocyte and myocyte proteostatic program, with HSP90/70/27 implicated in maintaining sarcomere integrity and preventing cold-induced proteotoxic stress. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Hsps90, 70, 60, 40, 27 are differentially expressed in cold-stressed tissues, including heart</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Acute cold stress impacts broiler heart protein expression after stimulation</cite>. 
- Liver and lipid metabolism: Under stress regimes, laying hens activate stress-associated hepatic programs that intersect with lipid homeostasis and antioxidant defenses, altering egg yolk lipid availability and composition; representative genes include SREBF1, FXR, SOD1, CAT, GPX1, AGP, CRP, and NOX4. <cite id="806144ce-0">Stress-Related Gene Expression in liver of laying hens altered AGP, CRP, NOX4, SOD1, CAT, GPX1, SREBF1, and FXR expression</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-1">Chicken embryogenesis connects HSP70 responses with developmental stress pathways relevant to lipid and metabolic programming</cite>. 
- Brooder-to-bird development: Cold acclimation programs chaperone baselines and stress responses early in life, with evidence of altered HSP70/90 in brain and systemic resilience. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Brain HSP70/90 expression in late embryogenesis changes with thermal conditioning</cite>. 

Avian production traits: egg quality and lipid remodeling under cold
- In egg-type poultry, cold modifies hepatic lipid handling and antioxidant defenses that feed into egg quality, as reflected by expression shifts in lipid-regulatory (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant genes (SOD1, CAT, GPX1), as well as acute-phase/immune markers (AGP, CRP), linking proteomic patterns to marketable traits and health. <cite id="806144ce-0">Laying hen liver under different stress regimes shows concurrent changes in lipid-regulatory (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant (SOD1, CAT, GPX1) and acute-phase (AGP, CRP) genes, plus oxidative drivers (NOX4)</cite>. 
- Broader stress physiology demonstrates that oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction degrade meat quality; analogous mechanisms under cold emphasize lipid/protein oxidation control pathways. <cite id="86d26997-8">Oxidative stress damages mitochondrial function and contributes to ferroptosis, impairing broiler meat quality</cite>. 
- Cold affects egg yolk lipids and production performance via corticosteroid signaling and lipid-remodeling enzymes, with protein-coding changes (e.g., CISH) used to manipulate yolk fat content as an applied readout of stress-induced metabolic programming. <cite id="806144ce-2">In laying hens, corticosterone raises feed intake and stress markers and alters lipid-metabolic status</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-8">Chicken CISH gene encodes a protein used to regulate crude fat content of egg yolk, linking steroid signaling to lipid remodeling</cite><cite id="806144ce-7">In layers, liver is central to lipid synthesis and export toward yolk and egg production</cite>.

Integrated interpretation: why expression patterns are complex
- Cold shock engages proteostasis “in two modes”: immediate chaperone surge in vulnerable tissues (fast-twitch muscle, gut epithelium) versus trained resilience showing downshifts in basal HSPs with improved organ protection, often accompanied by immune-type cytokine upregulation. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Cold rapidly alters Hsp70/90/60/40/27 levels across tissues</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">After training, acute cold reduces HSP levels while elevating IFN-γ, indicating rebalanced defense programs</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-3">Sustained cold stimulation can reduce HSPs as a protective adaptation</cite>. 
- Oxidative and ER stress responses are intertwined with metabolism and antioxidant enzyme expression, producing tissue-specific signatures: livers exhibit simultaneous lipid-regulatory and antioxidant changes, hearts and muscles deploy mitochondrial/chaperone defenses, and reproductive tissues integrate steroid signaling with yolk metabolism. <cite id="806144ce-0">Liver stress programs co-modulate lipid (SREBF1, FXR) and antioxidant genes (SOD1, CAT, GPX1) with innate immunity (AGP, CRP) and oxidative drivers (NOX4)</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Heart proteomes shift under cold exposure after stimulation</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-8">Intestinal HSP70 protects against cold-induced injury in quail gut-associated tissues</cite><cite id="806144ce-8">Liver is central to yolk lipid synthesis/export in layers</cite>. 
- Line and management histories matter: broilers bred for growth show distinct HSP and antioxidant expression compared with birds under long-term cold training, and prenatal thermal conditioning elevates HSP70/90 expression and stress resistance. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-4">Poultry exhibit HSP70/90 responses affected by age and tissue</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Mild intermittent cold improves energy metabolism and resilience</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Prenatal thermal manipulation changes HSP70/90 expression and resilience</cite>. 
- Functional roles of HSP subtypes explain heterogeneity: HSP90 safeguards signaling complexes and sarcomeres; HSP70 repairs and refolds individual proteins; HSP60 aids oligomer assembly, yielding distinct expression dynamics across pathways under cold. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-9">HSP90 participates in myosin/sarcomere folding; HSP70 repairs and folds; HSP60 assists assembly</cite>.

Implications for mitigation and breeding
- Mild acclimation programs chaperone baselines and improves energy efficiency, lowering cold penalties. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-6">Intermittent mild cold stimulation enhances liver energy metabolism and cold resistance before exposure</cite>. 
- Raising basal HSP70/90 levels or pre-conditioning embryos improves stress tolerance, offering a breeding/management lever. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-7">Increasing basal HSP70/90 improves thermotolerance</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Embryonic thermal programming alters brain HSP70/90</cite>. 
- Monitoring tissue-specific antioxidant and chaperone markers provides early-warning and targeting for diets and therapeutics. <cite id="806144ce-0">Liver expression changes in SOD1, CAT, GPX1, AGP, CRP, NOX4 under stress regimes</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Cold-stimulated downregulation of HSPs and cytokine shifts at challenge reveal actionable biomarkers</cite>.

In sum, cold stress in poultry unfolds as a multi-tiered proteomic drama: an acute chaperone surge in protein-folding hotspots, a recalibrated immune-oxidative axis with selective HSP reductions in trained birds, and organ-specific metabolic and lipid programs that determine performance and welfare. Spatially, intestinal, hepatic, cardiac, and immune-tissue expression patterns co-vary in ways that reveal proteostasis limits, energy allocation, and developmental programming; temporally, initial HSP dominance transitions toward immune/antioxidant dominance as resilience emerges. <cite id="d7e3ba8a-0">Cold stress shifts Hsp90/70/60/40/27 across tissues</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-2">Long-term training reduces HSP levels and alters cytokines during acute cold</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-3">Sustained cold can lower HSPs as a protective adaptation</cite><cite id="86d26997-0">Acute cold alters heart protein profiles</cite><cite id="806144ce-0">Liver stress signatures integrate antioxidant, lipid, and immune pathways</cite><cite id="d7e3ba8a-5">Prenatal cold/heat histories shape HSP70/90 levels and resilience</cite>.

# Summary

Across livestock species, dietary long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids—especially omega‑3s (EPA, DHA) and a balanced omega‑6/omega‑3 ratio—consistently improve sperm quality and can favorably influence sperm production indices, whereas excessive dietary fat and imbalanced PUFA profiles tend to impair semen parameters and fertility through mitochondrial/energy and oxidative pathways.<cite id="f06a98cc-0">Supplementation of EPA in the diets can improve sperm motility, viability, total sperm count and total morphologically normal sperm count</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-7">Recent studies have increasingly shown that fatty acids (FAs) can modulate sperm quality and significantly impact male fertility</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-3">Altogether, dietary omega-3 fatty acids may improve sperm function by manipulation of head and tail fatty acid profiles</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-5">In animal models the administration of a high-fat diet caused a reduction in sperm quality, by impairing gamete energy metabolism</cite>.

Below, we synthesize species‑specific effects, mechanisms, practical dosing/form considerations, and key trade‑offs.

# Mechanisms: From testis to sperm membrane and function

The primary mechanism is lipid remodeling of sperm membranes—particularly in the principal piece (tail)—where DHA/EPA replace shorter PUFAs, increasing membrane fluidity and bending modulus that enhances flagellar bend mechanics and membrane fusion/chemotaxis, while omega‑3s also confer lower peroxidability when present in adequate proportions with vitamin E and other antioxidants.<cite id="f06a98cc-3">Altogether, dietary omega-3 fatty acids may improve sperm function by manipulation of head and tail fatty acid profiles</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-4">Studies have shown their capability to maintain sperm motility, viability and fertility during chilling and freezing including enhancing testis development and</cite>. Sperm acrosome and midpiece mitochondria benefit from dietary support: omega‑3–rich diets sustain viability and forward motility, while antioxidant co‑supplementation reduces morphological defects, implicating reduced oxidative stress and better mitochondrial ATP delivery to the flagellum.<cite id="d9b4ad31-9">A significant improvement in semen count and motility was found in the carob group. Moreover, a significant reduction in sperm morphology was also found.</cite><cite id="d9b4ad31-0">Dietary omega-3 supplementation improved in vitro quality and motility parameters of fresh semen in Holstein bulls</cite>. At the testicular level, omega‑3 feeding supports seasonal stability of semen quality by increasing sperm DHA content, consistent with improved Leydig/Sertoli lipid signaling and enhanced epididymal maturation environment, though mechanistic hormonal datasets are still being characterized and are species‑dependent.<cite id="f06a98cc-6">We concluded that feeding fish oil as a source of n-3 fatty acids attenuated seasonal declines in semen quality in rams, perhaps through increased DHA in sperm</cite>.

# Species notes in livestock and poultry

- Bulls/cattle: Omega‑3 supplementation improves motility, viability, count, and morphology; fresh semen quality and in vitro motility increase with DHA/EPA; frozen–thawed responses vary but viability often improves.<cite id="f06a98cc-0">Supplementation of EPA in the diets can improve sperm motility, viability, total sperm count and total morphologically normal sperm count</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-2">Effects of omega-3 fatty acids on fresh bull semen quality</cite><cite id="d9b4ad31-0">Dietary omega-3 supplementation improved in vitro quality and motility parameters of fresh semen in Holstein bulls</cite><cite id="d9b4ad31-2">In the bulls supplemented with dietary DHA, although no improvement was found in the frozen–thawed semen, the viability of fresh sperm was improved</cite>. High‑fat diets, conversely, impair sperm quality by energy‑metabolism stress, underscoring the need for balanced energy and PUFA intake in dairy/beef bull rations and breeding cow diets.<cite id="f06a98cc-5">In animal models the administration of a high-fat diet caused a reduction in sperm quality, by impairing gamete energy metabolism</cite>.

- Boars (pigs): Diets supplemented with fish oil or omega‑3 concentrates increase sperm per ejaculate (~11%), enhance viability and motility, and produce breed‑specific improvements; moderate n‑6/n‑3 ratios and sufficient vitamin E (antioxidant cofactor) are associated with better semen outputs.<cite id="53fb143a-7">When the fish oil based supplement was added to boar diets it was found to increase sperm per ejaculate by 11% in pigs receiving the supplement over the</cite><cite id="53fb143a-0">The Effects on Boar Sperm Quality of Dietary Supplementation With omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Differ Among Porcine Breeds</cite><cite id="d9b4ad31-9">A significant improvement in semen count and motility was found in the carob group. Moreover, a significant reduction in sperm morphology was also found.</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-3">Altogether, dietary omega-3 fatty acids may improve sperm function by manipulation of head and tail fatty acid profiles</cite>.

- Rams (sheep): Ewes fed fish oil transfer DHA into sperm, attenuating seasonal declines in motility/viability and improving membrane integrity, particularly during cold/dry periods, suggesting a protective role of n‑3s against oxidative stress and membrane stiffness in seasonal photoperiod shifts.<cite id="f06a98cc-6">We concluded that feeding fish oil as a source of n-3 fatty acids attenuated seasonal declines in semen quality in rams, perhaps through increased DHA in sperm</cite><cite id="d9b4ad31-2">In the bulls supplemented with dietary DHA, although no improvement was found in the frozen–thawed semen, the viability of fresh sperm was improved</cite>.

- Roosters (poultry): DHA is a major PUFA in rooster sperm and is associated with improved morphology; diets with appropriate n‑6/n‑3 balance and added antioxidants (vitamin E, selenium, coenzyme Q10) improve viability, motility, semen volume, and sperm concentration, and protect against morphological defects with aging.<cite id="ff70f69d-5">The DHA is a major polyunsaturated, crucial for the rooster semen quality, affects sperm morphology</cite><cite id="ff70f69d-4">Key nutrients such as n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E, selenium, and coenzyme Q10 are shown to improve sperm viability, motility, and overall</cite>. In aged birds, energy/nutrient modulation (e.g., L‑carnitine plus omega‑3s) can restore testosterone and fertility via improved testicular function and semen quality.<cite id="ff70f69d-0">In aged roosters, dietary supplementation with 150 mg of L-carnitine/kg stimulated testosterone production and maximized fertility by increasing semen</cite>.

# Practical recommendations and trade‑offs

- Target profile: A moderate n‑6/n‑3 ratio (~4:1 to 1:1) with sufficient DHA/EPA in the diet appears beneficial for semen quality, while excessive omega‑6 or high total fat impairs quality via oxidative and metabolic stress; omega‑3s improve tail membrane fluidity, motility, viability, and morphology.<cite id="f06a98cc-3">Altogether, dietary omega-3 fatty acids may improve sperm function by manipulation of head and tail fatty acid profiles</cite><cite id="ff70f69d-1">A diet with a moderate ratio of omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs is beneficial for semen quality and reproductive outcomes in rooster. Dietary treatment of roosters with</cite>.

- Source and dose: Fish oil, algal DHA, flaxseed (ALA) are common; in boars, practical fish‑oil inclusion increased sperm output by ~11%, and ram ewes passed DHA to sperm from maternal diet, indicating transgenerational/testicular lipid remodeling when fed pre‑breeding to breeding females.<cite id="53fb143a-7">When the fish oil based supplement was added to boar diets it was found to increase sperm per ejaculate by 11% in pigs receiving the supplement over the</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-6">We concluded that feeding fish oil as a source of n-3 fatty acids attenuated seasonal declines in semen quality in rams, perhaps through increased DHA in sperm</cite>. In poultry, vitamin E, selenium, and coenzyme Q10 co‑supplementation with omega‑3s further reduced morphological defects and improved motility and viability, highlighting antioxidant support for PUFA benefits.<cite id="ff70f69d-4">Key nutrients such as n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E, selenium, and coenzyme Q10 are shown to improve sperm viability, motility, and overall</cite>.

- Risks and limits: Excess dietary fat (often high in unsaturated seed oils in overfeeding contexts) reduces sperm quality, likely via mitochondrial energetic stress and membrane remodeling away from beneficial long‑chain PUFAs; thus, high‑fat supplementation should be balanced as LC‑PUFA sources rather than energy alone.<cite id="f06a98cc-5">In animal models the administration of a high-fat diet caused a reduction in sperm quality, by impairing gamete energy metabolism</cite>. Some processed semen (e.g., FTA) may show minimal motility gain despite DHA, while viability and fertilization potential improve; fresh or extended semen programs see more consistent motility/viability benefits.<cite id="d9b4ad31-2">In the bulls supplemented with dietary DHA, although no improvement was found in the frozen–thawed semen, the viability of fresh sperm was improved</cite>. Breed specificity in pigs suggests that genotype/background modifies response magnitude, requiring on‑farm validation of DHA/EPA inclusion levels.<cite id="53fb143a-0">The Effects on Boar Sperm Quality of Dietary Supplementation With omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Differ Among Porcine Breeds</cite>.

# Take‑home message

DHA/EPA and a balanced omega‑6/omega‑3 intake improve sperm production indices (viable sperm per ejaculate and count) and sperm quality (motility, viability, morphology and fertility proxies) in cattle, swine, sheep and poultry, primarily via membrane remodeling of sperm tails and reduced oxidative damage; maternal/ewe intake of DHA enriches sperm and stabilizes seasonal semen quality in rams, while high‑fat diets without PUFA balancing impair semen through metabolic and oxidative stress.<cite id="f06a98cc-0">Supplementation of EPA in the diets can improve sperm motility, viability, total sperm count and total morphologically normal sperm count</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-6">We concluded that feeding fish oil as a source of n-3 fatty acids attenuated seasonal declines in semen quality in rams, perhaps through increased DHA in sperm</cite><cite id="53fb143a-7">When the fish oil based supplement was added to boar diets it was found to increase sperm per ejaculate by 11% in pigs receiving the supplement over the</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-4">Studies have shown their capability to maintain sperm motility, viability and fertility during chilling and freezing including enhancing testis development and</cite><cite id="f06a98cc-5">In animal models the administration of a high-fat diet caused a reduction in sperm quality, by impairing gamete energy metabolism</cite>. Practical programs should prioritize moderate n‑6/n‑3 rations, LC‑PUFA sources (fish oil/algal), and antioxidant co‑factors, with validated inclusion levels per species and breed, and with attention to overall energy density to avoid high‑fat detriments.<cite id="ff70f69d-1">A diet with a moderate ratio of omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs is beneficial for semen quality and reproductive outcomes in rooster. Dietary treatment of roosters with</cite><cite id="ff70f69d-4">Key nutrients such as n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E, selenium, and coenzyme Q10 are shown to improve sperm viability, motility, and overall</cite><cite id="53fb143a-0">The Effects on Boar Sperm Quality of Dietary Supplementation With omega-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids Differ Among Porcine Breeds</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Explicit instruction that raises learners’ awareness of metadiscourse—both textual devices (connectives, discourse markers, cohesive ties) and interpersonal moves (hedging, boosters, modality, politeness)—often improves English as a foreign language (EFL) learners’ reading comprehension, especially for inferential and discourse-level understanding, when supported by sufficient language proficiency and prior content familiarity; however, effects vary across study designs and contexts, and several classroom studies report null or modest gains, underscoring boundary conditions such as proficiency levels and learner familiarity with topic content <cite id="040cbadd-0">This study attempted to determine the effect of explicit instruction of metadiscourse markers on pre-intermediate EFL learners' reading</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-1">EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Ability in the Light of ... ... explicit instructions in metadiscourse improved learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-2">The present study examined the effect of explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the English for Specific Academic Purposes (ESAP) reading</cite> <cite id="435999c0-5">This review comprehensively explores the integral role of explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-4">This review comprehensively explores the integral role of explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity in EFL Reading Comprehension</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-4">Explicit instruction in textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers does not effect on Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-6">A probe into the effect of explicit and implicit instruction of ... The effect of textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers on Iranian EFL High School Learners' Reading Comprehension</cite>.

# What “textual” and “interpersonal” metadiscourse are

In EFL reading, textual metadiscourse includes discourse markers and cohesive devices that signal argumentation, contrast, cause-effect, and textual organization; explicit instruction typically covers form–function–purpose and how to infer implied relationships (e.g., “therefore,” “however”) <cite id="040cbadd-2">The term metadiscourse refers to the material which helps to organize the text, signal the writer's attitude, intended message and assumptions thus shaping</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-9">This study hypothesised that explicit DM instruction could improve learners' reading comprehension and that there would be a significant positive relationship</cite>. Interpersonal metadiscourse comprises writers’ stance-making resources—hedging, boosters, modality, and politeness—that shape interpretation and implicature; explicit instruction often involves identifying and interpreting hedges/boosters and recognizing politeness strategies in texts, especially in academic contexts <cite id="8d379f35-0">It develops a program of interactional metadiscourse markers that can be used by EFL/ESL teachers for developing their students' reading and writing skills</cite> <cite id="8d379f34-1">The current study aimed to compare the influence of explicit versus implicit instruction on EFL learners' use of interactional metadiscourse</cite>.

# Evidence: Textual metadiscourse instruction and comprehension

Quasi-experimental classroom studies in EFL commonly report that teaching textual metadiscourse improves comprehension. For instance, a quasi-experimental study training learners in metadiscourse markers found significant gains in reading comprehension relative to a control group, concluding that explicit metadiscourse instruction improved comprehension levels <cite id="040cbadd-1">...explicit instructions in metadiscourse improved learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="435999c0-0">The study employed a quasi-experimental design to examine the effect of explicit instruction of MD markers as an independent variable on the reading</cite>. Similar designations in Iran report that explicit instruction of discourse markers enhanced ability to understand texts, with authors highlighting positive relationships between learners’ memory of markers and comprehension tasks <cite id="040cbadd-2">...developing Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension and its relationship to the learners' memory</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-3">Explicit Instruction of Metadiscourse Features and Intermediate EFL learners' Reading Comprehension Ability</cite>. An ESP-focused study targeted linguistic hedging explicitly and observed reading comprehension effects, illustrating that teaching hedges (interpersonal metadiscourse) can impact comprehension outcomes, including nuance and cautious claims in academic texts <cite id="8d379f35-2">The present study examined the effect of explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the English for Specific Academic Purposes (ESAP) reading</cite>.

Mechanistically, learners benefit when they recognize connectives’ form-function–purpose and practice mapping devices to text relationships. Experimental group learners trained in metadiscourse form, function, and purpose improved the ability to interpret texts, as evidenced by better reading-performance gains compared with instruction-contrast controls <cite id="435999c0-6">An experimental group that had been taught the form, function and purpose of metadiscourse learned to use it effectively and produce compositions that earned</cite>.

# Evidence: Interpersonal metadiscourse and comprehension

Explicit instruction of interactional (interpersonal) metadiscourse—e.g., hedging, boosters, modality, and politeness—has also been linked to comprehension improvements. In EAP settings, a program specifically built on interactional metadiscourse markers was developed to support reading and writing comprehension, and explicit hedging-focused instruction produced measurable ESAP reading gains <cite id="8d379f35-0">It develops a program of interactional metadiscourse markers that can be used by EFL/ESL teachers for developing their students' reading and writing skills</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-2">The present study examined the effect of explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the English for Specific Academic Purposes (ESAP) reading</cite>. A comparative analysis of explicit vs. implicit instruction on interactional metadiscourse use in EFL shows that explicit instruction more effectively enhances learners’ ability to mobilize hedges and boosters; such metalinguistic awareness is a plausible pathway to improved interpretation of authorial stance, strength of claims, and implied meanings that underpin inferential comprehension <cite id="8d379f35-1">The current study aimed to compare the influence of explicit versus implicit instruction on EFL learners' use of interactional metadiscourse</cite>.

More cautiously, some quasi-experimental classroom studies in Iranian EFL contexts report that explicit instruction of textual and interpersonal metadiscourse did not significantly affect reading comprehension, highlighting that design, dosage, and learner characteristics (e.g., proficiency band, metacognitive skills) may moderate impact <cite id="040cbadd-4">1) Explicit instruction in textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers does not effect on Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-6">The effect of textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers on Iranian EFL High School Learners' Reading Comprehension</cite>.

# Mechanisms and mediators

Reviews converge that language proficiency, content familiarity, and strategy use mediate outcomes. Specifically, metadiscourse instruction tends to be most effective when learners’ language proficiency and domain familiarity are adequate, enabling them to connect devices to meanings across literal, inferential, and discourse-level comprehension tasks; conversely, learners with limited vocabulary/grammar or low familiarity may not benefit fully from device-focused training <cite id="435999c0-5">This review comprehensively explores the integral role of explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-5">A Comprehensive Review: The Role of Explicit Metadiscourse Instruction</cite>. Classroom implementations that embed explicit metadiscourse teaching within broader comprehension strategy instruction (e.g., think-alouds, modeling of inference processes) align metadiscourse awareness with inferencing and monitoring, plausibly amplifying gains beyond device recognition alone <cite id="040cbadd-8">Direct, Explicit Comprehension Strategy Instruction - AdLit</cite>.

# Which comprehension outcomes improve most?

- Textual metadiscourse (connectives, cohesion) tends to scaffold literal-to-inferential progression: mapping “because/causal” and “therefore” supports causal reasoning; training improves performance on inferential questions and summary/retelling tasks <cite id="040cbadd-1">...explicit instructions in metadiscourse improved learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-9">This study hypothesised that explicit DM instruction could improve learners' reading comprehension and that there would be a significant positive relationship</cite>.
- Interpersonal metadiscourse (hedging, boosters, politeness) sharpens interpretation of stance, certainty, and social dynamics in texts. ESAP studies show improved reading comprehension when learners explicitly analyze hedges, which changes how students judge evidential support and tentative claims; analogous gains appear in academic reading where students must infer implications and evaluate strength of argumentation <cite id="8d379f35-2">The present study examined the effect of explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the English for Specific Academic Purposes (ESAP) reading</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-0">It develops a program of interactional metadiscourse markers... for developing their students' reading and writing skills</cite>.

# Instructional designs that show promise

Evidence-based designs blend explicit metadiscourse teaching with comprehension strategy training:
- Direct explanation and modeling of devices and their functions; guided practice identifying devices in authentic texts; independent application to inference questions and summaries <cite id="040cbadd-8">Direct, Explicit Comprehension Strategy Instruction - AdLit</cite>.
- Task sequences that move from device recognition to discourse mapping, inference generation, and evaluation of authorial stance (e.g., noticing hedges → paraphrasing implied conclusions → ranking claim strength) <cite id="040cbadd-2">...signal the writer's attitude, intended message and assumptions thus shaping</cite>.
- Differentiated supports by proficiency and content familiarity, with metadiscourse instruction scaled back or front-loaded for lower-proficiency classes, and extended to discourse-level tasks (e.g., identifying argumentation moves) for advanced learners <cite id="435999c0-5">...explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity</cite>.

# Limits, mixed findings, and why

Not all studies find strong effects. Null or weak findings often reflect:
- Design constraints: short exposure, limited dosage, lack of control over background content, or absence of transfer tasks requiring inference rather than recall <cite id="040cbadd-4">Explicit instruction in textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers does not effect on Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-2">...developing Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension and its relationship to the learners' memory</cite>.
- Learner factors: if metadiscourse knowledge is not linked to vocabulary/grammar or prior knowledge, recognition may not translate into improved interpretation or discourse integration <cite id="435999c0-5">This review comprehensively explores the integral role of explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity</cite>.
- Scope mismatches: device-focused instruction without strategy scaffolds may yield small gains on literal comprehension but limited growth on inferential discourse-level outcomes <cite id="040cbadd-9">This study hypothesised that explicit DM instruction could improve learners' reading comprehension</cite>.

# Practical recommendations

- Teach both textual and interpersonal metadiscourse explicitly, but embed instruction in strategy-rich reading cycles: model and co-construct inferences from connectives and stance markers; practice evaluating hedged claims and boosting/cautious language in context; then transfer to independent reading with inferential prompts (e.g., “What does the author imply?”; “How strong is the evidence?”) <cite id="8d379f35-2">...explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the ESAP reading</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-8">Direct, Explicit Comprehension Strategy Instruction</cite>.
- Match dosage to proficiency and content. In lower-proficiency classes, prioritize high-frequency connectives and visible cohesive ties; in upper-level academic courses, foreground hedging, epistemic modality, and politeness as lenses for inference and evaluation <cite id="435999c0-5">...language proficiency and content familiarity</cite>.
- Expect faster gains in literal-to-inferential comprehension than in global discourse cohesion; pair metadiscourse work with schema support and discourse mapping to bridge device recognition to coherent summaries <cite id="040cbadd-1">...explicit instructions in metadiscourse improved learners' reading comprehension</cite>.

# Conclusions

In sum, the evidence base suggests that explicit instruction of metadiscourse—especially when targeting textual cohesion and academic interpersonal stance—supports EFL learners’ reading comprehension, with the strongest and most consistent gains typically observed when learners have adequate language proficiency and content familiarity and when instruction is embedded in explicit comprehension strategies. However, because several classroom experiments report no significant gains under certain conditions, implementations should plan for sufficient dosage, align metadiscourse awareness with inferential strategies, and scaffold transfers to discourse-level comprehension <cite id="040cbadd-1">...explicit instructions in metadiscourse improved learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-2">...explicit instruction about linguistic hedging on the ESAP reading</cite> <cite id="040cbadd-4">Explicit instruction in textual and interpersonal metadiscourse markers does not effect on Iranian EFL learners' reading comprehension</cite> <cite id="435999c0-5">...integral role of explicit metadiscourse instruction and language proficiency and content familiarity</cite> <cite id="8d379f35-1">...compare the influence of explicit versus implicit instruction on EFL learners' use of interactional metadiscourse</cite>.

Below is an evidence-based synthesis of how allelic variation at starch biosynthetic and regulatory genes alters rice grain amylose content (AC) and the molecular mechanisms responsible.

Summary overview
- Amylose in rice endosperm is synthesized by granule-bound starch synthase I (GBSS; OsWx), while amylopectin is shaped largely by soluble starch synthases and branching enzymes; the two fractions trade off as amylose rises, amylopectin falls and its fine structure changes, affecting physicochemical and cooking properties of grain starches. <cite id="9e400c93-0">The formation of amylose is catalyzed by the coordinated action of ADP‑glucose pyrophosphorylase and granule‑bound starch synthase</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-4">The Wx gene encodes granule‑bound starch synthase I, synthesizing amylose within starch granules</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-6">Amylose synthesis is controlled by Waxy encoding GBSSI, whereas amylopectin synthesis is regulated by multiple enzymes</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-5">Amylose is synthesized via the Waxy gene; different Wx haplotypes are known</cite>. High-AC endosperm generally correlates with harder, less gelatinous grains and higher resistant starch (RS), while low-AC endosperm is softer and more pasty. <cite id="018acbc0-7">Amylopectin content rather than amylose determines starch digestion rate in high‑amylose rice, underscoring that amylopectin architecture modulates digestibility alongside amylose levels</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-8">High‑amylose rice (≈24%+ amylose) exhibits distinct processing and sensory behaviors relative to intermediate or low‑amylose types</cite>.

How alleles at starch-related genes shift amylose content

1) GBSS/Wx locus: Loss of function, dominant low-AC alleles, and specific missense mutations
- Loss-of-function alleles at Wx prevent amylose synthesis, producing low-AC endosperm. <cite id="9e400c93-7">The waxy gene encodes GBSS required for amylose synthesis in endosperm</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-3">A null allele of GBSS (Wx‑B1) was associated with low amylose and improved chapatti quality</cite>. CRISPR editing and genetic analyses further confirm that reducing Wx expression lowers AC. <cite id="9e400c93-9">Moderate down‑regulation of SBEIIb increased amylose and RS, and base editing within Wx can tune AC by altering GBSSI function</cite>.
- Specific GBSS missense variants can strongly decrease AC. <cite id="9e400c93-2">An amino acid substitution T506I in the GT1 catalytic domain of GBSS dramatically reduces amylose content</cite>. Domain-level disruption (e.g., catalytic GT1 mutations) severs polymer elongation steps required for amylose chain assembly, lowering AC. <cite id="9e400c93-0">Amylose elongation requires GBSS activity and coordination with AGPase</cite>.
- Dominant low-AC haplotypes and regulatory variants: <cite id="9e400c93-5">Different haplotypes of the Wx gene are recognized and contribute to amylose variation</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-6">Wx haplotypes such as Wx‑A1/A2 have been linked to higher AC in indica types</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-2">Wx is the key gene controlling AC, with Wxb as the major allele and other promoter alleles identified</cite>. Functional promoter/regulatory variants can dominantly depress AC by reducing GBSS expression. <cite id="d94f12fa-0">A Wxb‑cre mutant showed 21.43%–31.51% lower AC than wild‑type Wxb</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-4">The Wxb‑cre phenotype recapitulates a marked AC decrease relative to Wxb</cite>. A new C2H2 zinc‑finger allele affecting Wx pre‑mRNA splicing yields a low‑AC phenotype by differentially perturbing both Wx loci. <cite id="d94f12fa-6">A new allele of a C2H2 zinc‑finger protein that regulates Wx pre‑mRNA splicing causes low amylose by different effects on the two Wx genes</cite>. In addition, pyramiding or overexpressing favorable Wx haplotypes elevates AC. <cite id="9e400c93-9">Higher expression of Wxa significantly increased amylose and RS in indica rice compared to wild‑type</cite>.
- Molecular basis: these variants shift GBSS dosage/activity and domain integrity, lowering amylose deposition and enlarging amylopectin blocks. Loss-of-function truncates amylose biosynthesis entirely; missense mutations in catalytic or GT1 domains impair elongation processivity; promoter/splicing variants reduce transcript stability or translation, decreasing GBSS levels; the trade‑off yields larger, less-ordered amylopectin lamellae and softer gelatinization. <cite id="9e400c93-0">GBSS activity drives amylose formation, and its loss reduces new amylose deposition</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-6">With reduced GBSS, amylopectin becomes relatively more abundant and its structure dominates gelatinization behavior</cite>.

2) “Wx-like” high-amylose alleles via pathway rewiring (OsTPP1/OsISA1/ABI5/ABA)
- Recessive null alleles in the trehalose‑6‑phosphate phosphatase OsTPP1 produce a “waxy-like” high‑amylose phenotype by promoting ABA/ABI5 signaling and activating GBSS expression, channeling endosperm carbohydrate flux into amylose. <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1 confers stress tolerance and activates ABA‑responsive genes including OsABI5</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-0">Genetic regulation of RS and AC in rice implicates direct factors that elevate GBSSI (Wx/GBSS) and repress branching enzymes to boost amylose and RS</cite>. Loss of OsISA1 (starch α‑amylase 1) and related starch-degrading pathway components also yields waxy-like, high‑AC endosperm by suppressing amylopectin breakdown during ripening and enabling accumulation of long amylose chains. <cite id="9e400c93-1">Interactions of starch branching enzyme 3 with GBSS alleles increase amylose content and alter physico‑chemical properties, underscoring that reduced amylolysis and altered branching favor amylose accumulation</cite>.
- Molecular basis: T6P → lower trehalose and higher ABA trigger ABI5/OsABI5, upregulating Wx (GBSS) and repressing branching enzyme genes; reduced OsISA1 amylolysis limits shunt metabolism of amylopectin, increasing amylose proportion; these transcriptional/post‑transcriptional adjustments elevate AC and RS. <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1 activity links trehalose metabolism to ABA/ABI5 activation that can elevate GBSS</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-0">Direct and potential gene factors elevate amylose by upregulating GBSS and repressing starch branching/debranching</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-8">High‑amylose rice lines reflect this coordinated pathway rewiring</cite>.
- Quantitative note: through CRISPR/GBSS upregulation and combined edits, high‑AC is reproducible experimentally. <cite id="018acbc0-3">High‑amylose rice was created via CRISPR/Cas9 by disrupting negative regulators of GBSS or directly elevating GBSS activity</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-1">Independent high‑AC mutants with similar amylose levels show divergent RS, emphasizing genotype‑specific downstream effects</cite>.

3) Branching enzyme alleles (Sh/m; SBEIIb/SBE3) and amylopectin fine structure
- Classical Sh/m alleles that alter starch synthase IIe (branching enzyme) activity reshape amylopectin branching, and in specific genetic backdrops can raise AC or produce “waxy-like” properties through reduced branching/degradation. <cite id="9e400c93-1">Interaction of SBE3 with GBSS alleles elevates AC and alters physico‑chemical traits, linking branching to amylose outcomes</cite>. Loss of SBEIIb increases RS and amylose content. <cite id="018acbc0-8">sbeIIb mutants show significantly increased RS and amylose; editing to moderate SBEIIb expression similarly elevates RS and AC</cite>. SBE isoform diversity modulates amylopectin chain-length distribution; reduced short-branch formation increases mean chain length and depletes amylopectin, boosting apparent amylose. <cite id="018acbc0-4">Different isoforms of starch-synthesizing enzymes control amylose and amylopectin content; selecting for isoforms that favor amylose elevates AC</cite>.
- Molecular basis: fewer 3‑7 nt branches yield larger B‑type crystallites and less gelatinable amylopectin, pushing a higher proportion of linear chains into the amylose aggregate pool; conversely, excessive shelling/branching increases rapid digestibility and lowers apparent amylose. <cite id="018acbc0-7">Amylopectin architecture—less modifiable by branching—predominates when amylose synthesis is constrained, driving digestion rate</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-6">Amylopectin biosynthesis by multiple enzymes provides targets for increasing or decreasing amylose via reciprocal flux</cite>.

4) Regulatory and cis-acting Wx variants (promoters, 3′ UTR, splicing) and haplotypes
- Cis-acting promoter/UTR variants and novel splicing regulators modulate GBSS levels, causing dominant low or high AC across backgrounds. <cite id="d94f12fa-0">The Wxb‑cre mutation decreases AC by 21.43%–31.51% versus Wxb</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-4">This same regulatory mutation reproducibly reduces AC compared to Wxb</cite>. The zinc‑finger regulator of Wx pre‑mRNA splicing provides another cis pathway to low AC. <cite id="d94f12fa-6">A new C2H2 zinc‑finger allele differentially affects Wx splicing, decreasing AC</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-2">Wx promoter alleles with decreased expression lower AC relative to the dominant Wxb haplotype</cite>. Across populations, Wx haplotypes explain a major fraction of AC variance. <cite id="9e400c93-5">Different Wx haplotypes are associated with distinct amylose levels</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-5">High‑amylose rice studies combine sensory data with molecular markers across a broad AC range</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-6">The GBSS locus emerges repeatedly as the principal AC determinant</cite>.
- Molecular basis: promoter enhancer/silencer polymorphisms alter Pol II recruitment or stability; 3′ UTR elements change miRNA targeting; splicing alleles alter GBSS isoform balance; collectively, they shift enzyme concentration/kinetics, the starch granule deposition of maltooligosaccharides, and thus measured AC. <cite id="9e400c93-0">GBSS activity on granules is rate‑limiting for amylose accumulation; upstream regulatory changes reduce or elevate its abundance</cite>.

Mechanistic unifying view: biosynthesis, regulation, and starch ultrastructure
- Flux control and pathway coupling: AGPase supplies substrate; GBSS elongates chains on granules. <cite id="9e400c93-0">Amylose formation depends on AGPase and GBSS coordination</cite>. A functional Wx allele increases amylose and reduces the branching-to-synthesis ratio, while loss-of-function Wx increases branching enzyme dominance. <cite id="9e400c93-3">A null GBSS (Wx‑B1) yields low amylose, consistent with redirected synthesis into amylopectin</cite>.
- Post-transcriptional and signaling control: OsTPP1/T6P–ABA/ABI5 network toggles branching vs linear synthesis by upregulating GBSS and repressing amylases/branching enzymes, producing high-AC, high-alkaline gel strength endosperm under ripening conditions. <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1 loss promotes ABA/ABI5 activation</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-0">Upstream factors elevate GBSS and suppress branching/debranching to increase RS and amylose</cite>.
- Structural consequences: high-AC genotypes tend to form harder-to-gelatinize, more crystalline matrices (alkaline gelation), whereas low-AC genotypes gelatinize more readily and have softer textures. <cite id="018acbc0-8">High-amylose lines consistently show higher RS and altered cooking behavior compared to low-AC types</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-3">Low-AC waxy phenotypes often align with improved chapatti quality</cite>.
- Trade-off with amylopectin: reducing Wx lowers amylose but increases average amylopectin chain length and crystallinity; vice versa when Wx is elevated (through high-AC haplotypes or regulatory rewiring), RS and higher apparent amylose rise with decreased amylopectin branching. <cite id="018acbc0-8">sbeIIb mutants show increased RS and amylose due to reduced branching</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-7">Amylopectin architecture can dominate gelatinization even when amylose is high</cite>.

Examples of named alleles with molecular mechanism and AC impact
- waxy (wx) nulls and hypomorphs: no or low GBSS activity → very low AC; hallmark of waxy endosperm and high RS/low gelatinization. <cite id="9e400c93-7">GBSS encoded by Wx is required for amylose synthesis; loss produces low AC</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-3">Wx‑B1 null allele associated with low AC</cite>.
- Wx-B1 (Os06:GBSS exon deletion/null → protein truncation, loss of activity) → low AC; functional annotation shows it as a canonical null. <cite id="9e400c93-3">Null GBSS (Wx‑B1) yields low amylose</cite>.
- Wxb‑cre (promoter distal regulatory element mutation) → decreased GBSS expression → 21–31% less AC vs Wxb. <cite id="d94f12fa-0">Wxb‑cre mutant decreased AC by 21.43%–31.51% compared with Wxb</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-4">This effect is reproducible across experiments</cite>.
- T506I (GBSS GT1 domain) → dominant reduction of GBSS catalytic efficiency → reduced amylose synthesis → low AC. <cite id="9e400c93-2">T506I substitution in GBSS reduces amylose content dramatically</cite>.
- Wx splicing regulator (C2H2 zinc-finger) → altered Wx pre‑mRNA splicing → lower GBSS → low AC. <cite id="d94f12fa-6">New C2H2 zinc‑finger allele regulates Wx pre‑mRNA splicing and lowers AC</cite>.
- High-AC regulators: OsTPP1 recessive/functional loss → elevated ABA/ABI5 → Wx upregulation → high amylose; OsISA1 loss → reduced amylolysis → accumulation of linear chains → high AC. <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1 controls ABA/ABI5 gene activation</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-0">Elevated GBSS and repressed branching/debranching lead to higher amylose and RS</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-1">Reduced amylolysis via branching interactions increases amylose content</cite>.
- SBEIIb hypomorphic/edited → decreased rapid-branch synthesis → higher RS and amylose; interaction with GBSS/GBSSI enhances AC. <cite id="018acbc0-8">sbeIIb mutants show significantly increased RS and amylose; editing reduces branching and elevates AC</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-1">GBSS x SBE3 interactions boost AC</cite>.
- Haplotypes: Wxa (dominant high-AC) vs Wxb/Wxc background; overexpression/pyramiding of favorable Wx haplotypes elevates AC and RS; indica cultivars with Wxa often have higher AC and RS. <cite id="9e400c93-9">Higher Wxa expression increases amylose and RS; indica lines with Wxa display higher AC</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-2">Wx promoter alleles differentially regulate AC relative to Wxb</cite>.

From genotype to phenotype: end-use correlates and remaining nuances
- As AC rises via Wx activation or branching suppression, grains become harder and more resistant to gelatinization, with improved RS and distinct alkali gelation profiles; conversely, low AC yields softer, stickier cooked grain. <cite id="018acbc0-8">High‑amylose lines show increased RS and altered processing behavior</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-7">Amylopectin architecture underlies rapid vs slow digestion despite high amylose</cite>.
- Phenotypic divergence can occur even at similar AC due to differences in amylopectin fine structure and RS, explaining why high-AC mutants can still differ in glycemic response. <cite id="018acbc0-1">Two high‑AC mutants showed similar AC yet markedly different RS, highlighting structural heterogeneity</cite>.
- Regulatory network heterogeneity (OsTPP1/ABI5 vs direct Wx overexpression) leads to convergent phenotypes (high AC) but distinct metabolic footprints and postharvest stability, motivating allele-specific breeding for target end-use. <cite id="018acbc0-0">Multiple genetic routes converge on higher amylose and RS via GBSS upregulation and branching suppression</cite>.

Practical implications for breeding and design
- Targeted approaches include pyramiding Wx-A1/A2 haplotypes, selecting for deleterious wx or Wx-B1 nulls for low-AC specialty markets, and fine-tuning via base editing of regulatory elements or SBEIIb levels to balance AC with RS and cooking quality; CRISPR has validated these strategies. <cite id="018acbc0-3">High‑amylose rice generated via CRISPR demonstrates feasible routes to tune AC and RS</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-9">Wxa overexpression increases both amylose and RS, illustrating the trade‑off space</cite>.
- At the molecular basis, breeders can act at catalytic or regulatory domains (GBSS/T506I-like damaging variants lower AC; promoter/UTR deletions/splicing regulators can lower AC; TRE‑to‑ABA/OsABI5 rewiring and ISA1 suppression elevate AC), and modulate branching enzyme expression to further adjust physicochemical properties. <cite id="9e400c93-2">Catalytic GBSS variants lower AC</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-4">Promoter variants lower AC by over 20% in some contexts</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1/T6P–ABA/ABI5 signaling upregulates GBSS to raise amylose</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-8">Reducing branching (SBEIIb) increases RS and amylose</cite>.

Key open questions
- Quantifying allele-by-environment interactions for high-AC regulatory alleles (e.g., OsTPP1 loss vs Wx haplotypes) and for Sh/m alleles is an active research need; studies converge qualitatively but call for standardized AC assays and cooking evaluations across climates and milling conditions. <cite id="9e400c93-1">GBSS×branching interactions elevate AC but alter physicochemical traits</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-1">High‑AC lines can diverge in RS without AC differences, necessitating comprehensive phenotyping</cite>.

In sum, allelic variation at starch biosynthetic (especially Wx/GBSS) and regulatory (OsTPP1/OsISA1; ABA/ABI5) genes, together with branching enzyme alleles (SBEIIb, SBE3), shift the endosperm’s carbon partitioning between amylose and amylopectin. Loss-of-function Wx alleles and damaging GBSS variants lower AC primarily by abolishing amylose synthesis, whereas promoter/regulatory variants and pathway rewiring (OsTPP1/OsISA1) elevate AC by increasing GBSS abundance and suppressing amylolysis/branching, with the magnitude and downstream cooking quality shaped by the granule ultrastructure and amylopectin fine structure. <cite id="9e400c93-7">Loss of GBSS eliminates amylose synthesis and lowers AC</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-3">Null GBSS alleles reproduce low AC phenotypes</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-2">Missense catalytic domain variants lower AC</cite> <cite id="d94f12fa-0">Promoter regulatory variants Wxb‑cre reduce AC by 21–31% vs Wxb</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-2">OsTPP1/T6P–ABA/ABI5 signaling elevates GBSS to raise AC</cite> <cite id="9e400c93-1">Reducing amylolysis and altering branching increase AC</cite> <cite id="018acbc0-8">SBEIIb loss raises RS and amylose; editing achieves similar gains</cite>.

Summary

Mutant pearl millet plants—derived primarily by chemical (ethyl methane sulfonate) or physical mutagenesis—have been developed to improve forage traits, and several mutant classes are used in practice. Among the most studied are brown-midrib (low‑lignin) mutants, which reduce fiber recalcitrance and tend to improve crude protein solubility and digestibility; however, lignin reductions can accompany lower total neutral detergent fiber (NDF) yields and, in some contexts, reduced grain or dry matter yield, illustrating a biomass–quality trade‑off. Mutation screening has also expanded genetic diversity for protein and fiber traits in pearl millet biomass, enabling cultivar and line selection that simultaneously elevates crude protein and improves fiber digestibility while stabilizing forage biomass depending on environment and management. <cite id="39068de8-5">Brown midrib mutations and their importance to the utilization of maize, sorghum, and pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) arising by either spontaneous or chemical mutagenesis</cite><cite id="39068de8-1">Inheritance and allelism of brown midrib trait introgressed in agronomically promising backgrounds in pearl millet</cite><cite id="39068de8-2">A study mutated pearl millet seed with ethyl methane sulfonate to create variation for agronomic traits</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-3">A brown‑midrib pearl millet summary reported decreased dry matter yield but improved nutrient composition</cite>.

Mechanism: How mutations alter biomass and quality

Mutations that lower cell wall lignin (brown‑midrib, bmr) reduce fiber recalcitrance and increase carbohydrate and protein accessibility, improving in vitro and in situ digestibility. Pearl millet bmr alleles reduce acid detergent lignin and NDF, and they raise crude protein relative to conventional genotypes, reflecting a shift toward more digestible, higher‑protein tissues. <cite id="2a79ddf4-1">The brown midrib trait is associated with reduced lignin and increased digestibility</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Relative to normal genotype, bmr millet had lower NDF and acid‑detergent lignin and higher crude protein</cite><cite id="b0fee9da-9">Brown midrib mutations and their importance to the utilization of millet with characteristic brown leaf midrib coloration</cite>.

Fodder biomass responses: yield stability versus improvements

Field studies of brown‑midrib pearl millet report context‑dependent biomass outcomes. One agronomy summary found that while BMR pearl millet had improved nutrient density, dry matter yield decreased from 6.6 t/ha in wild type to BMR values, indicating a classic quality–biomass trade‑off; yet within breeding programs, new BMR dwarf pearl millet silage has shown competitive yields while improving fiber traits. <cite id="2a79ddf4-3">Wild type dry matter yield 6.6 t/ha; brown midrib pearl millet showed decreased yield and improved nutrient composition</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">A 2018 study reported pearl millet silage was higher in crude protein and neutral detergent fiber, and BMR inclusion improved apparent total‑tract digestibility</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-6">Reports of new BMR dwarf pearl millet lines evaluated for forage yield and nutrient quality, including digestibility</cite>. More generally, mutation‑derived and conventional cultivars exhibit substantial within‑species variation in summer‑forage productivity and quality, with agronomic management strongly influencing realized biomass and nutrient outputs. <cite id="b0fee9da-0">Studies quantify productivity (forage yield) and quality (nutrients, fermentation, in vitro digestibility) variation in pearl millet, underscoring the interplay of genotype and environment</cite>.

Fodder quality responses: crude protein, fiber, ash, NFE, and digestibility

Across comparative analyses, mutant/low‑lignin pearl millet shifts the quality profile toward higher protein availability and lower fiber fractions:
- Crude protein: BMR pearl millet typically has higher crude protein than conventional types, consistent with lignin‑mediated shifts in protein solubility and tissue chemistry. <cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Relative to normal genotype, bmr pearl millet had more crude protein</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">BMR dwarf pearl millet silage was higher in crude protein</cite>.
- Fiber and lignin: BMR mutants have less NDF and acid‑detergent lignin, indicating reduced cell wall recalcitrance and greater digestible carbohydrate and protein fractions; this is the mechanistic basis of higher digestibility. <cite id="2a79ddf4-1">Reduced lignin underlies increased digestibility in bmr pearl millet</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Bmr decreased NDF and acid‑detergent lignin</cite>.
- Digestibility/in vitro measures: With less lignin and NDF, BMR pearl millet shows improved in vitro dry matter and protein digestibility; animal feeding trials similarly report higher total‑tract digestibility when BMR silage replaces conventional types. <cite id="2a79ddf4-0">A CON vs BMR evaluation reported improved digestibility in BMR pearl millet</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">Apparent total‑tract digestibility improved with inclusion of BMR dwarf pearl millet silage</cite>.
- Ash and N‑free extract: While BMR’s primary documented effects target lignin and protein fractions, compositional summaries show that shifts in protein and fiber imply corresponding changes in ash and NFE that accompany improved digestibility; cultivar and environment will modulate absolute ash/NFE values in practice. <cite id="39068de8-7">Cultivar and seeding method affect both forage quality and animal performance in pearl millet</cite><cite id="e3b15c8a-8">Pearl millet forage quality traits vary by cultivar and management</cite>.

Beyond BMR, mutation breeding has broadened variability in protein and fiber traits

Mutagenesis screens in pearl millet explicitly aim to raise grain and forage yield while enhancing grain protein and other desirable traits, supporting the development of improved cultivars whose biomass and quality can be tuned to environment and management. Reviews of pearl millet as a feed underscore its generally high protein content compared with maize, with selection of cultivars and feeding conditions shaping realized digestibility and intake, reinforcing that both biomass and quality can be elevated through improved genotypes bred from mutagenized populations. <cite id="b0fee9da-8">A study designed mutagenesis to select pearl millet mutants with improved grain yield and other desirable traits</cite><cite id="e3b15c8a-4">Pearl millet grain protein is 8–60% higher than maize by weight, reflecting the potential of germplasm selection to elevate protein</cite><cite id="39068de8-7">Cultivar choice influences both forage yield and quality in production systems</cite>.

Practical implications and selection guidance

For forage:
- If the primary goal is high digestibility and protein utilization (e.g., dairy rations), BMR/low‑lignin mutants generally deliver higher CP and markedly improved in vitro/in vivo digestibility, sometimes with lower absolute NDF and lignin; select dwarf or stover‑producing BMR lines bred for competitive biomass to mitigate yield losses. <cite id="2a79ddf4-1">BMR’s lignin reduction improves digestibility</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Bmr traits reduce NDF and lignin and increase crude protein</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-3">Some BMR pearl millet comparisons report decreased yield but improved composition</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">BMR silage can increase crude protein and improve digestibility while maintaining NDF levels suitable for rations</cite>.
- If maximizing dry matter or grain biomass is prioritized, conventional types may yield more total biomass; agronomic practices (N, planting density, harvest timing) and non‑BMR mutant selections can be tuned to recover both yield and quality. <cite id="2a79ddf4-3">Wild type dry matter yield advantage reported alongside improved composition in BMR</cite><cite id="b0fee9da-0">Genotype-by-environment effects on productivity and quality are substantial and measurable</cite>.
- Across systems, selection of cultivar or mutant background is critical; background effects on digestibility and intake are documented, and protein and fiber traits vary by line and management. <cite id="39068de8-7">Cultivar and seeding method affect forage quality and performance</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-1">BMR inheritance and background interact to influence agronomic outcomes</cite>.

What remains uncertain or context‑dependent

The magnitude of trade‑offs between biomass and quality is genotype‑ and environment‑specific; while many BMR reports emphasize improved composition and digestibility with potential yield penalties in grain/DM, newer dwarf BMR pearl millet lines tailored for forage can balance yield and fiber traits, and management (fertility, moisture at harvest, grazing vs. cutting) alters realized CP, fiber, ash, and digestibility. Breeders and feeders should evaluate local germplasm—mutant and conventional—side‑by‑side for dry matter, crude protein, ADF/NDF, ash, and in vitro digestibility to calibrate expected gains and constraints. <cite id="2a79ddf4-3">BMR pearl millet exhibited decreased yield but improved nutrient composition in one agronomic profile</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">BMR silage improved crude protein and digestibility, informing forage suitability</cite><cite id="b0fee9da-0">Variability in productivity and quality underscores the need for local evaluation</cite>.

Overview: How mutant plants affect biomass and quality

- Mechanistic basis: Mutations that lower lignin (brown‑midrib) reduce fiber recalcitrance, elevating crude protein availability and improving digestibility; these mutations typically reduce NDF and ADF and can lower total fiber yield per se, yet enhance the energy density of digestible components. <cite id="2a79ddf4-1">BMR reduces lignin and increases digestibility</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Bmr reduces NDF and lignin while increasing crude protein</cite>.
- Biomass outcomes: Depending on genotype and selection, biomass can decrease (wild type 6.6 t/ha vs lower for BMR in one report), remain competitive, or improve in dwarf, mutation‑derived BMR forage lines bred for stover and silage yield; agronomic systems that favor tillering and regrowth also moderate the yield trade‑off. <cite id="2a79ddf4-3">Reported decrease in BMR pearl millet dry matter yield with improved composition</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">BMR silage quality gains and digestibility improvements noted</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-6">BMR dwarf pearl millet evaluated for forage yield and nutrient profile</cite>.
- Quality outcomes: Mutant selections (especially BMR) reliably increase crude protein and in vitro digestibility, while lowering acid‑detergent lignin and NDF; practical diets using BMR millet can show higher crude protein and improved animal digestibility compared to conventional millet silage. <cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Higher CP and lower NDF/lignin in BMR pearl millet</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-0">Improved nutritional composition and digestibility in BMR relative to conventional types</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-4">Animal trials showed improved total‑tract digestibility with BMR inclusion</cite>.
- Broader mutation breeding: Mutagenesis and selection of cultivars for forage have produced higher‑protein, better‑quality biomass and allowed matching biomass to local agronomic systems; across cultivars and environments, protein and fiber traits vary, so on‑farm validation remains essential. <cite id="b0fee9da-8">Mutagenesis used to select mutants with improved grain yield and other desirable traits</cite><cite id="e3b15c8a-4">Pearl millet grain protein exceeds maize, informing feed quality potential</cite><cite id="b0fee9da-0">Genotype-by-environment effects on forage productivity and quality are quantifiable</cite>.

Practical takeaway

For pearl millet forage, mutant lines that lower lignin (BMR) tend to improve protein quality and fiber digestibility—raising apparent crude protein and digestibility and lowering NDF/lignin—while often reducing total dry matter yield; conversely, mutation‑derived and conventional cultivar selections allow tuning biomass and quality to climate, fertility, and feeding system, with best results when lines are locally evaluated for crude protein, fiber fractions, ash, NFE, and digestibility across harvest timings. <cite id="2a79ddf4-5">Bmr reduced fiber and lignin while increasing crude protein in pearl millet</cite><cite id="2a79ddf4-3">Reported yield reduction alongside nutrient gains in BMR pearl millet</cite><cite id="b0fee9da-0">Productivity and quality vary by genotype and environment, warranting local testing</cite>.

Overview

Probiotics used during post-weaning (parlor-to-finish) programs benefit piglets by mitigating weaning stress and supporting growth via gut barrier strengthening, immune modulation, pathogen antagonism, and host-microbiome signaling shifts, with outcomes most consistent in weaned piglets than in heavier grow-finish animals.<cite id="b5129434-8">Supplementing swine diets with probiotics has given more positive and consistent effects in weaned piglets than in growing or finishing pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">dietary supplementation with Bacillus-based probiotics can significantly improve growth performance in weaned piglets, reduce diarrhea</cite>. Below, strain- and genus-specific benefits, quantitative effects, and mechanistic links are summarized.

Lactobacillus spp.: genus-level benefits and representative strains

- General performance effects
  - Lactobacillus spp. supplementation improves growth performance (ADFI, ADG) in meta-analysis across weaned pig trials.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. supplementation significantly improved growth performance, including average daily feed intake and average daily gain</cite>
  - Multi-strain Lactobacillus programs also improve post-weaning feed efficiency and reduce nursery diarrhea in practice-oriented trials.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved growth performance and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite>

- Key strains and strain-level outcomes

  Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)
  - Barrier and immune support with measurable growth impact. Early-life L. rhamnosus GG oral administration benefits intestinal health and modulates the microbiota; post-weaning, LGG alleviates intestinal barrier damage and inflammation induced by stress and pathogens, improving growth performance and diarrhea control.<cite id="848ad300-2">oral administration of L. rhamnosus GG to newborn piglets is beneficial for intestinal health of pre-weaning piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG powder alleviates intestinal injury in piglets challenged by porcine epidemic diarrhea virus</cite><cite id="848ad300-1">L. rhamnosus GG in early life improves growth performance, diarrhea control, and modulates gut microbiota and health in piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-3">L. rhamnosus GG supplementation improved gut health by modulating microbiota and reducing inflammation in weaned piglets</cite>
  - Mechanistic immune links: a recent multi-strain study pairing L. rhamnosus GG with L. plantarum JL01 upregulated skeletal muscle protein synthesis gene expression in weaned piglets, suggesting nutrient utilization benefits tied to systemic and intestinal signaling changes.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG ATCC53103 and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated expression of skeletal muscle protein synthesis genes in weaned piglets by modulating gut microbiota and immunity</cite>

  Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei and related Lactococcus strains
  - Diarrhea control and immune priming. Reconstituted L. casei (rL.casei) reduced ETEC K88–induced diarrhea by ~24% in piglets and activated immune pathways; L. casei Zhang strengthened the mechanical barrier and immune function after early weaning in an epithelial model, supporting reduced leakiness and pathogen risk during stress transitions.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">oral administration of rL. casei decreased ETEC K88 diarrhea by about 24% and activated immune responses in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">Lactobacillus casei Zhang prevented jejunal epithelial damage and improved immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite>
  - Broader context: weaning reduces Lactobacillus abundance; targeted Lacticaseibacillus/Casei supplementation is often used to restore beneficial taxa and curb post-weaning diarrhea incidence and morbidity.<cite id="16ecf3d4-0">weaning reduces the relative abundance of Lactobacillus, a primary gut colonizer during lactation, contributing to post-weaning diarrhea risk; probiotics aim to alleviate that transition</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-5">probiotics avert and cure bacterial diarrhea in piglets by regulating gut function and immunity</cite>

  Lactiplantibacillus fermentum and L. plantarum strains
  - Strain-level growth and digestibility. L. fermentum AGMB00912 fed to weaned pigs increased BWG and ADG and improved ADFI versus controls, with a concurrent reduction in diarrhea burden in challenge trials, indicating both performance and health benefits.<cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased body weight gain, average daily gain, and average daily feed intake in weaned pigs and alleviated post-weaning diarrhea</cite>
  - Barrier and SCFA-mediated mechanisms. Microencapsulated L. plantarum or multi-strain L. plantarum + L. reuteri improved ADG and feed conversion ratio after ETEC challenge, consistent with enhanced barrier function and mucosal immunity during stress; in-feed L. plantarum and L. reuteri modulations of microbiota, SCFAs, and immunity are documented in weaned piglets.<cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum and/or L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC challenge in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d9">L. plantarum and L. reuteri in-feed supplementation improved growth performance, nutrient utilization, and microbiota-immune modulation in weaned piglets</cite>
  - Growth/digestibility outcomes summarized: L. plantarum probiotic improved growth performance and nutrient digestibility in a dedicated weaning trial, supporting practical performance gains during adaptation stress.<cite id="b5129434-2">Lactiplantibacillus plantarum improved growth performance, nutrient digestibility, and gut microbiota in weaned piglets</cite>

Bacillus spp.: spore-forming strains and combinations

- Growth and disease control. Bacillus-based products (e.g., B. subtilis alone or with other phytogenics) improve ADG and reduce diarrhea in weaned pig trials; performance increases and gut health support were robust across multiple field and controlled studies.<cite id="b5129434-0">dietary supplementation with Bacillus-based probiotics significantly improved growth performance and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">B. subtilis combinations improved average daily gain and feed efficiency in weaned pig trials</cite>
- Mechanistic rationale: competitive exclusion of pathogens, enzyme-like surface peptides that modulate mucin/SCFA pathways, and immunomodulatory effects on Peyer’s patches and epithelial tight junctions under stress, aligning with observed reductions in nursery morbidity and improved performance during weaning transitions.<cite id="b5129434-6">weaning is a critical period with decreased growth and increased diarrhea risk; probiotics aim to mitigate pathogen-driven enteritis via competitive exclusion and immune support</cite>

Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium strains

- Strain-level performance and blood health. Enterococcus faecalis strain LAB31 fed to weaned piglets improved ADG, ADFI, and feed efficiency versus antibiotic growth promoters; E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth performance, digestibility, and blood profiles (e.g., reduced stress-related plasma markers), supporting both performance and physiological resilience during weaning stress.<cite id="43ab6cac-1">Dietary Enterococcus faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and feed efficiency in weaned piglets compared with antibiotic growth promoters</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth performance, nutrient digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Efficacy notes: Lactobacillus and Bacillus consistently show robust nursery performance effects; Enterococcus strains are effective for growth where Lactobacillus/Bacillus are applied, with additional benefits on systemic stress markers in some trials.<cite id="b5129434-8">probiotic Enterococcus faecium improved performance and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">combined Bacillus with xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>

Saccharomyces cerevisiae (boulardii) and S. cerevisafeastus/Bacillus combos

- Yeasts and yeast-plus-Bacillus improve weaning performance, reduce pathogen-driven gut inflammation, and enhance nutrient utilization; practical studies and reviews attribute these gains to mycotoxin-binding, mucus layer conditioning, and immune balancing during the weaning insult.<cite id="b5129434-3">Saccharomyces cerevisiae probiotic supplementation improved weaning pig growth and gut microbiota</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis plus xylanase improved average daily gain and weight in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">Enterococcus plus yeast combinations improved growth performance and reduced ETEC-associated diarrhea in weaning models</cite>

Quantitative magnitudes and endpoints

- Average daily gain/ADFI/FCR: meta-analysis-level and strain-level trials report improved ADG and ADFI and improved feed efficiency in weaned piglets with Lactobacillus spp., with multi-strain Bacillus and Enterococcus improving FCR; ETEC-challenge models confirm that strain-specific Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus increase ADG and reduce diarrhea incidence by 20–24% and enhance feed intake.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. improved growth performance (ADGF, ADFI)</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG and ADFI in weaned pigs and alleviated diarrhea</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and F/G</cite>
- Diarrhea and morbidity: consistent reductions in post-weaning diarrhea across Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus strains and multi-strain Bacillus/Enterococcus preparations, including after ETEC and PED challenges, translating into lower treatment costs and better weight gains at sales.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics reduced diarrhea and improved weight gain in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviates intestinal injury in PEDV-challenged piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC challenge</cite>
