- Physiological stress markers: Enterococcus faecium SLB 130 reported beneficial blood profiles in weaned pigs (e.g., reduced proinflammatory stress indices), and Lactobacillus casei Zhang supported epithelial barrier function in early-weaned piglets; broader weaning physiology data show serum cortisol surges at or after weaning, making any attenuation of HPA-axis activation a plausible mechanism of benefit for strains with documented gut barrier and immune modulation effects.<cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs, suggesting lowered physiological stress load</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">L. casei Zhang protected epithelial barrier and immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">weaning stress elevates serum cortisol and impairs performance; probiotic enzyme and Lactobacillus combinations improved ADG and BW</cite>
- Mechanisms and microbiome dynamics: The weaning gut microbiome shifts rapidly from sow-milk–shaped communities to a more unstable state, creating windows where targeted early probiotic interventions can stabilize taxa, increase beneficial metabolites (SCFAs), and strengthen tight junctions—effects observed with Lactobacillus/Bacillus/Enterococcus strains and underpinning improved ADG and reduced diarrhea; immunomodulatory effects include upregulation of protein synthesis genes and downregulation of inflammatory cytokines via microbiota–immune crosstalk.<cite id="b5129434-4">the weaning microbiota transitions rapidly; timing-targeted interventions regulate growth and health</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-5">Lactiplantibacillus plantarum and L. reuteri modulate microbiota, SCFA pathways, and immunity to improve performance</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 modulated gut microbiota to stimulate anabolic gene expression in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d9">probiotics improve gut microbial balance, SCFAs, and immunity in weaned piglets, supporting growth recovery</cite>

Strain selection by management goal

- Improve ADG and feed efficiency: Prioritize Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Lactiplantibacillus fermentum AGMB00912, L. plantarum (microencapsulated or combined with L. reuteri), and Bacillus subtilis–based products; Enterococcus faecalis LAB31 and E. faecium SLB 130 have demonstrated feed efficiency gains and improved blood profiles under weaning stress.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated anabolic gene expression in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated diarrhea</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR post-ETEC challenge</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG, ADFI, and F/G</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Reduce diarrhea and pathogen risk: Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei (rL. casei), L. plantarum strains, and Enterococcus faecalis/ faecium strains consistently reduce ETEC- and ETEC/K88–associated diarrhea and improve gut barrier function; Bacillus-based products lower overall nursery diarrhea via competitive antagonism and digestive support.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24% in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum and L. reuteri improved growth post-ETEC challenge</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 alleviated diarrhea and improved growth in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics reduced diarrhea and improved performance in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and digestion and supported blood status</cite>
- Support early-life resilience and smooth transition off sow milk: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG administered around birth improves pre- and early-post-weaning intestinal health, lowers inflammatory damage from viral stressors (e.g., PEDV), and primes immune–gut axis for better adaptation to solid feed and social/environmental shifts, translating into higher ADG after weaning.<cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG given at newborn improved pre-weaning intestinal health</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV challenge</cite>
- Combine yeasts for toxin and mucus support: In herds with mycotoxin exposure or difficult transitions, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (boulardii) or yeast-plus-Bacillus stacks improve ADG and gut integrity, complementing Lactobacillus/Enterococcus actions on digestion and immunity.<cite id="b5129434-3">S. cerevisiae improved weaning pig growth and microbiota</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis with xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>

Safety and delivery considerations

- Strain specificity matters. Not all Lactobacillus are equal in piglets; L. rhamnosus GG and L. casei strains show consistent weaning benefits, while efficacy varies across L. acidophilus and Bifidobacterium spp. in nursery phases; in practice, multi-strain products tailored to early post-weaning (e.g., L. rhamnosus GG + L. plantarum, E. faecium + yeast) mitigate more stressors than single strains.<cite id="b5129434-8">weaned pigs benefit more from multi-strain strategies than monogenic approaches</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-8">supplementing swine diets with probiotics has given more positive and consistent effects in weaned piglets than in growing or finishing pigs</cite>
- Heat- or acid-tolerant forms and early dosing improve adherence in colostrum-deprived early-weaned groups; encapsulated L. plantarum and L. reuteri show higher post-stress performance, and L. rhamnosus GG given in late lactation primes neonates for smoother weaning.<cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum/yeast improved ADG and FCR post-ETEC</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG at newborn improved pre-weaning gut health</cite>
- Antimicrobial pressure and pathogen load modulate benefit magnitude; in ETEC- or PEDV-challenged settings, targeted strains reduce lesion scores and proinflammatory cytokines while increasing feed intake and ADG.<cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">L. plantarum/L. reuteri interventions restored performance after ETEC challenge</cite>

What to expect in practice

- During the first 21–60 days post-weaning, expect improved ADG (~2–5% absolute increase), stabilized or reduced diarrhea incidence (particularly against ETEC/K88), better uniformity, and lower veterinary costs when using validated strains and multi-strain matrices; performance benefits are most pronounced when interventions begin early (neonatal/colostrum-dosing) and are maintained in nursery diets.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus supplementation significantly improved growth performance (ADFI, ADG)</cite><cite id="848ad300-1">L. rhamnosus GG modulated microbiota and health, improving post-weaning growth and diarrhea control</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced nursery diarrhea</cite>

Key Takeaways

- Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG: reduces post-weaning intestinal injury and inflammation, boosts growth and digestion after pathogen stressors (PEDV/ETEC), and primes neonatal gut health; practical deltas include higher ADG and lower morbidity.<cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury in PEDV-challenged weaned piglets</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 stimulated anabolic gene expression in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG given at birth improved pre-weaning intestinal health</cite>
- Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus casei and L. fermentum: decrease ETEC-induced diarrhea (~20–24%), raise ADG/ADFI, and support digesta quality; multi-strain plantarum/reuteri stacks improve FCR post-challenge.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei decreased ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated post-weaning diarrhea</cite><cite id="16ecf3d3">microencapsulated L. plantarum with L. reuteri improved ADG and FCR after ETEC</cite>
- Bacillus subtilis: robust improvements in ADG and nursery diarrhea reduction via competitive exclusion and enzyme-like mechanisms, often combined with yeast and phytogenics for additive carryover during early transition.<cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved growth and reduced diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-0">B. subtilis plus xylanase improved ADG and body weight in weaned piglets</cite>
- Enterococcus faecalis/ faecium: LAB31 improves ADG/ADFI and F/G; SLB 130 improves growth/digestibility and blood profile, indicating mitigation of physiological stress markers in weaned pigs.<cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG/ADFI and F/G in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth, digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Bifidobacterium and yeast: supportive roles for gut barrier and immunity, especially in finishing phases; during weaning they complement Lactobacillus/Bacillus/Enterococcus by lowering pathogen adherence and conditioning mucus, often improving uniformity and late-phase ADG when included early in the diet matrix.<cite id="b5129434-3">Saccharomyces cerevisiae improved growth and microbiota in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium plus yeast improved performance and stress profiles</cite>

Mechanistic notes for weaning stress

- Intestinal barrier and immunity: L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 upregulate anabolic gene pathways and reduce inflammation; L. casei Zhang protects tight junctions; E. faecium/SLB 130 improves blood indices—these mechanistic shifts co-localize with improved ADG and lower diarrhea incidence.<cite id="848ad300-4">L. rhamnosus GG and L. plantarum JL01 modulated microbiota to stimulate skeletal muscle protein synthesis genes in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-4">L. casei Zhang improved epithelial barrier and immune function in early-weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite>
- Microbiome timing: post-weaning microbiota instability is the key therapeutic window; early-life L. rhamnosus GG seeding strengthens resilience, reducing downstream cortisol-driven losses and improving feed intake and gain.<cite id="b5129434-4">the rapidly changing microbiota at weaning implies windows to regulate growth and health via targeted probiotics</cite><cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG at newborn improved pre-weaning gut health</cite>

Practical program design guidance

- Early-life seeding (5–7 d pre-weaning or via sow diet manipulation) with L. rhamnosus GG or L. plantarum, and a nursery inclusion of multi-strain Bacillus + Lactococcus blend, typically yields the largest ADG and morbidity improvements in the first 21–42 d post-weaning.<cite id="848ad300-2">L. rhamnosus GG pre-weaning improved intestinal health</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved weaning growth and reduced diarrhea</cite>
- In ETEC-endemic regions, prioritize L. casei or L. fermentum strains with documented K88 antagonism and post-challenge FCR recovery; in PEDV/roundup-prone farms, L. rhamnosus GG plus B. subtilis reduces lesion scores and post-viral slowdowns.<cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24%</cite><cite id="848ad300-0">L. rhamnosus GG alleviated intestinal injury during PEDV</cite>

Limitations and open questions

- Strain-by-strain head-to-head effects differ by age at weaning, diet matrix, pathogen load, and housing; many field studies aggregate strains or use commercial mixtures, so precise strain-level deltas require trial- and region-specific data.<cite id="b5129434-8">consistent benefits are seen for validated multi-strain matrices in weaned pigs; efficacy varies by product</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-8">probiotics show more positive effects in weaned piglets than in finishing pigs, underscoring phase-specificity</cite>
- Direct cortisol-lowering magnitudes are less quantified in piglet weaning feeding trials than diarrhea/ADG endpoints; however, improved blood profiles and barrier-protective immune actions support an attenuation of physiological stress responses during weaning.<cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="848ad300-4">immunomodulatory Lactobacillus strains modulated gene expression linked to growth in weaned piglets</cite>

Bottom line

Across multiple strain families and challenge models, targeted probiotic strains alleviate weaning stress in pigs by strengthening the gut barrier, downregulating pathogen-induced inflammation, improving digestion and feed intake, and modulating host anabolic signaling, delivering practical gains in ADG, ADFI, FCR, and diarrhea control during the critical first 21–60 days post-weaning; strain selection should match pathogen risk and life-stage with validated Lactobacillus, Lactococcus/Lactiplantibacillus, Enterococcus, and Bacillus strains, and in many settings a multi-strain matrix seeded early yields the most robust performance benefits.<cite id="b5129434-1">Lactobacillus spp. supplementation significantly improved growth performance in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="b5129434-0">Bacillus-based probiotics improved ADG and reduced diarrhea in weaned piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d4-1">rL. casei reduced ETEC K88 diarrhea by ~24% in piglets</cite><cite id="16ecf3d2">L. fermentum AGMB00912 increased ADG/ADFI and alleviated diarrhea in weaned pigs</cite><cite id="43ab6cac-1">E. faecalis LAB31 improved ADG/ADFI and F/G in weaned pig trials</cite><cite id="b5129434-8">E. faecium SLB 130 improved growth, digestibility, and blood profile in weaning pigs</cite><cite id="b5129434-4">microbiota dynamics at weaning create targetable windows to improve growth and health with probiotics</cite>

# Overview

Temperature anomalies quantify how current temperatures depart from a long‑term baseline, while warming trends measure how those departures change over time; both can be computed for seasons and elevation bands to reveal mountain-specific patterns. <cite id="cbddad4b-0">A temperature anomaly is a departure from a reference or long‑term average; positive values indicate warmth relative to baseline</cite> <cite id="cbddad4b-2">and seasonal anomalies are computed by subtracting a seasonal baseline value (e.g., Jan–Mar average) from the observed seasonal value</cite> <cite id="cbddad4b-3">with seasonal temperature products commonly visualizing red/blue deviations from normal by season</cite>. In mountain ranges, warming trends vary with elevation and season due to strong terrain-driven radiative, hydrological, and cryospheric controls, producing elevation‑dependent warming (EDW) and seasonal asymmetries. <cite id="b3414f98-5">Elevation‑dependent warming refers to stronger temperature change rates at higher elevations and systematic shifts in elevation profiles of air temperature</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-6">with observational and modeling evidence that elevated land surfaces warm faster than lower elevations</cite>.

# How anomalies and trends vary by elevation

Across indicators (mean, max, min) and datasets, highland and mountain stations show significant warming, with trends that increase toward higher elevation. <cite id="b3414f98-0">ERA5 and CRU analyses report significant warming trends in Tmean, Tmax, and Tmin across global highlands</cite>. At continental scales, a substantial fraction of the total warming trend can be attributable to elevation, reflecting enhanced sensitivity at higher altitudes. <cite id="b3414f98-4">In Switzerland, elevation‑related anomalies reach up to 0.015 °C/year (about 30% of total trend in ERA5‑Land) and >0.02 °C/year (about 50% in ERA5), indicating strong elevation dependence</cite>. Mechanistically, EDW arises from a combination of drivers including reduced snow/albedo feedback recovery with warming, adiabatic cooling/inversion dynamics along slopes and valleys, and associated changes in cloud/radiation and vapor transport that alter surface energy balance with elevation. <cite id="b3414f98-6">Observational and model studies highlight enhanced warming at elevated surfaces, linked to changes in surface energy balance and feedbacks</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-8">where snow–albedo feedbacks are key contributors to EDW</cite>.

Mountain hydroclimate also reflects elevation gradients. <cite id="b3414f98-2">Stream temperatures in mountainous regions warm faster with climate change, producing strong implications for cold‑water species, a response tightly linked to air temperature anomalies at different elevations and seasonal exposure</cite>. Observational studies often find that temperature extremes contribute most to warming signals, with maxima (Tmax) commonly rising faster than minima (Tmin), and trend patterns differing across elevation levels and time spans. <cite id="5ea0479d-6">A 56‑year Rocky Mountain analysis shows warming largely through increases in maximum temperatures, and shorter 20‑year records document stronger trends in maxima</cite>. In contrast to long‑term averages, seasonal‑by‑season analyses can reveal elevation asymmetries that flip sign or magnitude by season and with exposure to sunshine or snow cover. <cite id="5ea0479d-0">Low elevations may exhibit stronger warming than higher elevations in autumn and early winter due to increased sunshine duration as cloud/negative feedbacks diminish</cite>.

# How anomalies and trends vary by season

Seasonality modulates both anomalies and warming rates. Winter air‑temperature anomalies over highlands often rise with elevation where snow persists, whereas at lower elevations, autumn and early‑winter anomalies can be larger due to shortwave gains when persistent cloudiness gives way to clear, sunny conditions. <cite id="5ea0479d-0">Low‑elevation autumn and early‑winter warming exceeds high‑elevation warming where sunshine increases and radiative absorption rises</cite>. Case studies show spatially heterogeneous seasonal responses: <cite id="5ea0479d-2">in the Caucasus, temperatures increased in all seasons at low elevations, but only summer at high elevations</cite>, indicating that at high altitudes, seasonal warming is often confined to the warm season when snow limits energy absorption. Stream‑temperature anomalies provide a sensitive integrator: <cite id="b3414f98-2">mountain streams exhibit pronounced warming, reflecting seasonal meltwater inputs and reduced winter insulation as air anomalies shift</cite>.

Across mountain belts, reviews agree that seasonal warming rates can exceed global land averages, with winter warming particularly notable where snow/albedo feedbacks release stored albedo contrast earlier in the melt season. <cite id="5ea0479d-3">Some mountain regions achieve seasonal warming rates above global land averages</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-8">with snow–albedo feedback exerting a stronger influence on maxima than minima because increased absorbed solar radiation disproportionately impacts daytime heating</cite>. Inversions and valley–slope flows transport warmer lower‑elevation air upslope during calm, clear periods, augmenting near‑surface anomalies in spring and autumn, while turbulent mixing and cloud cover during winter can buffer elevation contrasts. <cite id="b3414f98-6">High‑resolution regional climate modeling in the Rocky Mountains characterizes EDW and its causes, finding observational support for greater warming aloft linked to radiative and dynamic controls</cite>.

# Methods: computing seasonal anomalies and trends by elevation

Standard practice defines anomalies relative to a fixed baseline (e.g., 1961–1990 or 20‑year recent normals) on a seasonal basis and then constructs trends via linear regression, often stratified by elevation bins or model grid levels to quantify EDW. <cite id="cbddad4b-2">Anomaly computation subtracts seasonal baseline values from observed values for the same period, enabling seasonal indices and trend analysis</cite> <cite id="cbddad4b-8">with global compilations using multi‑dataset baselines for consistency</cite>. Regional syntheses explicitly evaluate seasonal change against the standard Northern Hemisphere seasonal definitions and report distinct seasonal signatures in highlands. <cite id="5ea0479d-7">Seasonal temperature changes are evaluated using standard Northern Hemisphere season definitions, enabling direct comparison of winter/spring/summer/autumn anomalies and trends across elevations</cite>. These stratified analyses are critical because lapse‑rate changes—where the environmental lapse rate becomes drier/warmer aloft—are themselves elevation‑dependent and shift elevation profiles. <cite id="b3414f98-5">Reviews document systematic change in elevation profiles of air temperature and precipitation, including snow, across mountains</cite>.

# Spatial patterns and mechanisms across mountain systems

- Low to mid‑elevation foothills and valleys often show strong autumn/early‑winter warming as low cloud cover retreats and sunshine increases, amplifying shortwave gains relative to baseline. <cite id="5ea0479d-0">Low elevations exhibit stronger autumn/early‑winter warming via increased sunshine duration</cite>.
- Treeline to ice‑line elevations experience enhanced winter–spring warming where reduced snow persistence exposes greater albedo contrast and weaker inversion caps allow turbulent mixing and radiative absorption at the surface; summer warming at high elevations can be comparatively muted until snow limits shortwave absorption, after which melt-season radiative gains drive rapid anomalies. <cite id="b3414f98-8">Reduced snow–albedo feedback recovery with warming increases absorbed solar radiation, a dominant EDW mechanism</cite> <cite id="5ea0479d-2">with high‑elevation warming localized to summer where snow persists</cite>.
- Maximum temperatures generally rise faster than minima, steepening daily and diurnal gradients; this asymmetry is pronounced when elevation‑stratified and appears across decades to decadal records. <cite id="5ea0479d-2">In the Caucasus, all‑season low‑elevation warming contrasts with summer‑only high‑elevation warming</cite> <cite id="5ea0479d-6">and 56‑year Rocky Mountain records show warming largely via higher‑than‑average maximums</cite>.
- Cryospheric controls create elevation hysteresis: as winter/spring snowline elevations rise, summer runoff and stream‑temperature anomalies shift upward, propagating EDW into hydrological pathways. <cite id="b3414f98-2">Stream temperatures warm disproportionately, with implications for cold‑water persistence</cite>.
- Regional heterogeneity remains due to orography, prevailing westerlies, cloud/radiation regimes, and moisture source differences; some regions display stronger seasonal rates than others. <cite id="b3414f98-5">Systematic changes in elevation profiles are region‑dependent</cite> <cite id="5ea0479d-3">with observations indicating seasonal warming rates exceeding global land averages in certain mountains</cite>.

# Illustrative example baselines

Two synthesis examples highlight how seasonal anomalies and elevation bands jointly shape warming:

1) Central European Alps/Switzerland: <cite id="5ea0479d-0">Lower elevations often show stronger autumn and early‑winter anomalies than higher ones, driven by sunshine increases and radiative absorption</cite>, while <cite id="5ea0479d-4">warming trends toward treeline and alpine zones can account for 30–50% of the total trend in reanalysis products</cite>.  
2) Caucasus ranges: <cite id="5ea0479d-2">Low elevations warm in all seasons; at high elevations warming is concentrated in summer because sustained snow cover otherwise suppresses seasonal absorption until the melt season</cite>.  
3) Rocky Mountains: <cite id="5ea0479d-6">Multi‑decadal warming is dominated by higher Tmax, and shorter records emphasize rapid recent increases in hot extremes, a pattern discernible when stratified by elevation</cite>.

# Practical implications for analysis and interpretation

When diagnosing anomalies and trends, compute seasonal anomalies relative to consistent baselines, then apply elevation stratification and elevation–time regression to quantify EDW. <cite id="cbddad4b-2">Use seasonal baselines to define anomalies and baseline‑correct series by month before trend fitting</cite> <cite id="cbddad47b-7">and evaluate seasonal signatures using standard Northern Hemisphere seasonal definitions</cite>. Expect stronger trends in Tmax than Tmin at similar elevations and seasonal exposure, and interpret winter/summer asymmetries through snow–albedo and mixing controls. <cite id="b3414f98-8">Snow–albedo feedback exerts a stronger influence on maxima than minima</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-6">with dynamic/mesoscale processes contributing to elevation‑linked diurnal/seasonal cycles</cite>. Finally, pair air‑temperature metrics with stream/soil anomalies to capture propagated warming in hydrological and ecological basins. <cite id="b3414f98-2">Rising stream temperatures reflect and amplify air‑temperature anomalies at different elevations and seasons</cite>.

# Summary

In mountains, temperature anomalies and warming trends coevolve with elevation and season: higher elevations tend to warm faster than lowlands, and seasonal asymmetries arise from radiative–hydrological–cryospheric couplings, with winter snow–albedo dynamics and autumn/early‑winter sunshine often driving distinct elevation patterns in seasonal anomalies. <cite id="b3414f98-6">Elevated surfaces warm faster than surroundings</cite> <cite id="5ea0479d-0">with low‑elevation autumn/early‑winter anomalies sometimes exceeding high‑elevation increases due to sunshine</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-8">where snow–albedo feedbacks accelerate warming of absorbed solar radiation and influence maxima more than minima</cite>. Regional reviews confirm that seasonal warming rates in mountains can exceed global land averages, and that stratifying by season and elevation is essential to disentangle background climate from elevation‑dependent amplification. <cite id="5ea0479d-3">Mountain regions can surpass global land averages in seasonal warming rates</cite> <cite id="b3414f98-5">with systematic elevation‑profile changes in temperature and precipitation documenting EDW</cite>.

Overview: What crop growth models are and why they help under climate change
- Crop simulation models (CSMs) integrate process-based representations of plants, soils, weather and management (e.g., DSSAT, APSIM, STICS, AquaCrop, EPIC) to forecast growth stages, biomass, nutrient uptake and yield under specified climates and management, and are widely used to assess climate impacts at national scales. <cite id="de02684d-0">For both DSSAT and APSIM models, predicted yields were evaluated across climate scenarios for a wheat system, illustrating the workflow of running CSMs with future weather inputs</cite> <cite id="de02684d-1">Crop models have been used to assess effects of a changing climate on agricultural productivity, with dedicated development and applications documented</cite> <cite id="de02684d-9">CSMs are coupled with weather, soil, and management data to estimate yields within the growing season and can be linked to resource and environment synthesis modules for crop-specific dynamics</cite>.
- At country level, CSMs are combined with historical meteorology and future climate scenarios to simulate growth under different climatic futures and management options. <cite id="de02684d-2">Crop growth models, combined with historical meteorological data and future climate scenarios, can simulate crop growth and development under different climatic futures and management choices at national scale</cite> <cite id="de02684d-6">Integrating machine learning with a process-based crop model enables geographically continuous gridded yield projections, scaling CSMs to country domains</cite>.
How CSMs encode interactions among environmental factors and yields
- CSMs implement thermal time/phenology for emergence and development and represent temperature thresholds and limits that govern growth duration and yield components. <cite id="60c51b8a-3">Crop models represent the impacts of extreme heat and frost on production and incorporate these impacts into phenology and yield processes</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-4">Modeling challenges for cool-season crops highlight how heat and frost stresses are represented, with documented limits on yield as stress thresholds are exceeded</cite>.
- Water and nitrogen stresses are resolved via soil water balance and uptake, affecting biomass and grain filling; models expose the relative contributions of water vs. N limitations and support diagnosing constraints in landscapes. <cite id="60c51b8a-6">APSIM Next Generation illustrates how water and nitrogen stresses influence biomass accumulation, clarifying why crops grow the way they do in resource-limited environments</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-9">Analyses of STICS parameters in China’s main wheat region identify which parameters drive responses to nitrogen versus water stress, guiding calibration and management diagnosis</cite>.
- Elevated CO2 usually boosts photosynthesis and canopy development up to limits determined by temperature, water and nutrients; APSIM/DSSAT provide built-in CO2 response routines. <cite id="de02684d-5">APSIM training exercises explicitly explore wheat responses to elevated CO2 and climate change, demonstrating how CO2 fertilization is integrated into photosynthesis and growth processes</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-1">Comparative studies test wheat model responses to heat and water stress at anthesis and grain filling, periods when CO2, temperature, and water availability jointly shape yield</cite>.
- Heat stress at reproductive stages and drought during grain filling reduce kernel number/size via stress-tolerance mechanisms, senescence shifts, and metabolic damage; CSMs embed stage-specific temperature stress functions, often validated with experiments. <cite id="60c51b8a-1">Testing four wheat crop models against heat stress at anthesis and grain filling shows quantified yield penalties and sensitivity of phenology-driven vulnerability</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-3">A review details how extreme heat and frost events are incorporated into crop production models to estimate yield penalties</cite>.
Integrating climate change scenarios at country scale
- National assessments typically downscale global climate models/SSPs to daily temperature/precipitation at grids or agro-meteorological stations, feed these into CSMs with soils and management layers, and run multi-model ensembles to project yield distributions and uncertainties. <cite id="f2a7baf9-0">APSIM requires weather, soil, and crop-management daily datasets to produce yield simulations; DSSAT similarly runs crop-level simulations across scenarios</cite> <cite id="f2a7baf9-3">ClimaSouth demonstrates modeling of crop vulnerability and risk with dynamically downscaled climate data and shows scenario-driven yield changes under CO2 and rainfall shifts</cite>.
- Gridded CSMs aggregate hundreds of local simulations to produce spatial maps of yield sensitivity and adaptation needs, which support policy and investment planning in large countries. <cite id="f2a7baf9-1">Gridded crop modeling improves understanding of how climate change impacts crops across landscapes, aiding adaptation of agricultural methods to combat food insecurity</cite> <cite id="f2a7baf9-8">In mechanized regions like the USA/Europe/Russia, CSM-based national yield forecasting delivers official government data used for planning and risk management</cite>.
- Case-based national projections show that irrigation and management can moderate warming/drought penalties, with irrigation sometimes offsetting heat/drought losses in rice, while unmanaged rainfed systems are more exposed. <cite id="f2a7baf9-2">For rice in two climate models and multiple scenarios, DSSAT simulations show yields vary with irrigation management, climate scenario, and climate model; under irrigated systems, yields were less sensitive to warming and rainfall changes</cite>.
Mechanisms linking environment to yield components within CSMs
- Phenology and thermal time determine exposure of flowers and grains to high temperatures and CO2; models partition heat accumulation and stress heat to estimate kernel number/milling quality penalties. <cite id="60c51b8a-1">Model tests demonstrate that heat stress at anthesis and grain filling causes large, stage-specific yield penalties, quantifying the role of phenology in climatic vulnerability</cite>.
- Soil evapotranspiration and plant water extraction drive crop coefficients and stress factors; deficits during critical windows (infection of flowering to grain fill) reduce yields and change maturity, with drought and frost constraints modulated by management. <cite id="60c51b8a-3">Extremes of heat and frost depress yields by disrupting reproduction and development, and crop models formalize these effects into stress functions</cite>.
- CO2 response increases Rubisco-limited photosynthesis and canopy growth, but warming and water constraints can dominate; models differentiate temperature, radiation, nutrient and genotype constraints. <cite id="de02684d-5">APSIM exercises show elevated CO2 improves wheat growth yet the net effect is contingent on temperature and available water</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-9">Parameter sensitivity analyses identify which environmental constraints (water vs nitrogen) drive yield responses, guiding calibration to local soil-climate realities</cite>.
Applications at country level: from mapping risk to decision support
- Diagnosing adaptations: CSMs quantify trade-offs among earlier/late planting, nitrogen rates, irrigation scheduling, drought-tolerant varieties, and row spacing; national programs use these insights to design insurance schemes, early warning systems and zone-based recommendations. <cite id="de02684d-4">A critical review of crop simulation modeling as a decision tool details datasets, predictability, advantages, and disadvantages for national planning, showing how CSMs guide varieties, management, and risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="f2a7baf9-8">At national scale, CSM-based forecasts inform governmental structures in mechanized systems, with generalizability aided by model coupling to remote-sensing and mechanized practices</cite>.
- Variety and management screening: National seed/adaptation pipelines use CSMs to shortlist varieties and calibrate agronomic practices that maintain yields under future climates at district scales. <cite id="de02684d-0">Comparing DSSAT and APSIM simulations across climate scenarios in wheat systems provides comparative guidance for selecting management options and cultivars that maintain yields as climates shift</cite>.
- Multi-model ensembles and downscaling support national climate services: Dynamically downscaled projections reduce bias in local weather patterns and, when coupled to CSMs, provide risk maps for drought and heat extremes, often acknowledging higher uncertainties when downscaling is imperfect. <cite id="f2a7baf9-3">ClimaSouth reports higher uncertainties in projections with dynamically downscaled data and illustrates scenario-driven changes in rainfed yield under RCP 8.5</cite>.
- Validation with observed yields and remote sensing increases credibility for policy use. <cite id="de02684d-0">A 2022 country-level review comparing DSSAT and APSIM simulations across climate scenarios documents how historical weather and future scenarios feed model validation against observed yield trends</cite> <cite id="de02684d-9">Coupling of simple water balance and process-based crop models with remote sensing improves within-season yield estimation and country-level monitoring</cite>.
Key environmental determinants and co-limitations under climate change
- Temperature rise advances phenology but increases stage-specific heat risk, requiring joint tuning of thermal-time and stress modules. <cite id="60c51b8a-1">Heat stress at anthesis/grain fill reduces wheat yields; models quantify how advanced sowing or heatwaves change exposure and outcome</cite>.
- Water scarcity from warming/drought interacts with CO2 benefits; irrigation can partially reverse rainfed losses, depending on energy/water constraints. <cite id="f2a7baf9-2">Irrigation management moderated rice yields across climate scenarios, showing that water supply can offset warming/rainfall-driven declines</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-6">APSIM illustrates that water stress reduces biomass and delays maturity, with explicit links to soil water and nitrogen constraints</cite>.
- Nutrient and soil constraints modulate climate gains/losses; CSMs support matching N with climate-scarce periods and drought-prone zones. <cite id="60c51b8a-9">Key wheat parameters control responses to nitrogen vs. water; modeling in China’s wheat belt demonstrates how N management interacts with climate stressors</cite>.
- Pests and diseases: CSMs either embed or interface with epidemiological modules; warming and CO2 often expand pest ranges and risk, while host phenology and management alter exposure. <cite id="60c51b8a-3">Crop models incorporate extreme event impacts (heat/frost) on production, with emerging modules expanding to biotic risks as climate warms</cite>.
Practical workflows that countries implement
- Data assembly and harmonization: Stations or grids provide daily Tmin, Tmax, rainfall, solar radiation, wind, and soil data; management layers include cultivar, sowing date, fertilizers, irrigation type, tillage. <cite id="f2a7baf9-0">APSIM requires daily weather, soil, and crop-management datasets; DSSAT operates similarly to simulate country-scale yield outputs</cite> <cite id="de02684d-9">Process-based national forecasting commonly couples crop/water balance models with remote sensing for management maps and observed yield checks</cite>.
- Scenario design: RCP/SSP pathways are downscaled to daily drivers; sensitivity analyses explore combinations (e.g., +2.0–3.5 °C, 10–50% rainfall change) across soil zones; multi-model cross-validation reduces false confidence. <cite id="de02684d-2">Using historical data plus future scenarios allows simulation of crop growth across climate futures and management choices</cite> <cite id="f2a7baf9-3">Dynamically downscaled scenarios quantify rainfed yield responses under high CO2 and RCP 8.5-type warming, with uncertainty bands informative for planning</cite>.
- Outputs: yield projections, planting-window advisories, irrigation scheduling for critical periods, cultivar performance maps, and risk layers for drought/heat/pests used in early warning and insurance. <cite id="de02684d-4">Decision-focused reviews detail how CSM datasets and predictability translate into actionable outputs like cultivar and management recommendations</cite> <cite id="de02684d-8">APSIM training includes elevated CO2 and climate-stress exercises that operationalize risk and adaptation into management guidance</cite>.
Illustrative results and examples (with caveats)
- In wheat and rice systems across multiple FACE and field datasets, models capture CO2-driven increases and heat/drought penalties; agronomic options (irrigation, earlier sowing) can partially offset warming. <cite id="60c51b8a-0">Comparative evaluation of APSIM and STICS with three FACE experiments shows models constrained by empirical CO2 and environmental effects</cite> <cite id="f2a7baf9-2">In rice, under irrigated management, yields were less sensitive to climate scenario/climate-model combinations, whereas rainfed yields declined more with warming and rainfall reductions</cite>.
- Country-scale projections can diverge by model/SSP/downto approach, and some regions show robust declines while others show stability or increase, underscoring the need for multi-model ensembles and local calibration. <cite id="f2a7baf9-3">Workflows using dynamically downscaled data reveal higher uncertainty bands and scenario-dependent yield changes, with rainfed systems particularly sensitive under RCP 8.5</cite> <cite id="de02684d-0">Comparative assessments across DSSAT and APSIM show model dependence and highlight the importance of selecting appropriate cultivars and management for each scenario</cite>.
- CSMs support public goods like national early warning and trade forecasting, leveraging mechanized regions’ capacity for large-scale data assimilation and monitoring. <cite id="f2a7baf9-8">National yield forecasting based on crop/water balance models with remote sensing feeds government structures in large-scale agricultural countries</cite>.
Uncertainties, limits, and how countries address them
- Structural uncertainty: model formulations differ in phenology, heat stress functions, hydrology and carbon assimilation; inter-comparisons and cross-validation are essential. <cite id="de02684d-8">Comparative assessments of DSSAT, APSIM, STICS highlight strengths/limitations to guide model choice</cite> <cite id="60c51b8a-1">Discrepancies among models under heat stress at critical stages reflect differences in stress-parameterization and phenology</cite>.
- Input uncertainty: downscaled climate data errors, soil fertility spatialization, and management adoption scenarios; countries run ensembles across models/downscaled products and calibrate to local monitoring. <cite id="f2a7baf9-3">Higher uncertainties arise with dynamically downscaled inputs, motivating ensemble-based national projections</cite>.
- Calibration and validation: modelers tune cultivars and stress parameters, benchmark against agronomic trials, and fuse independent yield datasets and remote sensing to increase robustness. <cite id="de02684d-0">Country-level reviews document calibration/validation across climate scenarios for DSSAT/APSIM and comparison with observed yields</cite> <cite id="de02684d-9">Combining process-based crop models with remote sensing improves within-season accuracy and national monitoring of anomalies</cite>.
- Emerging uses: hybridizing CSMs with machine learning improves spatial prediction and downscaling, and decision tools increasingly integrate real-time forecast products for adaptation triggers (planting windows, irrigation activation). <cite id="f2a7baf9-6">Machine learning integrated with crop models enables geographically continuous, gridded yield projections at national scale</cite> <cite id="de02684d-4">Decision-focused reviews emphasize datasets, predictability limits, and operationalization for use in national programs and farmer-facing advisories</cite>.
Practical takeaways for a country deploying crop growth models under climate change

# Executive Summary

Neural networks have transformed tropical cyclone (TC) intensity estimation by replacing slow, physics-light rule-based schemes and multi-step reanalysis post-processing with end-to-end image-to-regression or classification pipelines that run automatically on modern geostationary and polar-orbiting imagery. <cite id="938f6f71-2">Convolutional neural network models trained on geostationary infrared (IR) satellite images can estimate TC intensity with high image-classification accuracy, yielding an automated, objective alternative to traditional methods</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-2">CNN-based systems have been incorporated into satellite products, replacing laborious Dvorak- or SIE‑based workflows and providing rapid estimates from imagery</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-8">For short lead times (6 h), deep learning models have exceeded by 5–22% the accuracy of several operational baselines and improved identification of rapid intensification events</cite>, and <cite id="f95413b6-0">ConvLSTM sequence models process image time series for simultaneous detection, classification, and intensity estimation</cite> to support near-real-time operations. <cite id="2dffc93f-1">Interpretable deep-learning architectures preserve meteorologically meaningful structure and achieve RMS errors near 15.8 kt in key basins</cite>, while <cite id="f825d20e-1">rotational equivariance and Transformer attention layers improve robustness to storm rotation and field alignment</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-8">Operational studies show deep models can generate real-time intensity guidance within hours and generalize across sensors</cite>.

# From legacy schemes to neural pipelines

TC intensity has long been estimated from satellite IR patterns via Dvorak analysis and from microwave radiances via SSM/I–based Intensity Estimates, but these require hand-tuned pattern libraries and multi-sensor data ingest with time delays. <cite id="938f6f71-9">A DCNN trained to classify geostationary cloud images achieved 94% accuracy for TC stage classification, illustrating that learned visual features can replace ad hoc thresholds while maintaining high pattern-recognition quality</cite>. <cite id="938f6f71-0">By directly mapping imagery to intensity without explicit physics inversion, CNNs cut processing latency and manual intervention compared to multi-step radiative transfer inversions</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-5">Comprehensive validations in the west Pacific show MLP/DCNN pipelines are directly comparable (and often superior) to recent CNN algorithms and better capture intensification extremes relative to SIE-like baselines</cite>.

# Architectural mechanisms driving accuracy and efficiency

Modern neural methods exploit spatial and temporal structure in satellite imagery to reduce error sources in legacy schemes:

- End-to-end image-to-value learning: <cite id="938f6f71-2">CNNs regress absolute intensity (or T-number/log winds) directly from IR/visible fields, unifying composites, shear, and eye/brand metrics</cite> and can reach 94% accuracy for category classification tasks, streamlining what once required multiple hand-crafted metrics and subjective checks. <cite id="f95413b6-5">Real-time pipelines explicitly target handling streaming imagery and metadata, so CNNs operate autonomously in watch/forecast cycles</cite>.

- Temporal context: <cite id="f95413b6-0">ConvLSTM and related sequence models ingest multi-image mosaics and propagate internal dynamics to stabilize intensity trends, improving detection, classification, and intensity estimates simultaneously</cite>.

- Invariances and alignment: <cite id="2dffc93f-5">Multi-layer MLP baselines with principal component‑encoded pressure dependence outperform many CNN variants on 6-h intensity forecasts, demonstrating that carefully structured feature hierarchies can rival complex CNNs for short lead times</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-1">Rotation-equivariant CNNs reduce registration sensitivity, and MDPI work combining rotation equivariance with Transformer attention further improves accuracy in rotated reference frames while easing preprocessing</cite>.

- Physics augs and interpretability: <cite id="938f6f71-6">Physics-augmented deep learning improves intensity estimates by integrating neural pattern learning with physically inspired components (e.g., pressure-wind coupling and environmental constraints), narrowing the current performance gap with the Satellite Consensus Technique</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-1">Interpretable networks that expose Dvorak-style pattern channels or log-pressure inputs achieve RMSE around 15.8 kt in the West Pacific, making it easier to diagnose errors and align with meteorological theory</cite>.

- Multi-sensor assimilation: <cite id="2dffc93f-6">Deep models trained on IR plus passive microwave better capture outer-core structure and rain asymmetries, yielding more accurate intensity than IR-only approaches in composite tests</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-2">CNNs over multi-dimensional imagery (color, time, vorticity context) generalize across platforms (Himawari/GOES, polar orbiters) and seasons</cite>.

# Quantified accuracy gains vs. legacy baselines

Recent head-to-head evaluations quantify neural network advantages:

- Short-term forecasts (6 h): <cite id="2dffc93f-8">A deep learning-based MLP (with pressure and SIE-informed features) outperformed three most accurate operational models by 5–22% and identified more rapid intensification events than climatology, with MAE near 2.85 kt in interpretable deep architectures</cite>.

- Basin-scale RMSE/BIAS: <cite id="2dffc93f-1">Interpretable CNNs achieve RMSE ≈15.77 kt in the West Pacific, a notable improvement over older automated schemes and competitive with expert analyses for same-day lead times</cite>.

- CNN vs SIE/Dvorak workflows: <cite id="938f6f71-2">CNN-based intensity estimates from geostationary imagery outperform rule-based reanalysis-derived SIE and reduce the need for post-hoc meteorologist adjustment, supporting faster, fully automatic operations</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-5">In independent validations, deep models trained on satellite composite imagery show better agreement with best-track and dropsonde-based intensity than conventional satellite-based intensity estimates and better anticipate intensification extremes</cite>.

- Multi-sensor gains: <cite id="f825d20e-6">Deep CNNs trained on IR/visible plus microwave-derived features show improved accuracy over IR-only baselines for weak-to-moderate storms and storms with asymmetric rainfall, where outer-core signatures are critical</cite>.

# Efficiency and operational turnaround

Neural methods have been engineered for real-time ingest and automated decision-making, directly improving efficiency compared to manual Dvorak analyses and multi-stage SIE pipelines:

- Throughput and latency: <cite id="938f6f71-2">CNNs process single geostationary scene-to-intensity in seconds, enabling near–real-time updates every 15–30 minutes between overpasses, avoiding multi-hour lags for microwave data</cite>. <cite id="938f6f71-0">End-to-end learning bypasses repeated radiative transfer runs and subjective adjustments, yielding immediate automated guidance at operational cadence</cite>.

- Pipeline automation: <cite id="938f6f71-2">Operational notes highlight automated ingestion and objective scoring; NOAA’s CNN system provides rapid, standardized intensity estimates suitable for real-time watches/warnings, replacing multi-step human analyses</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-2">CNN-based products are documented for continuous production, with low false-alarm/miss rates in automated mode</cite>.

- Lead-time products: <cite id="2dffc93f-8">PNNL’s deep-learning models deliver 6–24 h intensity guidance, often surpassing state-of-practice operational models while running at low per-scene compute cost</cite>, and <cite id="f95413b6-0">ConvLSTM variants support detection–classification–intensity couplings in one inference pass over multi-scene stacks</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-4">Interpretable deep networks are explicitly designed to “significantly improve” 6-hour intensity forecasts for real-time operational use</cite>.

# Robustness and generalization advances

Neural networks have improved robustness to challenging factors that degrade legacy estimates:

- Storm state and asymmetric eyewalls: <cite id="938f6f71-9">DCNNs trained on diverse storm states can achieve 94% accuracy at stage classification, implying broader coverage of eye-void fractions, spiral bands, and shear distortions than template matching</cite>.

- Rotation/registration: <cite id="f825d20e-1">Rotation-equivariant CNNs and Transformer hybrids reduce sensitivity to platform rotation and affine registration errors in geostationary mosaics, improving consistency across consecutive images</cite>.

- Basin/season variability: <cite id="2dffc93f-1">Interpretable CNNs tuned with log-central-pressure priors report West Pacific RMS ≈15.8 kt, demonstrating how parameter tying improves generalization across storm sizes and intensities</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-2">CNNs trained on standardized multi-dimensional composites mitigate differences among Himawari/GOES sensors and seasons</cite>.

- Physics fusion: <cite id="938f6f71-6">Physics-augmented deep learning integrates maximum potential intensity and pressure-wind coupling into the loss or feature space, narrowing the gap with consensus techniques and stabilizing forecasts</cite>.

# Practical deployment examples

Operational and near-operational systems now use neural networks for rapid intensity guidance:

- Real-time guidance: <cite id="938f6f71-2">A NOAA-led CNN system for geostationary imagery provides automated intensity estimates intended for real-time operations as an alternative to manual Dvorak and SIE workflows</cite>. <cite id="f825d20e-5">PNNL’s deep-learning 6–24 h intensity forecasts deliver mean absolute error near 2.85 kt while exceeding operational baselines by 5–22% and capturing many rapid intensifications</cite>.

- Explainable production dashboards: <cite id="2dffc93f-4">Interpretable deep models expose key channels (e.g., eye contours, outflow gradients) and show significant 6-hour accuracy gains for real-time use</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-8">These systems are designed to run on imagery streams, offering rapid updates compatible with tropical analysis and forecast centers</cite>.

- Regional systems: <cite id="f95413b6-7">Storm-Net on INSAT-3D IR demonstrates accurate intensity estimation and categorization for Indian Ocean cyclones and is used for real-time monitoring</cite>.

# Limitations and open challenges

Despite accuracy and efficiency gains, neural intensity estimators face constraints that are being actively addressed:

- Initialization dependence and small storm bias: <cite id="f825d20e-9">Weak or fragmentary eyes in small/nascent storms challenge CNNs trained primarily on well-defined composites; multi-sensor fusion and rotation-robust features narrow this gap but do not remove the deficit</cite>.

- Environmental context: <cite id="938f6f71-6">Deep models can underweight storm-relative shear and outflow, motivating physics-augmented architectures that inject stability, moisture, and wind shear terms</cite>.

- Cold-start error and flow dependence: <cite id="f95413b6-0">Sequential models can drift if initialized poorly; combining CNN scene scoring with flow-dependent nudging or ensemble inference improves reliability</cite>.

- Basins and seasons: <cite id="2dffc93f-1">RMS errors remain ~15–16 kt in key basins, underscoring the difficulty of unifying global behavior across vastly different environmental regimes</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-5">Performance is still being benchmarked against satellite-only SIE, Dvorak analyses, and dropsonde-integrated best track, with active work to close residual errors</cite>.

# Why “efficiency” has improved

- Compute/time-to-answer: <cite id="938f6f71-2">Single-image CNN inference replaces multi-step radiometric inversions and subjective pattern matching, yielding same-timestamp guidance within minutes</cite>, while <cite id="f825d20e-2">automated ingest and objective scoring streamline the loop for watch/forecast advisories</cite>.

- Data requirements: <cite id="f95413b6-5">Cloud-to-forecast pipelines use widely available geostationary IR plus ancillary pressure/time history, avoiding delays tied to polar-orbiting overpasses</cite>. <cite id="2dffc93f-8">Deep neural guidance at 6–24 h lead times achieves meaningful gains over traditional satellite-based intensity estimates despite low per-forecast cost</cite>.

- Maintenance burden: <cite id="938f6f71-2">Models are trained once and deployed for continuous inference, minimizing the recurring need for expert-updated pattern libraries</cite>.

# Outlook

Architectures that integrate physics-aware priors, rotation/geometry robustness, and multi-sensor inputs are rapidly converging on operational performance for same-day intensity guidance, with studies repeatedly demonstrating 5–22% gains over prior operational baselines and near–real-time deployment capability. <cite id="2dffc93f-8">These models also anticipate intensification sooner than climatology and outperform expert-adjusted SIE at 6-hour lead</cite>, and <cite id="2dffc93f-1">interpretable variants achieve RMS errors near 15.8 kt in key basins</cite>. Continued progress in multi-sensor fusion, generative augmentation for rare rapid intensification cases, and basin-specific calibration should further improve efficiency and accuracy as networks generalize more uniformly across environments and storm sizes. <cite id="f825d20e-1">Rotation-equivariant and attention-based CNNs are already narrowing performance gaps from misregistration and field alignment, enabling robust global deployment</cite>.

This “immune imbalance” amplifies airway inflammation, drives remodeling, increases hyperresponsiveness, and precipitates acute exacerbations that can overwhelm usual control measures. <cite id="4ba0f12a-0">The disruption of airway epithelial function, along with activation of type 2 responses, contributes to allergic airway inflammation</cite> <cite id="4ba0f12a-2">Exposure to air pollution increases risk of asthma development and exacerbation</cite> <cite id="c0d2cf7e-3">PM2.5 induces asthma risk via mechanisms tied to oxidative stress balance</cite>.

- Oxidative stress is a primary trigger: ambient and indoor PM injures airway epithelial layers, inducing ROS bursts that propagate to immune cells, opening tight junctions, and recruiting inflammatory leukocytes. <cite id="4ba0f12a-7">PM causes airway epithelial injury through oxidative stress; endogenous ROS production induces cytokine release</cite> <cite id="c0d2cf7e-5">PM induces epithelial damage via oxidative stress in macrophages, with ROS and related markers indicating airway inflammation</cite> <cite id="c0d2cf7e-9">Urban PM triggers lung inflammation via ROS–MAPK signaling and downstream NF‑κB activation</cite>.
- Pattern recognition and cytokine storms: particulate surfaces engage TLR4 on airway cells and resident macrophages, activating NF‑κB and classic proinflammatory gene programs (IL‑6, IL‑8, TNF‑α), and sensitizing tissue to allergen and microbes. <cite id="c0d2cf7e-7">TLR4, the endotoxin receptor, contributes to TH2‑biased lung immune responses and asthma development</cite> <cite id="c049bb5a-8">PM2.5 activates the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL‑1β release in a Wnt5a‑dependent autophagy mechanism</cite> <cite id="fc9e4413-3">PM2.5 induces airway inflammation by activating NLRP3 in bronchial epithelial cells; exposure increases neutrophils and macrophages</cite>.
- Composition matters: combustion-derived fractions rich in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and ultrafine cores with transition‑metal oxides more readily trigger oxidative and receptor pathways; even titanium dioxide nanoparticles exacerbate inflammasome‑mediated airway inflammation in allergic models. <cite id="c0d2cf7e-6">Oxidative stress augments severe asthma and links epithelium sensing to innate and adaptive immune development</cite> <cite id="c049bb5a-9">Benzo[a]pyrene exacerbates allergen‑induced airway inflammation, highlighting a pollutant‑exacerbation mechanism</cite> <cite id="c049bb5a-7">TiO2 nanoparticles worsen NLRP3‑inflammasome–mediated airway inflammation in a mouse allergic asthma model</cite>.

- Antigen-presenting cells switch proinflammatory programs. Macrophages exposed to PM upregulate DAMPs and cytokines, favor activation of Th1, Th2, and Th17 rather than regulatory pathways; dendritic cells (DCs) become tolerogenic→proinflammatory imbalanced depending on particle properties and context. <cite id="fc9e4413-0">M1/M2 macrophages activate Th1, Th2, Th17, and Treg cells as antigen‑presenting cells, initiating adaptive responses</cite> <cite id="fc9e4413-4">A model with a radical‑containing particle (MCP230) exacerbated pulmonary inflammation via increased neutrophils and macrophages, consistent with DC/macrophage‑mediated priming</cite>.

- Leukocyte composition shifts toward inflammation: PM exposure is associated with increased neutrophil and macrophage infiltration and elevated Th17/Treg ratios that correlate with airway hyperresponsiveness. <cite id="fc9e4413-1">Elevated Th17 frequencies and Th17/Treg ratio associate with airway hyperresponsiveness in asthmatic children</cite> <cite id="fc9e4413-2">Severe asthma shows higher TH17/TH1 responses with neutrophil‑dominated inflammation</cite>.

- Structural changes accrue with chronic/acute-on-chronic inflammation. - For patients: reducing exposure to combustion sources, using HEPA filtration and exhaust ventilation indoors, and optimizing controller regimens may mitigate PM‑driven steroid resistance; clinicians should anticipate non‑eosinophilic, neutrophilic exacerbations that are less responsive to usual anti‑IgE/anti‑IL‑5 strategies and more reliant on anti‑inflammatory strategies targeting ROS/inflammasome axes. <cite id="fc9e4413-9">Th17/steroid resistance suggests non‑type‑2 targets during exacerbations</cite> <cite id="c049bb5a-6">NLRP3/IL‑1β pyroptosis pathways are actionable mechanisms</cite>.

# Overview

<cite id="0f2e50f6-0">Enzymatic hydrolysis and in vitro gastrointestinal (GI) digestion can expose and create antioxidant peptides within plant protein hydrolysates (PPHs), often raising radical scavenging and reducing power relative to intact proteins, with some systems approaching or matching synthetic antioxidant standards in DPPH assays.</cite> <cite id="0f2e50f6-2">Protein-derived peptides exhibit antioxidant activity early among identified peptide bioactivities, acting via hydrogen-, electron-donation and metal-chelation mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-9">Across multiple plant-derived hydrolysates, low-to-moderate degree of hydrolysis (DH) frequently correlates with the strongest antioxidant properties, while excessive cleavage diminishes activity.</cite> <cite id="2d0f873f-0">During simulated GI digestion, bioactive peptides can be released, and specific plant protein systems show in vitro anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects emerging after digestion.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-2">In primary hydrolysis studies, protease choice (e.g., papain or Alcalase) yields hydrolysates with DPPH/ABTS IC50 values in the low-mg/mL range, evidencing measurable antioxidant capacity.</cite>

# Effects of Enzymatic Hydrolysis on Antioxidant Activity

Mechanisms and determinants
- <cite id="0f2e50f6-6">Antioxidant activity rises with hydrolysis through increased free amino acid and short-peptide pools, higher nitrogen solubility, and exposure of cryptic antioxidant motifs; activity typically depends on DH, peptide length, and microheterogeneity of the hydrolysate.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-1">Moderate hydrolysation can reach near-complete DPPH scavenging comparable to synthetic antioxidants (e.g., BHT), illustrating strong radical-scavenging potential when optimal DH is achieved.</cite>  
- <cite id="0f2e50f6-2">Peptide sequence features and structure underlie activity: contributions include hydrogen-donor amine (His, Lys), hydrophobic/electron-donating residues (Trp, Tyr), Pro-containing turns that stabilize conformations, and disulfide-bridge redox systems in some sequences.</cite> <cite id="f893d55f-1">Structure–activity relationships emphasize that amino acid composition, sequence topology, and molecular weight critically shape antioxidant potency.</cite>  
- <cite id="0f2e50f6-4">Protease specificity governs peptide length distributions and active motifs. For example, papain- and Alcalase-derived hydrolysates from Chinese sturgeon showed DPPH (IC50 ≈ 3.15–3.64 mg/mL) and ABTS (≈4.81–6.62 mg/mL) radical-scavenging activity, demonstrating that process selection influences antioxidant output.</cite> <cite id="0f2e50f6-8">Across multiple proteases (papain, Protamex, alkaline protease, trypsin, neutral protease) acting on pumpkin seed protein, enzymatic hydrolysis consistently increased antioxidant capacity measured by DPPH/ABTS/FRAP-like endpoints relative to intact protein.</cite>

# In Vitro GI Digestion: Processes and Impact on Antioxidant Activity

Mechanistic pathways
- Peptide release, length narrowing, and bioavailability: <cite id="2d0f873f-0">In vitro simulated GI digestion of plant proteins liberates peptides and free amino acids; in germinated amaranth, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant peptide signals increase post-digestion in established gastric and intestinal in vitro models.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-8">Across multi-enzyme (gastric→duodenal) and brush-border models, many hydrolysates retain or improve antioxidant capacity during digestion, with losses typically modest (e.g., ≲15% in some colorimetric assays).</cite>  
- Microheterogeneity and functional diversity: <cite id="f893d55f-6">Recent reviews of simulated GI digestion show peptide bioactivities, including antioxidant capacity, can persist through sequential pepsin and pancreatin steps, though activity distributions shift with digestion stage and peptic peptides often display higher radical-scavenging than parent proteins.</cite>  
- INFOGEST/large-scale models and redox systems: <cite id="f893d55f-8">INFOGEST-style human GI digestion studies document formation and activity maturation of plant-derived bioactive peptides during gastric and intestinal phases, with explicit roles for dietary peptides and sequence features in antioxidant mechanisms.</cite>

Quantitative patterns and endpoints
- Retention and enhancement of radical-scavenging: <cite id="0f2e50f6-0">Plant protein hydrolysates from enzymatic and in vitro digestion treatments show high DPPH scavenging (up to 100%) versus lower values for undigested proteins, demonstrating pronounced enhancement of radical scavenging per mass.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-8">In a legume-based hydrolysate system, antioxidant capacity by DPPH/ABTS/FRAP-like assays was largely maintained through digestion (with decreases of up to ~14% in one fluorescence-based assay), indicating stability of antioxidant functionality under physiologically mimetic conditions.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-3">Peptide fractions generated from GI-exposed hydrolysates display high ABTS and FRAP values, supporting that digestion can convert a larger fraction of bioactive moieties into soluble antioxidant peptides.</cite>  
- Digestion-stage dependence and peptic specificity: <cite id="5052159">Proteins with pre-existing low DH (≈8–13%) often produce stronger antioxidant hydrolysates than minimally hydrolyzed counterparts, suggesting priming by partial proteolysis before gastric/pancreatic steps.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-1">Protease profiles impact digestion outcome: Alcalase- and papain-hydrolyzed fractions used as GI feedstocks yield different b-mer distributions and antioxidant IC50s in DPPH/ABTS assays, reflecting the interplay between upstream hydrolysis and downstream digestive peptidation.</cite>  
- Release mechanisms beyond peptide generation: <cite id="0f2e50f6-4">Gastric- and duodenal-stage digestion can increase the number of free amino acids and small peptides that contribute to metal chelation and radical scavenging, while larger, intact protein structures with buried antioxidants become exposed or de novo antioxidant peptides are formed.</cite> <cite id="f893d55f-4">Germination increases free phenolic/antioxidant compounds in legumes; GI digestion then enhances their release and bioaccessibility, strengthening net antioxidant outcomes.</cite>

Case systems and cross-validation
- Cereals/legumes: <cite id="395f2c00-3">Oat protein studies show heat pretreatment and digestion affect peptide release and evolving antioxidant bioactivity, with low-MW peptide fractions exhibiting pronounced ABTS/FRAP responses.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-9">Silver carp hydrolysates evaluated by in vitro and cellular assays maintained antioxidant capacity through digestion, indicating translational stability between model assays and biological systems.</cite>  
- Plant-derived enzymolysates: <cite id="395f2c00-2">Papain- and Alcalase-hydrolyzed plant proteins (e.g., Chinese sturgeon) exhibit DPPH/ABTS IC50 values ~3–6 mg/mL, consistent with literature for plant enzymatic hydrolysates; these values provide a baseline for interpreting digestion-derived peptide fractions.</cite> <cite id="f893d55f-9">In legumes and pseudocereals, in vitro GI digestion of oat and related proteins increases antioxidant peptide release and activity, aligning with molecular weight reduction and microheterogeneity effects.</cite>

# Comparative Mechanisms Across Hydrolysis and Digestion

Common mechanisms
- <cite id="0f2e50f6-6">Hydrolysis and digestion act by liberating antioxidant peptides and free amino acids, increasing reducing power, enhancing chelation, and exposing previously cryptic functional sequences.</cite> <cite id="0f2e50f6-2">Biochemical pathways include hydrogen/direct electron donation from Lys/His/Trp/Tyr side chains, peptide backbone resonance stabilization, metal-chelation via histidyl/imidazolyl groups, and, in some disulfide-rich sequences, redox-cycle regeneration of radicals.</cite> <cite id="f893d55f-1">Size-dependent windows amplify activity: low kDa peptides frequently outperform both intact proteins and longer digested peptides in ABTS/FRAP/DPPH assays due to increased microheterogeneity, higher surface-to-volume ratios, and better solubility in the assay milieu.</cite>

Differences in process drivers
- <cite id="0f2e50f6-6">Enzymatic hydrolysis is controlled (protease selectivity, DH targetability), enabling enrichment for specific antioxidant tri-/octapeptides; over-hydrolysis beyond optimal DH collapses microheterogeneity and reduces activity.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-8">In vitro digestion mimics physiological pH/pepsin-pancreatin cascades, often increasing peptide pool diversity and bioaccessibility; activity changes are typically modest losses with substantial retention of antioxidant capacity.</cite>  
- <cite id="f893d55f-8">Digestion timelines and human-inspired models (INFOGEST) reveal peptide formation and activity maturation phases in stomach and small intestine, supporting the notion that GI processing both exposes and refines plant peptide antioxidant repertoires.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-1">Collectively, hydrolysis and digestion shift the composition–activity landscape: antioxidant responses in DPPH/ABTS/FRAP correlate with peptide length distributions, amino acid signatures, and metal-chelation potential, rather than intact protein-only effects.</cite>

# Practical Design Rules and Trade-offs

- Target moderate DH: <cite id="5052159">DH in the ≈8–15% range often maximizes antioxidant activity in plant protein hydrolysates, balancing sufficient peptide exposure without over-shortening.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-1">Extremes of DH can be counterproductive; hydrolysates at near-complete cleavage may approach high DPPH values but frequently lose peptide diversity and potency.</cite>  
- Choose proteases to expose motif-rich b-peptides: <cite id="0f2e50f6-4">Serine proteases (papain, Alcalase) and broad-activity proteases yield different b-mer spectra; selecting enzymes that preferentially cut N-termini or away from Pro-containing motifs preserves antioxidant-rich sequences.</cite> <cite id="f893d55f-1">Including residues His, Trp, Tyr and maintaining turn-forming Pro/Asp motifs improves ABTS/FRAP and DPPH outcomes.</cite>  
- Pair pre-hydrolysis with in vitro digestion screening: <cite id="395f2c00-3">Assess DPPH/ABTS/FRAP before and after simulated gastric/duodenal digestion to identify process-stable antioxidant peptide fractions for fractionation and peptide sequencing.</cite> <cite id="395f2c00-8">Expect ≲20% assay-level changes across digestion with many plant hydrolysates; stability indicates process robustness.</cite>  
- Leverage germination/processing to raise free antioxidant pools: <cite id="f893d55f-4">Germination increases phenolic/antioxidant release from legumes; GI digestion then enhances their bioaccessibility and peptide-mediated scavenging.</cite>  
- Validate mechanisms concomitantly: <cite id="f893d55f-1">Correlate activity with chelation assays (Fenton/deferrioxamine controls) and competition experiments with radical probes; peptide sequence/microheterogeneity profiling (LC–MS/MS, Edman) identifies structure–activity relationships.</cite>

Practical recommendations to maximize phenolic recovery
- Prefer water–ethanol (30–60% v/v ethanol) with mild acid (≤10% acetic or citric) for most plant wastes; titrate ethanol within 40–60% and confirm with RSM whether edge compositions (lower or higher) outperform due to solubility or stability shifts<cite id="cc21a46e-8">40% ethanol optimized for TPC in olive pomace phenolic extraction</cite><cite id="cc21a46e-3">Response surface mapping demonstrates TPC as a function of ethanol and extraction variables</cite><cite id="cc21a46e-7">Acidic ethanol (5% acetic) coupled with short microwave exposure improved recovery</cite>. 
- Keep exposures short and pulsed (1–4 minutes), followed by solvent replacement or filtration/venting to renew fresh solvent at the matrix interior; avoid continuous overexposure that concentrates microwave power near the surface and promotes polymerization and solvent loss<cite id="f6800b52-6">Rapid and homogenous heating allows short extraction times in MAE</cite><cite id="f6800b52-5">Large solvent volumes can limit heating to penetration depth; use cycles/renewal to reach interior</cite>.

- For highly colored/polymer-prone matrices, reduce temperature 10–20 °C below dielectric-optimal to favor depolymerization over thermal degradation; add ≤1–5% weak acid or a small amount of metal chelator, and run under gentle venting to remove volatiles and suppress oxidation<cite id="cc21a46e-2">Extraction from multiple food wastes revealed profile-specific needs to balance yield and stability</cite><cite id="f6800b52-8">Orange waste microwave protocols tuned acidity and time to maximize phenolics</cite><cite id="3bf585f2-2">Antioxidant activity and phenolic composition respond to solvent chemistry and temperature/time</cite>.

Limitations and trade-offs
- Overfilling vessels with solvent increases coupling but can cap interior penetration; venting/short-cycle strategies mitigate this but lengthen cycle counts. High ethanol raises polarity and absorption but can skew profiles toward more soluble phenolics; profile-specific desirability is needed when antioxidants and sensory traits differ. Temperature/acid addition improves stability yet risks hydrolytic artifacts if excessive; pilot matrices should be screened for degradation markers alongside TPC<cite id="f6800b52-5">Higher solvent volumes can restrict heating to penetration depth; cycle design and venting are critical</cite><cite id="cc21a46e-3">Ethanol and extraction time/temperature trade off yield and profile across olive byproducts</cite><cite id="3bf585f2-2">Antioxidant activity and phenolic composition depend jointly on temperature, ethanol, and extraction time</cite>. 
- Microwave-only extraction may be limited by mass transfer into compacted solids; integrating short ultrasound bursts between MAE cycles can enhance maceration and gas desorption, but requires co-optimization to preserve phenolic integrity and avoid thermal interactions that raise peak temperatures beyond dielectric windows<cite id="3bf585f2-8">Ultrasound-assisted and microwave-assisted extraction optimized to maximize phenolics and flavonoids</cite><cite id="3bf585f2-2">Combined UAE/MAE showed interactions requiring careful parameter mapping</cite>.

Assay interpretation and cross-species consistency

- Why results differ by assay: DPPH and ABTS primarily capture radical-scavenging and hydrogen atom donation, whereas FRAP measures reducing power and metal-catalyzed redox capacity; including both radical and metal-based assays more reliably discriminates phenolic-driven chelation versus direct radical capture. Summary answer

Across multiple in vitro studies of plant pods and seeds, the most consistently demonstrated antioxidant activities are: (1) dose-dependent scavenging of stable/diphenyl radicals (DPPH) and peroxyl-type radicals (ABTS) in both pod and seed extracts—often most pronounced in methanol/ethanol-polar fractions rich in phenolics and tannins; (2) significant reducing power (FRAP/ORAC) that tracks phenolic/tannin content and is typically stronger in polar seed/pod extracts; (3) inhibition of lipid peroxidation models that parallels scavenging/reducing power profiles and correlates with phenolics; and (4) mechanism-linked “synergy” indices where chelation-capable phenolics (tannins) amplify radical-scavenging and metal-reducing activities, especially in seeds and mature pods. <cite id="b7fcad4c-0">Methanol extracts of both pods and seeds produced significantly higher DPPH inhibition than ethanol, illustrating consistent radical scavenging.</cite> <cite id="3e7d69ed-2">Polar extracts’ higher phenolic content underlies stronger DPPH, hydroxyl-scavenging, and FRAP in multiple legumes and oilseeds.</cite> <cite id="6112e7f7-4">Pod and seed ABTS and FRAP ranges across species (e.g., Clitoria) are measurable and consistent with phenolic richness.</cite> <cite id="3e7d69ed-1">Moringa seed studies demonstrate antioxidant activity across DPPH, ABTS, and FRAP and link these to phytochemical composition.</cite> <cite id="dfc98d2d-1">Comparisons across multiple legume seed/pod extracts consistently show DPPH/ABTS/FRAP differences driven by polarity and phenolics.</cite> <cite id="dfc98d2d-3">Seed-focused peanut analyses show strong DPPH/ABTS/FRAP values per 100 g, again aligning with phenolic-rich extraction and processing conditions.</cite> <cite id="dfc98d2d-6">Okra seed extract delivers highly significant in vitro antioxidant activity in DPPH and FRAP, consistent with phenolic-driven mechanisms.</cite> <cite id="3e7d69ed-5">Immature pods may be weaker DPPH scavengers, underscoring maturity-dependent variability within consistent assay patterns.</cite> <cite id="6112e7f7-6">Interpreting consistent in vitro antioxidant activities requires caution across assays and awareness that results may diverge from in vivo outcomes.</cite> <cite id="6112e7f7-7">Combining ABTS/DPPH/FRAP with phenolic quantification clarifies whether observed activity stems from direct radical scavenging, reducing power, or chelation mechanisms.</cite>

Overview

Berries provide rich polyphenol “plant compounds” (anthocyanins, proanthocyanidins, ellagitannin hydrolyzates, stilbenes such as resveratrol) that have been evaluated in eczema- and allergic contact dermatitis–like models for effects on skin symptoms (itching, erythema, swelling, barrier status) and inflammatory responses (mast cell–mediated histamine release, IgE, cytokine balance, NF-κB/MAPK signaling). Across Vaccinium (bilberry/blueberries), Vaccinium uliginosum (blueberry), sea buckthorn, and mulberry/gooseberry systems, preclinical studies report reductions in pruritus, erythema/edema/dryness, scratching behavior, and systemic markers histamine/IgE alongside modulation of Th1/Th2 cytokines and nuclear factor–related pathways, with some studies demonstrating barrier-function/water-content improvements after topical sea buckthorn oil.
