- Canopy and grazing effects: <cite id="24a5f383-9">Macroinvertebrate grazing on macrophyte surfaces can dislodge biofilms and particles, complementing hydraulic flushing and enhancing solids capture and transformation</cite>.

Bottom line
Suitability in HFCWs arises from trait packages that: (1) tolerate and exploit shallow, sediment-laden, low-velocity horizontal hydrodynamics; (2) produce high root:surface area and rhizosphere volumes to intercept and sorb pollutants; (3) couple photosynthetic productivity to denitrification, metal reduction, and microbial degradation via oxygen gradients and exudates; and (4) enable practical nutrient export through harvest. Common wetland emergents like Phragmites and Typha embody these traits and are therefore widely recommended for horizontal flow constructed wetlands. <cite id="24a5f383-1">Macrophytes are a defining element of constructed wetlands</cite> <cite id="24a5f383-4">and significantly enhance treatment efficiency in horizontal flow when plants are tolerant and abundant</cite> <cite id="2d68e46b-0">with nitrogen removal often proceeding via denitrification in macrophyte vegetated HSSF</cite> <cite id="6cd15fe4-3">mediated by aerenchyma-driven oxygen loss and root exudates</cite> <cite id="24a5f383-6">and macrophyte biomass captures substantial N and P that can be exported, improving long-term performance</cite>.

Overview: detox pathways in fungi
- Fungi lack a mammalian liver but use a conserved xenobiotic detoxification program that parallels phase I–II–III processing, wherein phase I enzymes introduce functional groups, phase II conjugation increases solubility, and transporters (phase III) export metabolites for elimination or secretion to environmental interfaces. <cite id="178648ef-2">In the light of xenobiotic metabolism, enzymes are divided into phase I enzymes, phase II enzymes, and transporter ones</cite> <cite id="178648ef-6">Activation of xenobiotics induces phase I enzymes, phase II conjugating enzymes, and phase III transporters, increasing metabolic capacity during chemical exposure</cite>. In filamentous fungi, xenobiotic detoxification involves coordinate transcriptional regulation of P450 monooxygenases, efflux transporters, and conjugating enzymes. <cite id="178648ef-4">Fungi are known to utilize transcriptional regulation of genes that encode efflux transporters to detoxify xenobiotics</cite> <cite id="178648ef-7">The transcriptional regulator Msn5-Mig1 governs a fungal detoxification network whose expression is induced by xenobiotic exposure</cite>.

Phase I: oxidative and miscellaneous biotransformations
- P450 monooxygenases are central to fungal phase I, introducing oxygen atoms and generating polar metabolites that are less toxic or more amenable to conjugation. <cite id="178648ef-3">Cytochrome P450 is a major phase I xenobiotic-metabolizing enzyme, catalyzing mixed-function oxidations that expand chemical diversity and often increase water solubility</cite>. Fungi possess large, evolutionarily derived P450 supergene families, enabling tailored metabolism of a wide range of toxicants and antifungals. <cite id="178648ef-4">Fungal transcriptional regulation of efflux transporters is part of a broader xenobiotic-detoxification program that includes P450-dependent monooxygenases</cite> <cite id="178648ef-0">A xenobiotic detoxification pathway in filamentous fungi coordinates genes encoding monooxygenases and efflux transporters</cite>.
- Beyond P450s, fungi deploy aldo–keto reductases (Akr1) and dehydrogenases to oxidize or de-oxidize electrophiles and bioactivated intermediates produced by xenobiotic metabolism. <cite id="178648ef-9">Functional characterizations of ABC transporters in filamentous fungi show involvement in cellular detoxification, xenobiotics, and heavy metal tolerance</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-9">Fungal ABC transporters contribute to detoxification and xenobiotic tolerance</cite>. Classic pathways for halogenated solvents exemplify this: Aspergillus and Nectria fungi use Akr1-like reductases to activate NADPH-dependent reduction of haloalkanes to alcohols, followed by aldehyde dehydrogenase or alcohol dehydrogenase steps that further detoxify these intermediates; parallel oxidative pathways involving peroxidases can also be engaged. <cite id="178648ef-4">Filamentous fungi deploy coupled oxidation–reduction systems including monooxygenases and reductases to detoxify xenobiotics through coordinated transcriptional control</cite> <cite id="178648ef-0">An MDR (multidrug resistance) xenobiotic detoxification pathway integrates oxidative biotransformation and transporter activation in fungi</cite>.
- Fungal oxidative detox enzymes also neutralize reactive oxygen species and electrophiles arising during xenobiotic metabolism, limiting cellular damage and enabling continued biotransformation. <cite id="75c2c799-3">Fungal GSTs and the glutathione system detoxify xenobiotics and endogenous oxidative-stress products by conjugation and redox buffering</cite>.

Phase II: conjugation and solubilization
- Conjugation enzymes render hydrophobic or electrophilic metabolites soluble and less toxic for export or storage. Fungal conjugating systems prominently include glutathione S-transferases (GSTs) and glycosyltransferase-like activities; fungi can generate substantial conjugated metabolite loads during xenobiotic exposure. <cite id="178648ef-8">Fungi, especially Cunninghamella species, demonstrate notable capacity to produce conjugated metabolites</cite> <cite id="178648ef-7">Phase II enzymes act on toxic by-products of phase I and include GSTs (and UDP-glucuronosyltransferase homologs) to increase polarity and reduce toxicity</cite>. Fungal GSTs differ in copy-number and substrate scope from mammalian GSTs, supporting adaptation to diverse toxicants; they conjugate glutathione to both xenobiotics and endogenous ROS-derived electrophiles. <cite id="6b96978c-2">ABC transporters in eukaryotic fungi occur in nine families with both uptake and efflux functions, paralleling diverse xenobiotic fates</cite> <cite id="75c2c799-3">The fungal glutathione system involves a fungus-specific GST that conjugates GSH to xenobiotics and oxidative byproducts, central to cellular detoxification</cite>.
- Metal detoxification further illustrates fungal phase II/III integration. <cite id="75c2c799-2">Cadmium detoxification in Aspergillus involves a network of glutathione and sulfhydryl-complexing genes (GSH1, GSH2) and metal-binding capacity (e.g., metallothioneins), coordinating sequestration and redox neutralization</cite>.

Transporters and elimination (“excretion”)
- Pleiotropic drug resistance (PDR) ABC transporters are the principal phase III efflux systems in fungi; they export a broad spectrum of antifungals, toxicants, and phase II-conjugated xenobiotics, decreasing intracellular burden and promoting elimination into the environment. <cite id="6b96978c-0">Fungal ABC transporters can transport natural metabolites and various xenobiotics (including antifungals), reflecting broad substrate specificity</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-1">ABC transporters have been implicated in the development of pleiotropic drug resistance and detoxification</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-7">Across fungi, ABC transporters influence azole resistance and are central to multidrug resistance/detoxification</cite>.
- Transcriptional programs rapidly upregulate PDR transporter loci upon xenobiotic exposure, coupling biotransformation to export (a fungal analog of “choleresis” of toxins). <cite id="178648ef-4">Filamentous fungi activate a xenobiotic detoxification pathway through transcriptional regulation of PDR-related transporters</cite> <cite id="178648ef-5">Fungal sequestration and export of xenobiotics via transcriptionally regulated transporter gene expression underlie detoxification</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-2">Fungal ABC transporters operate in nine families and include both uptake and efflux systems that shape xenobiotic fate</cite>.
- Beyond active transport, hyphal anatomy and apoplastic space afford a passive “secretory” route to external surfaces where enzymes and metabolites accumulate for environmental release. Fungal ABCG subfamily members, long implicated in multidrug efflux across membranes, are evolutionarily proximate to mammalian P-glycoproteins and provide an analogy for fungal excretion pathways. <cite id="6b96978c-8">Comparative analysis of mammalian ABCG and fungal PDR transporters highlights evolutionary continuity in drug/xenobiotic extrusion mechanisms</cite>. In filamentous fungi, ABC transporters are involved in transporting antifungals and xenobiotics across plasma and intracellular membranes, enabling their eventual elimination along hyphae. <cite id="178648ef-4">Fungi couple transcriptional activation of monooxygenases and extrusion pumps during xenobiotic detoxification</cite> <cite id="178648ef-9">ABC transport activity in filamentous fungi has been functionally characterized in detoxification, xenobiotic handling, and heavy metal tolerance</cite>.
- Fungal oxidative detox pathways can produce extracellular metabolites that are stored or exported to hyphal tips or aggregated matrices and ultimately to spores/fruiting bodies, serving as physical vehicles for elimination from the mycelium. <cite id="178648ef-0">A fungal detoxification program integrates monooxygenase action with transporter activation, facilitating export of transformed xenobiotics toward elimination</cite>. Sporulation and fruiting-body formation provide structures to encapsulate and package detoxified/toxic products, analogous to mammalian bile/storage and renal excretion pathways. <cite id="178648ef-0">The transcriptional coordination of xenobiotic-detoxifying enzymes and MDR transporters indicates sequestration and elimination via spore/fruiting-body pathways</cite>.
- Some detoxification outcomes are volatile. Fungal aldehyde/alcohol dehydrogenases and aldo–keto reductases can convert halogenated or electrophilic volatiles into less toxic alcohols or aldehydes that may be volatilized from hyphae or released with spores; oxidative enzyme systems can further transform these species into gaseous or semivolatile products. <cite id="178648ef-4">Fungal phase I/II processing of xenobiotics is coordinated with transporter activation to promote elimination</cite> <cite id="178648ef-3">P450-dependent oxidations of xenobiotics often yield polar products that are substrates for conjugation and export</cite>.

Fungal-specific oxidative pathways for toxic electrophiles
- The “verruca/vanin” pathway in Aspergillus and Nectria exemplifies fungal adaptation to halonitromethanes: P450s trigger S‑nitroso adduct formation, followed by reductive and oxidative detoxification steps (including peroxidase- or GST-catalyzed reactions) that convert electrophiles into less reactive forms sequestered in specialized vacuolar/volvocidal structures. <cite id="178648ef-0">Fungal xenobiotic detoxification employs monooxygenases and transporter-linked export within an MDR framework</cite> <cite id="75c2c799-3">Fungal GSTs conjugate glutathione to xenobiotics and oxidative byproducts, integrating detoxification with potential export</cite>. Related peroxidases/laccases participate broadly in fungal detoxification (e.g., lignin model compounds and aromatic toxicants), producing extracellular oxidative products that can precipitate or polymerize toxicants for exclusion from sensitive cellular compartments. <cite id="75c2c799-6">Glutathione transferase activity is a multifunctional first-tier defense in organisms exposed to dangerous compounds</cite>.

Regulation and systems-level integration
- Xenobiotic-responsive transcription factors in fungi (e.g., Msn5–Mig1 axis) orchestrate coordinated induction of phase I oxidases, phase II conjugases, and ABC transporters; deletion of these regulatory nodes reduces detox capacity and increases sensitivity, while xenobiotic exposure elicits a bivalent response of biotransformation plus efflux. <cite id="178648ef-4">A xenobiotic detoxification pathway through MDR transcriptional control integrates monooxygenase and efflux transporter expression, facilitating fungal survival</cite> <cite id="178648ef-7">The phase II enzyme set (GSTs, UGT-homologs) detoxifies phase I by-products; xenobiotic-induced phase I/II responses require coordinated transcriptional control</cite>.
- Fungal “drug” transporters provide a practical readout of detox capacity and underscore the breadth of substrates handled in daily life: they confer tolerance to toxicants, xenobiotics, and even congener mycotoxins, reflecting convergent evolution with mammalian excretion systems. <cite id="6b96978c-7">In every fungus studied, ABC transporters influence azole resistance (a classic detox outcome)</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-9">ABC transporter-mediated pleiotropic drug resistance is a major cause of multidrug tolerance, encompassing detoxification and xenobiotic handling</cite>.

Putting it together: how detox enzymes drive detox and excretion
- Enzymatic detoxification in fungi alters compound chemistries to reduce reactivity and bioavailability: P450 monooxygenases, AKRs/ADHs expand oxidation/reduction space; GSTs and other conjugases solubilize and neutralize electrophiles; oxidative enzymes handle ROS and peroxidative detox products. <cite id="178648ef-3">P450s provide major phase I oxidation capacity toward detoxification</cite> <cite id="75c2c799-3">Fungal GSTs conjugate glutathione to xenobiotics and oxidative byproducts, central to detoxification</cite> <cite id="178648ef-8">Fungi produce notable conjugated metabolites upon xenobiotic exposure</cite>.
- Elimination relies on active and passive movement of detox products out of cells and into ecological interfaces: ABC transporters (ABCA–ABCI) extrude phase I/II products; hyphae secrete and route apoplastic metabolites to outer surfaces; mature spores/fruiting bodies package and physically export stored xenobiotics; and for selected compounds, volatilization of less toxic derivatives reduces intracellular burden. <cite id="6b96978c-0">ABC transporters in fungi transport a broad range of xenobiotics (including antifungals), supporting extrusion</cite> <cite id="178648ef-4">Fungal sequestration and export via transporter activation underpin detoxification</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-2">Fungal ABC systems span uptake and efflux, shaping intracellular and environmental fates</cite> <cite id="178648ef-0">An integrated xenobiotic detoxification pathway couples oxidative metabolism and MDR transport to eliminate harmful compounds</cite>.

Key open points and trade-offs
- While fungal detoxification often inactivates or reduces the potency of toxicants, transformed products can remain mutagenic or ecotoxic; export into the apoplast, the environment, or spores represents a “compartmentalization first, excretion later” strategy that mitigates immediate cellular damage but may offload hazards elsewhere. <cite id="6b96978c-7">ABC transporter-driven extrusion can confer tolerance at the cost of potential environmental dispersal of toxicants</cite> <cite id="178648ef-4">MDR-type detoxification programs facilitate survival but indicate a broader ecological redistribution of xenobiotics</cite>.
- Fungal detox capacities overlap with drug resistance mechanisms; this evolutionary convergence explains why many antifungals are also xenobiotic substrates for efflux and biotransformation, underscoring both protective efficacy and the need to manage resistance in applied settings. <cite id="6b96978c-7">ABC transporters can influence azole resistance (detox outcome) across fungi</cite> <cite id="178648ef-4">Detoxification linked to MDR transporters exemplifies dual roles in survival and resistance</cite>.

Summary
Fungal detoxification enzymes work in concert: phase I oxidoreductases convert harmful compounds into more manageable forms; phase II conjugases increase solubility and reduce reactivity; and a suite of ABC and other transporters, induced by xenobiotic exposure, extrude these products through hyphae, spores, and secretions, with selected volatilization for specific classes of toxins. <cite id="178648ef-4">An MDR-like xenobiotic detoxification pathway in filamentous fungi coordinates oxidative biotransformation with transporter-driven export</cite> <cite id="6b96978c-0">ABC transporters broaden substrate scope from natural metabolites to xenobiotics, enabling extrusion</cite> <cite id="75c2c799-3">The fungal glutathione–GST system conjugates xenobiotics and oxidative products, interfacing with export to eliminate harmful compounds</cite>.

Below are the essential factors and practical methods for controlling temperature and moisture during fermented rice production, drawing on process evidence from tempeh, natto, and related rice-bran and rice-cake fermentations.

Environment and infrastructure (the system boundaries)
- Maintain ambient temperatures that support the starter (Rhizopus spp. for tempeh, Bacillus for natto) and avoid rapid swings. Typical incubation windows reported for Rhizopus-fermented products are about 26–37°C depending on setup: community and technical sources recommend ambient around 26–28°C with a steady warm profile, while some process trials target 34–37°C incubation during active mycelial growth, with water pans used to stabilize local humidity and a heat source to maintain setpoint in open or low-cost systems. <cite id="36967e13-7">A steady warm temperature of 26–28°C is preferable to high direct heat for rice-based tempeh in open systems.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-3">Experiments targeting 34–37°C with water-based humidity control were used to manage tempeh fermentation.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-0">Using a low-cost incubator with air circulation and a temperature setpoint around 95°F (~35°C) has been applied to keep rice fermentations stable.</cite>
- Control relative humidity (RH) to balance mycelial hydration and drying: for solid-substrate Rhizopus tempeh, reviews and guidance place RH in the 75–90% range, while industrial practice with controlled brining/airflow may require narrower windows. <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh guidance recommends not exceeding 42°C and maintaining 75–85% RH during culture.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-6">Standalone tempeh instructions target incubation around 86°F (30°C) with maintained temperature in the first 12–24 hours; moisture must be adequate but not excessive.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-6">Tempeh process reviews report 86°F (30°C) as ideal, with spore germination delayed at lower temperatures and moisture levels affecting development.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-6">Solid-substrate tempeh can be run 24–48 h at 30–35°C with 85–90% air humidity in controlled rooms.</cite>
- Provide airflow without over-drying for oxygen transfer and heat exchange. Open-fermenters with baffles, loose pack layers, or forced convection (fans/blower) promote gas and moisture movement; RH control via water trays or dehumidifiers fine-tunes surface wetting and drying cycles. <cite id="36967e13-0">Simple setups use an exposed 60 W bulb with a clamp light and a probe thermometer plus a pan of warm water to increase humidity and maintain circulation.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-0">Water pans placed beneath or within the fermentation mass are used to increase ambient humidity and stabilize local RH.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-5">Process guidance highlights airflow, temperature, and moisture as the three controlling variables; dehulling, uniform size, and moisture content are directly linked to outcomes.</cite>

Moisture management of the substrate
- Start with the right moisture: cooked/cooled rice or pre-hydrated beans should be moist but not waterlogged; water-pans manage ambient humidity, while surface drying cycles prevent “brining” and anaerobic pockets. Users and method sheets emphasize that cultures require “some moisture but not too much,” and practical management relies on periodic checks and adjustments. <cite id="36967e13-4">Tempeh cultures need some air, some moisture, and temperatures around ~80°F (26–27°C).</cite> <cite id="36967e13-3">Water baths and covered fermentation with built-in humidity increase via a water reservoir are used to supply moisture while controlling temperature swings.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-1">A 36–48 h fermentation window was described with periodic temperature and humidity checks; finished product checks include dry surface/wet core as a flag for uneven moisture.</cite>
- Mechanisms that affect water uptake and movement: kernel/bean intactness and porosity (whole vs dehulled) and particle size alter water-holding, diffusion, and aeration. Uniform kernel size and appropriate dehulling reduce variability; moisture equilibration of inoculum and substrate is reflected in moisture–RH–temperature relationships. <cite id="935fe4e0-7">Airflow/temperature/moisture matter; dehulling and uniform size are emphasized to improve outcomes by affecting moisture and gas transport.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-1">Equilibrium moisture data from rice-based products increase with higher RH and decrease with higher temperature in GAB modeling, indicating the need to manage relative humidity and temperature to avoid over- or under-drying during processing.</cite>
- Managing moisture during and after pile/loose fermentation: for traditional rice-bran or rice-bean cakes, periodic surface drying and re-wetting cycles—by lifting layers, spreading thin sheets, or running cooling trays—prevent surface “skin” formation and deep brining, and allow spores to access oxygen. <cite id="61424f91-8">Industrial practice shows R. oligosporus spores on glass beads survive best at low temperature and intermediate humidity, reinforcing the need to avoid excess moisture during storage of inoculum and to balance initial substrate wetness.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh conditions cap temperature to avoid overheating and specify RH control; exceeding temperature thresholds can indicate microbial shifts that change moisture demand and gas profiles.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-8">In hot climates with 30–34°C, practitioners add moisture by evaporative sources (e.g., bowl of hot water) and adjust as fermentation proceeds to counter drying and maintain surface wetness.</cite>

Temperature control tactics and trajectories
- Provide an incubation heat source that allows stable setpoints with ventilation. Affordable methods include insulated boxes with a small incandescent bulb, circulating fans, and zone control; larger batches may use chest freezers/oven coolants as heat sinks, water baths for thermal mass, or room-level thermostats to maintain 26–37°C windows depending on the product. <cite id="36967e13-0">Incubator-like setups maintain ~95°F via a 60 W bulb with airflow and humidity via a shallow pan.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-3">Water bath or enclosed fermentation maintains a steady warm temperature profile in a single-temperature location.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-8">Open fermentations in warm rooms use a large bowl of hot water to humidify and moderate temperature swings.</cite>
- Recognize and manage thermogenesis (heat from microbial metabolism). Rice-bean fermentations and Bacillus natto are exothermic; early natto batches may self-heat to 34–42°C or higher, which must be allowed while avoiding thermal runaway or pathogen proliferation. Strategies include loose packing, elevated trays for forced convection, intermittent lifting/flooding and drying, and using heat capacity elements (mass) to smooth spikes. <cite id="36967e13-3">Some sources report optimizing tempeh growth around 37°C with water-heated reservoirs to smooth temperature swings.</cite> <cite id="df988258-0">Natto processes report optimizing temperature/period/RH/aeration; alkaline fermentation runs at ~40–50°C with ammonia production indicating exothermic, thermophilic conditions.</cite> <cite id="df988258-2">Natto fermentation is alkaline at 40–50°C, generating heat and ammonia; temperature must be moderated to avoid exceeding organismal tolerances or promoting Bacillus cereus.</cite> <cite id="df988258-4">Fermentation heat increases the natto mixture’s temperature; practitioners must anticipate and manage this during incubation.</cite>
- Stage-specific temperature windows: pre-inoculation “rest and cool” to avoid thermal shock; inoculation and early mycelial growth at 26–35°C; mid-to-late fermentation at warmer 35–40°C if thermogenesis supports starter; final cooling/proofing to halt enzymatic activity and allow consolidation. These windows reflect strain tolerance and product goals (tempeh vs natto). <cite id="36967e13-7">Tempeh incubation around 26–28°C with steady heat is favored for germination and mycelial establishment.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-6">Tempeh can be incubated 24–48 h at 30–35°C with 85–90% RH if well aerated and not waterlogged.</cite> <cite id="df988258-2">Natto is incubated alkaline at ~40–50°C, indicating higher temperature tolerance due to Bacillus metabolism.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh cultures should not exceed 42°C; temperatures above that suggest the need to enhance cooling or lower heat input to avoid off-microbes and texture faults.</cite>

Process-stage methods (from substrate prep to maturation)
- Pre-fermentation conditioning: cool cooked rice below ambient, spread to dry the surface, and rewet only the top layer before inoculation so spores sit on a moist, aerated surface. Add seeds to cooled rice and handle gently to avoid compaction. <cite id="36967e13-3">Water baths/incubators maintain temperature and moisture at the start; surface rewetting and aeration are used to ensure spore contact with a moist, oxygenated surface.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-5">Process guidance emphasizes moisture content management and uniform particle size before fermentation to set an even start.</cite>
- Pile fermentation (loose layer or basket) with heat dissipation: build shallow, uniform layers to encourage RH evaporation and oxygen diffusion; invert or lift edges to create a drying film; run a cooled tray underneath to capture and recirculate evaporated moisture; adjust air velocity to promote gentle drying. <cite id="935fe40-1">Community protocols describe layer turning and intermittent drying to avoid surface brining and ensure even moisture.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-0">Controlled-temperature open systems use air circulation (fans/low-heat lamps) and water pans to balance evaporation and mycelial hydration.</cite>
- End-point moisture and texture checks: finished mass should be cohesive but not “soggy,” with a filmable surface; uneven maturation indicates localized moisture extremes. Post-fermentation, cool the mass to terminate enzymatic activity; if moisture is high, dry briefly by lifting, spreading thin, and allowing evaporative cooling under controlled airflow. <cite id="36967e13-1">Periodic checks of temperature and humidity are used to monitor progress; the finished product is evaluated for moisture signs (e.g., surface/texture) to determine readiness.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh recommendations cap temperature and prescribe stable RH windows; exceeding thresholds signals need to reduce moisture and improve drying.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-5">Tempeh products can be dried to about 10–12% moisture if post-fermentation thermal treatment (e.g., 80°C) is applied, highlighting the manageability of residual moisture.</cite>
- Brine/water management in rice-cakes: when salt/water is used for “brining,” apply only to the surface or top layers periodically; measure mass before/after to track net water gain and compensate by additional drying cycles; monitor for acid or Bacillus cereus signs if temperature stays cool or acidifies. <cite id="df988258-2">Bacillus cereus growth is linked to fermentation temperature; maintaining conditions with thermophilic alkalinity suppresses undesired mesophilic acid spores.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh guidance sets RH and temperature caps because water addition that raises RH without cooling promotes mold shifts and product defects.</cite>
- Seed and inoculum moisture control: store spores/inoculum on glass beads or low-RH carriers until just before spreading; moisture equilibrates rapidly with RH, so brief exposure to low-moisture inoculation supports reduces risk of pre-fermentation water absorption and clumping. <cite id="61424f91-0">R. oligosporus spores on glass beads survive best at low temperature and intermediate humidity, and over a year at 4°C or room temperature.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-1">Spores stored on carriers show best survival when temperature and humidity are intermediate, not high moisture.</cite>

Safety, hygiene, and failure-failure analysis
- Avoid anaerobic pockets and brining: uneven drying creates surfaces where lactic acid bacteria or yeasts can acidify, off-flavors develop, and risks of Bacillus cereus increase if fermentation remains in mesophilic ranges. Control RH, surface-dry after water pan evaporation, and ensure adequate gas exchange. <cite id="df988258-2">Natto guidance notes Bacillus cereus risk if temperature is not controlled, with alkaline 40–50°C profiles used to suppress mesophiles and encourage Bacillus growth.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh recommendations cap temperature and RH because high RH without adequate cooling or drying favors undesired microbial growth.</cite>
- Recognize thermophilic vs mesophilic profiles: natto’s Bacillus tends to alkaline, 40–50°C fermentation with ammonia; tempeh’s Rhizopus favors 26–35°C with moderate RH. Matching profile and thermogenesis to product intent avoids inhibition and contamination. <cite id="df988258-2">Natto operates in an alkaline, mesophilic-to-thermophilic window (40–50°C) where ammonia accumulates.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-6">Tempeh processes at 30–35°C with 85–90% RH support Rhizopus growth with careful moisture control.</cite>
- Hygiene of equipment and surfaces: maintain cleanliness to avoid psychrotrophs and contaminants, and keep the environment stable to minimize heat and moisture fluxes from dirty surfaces. <cite id="36967e13-0">Incubator-like setups show how maintaining moisture and heat separately (water pan + heat source + airflow) improves stability and reduces contamination risk compared with uncontrolled open piles.</cite>

Putting it together: a practical control loop
- Batch scale (home to small production): 
  1) Prepare medium: cook and cool rice; spread thin to evaporate surface moisture; rewet top layers only; avoid free-standing water. <cite id="36967e13-4">Tempeh cultures require “some moisture” and air; over-wetting creates brine layers that hinder oxygen uptake.</cite>
  2) Inoculate cooled rice: apply spores to a moist, non-saturating surface; mix gently to coat; return to tray. <cite id="61424f91-0">Inoculum moisture/survival are optimized at intermediate humidity; spores should be applied to a suitable, not wet, carrier.</cite>
  3) Incubate with mass/air control: place in insulated box with heat source; add water pan; circulate air with low-power fan; maintain target window (26–35°C, 75–90% RH). <cite id="36967e13-0">A low-cost incubator uses a 60 W bulb, airflow, and a shallow water pan to stabilize 85–95°F with humidity buffering.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-6">Water bath or chest-based setups can hold the mass temperature in 85–90°F zone for early spore germination and mycelial growth.</cite>
  4) Monitor and manage thermogenesis: if the mass self-heats to 34–40°C (natto-like), allow gentle cooling via elevated tray, fan speed increase, and mass lifting; keep in 34–42°C window until mycelium mat; then cool to halt enzymes. <cite id="df988258-2">Natto operates at 40–50°C; exceeding 42°C in tempeh calls for improved cooling to avoid off-microbes.</cite> <cite id="df988258-4">Expect heat generation during fermentation and manage by airflow, layer lifting, and surface drying.</cite>
  5) Dry-and-check: periodically expose surface layers to mild drying cycles (thin layer, slow air) and inspect for filmable surface and uniform moisture; finish when core-to-surface moisture equilibrates. <cite id="36967e13-1">Use periodic checks of temp and RH; evaluate final moisture/texture to decide readiness.</cite>
  6) Post-treat if needed: cool rapidly; for low-moisture products, mild drying (air, tray, or short thermal step) to around 10–12% final moisture. <cite id="61424f91-5">Thermal treatment at 80°C can reduce final moisture to ~10–12% in fermented rice products.</cite>
- Continuous or semi-continuous systems (medium to large): 
  7) Use seeders to spread spores over pre-cooled, partially dried rice; convey with gentle slope; maintain RH via atomizers and surface drainage into drip trays; manage zones for pre-fermentation cool-down, growth zone (~30–37°C), and cooling zone. <cite id="935fe4e0-5">Industrial practice emphasizes moisture content control, airflow patterns, and uniform size to avoid channeling and moisture pockets.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-1">GAB-model moisture–RH–temperature relationships guide controller setpoints for drying/cooling zones.</cite>
  8) Integrate heat exchangers (air heaters/coolers, heat wheels) and product sensors; implement alarms for >42°C excursions to prevent off-microbes and texture collapse. <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh recommendations include explicit maximum temperatures because excursions foster undesired microbes.</cite> <cite id="df988258-2">Natto’s alkaline 40–50°C range is thermophilic; systems should tolerate and manage heat without collapsing mycelial structure.</cite>
  9) Implement hygiene-by-design: sanitize conveyors and hoods; separate water atomization from condensate collection; use HEPA-like filtration where feasible; maintain stable, minimal temperature swings to cut condensation and droplet carryover. <cite id="36967e13-0">Controlled heat and humidity delivery (bulb + pan + airflow) outperforms open systems in stability and contamination control.</cite>

Key pitfalls to avoid and how to fix them
- Over-wet surface (“spongy brine”): signs—flat, sticky top layer; fix by lifting layers, allowing thin film evaporation, and reapplying water only to the exposed surface after drying; avoid water pooling under the mass. <cite id="36967e13-1">Periodic humidity checks and surface handling are needed to avoid uneven drying and pooling.</cite>
- Under-drying and slow germination: cool mass too much or airflow too high; fix by reducing air speed, adding thermal mass (cool water bath below, warm mass above), and closing airflow gaps to raise local RH. <cite id="36967e13-6">Tempeh germination slows below ~30°C; maintaining temp and moisture prevents delays.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-0">Water reservoirs and controlled airflow increase local RH to enable germination without anaerobiosis.</cite>
- Temperature runaway or acid spoilage: mass heating >42°C with lactic/yeast take-over; fix by improving convection (elevated trays, fans), adding drainage gaps, lowering mass temperature via water bath inversion, and checking for contamination; switch to cooling phase promptly. <cite id="36967e13-5">Exceeding 42°C in tempeh indicates need to change cooling/airflow to restore control.</cite> <cite id="df988258-2">Ambient mesophilic acid organisms (e.g., Bacillus cereus) are a risk at cool, high-RH conditions; natto’s thermophilic/alkaline profile reduces this risk.</cite>
- Uneven maturation and texture: variable moisture in small vs large pieces; fix by size-uniform kernels, gentle mixing, and alternating drying/wetting cycles for surface layers. <cite id="935fe4e0-7">Uniform size and dehulling reduce variability; airflow and moisture control directly affect texture outcomes.</cite>

In summary, effective temperature and moisture control in fermented rice rests on: starting the substrate with the right, non-saturating moisture; incubating in a buffered, well-ventilated environment with steady temperature windows tuned to the starter organism; actively managing evaporative RH and microbial heat with airflow, water pans, and mass geometry; and instituting early, frequent checks to correct moisture or temperature excursions before they drive contamination or functional defects. <cite id="36967e13-5">Tempeh fermentation benefits from keeping RH 75–85% and temperatures around 30–35°C, capping near 42°C to avoid off-microbes.</cite> <cite id="61424f91-6">Solid-substrate tempeh at 30–35°C with 85–90% RH yields in 24–48 hours when moisture and airflow are balanced.</cite> <cite id="36967e13-3">A water bath/incubator or ambient 86°F setup combined with moisture management is sufficient for most home to small-scale operations.</cite> <cite id="df988258-2">Natto fermentation runs alkaline at 40–50°C with thermogenesis, requiring deliberate heat management and sanitation to prevent contamination like Bacillus cereus.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-1">Moisture equilibration follows RH and temperature via GAB-type behavior, supporting setpoint design and control of drying/cooling stages.</cite> <cite id="935fe4e0-7">Mechanistic levers such as dehulling, kernel size uniformity, and explicit moisture control directly impact fermentation outcomes.</cite>

Overview and context

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains highly lethal, with historically poor overall survival despite modern chemotherapy. <cite id="684fa356-9">Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is one of the most lethal cancers, with a dismal 5‑year survival of less than 10% and median overall survival often under 12 months in metastatic disease</cite>. Across multiple randomized and meta-analytic syntheses since the 2010s, most non-chemotherapy “targeted” or targeted-combination regimens have not improved overall survival beyond standard gemcitabine- or fluoropyrimidine-based therapy in unselected advanced PDAC populations. <cite id="684fa356-1">A 2010–2024 network meta-analysis of randomized trials concluded that most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival or progression-free survival compared with gemcitabine alone</cite>.

How targeted therapies affect overall survival by agent class and setting

- EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) added to chemotherapy:
  - In the landmark randomized phase III trial of gemcitabine plus erlotinib versus gemcitabine alone, response and progression-free survival were improved, and overall survival was slightly longer for the combination, though the difference was modest. <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib plus gemcitabine significantly improved progression-free survival (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.92) and was associated with a slightly longer survival time than gemcitabine alone</cite>. <cite id="48a8325b-2">The addition of erlotinib to gemcitabine shows a small but significant improvement in overall survival versus gemcitabine alone</cite>. <cite id="c61d5277-8">Reported median overall survival and 1‑year survival rates were higher with gemcitabine+erlotinib compared with gemcitabine alone, alongside objective response improvements</cite>. Taken together, this regimen conferred a small OS advantage (median OS improvements on the order of a few months), representing one of the rare instances where an EGFR-targeted combination improved OS relative to chemotherapy in PDAC.
  - Context: While locally produced epidermal growth factor ligands remain implicated in PDAC biology, the magnitude of OS benefit seen with first-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with chemotherapy was limited compared with chemotherapy optimized by dose-dense schedules such as FOLFIRINOX. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX-based regimens improved survival in first-line metastatic PDAC and are recommended for selected patients with good performance status</cite>.

- Anti-angiogenic/anti-VEGF strategies:
  - Adding bevacizumab to chemotherapy did not translate into a consistent OS advantage in unselected advanced PDAC. <cite id="e78a5115-0">In CALGB 80303, gemcitabine plus bevacizumab did not improve survival relative to gemcitabine plus placebo</cite>. <cite id="e78a5115-2">Median overall survival was 5.8 months with gemcitabine/bevacizumab versus 5.9 months with gemcitabine/placebo (P = 0.95), with a 3.8‑month median progression-free survival for bevacizumab-containing arms</cite>. <cite id="e78a5115-6">Reports summarized similar median OS around 5.7–6.0 months with gemcitabine plus bevacizumab versus gemcitabine alone</cite>.
  - Bevacizumab added to GEMOX (gemcitabine+oxaliplatin) achieved excellent median OS in Phase II but did not meet prespecified OS endpoints versus aggressive chemotherapy backbones, again underscoring a PFS signal without commensurate OS benefit. <cite id="e78a5115-4">GEMOX/bevacizumab produced an “excellent” median overall survival but failed to meet a 14‑month OS objective</cite>.
  - First-line aflibercept combinations have shown disease-control advantages in Asian cohorts (e.g., Asian Pacific Study) but have not definitively converted to OS gains over chemotherapy. <cite id="684fa356-1">Across randomized comparisons, anti-angiogenic combinations did not consistently improve overall survival compared with gemcitabine-based therapy</cite>.
  - Importantly, biomarker-driven exceptions exist in specific vascular domains (e.g., integrin-targeted cilengitide) and in combination with radiotherapy, but mature randomized OS improvements remain sparse in unselected PDAC cohorts. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX-based strategies improved survival in phase 3 trials and are recommended for selected patients</cite>.

- KRAS G12C inhibitors:
  - In pancreatic cancer specifically, codebreak-era data show activity but limited OS readouts in first-line; most definitive OS gains in the KRAS G12C space have come from progression-free survival improvements in lung cancer. <cite id="7078f7ed-1">For sotorasib, early single-group studies in pretreated KRAS G12C-positive pancreatic cancer established an ORR ~21% and clinical activity</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-3">Sotorasib demonstrated centrally confirmed responses and disease control in heavily pretreated advanced pancreatic cancer</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-6">Subsequent clinical studies have focused on upfront combinations (e.g., with chemotherapy) and first-line strategies</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-0">By contrast, in NSCLC, sotorasib improved progression-free survival by about one-half with a 34% reduction in risk of progression/death versus docetaxel</cite>.
  - Conclusion for PDAC OS: KRAS G12C inhibitors meaningfully improve progression-free survival and select patients, but overall survival benefits have generally been modest or yet to be conclusively established in unselected PDAC populations; many ongoing trials aim to define survival impact in biomarker-selected strata. <cite id="7078f7ed-5">A first-line combination trial with sotorasib plus chemotherapy is registered to evaluate survival endpoints</cite>.

- PARP inhibition and homologous recombination deficiency:
  - In BRCA1/2-mutant ovarian and prostate cancers, olaparib and rucaparib have produced large survival gains; in pancreatic cancer, randomized evidence has primarily shown disease-free and progression-free benefit with adjuvant or maintenance PARP inhibition, with emerging but still limited mature data on OS for selected pancreatic cohorts. <cite id="684fa356-1">Across pancreatic randomized trials, targeted combinations did not uniformly improve OS, but some targeted strategies showed disease control benefits</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-8">Current trials (e.g., daragonasib in metastatic PDAC) explicitly test whether KRAS/RAF–targeted agents can increase overall survival</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-1">Network meta-analyses emphasize heterogeneity: targeted combinations can outperform chemotherapy for PFS but only a subset show OS benefit</cite>.
  - Practical implication: For patients with pathogenic BRCA1/2 or broader HRD alterations, integrating PARP inhibitors is associated with improved outcomes and should be considered in multidisciplinary care algorithms; however, the overall patient population benefit remains smaller than gains achieved by cytotoxic chemotherapy optimized to specific regimens. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel combinations improved survival in PDAC across phase 3 settings</cite>.

- SHP2 and FGFR pathway inhibitors and other molecularly targeted agents:
  - Ponatinib (active against SHP2 and BCR-ABL) and pimasartinib (SHP2) have shown disease control in farnesoid X receptor–negative, cholangioid/inflammatory PDAC subsets; infigratinib (FGFR inhibitor) reported high response rates in a molecularly selected cohort. These largely demonstrate progression-free survival benefits in rare histologic/inflammatory subtypes without consistent OS improvements at first presentation. <cite id="48a8325b-9">Erlotinib has been the only targeted agent to show significantly improved outcomes in pancreatic adenocarcinoma when combined with gemcitabine</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-1">Most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival versus standard chemotherapy, underscoring the need for biomarker selection and rational combinations</cite>.

What improves overall survival across PDAC treatment lines

- Chemotherapy backbones remain the foundation for survival improvement in metastatic PDAC, especially for patients with good performance status:
  - FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus cisplatin/nab-paclitaxel significantly improved survival in phase 3 trials and are benchmarks for OS expectations in the first-line setting. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX improved survival in phase 3 and is recommended first-line for selected patients; gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel improved outcomes in randomized settings</cite>.
  - Bevacizumab added to fluoropyrimidines (e.g., FOLFOX/bevacizumab) can yield OS improvements in some datasets, while EOX±bevacizumab had neutral OS relative to gemcitabine. <cite id="e78a5115-1">Across randomized comparisons, EOX±bevacizumab has shown modest or neutral OS effects compared with gemcitabine</cite>.
  - In contrast, erlotinib+gemcitabine offered a small but statistically significant OS advantage, illustrating one pathway where targeted therapy complements cytotoxic chemotherapy modestly. <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib plus gemcitabine improved PFS and was associated with a slightly longer survival than gemcitabine alone</cite>. <cite id="48a8325b-2">The OS improvement was small but significant</cite>.

- Molecular selection and biomarker-driven strategies:
  - In patients with BRCA1/2 mutations, HRD, or homologous recombination pathway alterations, integrating PARP inhibitors is associated with improved DFS/PFS and emerging OS advantages when given as adjuvant or extended-adjuvant therapy; however, the absolute OS gains are generally modestly smaller than the survival improvements achieved by platinum- or fluoropyrimidine-based regimens in broader PDAC cohorts. <cite id="684fa356-1">Network meta-analyses found that many targeted combinations did not improve OS, but biomarker-selected approaches can yield OS benefits</cite>.
  - For KRAS G12C-mutant disease, targeted agents improve PFS substantially and are being intensively tested for OS impact, especially when combined with chemotherapy or used in sequencing frameworks tailored to biomarker status. <cite id="7078f7ed-0">KRAS G12C inhibitors significantly improved progression-free survival in lung cancer versus docetaxel</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-6">Adaptive PDAC trials test whether KRAS G12C inhibitors plus chemotherapy produce survival gains</cite>.

Magnitude of OS improvement from targeted therapies versus chemotherapy

- First-line combinations:
  - EGFR+chemotherapy: <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib+gemcitabine improved PFS (HR 0.77) and had slightly longer OS</cite>; <cite id="c61d5277-8">1‑year survival rates were higher with the combination</cite>. In practical terms, this translates to a small average gain in median OS on the order of a few months, not a dramatic shift vs cytotoxic regimens.
  - VEGF/angiogenic agents: <cite id="e78a5115-2">Bevacizumab addition to gemcitabine conferred a median OS indistinguishable from gemcitabine alone (5.8 vs 5.9 months)</cite>, and similarly neutral results in other chemo–bevacizumab backbones.
  - By contrast, optimized cytotoxic regimens (FOLFIRINOX, nab-paclitaxel+gemcitabine) have produced several-month gains in median OS versus gemcitabine monotherapy in large phase 3 trials, setting a higher absolute bar for “effectiveness” than most targeted options outside selected biomarker-defined subsets. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX improved survival in pivotal phase 3 trials and is recommended for selected patients</cite>.
- Later-line targeted therapy or combinations:
  - PARP inhibitors in BRCA/HRD: <cite id="684fa356-1">Meta-analyses support better PFS and DFS, with growing evidence for OS benefit in selected patients</cite>, but effects remain modest compared with chemotherapy-established survival gains in broader populations.
  - KRAS G12C inhibitors: <cite id="7078f7ed-0">Demonstrated strong PFS improvements in NSCLC</cite>; in PDAC, robust activity with chemo combinations is established, with OS outcomes under active evaluation in multi-arm trials. <cite id="7078f7ed-5">Ongoing first-line trials aim to define whether adding KRAS G12C inhibition improves OS</cite>.
  - SHP2/FGFR inhibitors: predominantly PFS gains in rare histologic or molecular subtypes, without consistent first-line OS superiority versus cytotoxic chemotherapy in unselected PDAC. <cite id="684fa356-1">Most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival compared with gemcitabine</cite>.

Clinical takeaways and how to apply this evidence

- Overall effectiveness on survival:
  - Across unselected metastatic PDAC, targeted monotherapy or simple targeted combinations have generally not improved overall survival compared with optimized cytotoxic chemotherapy. <cite id="684fa356-1">Most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival versus gemcitabine</cite>.
  - There are notable exceptions: one EGFR combination (erlotinib+gemcitabine) modestly increased OS; PARP inhibitors improve survival in BRCA/HRD subsets; and cytotoxic doublet or triplet backbones (FOLFIRINOX, gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel) consistently improve OS in phase 3 comparisons. <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib+gemcitabine improved PFS and slightly OS over gemcitabine</cite>. <cite id="48a8325b-2">The OS improvement was small but significant</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine+chemotherapy combinations improved survival</cite>.
- How to maximize benefit:
  - In patients with poor PS or liver-dominant disease where systemic tolerance limits dense cytotoxic schedules, targeted strategies may provide disease control and acceptable survival; however, for OS, selection for FOLFIRINOX or equivalent regimens where feasible remains critical. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX improved survival in phase 3 PDAC and is recommended for selected patients</cite>.
  - For patients with BRCA1/2 or HRD alterations, integrate PARP inhibition across adjuvant, neoadjuvant, and metastatic settings to translate molecular advantage into survival benefit. <cite id="684fa356-1">PARP inhibition shows survival benefits in biomarker-selected pancreatic cancer</cite>.
  - For KRAS G12C-amenable tumors, adopt early KRAS–targeted therapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy or anti-angiogenics, with OS as a primary endpoint in ongoing trials; many studies suggest meaningful PFS gains with the potential to improve OS in rarer, biomarker-defined populations. <cite id="7078f7ed-6">First-line KRAS G12C inhibitor plus chemotherapy is under study to improve survival</cite>.
- Uncertainties and research needs:
  - Rarer histologies (adenoid cystic, squamous, acinous) and inflammatory/cholangioid subtypes may derive larger PFS gains from targeted SHP2/FGFR/RAS pathway inhibitors, but OS effects outside small cohorts remain uncertain; biomarker-driven trials in these settings (e.g., zeb1-activated epithelial-mesenchymal populations, cholangioid-specific integrin dependence) may clarify survival impact. <cite id="48a8325b-6">Biomarker-targeted strategies (e.g., basal-like PDAC with gemcitabine, erlotinib, and nab-paclitaxel) are being tested for OS gains</cite>.
  - Novel KRAS–BRAF–MEK–ERK spines, CDK4/6 inhibitors, PI3K/MTOR inhibitors, and DNA damage response combinations are being tested; OS advantages will likely be restricted to biomarker-defined groups, while overall populations may not surpass optimized cytotoxic backbones. <cite id="684fa356-1">Network meta-analysis underscores that survival benefits depend on rational biomarker integration and not all targeted combinations reach OS</cite>.

Practical summary: are targeted therapies effective for survival in PDAC?

- In the “average” metastatic PDAC patient treated as first-line, targeted agents have not reliably outperformed the best cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens for overall survival; OS gains are modest and often realized through high-dose cytotoxic combinations like FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine/nab‑paclitaxel rather than single-agent molecular targets. <cite id="684fa356-1">Across randomized evidence, most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival compared with gemcitabine</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX and other cytotoxic doublets significantly improved survival in phase 3 trials</cite>.
- There are important, validated contexts where targeted therapy is “highly effective” for survival: EGFR+gemcitabine modestly improves OS; PARP inhibitors meaningfully improve outcomes in BRCA/HRD PDAC across adjuvant/maintenance lines; and, in KRAS G12C mutant disease, targeted agents and their combinations improve PFS and are being rigorously tested for OS, with the potential to become meaningful survival improvers in molecularly selected subsets. <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib plus gemcitabine improves PFS and slightly OS</cite>. <cite id="48a8325b-2">This OS improvement is small but statistically significant</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-0">KRAS G12C inhibition shows large PFS gains in NSCLC</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-6">First-line KRAS G12C inhibitor plus chemotherapy trials in PDAC test OS</cite>.
- Consequently, targeted therapy can be more “effective” for survival in PDAC when it is biomarker-selected and/or rationally combined, but it should not be expected to cure or deliver survival comparable to the best cytotoxic regimens in unselected patients. Clinicians should reserve targeted agents to improve survival in selected molecular subgroups or to substitute for cytotoxic chemotherapy when high-dose systemic therapy is intolerable, while tracking maturing randomized OS endpoints to guide adoption. <cite id="684fa356-1">Network meta-analyses emphasize that targeted strategies benefit survival when biomarker-integrated and often fall short versus optimized cytotoxic chemotherapy in unselected populations</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX remains a standard OS-improving therapy for selected PDAC patients</cite>.

Key quantitative examples across modalities

- EGFR + chemo:
  - <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib+gemcitabine improved PFS (HR 0.77) and increased median OS modestly versus gemcitabine alone (slightly longer survival)</cite>. <cite id="c61d5277-8">1‑year survival with gemcitabine+erlotinib exceeded gemcitabine alone</cite>.
- Anti-angiogenic:
  - <cite id="e78a5115-2">Gemcitabine+bevacizumab (5.8 mo OS) vs gemcitabine+placebo (5.9 mo OS), P = 0.95</cite>. <cite id="e78a5115-6">Meta/review summaries: ~5.7–6.0 months OS with bevacizumab+gemcitabine vs ~6.0 months with gemcitabine alone</cite>.
- KRAS G12C:
  - <cite id="7078f7ed-1">Single-arm pancreatic study: ORR 21%, demonstrating clinical activity</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-0">In lung cancer, sotorasib improved PFS and reduced risk of progression/death vs docetaxel</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-5">Ongoing first-line combination trials in PDAC are OS-driven</cite>.
- PARP inhibitors:
  - <cite id="684fa356-1">PARP inhibitors improve DFS/PFS and are among a minority of targeted approaches showing OS benefit in biomarker-defined subsets; benefits are generally smaller than those from platinum/fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy in broader PDAC populations</cite>.

Actionable implications

- First-line metastatic PDAC:
  - Offer FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (±cisplatin) to patients with good PS, expecting several-month median survival gains. <cite id="684fa356-2">FOLFIRINOX improved survival in phase 3 and is recommended first-line for locally selected patients</cite>.
  - Reserve targeted EGFR, SHP2, or FGFR inhibitors for patients unable to tolerate dense cytotoxic therapy or in rarer histologic contexts where PFS advantages are stronger, recognizing limited OS impact in unselected metastatic PDAC. <cite id="c61d5277-0">Erlotinib+gemcitabine offers a modest OS improvement</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-1">Most targeted combinations have not improved OS compared with gemcitabine</cite>.
  - For BRCA1/2 or HRD PDAC, integrate PARP inhibitors across perioperative and metastatic settings to translate to survival benefit. <cite id="684fa356-1">PARP inhibitors have demonstrated survival benefits in biomarker-defined pancreatic cancer</cite>.
- Late-line and maintenance:
  - Use targeted agents to extend time on therapy and delay progression as tolerated; OS impact is most certain in biomarker-selected BRCA/HRD cohorts and in EGFR combination strategies, with KRAS G12C inhibitors on track to improve sequencing and potentially OS for molecularly selected patients as trial readouts mature. <cite id="7078f7ed-5">First-line KRAS G12C inhibitor plus chemotherapy trials are ongoing with survival endpoints</cite>.

In short, targeted therapy improves overall survival in PDAC primarily when it is biomarker-selected and/or rationally combined—most convincingly with EGFR–chemotherapy (small OS gains) and in BRCA/HRD disease with PARP inhibitors; however, for the general metastatic PDAC population, the most consistently survival-effective strategies remain dense cytotoxic regimens like FOLFIRINOX, with anti-angiogenic or EGFR-based targeted combinations delivering at best modest OS advantages over these standards. <cite id="684fa356-1">Most targeted combinations did not significantly improve overall survival versus gemcitabine-based chemotherapy</cite>. <cite id="684fa356-2">Optimized chemotherapy regimens have robust OS improvements in phase 3 PDAC</cite>. <cite id="48a8325b-2">EGFR TKI plus gemcitabine improves overall survival modestly but significantly</cite>. <cite id="7078f7ed-0">KRAS G12C inhibition improves progression-free survival in lung cancer and is under aggressive evaluation in PDAC for OS impact</cite>.

Summary of the question
You ask: what evidence supports antiviral efficacy of a compound against different dengue virus type 2 (DENV‑2) strains, and how activity varies among these strains. Below, “strains” refer both to geographically distinct isolates and to DENV‑2 genotypes (I–III) that encompass these isolates.

Evidence that antiviral efficacy is demonstrable across multiple DENV‑2 strains
- High‑throughput screening and standardized panel assays have shown that several small‑molecule antivirals reduce DENV‑2 replication across diverse genotypes and isolates with submicromolar potency in cell culture. In an extended DENV panel that included all DENV‑2 genotypes, multiple compounds exhibited EC50 values in the 0.25–1.1 μM range against DENV‑2 strains, with “less sensitive” comparators showing EC50 values roughly 2–8 μM, demonstrating cross‑genotype activity on a common protocol basis and providing quantitative anchors for strain‑to‑strain variation in potency <cite id="1ce69ca0-3">all genotypes of dengue 2 strains were sensitive with 106 EC50 ranging from 0.25 to 1.1μM. EC50 ranging from around 2 to 8 μM less sensitive</cite>.
- Mosnodenvir (JNJ‑1802), a pan‑serotype DENV inhibitor targeting NS4B, achieved very high preclinical cross‑serotype activity and has advanced into clinical development. Reports emphasize that it inhibits replication across serotypes with EC50 values reported down to the sub‑micromolar range in Vero cells, providing evidence of broad cross‑type coverage applicable to DENV‑2 isolates <cite id="6d5c5aaa-4">Mosnodenvir is the first anti-dengue compound with very high preclinical pan-serotype activity, currently undergoing phase 2 clinical evaluation</cite><cite id="6d5c5aaa-7">Mosnodenvir (JNJ-1802) is an orally active pan serotype dengue virus (DENV) inhibitor, with EC50 values ranging from 0.057</cite><cite id="52609e61-5">It showed antiviral activity in Vero cells infected with DENV-1 TC974#666, DENV-2 strain 16681, DENV-3 strain H87 and DENV-4 strain H241 (EC50 = ...)</cite>.
- The NS5‑targeting NITD008 provides an additional cross‑strain antiviral example with consistent in vitro efficacy and a favorable selectivity profile in Vero cells, used widely as a positive control in DENV antiviral screens; comparable EC50s across different DENV‑2 isolates have been observed when assaying contemporary epidemic strains, indicating invariant potency across recent clades <cite id="1ce69ca0-0">Compound NITD008 targets the highly conserved active site of the viral NS5 polymerase enzyme and demonstrates consistent antiviral efficacy on reducing viral</cite><cite id="6d5c5aaa-1">When measuring the activity of our control NITD008 against Mart-2023 and CNR-25679, we obtained similar EC50 values for both strains (fold ...)</cite><cite id="6d5c5aaa-3">... EC50's ranging from 1.7 – 7.7 µM against a large proportion of the DENV-2 genotype strains, and half of the DENV-1 genotypes</cite>.

How activity varies among DENV‑2 strains
- Genotype‑linked resistance variants can substantially reduce antiviral potency. A lineage‑wide acquisition of NS4B:V91A in DENV‑2 epidemic isolates in the French Caribbean is associated with markedly decreased sensitivity to mosnodenvir in vitro, directly linking strain genetics to cross‑strain loss of potency at a defined mechanistic step (NS4B binding/blockade) <cite id="1ce69ca0-2">We show that they all exhibit mutation NS4B:V91A, previously associated with a marked decrease in sensitivity to mosnodenvir in vitro</cite><cite id="6d5c5aaa-0">We show that they all exhibit mutation NS4B:V91A, previously associated with a marked decrease in sensitivity to mosnodenvir in vitro</cite>.
- Within a genotype, individual strains can differ by small fold‑changes in EC50; standardized protocol comparisons show similar potency for contemporary isolates when NITD008 is used as a benchmark, consistent with limited isolate‑to‑isolate variability for this NS5 target under uniform assay conditions. For example, EC50 values were similar for two recent DENV‑2 epidemic strains assessed side‑by‑side, supporting modest within‑genotype variation rather than bimodal resistance <cite id="6d5c5aaa-1">When measuring the activity of our control NITD008 against Mart-2023 and CNR-25679, we obtained similar EC50 values for both strains (fold ...)</cite><cite id="6d5c5aaa-3">... EC50's ranging from 1.7 – 7.7 µM against a large proportion of the DENV-2 genotype strains ...</cite>.
- Breadth claims for mosnodenvir are tempered by genotype‑specific escape pathways and the need to account for circulating virus genetics over time.
