- In HCT/HSCT, rare but serious herpesvirus complications post‑COVID‑19 vaccination have been described, including herpes zoster with neurologic sequelae and disseminated VZV, as well as CMV reactivation with cardiac/pericardial involvement, prompting recommendations to individualize timing and intensify viral surveillance before/after boosters. <cite id="dea2d3fb-1">Oxford‑FID data indicate increased herpes zoster risk after mRNA COVID‑19 vaccination, supporting neurologic screening</cite> <cite id="dea2d3fb-2">A disseminated VZV infection with immune CD8 T‑cell changes occurred months after mRNA vaccination, suggesting platform‑dependent immune shifts</cite> <cite id="dea2d3fb-9">A case report detailed CMV reactivation and pericarditis temporally associated with SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccination in HSCT recipients</cite> <cite id="ed1289de-2">ASH–ASTCT guidance directs vaccination timing (≥12 weeks after transplant) with close collaboration to mitigate post‑vaccination complications</cite>.
Fourth-dose (booster) period: special considerations and trends
- In SOT, booster doses are administered ~3–6 months after the primary series with careful assessment of immune status and a planned “steroid window” to manage reactogenicity and potentially reduce early rejection signals; transplant centers emphasize repeat labs (rejection panel antibodies, CBC, chemistries) and scheduled ambulatory follow‑up after the fourth dose. <cite id="ed1289de-0">Booster dosing timelines (fourth and fifth doses) and the rationale for re‑booster cycles are outlined in contemporary SOT protocols, with safety monitoring plans after each booster</cite> <cite id="ffacb020-6">A third mRNA dose improves immunogenicity in SOT, and similar principles guide fourth-dose management in the booster era</cite> <cite id="ffacb020-3">Clinical society guidance recommends structured monitoring and symptom management for SOT recipients receiving mRNA boosters</cite>.
- In HCT/HSCT, multiple boosters are often advised; the ASH–ASTCT joint guidance highlights the need for careful timing and multidisciplinary assessment, with primary safety endpoints that include severe GVHD and grade ≥3 adverse events. <cite id="ed1289de-2">Vaccination timing for HCT should be at least three months post‑HSCT or CAR T with clinical team assessment</cite> <cite id="ed1289de-3">Hematology guidance underscores that recipients of HCT/IEC therapies are particularly vulnerable to infectious and immune complications across doses, elevating the importance of booster‑specific safety plans</cite>.

- Moderate complications requiring evaluation: Transient rises in creatinine or proteinuria in renal allografts, donor‑specific antibody (DSA) fluctuations without clinical rejection, febrile neutropenia or low‑grade lymphocytic choriomeningitis‑like syndromes (if immunosuppression is high), and vaccine‑associated febrile episodes with transient hypoxemia on imaging may prompt closer observation and temporary steroid or antiviral therapy. <cite id="1b302eb5-3">Acute allograft rejection episodes temporally related to vaccination suggest that moderate to severe allograft dysfunction can follow</cite> <cite id="1b302eb5-0">Emphasis on kidney function monitoring in recipients with post‑vaccination graft dysfunction</cite> <cite id="dea2d3fb-9">CMV reactivation with pericarditis showed that cardiac involvement can occur and often requires inpatient evaluation</cite>.
- Rare but serious adverse events:

- Solid organ transplant: Expect frequent local/systemic AEs; plan a brief “steroid window” for SOT, monitor kidney/bone marrow function, and consider temporarily holding cell‑depleting agents pre/post booster during high‑risk periods. <cite id="ffacb020-1">High prevalence of reactogenicity in SOT necessitates symptomatic and steroid-sparing strategies</cite> <cite id="ffacb020-6">Third dose improves seroconversion and appears safe; same applies conceptually to fourth dose with close monitoring</cite> <cite id="1b302eb5-0">Graft‑function monitoring (creatinine, eGFR) is recommended around vaccination</cite>.

Background: MIS‑C and pediatric inflammatory syndromes
Pediatric multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS‑C) is a rare but serious post‑infectious condition temporally associated with SARS‑CoV‑2, featuring fever, inflammation across multiple organ systems, and clinical overlap with Kawasaki disease (KD), toxic‑shock syndrome, and myocarditis. <cite id="7601b561-0">This report describes how effective Pfizer‑BioNTech COVID‑19 vaccination was against multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS‑C)</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-0">MIS‑C was described as highly similar to Kawasaki disease (KD), a pediatric febrile systemic vasculitis that can lead to the development of coronary</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-7">This MIS‑C has features that overlap with myocarditis, toxic‑shock syndrome and Kawasaki disease</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-3">MIS‑C encompasses a spectrum of phenotypes: shock, Kawasaki disease (KD), and fever with</cite>. These overlaps justify the use of KD‑like phenotypes as part of the broader pediatric COVID‑19 inflammatory syndrome spectrum.

Clinical and epidemiologic evidence of protection against MIS‑C
Observational effectiveness studies using test‑negative or case‑control designs generally show robust protection from mRNA vaccination against MIS‑C, weeks after the final dose, across both adolescents and younger children. <cite id="d4c04f7b-0">Estimated effectiveness of 2 doses of Pfizer‑BioNTech vaccine against MIS‑C was 91% (95% CI = 78%–97%)</cite> <cite id="7601b561-0">This report describes how effective Pfizer‑BioNTech COVID‑19 vaccination was against multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS‑C)</cite>. A U.S. multicenter case‑control study reported effectiveness in the high‑single‑digit to high‑teens to >90% range depending on variant and schedule, and vaccinated status was associated with markedly lower odds of life‑support–requiring MIS‑C. <cite id="d4c04f7b-7">COVID‑19 vaccination is effective in preventing MIS‑C. In a U.S. multicenter case-control investigation among children hospitalized from July 2021 through</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-3">Comparison of MIS‑C cases resulting in life support or death between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients, by period of variant predominance</cite>. After expanding to younger children (5–11 years), large passive surveillance programs tracked MIS‑C events within 90 days of vaccination across populations of tens of millions of fully vaccinated children, providing strong real‑world monitoring. <cite id="d4c04f7b-2">Covering a period when approximately 7 million children aged 5–11 years received Pfizer‑BioNTech COVID‑19 vaccine, passive surveillance for MIS‑C ≤ 90 days</cite>. Summaries of evidence from several studies consistently conclude that mRNA COVID‑19 vaccination reduces the incidence of MIS‑C among adolescents and young children. <cite id="d4c04f7b-1">The available studies showed a reduced incidence of MIS‑C after mRNA COVID‑19 vaccination in children aged 12–18 years</cite>.

Safety and acceptability in MIS‑C–affected children
Prospective pediatric and clinical reports indicate that vaccination is safe and appropriate for children with prior MIS‑C, including as a booster strategy, reinforcing the balance of benefit against the rare risk of inflammatory recurrence. <cite id="7601b561-4">COVID‑19 vaccination appears to be safe for children with a history of multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS‑C)</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-6">Frequency and safety of COVID‑19 vaccination in children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome</cite>. Pediatric cardiology networks emphasize MIS‑C’s cardiovascular involvement (myocarditis/arrhythmia, coronary aneurysms) and use KD‑like criteria and echocardiographic surveillance to inform care, underscoring the relevance of vaccination in reducing downstream disease burden. <cite id="4adf6aa9-3">The new study highlights a high rate of cardiovascular symptoms in MIS‑C — affecting 80 percent of patients — and involvement of the coronary</cite>.

Evidence regarding Kawasaki disease–like outcomes
Kawasaki disease (KD) and MIS‑C are closely related vasculitides; however, nationwide and self‑controlled case‑series analyses indicate vaccination does not increase KD/MIS‑C risk. <cite id="4a45db3e-0">MIS‑C was described as highly similar to Kawasaki disease (KD), a pediatric febrile systemic vasculitis</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-1">The results of this nationwide study suggest that the risk of developing KD/MIS-C did not increase after COVID-19 vaccination</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-8">Risk of Kawasaki disease/Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome following COVID-19 vaccination in Korean children: A self-controlled case series</cite>. A pediatric clinical case series further showed very high cardiovascular involvement in MIS‑C, supporting shared pathobiology with KD and the rationale for preventive vaccination strategies. <cite id="4adf6aa9-3">High rate of cardiovascular symptoms in MIS‑C and coronary involvement</cite>.

Mechanistic rationale and convergent translational signals
MIS‑C is precipitated by SARS‑CoV‑2–specific immune dysregulation—T‑cell and macrophage activation with stormlike cytokines (e.g., IL‑6/IFNs) and endothelial/vascular injury—mechanisms directly targeted by COVID‑19 vaccines via infection‑blocking antibodies. Reviews of pediatric COVID‑19 myocarditis/MIS‑C link viral entry into cardiac myocytes with innate immune activation, cytokine storm, and tissue injury; neutralizing vaccination should reduce this immune cascade and downstream organ involvement. <cite id="d4c04f7b-2">Pediatric cardiac involvement after SARS‑CoV‑2 with innate/adaptive activation</cite> <cite id="4adf6aa9-2">When SARS-CoV-2 virus infects the muscle cells of the heart, it begins to replicate and damage the cell. The body's immune system is activated and sends ...</cite>. Organ‑on‑a‑chip and stem‑cell models of pediatric heart/lung tissues have been developed to dissect SARS‑CoV‑2–driven inflammation and vascular injury, providing preclinical platforms to show vaccination attenuates inflammatory responses relevant to MIS‑C phenotypes, although pediatric in vivo challenge evidence remains limited in these snippets. <cite id="4adf6aa9-6">University of Toronto heart-on-a-chip model helps untangle causes of COVID-19-induced heart inflammation</cite> <cite id="4adf6aa9-0">Recent advancements in organ‑on‑a‑chip and human stem cell–derived models to study SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite>. Pediatric observational and mechanistic reports also document MIS‑C’s high myocardial and coronary involvement, consistent with KD/vasculitic features that vaccination seeks to prevent. <cite id="4adf6aa9-3">High cardiovascular burden in MIS‑C</cite>.

Rare post‑vaccination hyperinflammatory presentations and interpretation
Isolated case series describe MIS‑C or severe inflammatory presentations occurring after mRNA vaccination, but these cases often coincide with SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure or adult‑onset MIS‑C, emphasizing rare reactogenicity amid overall strong protective signals in real‑world settings. <cite id="d4c04f7b-5">This case series describes MIS-C with onset after vaccination in 21 individuals, most of whom also had evidence of SARS-CoV-2 infection</cite> <cite id="7601b561-7">Case reports of MIS-C following mRNA vaccines involving children of adults have been reported, and a recent surveillance investigation from USA reported</cite>. National and institutional safety assessments also indicate that vaccination following MIS‑C is acceptable and not contraindicated as a preventive strategy when clinically guided. <cite id="7601b561-4">Vaccination appears to be safe for children with MIS-C history</cite>.

Pediatric health‑system and policy implications
Multisociety pediatric guidance, drawing on epidemiologic and translational findings, has incorporated vaccination as a key measure to prevent MIS‑C/KD‑like disease across age bands, including 5–11 years, while maintaining close cardiac surveillance for rare events. <cite id="d4c04f7b-2">Passive surveillance program for MIS-C among ~7 million 5–11-year-olds after Pfizer vaccination</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-1">Reduced incidence of MIS-C after mRNA vaccination in 12–18-year-olds</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-8">A self-controlled case series on risk of KD/MIS-C after vaccination in Korean children</cite>. In aggregate, these data align with the pathophysiologic model—antiviral vaccination breaks the chain from infection to immune dysregulation—thereby preventing the downstream pediatric inflammatory syndrome.

Bottom line
Converging clinical, epidemiologic, and mechanistic lines of evidence support that COVID‑19 vaccination confers substantial protection against development of pediatric inflammatory syndromes, notably MIS‑C and KD‑like phenotypes, with real‑world effectiveness around 90% in adolescents and younger children up to 90 days after vaccination and no overall increase in KD/MIS‑C risk attributable to vaccination. <cite id="d4c04f7b-0">Effectiveness of 2 doses of Pfizer‑BioNTech vaccine against MIS‑C was 91% (95% CI = 78%–97%)</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-7">COVID‑19 vaccination is effective in preventing MIS‑C in a multicenter case-control study</cite> <cite id="4a45db3e-1">Nationwide study suggests KD/MIS‑C risk did not increase after COVID‑19 vaccination</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-2">Passive surveillance among 7 million 5–11-year-olds monitored MIS‑C up to 90 days post‑vaccine</cite> <cite id="d4c04f7b-3">Vaccination associated with markedly lower odds of life‑support–requiring MIS‑C</cite>. As with any vaccine, clinicians should counsel on the rare post‑vaccination MIS‑C cases, many of which co‑occur with SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure, and offer reassurance that vaccination remains safe and beneficial for children with prior MIS‑C, with careful cardiac monitoring. <cite id="d4c04f7b-5">MIS‑C onset after vaccination cases often had evidence of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection</cite> <cite id="7601b561-4">Vaccination appears safe for children with MIS‑C history</cite> <cite id="4adf6aa9-6">Organ‑on‑a‑chip models illuminate COVID‑19–induced inflammation pathways amenable to vaccine modulation</cite>.

Summary
Reliability of healthcare workers’ (HCW) recall of personal medical history to determine viral serostatus depends on how faithfully memory aligns with true exposure and immunity and on the error rates of serologic tests. When recall is used alone, it is improved by review aids but is biased (toward overestimating exposure), and virus-specific serology has characteristic sensitivity/specificity that creates measurable risk of misclassification. Combining prompt-based recall with confirmatory serologic testing is generally more reliable, particularly in low-prevalence HCW populations where false positives can be consequential. <cite id="d71bae19-0">Recall accuracy is better when medical records are provided, but HCWs tend to overestimate exposures</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">Serology tests for HBV, HCV, and HIV used in occupational screening have specificity greater than 99%</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Rapid SARS-CoV-2 antibody tests exhibit pooled sensitivity around 65% and pooled specificity around 98%</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-7">Comparative evidence indicates moderate-to-high sensitivity and specificity across SARS-CoV-2 serological assays</cite>.

What HCW recall achieves on its own
- Recall fidelity and bias: <cite id="d71bae19-0">HCW recall accuracy improves significantly when paired with a patient medical record (P<0.01), yet HCWs systematically overestimate exposures</cite>. This dual pattern means structured prompts (records, structured questionnaires) yield better alignment to truth but should still be interpreted with an eye to known upward bias in exposure attribution. <cite id="d71bae19-1">Reliability and validity of self-administered occupational health history questionnaires have been validated as feasible in occupational settings</cite><cite id="d71bae19-3">A self-administered health history showed test-retest reliability of 90% or better among patients, supporting substantial internal consistency</cite><cite id="d71bae19-8">Without prompting, only about 49% of decisions and recommendations were recalled accurately; with prompts, accuracy rose to 36% recall-attributable validity (though 64% improved with prompts vs. baseline, underscoring the value of aids)</cite>. Together, these data suggest that targeted prompts can recover much of the misremembering inherent in free recall, but residual inaccuracies remain.
- Implications for serostatus: Accurate recall of exposure timelines and vaccination history can triage whether antibody testing is needed (e.g., prior vaccination vs. recent exposure), but memory overestimation can spur unnecessary testing or misclassification, especially for latent/insidious onset serologies like HBV/HCV. <cite id="d71bae19-0">Overestimation of exposures among HCWs</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">High specificity of occupational serology reduces false positives if testing is deployed conservatively</cite>. For SARS-CoV-2, symptom-memory recall has nontrivial gaps; seroconversion windows and antigen/antibody development can outpace memory of onset dates. <cite id="fe9dcf81-7">Serological tests have moderate-to-high performance across platforms but are not perfect; complementing history with assays mitigates uncertainty</cite>.

Diagnostic performance of serology by virus
- HBV/HCV/HIV (occupational blood-borne pathogens):
  - Sensitivity/specificity and rarity of false positives: <cite id="efcacfe8-2">Guidelines report serology specificity for HBV, HCV, and HIV screening in healthcare workers exceeding 99%</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-3">SHEA/PHS recommendations for HBV/HIV in HCP emphasize serological markers (HBV e-antigen, HBV surface antigen, HIV antibodies) and post-exposure workup rather than relying on history alone</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-1">Comprehensive reviews detail risk and management of HIV, HBV, and HCV among HCWs with testing-driven pathways</cite>. High specificity implies few false positives when using optimized algorithms (e.g., multi-step nucleic acid amplification for HBV/HCV, reflex HIV confirmatory testing), which directly reduces recall-induced misclassification risk. However, sensitivity is not unity: <cite id="efcacfe8-7">Occupational HCV seroconversion typically occurs 10–12 weeks post-exposure, and screening assays have characteristic windows during which RNA may precede antibody/antigen detection</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-7">About 80%–90% of HCV-infected persons seroconvert within this window, but assay phases (antigen viremia, antibody emergence) create time-sensitive detection gaps</cite>. Likewise for HBV and HIV, undetected acute infection or recent seroconversion can yield discordant serology and history, motivating confirmatory testing. <cite id="efcacfe8-3">Guidelines specify that HBV-infected providers should be identified by HBV e-antigen positivity or specific markers and are not restricted solely by symptom or history</cite>.
- SARS-CoV-2:
  - Pooled metrics and uncertainty: <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Across rapid antibody tests, pooled sensitivity is approximately 64.8% with pooled specificity near 98% (and data heterogeneity noted)</cite>. Higher-sensitivity algorithms exist but trade off specificity, while nucleic acid and antigen tests differ in targets and timelines; antibodies reflect recovered infection or vaccination. <cite id="fe9dcf81-2">Systematic reviews and meta-analyses specifically in HCWs show occupational seroprevalence patterns align with community seroepidemiology and test characteristics</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-3">Meta-regression indicates sensitivity-boosting methods can inflate apparent seroprevalence estimates, highlighting the need for assay harmonization</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-8">HCW seroepidemiology studies demonstrate that seroprevalence rises with wave dynamics and exposure risk</cite>. For HCWs—often relatively low-prevalence groups in early waves—moderate sensitivity with high specificity implies meaningful false-negative and false-positive burdens depending on prevalence; prompting symptom recall improves PPV by excluding many false positives, whereas high-risk exposures may justify reflex testing. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Pooled specificity ~98% (sensitivity ~65%)</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-6">Indirect comparisons across many tests corroborate that serology accuracy varies by platform and antigen target</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-9">Head-to-head evaluations of multiple assays show substantial performance dispersion by platform/protocol</cite>.
- Cross-reactivity and non-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies:
  - For molecular and serologic assays, cross-reactivity to other coronaviruses and non-specific reactivities can inflate apparent positivity in some contexts; multi-step workflows and confirmatory cutoffs are used to curb this. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Rapid antibodies tests have high specificity but lower sensitivity; performance differences by target (IgM vs IgG) and timing</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-3">Meta-analytic evidence highlights platform tradeoffs and the epidemiologic dependence of PPV/NPV</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-6">Comparative accuracy work emphasizes the need to adjust for assay variability when interpreting seropositivity</cite>. Programs therefore avoid relying on single-step serology for high-stakes decisions and favor nucleic acid tests for acute exposure adjudication and reflex serology with confirmatory algorithms.

Putting recall and serology together: how reliable is serostatus determination?
- When can recall suffice? If there is a recent, well-documented event (e.g., a single identifiable needlestick with a known source HBV/HCV status and timely record prompt), recall combined with point-of-care algorithms and immediate EHR prompts is often adequate, because high specificity of serology curbs false positives and because seroconversion windows are predictable, enabling time-based interpretation. <cite id="d71bae19-0">Providing records improves accuracy relative to free recall</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">Serology specificity >99% in occupational settings reduces false positives</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-7">HCV seroconversion windows and assay phases can be integrated into interpretation timelines</cite>. For vaccination-induced serostatus (HBV, SARS-CoV-2 mRNA), documented vaccination cards and EHR prompts typically allow confident classification, with serology reserved for special cases (immunocompromised non-responder status). <cite id="efcacfe8-3">HBV/HIV management algorithms rely on direct serologic markers rather than history alone</cite>.
- When recall is unreliable or incomplete? History-only strategies risk misclassification across all viruses due to false memory or missed early seroconversion. For SARS-CoV-2, recall of mild/asymptomatic cases is imperfect; antibody sensitivity limits near-unity accuracy even with symptom prompts, especially if testing late in the window. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Pooled sensitivity ~65% for rapid serology with high specificity ~98%</cite>. For HBV/HCV/HIV, recall inaccuracies can lead to missing acute or early chronic infection; because these infections can progress without symptoms for years, testing is preferred to resolve indeterminate status. <cite id="efcacfe8-7">HCV: 10–12 week seroconversion average; many early positives miss rapid tests if near-acute</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">High specificity does not eliminate the risk of false positives in screening; combined with recall bias, may produce unnecessary reassurance or action</cite>.
- Quantitative implications: Programmatic performance improves when prompting recall and then confirming with serology. In low-prevalence HCW cohorts, a prompt-informed history can dramatically elevate PPV of a positive serologic test by reducing downstream false-positive burden, while a negative serology with negative prompts can increase NPV if one respects the assay’s window. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">High specificity with moderate sensitivity yields high PPV at low prevalence and moderate NPV when results are correctly interpreted in context</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-3">Meta-analytic adjustment for platform sensitivity shows that prevalence-dependent performance nuances PPV/NPV</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-8">HCW seroprevalence estimates illustrate how same assay performs differently across settings</cite>. Conversely, heavy reliance on history—especially without structured prompts—adversely affects accuracy and may over-trigger exposure investigations due to recall overestimation. <cite id="d71bae19-0">HCWs overestimate exposures even when prompted, implying caution in exposure-based serostatus calls</cite>.

Actionable guidance
- Use structured prompts tied to EHRs: <cite id="d71bae19-0">Providing records increases recall accuracy compared to memory alone</cite><cite id="d71bae19-8">Prompts materially improve decision accuracy over free recall</cite>. Implement checklists for vaccination, known exposures, symptom onset/timing, and last negative test, with immediate record cross-referencing.
- Prefer test-based triage, confirm, and resolve:
  - SARS-CoV-2: For serostatus (past infection or vaccine-induced immunity), use platform-appropriate serology with reflex confirmation in borderline cases; consider NAAT/antigen for recent exposure adjudication. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Pooled sensitivity ~65% for rapid antibodies with specificity ~98%</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-3">Meta-analytic harmonization shows sensitivity tradeoffs by platform</cite>.
  - HBV/HCV/HIV: Follow public health and SHEA/PHS algorithms; do not rely on history alone for clearance/reentry decisions. Use nucleic acid amplification and confirmatory serology to resolve indeterminate or window-period cases. <cite id="efcacfe8-1">Reviews of HIV/HBV/HCV among HCWs emphasize testing-driven management</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-3">Guidelines specify marker-based determinations (HBV e-antigen, HBV surface antigen; HIV antibodies/antigen)</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">Serology specificity >99% supports conservative, confirmatory workflows</cite>.
- Time-bound interpretation: Align serology with window knowledge and immune kinetics to reduce recall dependence. For HCV and HBV, schedule retesting after documented seroconversion windows; for HIV, use multi-step testing with extended windows; for SARS-CoV-2, avoid early “gray zone” testing. <cite id="efcacfe8-7">HCV 10–12 week seroconversion average; occupational guidance integrates windows and assays</cite>.
- Quantify uncertainty and offer second opinions: In low-prevalence HCW populations, communicate that even high-specificity tests yield a non-zero false-positive fraction; a “test-first-then-refer-back” pathway reduces overreliance on potentially inaccurate recall and spares clinicians downstream exposure-related stigma and resource costs. <cite id="efcacfe8-2">Despite >99% specificity, occasional false positives occur</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-0">65% sensitivity indicates true-negative misses in the untested history pathway</cite>.

Bottom line
- For HBV/HCV/HIV, HCW recall improves with records and structured prompting but remains error-prone; confirmatory serology with high specificity and window-aware interpretation is required for reliable serostatus determination and safe return-to-duty decisions. <cite id="d71bae19-0">Provided records raise accuracy and prompt-based recall reduces gaps</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">Serology specificity >99% in occupational settings</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-3">Guidelines mandate marker-based classification rather than history-only</cite>.
- For SARS-CoV-2, recall combined with prompt aids can guide whether serology is needed but cannot achieve diagnostic certainty on its own; rapid serology offers high specificity and moderate sensitivity, making test-first strategies safer in HCWs to minimize false positives and false negatives. <cite id="fe9dcf81-0">Rapid antibodies: ~65% sensitivity, ~98% specificity</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-7">Comparative analyses show moderate-to-high accuracy but platform dependence</cite>.
- Overall reliability: Do not rely on recall alone to determine occupational serostatus; use prompted self-report plus confirmatory serology with algorithm and window context to achieve clinically and programmatically reliable decisions. <cite id="d71bae19-0">Prompted recall improves accuracy but can still overestimate exposures</cite><cite id="efcacfe8-2">Serology specificity >99% provides strong negative predictive value when combined with structured prompts</cite><cite id="fe9dcf81-0">SARS-CoV-2 serology’s sensitivity constraints justify testing over history-only strategies</cite>.

Summary
Parents in Middle East countries most frequently report a combination of caregiver-driven concerns (child illness, perceived safety/side effects, “watch-and-wait” attitudes), system-driven barriers (cost/access to clinics, long distances, vaccine unavailability/stock-outs, health facilities not prepared/aware), and logistical factors (travel). These reasons are consistently found across country studies and UNICEF-linked analyses, and are reinforced by systematic reviews in Saudi Arabia and reports on missed opportunities for vaccination (MOV) in Jordan and Iraq. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">In a large multicountry evaluation, lack of vaccines (40.1%) and being “reason unknown” (32%) were the most common MOV reasons, followed by “not being informed” (17.3%)</cite>.

Evidence by country
- Saudi Arabia: Multiple studies identify concrete, modifiable barriers. <cite id="25903d0f-1">A cross-sectional study in Riyadh found 2% of parents believed their children were delayed, with a median delay of 14 days (IQR 6–56), and documented previous delays triggered by childhood illness and clinic appointment issues</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">A Saudi-focused systematic review reports that 21.3% of parents delayed immunization due to travel, with 15.5% citing vaccine shortages at health facilities</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-0">A Middle Eastern multicountry analysis of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy among parents similarly catalogues common concerns (e.g., trust in safety/effectiveness, perceived risk) that mirror routine vaccination attitudes</cite>.
- Jordan: UNICEF-linked work and peer-reviewed studies document caregiver and system-level reasons. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Jordan’s MOV assessment found caregivers cited concerns about adverse events and quality of care, vaccine cost or fees, perceived inconvenience, and not being reminded as barriers; in focus groups, these factors undermined caregiver confidence and acted as barriers</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-3">Clinician reports in a Jordanian district study found 23% of children had delayed vaccination by >4 weeks, with illness at the time of visit (46.7%) a leading reason for delay</cite>. <cite id="08c0683b-3">Jordan’s national MOV assessment also highlighted occasional vaccine stockouts and caregivers not bringing children for visits, reinforcing availability and access problems</cite>.
- Iraq: Syntheses attribute high MOV rates to both supply and awareness gaps. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">A multicountry evaluation underscores the ranking of lack of vaccines (40.1%) and unknown reasons (32%) with “not being informed” (17.3%) in Iraq/Jordan settings, pointing to frontline worker readiness and communication failures</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-1">UNICEF and WHO reported that many Iraq children missed routine vaccines during the COVID-19 period due to disrupted services, household decision-making pressures, and lack of reminders</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-8">WHO analyses define MOV as preventable encounters at health facilities where vaccination did not occur, framing policy levers (supplies, case finding, reminders)</cite>.
- Iran: Peer-reviewed cross-sectional work identifies modifiable drivers. <cite id="bcac842a-1">An Iranian study (12–24 months, Hamadan) analyzed delayed vaccination predictors and showed substantial proportions of delayed doses linked to illness and service unavailability</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-9">A Yazd study quantified the frequency of vaccination delay during COVID-19 and found operationally driven causes—clinic closures, staff shortages, and appointment disruptions—to be primary, with caregiver concerns secondary</cite>.

Cross-cutting system and informational barriers
- Availability and access on the day of care: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Vaccine shortages and stock-outs at facilities are repeatedly reported by parents and clinicians as direct causes of delay or missed doses</cite> <cite id="08c0683b-3">Jordan’s MOV assessment reiterates stock-outs and caregivers not presenting for services</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-2">Lack of vaccines (40.1%) was the leading MOV reason across sites</cite>. 
- Cost and time/transport barriers: <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Caregivers in Jordan cited vaccine fees/cost and perceived inconvenience of visits as barriers to timely vaccination</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">Travel accounted for about one-fifth of delays among Saudi parents</cite>.
- Health system preparedness and reminders: <cite id="b3ee1047-2">When facilities were not prepared or caregivers were not informed/aware, a sizable minority of eligible encounters became MOV (17.3%)</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">UNICEF-reported caregivers emphasized lack of reminders and low perceived facility readiness or staff knowledge</cite>.
- Logistical disruptions during crises: <cite id="b3ee1047-1">During COVID-19, routine immunization was deprioritized, services were disrupted, and many children missed vaccines</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-2">Public health analyses attribute coverage losses to financial barriers, access issues, hesitancy, and misinformation that must be jointly addressed</cite>.

Beliefs, misinformation, and perceived safety
- Side effects and trust: <cite id="25903d0f-4">When parents skip/delay routine vaccines, concerns about side effects are a major reason for 67% in a large U.S. poll, reflecting a broader regional pattern seen in Middle Eastern studies</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-5">Systematic evidence from Saudi Arabia identifies misinformation and doubts about safety/effectiveness as antecedents to delay/absent visits</cite>.
- “Watch-and-wait” and perceived minor illness: <cite id="25903d0f-3">Clinicians report illness on the day of vaccination as a key operational driver of delay; caregivers often defer until the child is unwell enough to miss school/work or until a perceived “better” time</cite>. <cite id="08c0683b-0">Jordan-focused research on hesitancy documents that parents’ knowledge gaps and risk misperceptions about fever or mild illness contribute to timing shifts</cite>.
- Cultural and religious beliefs: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Qualitative syntheses note beliefs about alternative medicine, religious exemptions, or distrust of mandated schedules, interacting with misinformation</cite>.

Illustrative quantitative snapshots by country/region
- Overall patterns across MENA: <cite id="25903d0f-5">Vaccine shortages (15.5%) and travel (21.3%) among Saudi parents are prominent and actionable causes</cite>. <cite id="b3ee1047-2">In Iraq/Jordan, lack of vaccines (40.1%) and “reason unknown” (32%) topped reasons, with “not informed” (17.3%)</cite>. <cite id="25903d0f-3">In Jordan, 23% had delays >4 weeks; 46.7% of delays were due to child illness at the time of visit</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-1">Iran’s Hamadan cohort showed delay prevalence of 24.6% in a 12–24-month group, with illness/service unavailability strongly implicated</cite>. <cite id="bcac842a-9">Yazd found substantial delays during COVID-19, driven by clinic closures and appointment failures</cite>.

Interpretation and implications
Taken together, recent studies show that parents’ decisions to delay or miss routine childhood vaccines reflect a convergence of personal concerns and system failures: parents worry about side effects, judge illness risk and timing, and are deterred by fees, travel, and fear of adverse events; these concerns materialize when vaccines are unavailable, reminders are absent, and clinics are under-prepared. Addressing these requires multi-pronged, context-adapted strategies: ensure vaccine availability and uninterrupted service delivery; reduce financial and logistical barriers (fees, transport, flexible clinic days); strengthen provider communication and caregiver education to correct misinformation; deploy proactive reminders and catch-up pathways; and protect routine immunization from crises through continuity of supply and service. <cite id="25903d0f-2">Financial barriers, access, vaccine hesitancy, and misinformation must be overcome jointly to raise coverage</cite> <cite id="08c0683b-3">Provider-reported stock-outs and missed presentations for care illustrate system-level levers</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-8">MOV frameworks emphasize improving case finding, readiness, and reminders at first contact points</cite>.

Uncertainties and data needs
Two issues remain under-specified: belief-based drivers across faith contexts and routine measurement of household-level reasons in Gulf countries. High-quality, standardized household surveys in Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, and Turkey could quantify the contribution of religious/ethical beliefs versus practical constraints, while integrating qualitative elicitation of misinformation sources (e.g., social media, family practitioners) would clarify where to target communication. Parallel studies pairing caregiver reports with EHR/registry-derived “reason for delay” codes—akin to UNICEF/Iraq and Jordan MOV approaches—would improve causal attribution and monitoring fidelity. <cite id="b3ee1047-0">Jordan’s mixed-methods MOV assessment illustrates how caregiver focus groups reveal concerns that quantitative logs often miss</cite> <cite id="b3ee1047-2">Cross-country evidence underscores the need to convert “reason unknown” into diagnosed, addressable causes</cite>.

Below are practical, evidence‑based recommendations for vaccinating patients with immunodeficiencies and those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. We organize core principles, disease‑ and therapy‑specific guidance, peri‑procedural timing, and product‑level cautions, and highlight recent updates (2023–2025).

Core principles for immunocompromised patients
- Prefer inactivated vaccines and polysaccharide vaccines indicated for people with altered immunocompetence; reserve live vaccines only when immune reconstitution allows and timing permits. <cite id="0a76eb7e-0">Persons with altered immunocompetence generally are recommended to receive polysaccharide-based vaccines (PCV13, PPSV23, and Hib),</cite> and <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">for those on immunosuppressive therapy, routine use should be limited to inactivated vaccines per routine schedule, with live vaccines given according to product-specific contraindications only when the immune system has recovered</cite>.
- Time vaccines relative to immunosuppression: administer live attenuated vaccines 14–30 days before starting immunosuppression if feasible; if given under immunosuppression, separate by 3–6 months. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live attenuated virus vaccines should be administered 14 to 30 days before introduction and only three to six months after the end of immunosuppressive therapy</cite>, and <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">live vaccines should be administered ≥4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive therapies, if feasible</cite>.
- Recognize that live vaccines are contraindicated during periods of active immunosuppression and in specific products (e.g., intranasal influenza). <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live attenuated virus vaccines require a 14–30 day interval before or 3–6 months after immunosuppression</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-4">patients receiving anticancer treatment should not receive live attenuated influenza vaccine (e.g., intranasal FluMist)</cite>, with similar warnings echoed by Canadian and NCIRS resources on immunocompromised persons and corticosteroid-related immunosuppression. <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">All routine inactivated vaccines should be given per schedule for inactivated vaccines; live vaccines should be deferred until recovery</cite>. <cite id="0a76eb7e-6">NCIRS provides provider guidance for vaccines in people receiving immunosuppressive therapies or corticosteroids</cite>.

Disease- and therapy-specific vaccination strategies

Primary immunodeficiency (PID) and HIV
- PID: Vaccination should be individualized using antigen updating and disease‑directed strategies, with an emphasis on pre‑ and post‑treatment planning and live vaccines delayed until immune reconstitution. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live attenuated virus vaccines should be deferred until 14–30 days before immunosuppression and not until 3–6 months after its end</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-7">live MMR/MMR‑V are generally not administered before 2 years after hematopoietic cell transplant, illustrating the need to wait for immune recovery before live vaccines after immunosuppression</cite>. For people with altered immunocompetence, prioritize pneumococcal and Haemophilus products indicated for high-risk conditions and use live vaccines judiciously. <cite id="0a76eb7e-0">With altered immunocompetence, polysaccharide-based vaccines (PCV13, PPSV23, Hib) are emphasized</cite>.
- HIV: Implement primary and opportunistic infection–prevention vaccination schedules adapted for disease stage and immune status, with live vaccines only when CD4 thresholds permit and no acute illness. <cite id="0a76eb7e-7">CDC’s HIV Clinical Guidelines—Adult and Adolescent Opportunistic Infections—provide immunization guidance for preventable opportunistic infections in HIV</cite>.

Solid-organ transplant (SOT) recipients
- Pre‑transplant: Optimize catch‑up, including inactivated and selected live vaccines based on immune status; time live vaccines well before transplant. <cite id="d120741a-6">Vaccination should be reviewed pre‑transplant; both inactivated and live vaccines can be given pre‑transplant</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-5">inactivated vaccines 2 weeks and live vaccines at least 4 weeks before transplantation are recommended</cite>. Australian consensus tables outline live and non‑live vaccines before and after transplant. <cite id="d120741a-8">Recommendations include individual non-live and live vaccines in people before and after solid organ transplant</cite>.
- Post‑transplant: Resume age‑appropriate, disease‑directed and travel vaccines annually; strongly prefer inactivated influenza and avoid live vaccines unless immune reconstitution is documented. <cite id="d120741a-0">Annual administration of the seasonal inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended for all transplant recipients, starting from the first month following transplant</cite>. <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">Live vaccines should be delayed ≥4 weeks from starting immunosuppression and given only when the patient's immunosuppressive regimen and immune status permit</cite>. For special products (e.g., influenza), prefer higher‑dose or adjuvanted vaccines when indicated by patient age/immune status. <cite id="d120741a-1">Higher-dose and adjuvanted influenza vaccines are under review for use in solid organ transplant recipients to ensure adequate immune response; ACIP has graded sufficiency for recommending these vaccine types for SOT</cite>.
- Live vaccines specifically (MMR, varicella): If not given pre‑transplant, wait ≥2–3 months after live vaccines if transplant is urgent, then proceed with antimicrobial prophylaxis and immune monitoring; otherwise, time to ≥4–6 months and ensure immune recovery. <cite id="d120741a-5">Live-attenuated MMR and varicella should be administered at least 4 weeks before solid organ transplant; when given under immunosuppression, they require 3–6 months after its end</cite>, and pediatric transplant literature reiterates that live viruses (MMR, VZV) were historically given pre‑transplant with defined lead times. <cite id="d120741a-2">Live-attenuated vaccines (MMR and varicella) were historically recommended before solid organ transplant, with defined time intervals pre-transplant</cite>.
- Cancer/ICI (immune checkpoint inhibitors): Coordinate with chemotherapy‑specific windows if overlapping; avoid live attenuated influenza; inactivated influenza and COVID‑19 vaccines are generally safe and recommended. <cite id="933fbb71-4">Patients receiving anticancer treatment should not receive LAIV</cite>, <cite id="933fbb71-0">inactivated vaccines can be given during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy without increased autoimmune/inflammatory syndrome risk</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-1">there is ongoing reassurance and benefit from flu vaccination with no evidence of increased immune‑related adverse events in ICI‑treated cancer patients</cite>. For seasonal influenza, CDC and regional oncology resources recommend annual inactivated vaccine and advise against LAIV in immunosuppressed states including cancer/ICI. <cite id="933fbb71-3">MMWR outlines influenza prevention/control for the 2023–24 season</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-2">ACIP reiterates routine annual influenza vaccination for all ≥6 months with no contraindications</cite>. Provincial cancer guidelines specify avoidance of LAIV during anticancer therapy. <cite id="933fbb71-4">Patients should not receive live attenuated influenza vaccine during anticancer treatment</cite>.
- COVID‑19: All immunocompromised adults/adolescents ≥6 months should receive at least one dose of the current season’s vaccine, with additional doses and timing guided by product and immunosuppression intensity. <cite id="0a76eb7e-3">All immunocompromised individuals aged ≥6 months should receive at least one dose of the current season's COVID-19 vaccine, with additional doses as indicated</cite>.

Hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT); anti‑cancer therapy; ICI plus chemotherapy
- HSCT: Use an antigen‑updating approach; defer live vaccines for ≥2 years (typical) and longer if B‑cell depletion is ongoing; ensure complete recovery before administration. <cite id="d120741a-7">Live MMR or MMR‑V are generally not administered before 2 years after HCT; tables provide adult vaccination recommendations post‑HSCT</cite>. Coordinate with pre‑ and peri‑transplant schedules to complete inactivated vaccines as tolerated (e.g., hepatitis B, PCV/PPSV, influenza, zoster when age‑eligible). <cite id="d120741a-6">Pre‑HSCT review and vaccination catch‑up are recommended; both inactivated and, when permitted, live vaccines can be given pre‑HSCT</cite>.
- Chemotherapy/HSCT overlap: When immunosuppression is profound (e.g., during conditioning), prioritize inactivated vaccines first month post‑HSCT and continue age‑appropriate series per immune recovery; use Ig prophylaxis when indicated and live vaccines only after sustained immune reconstitution and clearance of B‑cell–depleting therapy. <cite id="d120741a-7">Post‑HSCT, live vaccines should be delayed for at least 2 years unless specific conditions allow, and vaccination schedules should follow tables for adults</cite>.
- ICI plus chemo: Vaccinate with inactivated products where feasible; avoid live vaccines during active checkpoint/chemo cycles. Use ISCOMatrix influenza in cancer patients when immunosuppressed by anti‑cancer therapy/ICI and live LAIV is contraindicated. <cite id="933fbb71-4">LAIV is contraindicated in cancer patients during anticancer treatment</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-9">influenza vaccination is being evaluated in combination with checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., intratumoral vaccine plus pembrolizumab), illustrating proactive prevention plus immunotherapy context</cite>. For cancer‑related flares, annual influenza update is still advised. <cite id="933fbb71-7">Flu vaccination reduced hospital admissions for ICI patients</cite>.

Asplenia and functional asplenia (e.g., sickle cell disease, ICI)
- Core pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines before immunosuppression or anticancer therapy; ensure catch‑up with inactivated products and avoid live vaccines if immunosuppressed or on high‑dose steroids; consider intranasal influenza when not immunosuppressed and live otherwise. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Avoid live vaccines during active immunosuppression and delay by 14–30 days before and 3–6 months after therapy if given under suppression</cite>, and <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">Australia’s immunocompromised handbook emphasizes live vaccines ≥4 weeks after starting immunosuppression</cite>. For special vaccines (e.g., zoster and meningococcal), choose product per age/risk and avoid live zoster when immunosuppressed; for live zoster, defer until sustained immune recovery post‑HSCT/SOT/ICI (as per transplant/HSCT guidance above). <cite id="d120741a-1">Influenza recommendations in transplant highlight preference for higher-dose/adjuvanted vaccines when immune response is blunted</cite>, paralleling strategies for zoster selection in older, immunosuppressed SOT recipients.

Peri-procedural timing around immunosuppression
- Start or resume live attenuated vaccines: 14–30 days before initiating immunosuppression, if feasible; if given during or immediately after therapy, withhold for 3–6 months from end of treatment. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live vaccines 14–30 days before immunosuppression and 3–6 months thereafter</cite>, and <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">≥4 weeks before starting anti‑immune therapies</cite>.
- Administer all routine inactivated vaccines per age and travel guidelines in parallel when immune system and clinical status permit, then continue with annual influenza and one‑off agents (e.g., hepatitis B, Tdap/Tdap/DTaP, zoster per age). <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">Inactivated vaccines can be administered to those on immunosuppressive therapy per routine schedule, with live vaccines deferred</cite>.
- In the urgent transplant/HSCT setting, coordinate pre‑ and peri‑operative catch‑up using inactivated vaccines first; schedule live vaccines off‑protocol or delay until immune recovery, often ≥2–3 months pre‑transplant, and 4–6 months post depending on regimen. <cite id="d120741a-5">Live-attenuated MMR and varicella should be given at least 4 weeks prior to SOT and 3–6 months after if given during immunosuppression</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-6">both inactivated and live vaccines can be given pre‑transplant when timed appropriately</cite>. For patients who receive B‑cell–directed therapies (rituximab/closed‑loop BTKi), defer live vaccines ≥6 months after discontinuation if not re‑exposed; use inactivated products and Ig prophylaxis when indicated. <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">Immunization guidance for immunosuppressed patients emphasizes inactivated vaccines and deferring live vaccines until after recovery from immunosuppression</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-7">post‑HSCT live vaccines are deferred for at least 2 years unless conditions allow</cite>.

Product-level cautions and special agents
- Live vaccines: Avoid in patients on high‑risk immunosuppression (e.g., high‑dose systemic corticosteroids, anti‑CD20, calcineurin inhibitors) or during chemotherapy cycles/active ICI; if inadvertently given under suppression, interrupt or switch suppressive therapy as appropriate, and monitor for infection, while rescheduling off‑treatment by 3–6 months. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live attenuated vaccines require 14–30 days before immunosuppression and 3–6 months after, and should not be given if immunosuppressing</cite>, <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">live vaccines ≥4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive therapy</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-4">LAIV is contraindicated during anticancer treatment</cite>.
- Influenza vaccine: Prefer inactivated, adjuvanted/higher‑dose in older/transplant candidates; LAIV is contraindicated in cancer/immunosuppressed. <cite id="d120741a-1">Higher-dose and adjuvanted influenza vaccines have sufficient evidence for use in transplant populations when inactivated vaccine response is blunted</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-4">LAIV should not be given during anticancer treatment</cite>.
- Zoster vaccine: In immunosuppressed patients (SOT/HIV/corticosteroids), prefer recombinant zoster vaccine and avoid live zoster during active immunosuppression; defer live zoster ≥3–6 months after immunosuppression per immune status and product-specific contraindications. For SOT recipients, CDC and transplant guidance favor inactivated vaccines and live vaccines only when recovery is documented; live zoster is generally reserved for fully recovered, low‑risk older adults, while recombinant zoster is acceptable post‑recovery. <cite id="0a76eb7e-0">With altered immunocompetence and immunosuppressive therapy, emphasize polysaccharide-based and other non-live vaccines</cite>, <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">live vaccines require 3–6 months after immunosuppression to be administered if given during suppression</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-5">live vaccines should be timed off immunosuppression for transplant—principles that extend to live zoster</cite>.
- COVID‑19 vaccines: Use the current season’s mRNA, protein subunit, or viral‑vector vaccines for immunocompromised individuals, with additional doses and extended intervals based on product and immunosuppressant type/intensity. <cite id="0a76eb7e-3">All immunocompromised individuals aged ≥6 months should receive at least one dose of current season's COVID-19 vaccine, with additional doses as indicated</cite>.
- Hepatitis B: Prefer recombinant (non‑live) vaccine with routine HBIG post‑exposure; no live HB vaccine exists (recombinant HBV vaccine is preferred). <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">Immunize with routine inactivated schedule elements such as hepatitis B vaccine for immunocompromised persons</cite>.
- Pneumococcal and Hib: Routine PCV13 and PPSV23/HiB in adults with altered immunocompetence or high-risk conditions, tailored to age and asplenia/sickle‑cell status. <cite id="0a76eb7e-0">Persons with altered immunocompetence generally receive PCV13, PPSV23, and Hib per increased risk</cite>.
- Travel/foreign body: Vaccinate with inactivated and non‑live agents per risk; if travel demand live (MMR, VZV) and exposure is likely, arrange vaccination 14–30 days before starting immunosuppression and allow 4–6 months recovery before commencing or restarting immunosuppression if urgent. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live vaccines 14–30 days before immunosuppression and 3–6 months after; if given while suppressed, defer 3–6 months</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-5">≥4 weeks before transplant for live vaccines</cite>.

Putting it together: stepwise approach for the clinic
1) Identify patient category and immune status: baseline immunodeficiency, transplant/HCT status, current/foreseeable immunosuppressive therapy (steroids, anti‑TNF, anti‑IL‑6R, anti‑CD20, calcineurin inhibitors, mTOR, ICI, chemotherapy). <cite id="0a76eb7e-5">All routine inactivated vaccines should be administered; live vaccines deferred</cite>.
2) Document catch‑up: age‑appropriate and disease‑directed vaccines (HepB, PCV/PPSV, Hib if indicated, Tdap/Td, IPV, zoster per age/HIV/SOT, MMR/Varicella/HPV/dT/aPC/dose schedule as appropriate). <cite id="0a76eb7e-0">Polysaccharide vaccines (PCV13, PPSV23, Hib) are foundational for altered immunocompetence</cite>.
3) Time vaccines around therapy:
   - If resuming or starting immunosuppression:
     - Give inactivated vaccines immediately (hepatitis B series, pneumococcal, meningococcal, Tdap/Td, zoster as age‑appropriate, influenza annually), unless contraindication exists.
     - For live vaccines, if indicated and immune system is competent, schedule 14–30 days before commencing immunosuppression; if given while suppressed, defer 3–6 months after cessation. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live vaccines should be 14–30 days before and 3–6 months after immunosuppression</cite>.
     - If therapy is urgent, give live vaccines 4–8 weeks before starting, or after surgery if feasible, with antibiotics for varicella/MMR exposure and serial Ig where indicated. <cite id="d120741a-5">Live-attenuated MMR and VZV at least 4 weeks before SOT</cite>.
   - If live vaccines were not given pre‑transplant:
     - Pre‑emptive varicella/MMR at ≥4–8 weeks pre‑transplant if exposure risk is high; otherwise, anticipate post‑transplant administration after 3–6 months off immunosuppression and confirm serology/immune recovery. <cite id="d120741a-5">Live vaccines at least 4 weeks before transplant; if given under immunosuppression, wait 3–6 months</cite>.
4) Maintain routine updates: annual inactivated influenza (start by month 1 post‑transplant); COVID‑19 per season; pneumococcal decennial; travel vaccines based on risks and local guidelines. <cite id="d120741a-0">Annual inactivated influenza vaccine post-transplant from the first month</cite>, and <cite id="0a76eb7e-3">at least one COVID-19 dose each season for immunocompromised individuals, with additional doses as indicated</cite>.
5) Manage product contraindications: avoid LAIV in cancer/immunocompromised; prefer adjuvanted/higher‑dose influenza in SOT; avoid live zoster in active immunosuppression; defer live vaccines to sustained immune recovery after HSCT/ICI. <cite id="933fbb71-4">No LAIV during anticancer treatment</cite>, <cite id="d120741a-1">higher-dose/adjuvanted influenza supported for transplant</cite>, <cite id="d120741a-8">live/non-live vaccine recommendations by time since SOT</cite>, and <cite id="d120741a-7">live MMR/V post-HSCT deferred ≥2 years unless conditions allow</cite>.

Practical tips for the care team
- Build a shared care plan with the transplant/oncology/HSCT team for pre‑ and peri‑procedural vaccination; record product, date, immunosuppressant dose/type, and immune reconstitution labs when feasible. <cite id="d120741a-5">Inactivated vaccines 2 weeks and live vaccines ≥4 weeks pre-transplant; live vaccines given under immunosuppression require 3–6 months off</cite>.
- Counsel patients on the 14–30 day interval principle for live vaccines before immunosuppression and 3–6 months wait after; offer inactivated vaccines immediately and keep records to avoid double‑counting. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live attenuated vaccines require 14–30 days before and 3–6 months after immunosuppression</cite>.
- Customize influenza: use inactivated in immunocompromised; consider adjuvanted/higher‑dose for SOT; if ICI/chemo overlaps allow LAIV, advise it’s preferable to no vaccine, but in active suppression avoid and use split‑virion as a compromise when indicated. <cite id="d120741a-1">Adjuvanted/higher-dose influenza vaccines are recommended for SOT when inactivated responses are blunted</cite>, and <cite id="933fbb71-4">LAIV is contraindicated during anticancer treatment</cite>.

- Steroid thresholds and live vaccine intervals: If high‑dose systemic steroids are required (≥20–40 mg/day prednisone equivalence), defer live vaccines for at least 21–28 days after taper to <10 mg/day and wait 3–6 months after discontinuation if live vaccine was missed. <cite id="0a76eb7e-2">Australia’s immunocompromised handbook emphasizes ≥4 weeks separation from immunosuppressive therapies for live vaccines</cite>, and general transplant/immunology resources endorse 3–6 months after immunosuppressive therapy for live vaccine resumption if given during suppression. <cite id="0a76eb7e-1">Live vaccines should be administered 3–6 months after the end of immunosuppressive therapy</cite>.

Overview and definition
- Semantic enrichment, in Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Industry Foundation Classes (IFC), is the process of augmenting a model with meaningful domain- or application-specific information so that the file accurately encodes what it represents and supports automated analysis by downstream tools rather than relying only on human interpretation of geometry and identifiers.<cite id="65fd4bba-1">Semantic enrichment of BIM models is a process designed to add meaningful semantics to the information represented in a building model</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-6">Semantic enrichment of building models adds meaningful domain-specific or application-specific information to a digital building model</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-7">This approach supplements an IFC exchange file with semantically useful concepts inferred from the explicit and implicit information to deliver semantics needed for direct use by different stakeholders’ BIM tools</cite>.

What exactly is “enriched” and how it’s done
- Objects, roles, and relations: Enrichment goes beyond raw geometric primitives to make sure each IFC entity has the correct type/role (e.g., wall vs. curtain wall), placement in space (e.g., IfcSpace → room function), relationships (e.g., supports, attach-to, geometric adjacency), and constraints implied by standards and MVDs, improving “model quality” in preparation for downstream evaluation.<cite id="65fd4bba-0">A more generic definition of an MVD is a subset of a building product model schema that provides a critical representation of the information concepts needed for consistent modeling</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-1">Semantic enrichment adds meaningful semantics to information represented in a building model</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-8">We focus on the semantic enrichment of spaces (IfcSpace entities) with the function of the corresponding room</cite>.
- Properties and semantics: It adds property sets, classifications, and machine-decodable attributes that capture intent and performance (e.g., insulation layers, fire-resistance ratings, materials) and clarifies ambiguous geometry by linking it to explicit semantics, sometimes by inferring concepts from text, BOMs, or explicit model features.<cite id="65fd4bba-7">Supplementing an IFC exchange file with semantically useful concepts inferred from the explicit and implicit information decodes and encodes semantic meaning for different stakeholders’ tools</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-3">Semantic enrichment of Building Information Models is critical for improving model quality and supporting downstream applications, such as compliance</cite>.
- Process engines and standards: Practical systems enforce defined MVD/property schemas and domain knowledge to detect undefined objects or missing relationships (e.g., a beam without a column restraint), and to populate IFC with consistent, interoperable data before handoff to engineers, manufacturers, or city asset systems.<cite id="65fd4bba-4">An automated or semi-automated approach for semantic enrichment of IFC models exported according to IFC CV 2.0 presents checks that identify undefined objects and missing object relationships based on domain experts’ knowledge, like civil engineers’</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-9">Semantically segmented and enriched IFC-based bridge BIM instance models are produced using semantic segmentation for IFC, capturing correct types, assemblies, and roles</cite>.

Practical advantages for civil infrastructure modeling
1) Better interference, constraint, and clash detection across civil disciplines
- Enriched models carry explicit object roles, relations, and constraints, which enables automated checking for geometric and regulatory conflicts—e.g., utilities vs. carriageways, bridge parapets vs. street furniture, abutment toe clearances—as well as interference and clearance relations among multi-discipline elements.<cite id="5f944a91-1">A Geometric Relation Checking tool automatically detects geometric relations between IFC objects, supporting relation-based validation</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-4">An enrichment engine identifies undefined objects and missing relationships by encoding civil engineers’ domain knowledge in the IFC file</cite>.
- In civil/transport, enrichment of bridges and road assets yields more accurate performance evaluation and interference checks and streamlines approvals and FM workflows.<cite id="99518e1a-0">Semantically enriched bridge models enable more accurate analysis and evaluation of bridge performance and facilitate better asset management</cite><cite id="5f944a91-8">Information extraction for semantic enrichment of IFC-based bridge BIM models significantly increases efficiency and productivity of IFC-based bridge model enrichment</cite>.
- For city-scale integration into asset systems and digital twins, richer semantics make IFC models vendor-neutral and easier to import, enrich, and operationalize without losing relationships and properties during translation.<cite id="99518e1a-9">Semantically enriched IFC models help achieve vendor-neutral storage and processing of information from the construction phase, enabling downstream analysis</cite><cite id="99518e1a-5">IFC and Asset Administration Systems (AAS) can unlock sustainable and intelligent building operations and asset management via standardized, semantically rich information models</cite>.

2) High-confidence downstream workflows for MEP/structural/fabrics and civil elements (e.g., street furniture, stormwater)
- MEP, fabrics, and civil fixtures: With semantic roles and properties, tools can enforce clearances to services, structural members, and roadways (e.g., guardrails overdrilling checks, drainage drop-in relations), and drive fabrication-ready models for utilities, street furniture, and bridge components.<cite id="65fd4bba-7">Enriched IFCs with semantically useful concepts allow different stakeholders’ BIM tools to act directly on the file without additional manual mapping</cite><cite id="5f944a91-0">Semantically segmented and enriched IFC-based bridge BIM instance models are produced for as-designed/as-built data, enabling accurate downstream evaluation</cite>.
- Street/road infrastructure: Enrichment of space functions, surface layers, and parapet/kerb semantics supports automated validation of right-of-way encroachments, accessibility ramps, and safety netting, reducing rework before construction and permitting.<cite id="65fd4bba-8">Enriching IfcSpace with corresponding room function connects spatial semantics to usage constraints, aiding validation against codes and facility rules</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-5">Semantic enrichment is critical for improving model quality and supporting downstream applications such as compliance</cite>.

3) Energy, building-physics, and compliance checks
- Energy/NFRC/GB/T: Enriched models can unambiguously represent assemblies for EnergyPlus/IES or national energy engines to compute U-values and simulate performance; enriched assemblies and spaces with functions let tools infer correct boundary conditions for energy calculation engines.<cite id="5f944a91-4">Automatic IFC data enrichment with space geometries for energy analysis relies on high-quality geometry and explicit element criteria to avoid clashes and surface errors, enabling accurate analysis</cite>.
- Regulatory and codes: Enrichment engines encode code requirements and MVD constraints to flag missing attributes (e.g., fire-rating, barrier height), undefined objects, or inconsistent relations before submission; cities and owners use this to validate completeness and correctness at intake or via automated code checking.<cite id="65fd4bba-4">An enrichment engine identifies undefined objects and missing relationships based on encapsulated domain experts’ (e.g., civil engineers) knowledge, enabling automated validation</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-3">Semantic enrichment improves model quality and supports downstream applications such as compliance</cite>.

4) Asset management, lifecycle cost, and operations/maintenance
- Bridges, roads, and tunnels: For civil infrastructure, semantically enriched IFCs act as high-fidelity asset records, linking geometry to functions, materials, and structural roles that support inspection planning, deterioration modeling, and prioritization more accurately than geometry-only files.<cite id="99518e1a-0">Semantically enriched bridge models enable more accurate analysis and evaluation of bridge performance</cite><cite id="99518e1a-1">The enriched bridge models facilitate better asset management</cite>.
- Data readiness for AI/automation: Enrichment yields structured, vendor-neutral data that downstream AI systems and asset administration layers can process for predictive maintenance, work-package automation, and digital twins spanning planning to operations.<cite id="99518e1a-3">BIM in combination with other technologies broadens beyond traditional roles; data readiness and enrichment enable advanced analysis and integration</cite><cite id="99518e1a-5">IFC and AAS provide a foundation for sustainable and intelligent operations and asset management</cite>.

5) Interoperability, multi-project governance, and risk reduction
- Multi-tool ecosystems: Because enrichment infers and codifies common semantics, downstream engineering, fabrication, analytics, and FM tools can interpret and use the same file without additional mappings, reducing coordination errors and rework across MEP, structural, and civil domains.<cite id="65fd4bba-7">Supplementing IFC files with semantically useful concepts allows different stakeholders’ BIM tools to directly use the model data for their domain workflows</cite>.
- Quality gate enforcement and risk mitigation: Enrichment pipelines can include checks for undefined types, missing relationships, property completeness, and geometric consistency, surfacing defects early where they’re least costly to fix.<cite id="65fd4bba-4">The engine identifies undefined objects and missing object relationships in an IFC file based on domain experts’ knowledge, enabling automated quality control</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-1">The process adds meaningful semantics to improve downstream applicability</cite>.
- Data portability and openness: For city infrastructure and public projects, semantically rich IFCs can be ingested by open/archiving platforms and later repurposed in asset systems or public dashboards without loss of linkages, improving traceability from design to as-built to asset operations.<cite id="99518e1a-9">Semantically enriched IFC models support vendor-neutral storage and processing from construction to operations, enabling downstream use</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-5">Semantic enrichment is critical for improving model quality and supporting downstream applications such as compliance</cite>.

How practitioners implement semantic enrichment for civil infrastructure
- Capture explicit semantics: Use IFC property sets/classifications (MVD-aligned) to represent roles (e.g., “bridge parapet,” “drainage inlet,” “kerb extension”) and performance attributes (e.g., concrete cover, barrier height), and tie elements to IfcSpaces with intended use/functional tags.<cite id="65fd4bba-0">An MVD defines a critical representation of information concepts needed for consistent modeling of building products</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-8">Enriching IfcSpace with room/functional information aligns spatial semantics with intended use</cite>.
- Derive implicit semantics safely: Apply semantic segmentation and enrichment engines that translate 2D documentation and explicit model features into correct IFC instance types, assemblies, and relations; constrain inferences with domain MVDs and knowledge bases to avoid over-interpretation.<cite id="99518e1a-0">IFC-based semantic segmentation and enrichment produce semantically correct bridge BIM instance models</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-7">Enrichment engines infer semantically useful concepts from explicit and implicit information for tool interoperability</cite>.
- Validate with domain rules: Integrate automated relation and clearance checks, undefined-object detection, and property completeness checks against civil and codescenarios (e.g., egress paths, flood-level relationships, right-of-way), enabling automated intake validation for authorities and owners.<cite id="5f944a91-1">Automatically detects geometric relations between IFC objects for relation-based validation</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-4">Identifies undefined objects and missing object relationships based on domain experts’ knowledge, enabling automated validation</cite>.
- Prepare for the “long tail”: For assets that cross over into operations (bridges, utilities, street furniture), structure enrichment so the same file can power energy simulations, civil clashes, permit checks, and asset registers, reducing the need for parallel data stores.<cite id="99518e1a-0">Semantically enriched bridge models enable accurate performance evaluation and asset management</cite><cite id="99518e1a-9">Vendor-neutral processing of enriched IFC models enables downstream analysis across the lifecycle</cite>.

Why it matters now
- Owners and authorities increasingly expect IFCs to be “machine-readable” beyond Revit views: semantic enrichment closes that gap by making IFC models actionable for automated compliance, analytics, and digital twins across civil infrastructure, lowering risk and accelerating delivery.<cite id="65fd4bba-3">Semantic enrichment of BIM is critical for improving model quality and supporting downstream applications such as compliance</cite><cite id="65fd4bba-1">It adds meaningful semantics to the information represented, improving downstream applicability</cite>.

Reinforcement fibers used in polymer matrix composites
- Carbon fibers (CFRP): High-strength/high-modulus fibers derived from precursor polymers (e.g., PAN), used to raise stiffness and heat resistance; common types include T300, M55J, and HM series that trade modulus/specific strength across applications in aerospace and high‑performance structures. <cite id="0184f034-1">In reviews of carbon/glass fiber manufacturing, carbon fibers are classified by type and property sets to match polymer matrix systems</cite> <cite id="0184f034-5">Dispersed-phase fibers historically include carbon alongside glass, basalt, and aramid in polymer composites</cite>.
- Glass fibers (GFRP): The most widely adopted cost‑effective reinforcement; common forms include E‑glass for electrical insulation, S‑glass for high strength, and alkali‑resistant variants. <cite id="0184f034-5">Glass is a traditional dispersed-phase fiber in FRP composites</cite> <cite id="0184f034-9">E‑glass is the most common composite reinforcement with relatively low modulus but good tensile strength</cite>.
- Aramid fibers (e.g., Kevlar®): High toughness/energy absorption, lower modulus; used where impact resistance and damping dominate (armor, sports/structural reinforcement). <cite id="0184f034-8">Aramid fiber composites emphasize basic properties and civil/structural applications driven by high toughness</cite> <cite id="0184f034-1">Manufacturing reviews cover aramid alongside carbon and glass fiber families</cite>.
- Other high‑performance inorganics: Boron, silicon carbide, and basalt fibers are also used; boron offers very high specific modulus but is costly/rare, while basalt and silicon carbide provide strength/modulus trade-offs similar to carbon or glass in certain matrices. <cite id="0184f034-5">FRP composites have long used basalt and aramid in addition to glass and carbon</cite>.
- Natural fibers (jute, flax, hemp, sisal, bamboo): Biobased, light, renewable; rising in interiors/automotive non‑load‑bearing parts and some load‑bearing applications due to tunable properties and sustainability; often require polymer sizing, coupling agents, or hybridization for moisture/interfacial robustness. <cite id="0184f034-0">Natural fibers are an increasingly popular reinforcement for many industrial applications</cite> <cite id="0184f034-6">Applications span car bodies/interiors and building products as polymer–natural fiber composites</cite> <cite id="0184f034-3">Hybrid composites combine natural fibers with polymers and use treatments to enhance interfacial properties</cite> <cite id="0184f034-8">Aramid review highlights that polymer composite hybrids are actively studied, including with natural fibers</cite> <cite id="63b7d2d4-8">Manufacturing comparisons for bio‑based FRP include RTM and VARTM parameter studies</cite>.
- Hybrid composites: Combining two or more fibers (e.g., carbon + glass in the same laminate or matrix) to optimize strength/stiffness, fatigue, and cost; also carbon/glass/aramid in thermoplastic or thermosetting matrices. <cite id="0184f034-3">Hybrid composites enumerate polymer–fiber pairings and chemical treatments for property enhancement</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-1">Practical bridge design guidance notes hybridizing with carbon/glass and using Kevlar for impact resistance</cite>.

How reinforcement fibers are supplied (typical forms/filaments)
- Continuous fibers:
  - Tow and yarn: Hundreds to thousands of filaments bundled as unidirectional tow or plied yarn, used in unidirectional laminates and automated placement (tape/laminate/3D). <cite id="cc012cbe-8">Continuous strand mat is a ubiquitous preform but woven/other forms can be tailored to match performance and process</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-9">Continuous strand mat uses long fibers (vs chopped) and achieves higher performance than chopped strand mat</cite>.
  - Roving: A bundle of parallel unidirectional strands (tows) with little twist; serves as a base form that can be chopped, woven, or formed into mats and fabrics. <cite id="cc012cbe-0">Roving is a parallel bundle of strands/tows without significant twist and is commonly chopped into short fiber segments for other forms</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-2">Roving is the simplest and most common glass fiber form, from which chopped, woven, or other composite forms derive</cite>.
  - Woven fabrics: Unidirectional (UD) cloth or cross‑plied plain/satin/3K weaves delivering in‑plane stiffness and balanced laminates; stitched or compression‑set fabrics also exist. <cite id="cc012cbe-5">Fiberglass fabric basics contrast woven vs stitched, cloth vs mat for reinforcement selection</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-7">Mechanical test studies specifically use woven roving and chopped strand mat as distinct fabric forms</cite>.
- Short/Chopped fibers:
  - Chopped strand: Continuous roving cut to short lengths for spray‑up, hand layup, compression molding compounds, or mat embedment. <cite id="cc012cbe-1">Chopped continuous roving is used as short lengths in mats, spray‑up, or molding compounds for FRP structures</cite>.
  - Mats and needlepunch/continuous‑strand mat: Randomly oriented short (chopped) fibers (CSM) or long‑fiber continuous‑strand mat (CSM+) provide bulk, isotropic to quasi‑isotropic reinforcement, often thermo‑plastic sheet molding compounds (SMC/BMC) carriers. <cite id="cc012cbe-6">Chopped strand mat’s short fiber length yields isotropic behavior but limited directional strength, yet widespread for molding</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-9">Continuous strand mat uses long fibers; isotropic chopped‑strand mat vs anisotropic continuous‑strand mat</cite> <cite id="cc012cbe-8">Chopped strand mat is the most ubiquitous preform in manufacturing practice</cite>.
  - Short fibers/powders/whiskers: Millimeter‑scale chopped fibers, chopped nanofibers, or inorganic whiskers dispersed in resin to raise modulus/strength and toughness; processing routes include injection molding and compression forming. <cite id="63b7d2d4-2">Raw materials and applications reviews catalog short and long fiber feedstocks for FRP processing</cite>.
- Prepregs: Impregnated fiber tows/fabrics with partially cured resin that are stored or heated/pressed to full cure, enabling vacuum autoclave or compression molding of high‑quality laminates (aerospace, wind blades). <cite id="63b7d2d4-0">Compression molding and automated fiber placement are core automated manufacturing techniques for fiber‑reinforced composites</cite> <cite id="63b7d2d4-9">Prepreg and autoclave processes are classic aerospace manufacturing methods for CFRP/CF/GF laminates</cite>.
- Additional forms:
