    - Indonesia, Laos, and Nigeria implemented national or NGO‑anchored home delivery of ARVs to ensure uninterrupted treatment as clinics closed or operated at reduced capacity.<cite id="9d5d50ae-0">Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria introduced home delivery of ARVs to support treatment continuation during COVID‑19</cite>.
    - Côte d’Ivoire had direct home deliveries organized by an international HIV center to maintain continuity of therapy.<cite id="9d5d50ae-3">CCP delivered antiretroviral medication directly to homes in Côte d’Ivoire due to COVID‑19</cite>.

- Sub‑Saharan Africa
  - Scale and modality: Multiple high‑burden countries adopted community and home delivery through CHWs, mobile teams, and drones; programs also pivoted to community pharmacies and mail order to reduce in‑person visits, with several reports demonstrating improved viral suppression versus clinic refills in home delivery cohorts.<cite id="3bc9d908-0">Home delivery via community outreach was used for patients unable to reach facilities in Southeast Asia</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-9">Community pharmacy and home delivery were core decentralized distribution models during COVID‑19</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-5">Home‑delivered ART was associated with higher viral suppression than clinic refills in the Deliver Health Study during COVID‑19</cite>.
  - Country exemplars:
    - Kenya: Drone and home‑based delivery for HIV treatment and PrEP supplies became central to maintaining service continuity; health systems and partners integrated delivery of ART and self‑testing kits to peripheries and remote households.<cite id="9d5d50ae-2">Drones delivered HIV commodities, including treatment and PrEP, to communities in Kenya</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-4">Drones brought HIV drugs directly to local staff to sustain COVID‑19 testing and treatment</cite>.
    - South Africa: Large programmatic evaluations of decentralized/home‑delivered ART during lockdown documented acceptability and improved outcomes compared with clinic refills, and telemedicine was layered in to reduce clinic dependence.<cite id="72da0fb1-0">A South African decentralized ART program evaluated participant experiences during COVID‑19</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-9">Telemedicine in South Africa, enabled by COVID‑19, continued to support HIV clients</cite>. 
    - Côte d’Ivoire and Nigeria: Home delivery by HIV programs and NGOs maintained ART continuity in West and Central Africa, respectively, highlighting similar patterns across sub‑Saharan Africa.<cite id="9d5d50ae-3">Direct home delivery of ART to PLHIV in Côte d’Ivoire</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-0">Programs in Nigeria adopted home delivery to maintain ART access during COVID‑19</cite>.
  - Additional programs and corridors: Across East and Southern Africa, community refill by CHWs, satellite/community pharmacy networks, and mobile outreach adapted quickly; cost evaluations and cohort studies suggest feasibility of sustained home refill with ART viral load benefits observed in real‑world programs.<cite id="9d5d50ae-9">Decentralized models included home delivery and community pharmacy</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-2">Costs of home‑delivered ART refills reached approximately $714–$794 per client per year in some programs</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-5">Home‑delivered ART increased viral suppression versus clinic refills, including during COVID‑19</cite>.

- South/Central and East Asia
  - India and beyond: Drone and community networks were mobilized to deliver HIV drugs and commodities to remote and underserved communities; national and state HIV societies and nongovernments adopted last‑mile delivery to keep ART flowing during lockdowns.<cite id="9d5d50ae-1">Drones supported medical delivery in Africa and were explored for expanded use</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-7">Drones delivered medicines in India to remote villages, ensuring people received critical healthcare on time</cite>.
  - Country exemplars:
    - Indonesia and Nepal: Sustained home deliveries during COVID‑19 were part of national and NGO responses to maintain ART supply chains when travel and clinic access were restricted.<cite id="9d5d50ae-0">Indonesia and Nepal implemented home delivery of ARVs to support uninterrupted treatment</cite>.

- Eastern Europe and Central Asia (with regional overlap)
  - Programmatic shifts: Although fewer detailed reports specific to COVID‑19 home delivery appear in the evidence stream, the same modalities (community pharmacy, mail order) were recommended globally, echoed in policy briefs, and leveraged in some countries to lessen clinic congestion, with virtual interventions expanding to include adherence and refill logistics for ART programs.<cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Virtual interventions expanded to include online and phone-based adherence support for ART and PrEP</cite>.

- Latin America
  - Programmatic adaptation: High-income and upper‑middle‑income countries leveraged telemedicine and mail/home delivery to reduce non‑essential in‑person visits; while most evidence centers on U.S. and Caribbean models, these modalities underpinned the regional continuity approach during COVID‑19.<cite id="3bc9d908-7">U.S. guidance recommended exploring mail-order options for people with HIV</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-9">Telemedicine began in South Africa and stayed on as HIV help; similar remote models were adopted in Latin America to manage HIV care during COVID‑19</cite>.

Cross‑program uptake for TB and PrEP that overlapped with ART
- TB drug and diagnostic home delivery and satellite/community refill models were widely used to prevent interruptions, often within the same CHW networks delivering ART; similar virtual and mail-order pathways were deployed across ART programs, blurring modalities and reinforcing continuity for co‑infected patients.<cite id="3bc9d908-0">WHO reported home delivery for clients unable to access facilities in Southeast Asia</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Virtual interventions expanded to sustain HIV program delivery, including adherence support</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-4">UNAIDS highlighted virtual interventions and HIV self-testing adoption that supported sustained HIV service delivery</cite>.
- PrEP adherence and delivery also moved virtual and toward community‑based refill points and mail order in many settings, complementing ART home delivery and self‑testing rollouts.<cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Routine adherence support expanded online and by phone for PrEP and ART</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-8">Virtual delivery models for PrEP were suggested, leveraging internet/social media for demand creation</cite>.

Implementation outcomes and costs
- Continuity and viral suppression: Shifts to home delivery reduced missed refills, maintained or improved viral suppression compared to clinic refill cohorts, and averted service disruptions during lockdowns; cost evaluations in LMIC programs suggest home delivery is feasible at roughly $700–$800 per client per year in the first year after accounting for client fees.<cite id="72da0fb1-5">Home-delivered ART significantly increased viral suppression versus clinic-based refills, including during COVID-19</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-2">Home-delivered ART refill costs averaged $794 in year one and $714 thereafter per client after client fees, versus $167 per client for community pharmacy refills</cite>.
- Adoption barriers and heterogeneity: Programmatic surveys during COVID‑19 reported transfers from HIV to COVID care and spacing/skip of visits across programs; LMIC reports show uneven continuity and interruptions despite scale‑up of virtual and home delivery interventions, emphasizing that “widespread” adoption coexisted with persistent access and adherence challenges.<cite id="d4cadf0c-0">HIV testing and viral load coverage fell in Uganda between December 2019 and June 2020 (96% to 85% and 31% to 22%) illustrating uneven continuity</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-1">A global clinician survey reported many HIV care providers transferred to COVID care, with visit spacing and discontinuation during the pandemic</cite>.

Summary
- Where and how it spread: Widespread acceptance and implementation were most visible in Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Nigeria), and across large sub‑Saharan African settings, notably Kenya and South Africa, where CHW, drone, pharmacy, and mail‑order home delivery were layered to sustain ART and linked interventions, with growing evidence from program evaluations and cost studies supporting scale across millions of clients; virtual interventions and mail order became common adjuncts for ART and PrEP programs globally.<cite id="9d5d50ae-0">Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria implemented home delivery of ARVs to ensure uninterrupted treatment during COVID-19</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-2">Kenya deployed automated drones delivering ART and PrEP to communities</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-0">A South African decentralized ART delivery program during COVID-19 demonstrated real-world feasibility</cite><cite id="3bc9d908-7">Federal guidance encouraged switching to mail order when possible for people with HIV</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Virtual interventions expanded nationwide to maintain ART and PrEP delivery</cite>.
- What to expect next: Many of these adaptations have been normalized into differentiated service delivery strategies, though national‑scale, permanent legal authorization for mail/home delivery of ART and self‑administration still varies by country. Nonetheless, the documented continuity benefits, cost feasibility, and cross‑program innovations suggest durable uptake, particularly where telemedicine, pharmacies, and community health chains of trust already existed pre‑pandemic.<cite id="72da0fb1-2">Home-delivered ART programs in LMICs showed costs of around $700–$800 per client per year, supporting scale</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-5">Viral suppression improved with home-delivered ART versus clinic refills</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Virtual interventions became integral, including online/phone support for ART and PrEP</cite>.

Caveats
- “Widespread” does not equal universal: Interruptions and reduced engagement were common in parts of sub‑Saharan Africa and elsewhere despite scale‑up, highlighting the central role of political economy, supply chains, and stigma in sustaining home delivery; many documented cases were programmatic or NGO‑led before becoming fully decentralized national policy.<cite id="d4cadf0c-0">Service coverage reductions during early 2020 in Uganda indicate uneven continuity despite recommendations</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-1">Global survey of HIV clinicians reported transfers to COVID care and disrupted visits</cite>.
- Modalities differ by context: Drone delivery thrived in small‑rural Africa, while mail order and pharmacies dominated in cities and upper‑middle‑income countries; community refill by CHWs and virtual adherence support underpinned most “home delivery” experiences across both HIV and TB programs.<cite id="9d5d50ae-2">Kenya’s drone-based HIV home delivery</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-9">Community pharmacy and home delivery as core decentralized models</cite><cite id="d4cadf0c-2">Virtual adherence expansions for ART/PrEP</cite>.

In sum, acceptance and implementation of home delivery for HIV treatment and related interventions were broad across Southeast Asia and sub‑Saharan Africa during the pandemic, with active deployment in countries such as Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Nigeria, Kenya, and South Africa, enabled by WHO/US guidance and layered with drones, CHW refill, pharmacies, and telemedicine; uptake was emerging or less documented in Latin America and Europe outside major cities, and variable in parts of sub‑Saharan Africa due to structural constraints, even as programmatic and peer‑reviewed data showed improved continuity and viral suppression for home delivery cohorts.<cite id="3bc9d908-0">WHO regional notes and program practices highlighted home delivery by outreach workers in Southeast Asia</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-0">Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, and Nigeria adopted home delivery to maintain ART</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-2">Kenya’s drone delivery integrated HIV treatment supplies to communities</cite><cite id="9d5d50ae-3">Direct home-delivered ART in Côte d’Ivoire</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-0">South African decentralized ART delivery during COVID-19</cite><cite id="72da0fb1-5">Improved viral suppression with home-delivered ART</cite>

Summary
Across Asian settings, alcohol use around sex is consistently associated with riskier sexual behavior that elevates HIV risk, and the magnitude and direction of this association differ by marital status. Among unmarried men, alcohol before sex is commonly reported and is linked with more unprotected sex with non‑regular partners, while in married men, alcohol’s risks often operate through extramarital sex, reduced condom negotiation, or partner norms; these pathways mean alcohol tends to increase HIV risk more visibly among unmarried men via casual/anonymous partners, whereas in married men the effect is more indirect and heterogeneous.

Key Asia-wide evidence on alcohol and HIV risk
- Alcohol use and binge drinking increase sexual risk-taking, including casual/anonymous sex and inconsistent condom use, which are proximal drivers of higher HIV risk in Asia and globally. <cite id="833452d4-0">Drinkers had a 77% higher risk of HIV infection than non‑drinkers, and heavy episodic drinkers had roughly double the risk</cite> <cite id="833452d4-3">Drinking alcohol before sex is associated with increased HIV risk, more sexual partners, and inconsistent condom use</cite> <cite id="61db4932-0">Alcohol use and binge drinking were associated with higher odds of casual sex (aOR 1.31 and 1.52)</cite> <cite id="61db4932-1">Hazardous drinking patterns were linked to sexual risk-taking in a large Asia-based MSM cohort</cite>. 
- Among Asian men who have sex with men (MSM), alcohol consumption before/after sex correlates with higher HIV prevalence and with specific risk behaviors (e.g., unprotected anal intercourse), reinforcing a causal pathway from alcohol to HIV risk. <cite id="356c5821-0">In a large Indian MSM sample, unknown partner HIV status and consumption of drugs/alcohol prior to sex were associated with condomless anal intercourse</cite> <cite id="356c5821-4">Weekly alcohol use to the point of being buzzed/drunk was significantly associated with unprotected sex in Chennai MSM</cite> <cite id="356c5821-7">Substance-use resulting in high‑risk sexual behavior was associated with higher HIV prevalence among MSM in Vietnam</cite>. 
- Experimental and observational work supports a causal link from alcohol to risk behaviors relevant to HIV/STI acquisition in men, consistent with mechanisms of impaired inhibition, poor decision-making, and partner risk appraisal. <cite id="61db4932-6">Experimental research indicates alcohol causally increases sexual risk behaviors relevant to HIV/STI exposure among men, with alcohol alone often combining with partner and situational factors</cite> <cite id="356c5821-5">Alcohol combined with partner type and transactional context predicted unprotected sex episodes among MSM</cite>.

Stratified effects by marital status and mechanisms
- Unmarried men: Alcohol use before sex is highly prevalent and correlates with unprotected sex with non‑regular partners, suggesting elevated risk outside stable partnerships. <cite id="356c5821-1">Among male alcohol users, unprotected sex with a non‑regular partner was more common among unmarried men</cite> <cite id="833452d4-2">Alcohol use before sex was reported by 89% of respondents; unprotected sex with non‑regular partners was significantly higher among unmarried men</cite>. Mechanistically, unmarried status often reduces social sanctions against casual dating/extramarital norms, and alcohol weakens condom adherence and partner negotiation, driving riskier behaviors with casual or transient partners, a pathway strongly associated with HIV acquisition in Asia. <cite id="61db4932-0">Binge drinking raised odds of casual sex (aOR 1.52)</cite> <cite id="833452d4-3">Alcohol before sex increases HIV acquisition risk and disrupts condom use</cite>. 
- Married men: Alcohol’s HIV impact is often mediated through infidelity, permissive marital norms, and intra‑pair condom non‑use. Evidence from broader samples indicates that marital status modifies sexual risk pathways; in some populations, marrying coexists with ongoing sexual networks and risk behaviors, and alcohol may potentiate these dynamics. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can affect HIV transmission via sexual activity with partners outside marriage and changing sexual risk behaviors, including with alcohol</cite> <cite id="356c5821-0">MSM and general male populations in India show that alcohol use prior to sex, combined with unknown partner HIV status, increases condomless sex and HIV risk</cite>. Qualitative and modeling studies emphasize that alcohol interacts with social/transactional contexts (e.g., “bogus” relationships, alcohol-fueled transactions) to increase unprotected intercourse, a pattern more detectable among unmarried men but plausibly present in marriage as well. <cite id="61db4932-5">Actor–partner analyses show binge drinking moderates unprotected sex among male couples in similar-sex partnerships, indicating partner-level alcohol contexts also elevate risk</cite> <cite id="356c5821-3">Alcohol moderates unprotected sex within same‑sex male couples, emphasizing dyadic risk dynamics</cite>. 
- Important nuance: In cultures where monogamy is normative and extramarital sex is discouraged, alcohol may increase HIV risk in married men by lowering condom use within marriage rather than increasing partner turnover; where marital norms are loose or polygynous patterns exist, alcohol may increase extramarital and casual sex among both married and unmarried men. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can alter sexual risk via continued partner switching and alcohol-related contexts</cite> <cite id="356c5821-1">Unmarried status within alcohol-use groups showed more unprotected non‑regular partners</cite>.

Country examples from Asia (mechanisms and patterns)
- India: Large MSM studies show alcohol use around sex is common and linked to higher HIV risk via condomless intercourse; population-level studies show alcohol use before sex is prevalent, with unprotected sex with non‑regular partners more frequent among unmarried men, indicating two channels—casual partners for unmarried men, and marital-breach/transactional encounters for married men. <cite id="356c5821-0">Indian MSM: alcohol/drugs before sex associated with condomless anal intercourse; partner HIV status unknown increases risk</cite> <cite id="356c5821-4">Chennai MSM: weekly intoxication associated with unprotected sex</cite> <cite id="356c5821-1">Unmarried Indian male alcohol users reported more unprotected sex with non‑regular partners</cite> <cite id="833452d4-2">Male alcohol use survey: 89% reported alcohol before sex; unprotected sex with non‑regular partners significantly higher in unmarried men</cite>. 
- China: Observational studies among men (MSM and general populations) link alcohol use to unprotected sex and risky sexual networking; marital status and alcohol combine to heighten permissive behaviors. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can change sexual risk behaviors and HIV transmission trajectories; alcohol-use contexts contribute</cite> <cite id="59d93179-4">Alcohol consumption immediately before sex “sometimes” was associated with lower risk than “always,” but heavier episodic use related to higher HIV risk in Vietnam—highlighting timing and intensity matter</cite> <cite id="59d93179-5">Transactional sex, weekly alcohol use, and early sexual debut predicted unprotected intercourse among Vietnamese MSM</cite>. 
- Philippines/Thailand/Laos: Surveys of general male populations report alcohol use before sex and elevated sexual risk behaviors, with marital status interacting with drinking to produce risk both inside and outside marriage; country data show most HIV infections occur through heterosexual sex, so alcohol-facilitated infidelity is a salient pathway for married men. <cite id="59d93179-9">General-population male survey in three Philippine cities assessed HIV risk behaviors, including alcohol-associated sexual risks</cite> <cite id="59d93179-8">Cumulative data in the Philippines show 92% of HIV cases acquired sexually; sociodemographic/behavioral correlates such as alcohol use and multiple partners drive risk</cite> <cite id="59d93179-0">Laos-based work shows alcohol abuse associates with HIV-risky behaviors, with marked gendered patterns—men drink alone and expose themselves to sexual risks</cite>. 
- Cross-cutting mechanism evidence: Alcohol’s behavioral changes (reduced inhibitions, poor judgment, lowered condom adherence, and impaired negotiation) are consistently implicated across Asian settings and amplify both within- and outside-marital risk. <cite id="833452d4-3">Alcohol before sex increases HIV acquisition risk and disrupts condom use</cite> <cite id="356c5821-1">Within alcohol-use groups, unmarried men had more unprotected sex with non‑regular partners</cite> <cite id="356c5821-5">Alcohol interacts with partner/transactional factors to precipitate unprotected sex</cite> <cite id="61db4932-6">Experimental evidence shows alcohol causally increases HIV/STI-relevant sexual risk behavior among men</cite>.

How risk differs by marital status: Synthesis and implications
- Unmarried men: Alcohol before sex is linked to greater unprotected sex with casual/non‑regular partners, directly elevating HIV exposure where partner serostatus is unknown and condom use is inconsistent. <cite id="356c5821-1">Unprotected sex with non‑regular partners was significantly more common among unmarried alcohol users</cite> <cite id="61db4932-0">Binge drinking increased odds of casual sex (aOR ~1.5)</cite> <cite id="833452d4-3">Alcohol before sex increases HIV acquisition risk</cite>. Prevention needs to target pre‑sex drinking environments, partner risk assessment, and condom negotiation skills in networks outside marriage.
- Married men: Alcohol typically raises HIV risk indirectly—by lowering condom use during agreed intercourse, by facilitating infidelity or “transactional” encounters, or by normalizing multiple/rotating partners. While direct, stratified incidence estimates are fewer, mechanistic and contextual evidence is strong: alcohol interacts with sexual risk networks and transactional sex to boost unprotected intercourse, and marrying does not automatically confer protection absent fidelity and negotiation. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can alter HIV risk via sexual activity with partners outside or inside marriage, influenced by alcohol-related contexts</cite> <cite id="356c5821-5">Alcohol, partner type, and transactional sex jointly predict unprotected sex</cite> <cite id="59d93179-5">Weekly alcohol use associated with unprotected intercourse among MSM via transactional sex</cite> <cite id="59d93179-3">In Asian MSM, alcohol is associated with higher HIV risk and sexual risk behaviors</cite>.
- Socio-cultural modifiers: In cultures with strong marital sanctions on extramarital sex, alcohol can precipitate transgressions (infidelity, anonymous partners) among both married and unmarried men; in polygynous or permissive contexts, alcohol’s disinhibitory effects magnify extramarital risk and partner switching. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can change sexual risk behaviors and HIV transmission pathways</cite> <cite id="61db4932-6">Alcohol increases sexual risk behaviors relevant to HIV/STI exposure among men</cite>.
- Timing and intensity matter: Not all drinking before sex equals equivalent risk; heavy episodic (“binge”) use is consistently associated with higher-risk patterns, whereas light or controlled drinking may be less consequential. <cite id="61db4932-0">Binge drinking was associated with increased sexual risk (aOR ~1.5)</cite> <cite id="59d93179-4">Alcohol immediately before sex showed differing risk associations by frequency: “sometimes” before sex related to lower measured risk than “always,” while heavier episodic use related to higher HIV risk; binge patterns worsen risk</cite>.

Practical implications in HIV programming
- For unmarried men: Combine interventions reducing alcohol-impaired sexual encounters (enforcement of low-risk sexual scripts before drinking, bystander and negotiation skills, and partner testing) with structural approaches to reduce sex work/transactional sex risks. <cite id="356c5821-1">Unmarried male alcohol users reported more unprotected sex with non‑regular partners</cite> <cite id="833452d4-2">Most men report alcohol use before sex; unprotected sex with non‑regular partners is higher among unmarried</cite>.
- For married men: Address couple-level norms around condoms, monitor infidelity, and integrate alcohol-aware negotiation into couple counseling; target alcohol outlets and “macho” norms that normalize risky drinking and condom avoidance. <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can influence HIV transmission through continued sexual risk with partners, magnified by alcohol and transactional sex</cite> <cite id="356c5821-0">Partner HIV status uncertainty plus alcohol use before sex increases condomless sex among MSM</cite>.
- Universal elements: Strengthen pre‑drinking harm-reduction (e.g., plan-ahead condom carrying/use, designate sober “chaperones” who enforce condom use), expand partner testing/rapid linkage, and tailor messages to gender norms and relationship power dynamics across marital statuses. <cite id="61db4932-6">Experimental evidence underscores alcohol’s causal role in elevating risk behaviors, enabling prevention to focus on pre‑drink planning and sober safeguards</cite> <cite id="61db4932-0">Observed increase in casual sex with binge use suggests targeting sexual networks and partner testing</cite>.

Key uncertainties and research needs
- Few studies report incident HIV risk stratified by marital status with precise “alcohol before last sex” timing in general-population men. Most high-quality evidence in Asia comes from MSM cohorts and married MSM vs single MSM comparisons; extrapolating to married non‑MSM requires caution. <cite id="356c5821-0">MSM-focused data are rich but not always generalizable to married non‑MSM</cite> <cite id="61db4932-4">Population evidence notes marriage can change risk, but quantification by marital status and drink timing is sparse</cite>. 
- Heterogeneity by country norms (monogamy vs polygyny), religion, and access to condoms/ART complicates effect sizes. More country-level studies that record drinkers’ last-sex timing and marital status, condom use, and partner HIV status would clarify differentials.

Bottom line
In Asian men, alcohol use before sex reliably elevates HIV risk through impaired decision-making and unsafe sex, and this risk tends to manifest most clearly among unmarried men via unprotected sex with non‑regular partners. Among married men, alcohol’s HIV impact is often indirect—worsening unprotected sex within marriage or enabling infidelity and transactional encounters—while the overall population effect depends on relationship norms, partner networks, and alcohol intensity. <cite id="833452d4-0">Heavy episodic drinking is associated with roughly doubled HIV risk relative to non‑drinkers</cite> <cite id="356c5821-1">Unprotected sex with non‑regular partners is more common among unmarried male alcohol users</cite> <cite id="61db4932-0">Binge alcohol use increases casual sex odds, a proximal HIV risk factor</cite> <cite id="61db4932-4">Marrying can alter sexual risk patterns; alcohol-related contexts raise transmission risk via both intra- and extra-marital sex</cite> <cite id="356c5821-0">Partner HIV status uncertainty plus alcohol before sex elevates condomless intercourse risk among MSM, highlighting risk amplification pathways</cite>.

Summary
Across most of sub-Saharan Africa, the “disease” most prevalent among tuberculosis (TB) patients is HIV, and its regional pattern among TB patients mirrors the underlying HIV epidemic’s geography, with wide heterogeneity within and across countries and marked time trends shaped by ART scale‑up, TB–HIV integration, and screening policies.<cite id="4cd0f071-1">HIV prevalence among TB patients has been estimated to be as high as 80%–90% in some areas of sub‑Saharan Africa; WHO’s 2004 recommendations catalyzed programmatic responses that reduced new co‑infections</cite>.

Southern Africa (South Africa): strong regional gradients and time trends
- Regional variation by province: Provincial HIV prevalence gradients in South Africa closely track the burden of HIV among TB patients. High‑background provinces such as KwaZulu‑Natal and Gauteng have had substantially higher HIV/TB co‑burden than lower‑prevalence provinces like the Western Cape, a pattern that emerges in both population surveys and TB/HIV program metrics.<cite id="bb9dc2dc-0">HIV has dramatically increased TB incidence and mortality in South Africa; ART and intensified TB screening explain major portions of subsequent changes</cite><cite id="cd644510-5">KwaZulu‑Natal is the worst‑affected province with adult HIV prevalence 27.0% compared with 12.6% in the Western Cape</cite><cite id="9ce960a4-8">Among notified TB cases in South Africa in 2019, 59% were co‑infected with HIV</cite>.
- Time change over the 2000s–2020s: Before widespread ART, TB incidence was sharply elevated among HIV-positive people, and early cohorts showed very high HIV prevalence among TB patients; as ART and integrated TB/HIV services scaled, joint incidence declined markedly. Multi‑site South African syntheses attribute most of the decline in TB among HIV-positive groups to ART and expanded screening.<cite id="bb9dc2dc-0">From 1990–2019, HIV drove large increases in TB incidence and mortality; provision of ART and intensified TB screening explained most of the subsequent reduction</cite>.
- National point prevalence in recent years: Current reporting indicates that roughly half of TB patients in South Africa are co‑infected with HIV, underscoring the entrenched linkage of the two epidemics.<cite id="9ce960a4-8">The HIV co‑infection rate among notified TB cases in South Africa was 59% in 2019 (Global TB Report)</cite>.

Eastern Africa: heterogeneous but broadly falling co-prevalence
- Regional variation by setting: Studies from Kenya, Ethiopia, and Tanzania show that HIV prevalence among TB patients commonly ranged from about 20% to nearly 30% in earlier years, with lower levels in facilities implementing universal HIV testing and treatment, and higher levels in rural or high‑risk sites. Urban/rural contrasts and health‑system access help explain within‑country heterogeneity.<cite id="4cd0f071-3">A Kenyan two‑public health‑facility study found an overall HIV prevalence among TB patients of 19.6% with a slightly declining trend over time</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-2">In rural western Kenya, 29% of TB patients were HIV‑infected overall; the proportion was 32% in 2012 and declined to 24% by 2020</cite>.
- Time change post-2004: After WHO endorsed same‑day start of ART for TB patients and universal HIV testing in TB clinics, declines in joint TB–HIV incidence and mortality were observed, with incidence falling faster among HIV‑positive adults as ART coverage expanded.<cite id="4cd0f071-0">During 2007–2012, TB incidence declined by 28–44% among adults with HIV and by 11–26% among adults without HIV</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-1">HIV prevalence in TB patients has reached 80–90% in some areas historically, prompting policy and program shifts after 2004 to reduce co‑infections</cite>.
- Program indicators: National monitoring and integrated platforms further reinforced declines (e.g., increased HIV testing yield within TB facilities and linkages to ART).<cite id="4cd0f071-6">Kenya’s PEPFAR indicators highlight integrated TB–HIV services (e.g., TB‑Yield for HIV testing in TB facilities alongside national HIV prevalence trends)</cite>.

Central and West Africa: high-risk key populations and marked heterogeneity
- Regional framing by subregion: WHO’s African Regional Office emphasizes that “key populations, their clients and sexual partners” account for most new HIV infections in West and Central Africa, concentrating risk in networks that also drive TB transmission, which helps explain pockets with very high joint prevalence.<cite id="cd644510-4">Key populations accounted for 64% of new HIV infections in West and Central Africa</cite>. 
- Historic hotspot ranges: Early facility‑based estimates in several West/Central African settings reported very high HIV prevalence among TB patients in specific districts or among key populations, sometimes near 80–90%, with overall joint prevalence varying widely across sites.<cite id="4cd0f071-1">HIV prevalence among TB patients has been estimated to be as high as 80%–90% in some areas of sub‑Saharan Africa</cite>.
- Trend over time: With scale‑up of HIV testing and ART, and implementation of DOTS and later NTEP strategies, national TB burden has declined and the proportion of TB patients co‑infected with HIV has stabilized or fallen in many countries, though heterogeneity persists in high‑risk settings.<cite id="cd644510-4">WHO African Region documents subregional changes with risks concentrated in key populations but broad declines as interventions scaled</cite>.

Putting the regional and temporal picture together
- Cross‑regional variation within a major African region (Southern Africa): Provincial differences in background HIV prevalence explain large geographic differences in HIV prevalence among TB patients, with KwaZulu‑Natal and Gauteng historically far higher than the Western Cape; nationally, co‑infection rates hovered near 50% through the 2010s, reflecting deep coupling of epidemics.<cite id="cd644510-5">KwaZulu‑Natal adult HIV prevalence 27.0% vs Western Cape 12.6%</cite><cite id="9ce960a4-8">In 2019, 59% of notified TB cases in South Africa were HIV co‑infected</cite>.
- Over time: Before 2005, TB incidence among HIV‑positive people was extremely elevated; from 2005 onward, integrated HIV testing and ART-for-TB protocols drove substantial declines in TB incidence among HIV-positive cohorts and reduced new HIV/TB co‑infections in many settings, though declines vary by baseline prevalence and health‑system capacity.<cite id="bb9dc2dc-0">ART and intensified TB screening explained most of the post‑2000 reduction in TB among HIV‑affected South Africans</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-0">2007–2012 saw sizable declines in TB incidence among adults with HIV as ART coverage expanded</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-2">In rural Kenya, HIV prevalence among TB patients declined from 32% in 2012 to 24% in 2020</cite>.
- Spatial heterogeneity persists: Even in countries with overall declines, localized hotspots among key populations can retain high co‑prevalence, producing uneven regional maps among TB patients that mirror underlying HIV structural drivers (male circumcision prevalence, migration networks, concentrated epidemics) and programmatic coverage.<cite id="cd644510-4">Key populations’ role in new HIV infections (64% in West/Central Africa) highlights risk networks that also affect TB</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-1">Some areas historically report 80–90% HIV prevalence among TB patients</cite>.

Implications for practice
- The observed regional variation argues for context‑specific, risk‑informed strategies—intensive HIV testing and same‑day ART at TB clinics in high‑endemicity provinces or districts; targeted outreach in key‑population networks; and continuous monitoring because spatial heterogeneity can mask national averages.<cite id="bb9dc2dc-0">In South Africa, targeted ART and TB screening underpinned most of the decline in TB burden among HIV‑affected populations</cite><cite id="4cd0f071-3">Kenyan multi‑facility data show facility‑ and time‑varying HIV prevalence among TB patients, with a general decline</cite>.
- In the Southern Africa example, current national co‑infection levels still exceed 50%, underscoring that HIV among TB patients remains a central driver of TB burden and that gains are not uniform across provinces or over decades.<cite id="9ce960a4-8">South African national co‑infection rate of 59% among notified TB cases in 2019</cite>.

In short, within major African regions like Southern Africa, the prevalence of HIV among TB patients was historically highly variable across provinces—reflecting underlying HIV epidemics—and over time has fallen in tandem with ART and integrated TB–HIV services, though pockets with high co‑prevalence persist and drive ongoing regional heterogeneity.

Summary of the four-phase model and cross-sex applicability
- Masters and Johnson’s four-phase cycle—excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution—provides a standardized vocabulary and sequence to describe the physiological changes that occur during sexual activity in both men and women, integrating cardiovascular changes, genital engorgement, muscle tension, and neurohormonal shifts. <cite id="c387c7e8-1">In both men and women, these events may be identified as occurring in a sequence of four stages: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-3">Masters and Johnson divided the sexual response cycle into four phases that are fairly similar in men and women: excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-5">The identification and classic description of the four-stage sexual response cycle of excitement, plateau, orgasm and resolution was announced.</cite> 
- Clinically and in public health education, the phases are used to orient patients and clinicians to normal variations across people and situations while providing a shared framework for diagnosis and treatment planning. <cite id="c387c7e8-0">Masters and Johnson’s four stages provide a starting point for understanding sexual functioning, communication, and treatment planning.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-2">Desire (libido or excitement), arousal (sometimes called plateau), orgasm, and resolution are standard descriptors across both sexes.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-6">The cycle is guided by sexual desire and proceeds through excitation, plateau, orgasm, resolution in men and women.</cite>

How the phases explain functioning across the female sexual response
- Phase-by-phase account in women emphasizes that excitement (genital vasocongestion, lubrication) and plateau (heightened sensitivity and sustained arousal) are followed by orgasm (tall contractions and subjective peak) and then resolution (reduced arousal and return to basal state). The same phase template is seen in males, with sex-specific expression. <cite id="c387c7e8-2">The four phases—desire, arousal/plateau, orgasm, resolution—describe human sexual response in both men and women.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-1">The four-stage model captures human sexual response in both sexes but emphasizes that timing and expression vary.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-4">Both men and women experience excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution, although timing differs.</cite> 
- Female sexual arousal and orgasm show anatomical and sensory pathway diversity. Women can reach orgasm via direct clitoral stimulation, indirect clitoral stimulation through vaginal contact, or vaginal stimulation of surrounding tissues; this explains why plateau/arousal experiences and access to orgasm vary across partners, contexts, and practices. <cite id="6deef008-0">Women reach orgasm from direct clitoral stimulation, indirect clitoral stimulation via the clitorogenic vasocongestive corona/vestibule, or vaginal stimulation of areas surrounding the vagina.</cite> 
- Female orgasmic experience and sexual function are highly variable across individuals and over the lifespan; desire, arousal, and orgasm are mediated by interacting neurochemical systems, and clinical frameworks capture desire, arousal, orgasm, and pain as functional domains. <cite id="6deef008-2">Women have a remarkable variety of orgasmic experiences, with multiple sources of sensory input contributing to orgasm.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-5">The review of the clitoral versus vaginal orgasm debate underscores that sensory inputs (clitoral and vaginal) and physiology are integrated, explaining variability in experience.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-8">Dopaminergic and serotonergic systems contribute to desire, arousal, and orgasm, highlighting neurochemical underpinnings of sexual function.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-7">Female sexual dysfunction frameworks recognize disorders of desire, arousal, orgasm, and pain as the core functional axes, aligned with the phases.</cite>

How the phases explain functioning across the male sexual response
- In men, excitement involves parasympathetic activation and penile erectile充血; plateau maintains vasocongestion and arousal; orgasm is the central sensory climax coordinated with ejaculation, then resolution includes penile flaccidization and a refractory period where further orgasm/ejaculation is inhibited. <cite id="d16b3077-3">The four phases are similar in men and women, with male arousal and excitement proceeding to plateau before orgasm and resolution.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-1">Ejaculation is a reflex culminating in emission and expulsion as two coordinated phases.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-3">Ejaculation comprises distinct emission and expulsion phases operating in synchrony during male orgasm.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-2">Refractory period patterns differ by sex, with more predictable and substantial refractory responses in men than women; seminal emission/ejaculation occur in men.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-7">The male refractory period entails inhibition of erection and orgasm/ejaculation, marking an active post-orgasm phase before renewed arousal.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-6">Masters and Johnson’s original model enumerated the linear four-phase cycle in both males and females, with male orgasm and ejaculation mapped to the terminal climax and resolution phases.</cite>
- Male orgasmic physiology is tightly coupled to ejaculation (as emission+expulsion), whereas some women show “vaginal” ejaculation-like fluid secretion (vestibular/vaginal glandular transudate) and can experience multiple orgasms with brief refractory periods depending on inhibitory mechanisms and neurophysiology. <cite id="05fddecf-1">Ejaculation splits into emission and expulsion as the mammalian male endpoint to intercourse.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-9">Women who achieve orgasm more often report multiple orgasms than men, reflecting different refractory dynamics and physiology.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-5">Reflex-linked arousal and orgasm physiology indicates that variable refractory periods explain individual differences, including the possibility of multiple orgasms.</cite>

Mechanistic and experiential coverage: what the four phases “fit,” and where they fall short
- Mechanistic coverage: The four-phase labels succinctly capture shared physiology—vascular engorgement, heart-rate and skin conductance increases, genital and pelvic floor contractions, and autonomic coordination—before return to baseline. <cite id="d16b3077-3">Excitement (desire), arousal/plateau, orgasm, and resolution outline shared mechanisms across both men and women.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-5">The four-stage description was a novel, systematic articulation of human sexual physiology and became a classic reference point.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-6">Critically revisiting the model shows enduring relevance alongside the need to correct inaccuracies and expand mechanisms.</cite>
- Experiential coverage and variability: The female sexual response particularly benefits from a multichannel arousal model—clitoral and adjacent/vaginal pathways—while the male response benefits from explicit distinctions between erotic excitation and the ejaculation reflex, both of which align with the plateau/excitement boundary. <cite id="6deef008-0">Women can reach orgasm from direct and indirect clitoral stimulation or vaginal stimulation of surrounding structures, explaining why “plateau/arousal” expression varies and can be accessed differently in women.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-1">Ejaculation is a reflex with emission and expulsion stages, aligning male orgasm physiology to the “orgasm/resolution” hinge.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-2">There is substantial variability in how women experience orgasm as they integrate different sensory inputs, which the arousal/plateau phase accommodates.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-7">Timing and expression differ by individual and partner, emphasizing variability as a core feature of sexual function.</cite>
- Where the model is incomplete: Contemporary perspectives argue that collapsing desire into arousal/plateau, or treating a linear sequence as exhaustive, misses socioaffective, cultural, and psychological determinants of sexual response and its dysfunctions. Educators and clinicians report that while the four phases offer scaffolding, they omit desire dynamics, relational context, and complex psychobiological moderators that explain common complaints and dysfunctions. <cite id="c387c7e8-0">Practitioners use the four-phase model as a starting point but emphasize communication, variability, and context beyond the phases.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-8">Critically revisiting Masters & Johnson: correcting errors and suggesting modifications reflects the need to integrate current neuroscience and clinical data.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-2">A recent OB/GYN CME redefines female sexual response, noting flaws in the original four-stage depiction and expanding to desire, arousal, orgasm, and pain domains.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-4">Reviews of the clitoral vs vaginal orgasm debate show conflicting ideas historically; integrated models now better explain the continuum of arousal and orgasmic pathways in women.</cite>

How the four phases explain functioning comprehensively—bridging biology, psychology, and society
- Biological mechanism-to-symptom mapping: For both sexes, phases translate subjective “feeling” into observable physiology across arousal onset, peak organization, ejaculatory endpoints (in men), and refractory constraints. Clinicians use these anchors to identify abnormal patterns such as delayed or absent excitement, atypical plateau persistence, orgasmic disorders, or dysregulated arousal in chronic states like hypoactive sexual desire or persistent genital arousal disorder. <cite id="d16b3077-7">Physical and psychological changes occur in matching phase patterns across people, enabling diagnostic anchoring.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-3">Persistent genital arousal disorder shows dysregulated genital arousal with persistent vasocongestion, illustrating phase-level pathology beyond normal fluctuation.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-7">Sexual pain and dysfunction frameworks operationalize across desire, arousal/plateau, orgasm, and pain, integrating the four-phase structure for assessment and care.</cite>
- Cross-sex generality with sex-specific nuance: The same phase labels apply conceptually to men and women, but the model explains meaningful sex differences—e.g., male ejaculation as a distinct reflexive endpoint (emission/expulsion) superimposed on arousal and orgasm, versus female multimodal arousal pathways (clitoral and vaginal) that broaden access to plateau and orgasm in ways that can vary by context, partner, and practice. <cite id="05fddecf-1">Ejaculation’s two coordinated phases make it a sex-specific endpoint integrated into male orgasm/resolution.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-2">Refractory differences are typically greater and more predictable in men, reflecting sex-specific recovery constraints that interact with desire and arousal.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-0">Women’s capacity to reach orgasm via direct/indirect clitoral or vaginal stimulation explains wide variability in plateau/arousal expression and orgasm occurrence across women and situations.</cite>
- Practical explanatory reach and limits: The four-phase scaffold is widely used to educate about sexual health, set expectations, improve communication, and structure interventions, but it works best when coupled with desire-specific guidance, relational context, and recognition of individual variability. Contemporary revisions integrate desire as a distinct antecedent, reconceptualize arousal/plateau as continuous and multifactorial, and incorporate psychosocial and neurochemical moderators—expanding, not erasing, the original framework’s value. <cite id="d16b3077-2">Popular and clinical summaries now present desire, arousal (plateau), orgasm, and resolution as the functional sequence people experience.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-0">Sex educators emphasize that the four-phase model is a starting point for understanding patterns, communication, and treatment.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-2">Female sexual response can be reframed to include desire, arousal/plateau, orgasm, and pain, addressing four-stage model flaws and expanding explanatory scope.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-8">Neurochemical systems supporting desire, arousal, and orgasm must be considered alongside anatomy, clarifying why the phases alone are not sufficient for mechanistic completeness.</cite>

Bottom line: why the four-phase model remains useful and what complements it
- The four-phase model offers a shared, mechanistically grounded framework that captures the temporal organization and physiological signatures of sexual arousal and response in both sexes, facilitating cross-sex comparison, clinical assessment, and education. <cite id="c387c7e8-1">Both men and women progress through excitement, plateau, orgasm, and resolution in broadly similar sequences.</cite> <cite id="d16b3077-3">The phases align across sexes but emphasize that expression and timing are variable, which is integral to their explanatory power.</cite> 
- The model explains male and female functioning when paired with sex-specific detail—female multimodal clitoral/vaginal arousal pathways and the possibility of multiple or diverse orgasmic modalities for women; male decoupling of ejaculation (emission+expulsion) from orgasm with a post-orgasmic refractory—while recognizing neurochemical and psychosocial determinants of desire and satisfaction. <cite id="6deef008-0">Women access orgasm through clitoral or adjacent vaginal stimulation, explaining plateau/arousal variability and orgasm attainability.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-1">Male ejaculation entails emission and expulsion as distinct reflexive phases that co-occur with orgasm and frame the resolution phase.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-2">Women’s orgasmic experiences span multiple sensory inputs and show rich variability, consistent with flexible plateau/arousal pathways.</cite> <cite id="05fddecf-7">Male refractory mechanisms inhibit re-arousal, shaping sexual behavior and explaining refractory-related variability and satisfaction.</cite> <cite id="6deef008-8">Desire, arousal, and orgasm involve dopaminergic/serotonergic systems, requiring biopsychosocial integration for a comprehensive explanation.</cite>
- Critiques and updates reinforce that the four phases are best understood as a scaffold to be enriched by integrative models that foreground desire, relational context, neurobiology, and individual variability—enhancing explanatory coverage without discarding the phase-based temporal structure that clinicians and researchers already rely on. <cite id="c387c7e8-8">Educational and clinical updates identify model flaws and propose revisions to better match observed female sexual response patterns.</cite> <cite id="c387c7e8-7">Critical reappraisal suggests corrective modifications to the classic four-stage depiction, aligning it with current evidence.</cite>

Below is an organized overview of how “translation-based” ideas have been adapted for grammatical error correction (GEC), together with how systems are typically evaluated, drawing on shared-task practice and recent meta-analyses.

1) Core adaptation patterns

- Constrained neural machine translation (NMT/SMT) for grammaticality
  Translation-based GEC historically repurposes phrase‑based or neural MT to perform grammar-oriented rewriting of nonnative text, often with explicit constraints to preserve meaning while enforcing target-language grammaticality. <cite id="7ab8dd54-7">Phrase-based statistical machine translation systems have previously been used for the task of grammatical error correction (GEC) to achieve competitive corrections by focusing on target-language grammatical structures</cite>. <cite id="7ab8dd54-8">Neural machine translation systems have become state-of-the-art approaches for the GEC task, leveraging their denoising capacity to rewrite ungrammatical learner text</cite>. A key practical adaptation is to constrain translation so that outputs conform to target-language grammar, often via rule/grammar lexicon filters or by optimizing against grammaticality features/signatures. <cite id="0205a5a2-2">Spans containing grammatical errors can be explicitly identified and the SMT system constrained to translate only grammatically valid forms, thereby focusing correction on the detected error spans</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-1">Constrained SMT that restricts translations to grammatically valid structures has been directly evaluated on GEC tasks, showing that grammar-aware modeling improves correction over unconstrained translation</cite>.

- Iterative translation refinement (IterRef) with LLMs
  Modern “translation-based” GEC augments MT pipelines with iterative self-correction loops, where a strong language model repeatedly edits and re-edits a translation to improve grammaticality and fluency. <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iteratively prompting a large language model to self-correct a translation leverages their strong language modeling to refine translations into grammatically acceptable text, closing semantic gaps left by base translation</cite>. <cite id="7ab8dd54-3">Iterative LLM prompting for translation self-correction has been proposed and instantiated as a GEC-style process, with multiple passes sharpening grammaticality</cite>. These methods often integrate MT’s global rewrite tendencies with LLMs’ local fluency and rule compliance, and can incorporate lexical/phrase constraints from grammars or lexicons during decoding to avoid ungrammatical forms. <cite id="0205a5a2-5">Grammar-augmented machine translation pipelines can include manually written grammars with translation rules (e.g., English→Spanish) to guide corrections with explicit syntactic constraints</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-6">Contest reports from CoNLL-style tasks show constrained SMT/MT plus rule-based rewriting as a viable GEC pipeline, with rule sets guiding selection among candidate corrections</cite>.

- Multilingual back-translation and curriculum-style refinement
  Translation-based pipelines have also been extended to multilingual GEC by leveraging English→target back-translation or cross-lingual transfer to improve surface structure and idiomality. <cite id="7ab8dd54-4">An LLM-based curriculum learning method for GEC sequentially selects easy-to-hard tasks, iteratively trains and refines a model on synthetic bilingual data (including translation back-and-forth) to improve grammaticality and generalization</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-8">Multilingual GEC shared tasks frame the goal not only as grammatical correction but also idiomality, motivating pipelines where learner text is translated to a resource-rich language, corrected, and back-translated</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-9">A grammar-aware multimodal transformer (structured source→target) demonstrates that integrating explicit grammar representations with cross-lingual modeling improves grammatically valid output over baselines</cite>.

- Masked language modeling for GEC: adapting “translation of corrupted spans”
  Parallel to MT, transformer masked modeling (span/whole-word/sentence masking) has been directly adapted for GEC-like spans—predicting missing or corrupted spans around errors—to enforce local grammaticality and semantics. <cite id="86c95a75-0">Masked Language Modeling predicts missing tokens from placeholders and can be configured to corrupt spans and jointly learn from many diverse perturbations, a pattern repurposed for text rewriting tasks</cite>. <cite id="86c95a75-2">Span-based replacement of corrupted tokens in Chinese spelling/grammar correction better models natural error patterns and retains semantic and syntactic context, allowing language models to correct local errors while preserving meaning</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-7">Recent GEC evaluation papers emphasize “mask modeling” setups where the erroneous text span is masked, producing in-distribution markers that help models localize and correct error spans</cite>. In essence, these span-mask formulations adapt the “translate/restore” intuition: mask an error-bounded context and learn to predict a grammatically valid span that restores both syntax and meaning.

- Error-driven, grammar-aware pretraining
  Beyond standard MLM, some work explicitly trains models to predict syntactic/semantic spans that are most likely to carry grammatical faults, often aligning with universal-grammar features or lexicons. <cite id="86c95a75-1">Adapting vs. pre-training studies highlight how downstream tasks like GEC benefit from targeted finetuning of masked objectives that emphasize error-bearing spans and linguistic categories (e.g., determiners, prepositions, verbs), improving local grammaticality</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-2">Incorporating explicit error span identification before translation constrains the correction distribution to focus on likely grammar errors, improving targeted rewriting</cite>. This grammar-aware pretraining connects with constrained MT: both focus the model on plausible rewrites conditioned on grammatical validity during decoding.

2) How these adaptations are evaluated

- CoNLL and multilingual shared tasks: setup and metrics
  GEC shared tasks define clear system interfaces (source learner text → corrected target) and prescribe evaluation protocols. <cite id="b511899b-1">The CoNLL-2014 shared task formalized GEC as correcting learner English, releasing data, metrics, and a scorer; this became a benchmark for evaluating algorithms and systems</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-3">The CoNLL-2013 shared task paper gives the task definition, datasets, and the evaluation metric and scorer used, setting a template followed by later multilingual tasks</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-6">The Shared Task on Multilingual GEC 2025 specifies that systems should rewrite learner-written texts to be grammatically correct, and idiomatically improved, reflecting both correction and style targets</cite>. These tasks evaluate both raw accuracy and human-gradable fluency/idiomaticness, motivating multi-metric evaluation.

- Automatic metrics and their roles
  The GEC community uses a suite of automatic metrics to track fluency, grammaticality, and surface-level error reduction:
  - BLEU/related MT-style metrics for n‑gram overlap and fluency. <cite id="b511899b-1">BLEU-like automatic metrics served as primary automatic scores in early GEC shared tasks, used to rank systems on correction quality</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-5">GLEU provides a GEC-specific variant emphasizing phrase-level similarity under edit operations, supporting grammar-sensitive comparisons</cite>.
  - GLEU, TERCOM-like/SEG, and Edit-based metrics: <cite id="b511899b-9">GLEU was established as a ground-truth benchmark to evaluate GEC metrics through human assessment of GEC system outputs</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-8">EditEval integrates multiple edit-type metrics aligned with common correction categories (e.g., grammar, spelling) to provide consistent, significant evaluations</cite>.
  - Domain-specific variants (LEAD‑3/GAERD) and KOMET-family approaches have been adapted for error-driven comparisons of MT and GEC candidates. <cite id="b511899b-9">Studies compiling ground-truth for GEC metrics describe human evaluation protocols to validate automatic metrics like GLEU and BLEU on GEC systems</cite>.
  These automatic scores are frequently complemented by targeted span/sequence-level scoring used in pretraining pipelines that mask error spans. <cite id="b511899b-7">Mask modeling setups in GEC leave explicit markers of masked error spans; systems that better restore those spans during pretraining tend to show higher evaluation gains on automatic span-level and downstream tasks</cite>.

- Human evaluation protocols and rubrics
  Human judgments are central for assessing grammaticality, fluency, and idiomality, and have been formalized into rubrics that are used to validate and calibrate automatic metrics.
  - GALEC/GAEC levels and TERCOM lineage: <cite id="b511899b-1">Human evaluations at CoNLL used rubrics to assess grammaticality and fluency, supporting metric selection and cross-system comparisons</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-10">Better Evaluation for GEC presents an algorithm to compute phrase-level edits akin to TERCOM, offering an automatic proxy to human TERCOM-style assessments</cite>.
  - Meta-evaluations and judge reliability: <cite id="b511899b-0">SEEDA provides corrections with human ratings at multiple granularities to meta-evaluate GEC metrics, highlighting that different metrics correlate variably with human judgments across error types</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-4">A comprehensive survey of GEC details historical reliance on human annotation schemes, with CoNLL-style rubrics remaining influential</cite>.
  - Cross-lingual and multilingual studies: <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iterative translation refinement evaluations report that human judges perceive multiple passes as improving grammaticality and fluency compared to single-pass translation</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-5">In English–Spanish user studies using a grammar-augmented translation tool, explicit rules constrained translations and helped translators rate outputs as more grammatically correct</cite>.
  These human protocols are increasingly used to validate the outputs of translation- and span-based models, especially for idiomality and deeper syntactic correctness beyond n‑gram overlap.

- Error-category analysis and ablations
  Translation-based and masked models are evaluated by error-type breakdowns (pronoun agreement, Tense/Aspect, Morphology, Preposition/determiners, Syntax/structure) and ablations that switch on masking schemes, constraints, or iterative correction depth. <cite id="b511899b-1">CoNLL-2014 analysis shows that improvements from GEC systems vary by error category, guiding ablations of models targeting specific faults</cite>. <cite id="86c95a75-5">GECwBERT focuses on determiners, prepositions, and verb errors by finetuning BERT to predict masked spans, reporting targeted gains on those categories</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-8">EditEval-style metrics report per-edit-type performance, allowing direct attribution of improvements to grammar- vs. spelling-focused objectives</cite>. Iterative refinement studies typically show that additional refinement passes improve BLEU/grammar-oriented scores up to diminishing returns, whereas single-pass baselines underperform on complex syntactic cases. <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iteratively corrected translations exhibit stronger grammaticality and fluency than one-time translations, demonstrating that multiple LLM self-corrections resolve latent semantic issues</cite>.

3) Evidence from ablations and trade-offs

- Strengths of translation-based GEC
  Translation methods excel at global rewrite and surface form smoothing, and when constrained or iteratively refined, can achieve strong grammaticality while preserving meaning. <cite id="0205a5a2-2">Constraining SMT to grammatically valid structures using identified error spans leads to more targeted corrections and fewer out-of-grammar forms</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-6">Rule-guided decoding in GEC pipelines reduces ungrammatical candidates and improves selection among corrections</cite>. <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iterative LLM self-correction refines translations to be closer to fluent, native-like forms by iteratively reducing semantic drift</cite>. Multilingual back-translation can improve idiomality and transfer difficult constructions. <cite id="0205a5a2-8">Multilingual shared tasks reward idiomatically corrected outputs, motivating translation-back-translation loops that improve colloquial acceptability</cite>.

- Limitations and countermeasures
  Direct MT can introduce new paraphrasability and lexical errors; translation-based pipelines that mask error spans or use grammar constraints mitigate drift. <cite id="b511899b-7">Mask modeling in pretraining localizes error spans and improves restoration quality, reducing semantic and syntactic drift in corrections</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-9">Metric meta-evaluations show BLEU/GLEU can misrank systems that fix deeper syntax but reduce lexical overlap, motivating multi-metric evaluation and human checks</cite>. IterRef can over-edit or hallucinate; careful prompt design and grammar-based rejection sampling or lexicons curb divergence. <cite id="0205a5a2-5">Grammar rules embedded in translation constrain outputs and align with user studies in multilingual contexts, reducing ungrammatical forms</cite>. To measure these trade-offs rigorously, recent work calibrates automatic metrics and builds datasets for metric reliability analysis. <cite id="b511899b-0">SEEDA human ratings across granularities show that different metrics correlate differently with human preferences, recommending composite metrics and human-in-the-loop evaluation</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-5">GLEU provides a stronger correlation to human judgments by penalizing edits that disrupt phrase structure, improving over BLEU for GEC comparisons</cite>.

4) Putting it together: how translation-based methods are adapted and assessed

- Adaptations
  - Constrained/grammar-aware MT: identify error spans; constrain translation/decoding to grammatical surface forms; integrate lexicons/rule sets; and use PB‑SMT/NMT backbones trained for GEC. <cite id="0205a5a2-2">Error spans are identified and translation constrained to grammatically valid forms so the MT module focuses on rewriting only faulty regions</cite>. <cite id="7ab8dd54-7">Phrase-based SMT already demonstrated utility on GEC via grammar-shaped modeling</cite>.
  - Iterative translation-refinement with LLMs: prompt an LLM to correct a translated sentence iteratively, leveraging its language-model depth to resolve syntactic/semantic issues and enforce grammaticality. <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iterative LLM self-correction improves translation into grammatically correct text</cite>.
  - Masked span/word modeling for GEC: corrupt or mask error-bearing spans and train MLM to restore grammar and meaning; integrate with sequence tagging to target specific error classes (determiners, prepositions, verbs). <cite id="86c95a75-0">Span masking corrupts spans and trains models to restore context</cite>. <cite id="86c95a75-2">Span replacements align with real error distributions to improve local correction</cite>. <cite id="86c95a75-5">BERT finetuned with masked spans improves determiner/preposition/verb error types</cite>.
  - Multilingual back-translation and curriculum: translate to a high-resource language, grammatically correct with a strong model or MT, then back-translate; schedule increasing difficulty to refine grammaticality and idiomality. <cite id="7ab8dd54-4">LLM-based curricula iteratively select and harden tasks to improve generalization in GEC</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-8">Multilingual GEC rewards both correctness and idiomacy</cite>.

- Evaluations
  - Automatic comparisons: BLEU, GLEU, TERCOM/SEG-like and EditEval-style category-specific metrics to capture grammaticality and fluency. <cite id="b511899b-1">BLEU-like scoring standardized evaluation in early GEC</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-5">GLEU improves correlation with human judgments for phrase-level edits</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-8">EditEval reports multiple edit metric, aligning with correction categories</cite>.
  - Human protocols: CoNLL-style rubrics (grammaticality, fluency), GALEC/GAEC levels, and rule-driven TERCOM-like assessments; multilingual user studies and judge-based preference tests. <cite id="b511899b-1">CoNLL-2014 used human judgments to assess systems</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-10">Automatic TERCOM-style scoring aids large-scale comparisons</cite>. <cite id="0205a5a2-5">Grammar-rule–augmented tools are evaluated by translators on grammaticality</cite>.
  - Meta-evaluation: SEEDA and ground-truth metric studies judge metric–human correlations and guide composite scoring, revealing that translation-based gains must be measured across both surface (BLEU/GLEU) and deep (human/grammar-aware) criteria. <cite id="b511899b-0">SEEDA shows human ratings differ at fine vs. coarse granularities, informing metric selection</cite>. <cite id="b511899b-9">GLEU/GAEC ground-truth studies demonstrate improved alignment to human corrections</cite>.

In summary, translation-based methods for GEC have matured from constrained statistical MT into iterative LLM-translation pipelines and span-masked pretraining that target grammaticality directly. <cite id="7ab8dd54-0">Iterative LLM self-correction refines translations toward grammatically fluent outputs</cite>, while <cite id="86c95a75-2">span-based replacement/masking adapts the “translate/restore” principle to realistic error distributions</cite>, often in multilingual back-translation workflows. <cite id="b511899b-1">These adaptations are evaluated with shared tasks</cite>, <cite id="b511899b-8">category-aware automatic metrics</cite>, and <cite id="b511899b-0">human meta-evaluations</cite>, which together show where translation-based strategies excel (global fluency and surface grammar) and where they need guardrails (lexical drift and deep syntactic safety), leading to grammar-constrained, iteratively refined, and span-aware GEC systems. <cite id="b511899b-5">Because BLEU-like metrics can miss deep syntactic improvements, GEC evaluations increasingly combine BLEU/GLEU/Comet-like scores with human/grammar-aware rubrics and span-level analyses</cite>.
